Frustrating, hard, painful, and oh, so, so much fun. I had some time to kill over the Christmas break (the in-laws' house is a bit dull), and this game inspired me to learn about WWI. The level of accurate historical detail is shocking. The guns are dead on, the trench design is perfect, they even apparently looked at historical photos (the fort Douaumont map is FREAKY ACCURATE, I mean, the French actually built stone barricades in the tunnels of the fort, and the map re-creates them to eerily perfect detail). Yeah the hit boxes at point blank are a bit wonky, and the weapon unlock menu is obtuse, but this game does a masterful job of re-creating historic battlefields. It's part FPS, and part (due to the bolt action nature of most of the historically accurate weapons) almost a fluid turn based game. Yeah, twitch skills help, but you have to be methodical and careful if you want to win. My only gripe would be that high lvl NCO artillery barrages seem a bit OP, but when you consider the fact that 70% of the casualties in WWI were due to artillery they almost seem weak. (If they went TOO historically accurate you'd basically just have to huddle in a hole until a high explosive shell blew out your guts) I got this game for 50% off on a sale and I almost feel bad. This isn't CoD, so if that's what you're looking for, look elsewhere, but if you want a gritty, atmospheric game that rewards situational awareness then stop reading this review and buy it already.

Pros: It improves almost everything about the first one in everyway. More enemy variety, more puzzles to solve, and many different levels to explore. The game is much longer than the first with more secrets, puzzles, and epic weapons to find.
There are more classes and races to choose from and the skill system has been improved. It is much simpler for the player to see the effects of each skill point.
Dungeon crawling is satisfying with clever, if not frustrating at times, puzzles along with plenty of combat.
Cons: Unlike the first one, the Grimrock 2 is more non-linear. Progress at times can be hard to gauge because of all the different levels to tackle, as well as some puzzles requiring hints from multiple levels.
Mimics have a tendency to scare the daylights out of you.
In short: If you enjoyed the first one, then you will very much enjoy the second one. Some may find the non-linear nature annoying yet others will in turn love it. You do not need to have played the first one to enjoy the second one, both games have self contained stories.

Although i don't have as much playtime on this as some others, there is a lot to be said about the first impression of the game.
Pros:
Maps are richly detailed, i actually had to turn down settings so it wouldn't lag as much.
Cars are nicely detailed, drivers side view allows you to look from side to side just like in real life.

If you can get past the cons, there is some fun to be had in exploring and doing missions. Personally, i enjoy what i have played so far. Get it on sale.

I've been looking for a Magic replacement for awhile, as it's a bit too expensive for me to be able to play as often as I want to (not easy to get a playgroup together in my area also). Hearthstone was a poor imitation, and never truly grabbed my interest. Eternal is great, and has firmly. The deckbuilding is interesting, with a ton of room for innovation. AI modes are nice for earning early gold and cards, then ranked gives better rewards and draft (!) is the highest point of the game.
Eternal is comfortably free-to-play, with early quests giving the player a jumpstart on a collection and introducing them to the different modes/formats (a weekly quest, for example, provides 2-faction decks for inspiration after the tutorial), then later quests continue the flow in a rewarding manner. Winning games and completing quests give the player chests to open of varying quality (bronze->silver->gold->diamond), and the best part of Eternal's reward structure is that every chest has a ~10% chance to upgrade to the next highest quality. It is possible to win a ranked game (usually only a bronze chest) and walk away with a diamond.
All told, Eternal's game mechanics are great fun, deckbuilding is still a blast, and the game makes you feel like your time playing it is valued. Highly recommended if you've ever enjoyed another card game.

I decided against my better judgement to give wrestling games a try again, what a mistake that was.
The port is very poor, the game always launches in windowed mode regardless of what you have it set to, there's tonnes of screen tearing even with v-sync on and entrances can very often tank the fps.
While the roster is very large there are some glaring omissions like Kurt Angle, Eddie Guerrero, Rey Mysterio, Rob Van Dam and Hulk Hogan, however Hogan is a more complicated issue. many of the characters are not in career mode and are mostly just there for free play.
The In ring gameplay is ok some of the new systems like the submission mechanic are downright awful but for the most part it's ok.
Career mode is where i spent most of my time. You start out in NXT and slowly climb the ranks till you face Finn Balor for the NXT title and then you are moved up to the main roster and can choose a belt to go after, The ambitious man that i am i went for the WWE title. For a while career mode was good i had a storyline since I'd come up from NXT which basically boiled down to the authority thinking i wasn't good enough. on the way to my first pay per view i had lots of cutscenes and interviews that helped develop the storyline which culminated in a ppv match against big show and kane. After that the story continues and advances to Triple H attacking me himself and running in on my matches, again lots of cutscenes and interviews to advance the storyline which ended with a hell in a cell match against Triple H where i pedigreed Triple H through the cell ceiling. This is where career mode took a turn for the worse, by this point i was pretty happy with career mode I'd had a good storyline and good matches but that all ended here. After the hell in a cell match i had no more storylines no more cutscenes nothing i was 4th in ranking for the title at this point and i was just playing matches against the likes of Ryback and Mark Henry over and over. Sometimes a wrestler would run in on my match and it would start a feud but after the run in it's back to the same old random matches and then i got a normal match at the ppv with a rival I'd have had no buildup for. Then the next night on raw the same wrestler i just ended a rivalry with comes out and starts it again so it's another month of the same match over and over to end in a ppv with no storyline or buildup.
By this point i was getting pretty bored of career mode and was considering uninstalling the game when i saw the next PPV was the royal rumble and i thought there's a storyline to be made there, then i got in a rivalry and thought ok i can eliminate this guy at the rumble and get the title shot this might be ok. Then the royal rumble came along and i saw i wasn't in the rumble even though i was the number 3 contender for the title, after some frantic googling to find out why it turns out if you are in a rivalry you can't do any special matches at a ppv so no money in the bank no royal rumble which is the dumbest thing I've ever seen if you made it so no one in a feud could be in the rumble then there would be like 3 people.
By this point i thought well ok I'll get in a feud with the rumble winner and make the title match a triple threat, well you can't do that either because the game doesn't tell you who won the rumble. After some more googling i found out it doesn't matter anyway because apparently the AI doesn't cash in money in the bank and doesn't take the rumble title shot so i thought I'll play till mania and get in a feud with the title holder then it happens... the message you are locked in a rivalry with a mystery opponent pops up I'm thinking ok another actual storyline this might be ok. Well as it turns out it was Triple H, i started getting the exact same cutscenes as when i started the game so i was playing through the single storyline this game has twice instead of getting the title shot at mania. After that i decided to just skip all my matches until money in the bank and go that route. I remembered not to get in a rivalry with anyone before it so i could be in the ladder match and on the day of the ppv I'm in a normal match with Kane even though i'm the number 1 contender.
The reason I'm telling this story is because anyone buying this game should know what they are in for a grind fest playing the same matches every week, no storylines, broken mechanics, and the game ♥♥♥♥ing you every time you try to make a storyline yourself.
The career mode was very obviously rushed out the door and not play tested because anyone who is even a casual fan of wrestling would pick up on some of the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t in this mode like the fact that once you turn heel it's impossible to turn face, it considers hitting someone with a chair in the Tables Ladders and Chairs match a heel move, if you get thrown out of the ring the game acts like you ran out the ring and it's counted as a heel move however there's nothing the game considers a face action to counteract this.
The pay per views are laughable most of the ppvs in the game none of the titles are defended and at night of champions the one where all titles are defended one is defended. You have to be very lucky to be in a special match 99% of the time you will be in a normal 1v1 match regardless of whether it's mania, extreme rules, hell in a cell or the rumble.
The custom wrestler creator is decent not great and once you've made your wrestler be prepared to shell out money for the skill boost or start out unable to wrestle.
The only really good thing about this game is the entrance maker and even then you have to get a 3rd party program to get custom music for your entrance. Avoid this game at all costs unless you want Maggle Cole telling you how great it is to be on monday night raw even more than he already does.

Most wrestling fans agree that showmanship is at least as important as technical, in-ring ability, and WWE 2K16 doesn’t quite nail all its big spots in this regard. Technically, it’s kind of all over the place: there are no load times between ring entrances, lending a seamless, TV-broadcast feel to match openings, but the loads between other modes, and even just to preview a costume piece in create-a-wrestler can be painful. Sometimes the AI behaves uncannily like the wrestler you know and love, like when Seth Rollins tries to DQ himself to retain the belt, and other times, they quizzically zone out and sort of stare off into space. This same inconsistency spills over into other areas. Visually, some character models and effects look terrific, like during Randy Orton’s ring entrance, while guys like Chris Jerico seem to be holdovers from the last-gen days.  WWE 2K16 doesn’t quite nail all its big spotsFinally, the commentary has improved greatly, with far fewer repeated phrases, and more specific insight into many wrestlers’ fighting style and history, but it’s not all the way there yet. There are still a few too many general move callouts, making the play-by-play a bit flat at times. No one issue is big enough to ruin the fun, but together they can periodically undercut the tension and excitement the in-ring action builds sort of stare off into space. via

Holy f*ck it's so good.
Verdun is difficult. It has a player base of highly skilled people. It is unforgiving and in the heat of battle, it's hellish and... it's great.
The gameplay is perfect, the realism is superb. You shoot someone? They die. Someone shoots you? you die. regardless of weapon or level, guns feel powerful as they should. Your character experiences shellshock, speaks in whatever language they're supposed to, and when you're shot, you don't comically ragdoll, you stop, fall and curl up like a human would. The MGs are snipers without scopes, in that they have a huge range, but they're heavy and you can't run around with them(like irl). The mp18 is sh*t (like it is irl) but you can still use it. The pistols are slow to reload but perfect for storming trenches. The semi-auto rifles are good, but clumsy and few and far between. In the main gamemode, scopes are rare, and only maybe 4 people on the entire sever of like 30 people can have them. The sheer amount of weapons, attachements, uniforms and squads is amazing.
But the best part of Verdun for me is the attention to detail. The worldspace is absolutely beautiful. Every map feels real, you find evidence of people actually living, fighting and dying in the trenches. Graves, small kitchens and beds, NCO quaters, makeshift foxholes, books and journals strewn about. Every corner of the map has a a unique and interesting feel. But that's not all, Verdun is realistic not only in mechanics but in history. The guns are well-modeled, well-researched authentic weapons of the time. The uniforms are authentic, the battles & maps, the ranks and commands, everything. It's all accurate.
If you want an incredibly fun, unforgiving, historically-accurate attrition simulator, Verdun is perfect.

To open: This is not a $20 game. Do not get it for $20. You will be disappointed and I wouldn't even blame you.
That out of the way, this is story-driven exploration game with you coming home after a year away in Europe to your house being totally empty, and you simply explore it to find out why through collecting notes. Some give narration from your younger sister, a punky late-teen trying to find her place in a new school without her older sister.
This game is well made overall. The house is put together in a realistic way, the voice acting is genuinely without being cheesy, and the music is pretty good (if 90's grrrl punk is your thing). I think most people would agree on these point. The main issues of contention come from 2 things: price/time, and appeal.
Price per hour of gameplay is pretty poor, unforgivably so at full price. It takes 1.5-2 hours to play - wait for an appropriate sale for that playtime if you're interested. It'll allow for a much more genuine experience.
Appeal is more complicated. This game achieves a certain atmosphere that many simply cannot or do not wish to connect with, and that's fine.
Do you like the mid-90's? Do you like punk music? Do you like stories about high school girls learning about their values and what's important to them? Do you enjoy "showing-not-telling" narrative style and piecing a story together yourself? Do you like teen romance? Do you like exploration games?
If you answered "no" to many of the above, probably give this a pass. I enjoy this game, and I have a lot of affection for the story, but it isn't so good that it'll convert someone who dislikes the concepts it's built upon. That being said, for those who are exploration game fans with an interest in the mid 90's vibe and coming-of-age stories, pick this up if you see if for a good price. It's a neat story with straightforward gameplay.

The only thing I didn't like was the awkward movement that involved you clicking through multiple screens to get anywhere. I often found myself confused and turned around. I also think it's more mysterious than scary but it definitely builds up a creepy atmosphere.

Homefront: The Revolution is an open-world(ish) first person shooter where you must lead the Resistance movement in guerrilla warfare against a superior military force.
Oh boy, is this one a tough nut to crack. tl;dr Homefront can be amazing, it's also glitched beyond belief. But let's start at the beginning. Homefront The Revolution is a first person shooter in an open world, if you can count several zones as an open world. It's a bit like Red Faction Guerilla - you gain territory influence by completing missions in a zone, a bit like Mad Max with outposts to conquer, a bit like Far Cry with similar general game mechanics.
The game does a surprising amount of stuff good. It looks great, it has great level design, fun weapons and interesting weapon modifications. It has also atrocious AI and some serious glitches. I like them Far Cries and Mad Maxes, and I had lots of fun with Homefront, so if you like these kind of games you might want to give this one a try. Single player campaign is interesting enough as long as you substitute the countries involved for something more believable (you can also just ignore the story) and there is coop multiplayer (which is really hard, but might be fun). Completing the game on normal took me about 40hrs with some grinding for achievements and some time spent trying to unglitch several missions.
I liked:
* great visuals
* the general feeling
* that you can be sneaky
* level design
I disliked:
* glitches glitches glitches (enemies seeing through walls or despawning when they're hit with a grenade, glitching side-missions that become impossible to complete)
* Dana, damn that psychotic weirdo
Get this if:
* you can withstand the glitches and like these kind of games (these kind of games being a mix of Far Cry and Red Faction Guerilla/Mad Max)
* seriously, mind the glitches
Don't get this if:
* you expect a fair fight in your fpses, AI can be extremely dumb so most of the time you have unfair advantage, or disadvantage as they see you through walls and hit you flawlessly from 100m away
* you cannot stand glitches, as you are bound to encounter at least a few on your way here
Overall this is a recommendation as the level design alone is worth it imo, but really, mind the glitches.

A true classic. On of my favorites. Still worth replaying 11 years later. Despite being a point and click game, it scared the &*^% out of me back in the day. The world is very eerily rendered, but it is also the idea that you're alone in the middle of this woods and there's an invincible haunted Stone out there, it is hunting you but patiently. When is it going to show up again and where might it be coming from? It was stressful gameplay from a psychological perspective.
Also, we don't have many games where neopagan conceptions of magick are realistically integrated as an intergal part of the game play. Barrow Hill is unique in that regard.
Barrow Hill came out in April, 2006, just a few months after the venerable Scratches January release in North America. They were both originally published by Got Game Entertainment. Of course, these both stood on the shoulders of Myst and The 13th Guest. The difference IMHO, is that the aforementioned classic both shared an aspect of "game-ishness" if you'll pardon my little term. That IS NOT an editorial statement. But Barrow Hill and Scratches both succeeded in suffusing the experience with dread which could and did escalate to real terror at various points. Both games took it up a notch. They are both relevant to the history of how computer games have gradually become so immersive. I do consider Barrow Hill and Scratches to be sister games.
And even as I played through Penumbra and then Amnesia (and probably have been carrying around a mild, mild case of PSTD ever since) I had never forgotten these earlier classics. My opinion is admittedly biased to the point of sentimentality, but I really don't think of Barrow Hill as a dated title.
It's availability of Steam was most welcome news as is the release of it's Sequel, Barrow Hill: The Dark Path, which I'm playing through quite happily at the time of this writing.
Highly Recommended.

This game starts off looking like a really bland, sort of overdone kind of point and click adventure game on the surface, and even though part of that is attributable to age, there were more advanced kinds of games out there. But, once you sink your teeth into it, it gives you this extremely interesting and frankly, subtly terrifying environment. Without spoiling much of the story, you're basically stranded in some sacred woods on one of the worst nights for something scary to happen, and turn to a nearby gas station to search for answers. As for the scariness aspect, you will be thoroughly spooked by one playthrough, but the conciseness of the overall game makes me play it again and again and again. And, the more I play it, the more I can think about what I know and the more connections I can make to the more unclear parts of the story, and that leaves me TERRIFIED. Sometimes, I feel uneasy in my own home thinking about it. I highly recommend this game to thrill-seekers who enjoy a deep story and some puzzle-solving, because this is a game you don't want to miss out on.

Ok I'm writing this review having finished Chapter 2, because I am currently pondering whether to continue or not.
Graphics:
The cut scenes are dated and painful, but the in games graphics are fine.  A little clunky but fine.
Puzzles:
Hit and miss. You start the game in a hospital room with a girl, but no real direction. From my persepctive I just wanted to leave the room or take her out, instead I had to work out that what the game wanted was a contrived solution to a problem that may or may not exist and would only work in very specific circumstances. Don't get me wrong I love point and click adventures and they have contrived answers, but they tend to layout the problem first. While I continued with the hope that this would change, it did not. There are some good ones and there is potential there but its just not great.
So why the negative?
The main character is instantly dislikeable and not intentionally. The script could have done with some editting and you spend a large amount of time in prolonged, boring and tedious cutscenes.
Why I might continue....
Ok with all this said there are two solid reasons why I might continue this game. They are "Yesterday" and "The Next BIG Thing". Both excellent solid games, with fun puzzles, intriguing stories, interesting characters. I mentioned potential earlier and these games show that Pendulo allowed that potential to come to fruition. I kind of want to continue this game as I know that the studio is capable of a lot more and there are more games in this series which could potentially pick up.
Overall:
Unless you have the same attitude like me, avoid this game. Buy Yesterday, The Next Big Thing, Gemini Rue and Shardlight if you are looking for fun Point and Click Adventure games.

The first Runaway game is probably the most confusing adventure I've ever played. It's a renowned hit by a small studio, which made me expect clever but restrained audiovisuals (see the Blackwell series), and then superb characters, dialog and story (see... well, also the Blackwell series, for example), and hopefully excellent puzzles. Instead, the game hit me with superb cartoon visuals, one of the most likeably atmospheric soundtracks I've ever heard, and then dialog that's trite in many places, uninspiring characters, an OK-ish story, and a wide range of puzzles from awful to pretty good, never really reaching excellence. Where does this mix leave me? I'd accept most of the negatives, but some the puzzles were absolutely off-putting. Pixel hunting is a well known puzzle crime, and Runaway has many of these, but the worst are the "recharging container" type of items, which you need to return to multiple times, and they produce new items based on the current game context. These and some others lead to many situations where you had to rescan the entire gameworld for the next step, which was OK in the 1980s, but since then, the genre changed significantly. It's weird to write down, but Runaway is more fun with a walkthrough handy - I checked it 2-3 times in each of the 6 chapters, and there was only one case where I thought it was dumb to do so.
Considering all of the above, I'd give Runaway a slightly positive rating on a multi-select scale, because the atmosphere is amazing, the game is more often fun than it's not, and the worst parts can be resolved by means of the evil of walkthroughs. But this is one case where I'm really uncomfortable with my choice in Steam's binary-only voting system.

Is
a good or a bad game? I’d say both and neither, depending on your personal preferences for the point-and-click genre.
Visually, the game looks dated, but alright and I even found it to be quite reminiscent of the old LucasArts classics (especially
). The movie sequences are less than spectacular, but never to the point of being bothersome.
The game shows its age not only in the graphics, but also in its content. Hailing from the less sensitive age that was the turn of the millennium, it cares not for our contemporary ideas about all-inclusiveness. The people you meet are mostly stereotypes, so the drag queens are fabulous freak-shows, the Italians are mobsters, the native Americans have spiritual powers, Gina is a scantily clad bimbo who is constantly in need of being rescued, et cetera… Personally, I don’t mind, but this is something to keep in mind if you think about buying this game.
As for the puzzles: they are often difficult and sometimes opaque to the point of absurdity. Even by the standards of the point-and-click genre, I often found there to be little logical connection between the problems and their solutions. There is also a lot of pixel-hunting going on. A more serious gripe I had with the puzzles is that every now and then, an object that you had already inspected before is bestowed a new function, so you constantly feel the need to check every object again and again.
Not that it’s all bad though. The game shows some creativity and certain turn of events are rather funny, such as
.
The main character Brian Basco is rather bland and is neither particularly appealing nor off-putting, yet I still look forward to continuing his adventure in the sequels.
Final verdict:
.
is neither great nor terrible. It has its good moments, but the dated content and the contrived puzzles keep it down. This is definately not Pendulo Studios best work, which is a good thing, because they have certainly stepped up their game since this one.

Where to start? I was/am a long time Magic: the Gathering player. I've been playing for 17 years and found some moderate success in the competitive environment a few years back. That said, I had no idea Luis Scott Vargas was a (the?) designer of this game and I certainly didn't know the game existed until just this weekend.
It feels like a terrific middle ground between Magic and Hearthstone. There's enough interaction on your opponent's turn that the game becomes about skill and making the right card choices, but not as much as Magic where the game gets bogged down by every little action to see if your opponent wants to respond and doesn't lean heavily on RNG like Hearthstone does.
At first I was like, "This feels very much like a Hearthstone clone." I decided to finish the campaign up to see what the game is like after that and it came as part of a surprise that the game is more like Magic than Hearthstone. Which is fantastic in my books. I guess it's most easily comparable to HEX, but does it without the annoying side effect of asking your opponent if they'd like to respond every two seconds.
Since Wizards can't make a well polished digital game for Magic, I could see this game taking off into being a premiere competitive online card game. That being said, if Wizards ever does hire a competent programming team, I could see this game losing a lot of points in that department and would drop down to being somewhere between Magic and competitive Hearthstone levels.
Comparisons aside, the game has a very clean looking UI, the art is fantastic on the cards, and the claim that the game is entirely free to play holds true. You'll be able to grind out the Gauntlet battle mode endlessly to claim small rewards, including gold needed to play the more interesting modes. Forge and Draft will help super boost your collection while being fun play modes by themselves.
I'd highly recommend the game as of this writing if you're a card game veteran or someone interested in card games, but have never given one a try yet.

Five Nights at Freddy's 2. A game many of the actual vets of FNAF one were pretty hyped for. But certainly not prepared to handle. I remember being in high school when this was announced and few details were given about it. But we knew there were 10 enemies to worry about and no doors. How the hell were we going to keep those savages at bay with no doors?? It was unbelievable. And watching foxy jump at you during the trailer, sent a familiar chill down every FNAF 1 vet's spine. We had to get this game and further contribute to Scott's fortune. But we were not ready. With a very strict learning curve, almost three times the enemies, and buffed up difficulty, the sequel to the first delivered. No longer were the first 4 nights a cake walk. We were constantly on edge seeing which new enemy we were going to face next. The new animatronics were nicely revamped and glossed over. (including the design of the old ones) so all the enemies don't look like giant walking pieces of old crusty clay with eyes coming at you. Some of them even look genuinely frightening as oppossed to just being creepy. My two favorites would have to be faceless bonnie and marrionnette. These two are incredible at what they do. scaring the living crap out of me whenver im not paying enough freakin' attention to the game. With all that being said, No game is without flaws. One being the lacking need for the cameras once again. Once you get a good feel for the game and you've been through many jumpscares and such, you notice in this game there really is only one function of the cameras and that's to keep the marionette away. Thats pretty much it. Even FNAF 1 had more use. The next flaw is that we realized that while there were 10 animatronics to worry about, many of them can be avoided in exactly the same way. He could just as easily made a few, but faster and aggressive. Taking away the uniqueness of the enemies. But that's a minor flaw. The next flaw I need to address is the crap your pants scariness that comes with not knowing which animatronics react to what when the game first came out or when you first play it. The phone guy tells us that foxy is affected by the flash light and that the mask will repel animatronics. That's it. When some giant freakin' animatronic is making it's way down the hall and you put on the mask, take it back off, check the hall and are crapping your boxers to find that the son of a shepard only got closer, you really don't know what to do unless you looked up videos prior to playing. At least thats just me and the friends I played this with. This game is much more terrifying than the first and is much more complex which I just love. But I have to admit, the game is quite scary at times. Not crazy terrifying, but it can make you jump and the ambience is creepy enough. For being an actually good sequel which does not happen often, I give it a solid 80/100

I'm going to get this out of the way at the start, this game includes both FF X and X-2, and I must say, for the price, you get 2 full-length games that are of pretty good quality.
Now, I'm going to talk mostly of FF X as it is the one I was more fond of, X-2 was generally agreeable, but I certainly wouldn't see myself playing through it again like I would FF X.
The combat system in FF X is simply amazing, and it really goes back to the idea of a turn-based with no timer or active time system, further enhanced by the option to actively tag in and out your party members from any given fight. This brings a new level of strategy to the combat, looking for mostly a melee team to burn the heavy magic def resistant boss out? Just bring in your 3 players focused on melee, need to switch to pure magic? Then you can do that too. Furthermore, on a similar point, your summons feel much more alive and relevant when you use them, as they stick around and build up their own limit breaks and whatnot, replacing your party temporarily.
Something else, that almost does not need to be said, but the musical scores are absolutely stunning and incredibly done, which seems to be a regular occurence for the Final Fantasy series, and they certainly did not disappoint in this one either.
Further over the PS2 port, they enhanced the graphics considerably, improved the cut scenes graphics too, they redid the soundtrack, with the option to still listen to the original one as well, and they also added some upgrades (for those who are more interested in the story as opposed to the combat and grind?) which range from speeding up the pace of the game to essentially having godmode (though not exactly).
Summing up what was said, the game is well done, remastered properly, allows some upgrades to compensate for a lack in difficulty choices, and it's 2 full games for a pretty good price.
Oh, and I almost forgot, they have Blitzball! I know it's not something for all, but I absolutely loved playing blitzball in this game...
It's almost impossible to say no to a game like this on sale (if it's your style of game, anyways).

The game is commendable for being much slower and tactical than most FPS games, especially since it captures the reality of trench raiding fairly effectivley. The class and squad progression system is interesting as well. The accuracy of the weaponry, uniforms, gears and maps is a great positive.
It encourages squad cohesion and discourages lone wolf actions, which makes the gameplay more smarter and tactical. Assaults are made or broken by squad cohesion and support, or lack thereof.

The difficulty of the gameplay however carries both positives and negatives.
As a positive? It's more challenging, forces you to think more about your surroundings and approach combat with more care and consideration. It makes you more aware of where you are, what the risks are. It keeps you on edge the entire time and it makes for what could be called a very authentic experience of war. I highly apprciate and commend the game for this. I can't stress that enough
As a negative? Well, at the end of the day it's simply not fun to die twenty times for almost no gain. You could argue this was the point, to show the common reality of the stalemate that plagued The Western Front from 1915-1917, but the game itself has a win state.
You put effort into capturing trenches, so clearly there's an end goal with a purpose, so the idea that 'dying constantly is the point' doesn't hold up.
I doubt the game is some sort of philosophical deconstruction of the FPS and has valuable things to say on how cruel it is to use real wars as backdrops for FPS games (which is a valuable and important thing to say), because the game incentivises killing by giving you points. Saying 'it's not supposed to be fun because it's WW1' is at odds with the games entire system.
The ranking system is there to encourage progression, you get points so you can unlock better weaponry so you can kill more stuff with more ease. There's an end win state, you get points for advancing, following orders, killing people, helping other people kill people etc;
If you want to say the game wants to make a point about how horrible WW1 was, maybe don't give incentives to players to kill more people in the game... It's the exact opposite of an anti-war message.
So then the simple issue is that, as a game and from a purely game design standpoint, it's not going to be fun for most people. Realism is great and again, i admire, respect and appreciate the game for it's 'realism', but 'realism' does not always mean 'good game design'.
I appreciate the game immensly, but to say i always have fun while playing it is inaccurate. The fun is incremental and depends severely. In some games even if you're losing you can say you had fun. In Verdun, losing is an exercise in frustration, soul crushing futility and fury.
Maybe the question is should this game be 'fun' at all? Maybe the question should be to define what 'fun' means? Those are questions for a more philosophical essay. Maybe i'll write it one day.
The game arbitrarilly deciding your 'attack lost momentum' and theatening to execute you and deduce your progress if you don't retreat back in time (which is almost certain death anyway because you'll most likely be shot in the back as you move with haste) is IMO, completely unneeded in the game. It would be better to simply leave the squads to do their own thing, assault at their own convenience and decide the battle based on their own terms and abilities, and not when the game tells them to.
At the end of the day it's simply not fun. There are plenty of hard games that manage to be more fun than this.
Ultimatley, even with all the positives, the gameplay is severely hampered by a janky engine and incredibly sluggish movements, to the point where even the niche appeal of difficult gameplay is nullified. I think the game would benefit greatly if the movement speed of the characters and the movement of the aiming was smoother, more fluid and more human.
It would give players, IMO at least, a more equal playing field. It would be easier for all players to aim and function better as players on the field.
The quality of the gunplay depends severely. Others work fine, some others have sights that are too large for you to actually see anything.
Not to mention that aiming in this game is almost literally painful, slow, sluggish, and actually hitting something feels more like luck than any actual skill. Even at the highest aiming sensitivity it never makes much of a difference, your character still moves like a robot with rusty gears. It doesn't fee natural, it doesn't feel fun and it will get you killed at the most inopportune moment, not because the enemy is more skilled, but because the stars aligned and they managed to fight the sluggish aiming to get a good hit on you at that specific moment.
Not to mention that hit detection itself is atrocious and some of the weapons are so hampered by beefy, chunky sights and recoil that aiming down the sights is useless, while also being unviable while hip firing, like the BAR.
Spawn points are poorly constructed and you can often be picked off by snipers from the other side of the map as you respawn.
A lot of the maps are also very poorly constructed and either impossible to defend or to assault. Despite them looking very accurate and appealing, as gameplay maps, they're heavily unbalanced.
Most of the roles in the game don't offer much variety, perks or agency. The only class with real agency is the NCO and to me personally, is why it's the most fun to play. It's the only class that makes you feel like you're empowered or useful besides just being a walking murder machine. As a consequence, the lack of an NCO is what destroys squads. There's no system in place to account for it.
The machine gunner class is, IMO, counter intuitive to the gameplay. It's a class that often times rellies on being visible, in a game where being visible is a death sentence. Most of the time you will spend with your head, shoulders and arms perched on an incline and failry visible for the MANY sharp shooters, which the game favours heavily.
Moving from one spot to the next to avoid being shot is torturous due to the sluggish engine and slow movements of the character.
The only actual use for the class i've found is to deny entrances into the trenches, rather than as an implement to deny movement across the whole of No Mans Land.
As an aside, the game is utterly unwelcoming to new players. There are a limited ammount of servers and none of them are organised based on skill level, which means new players will get stuck in a server with no knowledge of the map, pitted against veteran players. It doesn't give new and casual players any actual chance to like the game.
Another aside, having more representation of Colonial troops would be a welcome sight. Africans and Asians all fought in France and Belgium, and the game would benfit from more variety in roles and abilities.
So would i reccomend it? Only as a niche interest to history buffs who don't mind frustrating gameplay, and even then it's not certain. A friend of mine who loves this era of history as much as i do hates the game and described it as 'feeling like you're moving through molasses' and honestly i couldn't agree more.
I'm sad that Steam only allows you a binary choice, because it's not as simple as just saying 'don't buy this game' or 'buy this game'. If you're a history buff who appreciates accuracy and a different and more methodical FPS experience based on WW1 you may wanna check it out. But if you're looking for casual fun, please avoid this game.

I've played this game for 4 hours and I can tell you pretty much all you'll want to know about it. First of all, the gamemechanics are very similar to Crysis and Farcry blended together. The main premise of the game is that you're a resistance fighter in wartorn America and you're goal is to sabotage the tyranical leadership from behind enemy lines. You take over command posts similar to Farcry and try to win over the reputation of citizens and persuade them to join your fight.  You can customize weapons on the go, which includes while you're sprinting. Attachments vary from red dot sights, holographic sights, 4x scopes and sniper scopes. Under barrel foregrips, bipods and laser sights. Muzzle breaks and silencers. And finally, every weapon can have an additional schematic which transforms it into a completely different gun. For example, the assault rifle can be turned into a LMG, or a trip wire-mine launcher. The pistol can be converted into an SMG. Whereas the weapon customization premise seems cool at first glance, I only ever ended up using the base variants such as the normal assault rifle because the game lacked situations where any other weapon would seem plausible. The game tries to give you stealth opportunities in the form of incorpoating a Farcry-esque awareness meter. The stealth gameplay falls flat due to the poor AI and quick detection time. When you're detected, an alarm sounds in the city and alerts all gaurds nearby thereby initiating a fight for your life against several heavily armed gaurds. You can lose the gaurds by jumping in a hiding spot such as a dumpster or portable outhouse. All of this sounds fun and exciting, and if it was half as fun and exciting as I've made it out to be, I would reccomend this game. The sad truth, is that it isn't. The game appears to be a AAA open world FPS game, but it doesn't feel even remotely close to that when you're playing. The bugs are what really kills the experience. There will be instances where an enemy convoy and anti-personal vehicle is approaching you at the end of the street. You'll switch to your explosive RC car to drive up under the vehicle and blow it up right? Sounds like a cool way to off all of these guys at once right? Wrong. As soon as you set the RC car down and start to control it, there's a 50/50 chance that the entire enemy convoy you just saw has disappeared off the face of the earth. Gone. No where to be found. Rendered one second, the next second vanished. It's a ridiculous bug that I've overlooked 50 too many times. It happens virutally everytime you try and use the RC car. Heck, I've even had it happen without using the car and just going behind a wall real quick. Enemies will literally just dissappear. Oh, they also just pop up and spawn right in front of you too.
So, Tl,Dr. Don't buy this game for full price. If it goes on sale, and you've already beaten every Crysis game, and Farcry game, and very very desperately want to play a game that has similar mechanics to either one, then MAYBE pick this game up. But if you like those games and think this game is would be cool because it looks so similar, don't buy it, because it's not very fun.

Started out game and there is no tutorial or info on how to play the game.  Sure it tells you it's a squad based game, but nothing else. Once you read the guides, I played the squad defense, which is pve.  This works great for learning a bit how different characters work.
After playing a few hours on squad defense I worked my way into the main scenario.  I was looking forward to using the squad tactics.  After all, the entire concept of the game is that everyone belongs to a squad of four players, each with a different role.  Unfortunately, there really wasn't even any team play.  Everyone just spawns and rushes into battle.  Had no idea where my squadmates were.
I know the game supports coop and so decided to play with a good friend.  I created a squad and had him join me.  Then we launched into the both the pve and pvp scenarios. Half the time I would go into the normal map and he would find himself in the christmas truce map.  No idea why this happened half the time.
The games premises is a great idea, but lacking any sort of tutorial to help you get started, wonky coop support (which this game would be great for), and the fact that people don't seem to use the squad tactics in game, I can't recommend it.  Even when playing with friends and everything goes right, I just didn't really enjoy the game that much.
Maybe if I invested a lot of time into it to unlock different weapons and found a group of 4 other players to play regularly with I would enjoy, it.  Until then I think I'll pass.

This game was developed half way through by Crytek but was sold to Deep Silver as a way to escape bankruptcy.  This is clearly seen in the gameplay.  There are many "Crysis" aspects in this game, for example, weapon customization, open world type levels, and ledge grabs.  The main story for the game is slow and speeds up near the end.  The main characters are not too likeable until the DLC where they show their true colors.  It is pretty clear that Deep Silver bought the rights to the game thinking it was mostly complete when it still needed alot of progress.
My main problem with the game is the AI.  Not because they are "dumb" but they have unexpected spawns.  When you clear out a building of enemy AI, and come back the the building 15 seconds later, all the enemies are respawned.  Sometimes, they AI spawn right infront or behind you.  There is no sense of saftey.  At certain points in the game, I would run past the AI just to activate a cutscene, knowing more AI will respawn no matter what.  This makes the sniper rifle pretty useless for most of the game.  This is only a problem of the MAIN story, NOT the DLC.
I highly recommend buying the DLC for a true sense of "ending" to the Homefront universe.
I give the main story a rating of 6.5/10, an average game.  The DLC gets 7.5/10 a enjoyable story but is unfortnetly short (about 1 hour each DLC).
I bought the game for $15 including the DLC and I think I got my money's worth.

Barrow Hill is now 10 years old, but if you like old school point and click adventures then this will be right up your street. You are following the footsteps of Conrad Morse, a well known archaeologist and you have one night to solve the mystery of the standing stones as something is beginning to stir at the Barrow. Although not a time limited adventure time will move on as you complete the story line. It's not an overly taxing adventure it will keep you amused for a while with some interesting puzzles. As size goes it’s not huge but it has many atmospheric locations to visit and explore. Listen out for the voice of Emma Harry playing herself as the radio presenter. Many of you will recognise her as Lucy Reubans from The Lost Crown. Jonathon Boakes who wrote The Lost Crown also worked on Barrow Hill which was a Matt Clark creation.  If you like Barrow Hill look out for anything from Darkling Room who worked on Dark Fall the Journal, Dark Fall Lights Out and Dark Fall Lost Souls (although they were all licenced to Iceberg Interactive about 2009). Anyway those games were all from the same stable of people. Also as another side note Nigel Danvers from The Lost Crown first appeared in Dark Fall the Journal, but voiced by Stuart Banks. Jonathon Boakes voiced him later on in The Lost Crown. Finally Rhiannon Curse of the Four Branches is another Celtic mystery worth looking at. Although from two other houses Arbeth and Lighthouse Interactive it is not a bad point and click. Interestingly Lighthouse Interactive was one of the original publishers of Barrow Hill along with Shadow Tor Studios.
And for those of you who haven’t guessed yet…yes, yes I am a nerd.

I've always been a fan of racing games. Doesn't matter what type or style it entailed. The Crew has its good and its bad. Lets go with the bad first.
The only real negatives I can personally give is once you hit level 50 and can get Platinum level cart parts it's a straight crap shoot at getting a level 50 car part. This is my biggest complaint. It's purely random, meaning you might get it on the first try or not get it for fifty tries or more. Also on the car parts that you "unlock", which allows you to buy the car part on another car instead of having to Story/Skills missions for the same part is restricted to which car spec you use when you unlocked that car part so if you get it through a Street spec car you can only buy it on a Street spec car, Any other car spec you will have to unlock seperately.
The car assists are split into three types, all assist, sport, and hardcore. None of which can be changed for what you want or don't want when driving. This is mildly annoying, but it also knows if you're using a controller or a steering wheel. Avoid using a keyboard if all possible with this game.
The NPC cars in Faction missions and the Police are cheaters, to put it as nice as possible, since it doesn't matter what surface they're driving on they will never lose any traction. The Police are lacking in the sense of you can drive by them at ridiculous speeds and run red lights/stop signs and they do not attempt to chase you. The only way to get a police chase is to either run into them or cause enough collateral damage during a Police Watch to trigger them into chasing you. Maybe this can be patched later to make them more like actual cops.
The car selection is nice, it isn't on Gran Turismo or Forza level, but it's sufficient. Overall the customization isn't bad either. Visual car aestetics are fairly wide until you get to Raid and Circuit specs (Since they are only color, sticker, tag, and rims options.) Again it isn't at the level of being able to make your own designs and putting them on your car. (I know why, mostly in the sense of people making poorly designed gentailia...) There are enough stickers and color variety to not run into same design, unless everyone in your session is obsessed with The Fast & the Furious.
The achievements can be entertaining in their title and down right fun to do depending on the prerequistes.
This game isn't for the simulator type player, it plays more to your Test Drive, Need for Speed and Burnout types. Even the adventerer in you will find it fun to be able to drive across the United States finding known landmarks throughout. The story isn't anything new, but it was still fun to watch and have some sort of cinematics and build some level of character developement for the people you add to your crew over the course of your exploits.
Oh, make sure you have some friends too, this is far more fun with people you know than driving it alone. At the end of the opening credits it says, "Never Drive Alone" and for good reason. Despite the flaws in this game I still see more posistive than negative, but what do I know since I'm the same guy that's been playing APB/APB:R for 3+ years. :)

This is, by far, the best TCG Digital game there is. Design wise it makes hearthstone look like monopoly. If you have any intrests in TCGs (Magic the gathering in particular) this is the game for you.
It's amazing.
------------PROS-------------------------------
+ Free to play. Really free to play. It's sooooo easy to get cards. Not grind OR pay to win, it's just play. You get cards at 4x the rate of Hearthstone.
+ Great design. It has a perfect balance (like MTG) between Skill/Luck and lack of RNG. Never again feel ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥tted when your Ragnaros misses for the 3rd time when that control warrior finally is down to 8 health before the justicar back to 90 armor.
+ Great brew potential. 81 deck slots and so many great cards to build around. After playing for 20 hours I can already start brewing amazing decks with redicilous combos.
+ Great multiplayer AND single player. You can get cards in a valid pace by playing against AI if you feel uncomfortable playing better players. My guess however is that you wont as the ranked matchmaking is awesome. When I had a newbie deck, I only played similar players. But as I started winning the matchmaking quickly placed me among my peers.
+ Actual limited (Arena in HS is not actual) gameplay that works really well. You build decks on site and face people doing the same. This let's the newcommer play with other people competitivly without hurting from lack of collection, it lets you learn all the cards and archtypes, it let's you open packs at value (everyone likes packs) and finally it's the most fun format that builds your collection.
+ Overall amazing. I would rate the game 9/10 easily +++
-------CONS-----------------------------------------------------
- It's still in beta, and while the design of game is spot on (amazing designers, luv u LSV), some development issues. Things are fixed quickly and direwolf listens to their players (looking at you blizz), however, as of now it's not perfect.
- Sometimes the software itself can feel clunky, especially if youre used to Hearthstone fluidity. If you are used to MTGO though it's a MASSIVE improvement and I cant recommend the upgrade enough.
- No phone support. I havented tried their pad gameplatform.
- Some artworks are lackluster (Nowhere near MTG but on HS level atleast.)
- The lore is somewhat unaccessable even if it's there
-------------------------------------------Verdict -----------------------------------------------
Gameplay 10/10
Platform 5/10
Newbie friendlyness 9/10
Rewarding 10/10
Potential long term 9/10
Art 6/10
------ Personal verdict:
It's the best TCG made to play on a electronic device. It's amazing. It is bested by Magic but it is so much more accessable than Magic. It's slightly less accessable than Hearthstone but it makes up for that in 1000-fold once you get over the initial hump.
If you're new to TCG this is my nr 1 recommendation.
If you love magic but dislike MTGO this is my nr 1 recommendation.
If you love MTGO this game will feel uncessesary.
If you like Hearthstone this will be an eyeopener and a replacement.
9/10 game, I'll play it 5ever.

So much potential ruined by greed and Ubisoft's practices.  It's a AAA title you pay full price for, then has all the elements of a F2P title.
1)  After buying the game for $40-60, you're given a starting car that is very underpowered and handles like crap.  It takes a *lot* of time to grind out upgrades, level up your character, and earn perks.  OR, you can pay a few real dollars and unlock a super car straight away.  Not with premium currency, *literally* with real world money.  However:
2)  There IS premium currency.  You can buy packs of Crew Credits to unlock parts and upgrades faster.
This wouldn't be an issue if you could only buy cosmetic things, but the cars on sale for real cash and the parts you can get with premium currency give you an edge over most players in PvP.
Also, don't forget Uplay.  If you launch the game from steam, Uplay has to load up and sync, then the game tries to load.  Which can really bog down your system for no apparent reasons.
For some reason your car stutters and jumps all over the place in cutscenese.  However you're fine during the gameplay itself (albeit capped at 30 to 60fps).  This has been a bug known since before release from what I've been reading, but nothing's been done to fix it.
Your car handles like crap.  If you watch closely, when you're travelling at speed your car doesn't follow real world physics:
instead of turning.  This is extremely apparent if you visit a highway with steady curves or a race track, you can watch as the trunk of the car slides out and the wheels don't line up to where the car is heading when you're not drifting.
Speaking of wheels not lining up, visit an airport.  The aircraft (which are all scaled down and scaled up copies of each other) are just static models that slide around.  Their wheels don't spin and the nose gear doesn't turn.  Heck, they don't have any animations at all, and their engines are obvious polygons.  I haven't seen aircraft that poorly modelled since 1998.
In conclusion:  Hell no.  I wasted $40 on a game where you have to grind for days on end before you're even competitive, or give Ubisoft more money.
(The tiny straw that broke the camels back:  They made New York and Chicago huge and detailed, but my ENTIRE state gets a few highways and a handful of buildings?  The two towns they added and named are literally a dozen or so buildings.  And they're both tourist trap villages, they didn't add our biggest city or our capital.)
EDIT:  almost forgot!  The AI cheats.  Regardless of how much more upgraded your car is, they speed up to keep up with you, and
.  They get to fly at max speed as if they're on pavement, while you're struggling to stay on the track as you drift around corners.  Even if your Dirt Spec is levelled up far more than theirs.

After that, I tried my first wrestling game by renting it from a local Blockbuster (does anyone stil remember those?). It was Smackdown vs Raw 2006 for the PS2. The controls felt a little bit clunky because it tried to be something it was not: a grappling simulator. However, I enjoyed every single moment I spent on that game just because I could recreate what I saw on the show and fight with my favourite wrestlers.
Fast forward to 2016 and I'm still playing the same damn game with an updated roster and a graphic mod.
The main problem with WWE 2K16 is exactly that, they've been doing almost the same game for 10 years. Sure, they've added more game modes, characters and other stuff. They have even improved the grappling and striking system to make it more fair when playing with friends (oh the times when you had infinite reversals and they were performed just by smashing a button).
If you're a hardcore wrestling fan like me, you will probably enjoy this game, even if it has really strong weaknesses as a a PC port (fps drops, physics crashing, animations glitching...) and even if it adds nothing at all to previous WWE games but a wider roster that doesn't involve repeating the same superstar in different time periods (I'm looking at you WWE 13 and your 3-4 versions of Triple H).
However, if you're looking for a fun sports/fighting game this probably isn't the correct choice for you.

In not that much of a fan of the WWE, but I like wrestling games. I do recommend this game, since it's pretty good and perhaps is the best one available for PC. However, there are a few things that I don't like, I hate or I simply wished they haven't removed.
Cons
-No custom matches: Which means you may only play with the ones defined by the game. Not a big variety and you can no longer change things like "win by Finisher only" and stuff like that.
-No symetry when creating superstars or divas. You edit things with points and the lack of a symetry tool makes the process a bit tedius.
-I know it's the PG era and stuff, but I do miss the intergender matches. You can kinda "hack" wrestlers to be able to fight intergender, but it could increase the risk of crashing the game.
-Wrestler creation process is in general slow and lacks of previews... but keep reading. XD
Pros
-In depth wrestler creation. If you take your time working on this, you can get pretty awesome results. There are certain limits but in general creationg is pretty cool. Even when you can't preview anything and the process is slow, if you enjoy spending hours customizing, this game is good.
-Sharing content. Or if you're lazy and are looking for Deadpool, Rainbow Dash or Undertaker in another outfit... you can just see if someone already made it and download it.
-Universe mode. Kind of like a story mode, which can be customized. For example, you can select only your custom supersatrs to be part of the matches, set the championships and stuff. Way better than the actual story mode.
-Good gameplay. As any wrestling game lately, it takes a bit of time to get used to it, but it's pretty well done.
Long story short: If only intergender matches were a thing, as well as match creation/customization... I'd love this game. As it is now, I just think it's good.

The horror genre is a result of people wanting to subvert that idea that videogames are about empowerment, that being weak and powerless is just as fun as being one man army of chaos and destruction.
One day, a hack and slash and a horror game ♥♥♥♥ed in a dark alley, and I'm not talking about that smooth stuff, I'm talking about the kind of angry sex that was used to settle frustrations with each other and just get it over with, the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ child born out of that, was Dark Souls, who was heard from the trash can, got adopted by a few damn good parents and became a millionaire.

That, is Dark Souls.

You know, I think
is the kind of game where it's best to go in completely blind. No reviews, no pros and cons, no preconceived notions. Just dive in. The first few moments of the game are immediately gripping, and the introduction to the world you're going to be playing in is perfectly paced and intriguing.
But hey, if you insist on at least SOME information before you buy a game then here you go:
is a strange mixture of side-scrolling shooter, survival game, and a dash of management game. You're playing as the conductor of a small train during the
alien apocalypse, carrying important cargo that could change the tide of the battle plus whatever survivors you find on the way. The gameplay alternates between the shoot-y exploring-y parts where you scrounge for supplies in the outside world, and the parts where you frantically run back and forth in the train trying to keep you bleeding passengers from dying and the various machinery from breaking down.
The clever part of this, and the thing that ties the two gameplay sides together, is that your inventory is common for both. Meaning that the medkit you spend on yourself on the field is one less medkit you can use on your passengers, and vice versa. This leads to the necessity for strategy during exploration; do you spend bullets and health to get to the precious food and crafting supplies behind the enemy monsters? Do you quickly go to your objective and back, hoping the supplies you already have will be enough? Both of these options can leave you screwed if you're not careful.
And it's exactly this caution that puts you in the mindset of a survivor. Because while this is by no means a horror game, there is a certain tension and dread following in your footsteps. I had gotten into the habit of instinctively backing up when opening doors, paranoid about enemies rushing me. I would decide to conserve my dwindling bullets, only to waste them in a panic when surrounded by too many monsters. I would feel disoriented and suspicious whenever I visited safe zones populated by actual normal human beings. The game is very effective in achieving emotional responses from you, and there were even some parts that were surprisingly and delightfully creepy that definitely left an impression on me.
The story itself is left mysterious, with information mostly gained from the rumors and gossiping of your passengers, and from the remnants of various strange past events you encounter during your travels. The world-building is slow but clever, and the moments when the bigger picture starts becoming clearer are particularly memorable. All in all it's the general atmosphere created from its seperate parts that is the game's greatest strength, and it's enhanced by the beautiful pixel art in the backgrounds and level design.
Sadly no game is without flaws, and I'll start with a more personal nitpick: I thought the game just wasn't... well, hard
. There's some talk in the beginning about how maybe you can't keep all your passengers alive and should prioritize who to save, but honestly if you're a basically decent player and explore often you won't have that much trouble with it. Maybe I'm a masochist but when I play survival games sometimes I want a more hardcore challenge, especially on a second playthrough, and this isn't really an option here as you can't choose a difficulty level. There aren't even enough achievements to make any self-imposed challenges worth it. What you get is the same each time.
I should also mention the playtime, which is a bit short, with the game lasting about 4-5 hours. I actually don't think this is a negative point on its own, since there was enough content for me to feel satisfied, and anything more would probably end up being too repetitive and tiring. The negative aspect is that there is barely any replayability to it. The game can be loosely devided in 3 parts (plus prologue and epilogue) so I expected at the very least a chapter select option when I finished, but nope. You gotta start from the very beginning. And since like I said there are no difficulty levels to choose, you have bascially no incentive to start again.
So yes, this is a game meant to be played only once. However, in the end the strength of the experience you get is more than enough to make it feel worth playing. (I was certainly impressed enough with the game to write this way too long review to recommend it!) So if you like clever little atmospheric indie games that try to be something a bit more unique, then don't let the downsides deter you. Give this a try. It's worth it.

This review contains no spoilers.
The tags on this should have warned you from the beginning, but just in case: this is not a game, it's another "walk around and explore everything, eventually leading to a conclusion" type of experience.
has a main story that unfolds in linear fashion as you explore the surroundings, and also a lot of background detail that tells you more about these people you never interact with. All the characters actually have quite a bit of backstory, not just the one the story focuses on, and it's easy to miss all the little hints and clues that tell you everything there is to know about this world, so it's not quite as linear as your movements.
However, that still doesn't mean it's worth $20 at full price; there's just not enough substance to justify it. At $4 on sale, you could go for it if you really like these kinds of harmless, non-twitchy explore type interactive experiences. If you're open to it, and you like thinking about fictional people and what their lives could be like, well, you might even get your money's worth. The hard decision for me is whether I recommend it, and I'll have to go with "no". It's not terrible by any means, it's a charming little slice of life experience, but it's awfully short, and the emotional and narrative payoff is really too paltry. If I'd read this as a story or watched it as a TV show, I wouldn't have walked away satisfied, and dressing it up as a game doesn't change that.

Final Fantasy X is one of my favorite games from growing up. Great story and love the leveling system because it isn't very linear and you have much more freedom in your choices, especially on the remastered edition since it has the grid sphere system that was on the japenese version, which starts everyone near the middle to go whichever direction you want. The combat system in X is basically just your standard turn based battle but the variety of moves and freedom to build a character how you want keep it interesting. Plenty of side mission type things to do for you to be able to spend tons of hours playing.
Final Fantasy X-2 isn't quite as great by itself but as a follow up to X it does it's job reasonably well. X-2 does offer a more interesting battle system than X however. Still mostly turn based but you have different "classes" you can change between mid battle. This keeps the battle pretty interesting. The story itself if you don't get a "perfect" game maybe isn't as interesting, but once you achieve a perfect game it is pretty satisfying and a great follow up to X.
There's also a afterstory voice over called "Final Fantasy X/X-2 Will" that isn't really very well pointed out that it even exists. It's just a voice over showing pictures from the games, but it's kind of like an after story to show some things that happen after the events of both games. Decent side story that almost makes it seem like they want to make an X-3.

Highly visceral and deep gun handling and creepy distopian vibe are the two primary positive elements that this game has to offer. Nothing beats the feeling of learning the gun mechanics and successfully using them against the (sadly) 2 types of enemies you'll face during the game.
The map is randomly generated for each playthrough and each time you die but things will definitely start to look familiar the more you play. Your mission is to locate 11 tapes that are scattered around the map and listen to their dialogue while staying alive. Be very careful while turning each corner in this game because a single enemy shot will kill you and send you back to the beginning. Oh and did I mention the guns are also randomized? There are 3 guns total but how many bullets they have and whether they're loaded, cocked or with the safety on can vary between each start.
On the negative side, there are framerate hitches whenever you walk into new areas and the levels can get really dark. The short version is this: You're playing a movie, not a conventional video game.  It's exceptionally well told and is nice to look at, easily on par with high-end indie movies.  It's worth noting that Gone Home is priced about the same as a Blu-Ray movie would be at most retail stores, so no, $19.99 is not asking too much for a 1080p movie-like experience, in my opinion.
The long version below goes into a little more detail about why Gone Home is such a great experience, in my pseudo-intellectual opinion.
Gone Home is not a game.  Our interactions with the world are too minimal compared with other games.  There is no failure state, there are no puzzles, and we have zero impact on the narrative or even the environment.  Gone Home is not a movie.  The whole story is told in one big, long cut, where we are often left standing in place and looking at the scenery, and that's something of a no-no in even independent art-house film.  Gone Home isn't even a glorified audiobook, since the narrator doesn't exactly act, it's more like a long after-the-fact explanation for why the titular home is empty when the player shows up.  That kind of delivery might work for a non-fiction book, but not for something with an actual story to it.
Gone Home, instead, is something we experience in our imagination, with the help of the narration and the provided environment.  It took me an hour and 48 minutes to get through it all, which is, appropriately, about how long an independent film with a similar setup would run.
In a way, Gone Home is brilliant, because it provides a visual cue to let the player know what the rest of the world might look like, and then gives them narration to provoke the imagination.  The objects that we interact with to trigger pieces of the story narration also help give us a clue what the setting might look like.  Experimental high school garage band logos tell us what these kids might look like, and our mind conjures up the rest of the images.  With this, Gone Home is able to to cut out almost all of the descriptive language that might be in an audiobook while still letting the imagination run wild, something that can't happen in a movie or conventional game.
Gone Home is experienced at your pace, and that's a bigger strength that most might realize, since after every piece of narration, we can take a moment to absorb and add what we just heard to the bigger story.  Again, conventional film, games, and audiobooks can't really pull that off.
If you heard the story already from a friend, I absolutely feel like you will still get a great experience from it, regardless, since there's plenty of polish and attention to detail in the visual settings.  There are just so many great details and tiny awesome moments that you have to experience Gone Home for yourself.

Some people will say this game seems very realistic.
That argument couldn't be further from the truth.
Verdun hardly captures the essence of trench warfare at all.  The 16v16 nature of battles where people fight mostly with rifles and pistols doesn't represent the hundreds and thousands who participated in charges across no-man's land with machine guns, mortars, gas, and artillery all over.  Yes, there are mgs, mortars, gas, and artillery, but they're hardly used by officers, and they don't target entire battalions (AKA several hundreds) of troops at a time.  Instead, you find yourself using mortar strikes just to bombard a hard to take corner in a trench that's covered by one or two troops.
Granted the aesthetics of the game seem very realistic.  Yes, the trenches are dug into the ground with planks and posts, and there are craters and barbed wire everywhere...
...but the low numbers in the game make it feel more like you're playing a WW1 post-apocalyptic simulator or leading a special forces squad on an infiltration mission instead.  If everyone got to play an officer leading a squad of a dozen NPCs, it'd be great.  If the game played like Planetside with massive battles, it'd be great.  If the game wasn't plagued with snipers who can ruin an offensive just by taking one or two guys out here or there, it'd be great...
...but it's not.  By the way, did I mention you get executed if you're still attacking when the computer arbitrarily says your side has lost momentum and "overtime" is over?  On the other hand, did I mention how the game will say your side has lost a trench even if your side still has troops in it just because the opposition has been in it for a long time?
On top of that, your success in one battle doesn't impact your success in other battles.  Pushing the front doesn't happen from one match to the next.  In any given match, the scoring system works according to whoever takes the most trenches, but ultimately, there's no goal in mind.  You're not pushing for Paris as the Germans or to liberate France as the Entente.  There's no promotion system either to control High Command or allocate resources.  You never get to conduct massive artillery strikes or assign tanks to finish off elaborate trench networks.
The game just feels boring at the end of the day.  The only reason to play this game is if you have a high-end PC that can run it at 60 fps so you can camp and snipe all day at suckers who are desperate to run and jump over an obstacle course.  On the other hand, you can enjoy wielding a trenchclub too and take society back to the Dark Ages when you roleplay a barbarian just to whack someone over the side of their head while they're reloading after missing their one shot with a rifle before reloading.

Restaurant cooking simulator where you try to complete as many orders as you can, then spend your earnings on upgrades. I used an x360 controller to play. Cooking meals is somewhat like Cooking Mama, but here there's no gestures: you press a button/direction for a certain ingredient/action and almost all recipes are just inputting the right ingredients. You then cook it for a certain time and send it off before it gets burnt. A few early recipes just involve holding the down direction for a certain amount of time to fry the food, and a couple complex recipes require you to put the ingredients in a certain order. It's not too complex to learn (you start out with fewer ingredients/recipes until you upgrade the foods) but the biggest problem will be doing them fast enough so that your other orders don't suffer. I avoided upgrading certain foods to avoid the complexity. Upgraded wine can be pretty cost-effective if you don't like the complexity because it mostly requires mashing one button. Upgraded soup was my least favorite thing to do because of the sheer number of ingredients involved.
Campaign mode is the big draw for me (earn upgrades, do events, read random e-mails), but there's also a nice multiplayer and challenge/score attack mode. Pretty fun if you like simulations or mastering sequences.

I enjoyed this game but it did have some flaws. I would recommend it if you are a fan of point and click style adventure.
Pros:
-Unique Story. Not very cliche even though some parts of it can seem a little dated.
-Not overly long or overly short. I felt the last few parts were a little long but I feel that can be attributed to a flaw I will discuss below, but overall the developers didn't add in stuff just to make it longer, they also made it long enough to resolve the main story.
-Interesting voice acting. Now this is debatable. I personally liked some of the comical voice acting but it isn't necessarily good voice acting. I felt it matched the story and mood but I could see the voice acting being a con for someone else.
-Good Aesthetic. I liked the cartoonish vibe and the art stays consistent.
Cons:
-Brian walks WAY TOOO DAMN SLOW. It seems like half the game is just waiting for Brian to walk over to a clue or a new place. It would'nt be so bad if things were close together but they have some maps(like Douglasville) which can take 15-20 seconds to walk across. This was a severe oversight. It is really annyoing to watch Brian slowly amble everywhere when you are trying to solve a murder mystery.
-Hard to discern what can be interacted with. There are so many things everywhere and sometimes it can be hard to tell what you can and can't click on. The mouse pointer changes when you hover over something but it isnt enough. There were multiple times I missed an important tool becuase it was a rock on the ground surrounded by other rocks. They shouldve of added a feature ,like in Yesterday, that lights up everything you can click on momentarily.
-They needed to space the hit boxes for clicking on stuff a little more.
-The puzzels and their solutions seem contrived and confunding at times. I will admit I am not the best at these games but I feel it would of taken me 3-4 times longer if I hadn't used a walk through. Add the fact that it can be hard to tell what you can interact with it can get out of hand. And sometimes you will look in a closet or a bag and find nothing. But after triggering some event or getting a new objective you will look again and find something you need. THAT IS RIDICULOUS. If i looked in the bag before, why not pick up the scapel why do I have to wander around waiting for Brian the slow walker (his walking really annoyed me) to amble all over then be able to pick up the scapel after I have exhausted every option, I already looked in the bag why would I look again? (Rant over)
Take note that when I said unique story that it is quite pulpy/comicy. So if you want something really cerebral or something that has a deeper meaning this is not the game you are looking for.
So overall i liked the game, mainly from the story, and I would recommend it if you
-Like Point and Click
-Want a unique kinda pulpy story
-Dont mind using a little dated gameplay
I would also say have a walkthrough ready so some of the kinks in the game dont frustrate you too much. Here is the one I used, its pretty good.
