I was pleasently surprised.  When the game first was released, I did not purchase it because of the negative reviews.  I recently bought it during a steam sale, and I must say I spent a good 12 hours straight playing this game (not crashing once, I add).
The game for me runs very well (40-50 frames per second) with all settings on maximum and in 4k resolution.  Mind you I have a GTX 1070 overclocked to 2GHZ and a watercooled core i7 4790k overclocked to 4.7 GHZ, so be wary if your specs are lower.
Now, don't get me wrong, it has it's flaws.  The primary annoyance is tanks and troops sometimes teleporting in, right in front of you; however, it happens so infrequently that when it does happen, it feels more like a sudden death match than anything else, and I have survived all such instances by running for cover.  Overall, the level of visual polish and the storyline and atmosphere overcome the downsides.  Seeing yellowzones slowly transform from somewhat peaceful concentration camps, to camps with rowdy civillians, to civillians in open rebellion, as you complete more hearts and minds objectives, is quite amazing.  It is a feeling of immersion I have yet to feel from an RPG, let alone a shooter.
I feel somewhat ashamed now, having purchased this game on sale, when I have purchased other games at full price that have left me wanting.  If you are a fan of games like far cry and fallout, this is definitely a game you should try.

2003.... Yeah It feels like a game from 2003.
While I'm going to review this game negatively.  It's NOT an awful game.  It's actually good for the time frame.  However the biggest problem with this game is it's a point and click adventure game from 2003.  By this I mean you have a bit of logical jump, weird puzzles, and of course, everyone's favorite feature.  Pixel hunting.  I'm sorry but with no in game hint system, and being forced to hunt for a small object, the game just isn't fun.
I'll focus on the first chapter of the game.
Now first, let's talk about the main character Brian.  He's... oddly shaped.   But beyond that he isn't that interesting a character.   He works as the player character but he's verbose about everything.  EVERYTHING, and none of it is helpful.
On the other side of the story, there's a heroine (yes a heroine) and it's again a 2003 heroine.   Big breasts, skinny waste, cocktail lounge singer, with a cocktail dress, and a face... well I get that they were trying to make her sexy, but they missed, if Brian is oddly shaped,  Gina (the heroine) is plastic surgery gone bad.
Anyways there's a LONG opening, at least 15-20 minutes maybe longer, and not very interesting. It also  appears unskipable (save after you finish! just in case)   But I won't fault it's length, they're developing a story, I will fault it's presentation which is.... humorous for the wrong reasons.
So anyways, when you final get puzzles you get a total of three rooms to explore, one of them locked away.  There's a good puzzle to open the third room.  That is fine.  Then the problems start.  You need to save Gina, but the game really doesn't make it clear how, however every so often dialog will allude to something.  Making a decoy.  Well to make the decoy seems easy, however... it's not.  You can get the parts of the body with out a lot of struggle, but then you're told you need to cover the head.  "How do you do that" well this is where you either get it or you don't.  There's a bag in the room and if you found it, you're good... well almost.  If you search the bag once, you find an item, you need to search the bag again.  And mind you finding the bag in the first place is reasonably hard.
Then you have to pixel hunt and find a small piece of paper on one of the three rooms.  Good if you found it yourself.
Then you have to pixel hunt a third time and get a book.  Mind you the game doesn't even give you a hint where these objects are, you either find them, or you're stumped.  Thankfully UHS is a thing, and gives good hints.  But the hints I'm getting aren't "how do I solve the puzzle" it's "where is this object."
So after you get the book the worst puzzle comes up.  You need to give a Gina a shower (to wake her up).  you think "Grab a glass fill it with water and spray her."   No.. that's too simple.  You need to use a aerasole can and matches to set off a fire sprinkler.  The problem is the sprinkler is maybe two or three pixels wide.  I moused over it three times before I realized it was what I was actually looking for.
The thing is this isn't a fun game to pixel hunt, and the story could work if the game wasn't a chore to play.  Even the graphics aren't a total mess, though they are odd.  I like the idea, but the age of the game gets in front of it.  With Telltale games and others being able to be played, I can't really recommend a 12 year old game which expects the player to pixel hunt to find every little object.  And Little is the operative word there.   I would avoid this game, and look for better point and click games.  This one isn't really worth your money.

Let me start out by saying that I have a degree focusing on Political Science and have worked in the sector....
The Socioeconomic policies do not reflect what happens in the real world, more what someone idealizes how they should work. The Human Element is not well represented, such as in situations where a positive outcome is seen, but the electorate is unhappy due to outlying political/social/etc beliefs (e.g. the goal is accomplished, but not HOW the populace wanted it accomplished, etc).
The Political system is rather simplified and this makes a Democratic Socialist approach far too easy and ignores key psychological responses that have been observed in the real world when certain situations arise.
After playing for a few hours, using demographic knowledge of game developers, and knowing the political beliefs behind certain policies, I easily beat the game with a Social Democracy....which appears to be the ultimate point of the developers. Comparatively, I attempted a few other forms of government approaches that have been historically stable in the real world, but those forms were not nearly as friendly in the game world.
As this is intended to be a political sim attempting to replicate the real world, I cannot recommend this.
However, if this were a model that honestly stated its intent to show HOW a Democratic Socialist contruct can best be made and why it is best for them, in their view, as compared to other options...Then I would say that it accomplished its intent.

It was pretty easy to see that I was playing a game from a Russian developer not long after starting it up.  Trains? Dark violent monsters? People on the verge of death?  Mysterious authoritarian government?  All the hallmarks of classic Russian games.  The random bits of poor syntax and spelling made that more obvious.  Yet even with all of that, The Final Station created a surprisingly unique experience that took some tried and true mechanics and added some really bleak environments and story to create a game unlike many I've played before.
When I first purchased this game, I assumed that it would revolve more around managing your train passengers.  Even the description makes it seems like that's the core of the game.  However, I found that the majority of the gameplay and challenge was simply surviving the stations you stop at as you move to your various destinations.  You only spend a relatively small amount of time managing your train and its passengers, and the station stops that comprise the rest of the game involve a lot of health and ammo management as well as a good bit of weighing the cost and benefit of fully exploring areas.  While I spent plenty of time exploring every nook and cranny, there were some times I came to a dead end after fighting through a battalion of dark zombie creatures to discover no reward at all.  Even when I did find items it sometimes wasn't even worth what I invested in ammo and med kits to get there.  It was unique to encounter something that went in the face of how games normally reward you for exploration.  While it was frustrating, it was also refreshing to have something different in a game.
The real goal of any stop in a station was simply to find the code to open the “blocker” that, for each station, stops you from moving forward on the tracks.  It's generally one of the last things you find requiring you to explore a large portion of the station at the very least, but sometimes it can be found relatively early.  The rest of the process is for you to find ammo and supplies (medkits and food) to keep your passengers alive.  When you're on the train traveling to the next station, you not only have to feed the hungry and heal those with chronic injuries, you must maintain the locomotive and train cars' systems to keep them from harming the passengers.  Whatever passengers survive each leg of the journey reward you with money and items.  The money can be used to purchase small upgrades for the protagonist you control and supplies for your the rest of your journey.  The whole process seems to feel a bit Sisyphean, but I believe that's the emotional impact the game is trying to portray.
The dark design of the various areas in The Final Station is put together in a way that thoroughly conveys how dire the environment is and how quickly things went south.  With a 2D art style it can be hard to convince the player of exactly what is going on in a 3D space, but the use of beautiful backgrounds and detailed foregrounds make it easy for you to understand what sort of situation you're getting into.  Sometimes in opening doors to new rooms I'd be floored by the amount of story that was told through each new piece of the design.  Some rooms may be fully intact but only feature a note or opened laptop with a conversation explaining what had seemingly just happened.  Others would be filled with carnage of various types, whether of humans or these 'zombies,' and it may be spread to other rooms as you go further.  This often told the story much better than the actual text and conversation that you'd normally expect to tell it.  The story, in general, leads all the way to one of the more confusing endings I've ever seen in a game.  I usually pride myself in being able to decipher confusing stories, but I immediately had to find some resources to lend me some more clarity.  I'm not the only one either.  The first Google result for the game is “The Final Station ending” and by far the longest non-sticky thread in the Steam discussion forum is about the ending of the game – at around 15 pages now.
To me, it seems like it's both a problem with the writing itself and the translation lacking in some areas.   I do believe that it is the job of the developers to make an ending something that can at least be understood within the context of the game, and that doesn't seem to be what was accomplished here.  It's not a good design choice when so much of the dialogue you see is in the train cars among the passengers while you're desperately fighting to make sure they stay alive and the train keeps working.  I can't even be sure of what all I missed because it's impossible to monitor all of these statuses, watch their dialogue, and keep an eye on the amazing backgrounds that, in themselves offer pieces of the story.
While The Final Station didn't exactly meet my expectations given what I saw about it beforehand, it didn't disappoint at all.  It felt like it was just the right length for what it offered and I've always enjoyed games that require good resource management to be successful.  Without a doubt I recommend this game and hope that more people decide to take a chance on it.  It may be a little short for $15, but it has been on sale for as little as $5, so it's more than worth it at that price.  I plan on picking up the DLC whenever I get the chance – both because I want more of this gameplay and I'd really love to see if it clears up the story a bit more.

This game was worth the sale price. And it would have been worth the full price too in my opinon.
The atmosphere (stormy night, great sounds) and the general set up (mysterious mansion with weird history to explore) sort of made me (used to the RPGs set up) sort of mentally gear up for looking for jumpscares and hidden panels. No jumpscares (not for me) but definite yes for the hidden panels.
But once i managed to shake the initial anxiety and meta of trying to parse what the game was trying to do, i was able to get into the story. And what a lovely, sad (and yet hopeful? it's a story about life, What else can be that varied?) story it was. I love how it was unfurled through the objects and the audio journal entries from Sam. It made me feel for them, not just Sam but also for the struggles that the parents were going through. Did not stop me from being quite angry at them when i reached the journal entry in the Kitchen though. The plates may have been thrown).
If you come into this game expecting a full blown RPG experience, you will most definitely be disappointed. This game, if anything, is an interactive story. You must put yourself in Katie's shoes and look for everything, look for the things that will lead you to Sam, who will then lead you through the house and through her story. Only then can you really appreciate what they have created here.

A lot of videogames are a result of people wanting empowerment, they want to feel like they can take down armies alone, armored, and prepared for anything, that there is no point where they aren't invincible and vulnerable in any way.
The horror genre is a result of people wanting to subvert that idea that videogames are about empowerment, that being weak and powerless is just as fun as being one man army of chaos and destruction.
One day, a hack and slash and a horror game ♥♥♥♥ed in a dark alley, and I'm not talking about that smooth stuff, I'm talking about the kind of angry sex that was used to settle frustrations with each other and just get it over with, the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ child born out of that, was Dark Souls, who was heard from the trash can, got adopted by a few damn good parents and became a millionaire.
You, sir, are a mage/knight person in armor/robes, if you don't know Dark Souls, your first instinct will be to hop directly into the first enemy's blade with no care for how fragile you are, it's a videogame, it's not going to be that hard...right?
Hah, you'll die.
Over and over, you are vulnerable, weak, pathetic, compared to your opponents, you can die in very few hits, armored or robed, equipped with big weapon in hand or magic, you'll die, but mistakes can be learned from, things WILL get hard, but don't let your will falter.
Learn how to dodge your enemies's attacks, counter-attack, push forward at all costs, and you will succeed.
That, is Dark Souls.

Even though I am a big fan of old-school adventure games (such as Indiana Jones: Fate of Atlantis) and even though that this game has a similar approach to it , it is simply a badly executed example of the genre.
The story is ok. A little cliché but what the hell, it is bound to be like that anyway. A well executed cliché is a great taste in video games and movies alike, so there is nothing wrong with it. The problem is that they just couldn't execute it well in this game.
The puzzles are ok. They are not too hard or too easy. You can just think of possible solutions to a situation yourself. However the game is too rigid with its expcetations. You cannot be creative which is something you would expect from a video game at this age.
Having said that, some puzzles are simply ridicoulous. Especially the "SPOILER STARTS HERE" - locomotive steam puzzles. A jail key and sherrif's badge in a locomotive engine? Really? Very logical - "SPOILER ENDS HERE".
The voice acting... Oh god. Don't get me started with that.
And the musics, too. I just couldn't stand it.
Finally... The game is very slow. I don't mean FPS or any other technical aspect. It is annoyingly slow, especially the cut scenes where the main character goes on with his narration. You can see how slow the "chapter name" comes on to the screen and you just have to wait for it to finish, even after the guy stops talking. Why?
And why torture us even more with that final cut scene with the bridge and that terrible music and the closing credits? Why can't we skip all that with a click? For that terrible extra scene at the end, which means nothing at all and causes us to wait even longer for it to vanish in an eternally slow speed?
All in all, I am glad that people are still trying to make games of this genre. However, I would give a rating of 4 out of 10 to this game in general. It simply sucks as a production. I felt more torture than fun when playing it. So yeah, 4 / 10

I great improvement over the first game in so many ways, this game instilled a sense of adventure I haven't felt in many, many years.
I'll keep it brief and instead try to sway over people who played the first game, since there is plenty of gameplay videos and reviews of the game itself.
If you enjoyed the first game, or played the first game and felt it could have been better, I highly reccomend giving this one a shot, it's worth several playthroughs.
+Game is almost 4x as large as Grimrock 1 just by size alone
+Game is no longer linear, and is spread out both vertically and horizontally
+Exploration is amazing, varied landscapes and dungeons replace the single sets of dungeon tiles from before.
+Combat has been majorly overhauled, every enemy is now unique in their actions and abilities and combat as a whole is much more varied and difficult
+New classes and the ability system has been made global, anyone can put points into any skill, which leads to much more creative builds and more viable Solo runs.
+Story and Lore are based heavily on exploration, there's many, many more secrets to find and much more content to explore
+Puzzles are much less front-heavy, are more spread out and varied, and are much less headache-inducing because of the game non-linearity.
+Excellent replayability, whether it's trying new builds with the global skill system, searching for all the new secrets, experimenting with new classes, or trying different routes through the island.

I started playing Pendulo games back when The Next BIG Thing came out, and I felt like revisiting their arsenal. I read through the majority of reviews before playing this game and was quite worried at what to expect. I will start out by saying that yes, I do believe it deserves a thumbs up.
[WARNING: Save regularly because the game can crash occasionally]
The immediate follow-up to that statement is that it's not a perfect game. This game has a lot of things to talk badly about, and I find the majority of mine come down to having puzzles that require nonsensical logic to complete. The answer to this problem is to have a walkthrough handy. I don't support using walkthroughs in most games, but this one actually requires one. The rule of thumb should be, give yourself 10-30 minutes of being stuck/lost before you look up the next step. Most of the time, one step will be enough to get the ball rolling, and you won't need another. A couple of the sections of the game shouldn't require looking anything up, but I'd say that 50% of them do (3 out of 6 Areas).
The story is basic, and relatively easy to see where it's going to go, and I felt a lot of nods to Full Throttle in there as well. The voice acting can feel distracting more often than not, but some of the characters redeem this issue. Oscar stands out as a lovable oaf that reminds us all of Lenny from Of Mice and Men. Another thing that might distract people in a time where female characters are becoming more complex and fleshed out, is Gina, who plays the generic damsel in distress. Beyond that fact, she also tends to be clothed in practically nothing throughout the entire game. Her male game equivalent is seen outside of a barn in one of the areas, baking shirtless in the sun, chucking beer cans in a metal tin, but I digress.
This game is a decent ride, and on sale, it's a solid playthrough. Not to mention the fact that it's the first of multiple installments. You'll walk away remembering side characters like Sushi, Lula, Rutgers, Oscar, and possibly Saturn. The art style and story are certainly enough to make the game warrant a thumbs up in my book.

Although the game certainly has solid combat and storytelling level of detail put into the world is what makes it extraordinary.  It is amazing that the developers put so many secrets into the game even though they were most certainly sure that no one player would ever uncover them all on their own.

So, I'm not sure what technical issues this game had at launch to get it downvoted this much, but I'll give my perspective the game as it stands now.
In my opinion, the gameplay doesn't spend enough time really properly building up characters to make me care enough about the story. I'm into the whole "red dawn" like setting of the game itself, but I really wanted more gameplay revolving around the story than I did an open world game.
Overall, I didn't feel like anything about the singleplayer experience was anything but basic in execution. It just felt like a very generic, semi-open world shooter.
This is where the game really shines for me, at least right now. The map selection isn't huge (I think around 8-10 maps or so), but there are a few elements that make this really fun to play for me:
1. It has a progression / customization system, to make you always interested in opening reward crates with the cash you earn from missions, and make your soldier that much better.
2. The enemies sometimes can swarm at you a bit, and sitting in one spot to fight them all isn't always practical vs just being mobile. So you get more of a feeling of urgency to make tactical decisions vs the singleplayer experience -- at least, sometimes.
3. You can play with friends, which, generally makes things more interesting when you're playing with intelligent partners. While there aren't a ton of people playing, the people that do play you can often keep in contact with and get games going regularly.
4. There is some degree of variation between mission runs. It's not a whole lot, but sometimes enemies will approach different directions in the same map, but on different runs. Sometimes there may be slightly different enemies (I've seen that too.) While I wish there was more of this, since this is somewhat minimal at the moment, it does help contribute to keeping things interesting.

Banished is the vision of a single person. The developer has single-handedly created the world, where your handful of exiled people must thrust their roots into virgin soil and survive. At first look, it may be easy to confuse the game with some cheery mix of the Anno series and SimCity, with a few other influences thrown in, but this is the first of many mistakes you'll make when it comes to Banished. The singular vision means that this is a truly unique game. There are no unlocks, no tech trees, no upgrades or hidden extras. In this world, your people have access to everything, all the time. But you have to make sure they can survive their first winter, most often by scouring the forest for roots and berries, before you start sending them off to build trading posts and mine coal. It's a delicate balancing act and one that, despite the outward appearance of a limited palette of buildings and actions, offers surprising depth, although in the early stages this depth often is focuses on a narrow path to achieve success. Beginning farming too early drains resources and one bad harvest can hollow out your population through starvation in a single year. Blacksmiths provide the tools which can almost triple the working speed of your townsfolk, but you have to figure out the best way to get the iron he needs: a mine is a costly and draining venture, but deposits on the surface can dwindle quickly and if your people have to go too far to collect them, they may not make the return journey without food or adequate clothing.
You can fail in a dozen different ways in this game, but with every map being different and offering its own challenges, plus the ability to help or hinder your efforts with a variety of terrain and weather types, and different starting conditions, it doesn't feel like just doing the same thing over and over when you once more welcome your cluster of exiles to their new home. It can get a little repetitive in later stages for areas such as building housing and such, but you then have the world of agriculture to keep you busy, which is a whole new area of expertise in and of itself.
In terms of game flaws, my personal feeling is that the information management system is a little lacking. By building a town hall you can track all kinds of data, but this is very raw data and there's no way to extrapolate it to predict how your current growth will affect certain resources (which is a huge part of the game's dynamic). Most often, it's not until your people are running around without any tools, for example, that you realise your lone blacksmith can't keep up with their demands any more. The other area of the game that I feel could do with some work is the customisation of certain areas. Upgrading or adding onto buildings is almost non-existent, except for the upgrade from wooden to stone housing (although the word to the wise is to avoid wooden houses as much as possible anyway). So every forester looks and acts the same way. As does every other profession. This adds a welcome element of stability and familiarity to a game with such a steep learning curve, but a little later on you can't help feeling that if you could just tweak this or that particular workplace in a certain way, it would provide significantly better results than just building another.
Minor flaws aside, Banished is a niche game that won't appeal to many for its steep learning curve and intense focus on survival that has nothing to do with a zombie apolocalypse or alien invasion, but more to do with getting the harvest in before winter and making sure there's enough firewood to last out that same winter. But for many this game resonates in a way that makes it hard to put down, providing a huge sense of achievement for relatively simple acts and instilling a sense of calm when you've got everything working in the right direction and are just able to sit back for a few minutes and watch your population no longer just survivng... but thriving.

The design choices in this game are baffling, and lead to it being genuinely unfun to play.
Every opponent no matter how weak no sells like ♥♥♥♥ing crazy and will happily kick out of multiple finishers with no problem. This leads to the same problem you'd get if this happened in real wrestling: finishers feel weak. And while you can change the difficulty from the main menu as far as I can tell it only changes it for optional modes, so you're stuck with enemies who will endlessly no sell everything you do refusing to go down drawing out matches longer than they need to be even for minor matches.
Add to that how the new pin and submission minigames absolutely break the game going the other way, relying totally on your reflexes leaving you vulnerable to suddenly lose a match you've been winning the whole way thanks to a cheap finisher and bad timing. Unless someone mods in a button mashing mod for these systems I honestly don't know how long I'll continue to play the game.
And you'd think that since this game has such a focus on reflexes for something as vital as kicking out of pins and surviving submissions that surely the rest of the game must have the same reflex focus? NOPE. It's a SLUGGISH simulation, which at times makes absolutely no sense and feels like it's taking control away from your character. The simulation style makes the battles look good, but it's absolutely at the cost of control and fluidity. Matches turn in to momentum driven slug out matches where the only way a character can get out of being endlessly chained is to counter, boiling battles down to whoever ends up draining their counters last and therefore ended up on top for a long series of grapples and strikes (or whoever has the best abilities and stats relating to counters).
The game is both super easy (in the whole: slow simulation, all you need to do is counter at the right time, thing) and frustratingly hard (in the whole: reflex based kick out and submission system) making it an absolute chore to play. You can't feel like a bad♥♥♥♥♥for beating a challenge becuase the wrestling is actually as easy as it gets, and you can't just enjoy playing the simulation because you're likely to get jobbed out unless your reflexes are beyond insane.
Shame too because there are some nice features, and a nice big roster, solid presentaiton, as well as community creations and what not... But none of that fixes that the core of the game, the wrestling engine, feels absolutely horrible. The most fun I have "playing" this game is when I'm watching the AI go at it.
I'm posting this hoping that someone sees this and they end up fixing things for 2k17, but as it stands I absolutely cannot recommend WWE 2k16. Save your money and hope it's better next year.
Edit: And it just crashed on me at the end of showcase match totally erasing my progress in the match. This is the first crash I've encountered but it's safe to say as of the 5th of July that they STILL haven't fixed the crashing issues. Honestly add in crashing and now I think this game is a full on peice of♥♥♥♥♥♥and won't be buying 2k17 unless I hear amazing things.

Game is side-scrolling shooter set during a zombie apocalypse. Hordes of undead waiting to pounce in darkened, abandoned areas that you explore, and a distinct lack of weapons and ammo to make everything a little challenging. You coast around the remains of civilization, exploring infested locales in search of supplies and a means to progress down the tracks, all while zombies nip at your heels.
The zombies you fight aren't pushovers; it only takes them three quick hits to put you down, and they love to attack in pairs. You can easily tackle a slow, mid-sized zombie with melee attacks, but smaller, faster monsters require bullets to the head.
There's always a passcode to find in order to reach a new area, which yields an abandoned town to explore and a safe zone where you can catch your breath. These areas give you an opportunity to upgrade your arsenal and chat with other survivors. In between missions, you're forced to take your train between towns, managing any survivors you may have saved during your journey so far. The train only has a few cars, and if you do manage to bring a few survivors on board, you’re tasked with feeding and healing them. But to do so, you only need to pick up a meal from a nearby dispenser and give it to the desired survivor. After leaving MtG for the convenience and accessibility of online CCG's, I've tried about a dozen different ones. Since most have clunky interfaces, slow gameplay, or oppressive new player experiences, I've only ever stuck with Hearthstone, but that has never been fully satisfying, since the developers have done a poor job of creating a healthy and balanced strategy-oriented meta. Eternal (designed by a bunch of big MtG names and game developers) is the card game I've been looking for for a long time. They've skillfully reduced the least relevant MtG mechanics to smooth out the computer-based player experience, developed an easy-on-the-eyes aesthetic, and taken advantage of the online platform with some interesting and well-designed mechanics that can't be pulled off with paper cards.
I've played since closed beta, and I've seen the devs make several active changes to card balance - both nerfs and buffs - which have always resulted in a more interesting and diverse meta. I also hear that they're working on character voice overs and all the fluff that will really enrich the player experience, which gives me even more hope for the future success of this game.

Finished in around 3 hours, with almost an hour spent on the DLC and just AFK while the game was running.
Overall I enjoyed the game, but was a bit disappointed about the fact that it wasn't a roguelike game according to my expectations since the main game turned out to be a very linear experience with only a few short hallways to explore during your visits to the different levels. This didn't stop me from playing until the end, though, as the levels were beautifully handcrafted and most of the areas felt like they had purpose and story behind them.
The story builds up nicely, but in the end leaves everything quite open for interpretation. This left me feeling bummed out, as I don't really enjoy having to sift through forums and discussions to find out what actually happened.
The gameplay is rather simple and to my liking a bit too easy. The monsters aren't really a threat and can be killed in cheesy ways where they can't really do anything to you. Caring for passengers and the train is a bit of a chore (but manageable) and make it a bit hard to follow the story through their dialog and the changing background scenery while on the train.
Mostly you will die to making a stupid move (accidentally throwing a fuel canister and killing yourself, anyone?). Getting killed isn't really that bad, though, since the checkpoint system is very lenient, usually restarting you before the door of the room you got killed in. This is a good and a bad thing, since it makes getting through the levels a breeze, while making the challenge and fear of death almost nonexistent.
The dialog is interesting and builds up the world nicely, but there is an overuse of ellipses (...) throughout. That's all the main character ever says: "...".
The game lacks replay value, but is worth the 3-4 hours you spend playing through it once. I got it through Humble Bundle, so the price wasn't bad. I wouldn't pay 15€ for it, though.
Overall if you enjoy a story driven linear experience with beautiful pixel art and an intriguing world, get it. Preferably during a sale.

Well, this is really a hard review.
Whether you like the game or not really depends on your willingness for retrying a situation.
Let me tell you this: this game  is hard. You will die pretty often - even more in later places.
Don't get me wrong, the atmosphere is great and I like the art style, the little details like the dialogues with the NPCs etc.
But what really brings me down is the try-and-error precedure each "room".
So in the end you walk through abandoned cities just to die all the time when opening a new house etc.
There - THEM are waiting for you so you have limited options for solving the problem. Shoot them, beat them or escape. The problem is, this is a game with very limited ressources. Your health is enough to survive 4-5 hits which is not much (especially since there are many times more than one enemy per room). Ammo as well as medi packs are pretty limited. Whats making it even harder is that you may decide whether you give the food and medipacks to your passengers or use it on your own.
This might actually give some interesting moments. You might relate the situations a bit to "Gods will be watching us". But what makes it frustrating is the die-all-the-time moments.
So if games like "Limbo" are great for you, you might actually enjoy it. The art style is somehow similar. As are the "die first, than retry until you survive" moments.
For others that like sneaking and puzzeling (or even alternative solutions a la Deus Ex etc.) this game unfortunately will be frustrating pretty soon.

I would recommend this game to just about anybody who is a fan of the first-person shooter genre or has any kind of interest in guns. This well crafted gun simulator is, like they say, easy to learn but hard to master. Learning each weapon and how it is operated by muscle memory is fluid and satisfying; I never tired of loading and charging a weapon.
The minimalistic presentation of the game environment allows the gun to be the focus of the game, as it should be, but each section in the procedurally generated world has its own challenges and secrets. After some practice you will grow well versed in traversing these environments and scanning them for threats and loot, which brings its own satisfaction.
Perhaps the most satisfying of all the game's elements is its actual combat. Enemies come in two types: hovering taser drones and static turrets, both of which can deliver instant and fatal damage to the player. The gameplay here is challenging, but never unfair, and the quick restarts allow you to dive straight back into the game and apply what you've learned from past mistakes. The trial-and-error nature of Receiver's gameplay gives it a visceral and ephemeral feel comparable to that of Hotline Miami, although with a vastly different tone.
Like the rest of the game, Receiver's story is delivered in a minimalistic and really quite interpretive style. You are tasked with exploring the world and collecting all eleven casette tapes, which contain a wealth of esoteric knowledge, accessible only to the specially mentally conditioned, known of course as 'receivers'. Despite their monotone delivery, I never really became bored with the tapes even after repeated listens. By the time you have heard all eleven, you will have memorised a great deal of background story information, which gives the feeling that you
a receiver. The casettes mention important story threads such as 'the Threat', 'the Mindkill' and multiple realities with such passing apathy that one is forced to imagine what exactly they entail, making the story that much more interesting. Without so much being left to the imagination, the game's story could not have had nearly the same effect.
All told, Receiver is a simple but beautiful game. Its developers set out to create in seven days an engaging and accurate gun simulator with minimalist storytelling and they have succeeded by all measures. Receiver is a cheap buy and well worth a look from a fan of the shooting genre.

This game is equal parts frustrating and ridiculously fun.
Make no mistake, this is a puzzle game first.  Yes, there is fighting and an RPG element to it, but the puzzles are how you get through the game.  Some of the puzzles are as easy as stepping on a pressure plate, others are as complex as hitting levers in a specific order even though the trap doors open and close below you as you are moving.
So believe me when I tell you that you will have to step away occasionally out of sheer frustration.  The developers do indeed give you clues as to how to complete most of the puzzles, but they are vague and definitely subject to interpretation.  That said, when you figure out a particularly difficult puzzle, it will be one of the more rewarding experiences in your gaming life.
Another aspect of this is the secrets in the game.  Some of them are just hidden buttons in walls that open up secret passages to treasure.  Others are teleport patterns that lead to artifacts.  If you are like me, you love discovery, so you will spend WAY more time than is necessary checking the walls for buttons and trying different patterns on pressure plates just in case.
In short, this game is awesome!

I loved the first Legend of Grimrock, it successfully updated the old Dungeon Master first-person dungeon crawler. It was one of my favourite games of 2012. If it had flaws, it was the lack of variety in combat and environment.
Legend of Grimrock 2 fixes all those flaws, and is immediately a much better game for it. The only thing it loses is its gradual "descent" into the depths of the dungeon. Here the world is laid out across a much wider area, although there is both depth and height to most dungeons now. The outdoor areas are the most noticeable change when you first start, and they add much needed life to the game. Some of the sights you'll encounter are impressive, not something I was expecting from a grid-based crawler, but the game can be often beautiful. Indoors the engine now deals with height within the same dungeon level, so ladders lead up and down onto platforms, and coupled with quite a few different mechanics leads to a lot more variety in the kind of puzzles that are possible. I didn't find the puzzles to be quite as challenging as Grimrock 1, some of which relied heavily on very tight timing, and in the sequel clues tend to be spread across the map rather than being just around the next corner. A lot of hints are very opaque at first, but gradual dawning realisation will occur much later in the game as you start to piece it together. Personally I really enjoyed this, and being able to make notes on the map is pretty much essential to keep track of them.
Combat is a vast improvement as well. There's much less reliance on dancing around enemies to stay out of harm's way, facing-off is far more feasible this time (on normal difficulty at least!) due to better character balance, progression, and smarter use of character traits. Of course, there are always exceptions, and the developers are clearly having fun keeping the player on their toes with new enemy types. This is not a turn-based game, but it should be manageable.
It took me a little over 40 hours to beat the game, although I've been quite thorough. I know others who did it in half that time. Even after beating the game, there's one major secret that I've yet to conquer, a way of ending the story more satisfactorily. I'm sure it will keep me busy a while longer. This is easily a contender for my favourite game of 2014.

is the first game in Runaway series made by Pendulo Studios, back in 2001. It has its ups and downs, coming into a résumé of being cheesy and needlessly complicated with a crude, childish charm on the side. It is only interesting enough for an old school adventure gamer, who wouldn't mind empty character stereotypes.
Let's see... There is an interesting variety of graphic and art display used in this first game; including old school hand drawn cartoons, slightly computer animated skylines, 2D characters wrapped with vibrant colors in gameplay - similar to original
series - and creepy plastic 3D models used in between cut scenes. It feels that someone failed to pick a homogenous art style for this game. 2D models + hand drawn cartoons is a great combination which we are already used to from older adventure titles, but 3D models? Well... I personally think the 2D + 3D artwork combination is a tricky one, and it wasn't well produced here. Some of the character designs were okay, but they mostly ended up being exaggerations of stereotypes. Brute and ugly rather than being funny, and character movement animations - especially ones from Chapter 2 and Chapter 3 - were downright spastic.
I don't know a lot about you, but a strong and unique protagonist with well-arranged character is really important in adventure games in my opinion. For the acquired immersion, you have to like the main character, or at least find him/her interesting. Brian Basco was neither likable nor interesting. For a supposed boy genius, he spoke and acted as a real dimwit who ends up becoming a Ken doll stereotype eventually. Gina - the supporting female character - isn't anything interesting or genuine either. She is there to live up to the labeled existence of being an exaggeratedly sexy bimbo.
The scenario is meaninglessly complicated and it seems that our characters have no actual control over any occurrence. On a series of quite random and unfortunate - or amazingly fortunate events - they manage to get by, but there is no exact brilliance to their progress. They always go through any kind of progress through the help of absurdly friendly random individuals with eccentric backgrounds that they meet around. The story itself is so fragmented and scattered, it doesn't really make any sense until the last chapter of the game. During the last chapter, every random plot hook are properly arranged and tidied up by yet another collection of random people - not our protagonist. In all events and occurrences, Brian Basco may be one of the most naive and ridiculously shallow characters in adventures games that I've played so far.
If we are to talk about gameplay, I have to confess that it has a ridiculously slow progressing game play for a ridiculously fast progressing storyline. There is odd repetitions in actions and with the speed Brian moves around, you'd better spare a whole day. It is a killer pixel hunt to collect items, or even notice that certain items are actually collectible. Some item combinations are just fine, the others... well, without a walkthrough I wish utmost patience for you. NPC interactions and dialogues are pretty much straight forward, but even though you'd be pretty confident about what you should do, the game forces you to either confirm that through making Brian realize the needed action, or at least try what you absolutely cannot do first as an elimination process. It ends up being tiresome after a point.
All in all,
is nothing miraculous. There is a great selection of adventure games you'd enjoy without a doubt. This is not really one of them if you are not a fan of cheesy character stereotypes and crude elementary level humor. I've been hearing a lot of good things about the other games in the series - especially
- so I'll finish the series to get there anyhow. Apparently, story arcs follow each other with references so it is not possible to thoroughly enjoy the last game without playing the prior ones. Take this one if you are curious enough, or wait for my reviews in other titles in the series!

Political sims are  hard to do well. The ones that try often go for a grand scale (eg Supreme Ruler) and tend to fall flat. The only quite successful one which comes to mind is Shadow President. Democracy 2 is more confined than most, limiting the outside world and turning everything into sliders and charts. It's a nice try, but aspects of it really don't come off well at all.
Superficially, it seems quite good. The interface is fairly well designed, presenting most of your key info on a single screen - although the inability to change the resolution (leaving me, on a widescreen monitor, with either bits of the interface cut off or a window which can't be enlarged at all) is frustrating. There are a wide variety of potential policies, each with adjustable levels.
Unfortunately, the gameplay doesn't hold up. It is far to easy to "game" the mechanics - just pour money into tech and universities and suddenly you are making massive income through technological advantage, which lets you build up everything else to win votes. The difficulty comes from random, arbitrary and unfair events. Random factors can completely decimate your popularity - slowly build up to an election winning lead over the course of years, then suddenly lose half your voters in one turn because the global economy drops.
It's also littered with grammatical errors, rather unfortunate for a game targeted at a more intellectual audience.
I wanted to like it, but found it a frustrating and unsatisfying experience.

FFX is a game very close to my heart... Although my playtime right now do not tell it I have most likely clocked in well over 300 hours of this game on the old PS2.
I remember the first time I boot up FFX which was after buying a friends old PS2 with couple of different games. Among them was FFX. I had never really heard of the Final Fantasy franchise from before, and I was about 13-14 when I got this game. I had just started to learn the true value of a good story. But I booted this up, and soon found myself being stuck forever in this game. It was something that ended up for me returning to now and then even after the story was done. And the story is so enticing that even though I am now playing this a fourth time over... I am still not tired of it. It is a great game.
Now you get a second game with it called FFX-2, the first Final Fantasy game that became a 2, which continues the story after a movie clip you get with this game takes place, that gives extra closure to the Final Fantasy X story, and thus the that story to. I have only clocked three hours or so of it, but it is quite nice to though from what I have seen.
Pros of FFX/FFX-2
-    A great story with many interesting characters, many who spans over the two games.
-    A good amount of game for this low of a price. With the end game stuff that I know off in FFX (Penence and the Dark Aeons) you can easily sink two - three hundred hours to attempt in beating them. And FFX-2 seems just as good with this, as you can catch and fins stories of all different enemies you fight... which is more than a bakers dozens of
-    Interesting mechanics that shift between the games. Enjoy really only turn-based extrem stragtegy builds and fights? Final Fantasy X got you covered. Enjoy the action battle system present in the eariler games, well X-2 got you covered.
-    Good remaster from the original with updated graphics and addition of cheats and speed ups of the games.
-    Overall one of the best musical scores I've ever heard. Zanarkand, Otherworld among others are still some of my favorite soundtracks to this date for me. And none fall to far behind for me.
-    At least for FFX there is an allowance for some insane builds as all characters can get every single node on the Sphere Grid for their use. With the addition of the "Customaization Spheres" as I call them turning empty nodes to whatever you need extra off.
-    Customize gear with many different buffs and aids.
-    Nice feeling menus that are easy to understand.
Cons:
-    Bit on the slow side sometimes, story in of itself takes easily sometimes up to 15-20 hours on its own if you ignore everything else...
-     I myself did not enjoy Final Fantasy X-2 to much, but this is personal thing mostly as it is bit different from Final Fantasy X and can imagine myself after growing into it a bit more finding it more capable as you get more immediate responses from your and enemies actions.
-     ... *Tidus awkward laugh*
TL:DR
This is worth to buy if you like any Final Fantasy or turn based RPG. HECK YOU OWE yourself to play it. And as I said with easily 200-300 hours of gameplay on only ONE of the two titles (!!!) this is some of the best spent money really. If you truly enjoy creating plans, doing character builds and create gods from scratch so you can fight the end game stuff. ♥♥♥♥ing go. FINAL STATION
PUBLISHER - tinyBuild
DEVELOPER - Oleg Sergeev, Andrey Rumak, Do My Best
GENRE – Indie, action, adventure
THE BASICS:
In a world in danger of being overrun by walking shadows, you are an engineer who has been forced into the role of troubleshooter. You have the only remaining operational train in the devastated land, so you get to deal with whatever comes up.
THE FLOW AND THE STORY:
Keep your train moving by regulating the power in various components, and keep your passengers fed and healthy for as long as you can, in hopes of getting them to their destinations alive. Succeed, and be rewarded. In between, explore the corrupted stations and towns that are being taken over by the shadows, collecting ammo, money, medicine, and food for your precious human cargo. Do you use the meds you find to keep yourself alive a little longer, or do you save it for that passenger with the bloody cough?  Fail, and you die...well, you just get kicked back to the last checkpoint, anyway. Death is cheap in this game, at least for you. For your passengers – not so much. The game autosaves frequently, so screwing up on the train may mean starting over again.
In each corrupted area, you explore in order to gather more supplies and ammo (while hoping you find more than you use), while searching for survivors willing to pay for a train ride so that they can get the hell outta Dodge. You will need to seek out a Blocker code in each area – near the end, of course – which allows your train to move on to the next station. Your ultimate goal is to get your train all the way to the ultimate end of the line intact.
CONTROLS:
Keyboard & mouse or native XBONE controller support. Fairly standard: Aim with right stick/mouse, fire, reload, punch/power punch, action (open door, pickup/throw), cycle weapons
GRAPHICS:
8-bit style that serves its purpose well. Plenty of detail in the towns to distract your eye (not always so much in they skyboxes).
SOUND:
Ambient sounds and music help to convey the feelings the designers want you to feel. Train sounds when riding the rails feel beefy and “big.”
OVERALL:
A solid, if short game that could greatly benefit from a clear explanation of how the train works. Great atmosphere, creepy vibe to what few enemies there are. Decent combat, even if it does feel a little bit laggy at times. Think “Out of This World” or ”Flashback” for a good idea of the punch speed. Guns are satisfying to wield and fire, even if they suffer the same delays. You won't be fanning the trigger in this one; you need to make every shot count.
SYSTEM REQUIREMENTS:
Minimal/Integrated graphics & 1 GB RAM. Windows XP or higher/Mac OS. In their words, a toaster can run this.
REVIEW BY: Eric_Kei
STORY: 85
GAMEPLAY: 85
GRAPHICS: 90
SOUND: 85
FUN FACTOR: 75
ATMOSPHERE: 90
Pros:
Great atmosphere
Some enemy groups seem insurmountable, at least, until you find a nice heavy TV to drop on them. That, or until you use some of your hard-to-find ammo to snipe them from the top few rungs of a ladder
Lots of world detail, including letters characters have written to one another, notes that died with their recipients (or on the way to them), and so on
Has a brief “preview” section which serves as a basic tutorial for the combat areas
Cons:
Fiddling with the train's components, messaging other engineers to get news along the rails, and crafting ammo and supplies takes you too far away from the passengers. They have plenty to talk about, but you never get to see 90% of it
Some issues with enemy encounter balance. While some are beatable with clever thinking, some just require going hit-and-run and hoping that they run out of HP before you do
Game doesn't explain the train controls at all, nor why they are important (hint: they are)
Could use a Help screen with something more than just the controls on it

I wouldn't say GONE HOME is worth the full price. If you can get it on a discount like 75% or higher, then I say get it. The voice work is fantastic, the house is incredibly well designed as a throwback to the 90s, and the short story is engaging.
Personally, I think this is a good example of "walking simulator" or "interactive storytelling," like Dear Esther. Unlike Dear Esther, though, there is more interactivity. You need to solve a few puzzles in order to progress through the house and the story (such as finding lock combinations, keys, and maps to secret passages). The game rewards these puzzles by furthering the story of a teenage girl. It's a good, short coming of age story, actually, as the girl discovers more about herself.
BUT, it is short. As engaging as the story is, you can beat the game in only a couple of hours. Which is why I don't believe it's worth the full price. But I think it's worth experiencing it at least once.

Homefront The Revolution is the very definition of a hidden gem.  A semi-open-world FPS that tasks you with rising up against a brutal North Korean military occupation in Philadelphia, it offers a surprisingly wide variety of gameplay and an engaging story to boot.  Below are some of my favorite things about the game.
A page ripped right out of Crysis' playbook, Homefront's weapon customization system allows you to modify weapons even in the middle of combat.  You can swap out several different optics, underbarrel attachments, and more.  Homefront even takes this to a whole new level with full-on weapon conversions that drastically change how weapons behave.  Pistols can be converted into makeshift SMGs, for example, and Battle Rifles can be converted into firework-spewing "Freedom Launchers."
Homefront's world is broken up into these two types of zones which offer totally different types of gameplay.  Red zones are essentially war zones and consist of resistance cells facing off against the North Korean military.  Here you must liberate outposts and obliterate KPA forces.  Yellow zones, however, are littered with civilians and heavily policed by the North Koreans.  In these zones you must avoid detection while performing acts of sabotage in order to inspire the people to rise up against their oppressors.
I won't spoil anything, but the story is full of twists and turns and almost all of the characters are memorable and well-voice acted.
Homefront looks gorgeous and performs really well on capable hardware thanks to its post-launch performance updates.  Characters and environments are well-textured and full of detail, and the dynamic day/night cycle and weather make the world feel alive.  It certainly doesn't hurt that the game runs on CryEngine 3.
If you're hunting for an awesome (and in many ways unique) open-world shooter, please don't pass this one up.  Homefront The Revolution might have been dogged by critics at launch, but today it stands as arguably one of the best games of its class.  It looks and plays great and will undoubtedly keep you invested in its story from start to finish.

Simple premise, beautiful execution, and a lot more meat on its bones than you might expect.
Of course, twitch reflex business micro-management by way of countless variations of hotkey sequences is not going to be of interest to everyone. But if you're tempted, I highly recommend this one.
This frantically fast multi-tasking game is challenging by nature, but manages to avoid being punishing with an excellently modulated difficulty curve and a lot of player control in their own difficulty experience; Things too fast for you? Ditch some of the more time-consuming items on your menu, "practice" any that are giving you trouble until your fingers know where the right keys are almost before you do, and don't optimize your "buzz" as much - then you'll be faced with easier tasks coming at you more slowly, for as long as you want until you're ready to step it back up.
It's delightfully easy to pick back up after not playing for a while. Tutorials and practice tools are available to you whenever you need them. You can even practice cooking a food you haven't even bought yet, to help you decide whether you want to commit to the time and effort it will take.
Beyond the basic structure, the game also incorporates a lot of extra material, including catering events, TV appearances, being robbed, betting on your own skills, holding a romantic text message conversation and funding projects on the game's version of kickstarter; and they are all integrated with impressive fluidity into the existing system.
If you want even more than that, there are weekly time challenges in which you can compete with the whole online community, and apparently there's even a mode in which you can play this game with local multiplayer. I haven't tried it myself, and have no idea how it would work, but it's there.
That said, the game isn't completely perfect. There are so many different foods and hotkeys that it can be hard to remember that onions can be O for one food and N for another. Accidentally hitting 4 instead of 5 (for instance) can mean an immediate bad order as you hand off raw chicken to a customer. For some reason tossing out garbage bags always feels unresponsive in the throw unless you slow down for it.
But these are all minor quibbles, and if you do make one of the many easy mistakes, it's not the end of the world. You'll take a minor hit to your reputation for the next day, and don't get the coveted Perfect Day this time around. No biggie. Maybe you'll manage to achieve perfection in the next round.
After all, nobody claimed this was going to be easy, right?

I will preface my thoughts by saying that I have not played the first Homefront game, I am not a huge fan of first-person shooters, and I had no interest in this game prior to finally purchasing it a few months back. I also played the campaign solo and have not touched the DLC yet.
Around a forum I frequent, I like to lurk on the Steam thread, never posting much, just... Listening. One thing that caught my attention was a few posters bringing up this game, and how they had enjoyed it quite a bit. Finally, I decided to bite the bullet and pick up the Freedom Fighter bundle for relatively cheap. I figured I've spent $11 in worse ways before... Hell, probably even that day. Regardless, I picked it up, installed the massive game (god, was the bandwidth worth this as well?...) and booted it up for a few minutes. Cool, I thought, interesting. At that point, into the backlog it disappeared, to forever stay unplayed or picked at here and there...
I don't know what decision I fell upon that made me pick it up again, but I did... And I found it to be... Stiff, but intriguing. The most common comparisons I find are with the more recent Far Cry offerings, and I do agree with that. What turns off most, seem to be a particular interest for me... In this game, you have to "collect" different areas on a map, taking the power back. Welp, I decided, I guess I'm in for the long haul...
After 22ish hours, completing the campaign and a hefty amount of side-missions, I find that never once did I feel the game overstayed its welcome. I truthfully enjoyed this game much more than I would have anticipated, and I hope that others will give it a chance. I know that the game suffered from debilitating bugs at launch, but aside from a few non-game-breaking issues, it was pretty flawless for me. The pallette is pretty drab, but I found enough variety in different districts to keep it interesting. The gunplay felt tight to me, the story was pretty by-the-numbers with a few intriguing points to keep me invested, and I particularly liked the character of Dana, who many seem to think was too poorly written and acted. Sure, she felt more like a character than a person, but she has spunk and one of my favorite lines in the game.
In the end, I think Homefront: The Revolution is an often-overlooked gem that is well worth $10 if you've run the FPS-supply dry and want something that takes pieces from a handful of other franchises. Reading the note from the creative director at the end of the game was nice too, as I didn't realize the game had gone through such a tumultuous journey over four years. I hope the devs got a decent enough response to make it feel as though their hard work didn't go unnoticed.

It takes a family and delves deep into who each of the people are and tells a compelling tale that you discover as you move through the house. Of course, you won't get nearly as much from the game if you don't actively explore and look in all of the nooks and crannies to find out about each character. Fortunately, the writing is well done to the point that every character drove me to ridiculous searching, regardless of their importance in the 'main' plot. Every piece of information you can read just contributes to the sense that the characters are really alive and breathing, just not in sight.

In the past few years, I’ve tried several party-based RPGs which were developed by Indie companies and marketed as “old-school”. Unfortunately, these games were held back by clunky/unintuitive interfaces and skill systems, or did not run smoothly despite decent computer specs. Legend of Grimrock 2, on the other hand, is old-school nostalgia done RIGHT. Easily my most-loved game of 2014 (unless something crazy happens in December), Legend of Grimrock 2 is one of the most immersive, challenging and rewarding games I have played.
Gameplay feels very crisp and intuitive. It’s an amazing feeling, to tentatively stick your head out from behind a dark corner, wondering whether that giant Rat-man dressed as a pirate is going to one-shot your squishy party members with his enormous hand cannon. It’s an amazing feeling, to finally put together a bunch of vague clues scribbled on parchment paper, locating a hidden treasure chest containing epic phat loots – and distributing this loot amongst my fully customized party of 4, each with their own distinct fighting styles and weapon/magic inclinations.
There’s a good balance between combat, puzzle solving and exploration in Legend of Grimrock 2, and for me most of the puzzles were difficult, but that’s what made playing this game feel so rewarding. I often found myself saying “I’ll just explore one more area before I quit!” – and that didn’t work out too well. The developers did a fantastic job with level and sound design -- exploring the Laboratory for the first time actually made me very frightened. It’s a game that totally gets you in the zone and allows your imagination to run wild, and I appreciate that.
My thoughts comparing Legend of Grimrock 1 & 2: The first game was a fun, linear dungeon crawler with a rather repetitive environment. Legend of Grimrock 2 is a much larger epic adventure across many different (but always beautiful) environments, both indoors and outdoors. The combat in both games aren’t the strongest selling point – in fact, it feels rather cheesy to constantly “run in circles” around monsters on hard difficulty (as facing them directly would be too dangerous). That said, both games are very high quality in terms of puzzles, atmosphere and exploration, but if you’re on a gaming budget and can only purchase one game at the moment, you may want to play Legend of Grimrock 1 if you prefer a more linear, focused adventure. There was quite a bit of "wandering-around-lost" downtime for me in Legend of Grimrock 2 compared to Legend of Grimrock 1, but it didn’t bother me that much. However, I can understand that if you have limited time to play, you may be looking for an adventuring experience that feels more cohesive – in that case, buy the first game.
I’m pretty close to completing Legend of Grimrock 2 and I’m a little sad. I’ll stress again what I said at the beginning -- Legend of Grimrock 2 is old-school nostalgia done RIGHT.

The Legend of Grimrock 2 is the sequel to an award-winning hit series, and it just keeps getting better and better.  This series is the new king of dungeon crawlers with hours and hours of content to traverse through.
Similar to its predecessor, the story of LoG 2 is a bit on the lacking side, but is every bit made up for by the gameplay, character design, and intensive replay value.  By controlling a party of up to four, choosing from multiple races and classes, you can pick and choose the level of balance (or imbalance) you can have with your team members.  Between having a Human Battlemage, or a Ratling Alchemist, a Minotar Barbarian, or possibly an Insectoid Farmer (yes, farmer) if you like the trolling side, you can set up your party how you wish.
A single playthrough of this game will easily take beyond 25 hours of gameplay, and that is if you are cruising through not looking for secrets and treasures.  There are puzzles galore, and many are extremely DIFFICULT puzzles that will challenge the most intellectual minds.  Most of these puzzles you will have never seen in any other video game, and some especially new in style to the LoG series.
Beyond the extensive puzzle-solving, quick reflexes and a little bit of finger dexterity is needed in this game to survive, especially if you enjoy playing on all of the hardest difficulty settings the game offers you at the start like I have.  LoG 2 offers three difficulty levels (Easy, Normal, Hard), Ironman mode, which allows saving only at health crystals, and Single-use Health Crystals mode, where you are only able to use the crystals once.  On top of all that, they brought back Old-School Mode back, which takes away your trusty map, leaving you in the dust with nothing but your compass (if you find one) and pencils and graph paper.
The layout of the game is fantastic, as it starts you on the shore of a beach, and the environment takes you into swamps, dens, lairs, catacombs, pyramids, jungles, etc...there is a wide array of refreshing map tiles that will keep you entertained, if not perhaps somewhat confused and lost.  Keep your eyes open, though, and look for levers, hidden buttons and switches, and traps everywhere.
This game can be very taxing on the mind and body, but does wonders for the soul.  If you like dungeon crawlers, this is the BEST in the genre, and is worth the money.
I rate this game a 9.6 out of 10.

It's really just about familiarizing yourself with the relationships and dynamics of the various functions withi the game, and then 1) immediately fixing the emergency problems upon starting a new game, folllowed by 2) micro-managing and tweaking these elements, which doesn't change very much from game to game once you've taken care of #1 and have some general control over the country's economy.

I'm hoping that's what Democracy 3 is.

I first heard about this game when I watched a Rooster Teeth: Rage Quit video about it. I did some more searching, briefly watch a video that Nerd³ made about it, and thought it looked interesting. So despite my rib-crushingly small budget this week, I bought this game. After all, it's only $5.
I launched the game, having a
idea as to what I was doing, meaning I knew there were guns, they were complicated, there were enemies I had to kill, and there were tapes (which tried to get me to question my existence) to be collected. And I found out very quickly that I wasn't far off.
When you start, you're given one of three handguns: A Colt M1911A1, a Glock 17, or a Smith & Wesson Model 10 Revolver. In your average FPS, all of these would be no-brainers; you would simply point, shoot, and keep half an eye on an ammo counter on the bottom right of your screen. In Receiver, on the other hand, all of these weapons work differently. In addition, there is no ammo counter. "Well,♥♥♥♥♥♥" I said to myself. I brought up the help menu (which is paired with a helpful, behind-the-scenes AI that will help you get your gun in to working order!) and figured out the controls for my gun. I got my weapon ready to fire, and set out searching for tapes. Shortly thereafter, I died. "Alrighty then," I mumbled to myself as the game reset. Luckily, I got the same gun next round, this time it was one step away from being ready. Same thing again. Set up gun, go find tapes, die. This will happen a
. The game randomizes the state your weapon is in when you
it.
After playing for a few hours, I went to sleep, and the next day I came back to it. Having become familiar with the controls the previous night, the second playthrough was a breeze. The first time I reloaded my gun from muscle memory made me feel awesome. I still died a lot, though. But at least I can load my gun faster.
Receiver is a good game. Well worth the $5.

-Combat that sticks to its roots pure turn based combat at it's finest. Some tough late game side bosses.
-Beautifully crafted characters and enviroments.
-Truely unforgettable Soundtrack.
-First Final Fantasy game with voice acting! no more reading from text boxes. (Most Minor NPC's still have them though.)
-Custom weapons and Armour
-Aeons or Summons that can truely turn the tide of battle. Each with beautifully rendered cutscenes as they enter battle.
FFX Eternal Calm/Another Story
This is a short video that takes place 2 years after X and bridges the events of both games. Great watch if your intrested to know why the new adventure begins.
FFX-2
-While still being a great sequel to "X" is not as strong story wise. But is great if you want to get some closure on certain events and characters after the previous game.
-Free-roam pretty much from the start.
-Combat Switches to "ATB" which stands for Active Time Battle. This is a step up from the previous game in my opinion as you still get "turns" but they are now not only predetermined by "Luck" and "Agility". You are never safe as freeflowing combat now takes over. You can now be attacked while you are picking moves or even casting them but this also means you can chain attacks together with your party members by timing attacks at the same time.
-Dressspheres! Characters get true classes! (Warrior, Black Mage etc.)
-New Monster System which used to be only avaliable in the international version. Swap out "YRP" for many different monsters and characters. (NPC controlled without mods).
-Leveling system becomes basic normal XP to gain "X" Level to gain "X" stats. one of two minor problems i have with this game.
-More sidequests than X which makes the game more open and racks up the hours.
-Blitzball makes a return but is a major downgrade from the first game in my personal opinion but atleast it is here.
-Monster Arena! So much new content! see how your team stacks up in tournament battles.

I haven't played this game since Summer 2014 but I distinctly remember a period of time about a month long (or at least several weeks), where I was playing this game pretty regularly everyday.
As far as sim games go this one is fun and light and functions moreso around speed and reflexes then one would expect going in. It's rewarding to string together dish after dish and most of the food and other upgrades feel worth (not so much some of the chore upgrades, however). Even little details like going through your email can be enjoyable at times. The way different food combinations on the menu interact can make changing the menu a fun little mini-game (although more often then not the best option is just to build a menu around a number of staple health foods like soups and salads).
I'm pretty sure most people will reach a point where they're quick reloading their saves as the game more or less demands higher and higher levels of persistent perfection to earn the best cash bonuses and a steady stream of unlockables once you get to the 3 star restaurant and above.
Around the 4 or 5 star restaurant unlock I reached a point where perfection felt impossible as I juggled increasingly difficult (but pricy) dish upgrades with the looming pressure of the impending lunch/dinner rush crushing down upon me.
Unless you're a huge fan of the gameplay, progression and eventually punishing challenge of time management and reflexes, you may not get more than a few months of play out of it. Still a 4/5.

The first Runaway game is an extremely beautiful point ‘n’ click adventure with bad voice actors, and needlessly overcomplicated plot and puzzles, completed with a last act that redeems most of the game in one swoop. Be prepared to use a walkthrough from the start though.
Pendulo, a Spanish studio tried to revive the dying point ‘n’ click genre at the start of the century by releasing their first decent hit, Runaway: A Road Adventure. The game stood out with its spectacular, lushly coloured, hand-drawn backgrounds and cell-shaded 3D characters. (The latter technology was a big rage at the time.)
And this is also where most of the budget went, because the lavish exterior hides a rather lacking adventure game.
The most apparent issue is the audio. The main theme is catchy (albeit dated), and the soundtrack is good, but the voice acting ranges from somewhat tolerable to downright horrible.
The less-apparent problem is the writing. Initially it seems great: a rather everyday protagonist accidentally gets dragged into a spy thriller by accompanying a beautiful woman. Then it just flips out and throws in locations and characters at random without any coherence. Heck, it even resorts to using aliens and magic.
Thankfully this mess is sorted out by the end, resulting in a good mafia story, but this is a very small compensation for all the stupidity you have to endure before it.

The puzzles are worse. Remember the infamous passport sequence in Gabriel Knight 3? Imagine that as the starting difficulty, getting more convoluted and illogical at every new step you take. And the solutions themselves are on rails: you cannot do what you are supposed to do unless you find out all requirements for even the most basic actions.
At its time, Runaway was a welcomed comeback of the adventure genre, but today it is just a pretty, but dumb piece of point ‘n’ click history.

This game works well in making you really feel like you are the under dog, there really is almost a struggle to work your way up and get better gear just to put the flow of funk back into the right direction. However there is a real sense of reward upon getting through that struggle, not only storywise but with all the goodies you get, but more on that later.
The main story could take you a good 8 hours, about 12 if you manage to clear all the areas and "strikepoints".
I'm a simple man, so I'll try to  make it simple. The map needs to be unlocked in sections much like Far Cry in a sense, you essentially plug yourself into the matrix at various places and then the map will reveal it's goodies to you. In order to get parts of the map back under your control you have to unlock and claim areas of strategic value called strikepoints.
Then you go about working up the peoples' spirit by stabbing a few ♥♥♥♥♥es, breaking attennas, twisting big wheels to make various monoliths explode, ya know the usual stuff.
One of the realllly cool things is the ability to Go Go Gadget your guns on the fly. Need an LMG? Don't worry, your assualt rifle can swap into one. Want a sniper rifle that can turn into a firework launcher? You didn't even know you wanted that more than anything in your life until you read that... I know, I was the same.
The only downside is keeping track of what gun has transformed into what, the amount of times I went to swap to my assualt rifle to only launch a mine harmlessly short of my target as I gain a for more holes to breath out of. But that's more my inabilty to keep track of things.
Besides having guns with identity issues, you also get some cool♥♥♥♥♥♥with the various grenades. Not only can you have the standard "throw, wait, boom." you can gain access to an RC car, teddy bear and a remote detonator. Now you can attach whatever 'grenade' to whichever item you want.
So like any decent human being, I blew peoples balls off teddy bears. I regret nothing. Besides that of course, there are many strategic RC sized vents laying around the place. So if you love all that sneaky sneaky hacky hacky stuff then you're covered.
Anyway. I would personally would reccomend this game. It was enjoyable to play and not too mentally challenging. Except for that ♥♥♥♥ing medical stash ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t, but that's a surprise for anyone who picks this game up.
Thanks for making it this far through my rambling.
