I think LoG 2 is an outstanding game, and there is nothing else quite like it (and here I mean a dungeon crawling game made modern). There have been a few attempts, but none come near the quality that this game has.
The game's world is huge and very varied. In every direction you turn there is new adventure, secrets, puzzles, things to explore. In that sense it actually reminds of Skyrim in its scope, although fundamentally different in style. Grimrock's world is really immersive. I especially loved the dark ambient soundtracks for each location (which are in same fashion as i.e. Stalker games), which set the mood. The visuals are fantastic and convincing, you really feel that you are deep underground in a deadly dungeon filled with secrets, traps, and places buried by time and dust.
Gameplay is great. The story is mysterious and fun. Combat is varied enough, and the puzzles are all fantasticly made. All of them are logical and can be figured out by careful attention to detail and hints. Some are easy, some are difficult, and a few are very difficult, but very fun to solve. Best part: no bugs and no broken puzzles. This game has what I greatly miss in modern games: that feeling of excitement when you finally solve a level and unlock another one, and can't wait to see what's inside.
For me this is the game of the year. I would suggest it to players who like mystery, adventure, immersive worlds, puzzle solving, and exploration, but I think it is so oustanding in all aspects that I simply think that everyone should try it.

This game is one of the worst experiences I have had, though I suppose part of it can be forgiven considering the age of the game. The game starts right off with you saving a barbiesque girl from some thugs. The protagonist is sure to tell the audience direcly about how beautiful the girl is and that this the main reason why he won't refuse to help her. The game is contradicting at times between the antagonists wanting to kill the girl at first, but then after catching her they want to interrogate her. The game also weirdly dips into native americans and then the supernatural, before ending on a relatively normal note. The final revelation of the plot is probably the only thing interesting about it. Mostly, the game seems to take itself too seriously for how bland it is.
While the models are simple and cel-shaded, the animations leave something to be desired. Talking animations often appear to be 2-frame mouth open/mouth closed animations. Interacting with people is often delayed while they finish an idle animation they are in the middle of. Characters aside from the main ones often stomp or shuffle around in ways I can't tell to be intentional or not.
The first few 2 chapters had some decent puzzles, but afterward it is increasingly difficult to determine what you are supposed to do. There are multiple times when you have an idea of what to accomplish, but with no idea of how it relates to your current goal. As the game approaches the end, the puzzles seem more like exercises in mind reading on the developers. At one point I had to give the name of a movie director and one of their movies to another character as it was tangentally related to a solution for a problem the protagonist had at the time. There was also a time when I was to cut a "rock hard" object with a knife that had been heated, because it would cut better. A third one involved throwing a basketball to a particular character because they were secretly used to be a famous basketball player. In none of these scenarios did I find any clues to the answers.
A few other bullet points:
- One part of the game involves you performing the same task 5 times, each time taking about 6 room transitions.
- The end of the game gets pretty tedious as you repeatedly leave objects for other characters to examine, leave the room, and come back.
- There are also times when a searchable object or container will need to be examined multiple times or at different times before new needed objects will be available to be picked up.

I guess I have to give this game a negative review!  It's *such* a cool idea, and the implementation is smart: nodes showing problems, issues, and policies, connected by red and green lines that show how they're related to each other.  But this game needed a lot more testing.  I dare anyone to get reelected in Zambeezia; you start out terribly unpopular and simply can't get enough people to join your party in four years, and unaffiliated voters mostly do not vote.  There are strange omissions ranging from "CO2 emissions apparently do not affect air quality in this universe" to "I have no tools to fight terrorism other than military spending."  And maybe weirdest, it seems that my voters' and ministers' opinion of the issues is absolute, not relative.  That is, if a country starts out very un-capitalist, I can do nothing but pass capitalist policies and still get resignation threats from my capitalist ministers, because capitalist voters hate me.  (One wonders whether they've seen the opposition party's policies!)
And, you know, fair's fair -- it's a one-man studio, and this is a pretty awesome game for one person to have made.  If I'd made it I'd be pretty pleased with myself.  But I really can't recommend it as a commercial product unless you're interested in game design, where this game has various good and bad lessons to teach.  Extensively modded, it might be salvageable.  As-is, no.

Eternal has the look of Hearthstone and the mechanics of a MTG card game.  Some cards are also very similar to Hearthstone, for example a 2 cost 2/3  or 3/2. Also you don't earn mana automatically each turn.  Although there are many mana altering cards, like Magic, you play one of your mana (if) you drew/had one each turn.  Think of "looks/simplification" of HS and "plays/feels" of MTG.  Awesome deck themes with similarities to MTG(green, red, etc).  I was waiting for something to combine some of HS and most of MTG and Eternal did that for me.  Eternal took my favroite parts from HS ( layout and simplicity ) and combined that with MTG (different attacking/blocking and mechanics).  While HS is a constant battle for board control, where your creatures can actually choose what to attack on their attack turn..  In Eternal you can't choose what to attack, only what to block, (BIG thumbs UP from me).  So far i have felt the FTP model for the game is fair and the changes that are being made are done so thoughtfully.  I have quite a collection building and havn't spent any real money.  It adds a few new mechanics to cards.  Weapons for your heroes like in HS. Enchantments for in play cards like MTG.  Replayable single player content.  More than fair reward system for any type of game played.  You keep the cards you draft.  So much good!  May Magic styles TCG's live on!

The Crew is an awesome game that really takes racing games to the next level. It also adds a community aspect to the story of racing games like I've never seen in a racing game before. Whether you are looking to play alone or with friends, this game is incredibly fun, and I recommend it completely.
Additionally, the driving mechanics in The Crew are great also. While there is a bit of an arcade feel at times, it is actually hard to progress in the story, and it does take some time to progress and get to the top cars in the game. I feel like this is a very positive aspect as it forces you to invest in the story and really play the game for a great amount of time before progressing to the best cars unlike other racing games that make everything super easy to do.

With that being said, there are some problems. One of the main problems that I have had is one where you are disconnected after a story mission, and once I reconnect, the result of it does not show. Thus, I have to completely replay it. This is game breaking at times if you are only playing multiplayer, but if you are a single player guy, you're still good to go. There are also some other bugs such as skipping, cars disappearing, and issues getting in the same lobby as a friend. These, however, are nothing compared to the original one where are disconnected without getting the progress you deserve.
Nevertheless, this game over all is pretty freaking good, and I would give the game a 80 out of 100. This is the best street racing game I have played in a very long time, and it is a must buy if you love racing games.

This is a game that makes me wish Steam had a "meh" button. It's hard to rate this game on a strict thumbs-up/thumbs-down basis because it does some things very well while other things aren't handled as elegantly, and, depending on what you enjoy the most, it can impact your overall enjoyment of the game. It's length means that you won't feel entirely cheated by the end of it (I beat it in less than 3 hours), but personally, it left me wanting more.
I'll start with the mechanics and overall gameplay. I initially purchased this game because I thought it was a take on the Oregon Trail or Organ Trail, where I had to get from point A to point B with some stops in between to scavenge or engage in combat. I would then have to divy my supplies among my companions and would ultimately decide who lives or dies. I was...half right. While you do scavenge and fight enemies and help your companions in between locations, there is very little that can impact them that is out of your control. No diseases, no dysentery, or no sudden hordes of enemies. Your downtime between locations was just that: Downtime. There wasn't any particular reason to stay on edge, unlike Organ Trail, but there were things to keep you engaged that I'll touch on later.
Station mode, where you explore abandoned zones full of enemies, is half of the gameplay and felt the best to me. You're given a pistol, then a shotgun, then an assault rifle by the endgame, and you have to make the best with your meager amount of ammo. Some enemies die in one headshot, some can be finished off with a shotgun blast, and some just exist to eat bullets. The variety was low, but for lore reasons, I was perfectly happy with it. It meant that even in the most chaotic situations, there are still rules to how these creatures worked and what you would be facing. You also had a melee attack which could be used to knock back or kill enemies and punch your way through certain walls. You were also able to pick up and throw certain objects that could kill enemies if you landed your throw. No problems with the combat but also nothing that felt amazing. It's a 2D game with no lock on so sometimes some shots will miss because your cursor wasn't in the right spot. Also, when going up and down stairs, you can't aim past a certain angle, so taking out enemies from above can be a hassle.
Train mode, the other half. was okay, but felt half-baked. While exploring locations, you could come across people who would board your train. You could find six in each "act" of the game and while taking them was optional, keeping them alive until the end of the act would handsomely reward you in the form of money or items. The harder someone was to keep alive, the more they would reward you. Also, one or two things would go wrong on your train during these lulls and you had to do short minigames in order to return your train to working order. The longer the problem went unsolved, the faster a passenger's health would drop. The minigames weren't hard and they were decent distractions, but the game didn't feel it necessary to at least drop hints of the mechanics. This is where The Final Station suffers the most on the gameplay front: very little is explained to the player. I didn't discover I could craft extra ammo or healthkits until the second act and some minigames weren't exactly clear on what had to be done in order to "win." On certain minigames, if you screwed up, the problem would actually worsen. That's really the worst part of the gameplay for me. On the whole, it's good, but not exactly memorable. Nothing that hadn't been done before.
The story is the subjective part. I've been going back and forth since I finished the game and I'm still not sure where I stand on it. I'll do my best to summarise the story and point out where I think it falls flat. Firstly, most of the game's story is given through dialogue and scraps of paper or other texts you find while scavenging. While on your train, passengers will talk amongst themselves about what's going on and there's a lot you can piece together. However, if you don't keep your passengers alive or just don't talk to them, you will know and learn very little. The Final Station takes place in a postapocalyptic future, 106 years after an alien invasion. You are the conductor of one of the last trains that is running and you must transfer components for a giant machine (and any survivors you find) from station to station. I won't spoil the game's story here, but there is a lot that is...up to interpretation. I'm all for symbolism, especially in gaming, but if you don't give your player something resembling a cohesive narrative, interest dwindles. I was certainly gripped by the world and setting because I kept playing just to see what happened next. I wanted answers...and then I got to the end. The best advice I can give is to keep every survivor you find alive to the best of your ability and listen to what they have to say and to read every note you find, ESPECIALLY from the third act on. There are very small details that will keep the ending from making sense unless you find them. I really like this organic storytelling, but I feel like the devs went overboard in this case. I went to look at a playthrough of this game on YouTube to refamiliarize myself with the ending and it irked me to see people summarizing The Final Station's story with "the way I see it." There's too much style with too little substance.
On the whole, I think I would recommend this game. The story is at least interesting, the presentation was neat, and the gameplay was intense enough that I frequently felt like my back was against the wall and one bullet made the difference between life and death, but it's easy to feel robbed if you don't pay excessive attention to every line of dialogue and every scrap of paper by the time you complete your adventure.

Once in a lifetime you'll come across a game that truly captures the history and cultural distinctions of the modern world the way a person can subjectively perceive it through our guided field of perspective. I have to admit, I had my doubts when I first learned of the game. After all, Amazing World? Will this game even be good? How ignorant was I to even have these thoughts. Little did I know I was about to indulge in what may have been the best 3.5 hours of my life. The game started out strong. The opening scenes enticed the audience with a captivating enigma. I was so taken aback from the next-generation animation that I almost didn't even realize the underlying symbolism in the ongoing scenes. It wasn't until my twenty sixth gameplay of this masterpiece where I finally got my bearings together and was able to focus on the gripping and labyrinthine stratagem. The underlying analogy for 19th century distopianism and the evangelical deviation of typical orthodoxy was enlightening to say the least. Just when I thought this game could not get any better, the increasing conflict before the climax began. I could not believe the complexity of the story as my character struggled with the everyday endeavors, for a quintessential cute cow with a funny hat, such as the consistent up- hill altercation of the fight against misogyny and the fiscal synergy of opposing interplanetary dynamisms. There I was, gripping to my chair as the conflict of the game began. I was so enticed by Amazing world that I felt as if I was both practically and relatively apart of the game. This is a special kind of high that not even the strongest of drugs can give you. Was I part of the game? Am I inside the game right now? This game will leave you questioning existential nihilism and the objective skepticism of our perceived valuation of anthropological existence. At this point in the gameplay, I was fully intoxicated by the avant-garde animated art style. That's when the plot finally aggrandized and I was completely stupefied. You could have lived a thousand years of isolation trying to predict the plot twist and you would never even scratch the surface of what actually transpires in this game. I was so bewildered that I actually had to rage quit, so that my existential crisis didn't dive too deep inside of myself. Even rage quitting was surreal. It's almost as if life rage quitted with the game. I felt as though I had actually become a cinematic tangent quantum. The effects are still wearing off and I haven't been able to play the game in several years. I spent the following seven years afraid of what outside of my house actually looks like. Every single day and night I live in misery because I became fully aware that happiness is never achievable. I realized that human life has absolutely no meaning and that no matter what I ever do, it is of complete unimportance and in years from now, no recollection of my existence will prevail, meaning that if I died years ago, died now, or die sometime in the future it will not matter whatsoever to anyone. But, then again, the fact that I'm living doesn't matter either so I might as well stick around for awhile, living in complete isolation, condemned to a life of traumatic memories and a completely corrupted sub-conscience.

Final Station takes 2D action side-scrolling and throws in some narrative driven clues and interactions in an apocalyptic setting where the world is on the brink of extinction from the infected. Instead of taking classic scenarios, the creators spin their own narrative involving this style of apocalypse. As the player, we begin playing the game in this weird setting where we are a train conductor(or engineer in this game) armed with a pistol walking around in a place about to be overrun by the infected and preparing for the worst. The engineer is quickly swarmed by the infected and promptly slaughtered. That is where we wake up. As it was a dream and a nightmare for the engineer just had visions of the Second Visitation.
This is when we slowly become aware of the setting through pieces of paper, dialogue with NPCs and a handful of messages scattered on computer terminals. The First Visitation took place some time ago and the train engineer lives in a world slowly rebuilding after already being overran once by infected. We find out that the First Visitation is traced to a crash landing by a UFO and exposure to gas which turn people infected. Along with that, there appears to be some form of alien invasion that the government barely managed to push back in the first encounter.
Overall, I enjoyed the game and if you are into apocalyptic settings or like story-rich games with some combat, then Final Station is worth checking out. For those interested my full review is down below. Have a great day gaming!

A really fun experience, held slightly back by a few small design decisions.
Mechanically, this The Last Station is responsive and provides solid feedback. The visual and sound design is absolutely excellent - pixel art is a glorious blend of traditional pixel-art and scanned images, and the effect is a treat.
Some people might be put off by the vague story, or the heavy 'found notes' style of storytelling, but I think the game gives you enough information to have a solid enough idea of what's going on by the end.
I was a little bit frustrated by the design of the train sections and the way money is used in the game. Shops are way too infrequent, and the cost of upgrades doesn't seem balanced. And having to hand feed your passengers on the train feels like pointless busywork - I would have preferred to do nothing so I could take in the gorgeous scenery, or focus on passenger dialogue!
This is still a really polished game, and comes incredibly close to being a classic. I would have really appreciated this game as a roguelike - the same kind of idea has been done in games like Dead Pixels and Death Road to Canada, and the mechanics here seem made for it! My playthrough was a tight experience lasting 4 hours, and I don't regret my time with the The Last Station at all.

Gone Home is an interactive short story of about an hour and a half. During that time, you are Katie who has just returned home from Europe and finds nobody home. So she explores the family mansion, to find out where her parents and her sister are. The graphics are nice enough, sound effects are ok and the voice acting is not bad either, which is a rare feat for indie games. But the story is what an interactive story is mostly about, of course, and unfortunately that's where Gone Home will be severely lacking for most people.
I don't want to spoil the story for people who may want to experience the story for themselves, but I can say that the story is a huge disappointment if you get your expectations from elements like 'a huge mansion to explore', 'an empty house', 'mystery: where is everyone?' etc. It's nothing like what you'd think. There are no unexpected twists in the story and there is nothing supernatural going on or anything like that.
The description for the game on the Steam page contains some quotes from reviews. One of the quotes mentions that the story of Gone Home is a love story. So that's no spoiler either, it's in the product's description. The story is indeed a teenage love story like you might have seen in an After School Special from the late 20th century. I don't mean that in bad way, there is nothing wrong with After School Specials, it's just so you know what to expect and who the target audience is.
If you think you might enjoy a teenage love story being told while you explore every room of a mansion, you should still be careful before deciding to purchase Gone Home. It's a completely linear experience and the interactivity required is very limited, so there is no reply value whatsoever. Moreover, the whole experience only takes an hour and a half.
So we should really talk about the price here. That isn't easy, though, because money is subjective: to some people, €20 or $20 means practically nothing but for other people, that's half their monthly budget for gaming. I usually tend to recommend buying games if they're on sale when I personally think they may be a bit overpriced for the value they actually offer. But in this case, I think it's safe to be blunt and say that pricing a short novel (emphasis on 'short') with extremely little content at €20/$20, is nothing less than a complete rip-off. I think I personally paid around €3.5 for it and I still feel that I paid a bit too much for what I got.
For people who are sure they won't want to experience Gone Home for themselves, I'll tell you the whole story just so you'll see what I'm on about in this review. So needless to stay, HUGE SPOILER coming up...
. Even for an After School Special pitch, the producers would have said: "Hmm ok, it's an interesting start for a story but what else is going on?". To which Gone Home would reply: "Nothing else. That's it. And that will be 20 dollar/euro please."

Intro: For me, Legend of Grimrock 2 came out of nowhere. I didn't ever expect a sequel to the first game, but when I saw it I picked it up based on how good the first game was. If you are new to Grimrock or new to Dungeon crawling games I recomend playing the first Game. The original game is slower and teaches you the basics much better than its faster cousin.
Gameplay: Much like the first game, you have the same style of dragging and dropping for inventory management. Clicking on characters weapons to attack and drawing patterns in the runes to cast spells. Navigating the menus can be clunky if your in a pinch, but if you use the numbered hot keys you shouldn't have a problem.
Puzzles: Puzzles are a big part of Dungeon crawling games. The puzzles in Grimrock 2 are weaker than the first game. Most of the time with puzzles you won't even know there is anything to solve. The game progresses along until you hit a brick wall and are stuck. And unless you did a super specific thing the game didn't elaborate on you will be stuck. The puzzles are challenging don't get me wrong, but when you don't receive enough information to know there is a puzzle to solve, it's frustrating.
Open World(Not really but we will call it that): Unlike The first Grimrock, the second opens the player up to a bunch of areas really fast. Much like Dark Souls, going to areas you are not prepared for will get you killed. The "open world" gives the player a sence of exploring foreign lands and although the back tracking sucks, it makes the player learn the island and get familar with it as their home.
Random thoughts: This game is exactly as it looks: Challenging, fun, and thought provoking. Prepare your internet browsers, because some of these puzzles are random af. Involving time of day, standing in certain spots for periods of time or digging multiple times.
Conclusion: All in all its a good buy for a fan of the  genre or franchise. If your new to these kinds of games, wait for a sale and pick up the first game. Who knows there could be a christmas bundle.

The first game of the series puts you in the shoes of Brian, a high school graduate who takes an off state road trip to college. Unexpected circumstances throw you in a middle of events that hinder with the initial plan. The plot takes place.
The game itself is fun and funny for the most parts and to an adventure game enthusiast like myself it has the proper feel to it. The interface is simple, though there is some room for improvement. Yet, after the first chapter it is pretty much obvious and doesn't get in the way of the story.
There area some chapters where an overwhelming frustration tends to kick in because you simply can't get ahead because you haven't found an item that is in some weird place blended so smoothly into the environment that you just don't notice it. Thanks to low frame rate moving the mouse too quickly over the item that is only few pixels in size won't reveal it because the mouse hover won't have time to change. This is why I, for a few times did something I usually never do when playing an adventure game; I took a brief look at a playthrough just to get a hint of what I am missing.
It was always either a small item in some corner that I had looked already but hadn't touched the tiny highlight area on screen or an item that was found in a place where Brian had already states there's nothing else to be found. This is the second annoying thing that I haven't encountered in any other adventure game I've played. If there is an item to be taken it can be taken straight away or the character tells that something is preventing him/her from grabbing it but not in this game.
Pros:
- Classic adventure game look and feel
- Hand drawn backgrounds
- Smooth animations
- Somewhat logical puzzles
- Story for the most parts
- Real world references
- Most of the over exaggerated characters
Cons:
- Finding items that are just couple of pixels in size and blended into the environment
- Finding items that are in places where you looked already and none were found
- Illogical item puzzles (like oil can vs watering can)
- Brian's tone of voice sometimes way off considering the situation
Overlooking the cons this game it is worth playing.

A huge, epic adventure that fans of first-person dungeon crawlers will devour. Designed with nostalgia in mind, but also sleek and shiny with modern graphics and great sound design. Better than the first game in every way, and worth it if you're even remotely interested in this kind of game. Play the first game before this one to help you ease into the mechanics and appreciate the improvements.
The challenge level is steep but fair, and difficult enemies can be taken down through tactics and manuvering rather than brute force. There are tons of secrets to find and an overall sense of mystery and wonder in every dungeon and area. Atmosphere is thick and the sound really makes the world feel alive, and threats ahead can be anticipated with keen ears. Overall the presentation makes for a immersive experience coupled with solid gameplay and combat.
The puzzles are mostly logical and can be figured out with a little thought and experimentation, though a few are so unclear that guesswork is almost neccessary. I'll fully admit I had to consult a guide for a few spots, and while some solutions made me feel stupid, a few just made me go "really?". It's much more satisfying to work through the puzzles yourself, but some of the nastier ones can get frustrating enough to encourage cheating.
A few minor balance issues made me rethink my initial party and start over after a while, but I'm terrible for that in any game like this. Almost any party combination can work, but some weapons are simply found more often and in better quality than others. Consulting a guide or a friend before setting out with your party can help a lot, especially since a few of the classes don't necessarily work the way you might expect them to.
Being out in a bright, open world makes the grid-based movement seem a bit strange, where it mostly made sense in the confined halls of the first game. It's not just there for nostalgia though - the movement system and the logic that governs it is central to the combat and puzzle-solving systems and removing it would have required a complete overhaul in design. The game wouldn't work otherwise.
The more open-ended design makes for a lot more exploration, but it can be overwhelming. Puzzles that need keys or information from elsewhere to solve don't always indicate that clearly, and if you leave the game for too long and come back to it, you'll likely be hopelessly lost. The progression path isn't clear, but that could be said to just be part of the game's philosophy. Here's an island full of monsters and traps and secrets, good luck.
Nostalgic, polished, immersive, and challenging enough to deter some players, this is almost everything you could possibly want in a dungeon crawl and one of the only modern examples of the genre. Worth the purchase, and then some.
This creative inversion of the platformer is an intersesting and sufficiently challenging diversion from the traditional platformer; an exciting and fun soundtrack is icing on the cake.

When it first came out, the adventure gaming was in decline, and many people considered Runaway to be some sort of a genre messiah. Sadly, it wasn't. While Pendulo surely tried to match Sierra's scale and Lucas Arts' wit, they failed in recreating the two key aspects that made adventure games great: puzzles and characters.
Too many of the challenges the player faces in the game are stupid, if not completely Illogical (getting the wrench and filling the tank, to name a few). And the two main characters are as underdeveloped and unlikable as they can get. Gina is nothing more than a damsel in distress, completely objectified and helpless; and Brian is shown as a self-centered jerk, totally unmoved by anything that happens around him, while stopping at nothing to fulfill his, often questionable, agenda.
Those hoping to find another Guybrush and Elaine, or Gabriel and Grace (or even George and Nico, for that matter), should skip this game.

Yes, as you can guess,
is a game aimed towards kids, but the painful fact of the matter is, it's a bugged game that acts like a free game, yet stops the player at a certain point by saying "You have to be a member to continue this part of the game" after proceeding to a certain point...basically, that means you have to pay for a limited time membership to continue.  Yes, a membership that expires.
Aside from that, there are times where your avatar (called a "Zing") changes in one of the minigames to be a yellow bear splattered with purple paint, even if you're something else like an orange fox.  There are also some minigames that auto-complete (like with the artist), and of course...there's awful controls.  You're able to move around with the directional keys (Up, down, left right) and the WASD keys (which make you take a few steps before freezing in place).  In addition to this, there's the driving controls, which are some of the worst car controls I've seen in a game (heck, it spawns you in a vehicle dropping from the sky onto the ground, rather than on the ground).
There's an achievement in the game that awards you for unlocking a minigame (Crystal Capers).  Strangely, it's already unlocked and therefore impossible to unlock the achievement.  Upon trying an alternate in-game account to see if I could unlock it, I could verify that it was still locked...however, upon logging back into my original account, my already unlocked achievements re-unlocked in bulk, instantly changing the unlock times of the achievements I've already gotten.  Adding to that, there are some achievements that require you to own certain items that strangely do not exist.
This buggy mess seems like it has potential to be a decent game, but with several bugs, I don't see even children finding this game enjoyable.  Several missions are repeats, reusing the same maps/missions, but with slightly different graphics for targets.
Now, as far as positives go, I enjoy the effort that went into the graphics and the world and also find it impressive that the whole game is fully voiced by various voice actors.  But that's about all I can say about that.  The story is boring, cringey, and full of furries.
If you're looking for a good game to play, then you might want to look elsewhere.  You can only unlock about 12 (17%) of the achievements as a free player before having to pay for access to the rest of the game.  Even given the quality of the game, I wouldn't justify paying for temporary access to the rest of the game unless you support this particular developer.

A rather disappointing 2D platform zombie/survival game that showed a lot of promise.
I saw this game a while ago and was looking forward to play it as the it looked really good, it seemed to have a pretty nice idea and looked very promising.
Sadly the game falls short. The visuals are nice, the pixel art is of hight quality. The theming does look also good. But the game is not that fun to play. The story behind it is a standard zombie outbreak of some sort - nobody knows what's going on really apart from the fact that people are turning to zombie like creatures. And it turns out you're the last train driver around tasked with transporting something somewhere for the military.
The game is divided basically into two parts - in one you're riding the train from station to station taking care of the machine and managing your supplies to keep your passenger alive in the other you explore each station in search for survivors, supplies and a code to let you go through.
The train riding part serves as sort of exposition - your passengers talk about what they heard and what they feel is going on - but it's mostly gossip you don't pay much attention to. Some of them are wounded, some hungry - you need to distribute food and med kits among them to let them survive. If they survive to a specific station you'll get a reward. Apart from that you need to keep an eye for a specific element and tweak it so the train doesn't stop. It's an interesting idea I guess but it feels just so boring. Totally unnecessary.
The second part of the game is exploration. Once you meet a station you need to find a lock code to progress further. You have a gun, fists, later on shotgun and machine gun. The ammunition is very little so you need to make every shot count. That is until you learn you can punch the zombies to death and with the use of ladders which zombies can't climb - well to say I was definitely not lacking the ammo. There is no jumping and while the levels look cool they feel very much the same. You walk left, kill some zombies, collect supplies, climb down, progress through some kind of underground area and you're back at the train. Every time it's the same thing.
The number of zombies is also quite limited so it feels a bit same all the way. I've finished it - but I can't say I enjoyed every moment of it. Maybe first half an hour - later on I was just curious to see how it ends - and the ending was especially disappointing.
Overall a decent game that just didn't catch my attention and felt it had much more potential than it turned out. Would probably not recommend.

While you take the cargo to its bunker you also have explore each station along the way so you can find more ammo, food, medicine, survivors and a passcode that will unlock the tracks and let you proceed to your next objective.
While you're traveling you also need to keep your train from "exploding" and manage a random system that will be going haywire.
You either need to cooldown the cargo, release pressure from the train's suspension or take care of the cabin's ventilation. If you have any survivors in the passengers cabin you may also need to give them food (which may be found at the stations) or treat them with medkits that will stop their bleeding. If you fail to do so they will die and consequently the reward that they give you for getting them to the next bunker, will not be awarded. The rewards consist of bullets, money (that can be used to restock the train's supplies) and weapon upgrades.
The main story is really well delivered through small talk with other characters (no longer then 2 phrases) and a more in-depth view about what is going on is told through pages, books and emails at the stations (you are not forced to read them if you don't want to and there's no big boring exposition parts).
I didn't find any technical flaws, no crashes, no weird gameplay mechanics and the menu is organized and simple.
I really enjoyed my time with 'The Final Station' but i recommend you get it either on sale or from another reseller (it goes for around €2.40 at the time of this review). In my opinion it's worth the full price but you will definitely feel like you got more for your buck if you buy it cheaper.
The only thing i didn't like much was the inexistence of voice acting or any sort of noise (other then ambient and music) when in dialogue with the NPC's. At least the classic "grunts" should have been included, but that's not a big problem since the dialogue is so scarce and short.
My final score is a 9/10 - 'The Final Station' really stands off from the competition in it's genre, with a beautiful art style, amazing story and a entertaining gameplay. This game is going to get you hooked from start to finish.

All the depth of a mobile game with a story held up by rotting vegetables.
The Final Station is a 2D pixel art game that combines twitch shooting and basic resource management into a (kinda-not-really) post-apocalyptic wrapper. You play the conductor of a new prototype train and are tasked with going across an unnamed country to stop a deadly plauge that turns people into squid ink puking zombies.
Side note: Between Stick it to the Man, The Final Station, Gloom, and others...I'm getting really really bored of 2D enemies made of shadow with glowing white eyes.
The gunplay...gets boring really really quickly. This is partially due to the game's 2D environment. You only have so much tactical initiative when you're faced with enemies who stack on top of eachother and can only come at you in a straight line. The starter pistol is your only weapon for most of the game, but you'll quickly learn how to cheese the punching mechanic when things seem desperate. Additionally, because checkpoints are extremely generous and there's no penalty for dying, you'll learn how to complete every level in the game without a single medkit. The result is a tedious combat portion that you only play to unlock more of the story.
Your goal in each exploration level is to find a code that will all your train to leave the station. Unfortunatley, the game might as well be on rails as exploration is bare bones. Again, this is partially due to a 2D environment which confines you to either going left, right, up, or down. I liken the action in this game to Fallout: Shelter. Rooms and hallways are hidden in blackness until you explore them, creating the illusion of a much larger and more mysterious world. Once you realize this and once you clear room after room and find nothing to reward your troubles, you'll understand why gunplay gets boring.  The game is only about 4 hours long, but it feels like 7-8, if not more.
Resource management, the game's other key feature...is a complete and total disaster beyond saving. The section goes like this: At each station you pick up a survivor. During the train ride to the next area, survivors discuss the world's backstory. While this is happening, the player has to play tedious and trivial repair minigames to stop the train from breaking down. The player also has to feed hungry passengers and bandage bleeding passengers with their precious medkits. The problem is that passengers only speak while the player is in the passenger train car. Going to get supplies or playing a minigame stops the conversation. Worse, these sections are on a timer so you'll miss huge amounts of much needed dialouge trying to keep your passengers from dying. You can continue listening to passengers after your "you have arrived' notification appears, but passengers will continue to starve and bleed and the train itself will continue to breakdown. The entire travel section doesn't accomplish anything. It doesn't help tell the story because the player is burdened with a mountain of unengaging busywork.
The reason you NEED to hear what the passengers are saying is because the story is incredibly vauge. All we start with is that it has been 106 years since something called 'The First Visitation." We never learn the details of this event. All we get is that pods of a mysterious make and material dropped from the sky and are emitting a gas that turns 99% of people into black sludge spewing zombies. The game has an illusion of deep and expansive lore, but ultimatley leaves you disappointed, not because the story is difficult to understand but because there isn't as much there as you are lead to believe.
Just as an example, we don't even know if this game takes place on Earth because its set far in the future, looks like the Combine from HL2 have invaded, and the only time you see the night sky, there are two moons. Yet none of this matters. Thats not what the story is about.
Here's the overarching problem: When you have a really complex world, you need to anchor your audience in the setting with some kind of introduction. Warhammer 40k does this, Star Wars does this, Dune does this, Fallout does this, Mad Max does this. Every franchise that wants to grow and build a fanbase does so by anchoring and immersing the audience. The Final Station drops you into a 2D world populated by two-dimensional lore and one-dimensional characters.
Tedious gunplay, awful resource management, and a story that teases and prods without going anywhere. I might be more lenient to a $5 game, but The Final Station retails for $15. For all these reasons I cannot recommend The Final Station.

i bought this game with all its DLC when it was on sale for about $10, and while it was a good price the game has some glaring issues *Some Spoilers*:
Story:
This is your average war hero story, nothing more nothing less, it doesnt do anything new or even try to for that matter, the best bits of the sotry are actually the DLC, all 3 campaigns are very tight and tell a cohesive narritive. Honestly if they had gone the route that they did with the DLC itd deffinatley be a higher rated game. In the campaign your carecter is mute the entire time, witch is a huge turn off for someone like me. The ending is very lackluster with none of the carecters really going through anything major other than things you will read in journals. Witch is by far the worst way to convey your story. It has a twist youll see coming from a mile away, the minute they say it youll be like "oh well duh ya idiots."
Gameplay:
This game has a semi open world. I say that because you cant travel seemlessly through the areas and most of it is very small city sections with more interesting things blocked off. The gunplay however is very responisve and is fun to shoot and kill, even if some of the weapons dont pack a huge punch. Also the feature from crysis to swap attatchments on the fly is back and fits very well into the world this game is trying to create. The driving is as good as any other FPS with driving, mostly works other than some strange glitches when exiting a vehicle (sometimes when you exit a vehicle you cant aim or shoot your gonna without switching weapons). The mission structure is fun enough to keep you playing in bursts like I did, my main complaint is the AI is super stupid. Freindly and enemy AI have no idea what they are doing even on hard.
DLC:
Im giving this a section mainly because the DLC is amazing for this game, they give your carecter a voice and tells what happens moments before the opening of the game, witch I actually wondered myself. The first DLC follows walker before everything hit the fan and you play as him while getting your insurgant team to saftey. VERY fun to play. The second DLC takes place a few months after the end of the main story and even pokes fun at the fact that you were a mute in the main story. You play as Brady again now trying to go rescue walker from KPA hold. This is fun because if your smart you can stealth your way around the whole level. The third DLC we are again following Brady, I refeer to this as a "what if" story. I do this because it completly ignores the first to DLCs, witch is extremley dissapointing because i wanted to see what happened after rescuing walker. BUt you help NATO scientists put up a final front against the KPA in a last ditch attempt. Ill be honest i couldnt finish this one cause the game kept crashing on me.
Co-Op:
No one in the servers dont bother.
I reccomend this game based on the DLC (witch really sucks to say). But also on the fact that even though the story is a mess its still a damn fun playthrough and for when its on sale, this game is honestly a no brainer.

Silly AAA industry; you keep trying and trying to make the most realistic shooter ever, but an indie dev beat you to it. And he did it in one week.
Receiver is, without a doubt, the most realistic shooter there is.
-You die in a single hit. (To be fair, a single bullet will not always kill you in real life, but if it hits your body or head, it WILL disable you such that you are at the shooter's mercy)
-You hold your gun and flashlight in the exact same way that US investigative and miliraty forces are trained to.
-Your gun behaves exactly like a real one would. You can fill a magazine, load it, chamber a round, eject the magazine, and put another bullet in it. And you can fire the chambered round with or without a mag loaded. I could go on.

Runaway: A Road Adventure is a great game after what I thought was a mediocre execution of the introduction. Before you take control of the main character, the game plays a rather lengthy cutscene that lasts for about 9 minutes and it serves as a prologue.  The problem is that while the story in it is worth knowing and some of the animation was nice, the overall quality of it suggests that it would have been better if it was shorter. At one point in the cutscene I was wondering if this game was worth getting into.
But after the first chapter things really kicked off.  The puzzles are interesting; the side characters flesh out the charm of the setting, such as the janitor who is also a "businessman" that sells high quality optics; and the main characters become more attachable as the story develops. The story can get a bit corny at times, but combined with the previous qualities the game turned out to be quite memorable.
If you're looking for an adventure game saga, the Runaway series is definitely worth getting into.

As far as shooters go, you can definitely do better than Homefront. You can also do worse. Although I found the game difficult to enjoy, it gave me a good amount of playtime and scratched that shooter-itch I had. I'm Recommending the game insofar as, at a sale price of almost nothing, the game was a decent enough value. I wouldn't recommend paying more than $10 for it.
Homefront is, across the board, extremely average. I didn't find that much of the game really stood out from a sea of samey, uninspired shooters. Ambient noise was pretty decent; the level of immersion was decent enough. However the gameplay mechanics really hinder that a lot. There are 5 or 6 zones in the game and each time it is the exact same fare: run from base to base capturing them, finding radios. The game took a bunch of pages from Ubisoft's playbook with the open-world "activity hunter" style of gameplay but didn't add any of the parts that make that fun - rewards. There is seemingly no benefit to actually capturing bases. Your primary source of money is actually doing main missions because loot is worth next to nothing and there is no actual benefit to exploring.
Generally in an open-world game, you are rewarded for finding things and exploring; a new weapon, new gear, character upgrades. Not here. The only things to find are loot items and rebel stashes which don't contain anything you can't quickly or readily find elsewhere. All of your weapons and gear are purchased through gun cabinets which you will find at just about any base you capture. So that big, beautiful, destroyed city you're roaming around will almost go completely unnoticed because there is no incentive for you to deviate from your path.
There are only a handful of weapons, most of which can be modified to other, less useful varieties. For example, your handgun can be modified into an SMG or a suppressed pneumatic dart gun. Because the stealth mechanics are very shallow, and because the handgun and SMG can both be suppressed, there's never a compelling reason to take the dart gun. Gunplay is so-so; weapon sounds are adequate. Nothing you're ever carrying feels lethal or that it has any weight to it. Animations play really quick and just feel unsatisfied, especially when you are modifying your weapons. Your assortment of weapons is extremely small, which is another disappointing factor considering that America is notorious for it's gun culture. As cheesy as it is having weapons in games renamed for licensing reasons, it's even worse when your weapons are literally "pistol" and "assault rifle."
Equipment and upgrades are also extremely weak, and part of me wonders why it was even included. Most of the gear you buy provide bonuses that don't make sense. Kneepads for crouch speed and boots for quiet moving, but not things like gloves to help you search corpses faster, or maybe climb faster. Things that would have benefitted exploring. Weapons have attachments but they are also lacking in utility, function or variety. Aside from a crossbow, the only quiet weapons you have are made from your pistol.
My other main problem is the writing and story of the game. The story is that the American economy collapses and racks up a huge debt to North Korea so they invade as a "peacekeeping" operation. I'm perfectly fine with the concept of America being invaded and occupied by a foreign power. However, for that foreign power to be North Korea, a country that is 1/5th the size of Texas and with 1/10th the population of the USA, I find that to be a stretch. If it had been some coalition of countries, maybe. Also, the fact that somehow, North Korea is able to invade the USA without any opposition from foreign governments seems so implausible as to be ridiculous. Especially when the North Koreans are actively engaging a civilian population with chemcal warfare. The characters you meet are all cardboard cutout stereotypes. You've got the "grizzled but justified" leader, the "psychotic, whatever it takes" second-in-command and of course the "resentful, there's got to be another way" doctor. None of them are compelling and literally nothing any of them says makes any difference.
Throughout the game resistance members chat about there being no food, no medical supplies, no ammunition, etc. Yet none of this materializes in the game; at no point are any of these shortages worthy of you actually doing anything about it. You don't ever capture Nork weaponry other than for a story mission. You have an occupying force of well-equipped, high tech soldiers and we're still running around with rifles wrapped in rubber bands.
The tone and pacing of the game is, predictably, all over the place. You go from a new recruit to literally the savior in under 30 minutes of gameplay. Despite  being a resistance member, you are openly killing and defying the occupying military with almost no trouble to show for it. In fact, absolutely everything is going in the resistance's favor up until the exact second that the script calls for conflict; people die, the army starts a massive "crackdown" operation and all of your heroes start shouting doom and gloom. And then 10 minutes after that, they devise a hail mary and everything is coming up Milhouse again.
Visuals are pretty decent. The game looks nice and effects are pretty solid. Your explosives all create a wonderful explosion of smoke and fire and the accompanying screams. The city looks like it has survived a war which creates a great atmosphere. Unfortunately, the rest of the elements that go into world that are severely lacking and can't tie everything together.
The game also has it's fair share of mechanical problems. Multiple times I had to reload checkpoints (or restart the game completely) due to gamebreaking bugs. At one point while I was standing in line at the shipyard, the person that was in front of my escort bugged out and wouldn't move with the line, blocking my own passage. At one point I fast travelled late in the game to sell loot and had no fast travel point to return; which wouldn't have been so bad if the tunnel locations on my map hadn't disappeared. When you break Homefront down to it's component pieces, it looks like multiple teams all made different games and then taped those pieces together. The concept of a resistance movement fighting off an occupying force is a good one, unfortunately it just wasn't properly executed.
Verdict: Buy it on sale if you're looking for a so-so shooter. Otherwise, you can do better.

When I play adventure games, usually I like to play a compelling protagonist, solve ingenius puzzles, and meet a colourful cast of interesting characters. Unfortunately, Runaway fails on all counts, and then finds some more levels to fail on, in case I was not sufficiently put off from it with it's sheer audacious ineptitude alone.
The art, while competent in it's backgrounds and interesting in the execution of the cel-shaded comic style, fell short when rendering the characters, whose bodies float around while their mouths snap into keys, a discordant, stilted animation method that only serves to both highlight the failings of the watery bodies and the limited mouth animations. The character designs ranged from by the numbers boring, to overwhelmingly offensive and reductive. Racist stereotypes pop up again and again, gentle and unassuming, as if the writers thought nothing of their inclusion, with a literally yellow faced asian lady at one juncture, and a Tojo-style bucktooth japanese stereotype popping up later. The game seemed to take great pleasure in exaggerating features that weren't part of the caucasian face. While Brian and Gina were bland to the point of soporific, some of the supporting cast were so caricatured as to make them inhuman. The resulting mashup was incredibly distracting, and often insulting. It didn't fit together well.
The puzzle design was some of the worst I've ever seen - and unquestioned in it's sociopathy. Oftentimes the solution to a puzzle is to destroy some great work of art, or a career, or simply make someone's life worse for Brian's gain. Other puzzles involve leaps of logic so great as to bring into question the world this game was made in. Filling lipstick tubes with gunpowder, for instance, apparently makes for bullets. In what sane universe would this not just melt the lipstick and cause a jam in a gun? And Peanut Butter made by heating butter with some peanuts. Not only do the puzzle solutions often not make sense, but are literally antithetical to the goal you are trying to achieve. Brian will, at times, do something that is counterproductive to his aims for no real reason other than to prolong the game's running time. He is also an incredibly inconsistent hypocrit, refusing to steal some things because "he is a decent guy" and gleefully stealing and destroying other items because "they won't miss it". The amount of unquestioned property damage in this game is staggering. I was actively rooting for something horrible to happen to the protagonist by the end, as he got everything he ever wanted and more, as he complained about being lied to while lying out of his♥♥♥♥♥at every opportunity, and as he made everyone's lives a living hell while they did nothing but be accomodating to him.
From the very beginning, the insufferable Brian Basco comes across as a bland, entitled dudebro, whose complete disregard for his fellow human beings' safety is only matched by his lack of personality traits. I can only sum him up as some kind of dark, unfathomable void-beast who wants to go to Berkley University. In his quest for getting the female supporting protagonist, Brian poisons, strongarms, and causes the death of all who get in his way. He is unaffected by the death of friends, loved ones, and nothing bad that happens around him ever seems to stick - upon being told to not mourn by a Hopi Ghost, for example, he instantly feels better and snaps back to being the insufferable twit that he normally is.
Mentioning the Hopi, an important point has to be brought up. The Hopi, in the game's setting, appear to be a extinct tribe that have only a presence through spirits and ghosts, when in reality the Hopi are still a political presence in Arizona, with several towns. It reinforces the awful "Native Americans are Already Dead" tropes that resonate throughout media, which is part lie and part incredible racism, of which this game has in spades.
The story is at it's heart, forgettable, but only through Brian Basco's audacious awfulness is it elevated to a travesty. The twist in the plot takes five out of six chapters to come to fruition, and it is such a damp squib of a twist that you question why you even bothered with the game in the first place. The game's setup promises intrigue that the game ultimately does not deliver on. It barely engages more than morbid curiousity, let alone any proper intrigue. The game sets up a mystical element that ultimately only serves to give our hero yet another item and a pat on the back when he loses something. The love interest element is sickeningly underwritten and overemphasised, mainly when our hero reminds the supporting cast, and the player that he is not gay. His love interest spends most of the time unconscious, indisposed, or absent. What spark they could have had is never shown on screen, just that he thinks she is beautiful, and ergo he needs her. And she wants him for an unknown reason, probably because he hit her with his car and she needs protection. She is an eternal damsel, and her story is never expanded upon, even though it is far, far more interesting than his,
Describing Runaway as a power fantasy would be completely apt - Brian Basco represents the nadir of the human being, but still gets everything he ever wanted while reassuring himself, and being reassured, that he is the Decent Nice Guy Who Gets The Girl. It is almost sickening how pornographically this game presents us our "hero", in the sense that everything he does brings him everything he ever wanted, he never faces any real, lasting trauma or tragedy. No character development, just a stagnation into the awful person he always was, and will always continue to be.
Runaway is exactly what you should do when faced with this game.

F1 2016, in my opinion, is one of the best Codemasters game by far. It just never gets boring and I really enjoy playing it!!
Here is my review.
Handling. The handling really feels awesome on a pad and I feel no understeer unless my front wing is broken or I have dirty air from the car in front. I do have oversteer sometimes, but not very often as I can manage the throttle well. I like the handling, it's
but it's a very good model. UPDATE: I still like the handling, but it's the Mercedes which is understeery, which then makes me angry about it
AI. They are really aggressive and they go for moves on you everywhere, I really like that as I can have a lot more exciting battles with them. They can sometimes cut you off and smash you but I don't deal with that at all. That's in single player anyway. I enjoy playing quick races and career with them, they are really fun to race with.
Career Mode. The career mode is really cool, I like the agent who gives me updates and contract offers, and rivalry updates. In general this is my most enjoyable career mode, with all the practice programs which give the team data and information heading into qualifying and the race. The paddock is awesome too, it is very realistic and my team members are walking and stuff like that. The unfortunate thing about my career is that Mercedes are still winning races 8 races into the season. UPDATE: After Malaysia, Ferrari are now the fastest team of my season!!!
New features. The new features (like the formation lap) are really enjoyable and when I heard that it was announced I was like "OMG this game is awesome!! Formation lap?! :O Manual starts?!". The manual starts are cool as you click your gearshift up button to hold the clutch and then release it. I really like that feature. The formation lap makes the races a lot more realistic, as it gives the feel of your car before the start of the race. I really wanted to manually control the car while lining up on the grid though, it would've made this feature better imo.
Graphics. The graphics are absolutely beautiful and it makes me feel like a real F1 driver. I take some awesome screenshots from races (as you've seen on my Steam activity if you're my friend), and they look really cool.
Online features. Overall I don't enjoy online but the new features are cool, especially when you pause the game and the AI drives for you and then you continue on. AWESOME!!! I keep my position and keep on driving!!! Spectator cam is very cool, you can switch between broadcast mode and onboard camera, and it's good to watch other people race from that.
Engineer. I like the engineer in this game, despite him not shutting the ♥♥♥♥ up. He is really detailed with information, like weather data, race data, position, cars behind or in front, championship status, etc. I also love the "Shut up Jeff" option cause it's funny XD
I am 173rd at Malaysia on this game, my best ever leaderboard position in a racing game, which is brilliant!! And in most of the tracks I am under 1000th, maybe even under 600th or 500th!!! I am very good at this game, which is my hardest game imo.
Now despite there being so many positives, there has to be negatives too.
No driver statistics. I can't believe there are no statistics available for online or career mode in this game, I like looking at them to see how well I've done in them. I've had 1 pole and 1 podium in career mode, and many many wins in quick races. And around 30-50 wins online. I can't tell exactly how many cause there are no stats available!
Online AI. The AI, despite their brilliance in single player, are actually terrible in online. Why is that? Because they always brakecheck you, cut you off, don't see you coming. It's possible to overtake them but it's really hard to avoid them doing this. I find it really annoying, especially when I'm fighting at the front.
Some bugs and glitches. The bugs and glitches in this game are annoying, there's not many but if there is one, then it's annoying. Some examples: illegal overtakes when you overtake spun cars, getting a warning for a cut when you have 2 wheels off the track, replay cam glitch where the game stays on a particular replay screen (I had that in career mode), glitch where AI have impossible times, etc.
Physics. The physics are not good, when you hit a wall lightly you spin wildly and it generally keeps going for another 5 seconds before you stop. Also when you touch the back of someone, you get pretty much connected to their car and you go off with them.
That concludes my review of F1 2016. Overall I really enjoy it and it's a great game, I don't have many things against it at all. I hope F1 2017 is equally as good. Have a nice day :)

The Final Station turned into a far more story heavy game than I thought it would be. This isn't really a bad thing, as the story was pretty enjoyable and well told. The game itself breaks down into two main phases: The train, and scavaging.
The train sequences are basically a management game. You have to keep your passengers alive by providing them with medkits and food, while also keep various parts of your train working properly. During this time you also get some story from the passangers, as they'll chat with you and the other rider.
Whenever you reach a new town or base, you'll stop the train and get out. To move onto the next level you have to find a code somewhere. While you're searching for the code this is also your opportunity to collect ammo, food, medkits, and crafting materials to make said items. Occasionally you'll get to a main hub where you can drop off your current passagers and spend the money you've earned.
Overall I think the game warrants a playthough, but I do find that it was really starting to drag out towards the end. I probably would have enjoyed the experience much more if it was an hour or two shorter. After you reach a certain point you'll stop seeing anything new as far as enemies or mechanics, making the last half of the game quite repetitive while waiting for the story to progress.
In short: Worth a playthrough if you find it on sale, but could benefit from being compacted into a shorter experience.

F1 2016 is a good game. A very good one indeed.
I will start with the pros.
The performance of the teams mirrors well (not perfect) the performance of the car in real life.
The handling is good, i play with a pad and i can take most corners without problems unlike in previous F1 titles, however if i press throttle just a tiny bit it registers as if I floored it. The same applies for the brakes therefore the rear end can be unstable at times.
I really like the fact that if even one wheel hits the grass you can lose control of the whole car which in my opinion makes the game feel more realistic.
Simulation damage seems OK but i think it can become even more realistic in future titles
Formation Lap is awesome aswell no pit assistance which give you more immersion. The new starting mechanic looks cool and you can jump start if you are not careful enough. Makes the game more immersive.
The career is also very good although upgrading can be done very quickly and make a Manor-Marussia a fronttier fighter by the end of season 1. By mid season you can stop r&d development so that you can focus on next seasons car making the game even more realistic.
The new stuff you can ask your engineer is also a nice addition although most of it isnt really helpful you know for example who is in front of you.
I also like the AI being more agressive (I play on expert) they will also try to divebomb you from time to time which can cause accidents, the same applies for the start i have spun a couple of times when starting in the middle.
Cons
Many people who drive dirty in MP
The game registers "Left the track" too harsh. If i for example go a bit further out of the track in time trial my lap will be invalidated. While is true that i left the track you actually get a penalty in real life F1 if you gained an advantage from it (Corner cut excessive squeezing, overtake etc).
Hard to Mod. I miss those classic seasons mods like 1999

TL;DR Holy♥♥♥♥♥♥is this game a good surprise! Just picked it up at 2016's steam summersale, and I am hooked. Im really awful at fighting games and normally don't have any interest for them but this game is different being noob friendly (if ur a hardcore guy u can ramp up all the difficulty options). Buy this game if you want a fun sandbox fighting experience making matchups between the terminator and hitler.
Now for the guys that want the full review:
The big selection of superstars is amazing since the old timers like randy savage to john cena! You can even play as the terminator.
The career mode is way better then people believe it to be. In my example I created Adolf Hitler, a Heel wrestler, who will gain all of the popularity of the WWE. The character creation is amazing (if you want you can look at my wwe hitler screenshots) and the entrance creator is too! Going around about 2 hours I finally chose Mr.Perfect's theme and mixed movements with Colin Cassady and Paul Wight (wierd mix IKR). And after that I spent one more hour making my choice of movements that I think Hitler would fight with. As you can see you have insane customization oppurtunities with these but also with the skills atributes and abilities of the character. You will have to manage points into upgrading your character being many upgrades important from stamina strength and speed. If you are lazy like me you can use a boost to rise some atributes to the max until your overall is 90 but if you like a challenge do not rise this as it will make the game faster and easier. Another plus about the career is that you will have many hours of playtime if you are a completionist like me.
The showcase mode is also very interesting, specially if you are a WWE enthusiast. My favorite "campaign" is certanly the hall of fame one, as it goes around some of the best wrestlers and most interesting feuds like the rikishi vs the rock and randy savage vs jake the snake.
The online is really fun but bewary, in singleplayer the bots play fair but in online I have had myself several times thrown out of the ring incapacitated before the count of 10 and then disqualified. Most of the online players want to WIN and not have a fun match. If you want a more fun multiplayer experience get a friend to play with you locally, if you have a xbox controller you can play one the controler and your friend can play in your keyboard!
The community created items are also a really fun adition as they bring new content to your WWE experience, since new fun created characters like mario and luigi, to new logos and anything you can imagine. You can also create your own and upload them, and if you want to see yourself as a wrestling abomination you can upload a photo of you or anybody else to morph it into the face of a wrestler that you create.
The universe mode isn't something I really enjoy but if you want a more extense sandbox experience then single matches or the career then by all means dive into this and enjoy it.
Concluding my review I think that anyone that enjoys a good fighting game or is a WWE fan should buy this game. It is fun in almost everyway and most criticisms you see in the reviews are nitpicking because this game is a fairly well optimized game and there are almost no glitches or bugs. So what are you waiting for BUY IT.

I'll thumbs this one up, but to be honest, it's more of an average rather than a wholehearted recommendation.
Basically: what you see is what you get. Simple survival elements where your best bet is to charge a punch and then hit the enemy, to conserve ammo. Everything is scarce (which is good) and has barely any variety (which is not so good).
Main advantage of this game is the story element. You have to navigate a train through an increasingly bleak landscape. This pitch is pretty powerful, and motivates to finish the levels (which always consist of finding a four-digit code). It may just be the next zombie apocalypse game (or not...haven't finished it yet), but the notes, the people you meet and the atmosphere really makes it believable.
The game itself is put a bit below that, though. Yes, it's purposely hard (but not insanely so), but that's not the problem. It's that it's so repetitive. Every level has you searching for a code (which has you basically follow the trail). Then there's a bit of a train section that is pretty much a minigame of 'keep the voltage okay' and 'feed the passengers'. This part is more an interactive cutscene, to be honest.
End result: I'd say about 6 or 6.5 out of 10. It does what it sets out to do, doesn't have mayor gripes (to my opinion) but nothing spectacular going for it either.
I got this in a bundle, so I got the value's worth out of it (and am still playing). Can't say if I would want to pay full price for it, though. :-\

First of all I would like to start off by saying that I have played approximately 20 hours of the game.  This has basically put my most of the way through the campaign.  My background with the game started earlier this summer when I got invited into the closed beta.  (Played about 6-8 hours)  The very first problem with this game is that you can't just use steam, on top of steam you have to use UPlay(Only works about half the time and takes forever to get into the game)  The next problem is that once you get into the game (assuming you have an internet connection) it tends to be rather buggy.  There seems to be an issue with optimization because my computer is rather capable and more than meets the minimum and recommended specs.  As with most AAA titles lately if you have AMD hardware you definitely need to beware  (my laptop with Nvidia hardware runs the game much better)  The main problem seems to be around the cities(Lots of buildings and poor optimization).  All in all this fits together to be a rather poor title but the one thing that keeps nagging me is the physics of the game itself.  I could probably get past the online all the time (Wasn't explicitly stated that you have to be) or even the sometimes poor framerates.  But the poor and might I add inconsistent physics and handling between cars is terrible.  Now I can personally say that I have never driven most of the vehicles in-game, but last time I checked a 600-900 horse Ferrari should be able to drift much better than an off-road Chevy Silverado(Actually have driven this).  However this is not the case all the muscle cars that people have been sliding around for years and years are impossible to drift.  The only game mode that seems remotely realistic is that of circuit racing.  I wasn't expecting this to be Forza Motorsport realistic but I at least expected it to feel something like Dirt 3 or Grid (Something sim-cadeish).  Finnally about the physics we are looking at the terrible bug where sometimes you will be cruising along and hit the same curb or patch of dirt you have hit 100 times with no consequence and now all of a sudden you are tossed into the air and are placed miles behind your competitor.  All in all I am extremely dissapointed with the crew as I have been waiting for a U.S. playground for cars for years.  Guess I am still waiting.
