I won't go into too much detail on the game mechanics, it does a pretty good job explaining that already.   I will go over the things I don't like about it, but most of that is just my opinion and not the reason I don't recommend the game.  The only objectively bad thing about this game, and the singular reason I can't recommend it, are the crazy long laod times.
The meat of this game is taking your troops to battle against other players maps.  You battle one player, get some cards, and immediately go into another, over and over and over.  You will do this hundreds to thousands of tmes (depending on how long it takes you to get bored) and every single time you will sit through a full 5 second load time to load up their map, and a full 5 second load time to load back into your map.  With matches that last about a minute and a half and the limited number of assets and the small map sizes this is completly inexcusible.  I can understand a 1 to 2 second laod up to connect to another player's map, but not the load time to get back to your own.  EA is not the culprit here, this game has been out for over 2 years and should be streamlined to a mirror finish by now.  When I can play Elder Scrolls Online or Black Desert and they can load up to their overworld from a transition from a dungeon faster than this can load up it's pittly little maps, something is wrong.
Other than that the only complaints I have I can admit are just my opinion and others might consider features.  For instance I find it odd that you spend your in game currency primarily on upgrading your base defenses, and you can only use randomly given cards to upgrade your troops.  When you consider there is really no reason to upgrade your base, as you lose nothing but dog-tags (I have no idea what they even do) if you lose, and you gain nothing if you win, it would seem to me you should be spending your currency on increasing your troops stats.  This would give you a steady stream of increasing your power as you played, rather than sometimes going for hours on end without getting a better card only to suddenly get an epic rare card that boosts you significantly.  This would also prevent you from running into the situation I found myself in.  The first 12 levels or so you can pretty much skate by, then it starts unlocking the mid tier troops and it becomes a bit more difficult.  It costs a one time payment of in game currency to unlock these troops as you get to the appropriate level.  Unfortunately I had spent all my money on base upgrades and couldn't afford to unlock these new troops until I grind some.  Okay no problem, except for some reason the match generator stops giving an appreciatible difference between the easy (one skull) and normal (two skulls) maps.  Sometimes the one skull maps would actually be listed as more difficult then the two skull maps.  Now at this point I had a backlog of attack cards (randomly given at the end of matches) because I was primarly grinding on easy maps that barely required my attention before now, so I could brute force my way through if I wished.  However I can easily see someone backed into a corner where they are out of attack cards, don't have money to unlock stronger troops, and unable to really continue without losing a lot of matches before they finally made enough to get something stronger.

Single sentence review: The zaniest and most challenging restaurant sim slash time management game you will ever come across on Steam.
Cook Serve Delicious is an incredibly fun, potentially maddening cooking/restaurant "sim" - although using that word to describe it is doing a disservice. While you do indeed play owner and choose the menu, check your emails and so on (some of the emails are hilarious by the way!), the core focus of the gameplay boils down to you as chef. From open to close, it's your job to multi-task your customer's orders, using keyboard hotkeys to manage up to eight (!) dishes simultaneously. Cook each one with no mistakes and get them out on time to rack up your combo, win bets, unlock cool stuff and eventually showcase your talents in front of a culinary secret society! I'm not joking.
Now. This game may look like another Diner Dash, but considering that some dishes use nearly every single letter (A-Z) on the keyboard plus the arrow keys and space bar, this game can reach a level of difficulty which will have even the most hardcore time-management fans palpitating. Combine this with a realistic peak time mechanic, your food choices having a PROFOUND effect on how the day will pan out, needing to compelete chores simultaneously alongside your cooking to stop bad publicity, navigating ever more complex bets from Crazy Dave or an orange robot to boost funding to your restaurant, and suddenly needing to respond to a potential girlfriend/boyfriend's crappy chat-up lines in the middle of a five second flash-fry...
... yeah. This game can get as hectic and random as all hell, but it is one of the richest and most challenging time-management games I have ever played and I cannot recommend it enough. I would especially recommend it if you have never felt challenged by a time management game before. Too many games in that genre go down the route of being too easy, doing lots of hand-holding or very quickly running out of new features to keep you interested. Cook Serve Delicious manages to deliver on all of those aspects while remaining colourful and wacky enough to stop you from throwing your laptop at a concrete wall.
Bon appétit!

Short version: This is no different to last year. The only change is now you have a set amount of reversals (that you regain over time) to avoid the ridiculous amont of reversals of yesteryear. Unless you REALLY love Showcase or somehow weren't bored of the Career or Universe mode's repetition, you won't miss this. It's probably better than what THQ would still be producing, but 2K are just like WWE - phoning it in now they have no competition. Why try?
Long version:
Exactly as I said in my review of last year's game, there are moments of huge potential hidden in here.
The movement is so fluid nowadays that things look a notch more realistic (like playing a tag match as The Outsiders, and Hall slips out of a move and pushes the guy in your direction as you run up and deliver Nash's Big Boot finisher, beautiful).
The tech is advanced enough to have physics for satisfying impacts on weapons and through tables now too (X-Pac's Super X-Factor onto a ladder or table you conveniently laid below is a bit more satisfying now, but not as much as setting up a table next to a ladder, fighting on top of the ladder, and powerbombing the guy off it in exactly the right place where you laid out the table, which you may or may not have set on fire beforehand.
But it still needs a lot of tweaking. They're clearly aiming for the more thought-provoking game we once had around 2007, with stamina and limb damage and how it affected your moves, but they're still not there yet. Even when they do add things, there's no tutorial and no real manual so people are tasked to find out themselves what icons mean or how to do things.
Another notable thing is finisher spamming and no-selling. Spamming finishers and kicking out of them has become cool. This has been replicated in the game, and it's just as ridiculous. Your matches can go 10 minutes too long because Rusev kicked out of his 10th F-5. It makes the health bars meaningless.
Unfortunately the graphics have always been a generation behind. There's been no major graphical overhaul in this version, it's still cartoony, and the Divas are still creepy as hell and have ♥♥♥♥ed up Joker smiles. Funnily enough, Steph finally looks a lot like Steph now - she seems to have a face that's been impossible to recreate in digital form thus far.

I always enjoyed Showcase mode (and it s predecessor Legends of WrestleMania), but it's not very interactive now. Here's how it goes now:
1) You start a match
2) 5-minute cutscene of entrances and opening moments of match, very slow-paced.
3) Get given an objective as you start the match (e.g. irish whip your opponent, do your finisher, throw them out the ring), this can take anything from 3 seconds to a minute or two.
4) Very slow-paced cutscene plays of what happened next in the match, this can be a few minutes, because they've got to show every second! You've now been sat here 10 minutes and only played for 2 of those minutes at most.
4b) Sometimes there's a QTE, which means you spend 20 seconds watching the buttons waiting to see which flashes, so now you're not even watching the cutscenes!
5) Go back to 3 until match is over.
This is combined with the familiar half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥unemotional commentary from J.R. He and King are slightly more believable, but now just sound mildly interested. I picture them sitting on the sofa, feet up in front of the TV and commentating on the match to each other.
My Career mode is where you create a guy and climb the ranks. In the last game it was just a load of meaningless matches, and it's not any different this time around. Again there's huge potential here. When I reached rank #1 for Kevin Owen's NXT title, I made sure my bosses (the game) gave me my shot by taking out Owens. He was having a match, so as he was doing his title pose during his entrance, I appeared into camera shot behind him, the crowd went mental, and I laid him out.
When I got promoted to Raw, I needed to fast track myself to the title, so I made a statement by going after the #1 contender for the world title: Brock Lesnar! He was having a match, so as he was doing his little pose during his entance, I appeared into camera shot...
Ah, you see where I'm going. That's the problem. You can go after people, make statements, do your thing, but there's only one way to do it, it's the same old♥♥♥♥♥♥ and there's no intricate storylines. Just as in Universe Mode, two guys beat each other up each week then have a PPV match. Same every month. Even if something major happens, like joining The Authority, it's like nothing happened, just a random cutscene that played.
The unintentional highlight of this mode is the promos, delivered awfully and eerily similar to one of the Family Guy voices. "Nothing but net."
Every week you're very awkwardly interviewed by Renee Young. She asks you about a guy, you stare silently at each other for 10 seconds, then you get a choice of reply. A lot of the time these choices are vague, or it's a meaningless choice. You'll randomly turn heel for not trashing your bosses (The Authority) in your first month in the job as an NXT jobber, or you'll pick a harmless looking response and your guy will insult the fans or something.
There's nothing sophisticated though. All you're doing is saying if you want to feud with a guy and if you want to be heel or face. Every ♥♥♥♥ing week. Then do random matches and see random cutscenes, the same ones you've seen every month.
Universe Mode is completely unchanged. It and My Career are pretty much the same now. I've seen a lot of people say they stopped playing Career when they realised it was the same as Universe.

Originally, I started playing because I wanted to test the gaming capabilities of my school-required laptop. Then I couldn't stop. The efforts of making a cute, engaging, kid-friendly game resulted in something pretty relaxing for a jaded twenty-something like myself. Things are kept PG and that includes player interactions/chat/player names. It's a nice break from the usual toxic wastelands of other MMOs.
There's an Animal Crossing quality to the overall game experience with the cute characters, wide variety of costumes, home (and yard) decorating, and minigames. Everyone in Amazing World is an animal, though- players get to choose from several different bases at the beginning and give them a basic outfit before setting off.  Despite the simplicity of many early clothing items, the 10 equip slots combined with crafting and quest rewards enable players to create their own unique looks.
Skill levels stop for free players at skill level 5. You can still level up your character through fishing and multiplayer minigames but quest givers will eventually stop interacting with you and will have a little "Members Only" bubble above them. It should be noted that I clocked in 5 hours and still had 4 skills to "finish." Membership is $3.99 per month and opens up the rest of the quests, lets skills continue leveling, gives access to buying certain shop items, and gives you a cosmic bear character to play as.
The home/yard decorating can be a little wonky. It works on a grid system but items seemingly don't want to be too close to each other. I admittedly haven't put much time into that aspect of the game.

This is a great digital CCG for Hearthstone players looking for less randomness and more interesting strategy.
This is also a great game for Magic the Gathering players looking for a less expensive version of what they already love with a fully competent online client with a good UI.
This game plays very similarly to Magic the Gathering. Units attack all at once and blockers are selected by the defending player. There are fast spells (instants) which can be played during your opponents turn. There are several keywords and tutoring effects which are designed to take advantage of the digital format to create opportunities for clever plays without having to keep track of tokens or constantly shuffle your deck.
It is possible to play the game without spending real money. Everything can be bought with in-game currency gained through winning games vs real or AI opponents. There is also a draft mode in which you keep all cards drafted which will let you build your collection quickly, especially if you're able to win consistently.
Tl;dr if you're looking for a strategic upgrade from Hearthstone or a digital evolution of Magic the Gathering look no further.

I like the concept of Receiver, vs the genre of Modern Military shooters, where the protagonist is always steady under pressure, can reload almost instantly, his gun never jams and has nearly magazines.
Recevier feels like a trip to the gun range, where you are given a randomized pistol, and told: "Here, figure this out. GL HF."
Just figuring out the sequence of "Click off the safety, check the chamber, eject the magazine, holster the pistol (if necessary), fill the magazine (if necessary), ready your pistol, insert the magazine and rack the slide" takes time, but is very rewarding. Sometimes the randomized nature of the spawn points means you're trying to do all this while flying taser drones are patrolling the skies above you, or worse, actively hunting you down and zapping you. Game over.
That leads into the story of Receiver, which while basic, adds background and urgency to game... the player takes the role of what can be described as a near future, cyber punk, noir detective.. searching rooms for tapes that provide information and ammunition to stay alive against the constant threat of spinning stationary gun turrets and flying, seeking taser bots, both called Kill Drones.
I agree that I would love to see these gun mechanics carried over to the survival horror genre... adding another layer of tension to hording and scrounging bullets, avoiding monsters, and fumbling to top off a magazine and ready your weapon while a Silent Hill nurse or Resident Evil zombie comes lurching at you to nibble on your succulent flesh.
TL/DR:  Matrix like, minimalist room clearing and gun handling simulator. 9/10.

Excellent game mechanics. Better than a point and click because there's little aimless point and clicking and better than a sidescroller shooter because of the exploration element. Gameplay is fluid.
The game's music, sounds and graphics go a long way to immerse the player in its somber atmosphere. Its design language is coherent, never deviating from its purpose but is always fresh, as the stations have all different themes and game resources are only re-used if the object portrayed is the same. This train's next stop is to impress your senses.
The motive power behind the game, however, is the story. And this game tells its story through the eyes of a man that has little influence in the world around him. The events that happen are not deliberately told to you, there are only clues, and those clues come from comments and remarks your passengers make, paper notes in billboards and fragments of newspapers and eventual radio transmissions you happen to listen during your work.
Many people regard this as bad because they feel powerless or opressed by those circumstances but this very overwhelming is what makes this game stand from most others. Playing it makes you feel overwhelmed. The story makes no sense. People are going insane everywhere, there are no reliable news sources, bombs are falling -but are not launched- and the government has no clue what to do.
In the middle of this stands you, a train driver, doing exactly what you have been doing for the past years of your life: driving trains and filling paperwork.
How many games do you remember made you search online for its backstory? As with Alfred Hitchcock's The Birds, lots of questions remain unanswered after completion but this is -precisely- the very definition of "suspense". According to the Cambridge Dictionary: "A feeling of excitement or anxiety while waiting for something uncertain to happen".
Buy the thing and delight yourself with this Cyrillic masterpiece.

Receiver is a unique, unforgiving, fps.
I should start by warning you that the graphics and sound design to this game are okay at best, and given that this was part of a game jam, that is understandable. The real attraction here is the gameplay.
It is unique in that I have never before seen an fps that goes into such detail with the gun mechanics. There are lots of controls to learn, so you may find yourself with the help menu open for a while. However, as you become accustomed to the game you begin to learn the controls, making the game more fast paced.
The aim of the game is to locate randomly scattered tapes that tell the story, while avoiding enemies. This game can be hard to get into because the enemies operate on a one-hit-kill basis, but that is again quite refreshing in a world where many games let you take entire clips of ammo straight to the chest, only to auto-recover health after a few seconds.
This is also a perma-death fps. You get killed, you have to start collecting tapes from scratch. You are also assigned a weapon randomly each time you spawn into a world. This can get a bit annoying, but it is all part of the challenge.
If you're a gun fanatic, I can't vouch for the accuracy of the game, but you may enjoy this, as well as any fans of both difficult rogue-likes and fps games.

Reciever is a short game with fun gun mechanics. It was initially made in about 42 hours or so for a competition, and it shows. The environemnts are repeated heavily, the textures are bare, and it feels kinda cobbled together. That being said, the gun mechanics are its main selling point, and you're probably not thinking of buying it for its minimalistic style. So, let's address that aspect of the game.
The gun mechanics are very complex and realistic, and unique because of that. Now - to be clear - I've never owned nor fired a gun. However, I do have a pretty decent grasp on the basics of how modern ballistic weapons work, as should most people. The game portrays them accurately as far as i know, but someone that actually owns a firearm might say otherwise. Reloading the weapon is a complicated multi-step process, priming the weapon must be done for it to fire, and you even have to turn of the safety. There is also no ammo counter, you have to count shots or look at your clip for a vague idea of how many bullets you have left. You have to make sure a round is actually chambered, and cocking the gun while a bullet is in the chamber already ejects the perfectly good, unused round that you then have to pick up in embarrassment. If you're looking at buying this game for the mechanics of it, I'd say it's probably worth it.
However, if you want a game that is more than just a bare-bones proof of concept slapped together over a short amount of time and sold on steam, then you might wish to look elsewhere. While it's not expensive by any stretch of the imagination, it is - however - still 5 bucks. While I've derived a lot of enjoyment from messing around with it - as it's a rogue like - there's a distinct lack of a real story, varied enemies, guns - even through there's 3 now - and other content you'd expect from a normal game. It's good, but if you don't think the shooting mechanics are interesting enough to warrent a purchase, then you should probably think hard about whether or not it's worth it. I won't tell you that you won't end up liking it - because you might - but know that when you get into this thing it's not to reach reality A.

First off, yes this is a "Walking Simulator". So if you already made up your mind that you hate those types of games where you cant die and its focused on simply unravelling the story, then this isnt for you.
Still here? Great, because Gone Home is a fantastic game/experience that should not be missed for those itching for a great story. But i'm not going to tell you what the story is about. Suffice to say, you come home after being away for a few years to an empty home. While waiting, you poke around the house, and discover why everyones missing, and the stories hidden inside the house.
To put it simply, the story is incredible in the way it is told to you, and part of the fun is the mystery and intrigue of discovering why everyone is missing. Unlike most games, Gone Home felt genuinely real to me. Terrific voice work helped to cement the experience, and the result is one of the most involving stories i have been a part of in years. (and i loved The Last of Us and Mass Effect)
Its sad to see such hate being thrown at the game because of its subject matter, and its "lack of gameplay'. Yes, there are no death states in the game, no bosses, no fighting mechanic. You walk, explore and interact. Which is not a bad thing at all. The only downside i have to warn you about, is the game length. Its 3 hours for 20 bucks. Personally, that is overpriced, so i reccomend getting it at a sale. But it is a must play game.

This is a WWII class-based shooter game pitting the allies against the axis, only with a twist: you get to play as dinosaurs. It's very much like TF2 in that you are free to switch between teams and classes and you have to complete a certain objective (most of the time it's a deathmatch). It's a fun concept and while this isn't a perfect execution of it, it does a good enough job of giving you your daily dose of dinosaur action.
Pros:
1. Variety of classes - The game has 7 playable dinosaurs and 9 human classes, all of them providing just enough variety to keep the game entertaining. You can play as a velociraptor and assassinate your enemies, be a Dilophosaurus and throw goats and humans around, or if you're lucky, a walking death machine that is T-rex.
2. Casual and entertaining - This game is good for when you're bored and looking to drop by for a quick game or two before you move on to something else. The game might feel unfair at times with how easy you can die but it's still immensely satisfying when you maul someone as a dinosaur (unfortunately, most dinosaurs are only playable by axis team).
Cons:
1. One downside that comes with these niche games is that the playerbase is low. However, there are just enough people for 2-3 servers so if you're up for a couple of quick rounds you don't have to worry.
2. Another criticism is that some of the larger dinosaur models can get stuck in narrow corridors which makes it hard to navigate them. I've heard other people comment that the controls can be finicky, especially for models that move fast.
The whole premise of the game has a lot of potential but after a few hours of playtime the maps seem repetitive and gameplay can feel dull. More frequent updates and maybe the addition of brand new dinosaurs could definitely make the game feel more refreshing again. It seems like the developers have released a couple of updates with different game modes but unfortunately the game is in a difficult position of not having enough playerbase that can fully experience these new contents.
Overall, though, I'd still rate this game pretty high. It's not a top tier shooter game (far from it), but it's definitely entertaining and the dinosaurs make it all worth it. It is a good break from all the competitive games you might be playing. I'd recommend getting this game during sales when its price drops by 50~60%.
tl;dr: Fun casual game where you can play as Nazi dinosaurs. Entertaining but can feel repetitive if played a lot. Recommend getting it on sale.

I bought this on sale with all the DLC for next to nothing.
That being said, I actually enjoyed it. Do I see it being a full price title? No, not really. But I do see it being a fun experience in its own right. It's not the best, it's not the hottest title ever, it's not one that people will be talking about for the next decade; but it's overall it's okay. The game's biggest downfall? The open world.
Before people burn me at the stake for saying something against open world, it's not that open world in general is bad. But the open world in this game is small, and mostly empty. Could it have been better if this game hadn't gone through development hell just to make it out at all? Probably. But as it stands all the open world really is is just running to your next mission and shooting some cameras to instill unrest.
The part where the game really shines is the DLC. If the entire game had been like that, it would have been a much more enjoyable experience. The story was more driven and scripted to remove the most boring parts of the standalone story. And your character actually speaks, wowie! But they're very short, sadly. Each DLC is basically one mission.
Beyond that, I had no issues. No glitches, no hangs ups, not anything else to gripe about. And underneath that, I still found myself having fun, running around capturings towns and shooting Norks. It's a mindless timekiller, but one I didn't hate.
If it's on sale, pick it up and play it. You won't be impressed, but you might be pleasantly surprised that the reviews that call it the worst game ever are greatly exaggerated. I applaud the devs for sticking to a game that seemed outright doomed, and the DLC ending even made me kind of wish there'd be another... But that won't be happening anytime soon (or ever).

like Homefront: The Revolution, whose publishers unfortunately give them terribly botched launches. The pressure on a dev team to deliver the finished product, especially with games like Homefront that have had a very long, twisty development history, is immense and often responsible for the botched launch and/or the parcelling-off of content into DLC. So as a potential buyer of this game, reading the Steam reviews before you purchase, the first thing you need to do is divorce yourself from all the anger and bitterness surrounding its flatulent launch, and examine the game as it stands now (June 2017 as I write this). And as it stands now, it’s an absolutely brilliant open-world FPS, with beautiful CryEngine graphics, smooth animations, detailed textures and fantastic lighting, and a really solid-feeling set of controls. Most excitingly (for us newcomers) and terribly (for those who were burned at launch), it’s immensely good fun to play too.
a twitchy Call of Honour: Medalfield man-shoot, but something in-between all those sugar-addled rage-baiters and the more ponderous ARMA-like milsims. The weapons have a nice, hefty feel, and the differences between a Battle Rifle modded with a muzzle brake and a short/mid-range scope and an unmodified Battle Rifle are quite apparent. The base selection of weapons is quite limited, but each one can be converted into 3 different sub-weapons. For example, the crossbow can become a blunderbuss or a flamethrower, the pistol an SMG, the assault rifle an LMG and so on. Each variant is then modifiable with different scopes, muzzles and grips or bipods. On top of that, there’s a really fun range of craftable explosives and ‘hacking devices’ that can be thrown, planted, disguised as teddy bears or driven around on RC cars with tiny cameras attached. Some of these tie in to the different approaches you can take to various enemy compounds and blocked-off bonus areas, and each one is fully satisfying to use.
around a dozen or more different urban zones, ranging from Really Large to Bloody Huge. It’s mostly post-war destruction and very Fallout (not least in the way you collect random junk from rubbish bins and old sofas to help you build your Molotovs and grenades, etc), which is no bad thing really, especially as rendered in CryEngine. And despite the general theme of guerrilla fighting amidst the dusty ruins of broken houses and office buildings, rubble-filled streets and over-grown rail and dockyards, there is a surprising amount of variety between the zones too. As the story progresses through each new area, it’s sort of a nice treat to see what new scenery you’ll be crawling over, under and through each time. The zone maps are filled with icons representing different optional activities, special items to explore for and various story and side-story objectives. A zone is ‘completed’ (although you can still go back to it at any point) once all of its main objectives have been achieved, i.e. capturing various enemy strongholds, often by force, but also by completing simple environmental puzzles and exploring and climbing.
there is a very nicely done day/night cycle, and the enemies’ MGS-style awareness of you and their minimap-visible alertness levels are significantly influenced by the time of day. Speaking of the enemies, they’re generally pretty sharp. They see you, they’ll organise and chase you down. They’ll flank you, encircle you, try to sneak up on you and do all sorts of interesting things. Many’s the time I crouched quietly in a corner healing or re-loading, only to watch in horror as the red dots on my mini-map fanned out and zeroed in on me using routes I wouldn’t have thought a computer game mob would be smart enough to use. They’re a good challenge on normal difficulty, on hard they might be really tough.
but ultimately not as interesting as the motion capture and voice acting, which are simply captivating. There are only very, very few pre-rendered moments in which you just sit there watching, but the rest of the time it can feel quite close to actually ‘really being there’. Good stuff, in other words, and it really does help buoy the story along. Where you can really see the aforementioned publisher clock-watching and content-chopping is in the fact that the game ends on something of a muted victory – in fact, the entire story is quite intimate, but happens to be set in a larger context – and that only by playing through the 2nd and 3rd DLC do you really get a meaty conclusion to that larger context. The 1st DLC acts as a direct prequel to where the game begins, so that if you play all 3 DLC and the main game, you do then feel as though the whole world of Homefront (literally) opens up into something truly cinematic – a Kelly’s Heroes or Dirty Dozen for modern times.
because a lot of the original outrage was based on glitches, bugs and errors – the game as it stands now played perfectly for me. It ran beautifully smoothly at my desktop resolution of 1920x1080 and never crashed or froze once. And I can count the number of visual glitches I saw on one hand. This is with 34 hours played to complete the main game and all DLC, on a five-year-old i5 3.10 GHz CPU, 16 Gb of good RAM, and an ancient nVidia GTX 750 (yes, I am a terrible human being). Of course, performance and the appearance of bugs and glitches is mostly subjective, so the fact that it ran well for me doesn’t mean (obviously) that all the people for whom it didn’t run well were imagining things.
part UbiSoft Map ’em-Up, Homefront: The Revolution also has buckets and buckets of its own charm and good feels. The DLC is uniformly excellent, so if you can get that too, it’s a huge bonus. Most importantly though, and the question I always ask at the end of my reviews, is it worth the price? Well, if you’ve read this entire thing without skipping ahead to the end to tell me what an absolute idiot I am, the answer might surprise you: Not completely, no. I couldn’t recommend it for EUR 60, or whatever it debuted at. And in spite of the enormous fun I had with it for almost 40 hours, I can’t in good faith recommend it for the EUR 30 it’s listed at now, here on Steam (even though the production values appear to be sky-high and I’m sure Deep Silver would like to recoup them). Honestly, and I’m not even sure why, but this feels more like a EUR 20 game. I think that if the DLC were integrated parts of the whole, 30 would be reasonable, but without them the base game is a good story that starts too slowly and confusingly, and ends with a TV-budget bang. But the good news is, you can find it on most non-Steam sites for around 20, and sometimes even 10, anyway. So if you do, pounce on it and you won’t regret it.

This game has several flaws, but overall it was fun to play and I would recommend it.
PRO
Good FPS action with reasonable AI opponents and the ability to recruit supporting fighters. There is no squad control, but the supporting 'good guys' do actually help out with raids on major enemy installations making reasonable choices. I  like single player FPS games, so this lack of complexity (squad control) made it easy to enjoy the fight and balance the odds when the enemy had a lot of troops, without worrying about the admin involved in leading a team.
Nice story, bit far fetched (USA conquered by N Korea), but once you get beyond that the story links the missions together nicely and there are about the right number of cut scenes to drive the narrative along.
Easy to die - unlike many FPS games, you are not an invincible tank that absorbs multiple hits while the enemy troops collaps around you. A few solid hits and you are down. So preserve your health, use cover, and keep your head down. I liked that.
There are a few puzzles to solve, mainlly how to acecss some buildings to get a reward. I enjoyed these, there are some clues, and working them out was a nice distraction from the fighting.
CONS
Two major flaws. The game progresses through a number of sectors, basically the task in each one is the same, capturing strong points and carrying out acts of sabotage. This is a bit repetitive. The sceenery changes between sectors which helps and some have more and some less resources. But there could have been more variety in the tasks required acrosss the regions.
The game allows you to customise weapons, but switching between configurations is not something to do in a fire fight. The interface is horrible and and you are vulnerable to enemy fire while doing it. So this basically excludes this option once the shooting starts, so you can't fully configure your load out to match the task.
If you go into this game expecting a demanding, story driven adventure (e.g. Far Cry), it falls a bit short. However as a fun FPS, with some interesting characters and quirky weapons, and a interesting backing story, it is a lot of fun.

This program has turned into a fantastic survival, city builder game.  It's not about your survival, it's about a group of people who were banished from their homeland, probably caused by an invasion or religion.  They're not bad people, they were just pushed out and with your help they may survive and prosper or die trying.
The game has always been good, right from the start but with new modding allowed it has become a leader of this genre.
You can make the game into whatever you wish, easy, hard or extreamely hard.  Personally I hate snow and winters so since the mods came out,  I start my towns in a very mild climate, where they don't have to worry about freezing to death.
The citizens get married, have kids, grow old and die.  You can't control individual citizens but you do control what they do as a group.  You can send them out to gather resources, build houses, businesses, schools etc.  You can assign jobs by telling the program what laborer is needed and a citizen is assigned to fulfil that request.
Every decision you make has consequences, good or bad, so you must plan ahead or your citizens will starve, get sick or suffer from some other disaster and your population will plummet.
It's challenging and fun.  I highly reccomend it.

So much better on PC than PS4!  That said, I had tons of hours when I played this on my console, yet I stopped because the Playstation network timeouts made it frustrating!  Since I've started over, here are some tips that might make it more enjoyable...
1 - Forget worrying about PvP at early levels.
Your early objective should be to build a simple base that can withstand a 3 minute CPU attack.
Once you get your base to be able to "auto defend" for 3 minutes, you can just let it grind in the background for munitions.  Yes, this can get tiresome early on, but if you are working on other projects, listening to music, watching YouTube, etc...it makes it easier to slowly build up and UPGRADE your Sniper Towers, Machine Gun Bunkers and Walls.  If you have time to be attack other players for cards, bonuses, etc...you will get there faster!
2 - In order to get your base to be able to "auto defend" for 4/5/6/7 minutes...work on strengthening your Grunts!
You can do this by using PERKS to add health, damage, fire rate, accuracy, etc. In addition, you can attack 1 Skull player bases by just spamming grunts.  The SPECIALIST medal will help reduce cooldown by 25% and the SURVIVALIST medal will add 20% health (work on this once you get to 15+ level.  When attacking player bases with grunts only, add in a couple of Medics and you can hammer out more 3 Star Wins!
3 - Don't worry about the loot crates that you have to scrap because you don't have keys or gold.
Remember these items are just there to push you into spending money.  People that pay to play are impatient, you can BEAT the developers by grinding and let the impatient players pay for your eventual free content that gets added over time.
If you want a real sense of accomplishment...then let other players pay for YOUR free content!  Regardless of your philosophy about in game transactions, you can have a TON of fun playing this without spedning money.  If you focus on extending your "auto defend" for CPU attacks, you will get 100+ hours of free entertainment.  When I eclipsed the 30 minute mark on auto defend on PS4 that seemed to be the end of the grind, but considering that there are all the medals and heroes to get...you can probably expect another 200+ hours!

While it looks like a Hearthstone clone, Eternal has really surprised me with deceptively strategical gameplay, and in my opinion, is a VERY nice change from the aggressive, non-chess minded game that Hearthstone has become.
Eternal has a lot of the same mechanics you would find in other card-based RPGs.  You have minions that cost a certain amount of mana, they have health and attack power, you have spells that cost mana, and abilities/weapons you can equip minions with that will boost their stats.  However, rather than gaining more mana every turn, you have to use sigil cards that belong to one of 5 "factions" that will increase your mana pool permanently while giving you influence in the faction it displays.  You need to have enough Fire influence, for example, in order to use some of the stronger minions of that faction, while also expending the needed mana to summon them.
There are lots of other interesting mechanics such as Fast Spells and using your minions to block attacks on your opponent's turn that really bring more depth to this game.  Deck building is also huge, since you can make whatever deck you like while mixing and matching cards from any faction.  You do not select a "class" character to play with and thus are not limited to "class" specific cards, you simply use any cards you like and work for you.
The graphics are all good and very smooth, with one complaint being the UI not being so friendly at times.  Also the game is pretty quiet compared to Hearthstone since the minions aren't voiced.  But the game is definitely worth a try, and it's free with some pay options to unlock card packs.

The Crew
The crew is a large, open world environment with lots of multiplayer aspects and huge POTENTIAL. But from there, it’s all a bit downhill. I bought it because I wanted a driving game where you could customise your car, get chased by cops, play with friends even for a nice little drive down a motorway at 200km/h.
I got what I asked for, but not what I paid for. I get my custom car, which then gets pulled away from me for mission specific cars. Now, I’m in a mission with an unfamiliar car and AI designed to be perfect. I know they are. Get the perk which shows you the lines to a race mission, I almost guarantee that the AI in 1st will be perfect to that line. Have all the skill you want, if you don’t take shortcuts or have the better car, you won’t win and if that’s the case, don’t even bother going for a perfect score. I know there are people out there who are pros and know every corner, every braking point and every shortcut. I can only imagine how much time they spent and how much sass from the NPCs they got. And then there are the regular AI cars. Not the race ones, just the normal run-of-the-mill pedestrian cars. God help if you’re going for a high score and one of those come along and pull into the lane you’re in about 50m from you.♥♥♥♥♥♥happens, but not to the AI racers.
Then the authorities. Hands up all those who love a good chase scene. I do, and I thought “Yeah, lots of road and different terrain, this should be good.” Oh sweet innocence. First, find a patrol car and then crash into stuff. Problem. Find one. I’d hate to believe that there are only two patrol cars in New York. This game had a lot of potential, but in the end its just a giant failure.
Graphics: The game looks really nice and runs pretty smoothly when other players arent near you, i am able to maintain a constant 50-60 FPS, my system stays cool and i dont get stuttering too often unless im driving over 200 MPH. The enviroment is attractive and makes exploring the huge map even more worthwhile, the waters not the most attractive but its not an issue since you should be spending most your time staring at the road or the cars.
Customization: Theres enough to make your car unique and the game allows every spec to be different so your car can look completly different in street then it does in performance. However Raid and Cicuit spec have almost no custumization available and dirt spec is sometimes lacking as well. Also higher end cars ussually have less then cheaper cars meaning aventadors and vipers ussually look identical while mustangs and camaros can be heavily customized.
Map: Its large, it takes about 30-60 mins to to drive between 2 major areas (ex. Detroit to Miami, Maine to Texas, NY to LA) mostly highway averaging around 160MPH. Most areas look pretty accurate and you can ussually guess where you are if you have seen the place in real life, however many areas are located FAR from where they should be and some are sized quite oddly, for example Salem MA is up in Maine and Miami is most of florida.
Cars: This is one area where the game fails miserably, while it does have some great cars the balance is horrible and very unrealistic, mini cooper is one of the fastest cars in the game, bentley continental outruns sklyine gtrs and vipers with no issues, no point buying an expensive dirt spec since the ford focus is pretty much the best for dirt, mustangs are faster, better handling, and have better traction then the 370z, the murcielago feels like its on ice all the time ect. Many cars cant be put into specs that make perfect sense to be available, most supercars cant be circuit, f150 cant be raid spec, golf gti cant be anything but street spec, high end cars can ussually only be performance spec and thats it. AI uses vehicles in specs that you cant for example circuit spec trucks, Some cars are just pointless like the golf gti and  jeep cherokee, and others are so expensive its not worth getting since there are faster cars for half the price. Also when theres only about 30 cars in the game why would you have 4 lamborghinis, 4 mustangs, 3 Trucks and 2 SUVS, 2 camaros, and 2 chargers, but not include any hondas, mitsubishis,porches or toyotas and leave out cars like the suburu impreza and lancer evo despite how well they would work for street and dirt spec.
Driving: Suprisingly the game worked perfectly with my g27 racing wheel as well as an xbox controller without needing any configuring or calibration(other then turning driving assists off). It has a lot of options for adjusting force feedback, steering deadzone and sensitivity making it easy to get a comfortable set up as well. Unfortanetly despite good settings the game feels very unrealistic, collisions never make sense sometimes you go flying 1000ft into the air other times you bounce off like nothing happened, other times a bump at 10MPH totals your car, some cars spin out randomly for no reason, traction is terrible for some cars, theres no difference between FWD, RWD or 4WD , for some cars the game handles very arcadey much like an old need for speed game where you can just drift sideways through a corner without slowing, other cars you NEED to brake before a corner like you would in a simracer. Also if you play manual transmission on a controller expect to be heavily disadvantaged since the only way to reverse is to shift all the way down to 1st, then down to nuetral then into reverse and theres a forced pause between every shift so you cant just drop two gears quickly.
Online: Honestly, dont even bother. For one the game has no level scaling so all pvp is mixed together meaning a lv 300 f150 will be expected to race lv 1299 (max lv) lamborghinis and vipers. PVP is very buggy and laggy cars teleport 500yds ahead of you, cars lag into you causing you to crash, and disconects are very common, back on track feature sometimes places people far ahead of where they were, and sometimes you can clearly finish in 2nd only to have the game tell you you finished in 4th. PVP is also full of hackers and the developers dont seem to care, expect to see a lot of people with infinate nos, 300MPH cars, invincible cars that dont get slowed or moved when rammed into and even some people who just instantly win the race shortly after it starts. even if you do get a match without hackers or terible lag its boring since everyone only chooses highway races in performance spec with traffic off and then everyone is in either an aventador, bentley, or one of the free cars from the season pass, ive never seen a pvp in dirt, street or raid spec, ive only found a couple of circuit specs, and ive only seen about 10 of the 30 cars in the game in pvp. Outside of PVP the other players on the map can be really annoying, you will probably never see them while dirving around exploring but go to a skill challenge and expect 5 people to telaport there after you and start parking in the way or even trying to ram you off the road for no reason.
AI: the AI cheats...A LOT. doesnt matter what car your in or how fast your going the ai will be faster, cops will catch your 250MPH ford GT in a crown victoria, ram your Hummer H1 off the road easily without damaging their own car, cops can arrest you if your driving below 40MPH for more then 3 seconds and they teleport to your position sometimes if your escaping. Races against ai can be really annoying because the game decides to tell you that you were in 3rd place despite finishing 1 mile ahead of the 2nd place guy, the AI will teleport miles ahead in a race sometimes and you cant ram them off the road but they so much as bump you and your sent flying off the road.
Multiplayer: The games really fun to play with friends however i played the whole story mode with a friend and we did all but 3 mission at least twice due to the game disconecting one of us after winning and not giving us credit for completing it on almost  EVERY SINGLE RACE.
Overall: Its a fun game to play with friends, tons to explore, cars are expensive so theres a lot of farming to do, plenty of acheivments, skill challenges and multi hour races if your a completionist, however its a mess of flaws, bugs, cheating AI, lag, disconects after races, and the pvp is honestly by far the worst pvp i have ever played.

1) There are like 12 cars in the game, so no one has anything different.  If you're used to Forza 4 or Horizon, don't buy this.
2) There aren't any massive servers.  There are only 8 cars roaming around including yourself.
Overall, I'd give this game a 6/10.  It's really fun for the first two days; I'll give it that.  Once you finish those two days of cruising, it gets boring.  It gets to be a pain to play.  It becomes a grind to get what you want, which wouldn't benefit you in the long run anyway because unlike Forza, where certain cars have more potential, you can take a 370z and make it faster than a Pagani Huayra, both in handling and speed.
And the AIs.  Oh my god... The AIs.  They're not part of the physics engine.  If your car is one point behind the "recommended level" they leave you in the dust.  If your car is one point within range of being too low, you leave them in the dust.  It's not even about skill.
This is my first time leaving a review, so I'm not sure if you guys can message me or not. If you can, feel free to ask a question about the game.  Message me.
Once again, 6/10.

The Crew is an open world MMO racing game with some RPG elements. It was developed by Ivory Tower and Ubisoft.
The Crew is set on miniature version of the USA. But dont get me wrong, it has huge map open to explore from the moment you start the game. Map is split into five regions: Midwest, East Coast, South, Mountain States and West Coast. It take over an real life hour to drive decent car from Atlantic to Pacific. The Crew's handling model is a bit arcadey but not totally unrealistic. Physics engine could use some refinement though. Graphics are good, especially lighting effects, but if you stop for a moment and look, many things lack in detail. Game's audio isn't very good. Sounds just dont have that "depth" in them.
Gameplay is enjoyable and all Specs (car classes) handle differently. A warning for wheel users though: Force feedback effects are really strong so it can be hard to drive with wheels that have high steering angles. Story isn't that great bit it took about 10 hours to complete alone and that is a lot in todays standards. Although there is much more content than the story. The game is constantly online so you come across other players all the time. You can form a crew with them to play missions together. Or race against them. Its your call! There is some problems in PvP matchmaking but developers are fixing them currently. All missions are based on basic modes like race, checkpoint time trial and other more unusual modes like smash the target car. It can get repetitive sometimes but Specs mix up things nicely. There's also very long missions for hardcore gamers like over 4 hours long race!
You progress trough the game by playing missions and completing Skill challenges. Skill challenges are quick freeroam challenges that give some money and experience but most importantly car parts. Car parts are upgrades to your car that increase its stats like accerlation or handling. You also earn carparts from all missions but Skill challenges are the quickest way. Car cost quite alot but it isn't necessary bad thing as there's content and reason to play longer.
Overall The Crew is quite successful racing game thats easy to pick up and enjoy. It had potential to change the standards of racing games but it just could not bring the needed quality in certain aspects. I recommend it for racing fans but also for those who dont usually play racing games.
Pros:
+ Huge open world
+ Graphics
+ Handling
Cons:
-Physics
-Audio
-PvP matchmaking

+ the story is fantastic and is told through subtle hints here and there
+ there are great sub-plots of different people which are also cool to discover

+ ammo is scarce, but not to a super frustrating extend, loved the balance of the gameplay
+ you really have to think about clever ways to advance
+ riding the train lets you manage people that you picked up, it switches to a resource management mini game

“Definitively, the THINKING player’s rolling-ball game!”
Admittedly, though this reviewer acquired The Little Ball That Could (TLBTC) on Day One, judgement was not immediately ready to be assigned. Though a long-time fan of rolling ball games, it’s another matter to have any degree of success with them. Of the dozens in this player’s collection, none have yet been completed (for various reasons.). TLBTC shows every indication of being THE exception to this long-time rule.
At first look, TLBTC seems to be rather sterile, and overwhelmingly repetitive. However, gameplay indicates that there is vastly less truth to that than at first appearance. Each of five areas of 24 levels each simply requires a significant amount of real estate in order to fully utilize that zone’s concepts and possibilities fully. And that is a huge plus, as you listen to very pleasant music.
TLBTC is actually more than a single game. True, in order to unlock additional of the four locked worlds (after the original unlocked one) a certain number of tasks need to be accomplished, but the quantity is very accommodating to the vast number of players. Each of 120 levels (seemingly) has the same three tasks: finding a single puzzle piece, finding all three diamond shapes, and completing a speed-run in a generally quite generous time limit. Without conscious effort, this player unlocked the third world while still well within the second one. (The speed-run, generally to be attempted separately form the "searches", also has a highly motivating three-tier leaderboard.) Additionally, TLBTC has achievements with purpose, and not simply “participation trophies”, as is far too common. (Even numerous achievements for failure!)
Where TLBTC may seem repetitive is when players originally see the complexity of each level. It can be very daunting indeed, and more so to realize that of each level’s (often) DOZENS of path possibilities, there may only be one optimal path for speed-run success (but likely more), and only one path for locating the needed items. (Thus, an achievement for starting any level ten times.) And to add to the challenge….no control over camera movement, and only a small section of the level available at any time, with the ball dead center. It’s frequent to not see a spot where the ball must go, so the walls become partially transparent for that place (but won’t show a drop-off. HINT: Hidden places very often contain needed objects.) Also fortunate, the player has control over save locations, within the parameters of the “save buttons” that may, or may not be rolled over as is frequently the player’s choice.
The ball control within TLBTC is basically perfect, which is necessary considering the many dangers to be encountered. Balls can fall into the ocean, be crushed behind “ball pushers”, be explosively “spiked”, or fall without landing on a cushion pad, breaking into shards. And all this may be overcome just to discover that the level is complete….but without finding the necessary objects. But no worries! Each traverse causes the pool of knowledge of that level to grow.
Perhaps TLBTC isn’t as inexpensive as comparable games, but are there comparable games? If this game genre is your passion, there is no reason to delay purchase even another minute.

The original "Homefront" (2011) was awful. A badly made "Modern Warfare" clone, it took all the bad aspects of the genre - linear levels, straitjacket scripted encounters, stupidly bombastic storyline - and wrapped it in generic gunplay, visually unappealing graphics and an idiotic set-up. The core of the game - playing as freedom fighters waging war against foreign invaders in downtown USA - was interesting enough, but the implementation was terrible. So when the sequel was announced, you can understand if I approached the game with a great deal of trepidation.
There is a lot to dislike about "Homefront: Revolution". The voice-acting stands out with how terrible it is, and the backstory remains idiotic even after they turned the whole thing into an "alternate history" in some vain attempt to make a Korean invasion seem more plausible (it doesn't help). The bad-guys are cartoonishly evil, apparently now poison-gassing whole cities just for the LOLz. The good guys aren't much better - some taking vicious joy in torture - perhaps because the developers were aiming for a whole real-politick, shades-of-grey attempt at realism -  but when the villains are so unbelievably evil the whole thing just feels nasty and flat.
The levels are fairly large and reasonably detailed but disappointingly the world is divided into distinct maps and transit between them is controlled through mission advancement, completely ruining any feeling of an open world. Within each map the game falls back on the usual tropes: hidden goodies and the usual capture-the-base missions that have been the standard since 2008 and Far Cry 2. The game does expect you to stealth often, but - again - this system is poorly implemented, largely because the enemy attacks immediately upon spotting you. "Revolution" also relies heavily on respawning enemies to bump up the difficulty level rather than utilizing strong AI, and at times the game feels almost like Robotron with how many soldiers it throws at you.
So, another terrible Homefront game, eh? No surprise given its legacy, right? Well, not quite.
"Homefront Revolution" isn't a great game; I'm not even sure it's a good game. It is, however, head-and-shoulders above its predecessor and not completely without merit. Graphically, the game is surprisingly appealing, with some very good lighting and textures (the animations could have used some work). The firefights were solid, with good gun-play and level design that supported the close-quarters urban combat. I found the motorcycle - the sole player-controlled vehicle - a bit pointless; between the too frequent enemy spawns and the rubble-strewn streets, it was just faster and easier to run everywhere and I almost never used the thing. But the game had a solid foundation; it was just everything built atop that foundation that was awfuk. More variety in enemy types, a larger, more varied and cohesive game-world, a more robust stealth system, more mundane enemies who were individually threatening - rather than dangerous because they were thrown at the player in waves - and more things to do in the game beyond the token collectibles and base-capture would have made the game far more enjoyable.
(As an aside, the game's visuals - especially at night, with all the tracer-fire and the imposing steel-clad fortress of the Koreans - looked peculiarly post-apocalyptic and made me wish for nothing more than this game be re-done using the Terminator license, perhaps as a remake of Bethesda's "Terminator: Skynet" game from 1996. Anyone else feel the same?)
"Homefront: Revolution" surprised me in that it wasn't as horrid as I expected, and honestly I don't really regret the 20 or so hours I invested into playing it, but it's really quite flawed and not a game I expect to return to anytime soon. I'll reluctantly give it a recommendation, partly because the gunplay was solid but mostly because it was such an unexpected improvement over its predecessor, but it's definitely a game you'll want to pick up on sale.

This game had some absolutely MAJOR problems at launch with AI and bugs. However, after a year, I came back to this game after they started patching a lot of things up, such as major graphical issues and AI problems, so what is the state of this game now? It's bug free for me. This game really can be seen as an urban far cry with better weapon customization, an ok story, and some really good fights that you can get into. The AI for the enemy tries different strategies when they can to counter what you do, such as when you are behind cover and wont move they might try to flank you or throw a grenade to flush you out. Your friendly AI, however is quite stupid at times, sometimes just blindly start rushing forward and dying because of enemy fire. Graphically, I think the graphics are great and this game really shines at night. Night in this game has superior lighting effects, coupled with heavy rain, ruined buildings, you got yourself an immersive experience right there.  Story-wise, this game is nothing special. The characters are good but the writing simply is not that great, they should have developed the story more in terms of the main missions. Gameplay is basically your generic far cry-esque shooter that is somewhat more difficult as your health is fragile BUT this game has more verticality to it (meaning you can use buildings and rooftops to your advantage in a fight) and two different types of gameplay zones that play completely different from eachother. In one of these zones the actions you take directly impact the world around you because when you start undermining the KPA, the revolutionary spirit in the civilian population grows, and you will start seeing things like the american flag being posted around the area or violent rebellious actions against the KPA. The other zone type is basically a chaotic kill everything area. So now what about multiplayer? If you want to play it do it with friends, I dont remember anyone playing it. So now should you get this game? You should pick it up but I believe $30 is pushing it a little bit, however you should definitely get it when on sale, you will enjoy yourself.

I cannot recommend this game. It had a ton of negative feedback from the beta, with a load of bugs and other glitches of the sort. They had plenty of time to fix this before launch, and even with the launch it's buggy as hell. Five days after launch, players discovered a bug where you can't load your save (or even restart the game) without being inexplicably returned to the title screen with no message. A staff member on the forums said they were going to look into this, seeing as how a number of people were complaining. It's been over a year since release and this complaint has been filed and noticed, and it still hasn't been patched. Not to mention the amount of bugs leading up to before I personally even experienced this particular bug.
Bugs and defectiveness aside, let's talk about the campaign. It's definitely trying to seem deep, and it did a lot better than the original Homefront did in that regard. I hated the first Homefront, it was really just a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ CoD rip-off.
However, the more I tinkered with this game, the more I realized it was just a Far Cry 3 rip-off.
Not a perfect rip-off per-se, but they were trying REALLY hard to have some of the same features it had. Tagging people with your camera, recommended stealth paths, hidden collectables, fort taking and defense, etc.

Having played (usually for quite a while and with cash invested) Magic Duels, Hearthstone, Duelyst and The Elder Scrolls: Legends, Eternal leaves me slightly saddened. Considering Dire Wolf are involved with both TES:L and Eternal, I find myself confused over some of the UI design choices (navigating the collection and creating decks is decidedly unwieldy in comparison to every other game named above). The freebies at the start of the game feel quite unrewarding (the campaign is rather long and the rewards for it seem underwhelming), but the rate of gold, Shiftstone (dust) and cards gained through play in any mode is more than fair (in ~20 hours of play I have earned 100% of commons and uncommons in the game, 35% of rares, 10% of legendaries, 3 drafts and 2 forges). Also, to my understanding, once a week you get a pre-made deck for free for a daily quest, and you get to keep all of the cards in the deck for your collection.
The gameplay is fun, a slightly different twist on the genre from the other games, nothing groundbreaking and you can't go wrong if you don't mind the usual "annoyances" that MTG style card games offer (like mana-flooding/-screwing and fliers). The art style (of the game outside of card arts, which are largely great) is of course entirely preference, but it doesn't do much for me- the cartoony-looking card frames are the worst. The lack of voice lines when you play cards/attack really takes away a lot of personality not only from different factions/colours, but the game as a whole (edit: apparently they have been working on voiceovers since late August). A game that isn't based on another IP (obviously this is, but only in terms of gameplay) needs to have its own strong and defined personality- Eternal doesn't imo. The steampunk influences are nice and could be built upon for example, but a lot of it is generic fantasy fare.
At first I wasn't really hooked at all, but the game has grown on me tremendously now that I have played a couple drafts. It's like HS arena, except you get to keep all the cards you draft. The format is like actual drafts with packs being passed from player to player, and the decks you create will be more consistently good than in arena in other games, at least it seems that way in my experience so far. I can't see myself playing any card game that doesn't have draft anymore now tbh.
The only mode I thought wasn't designed very well was Gauntlet- you go against 7 AI opponents, the 7th of which has special rules (draw an extra card every turn, all units have 1 health, things like that selected at random) and ranks you up to the next higher difficulty. The only problem with this is, it ranks you up after a certain number of games regardless, so that you can't throw the 7th game and farm the easy AI. I missed the rank-up chest from gold to diamond, failed to rank up 2 or 3 more times after that due to increased difficulty/being bad/RNG and now I'm facing what must be diamond level opponents with super aggressive decks and multiple legendaries while I'm sitting at "gold" difficulty level with few cards to my name. Essentially I missed my chance at getting 2 rank-up chests (they're the valuable ones) until I can build better decks some time in the future or find the energy to ram my head against it stubbornly until I get lucky, which feels pretty bad. This seems kind of poorly designed overall, and I can't decide whether that's fine because it's free. It would certainly feel a lot less frustrating if you had a second life, but I guess that's what you pay for in Forge. I'll just play ranked, thank you.
I recommend you download the game and give it a whirl, it's a really good CCG if you allow yourself to persevere through the bland first impression.
tl;dr:
Pro:
- DRAFT
- generous rewards with no daily cap
- good/hard AI that allegedly doesn't cheat
- balanced starting turns and offense/defense roles
- interesting interactions and archetypes not found like this in other CCGs (such as Armory)
- mana flooding/screwing adding another layer to deckbuilding
Con:
- no voiceovers yet
- small playerbase thus far, you will run into the same players repeatedly
- art style and IP as a whole not particularly well defined/interesting
- only 1 mulligan which can worsen the flooding/screwing situation
- mana flooding/screwing adding another layer to my immeasurable supply of sodium

Cook, Serve, Delicious! is a restaurant/cooking simulator where you start with a rundown little cafe and turn it into a five star restaurant all the while cooking numerous dishes, fending off robbers and flushing blocked toilets. While the game might not sound like everyone's cup of tea it combines addictive gameplay with a good progression system to make a  fun gaming experience. As a huge fan of the Papa's Pizzeria games this was a must buy for me and I was not disappointed.
+Nice simplistic graphics, food and drink is well designed and the UI is nice to look at as well
+Incredibly addictive, simple gameplay that keeps you coming back for more
+You can take place in bets each day which require you to get a certain combo with certain foods
+You are rewarded for perfect orders and penalised for bad orders which helps push you to try as hard as you can
+Lots of different dishes including drinks
+Most dishes have upgrades which adds a new ingredient and new recipe cards
+All recipe cards have specific names
+Local co-op game mode
+The hotkeys for the different ingredients are for the most part intuitive, i.e. the first letter of the ingredient is the hotkey, and if you don't like them the hotkeys can be edited
+Full controller support for both the Xbox 360 Controller and the Dualshock 4 Controller
+Great music
+There are special events in the game which you can take part in such as catering events which earn you more money
-The frequency of work orders (flushing the toilet, cleaning the dishes, taking out the trash and setting rat traps) seemed a bit too high, in particular the flushing the toilet job seemed to be very frequent even when the toilet had been upgraded
-The progression on the star system is very slow and food upgrades are very expensive
-Once you start unlocking more order slots (you start with four and then it increases) it becomes increasingly difficult to keep track of all of the orders you have on the go and I often pressed the wrong key and sent out an order early, breaking a combo
-I had a couple of issues where I lost saves and had to replay about 2 hours worth
-You can't upgrade the appearance of your restaurant apart from the automatic changes when you get a new star
Verdict:
7
A great restaurant/cooking sim that is perfect for fans of similar games but might be quite boring for most, best to pick this up on sale.

Ok, basically what you get is a comfortable exploration game where you uncover the background story by exploring your way through a normal (though somewhat large and messy) home. It plays out more like an interactive story than anything else.
The setting is your home and it was a dark and stormy night... but that's the extent of the tension (again no scares).
Things you won't find in this game:
-Enemies to defeat
-Unusual puzzles scattered about to solve in order to progress through the home.
-Ghosts
-A button that says "8" when you push it.
Things you WILL find:
-90's references (does anyone else remember the Laserdisc or is it just me?)
-A primary background story focusing on your little sister and two smaller stories for your parents.
-Various rock music on various Cassette Tapes to play while rumaging through your family's belongings. (Note: Cassette Tapes are what 90's kids listened to music on before CDs rose to power in the mid 90's, they existed before CDs yet after 8-Tracks. You are forgiven for not knowing this if you were born outside the years 1990-99 as only 90's kids remember the 90's. In such a case just accept my statement as simple fact and you will be fine, and remember there is no shame in being born outside the 90's... not everyone can be cool.)
-A realitically believable yet heartwarming tale of love and the hardships of growing up.
Things to consider before buying.

I really like the tension in this game when you sneak around hoping not to be killed by a turret or a flock of drones waiting around the next corner.
The gun mechanics contribute to the tension. It's like an elaborate gun simulator.You have bullets. you put the bullets in the magazine (one by one) and jam the magazine into the gun. Drones! Shoot it! Click, click, click! You just died because you forgot to put a bullet into the chamber by pulling back the slider thing on the gun.
There's no interface showing you number of bullets and such. You'll have to pull out the magazine and look at it to see how many bullets you have left. You can also pull back the slide a little to see if you have a bullet in the chamber.
The gameplay is simple, but pretty fun if you like realism. Take one bullet and you're dead. Run around and you'll be dead pretty soon.
The purpose of the game is to find 11 cassette tapes hidden around. It's a rather difficult goal, and I wish there were some alternative game modes (like getting from A to B or clearing buildings/blocks). I'd relly love to see more games with similar gun mechanics and damage.

I really like this. The idea, the feel, the game really makes me think back to old text adventure games, just with added freedom and a wider choice of what to do.
The game is admittedly difficult at first, especially if you didn't go through the full tutorial. However, the feeling of not knowing exactly your place in this place really settles in quickly because of it.
Gameplay is pretty simple. Honestly, it does feel a little dated, but in my opinion it adds a lot of character to the game. People you meet will speak somewhat plainly, but it helps in conveying the emotion of being out in the expanse of space and speaking to a complete stranger that has lived his life totally separated from you by literal light years.
Hell, even a few of the things I've played through in my short 100 minute play test hit me in the emotions. Without giving anything away, moral choices are a thing here. I haven't played enough to tell if choices affect anything, but if I find out I'll update this.
It isn't without cons, though. Some text is hard to read, the first example that comes to mind is in the stats screen. Some of the text is bright green on a grey background. Why?
Secondly, while the game being somewhat empty-feeling does add atmosphere, sometimes it makes the game feel a little, well, empty. There's not many types of ships, and all the icons for items look the same. An engine and an engine mk2 for example. Maybe add a bit of variety to make it easier to discern between the kinds?
Overall, I like this game. I'm going to keep playing it, and I hope to see changes for the better come about. I've been wanting something exactly like this for a while now.
Edit: After about three hours of gameplay, I've noticed a bit more about the game. Combat is a little difficult, I've tried a few different weapons and not much changes, in the end I have a hard to aiming and the enemy just barrages me with missiles. It's not fun, but running away from pirates or flying through territory that the Empire doesn't protect can be exhilarating if you can actually get away with it. Pro tip: Try the ship that has Instant Warp, and set it so you're only slowed down if you take armour damage. That'll let you slip right past and start opening up stuff way easier than using the base ship.
The UI is also set up to where it's kinda hard to find things. I bought a UI look from a planet, but I have no idea where to go to apply it. The in-game tooltip just says "for you to apply". Where??
Continuing on from this, perhaps add a feature where when you hover over something, a tooltip comes up. The stuff in the top right is meaningless to me (albeit I didn't go through all the tutorials, I have to admit that). Just a small description when your mouse is over an icon or something would disperse a lot of confusion.
Thirdly, I know this game is pretty new, so it's exusable, but there's not much variation in the items' function. I have never upgraded my engine nor my CPU or armour plates because the ones I got in the start and with the ships I have bought have all been better. What's the point in only having items that aren't even worth using? Even the cost for buying them is zero credits.
I guess lastly I should bring up the stats of ships themselves when compared to other ships. My main cargo-hauling vessel holds 56 tons, and my second one hold 13. When I select my second ship and compare it to my first, it says the second has +10% cargo space, when it surely does not. Broken or are they meaning something else, in which case the wording should probably be changed to make it more clear what the player is looking at.
I've torn this game a new a$$hole, so lets talk about the good parts of the game :)
The world is massive. As in, for a 2D clicking game where all you do is fly around on the x and y axis, its huge. I've found 20+ systems, all with usually 3+ planets or space stations. Some planets have moons, and some space stations orbit planets. They're different sizes, all look different and every one of them has their own bio about the history of the planet, or a story about how the name became what it is. I expect myself to take about 10-15 hours at this point to go through and explore everything I've found, and I haven't even uncovered half of the map.
The more you learn the world, the better the experience becomes. I can tell what ships are what factions, who to be careful about and who are my friends. I've met people in the ranks of the Empire and been on their bases, I've talked to and worked with pirates and bandits. Some places run out of ore often, and some places are a thriving economical marketplace. The longer you stay in Naev, the more you feel like you're a pilot out in a universe where you are not familiar with everything, finding your own way to survive.
TL;DR It's good, play it

Unlike the Farcry games however: Dont go in expecting a highly streamlined and polished experince, you'll likely encounter quite a few non-gamebreaking bugs, and quite a few level design decisions that'll leave you scratching your head, wondering how you were ever supossed to figure out exactly what the designers meant for you to do. Neither of these should ruin your playthrough, but if you for some reason should be unable to deal with bugs in a videogame you may wanna stay clear of this one.
