Classic RPG elements and beautiful environments blended with satisfying puzzle solving.
Although I never played the first Legend of Grimrock, it did not stop me from getting this gem of a game. Luckily no knowledge of the predecessor is required to enjoy this game. It does help if you know the core concept though, as the game never holds your hand apart from at the very start. The semi-turnbased classic RPG elements are not for everyone, as it does require strategic thinking while in combat, especially later in the game. The game often does not show any mercy in unexpected tough situations. It challenged me and kept me immersed at all time, which I greatly enjoyed. An aspect that I personally had great fun with is the puzzles. These puzzles are hardly ever straightforward and really make you think. Look around for clues. Any secrets? What does this text mean? And when you finally find the solution, you feel like a master of puzzlesolving.
There are some things that bother me. Some monsters seem just too strong in comparison to other in the same area. It catches you off guard, making you think you can take on the area while you definitely cannot. Also I think accuracy is always quite a bothersome thing for me. My characters keep missing their attacks, making me frustrated at times of danger. This is a common mechanic in classic RPGs so I just have to get used to it I suppose. And finally, although I love the concept of tilebased movement, it did take me a while to fully grasp it and gave me some issues along the way. In the end, mostly small subjective complaints.
Finally, I absolutely love the level editor. As a level designer, I greatly enjoy this feature and it definitely was one of the selling points for me.
I recommend this game to all hardcore players who enjoy a beautiful and expansive classic RPG.

If the first Homefront tried to copy Call of Duty this one is more similar to the Far Cry games. The story puts you in the shoes of Brady who goes around pretty big open world maps where you have to take over towers and clear up various points in order to clear the streets of the KPA occupation. The story is peppered with drama and characters have a tendancy to die. While not everyone is flushed out the story is good enough to keep you going and see it thru to the very end. The main campaign took me around 9 hours to finish however there are a lot of points that you can capture.
The biggest problem this game has is the mission structure which forces you to clear a certain ammount of the KPA occupation in order to progress further. And this happens way too much and gets in the way of the story's pacing. The areas aren't too varied but they're all well flushed out. The enemies are way too similar and the quests are a bit basic. The RPG elements are a bit underdeveloped and there isn't much of a weapon variety. You can no longer pick up guns from enemies and instead just ammo for your regular guns. You will find 2-3 that will work for you and keep to just those as the upgrading costs are very high and lower level weapons do not pack a puch.
The sound design is ok with some really great voice acting from Dana's and Jack's actor. What bothers me a lot is that your character is mute and in this game, where people always tend to ask questions, you don't say anything but just go along for the ride even tho there are a lot of moments where you could actually make a choice but the game takes that away from you.
Overall the game is pretty good. The visuals are stellar for an open world game and there is quite a lot to do even after you finish the campaign. There are quite a few story DLCs as well which I'm going to play and the gameplay is good. In some aspects however it is a step down compared to the first game. There are very few setpieces in the game and not enough character development. The pacing is thrown off because of the Harts and Minds system (where you have to grind out camps in order to progress further in the story) and the fact that you can no longer pick up weapons makes the game a bit too repetive as you're stuck with the same few weapons the whole game.
I'd recommend it to anyone who has played the first game or wants to try a more down to earth "muddy" FPS where the story isn't all rainbows and sunshine.

- great graphics and good performance

The Bad:

This is by far my favorite shooter. If you like games that are tactical, suspenseful, and have a hard learning curve. you will love this game. You are a bit dependent on your team, but that is by design, there are slow moments, which are also by design, despite these deviations from the norm of shooters, it still manages to be consistently entertaining, even when you lose. It has a great atmosphere. If you want a game which is all sitting back and sniping, you'll probably be satisfied by this game's emphasis on marksmanship. If you want a game that's always fast paced, adrenaline pumping, and up close and personal, you probably won't enjoy this game's slow pace. But this game does have its fast paced periods while trenches are contested and the teams are brutally killing each other with trench clubs, grenades, bayonnetes and pistols. For me, this game is the perfect balance between skill and strategy based gameplay, where marksmanship is encouraged, reaction speed is useful, and a strategic and patient mind is necessary. The only real downsides are that the learning curves have become steadily steeper, and the community has become steadily more toxic as time has gone on.

Excellent game! I just played it for hours. It's roughly like Diner Dash, but way more invovled. I like that it's repetitve enough that you can memorize certain tasks (so the game doesn't feel impossible!) but not so repetitve that it turns into a rote timing game (like Diner Dash can). Most items can have multiple recipes (which you can get by purchasing upgrades as you go along) which keeps the novelty factor alive and continues making it challenging for a long time.
I also like that the customers don't really get impatient like they do in DD - items have a wait time in the queue and will contribute to a bad score if you don't get to the fast enough, but it's not like DD where certain people are more annoyed than others. Similarly, I like that you can get an order kinda wrong and it doesn't really penalize you. You wouldn't get a perfect score, but the customer isn't angry either. (If you give them the entirely wrong order, they will be mad, of course, but if you just forget one ingredient or something, they're just mildly annoyed).
Another cool feature is that you don't have to use your mouse (unless you really want to) but instead can use keystrokes for everything. The default keystrokes are pretty self-explanatory (c for creamer, s for sugar, etc), or else easily learnable (n for onion, v for olive). And if you just can't rememeber them... they let you change the default keystrokes, per food, to whatever you want them to be. Love how flexible that system is!
Besides being like a highly improved Diner Dash, this game also has a touch of Tycoon in it as well, which I love. They did a good job of giving you warnings of things (Rainy day coming! May want to have rainy day food on the menu!), but still not making it super tedious (for example, you only have to buy equipment and recipes, but don't have to keep on eye on / purchase supplies). They have a health inspector that comes every 5 days, but all she checks is that you're cleaning the toilet, etc. Since you know ahead of time that she's coming, you can opt for an easy menu that day to save yourself some time and make sure you get her demands met.
There are also some interesting side options you can do. There are occasional bets you can take (or not) that can make you some extra cash. You can also take catering jobs once you've upgraded a bit for some SUPER easy cash. :) And if you happen to have a perfect day (I've only managed this once so far!) you get a cash bonus for that as well.
I definitely recommend this game! It's straightforward enough to have zero learning curve (and they even allow you to repeat tutorials anytime you want to learn the different recipes!), but it's complex enough to not get boring and to give yourself something to work towards (gotta buy that pizza oven!).
(PS: The only real downside I found was when the robber comes. I've only had that happen once but it was during rush hour and giving a description to the police was pretty tedious so I lost several food orders b/c I couldn't get to them fast enough (also there was a time limit on the description-giving and I didn't do it fast enough because I was distracted by my food burning so... I didn't get the report filed quick enough to get my money back! Boo....) Luckily the robber doesn't seem to come often and I also noticed some upgrades you can buy to make him even less so.... yeah....)

Warning: MP is relatively dead! (Add me if you want to play because I'm always down for a game!)
Now that the warning (and the expression of needing friends for the game) is over with, let's move on to the actual review.
From what I played of the SP campaign (only a couple of missions) it's a really thought out game. Although it is a bit awkward since the main character and Jun talk about something in their past. It's very vague and confusing for me. (Maybe it's explained during the campaign, I just have to continue playing in order to find out!) The game feels like a dumbed down 4X game.
EXplore, eXpand, eXploit and eXterminate are all there with some dumbed down just enough to allow you to get into the action as quickly as you can. EXpand was dumbed down to the bare essentials, with a handful of buildings. The Command Center, a Refinery, a Shipyard, Energy Generators, Missile Defense Pads (I may be wrong on the name) and maybe one or two other buildings.
That being said, I know the game is more a space-based RTS than a 4X game, it doesn't hurt to compare the similarities. As the dev said in their response to the review, they since played down the 4X description. Of which I either didn't pay attention to when I added this to my wishlist, or didn't even know existed as part of it's original description. The game isn't true to the 4X genre and has abandoned a good deal of what makes up some of the elements in said genre.
And it did it well too, because makeing it more of a space-based RTS helped it bring a good level of strategy within itself. Due to the fact that the game is litteraly about strategy and thinking things through, which would not have worked out as well as it could have if it was 4X. I hope no one will think (or continue to think) I have the wrong impression. Because the impression of it being a sb RTS was always there.

Eternal is an entirely successful effort to create something that keeps the flow, flash and fun of a game like Hearthstone with the depth, complexity and strategy of a game like Magic: The Gathering.  The result is something that in many ways exceeds both, but most importantly, stands on its own as a fun, free experience that rewards all of the time you spend in it.  This game is leagues above other CCG's and it's only going to get better with each successive set.
Eternal is quick and easy - games are five minutes on average - but is engaging from the lowest levels of play to the highest, and has a staggering depth of strategy to explore. I opened some 2,300 packs in the closed beta of this game without spending a dime, and plan to open many thousands more. This is what Hearthstone should have been.
I've been dabbling in online CCGs ever since I gave up MTGO a decade ago and I think we finally have a winner here. I immediately dismissed this game, even though I never bothered to activate my closed beta key, because it just looked too much like the 500lb gorilla in the room- Hearthstone(HS). I've seen so many promising CCGs never get off the ground or given the attention they deserve (Might and Magic DoC, Infinity Wars, SolForge, Scrolls, Hex, Duelyst), but Eternal is a real gem that tries to incorporate the best of what CCGs can offer, without straying to far off the beaten path of success.
Here's a list of everything I think this game does well or improves upon:
-Hearthstone-like ease-of-play
-Most accessible Free to Play CCG I've ever played. Sure the rarer the cards the better, and usually more difficult to acquire, but the mountain to earn them is hardly steep.
-Interactivity on both players' turns without being cumbersome like MTG or Hex with 10 different "turn phases".
-Instant/interrupt spells and abilities are here- COUNTERPLAY! Thank god
-Blocking is reintroduced, which curbs a lot of the mindless tempo/zerg strategy that is constant in HS (there's still aggro, but it's not as mindlessly frustrating)
-Non-monster permanent effects exist! Curses and Relics (basically enchantments from MTG). This just gives much more variety to card design.
-Weapons- but they're rebalanced so they don't feel overpowered like they do in Hearthstone. A weapon's durability is based on how much damage it can do, not how many times you're allowed to swing it.
-Multi-class combinations. Everything you love about faction synergy from MTG is here. Not stuck in a one-dimensional class archetype. Dual-color decks, tricolor decks, rainbow decks- OH MY!
-Dual-power resources (lands/mana in MTG)  are easy to acquire (unlike in MTG where they are a very necessary, but a very expensive premium resource). Basically Direwolf has taken great strides to even out the RNG with land drawing. While drawing power (lands/mana) is still random, it's significantly toned down.
-No stupid RNG, which is like 50% of what Hearthstone relies on to create interesting and dynamic mechanics
-AI formats are included to farm in-game currency. You don't HAVE to farm games vs. other players to acquire gold/cards. It might not be the most efficient, but it's still a ton of fun.
-Drafts you don't have to pay for with real money, BUT you get to keep your cards!
-4 copies of any card in a deck, which IMO,  greatly increases the focus and strategy of a deck.
-Interface feels very polished and easy to use.
I could go on and double the size of this list, but for me, this game is basically what Hearthstone should have been- a very polished and streamlined version of MTG without dumbing it down so much it loses all of the fun mechanics and strategy.
Really hope this game gets noticed by the masses, because it's a wonderful evolution of where the CCG genre should be headed.

Short review: Everything seems really good, except of manasystem which is from last century and is the thing that I hate most about MtG. If this is fixed, then this game could seriously contend with HS. Also the monetization model is much greedier than HS. I would give it a neutral review, as I enjoy the game and will continue to be playing it despite the shortcomings, but since that is not an option: the greediness of the monetization means constructed is locked out until you grind nonstop for a few weeks, which makes me give it a negative one.
Sidenote: So that I don't sound like a whiny kid, I will admit that I did spend more than 40$ on the game, which denotes how much I enjoy playing it as it's one of the better online ccgs out there. At the same time it does not deny the shortcomings, because of which I cannot recommend it to my friends. To be fair I don't think there is any online ccg I can recommend to my friends as this industry is really greedy... Well except for faeria, but that game is killing it's potential and creativeness is declining, so I am considering changing my review for that as well.
Extended version:
I really love how the things this game does and how it plays out. Mechanics, flavor and other things are great. It doesn't rely on RNG as much as hearthstone but still manages to keep simplicity of HS while providing plethora of interesting options. Basically if you enjoy any of the current CCGs like Hearthstone, MtG, Spellweaver, Star Crusade, Elder Scrolls Legends or any others you will have high likelihood of enjoying this.
There are a few minor issues UI issues that will be fixed later (like button on the screen to declare all attackers or a bit more seamless casting of spells) BUT there is one issue with the current game that I find troubling: Mana system.
Basically the reason I cannot recommend this game is because of the manasystem that is straight rom last century. Manascrew and Manaflood are same as magic so even with all the upsides, this game doesn't solve this issue, which is the worst issue in magic. Unless new game mechanics are introduced to alleviate manascrew, this game will not have lasting appeal. Overall this game seems good and interesting and I will follow the development of this game, but if this game will still have same manascrew/manaflood issues that I am fed up with in magic, then I cannot recommend this game. Another minor drawback is that there are no hero powers like in HS (Star Crusade and Spellweaver do this part really well), but I could live with that if not for the manasystem.
Update: After playing the game longer (basically for whole week nonstop), I have to admit that manascrew is not as much of an issue in this game as in MtG as there are a few mechanics that help it. Though I still consider this to be quite a big issue. But the bigger issue I have found in this game is how greedy the monetization model is.
It might seem like you are getting more stuff from boosters and drafting as you get to keep the cards you have drafted, but that is counterbalanced by the fact that to get enough gold for another draft you will have to win the draft. The crafting costs and the fact that you need 4x of any card (including legendaries) mean that it will take quite a lot of time/money until you are abe to build half decent deck. Although there are a few aggressive archetypes that you can build quickly and don't require legendaries, but if you want diversity and deck brewing, then you are out of luck.
Update2 with new set: After half a year of unchanging metagame we finally get a new set... Half of which is are reprints of first set. I could technically be fine with it if this had some redeeming qualities, but the sad part is keywords aren't nearly as well designed as in the first set (they still have interesting interactions, but they are much worse). The cards are overall less exciting and the game isn't even trying to be creative anymore. Feels like they just stopped putting real effort into making the game itself better and are only focused on making it look better. If I wanted something that looks good but pays bad and is rng-dependant, I would play Hearthstone...

: The copy of this game was provided by the developer for review purposes, yet it doesn't affect my review in any way.
Foresight is a RTS where you can lead your fleets into an epic battles in space. You're playing as a commander with a mission to recruit other commanders, that will help you both, forces and advice in battles. It's totally up to you how you will manage your resources!
Full disclosure - I am not a real-time strategy games player, I played only few strategy games in my whole life and it's not my type of a game, but I'm trying to be reliable and objective in here as I possibly can.
First of all, at the first sight you can easily tell that devs love what they're doing. This might not be some great AAA top title on steam, but they're obviously trying their best in here (Look at all those news, patches, upgrades and even their responses to reviews). Their love towards their game is a huge advantage for game itself!
Now finally about the game itself, yay! Graphics looks old, indeed. But here it's not about graphics but about gameplay, so I like to think about them not as "bad" but as "retro". Music is not wonderful either but it's nice listen. I didn't got far enough into the game to fully explore its possibilities, but I clearly see all the potential in it and I will surely play more of it in future. Missions and battles themselves are highly rewarding, building up your fleets, preparing to battle and standing over destroyed ships of your enemies is awesome!
I'd love to compare this game to some other RTS titles, but as I've said before, my experience with them is quite limited. But there's one thing I've noticed in here and what is not that common from what I know. I'm talking about how tactical this game is. It's not about how big and heavy your fleet will be, it's about how you will manage to lead it. For example, commander ships can only shoot forward and it takes time for them to turn around. Without those ships, bombers and fighters become useless and if you're using little and fast battleships to flank commander ship, you're gaining a huge advantage. I might be a bit too into this game...
Yes, there are some cons to this game, but it's understandable and game is fully playable and totally enjoyable despite them. One thing that bothers me is why this game is not in early access? It's constantly updated and fixed for better and better AND it would avoid some negative reviews from people who review "fully out yet bugged" game. But I guess there's developers reason behind it.
So yeah, long story short, an exemplary game from an indie studio. Recommended for everyone, obligatory for RTS lovers to see its potential.

This is a great game. The market is getting flooded with CCGs nowadays. It is good to see something that is not cookie cutter. The game rewards free to play players well, and is generous if you choose to buy into it.
First things first, it is great to play a game like this where you can respond on your opponents turn, rather than just sit and wait for your turn.
The different game modes are well done also. You can play Gauntlet (with a deck you make) vs the AI for free for rewards.
A step up from that is Forge where you craft a deck by picking from between 3 cards ala hearthstone, then play the AI with it. This is a great mode, and good for people learning the game and working on there collection

Again all on your own time you can stop after any game and pick it up later.
Then there is Ranked, where there is a ladder system you can work on finishing as low as you can monthly for rewards.
This is by far my favorite game of this Genre and have played most since beta that have been out. It has more that Magic feel to it, as they have several people helping on the game that are huge in the Magic community LSV (Louis Scott Vargas) to name one.
Do yourself a favor if you like these games try this out and give it a whirl.
Also make sure to join the Discord chat where the Devs hang out and the public are very helpful.

Foresight was developed by Strides Interactive and published by KISS ltd. It is a Real Time Strategy game that focuses on creating a space fleet and destroying the enemies side. The game was published on the 28th November 2014 and is still having updates.
Foresight is a true RTS space themed game, and the game proves that to us the more that you play through this game. The start of the game is obviously the tutorial, it helps you grasp the basic concepts of what you have to do to build ships, attack enemies ect in order to progress through the game. The tutorial is very helpful, I felt like the it didn't drag on very much and I felt like I knew what I was doing when I got into the actual first level because this game is fairly complex. It explains each of the mechanics very well and waits for you to complete that one task before they move onto the next part. If you are into these sort of games then this tutorial will be pretty easy to follow, but if you are more of casual player this might seem a bit difficult to get used to everything and learning everything at once.
Once you are in the levels you will find that the game isn't as easy as you thought it would be. The game doesn't really require you to be speedy at creating your ships, but more strategic to create the right sort of ships to defeat the enemy team. There is a interesting mechanic that is in the game, that is if you find a wormhole you will be teleported to another space on the map, this could give you a great advantage as you could be behind the enemy and ambush them. The story isn't all that much in-depth as the game focuses mainly upon the RTS side and not the story which isn't really considered a bad thing in most cases for RTS games.
The controls of the game are very well made and designed. For the casual players they will probably use the default controls that are in the game. But for the more 'hardcore' RTS fans there is a huge section for the hotkeys where you can assign pretty much everything for if you are that sort of person who likes to do that.
The game's graphics are very well designed, with all the ships having that sci-fi sort of look to them. they have all had the same amount of detail to them. The space background and the sort of detail that the cutscenes go into are a different sort of style to what the actual game is. The cutscenes are kind of weird compared to the style of the actual game, and for me doesn't really fit in very much.
+ Great tutorials
+ Great level design & mechanics
+ Simple and Advanced controls
+ Unique type of RTS
+ Steam Achievements and Cards
- For casual gamers might be a bit tricky to start off with, there is a lot that you need to learn
- Cutscene graphics are completely different from the gameplay graphics.
Foresight is still a great RTS game, with the game being fairly complex it is great for both casual and hardcore RTS fans although casual gamers may have difficulty to play to start off with. The gameplay graphics are great, but the cutscene ones seem out of place. Overall a great RTS game

The Crew attempts to be another TDU 2 and as long as you stick to stree or performance cars and don't go off road it does an ok job of it. The first and largest issue by far is the surface textures. All the surfaces from roads to dirt to snow to desert and grass and so on are very low poly meaning that it often sends you careening out of control because of a very sharp bump. Most cars don't handle well enough to hold those kinds of irregularities, not even the raid specs, making any time sensitive mission or race a very challenging and very very frustratring endeavor. A 16.5 GB game with a very large map results in a very poorly detailed map.
Its second large issue is the AI. The chase ai (cops or other 'baddies') is extremely broken. Cars that apeear fullstock or large police trucks are able to out-perform your car in every single way as long as you are in visual range, which is very hard to drop out of without some very tight and frequent turns, and they will follow you even offroad with all the aforementioned capabiliities. The race ai is equally stupid. The second place and often third place cars will outperform their own specifications simply "to provide a challenge". Whatever the point of all those parts i grinded for is, it is lost on me because of this. They will also ram you without a second thought  but when it comes to traffic they dodge it as if the traffic was christ himself.
Its third major issue is connectivity. Ubisoft has not yet fixed any of its server issues. My friend and I have crashed regularly at the end of races because of that and often times you will be driving around when everyone drops off mysteriously from your hud. This isn't as bad an issue except in co-op, which I highly encourage to tackle some of the missions to get the high ratings and therefore the great parts.
There are many other smaller issues. The traffic is horrid once you've spent even a few minutes on one road. Midnight highways resemble rush hour traffic and city roads are always crowded, which, combined with the low poli textures (especially felt in san fran, seattle and chicago) makes for a very difficult time to accomplish missions or skills. The mirrors in cockpit mode still do not work whereas they work fine in third person view. The wooden and weak metal fences seriously sap out your speed (though this is more a quality of life issue). The UI is very intrusive on occassion, especially when you're trying to escape cops and hit some skill challenge.
The small number of cars is rather dissapointing but the ones that are do add some substance. Unfortunately, for the cars I did drive and enjoyed, there never was a large difference once in the way they handled or overall 'felt'. TDU2 had about 2 to 3 times the number of cars, if not more. The challenges, while some are fun, especially the jumps, are very dissapointing in their variety and method of approach. Generally a high enough speed at the beginning of the challenge and at least half-way decent handling will get you gold/plat on nearly everything.
It does have some great things for it. Large map,, beautiful terrain (to look at) and pretty great sunsets and sunrises as well as overall good terrain variety. The story is pretty good if rather predictable with a terribly bland ending cut scene but a very satisying final mission. Mind the pre-rendered 30fps cutscenes and terrible stuttering. Some ocassional frame lag however takes from this though it has been rarer in its occurance. It is very very enjoyable to just take out a performace and drive the entire map (on road) and just see the sights and I found snow driving fun.
As the specs go, these are my thoughts:
Street: Basic racing spec. Good on road but rather terrible off-road (as expected). Enjoyable until you get a performace spec.
Dirt: The shiftiest early car spec you get. Terrible grip and acceleration unless specifically stocked for those. High level very enjoyable and a whole lot of fun to drift for a mile with.
Performance: Likely your car spec of choice. Great turning with good acceleration, grip and speed. Spin out rather easily early because of the power to weight discrepancy but overally very very fun to drive.
Raid: Roads? We don't need no roads. 'Nuff said
Circuit: NO NO NO NO NO. Spins out more often than the drift car on road, turns like a thrown brick, the first two gears might as well be non-existent making for a very harrowing off-the-line. Very very high speed but few roads will let you attain those. Maybe the Boneville salt flats. Terrible braking meaning you have to do it early. Mind the ramming ai.
Good concept. Poor execution. Surprising since part of the Ivory Tower team worked on TDU2 but I think they recruited the frustrating part of that team instead of the logical one.

I loved Gone Home's method of storytelling, but the story it told was, at most, lackluster. That really sucked, because I was super, SUPER excited about playing a game about a lesbian. There was a single moment near the end of the game that I found myself emotionally invested in the story, but at least for me, a moment of concern doesn't make up for a whole game that fosters indifference.
There is, however, an interesting side narrative lying around. The thing is, there's barely any content for it, and it is about a man. After hearing so much hype about Gone Home's presentation of women, finding that the game is best at making the player (at least me) invested in a side male character is really disappointing.
The most exciting thing that happens in Gone Home is discovering a cross. It is a red herring that is pretty much unrelated to the rest of the game, because, uh, ♥♥♥♥ you, I guess.
This is a super short game. I looked over every single inch of the house and read every single document, and the game still barely lasted two hours. This brief, uninteresting story is not worth anywhere near $20. Gone Home shows off a lot of potential that future games can hopefully make the most of, but couldn't pull its own self together enough to make a decent game.
In the end, I'm glad that I experienced Gone Home, but if I could do it over again, I would not have bought it. It was worth the little time and effort that I put into it, but it wasn't worth my money.

My gaming dollar was well spent on this game. Every so often, I like fighting games. This one I have a hard time puting down. There are many useful tools to make your own wrestler as plain, serious, or silly as you want. There are an almost overwhelming number of moves to pick from. You can even customize your entrance theme.
I got my fair share of OMG moments and laughs from this title. You don't even have to be a wrestling fan to enjoy this. This game is as chaotic and full of scripted nonsense as the "real" thing. The triple threat matches are insane, and so is the 6 man tag team events. The simulated ref will have his hands full.
What else do you need to know before purchasing, and how do you get the most out of it? Read further.
First, I have a four year old PC. My video card is an Nvidia 760. Memory is 12 gigs. So, my PC is very basic and out of date a bit. So, how does this game run? Almost flawlessly. The only slowdown I get is with some of the entrance sequences. These seem to be locked at 30 fps. Otherwise, I have had perfect frame rate during matches, and zero crashes. The sound in the game is top notch.
The game also has nice touches. There are a lot of little things that make a difference. The detail you can get into is almost intimidating.
The universe mode is fantastic. I, however, spend most of my time playing the career mode. You will see that most of the complaints are about the career mode. Yes, it could use some work. Some things are repetitive. The interviews after the matches are pretty basic, with only one voice-over. It's a minor thing that doesn't spoil the experience.
The best way to get the most fun out of the career mode is customizing your wrestler. Changing your moves around to create a theme and fluid move set takes some time but pays off. Change you moves around to eventually create your own vision of your wrestler. Start by picking some signatures and a finisher, and work your way backwards. Remove ones that seem out of place, and add ones from beat rivals.
Your first wrestler will probably be a mish-mash of moves, like mine was, until I learned to group my moves that made sense. Your wrestler will eventually grow on you, and the more fun you will have. Mistakes can be fixed in this game. Do not worry too much about your decisions you make in the interviews. Mix it up if you want.
Be aware that the first bracket of matches is pretty basic. Once you move on, things change a bit. The story line is full of nonsense, and doesn't make much sense, just like watching it on TV. "Real Life" wrestling is just as repetitive, just like this. How many times do you see the ref get knocked out during a match on TV? You know it's going to happen. This game just makes the same old thing more fun.
Just like any game, though, you may become bored with it. I have to say out of my 50 hours worth so far, I got my money's worth already. I sure hope the next version is even better, and I do hope they port it to the PC without waiting too long.
As far as short-comings, there is mentioning of save game corruption in some forums. My only advice about this is to avoid mods. I am not in anyway saying that this is the cause of it, but some games that aren't mod friendly can cause this. Modding is always done at your own risk. Another disappointment is that you can't try Divas in career mode without modding. It may have been fun to try, but there isn't than many of them to begin with. Divas do work fine in the universe mode, though. So, no big deal.
As far as gameplay goes, it plays at a good pace. Button mashing doesn't work. The reversal system is great. It takes a bit of getting used to since ealier versions of this type of game are just plain button mashers where the same thing works all the time. This game does force you to think ahead a bit. Again, just like "real life" wrestling, some cheap shots feel pretty cheap. Be prepared to say "Ohhhh, come on....!" or "WTF ?!?" from time to time. Being a poor sport in this game won't help you. Take it on the chin, and take it out on the next poor digitally simulated jerk to boost your ego.
Lastly, this game is great fiddleware. There are lots of things to try and creation tools to fool around with. Its not perfect, but what game is? For a tank of gas, you can have a good time.

To be frank, the game is half-baked.
The retro-style pixel graphics are great - really, the best thing about the game.  The combat is okay - not good, not bad, just rather simple and functional.  If you're looking for a pixel-shooter, you can do much better.
The survival mechanics are just busywork.  Granted, that's basically any survival game, but here they become a chore more than anything.  Likewise the simple minigames and you engage in to keep your train running.  Both of these things will distract you from the bulk of the story, which is odd because it's pretty clear the devs are very much in love with the story.

The dialogue is actually pretty bad, at least in its english version; the devs really should have hired someone with a better grasp of the language to write the localization.  The ending... As it is, I really can't recommend it.

So, I bought this game mainly to see what all the fuss had been about, a few years ago, when it seemed like half the gaming world hated it with a visceral passion.  When they hated it, and games like it, enough to start a shambling, deformed movement in protest.  I expected to find something at least modestly objectionable, because even though I disagreed with the people making those complaints on principle, on some level I thought that that many people couldn't be entirely wrong.
They were.
Where they complained that this wasn't really a game, and that it didn't deserve the praise it had received, I found an experience which constantly played with my expectations.  The setting, a dark, old, and empty house, with a mysterious and somewhat sinister past, in a thunderstorm, with a missing sister to find?  My mind said be be ready for jump scares, or some type of horror, and yet, aside from the general darkness, there was nothing overtly threatening to be found.  I continually expected to find that something terrible had occurred, that a weird old acquaintance, or perhaps a ghostly relative, would spring out, and that I'd suddenly be in Amnesia.  In other words, I expected this game to take the easy way out.  I was wrong, but I'm glad that I was, because the game let me slowly piece the story together, not just from Sam's diary entries, but from various documents and items, and from the setting itself, allowing me to realize that I'd been wrong just in time to be wrong again about where this was all going.
In the end, the story was nowhere near as complex as I was expecting, and I'm glad for that.  Not every story has to have you defeat the evil and save the world.  Sometimes, it's enough to just understand what another person is going through, and why they made the decisions they did.  I won't go into too much detail regarding the final reveal, as obviously I'd encourage you to play it yourself, if you decided not to heed the spoiler warning.  But I will say that I can relate, very strongly, to Sam's predicament, and the story she gradually reveals was touching in a way that most game plots can't even approach.  And as curious as I am about what happens afterwards, how, or even if, Katie explains what she's found to her parents, I'm glad it ended where it did.  A good story always leaves a few questions unanswered.
In the end, Gone Home isn't a traditional game, by any means.  It is, essentially, an interactive story, and if that's not your cup of tea, then I'd suggest giving this one a pass.  But if you want to experience a really nice story, and see what tricks your expectations may play on you, then I wholeheartedly encourage you to play.

Receiver manages to create a dark sci-fi setting with the use of a few short tape recordings. The game itself focuses on detailed gun manipulation that turn the automated actions of reloading, swapping mags or just checking how much ammo you got left, into detailed keystrokes that can end in disaster if used wrong in a combat situation. This is a great basis to give the game a lot of replayability even though it only features 3 weapons and two types of enemies as, like in a good action puzzler, your precise timing and situational awarness are tested over and over again even if you played through it before. The randomized layout and placement of enemies and pickups further adds to the replaybility of the title.
If you are not turned down by perma-death and the inability to safe or load a gamestate and you have a soft spot for punishing first-person action combined with a fresh look at gun play, this might be the title for you.

This isn't a terrible game. Yes it has it's flaws, but it's not TERRIBLE. Number one, glitches galore. Every single time I played this game there was usually four, I counted. While it doesn't constitute the game being bad, the glitches constantly break the immerson and makes the game feel rushed. Number two, melodramatic story. Now, I played the first homefront. And while the story was ok, I thought the characters were pretty unique and I enjoyed fighting with most of them (
), some of these characters were a little...too much. Voice acting was ok, but some of the lines were just...ugh. Edgy fourteen year old♥♥♥♥♥♥ Especially from the NPC's, they were the worst offenders there. Story-wise, the game is...pretty aight. There's predictable twists and turns (THEY WERE THE TRAITOR ALL ALONG? 'GASP), and some things that are left pretty vaugley unclear, but it's not a bad story by any means. Now, the gameplay. Comparing it to the last game, it's leap and bounds ahead. They turned a "meh" FPS into a pretty good open world game, where conflict is constantly arising on the streets and there's war everywhere you go. The story missions are usually pretty interesting, as are some of the strikepoint missions, which help you take back the city stronghold by stronghold, but shooting up the same fortress to turn the same nozzle on the same gas valve gets pretty tedious after awhile, I must say. The only thing that really made me groan were the flashpoint missions. THESE WERE THE SCORN OF MY PLAYTHROUGH. I'd just be walking down the street, shooting some KPA and getting so close to my objective when I would hear over the radio, "Hey guys, I'm gonna have to call a flashpoint here." Then, being the morally righteous prick that I am, I'd have to turn around and help the same three people fight the same eight bad guys or stop the same missile launcher from launching its missiles. These missions did almost nothing for the game expect annoy the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of me. ♥♥♥♥ flashpoint.
Anyway, game mechanics. During your playthrough, you can buy a multitude of weapons, and use these upgrade token-like thingys so that one gun can become another gun at a moments notice. You can modify your weapon on the go with attachments you've bought, i.e. your submachine gun with a muzzle flash can become a pistol with a silencer with a few clicks. You've also got your standard upgrades, stuff that makes you take more damage, stuff that makes you run faster, things like that.
Now throughout the whole thing, one thing really bothered me out of everything. The KPA, the seemingly unbeatable army that crippled america, the superior fighting force that had crippled America was...just filled with a bunch of kittens. (I'm sure you know what I mean.) Taking these guys down was super easy, even the heavy guys. Mostly. In large numbers, they could be a problem, but it was nothing that a LMG couldn't fix. And vehicles? Once you got a rocket launcher, not a problem. Blew up with one shot. The only thing I found kinda annoying was the airships that would fly around and alert the entire map worth of enemies to your position. Once it saw you, the alarm that sounded always made me want to punch my screen. So annoying. Anyway, point-being, the enemies were hyped up and didn't really show up to play, it never really felt like I needed to use the guerilla warfare that the game advertised, I could walk down the street and leave a trail of bodies in my path.
Bottom Line: This is NOT bad game. But it's still not a great game. But it's still a game I enjoyed playing, so I'm still gonna recommend it. If it's on sale, pick it up. You probably won't regret it.

I've played Dino D-Day for 22 minutes and I can already recommend this game highly. In these 20 minutes I have had more fun that in 2 hours of some games. I knew about this game but never looked at any videos or pictures of it or anything, I just knew it existed. Then I saw it was on sale this week, and I've been on a WWII kick with Call of Duty and Day of Defeat. I snatched it and installed it not knowing what to expect, I was delightfully surprised. This game is fun, fast paced and an interesting parody on history. I am a history buff and of course I know that WWII is probably one, if not the most horrid and deadly conflicts in history, so parody shouldn't really exist. Yet at the same time, the WWII setting is only a backdrop for this fun and fictional world in which the Germans use dinosaurs as weapons. With such a parody it makes sense that things like Swastikas aren't used because there is really no point in enforcing that realism, it just remains kind of upbeat. When you win, similar to most Valve games, a box shows up stating who won, this time in the form of a newspaper with a funny picture of a world leader and a funny fake quote. It really adds to the hilarity of dinosaurs already running around. The Axis, from the little I've seen, is the only side that seems to have dinosaurs (Although I may be completely wrong) but these creatures remain balanced with normal gun play and it works greatly. Overall, if you're looking for a fun, new WWII experience with TF2 style antics then definitely pick up this game. Some people say the servers are dead but I found at least one this late (Like 12:30 AM while writing this) so it seems fine to me.
Dinosaur D-Day: 8/10

Excellent game! I just played it for hours. It's roughly like Diner Dash, but way more invovled. I like that it's repetitve enough that you can memorize certain tasks (so the game doesn't feel impossible!) but not so repetitve that it turns into a rote timing game (like Diner Dash can). Most items can have multiple recipes (which you can get by purchasing upgrades as you go along) which keeps the novelty factor alive and continues making it challenging for a long time.
I also like that the customers don't really get impatient like they do in DD - items have a wait time in the queue and will contribute to a bad score if you don't get to the fast enough, but it's not like DD where certain people are more annoyed than others. Similarly, I like that you can get an order kinda wrong and it doesn't really penalize you. You wouldn't get a perfect score, but the customer isn't angry either. (If you give them the entirely wrong order, they will be mad, of course, but if you just forget one ingredient or something, they're just mildly annoyed).
Another cool feature is that you don't have to use your mouse (unless you really want to) but instead can use keystrokes for everything. The default keystrokes are pretty self-explanatory (c for creamer, s for sugar, etc), or else easily learnable (n for onion, v for olive). And if you just can't rememeber them... they let you change the default keystrokes, per food, to whatever you want them to be. Love how flexible that system is!
Besides being like a highly improved Diner Dash, this game also has a touch of Tycoon in it as well, which I love. They did a good job of giving you warnings of things (Rainy day coming! May want to have rainy day food on the menu!), but still not making it super tedious (for example, you only have to buy equipment and recipes, but don't have to keep on eye on / purchase supplies). They have a health inspector that comes every 5 days, but all she checks is that you're cleaning the toilet, etc. Since you know ahead of time that she's coming, you can opt for an easy menu that day to save yourself some time and make sure you get her demands met.
There are also some interesting side options you can do. There are occasional bets you can take (or not) that can make you some extra cash. You can also take catering jobs once you've upgraded a bit for some SUPER easy cash. :) And if you happen to have a perfect day (I've only managed this once so far!) you get a cash bonus for that as well.
I definitely recommend this game! It's straightforward enough to have zero learning curve (and they even allow you to repeat tutorials anytime you want to learn the different recipes!), but it's complex enough to not get boring and to give yourself something to work towards (gotta buy that pizza oven!).
(PS: The only real downside I found was when the robber comes. I've only had that happen once but it was during rush hour and giving a description to the police was pretty tedious so I lost several food orders b/c I couldn't get to them fast enough (also there was a time limit on the description-giving and I didn't do it fast enough because I was distracted by my food burning so... I didn't get the report filed quick enough to get my money back! Boo....) Luckily the robber doesn't seem to come often and I also noticed some upgrades you can buy to make him even less so.... yeah....)

This is a great game. The market is getting flooded with CCGs nowadays. It is good to see something that is not cookie cutter. The game rewards free to play players well, and is generous if you choose to buy into it.
First things first, it is great to play a game like this where you can respond on your opponents turn, rather than just sit and wait for your turn.
The different game modes are well done also. You can play Gauntlet (with a deck you make) vs the AI for free for rewards.
A step up from that is Forge where you craft a deck by picking from between 3 cards ala hearthstone, then play the AI with it. This is a great mode, and good for people learning the game and working on there collection
Draft mode is like Magic, you pick from a pack and it gets passed. You can quit after one pick, and pick it up whenever again. There is no time constraint. After you open 4 packs and build your deck (75 cards, min 25 power) you head to winning 7 or losing 3 whichever comes first. Again all on your own time you can stop after any game and pick it up later.
Then there is Ranked, where there is a ladder system you can work on finishing as low as you can monthly for rewards.
This is by far my favorite game of this Genre and have played most since beta that have been out. It has more that Magic feel to it, as they have several people helping on the game that are huge in the Magic community LSV (Louis Scott Vargas) to name one.
Do yourself a favor if you like these games try this out and give it a whirl.
Also make sure to join the Discord chat where the Devs hang out and the public are very helpful.

Excellent game, similar to MTG (including similar resource system), but without with a more restricted window to interact with your opponent, making the it more streamlined, but a little less deep. It also takes advantage of the digital format to add new mechanics that cannot be implemented IRL (like keeping track of stat buff outside the battlefield).
The F2P progression is nice, if you're willing to play draft. You keep the cards you draft, making the cost of entry effectively low (you pay 5 packs worth of gold to get in, handpick cards from 4 packs, and get 0.5 pack in gold even if you lose all matches). You cannot go infinite without winning 6 or 7 out of 7 matches each time, but you can grind that last bit of gold with AI matches.
I don't love the UI, but it's quite polished. I think the battlefield is too small when there is plenty of real estate wasted with interactables. I'm, also not a huge fan of the cartoonish art style. But these are all small details.
The greatest problem with the game comes from the choice of resource: sigils (similar to mtg lands). Although it gives more depth, being stuck with a bunch of cards and no sigils or vice-versa (MTG "mana screw") can and will lose you a game here and there. These are the moments where I think "this is the one think I
miss from MTG". Even though the game has a few mechanisms to help prevent this, it still happens, and you have to be prepared to accept it.
Overall, this is an amazing game!

Foresight: A Space RTS, with Base build, Armadas and Commanders.
Well you can compare this game to such classics like The Outforce or Conquest: Frontier Wars and Starwars Empire at War.
You do build in Space a Base , collect Resources like in C&C  and can jump to other systems like in  Conquest: Frontier Wars. So the map is separated in sectors like just 4 to. 20 or more.
in each sector you can build a base to collect resources and they all are connected with wormholes.
You have 3 Factions here, 2 really on energy like in C&C, so no energy no turrets power and slowly production, the other is unique, they need blood banks. Not enough blood and you units start to lose Hit Points.
Units are like in Starwars Empire at War. So you can build from small scouts to huge Capital Battleships.
The Unique idea is here you must place fighter and bombers in bigger ships to move them around, like the Protoss Carrier, but you build them in Shipyard, not on the capital ship.
Lots of Corvettes, Gunship and other support ships are here too.
Well best part is the unit limit, to increase this you must get a "Fleet Captain" on a ship, that you can assign ships to him. So you have like limit for 10 units, Assign them to the captain and now you can buy another 8 units and so on.
So if you loose a Fleet Captain you have like 18 Units and cant buy more units. Because you are with 8 units too high by the limit. Pretty interesting mechanic in my Opinion.
In most RTS its just some kind of house that is placed somewhere randomly. Here its you fleet commander. Story is challenging and interesting, the AI is like in Tiberium Wars, the game itself feels like an Space C&C.
You can by the way choose here the Tech Level like in Red Alert 1 or set the Amount of Start Resources. Like in Starwas Empire at War you can increase the game play speed, yes you have game speed controls here.
For this game I can put my Hand in fire, an extreme good AAA Indie RTS game.
The controls suck. The games are very easy. But.. I CAN'T STOP PLAYING. It's a decent time waster. You could do a LOT worse.

Probably the best card game I've played in my life. No, the BEST card game I've played.
Recently I went on a card game streak, as I've been waiting to settle on a new CCG/TCG for a long time. I've tried 6 different ones (excluding Hearthstone, I'm done with that RNG, shallow mess), and I tried this one the least, as I've thought I would like it the least. And my god, I've started playing last night, and I can already safely say I will not touch any other card games for a long time.
It strikes the perfect combination of complexity (color system, deep mechanics, great combos, many different card types, power cards), and simplicity (the look and feel of Hearthstone).
This is essentialy a dedicated crossover of HS and MTG, and it's executed perfectly, and it has enough base content to satisfy the game for weeks and months to come.
ALSO the economy is perfect for a f2p CCG game. Booster packs have a great amount of cards, and gold earning is fair and balanced without paying. And like normal MTG, it has game modes where you construct a deck from booster packs and you get to keep all the cards, on top of the game rewarding you cards ALL THE TIME.
Now while the game does need a lot more polish round the edges to make it feel *perfect*, the game progress from closed beta has been wiped and after last AMAZING patch we are officially on set 1 of the game, so it's a perfect time to jump into the game and start collecting and duelling.

To be frank, the game is half-baked.
The retro-style pixel graphics are great - really, the best thing about the game.  The combat is okay - not good, not bad, just rather simple and functional.  If you're looking for a pixel-shooter, you can do much better.
The survival mechanics are just busywork.  Granted, that's basically any survival game, but here they become a chore more than anything.  Likewise the simple minigames and you engage in to keep your train running.  Both of these things will distract you from the bulk of the story, which is odd because it's pretty clear the devs are very much in love with the story.
I don't know why, it's not a very good or interesting story.  The dialogue is actually pretty bad, at least in its english version; the devs really should have hired someone with a better grasp of the language to write the localization.  The ending...  Well, I won't get into any spoilers, but it leaves a lot to be desired.
The odd thing is the game style was really begging for a roguelike treatment, and I'm confused as to why the devs didn't go that route.  Not every game needs to be a roguelike, but I think it would have done well for this game.
As it is, I really can't recommend it.

I would like to recommand this version of F1 if Codemaster fixes bugs. Being a Formula 1 fan and having played F1 2005 on PS2, F1 2009 on both PSP and Wii with 100% race on careers, and F1 2015 during the freeplay (which was kind of rubbish tbh), F1 2016 is way better than its predecessors (Graphics, gameplay, tire management and settings, etc.).
So for its pros:
-Awesome graphics and framerate for middle-end GPU (you can race at around 30fps on heavy rain with a car crashing in front of you)
-Realistic sounds (the motor sound is quite original to the V6 hybrids)
-Safety car with VSC both back
-Choice to manually control the speed when entering to the pit lane
-Choice to start a race manually, needing to wait the red light to go off and engage the clutcher
-Possibility to have a race at any time during the day, eg Abu Dhabi at noon (rip tires)
-You can let your engineer via TR to shut up ("Shut up Jeff" is actually an achievement)
-An indicator that shows you how far is the DRS line
-Tire management improved, the effects of the rain on slick tires are more obvious (drop of tire temperature and lap time)
Cons:
-UNAVAILABLE Career mode. I just simply can't start a career as the game crashes each time I start the FP1 in Melbourne. It crashes right after the presentation of the circuit, no matter how many times I reinstalled the game.
-The track dries too quickly, being a bit unrealistic (Two laps after the rain stops on full race, everyone enters to the pits and changes inters to soft tires.)
-A bug about TR that happened several times, I am playing on X1 controller, but sometimes when I just want to get "Full race updates"(on the first page, second choice) it chooses mysteriously "Get intermediates tyres (on the second page choice 4)".
- Jeff says "The weather is unavailable" during weather changes (eg from heavy to light rain), so you don't know if you need to continue on your current tyres or going back to the pits to cahnge tires, and it will be much decisive if you do not want to be undercut.
-Both hands of the driver being away from the steering wheel at the end of a race (if you achieve first) but the car turns magically (eg after crossing the finish line in Mexico).
-Formation laps are meaningless as you can hit the wall and overtake as many times as you want, without having any penalities or damage on the car.
-A bug when the safety car is out, the driver in front of you may be overtaken if he goes off the track just a little
-Kimi smiles at the podium XD
In overall, F1 2016 is a great game IF bugs are being fixed. :-(

Like many others, I came to Eternal from the RNG fiesta that is Hearthstone currently. This game is truly a breath of fresh air in today's digital CCG landscape.
PROS:
1. Although there are microtransactions, this game is truly F2P thanks to the generous rewards system. For example, in Draft Mode (like Arena in Hearthstone) you get to keep ALL 48 cards that you choose, on top of the usual rewards for winning. There are also free random cards and gold for ranked wins.
2. Minimal RNG. However, because of the way the mana system works (similar to lands in MTG) you can get mana screwed but proper deck building should mitigate this,
3. Interactive combat system. This is similar to MTG where you can take some actions (e.g. Fast Spells) on your opponent's turn, such as when he attacks you. Again, I compare this to Hearthstone where you pretty much can't do anything on your opponent's turn.
4. Complex strategy. The cards in the first set are varied and allow for many different deck types. There are 5 factions and you can have all 5 in your deck (albeit risk getting mana screwed).
5. Complex tactics. Here I'm talking about the skill you need to assess the board state and make plays. Each player can have up to 14(?) units on the board and this can lead to deliciously challenging decisions - which units do I attack with and when? which  of my opponent's units do I block and with what units?
CONS:
1. Clunky UI. This is a minor gripe as it's already in a decent state, just needs a few tweaks.
2. Small player base. This game isnt hugely popular now and there aren't alot of web resources (no net decks :(). Hopefully with the steam release this game will pick up in numbers.
Overall this game is one of the better CCGs out there. And it's F2P, so there's really no reason not to install it and give it a go.

The story starts in the beginning of the 10th century BC and ends the last day of 901 BC. This period followed the Bronze Age collapse in the Near East, and the century saw the Early Iron Age take hold there. The Greek Dark Ages which had come about in 1200 BC. The animals had begun their takeover. As each of the animal legions joined forces, human cities fell to their knees. As the pharaoh gold mask is buried, Archippus, Archon of Athens dies after a reign of 19 years and is succeeded by his son Thersippus. The blue bear species had increased in population due to their important niche. As King Gong of Zhou becomes King of the Zhou Dynasty of China, the legion of animals pursues the Egyptian empire. Solomon, king of the ancient Israelites calls for aid as an Owlbear terrorises their rein. The Senate of the Great Galactic Republic watches closely from above as FOXHOUND begins their development of a weapon to surpass metal gear- MCPON John 117 codename: "Master Chief". As they create this "One man army" a man "Alan Wake" travels to India searching for the shortcuts on Garfield Cart. He encounters only the hardest resistance. A notable force working against him is the infamous Lena Oxton who pursues a battle against Claire Farron (Lightning not to be confused with lightning McQueen - Kachow). You are introduced to the evil Queen Vexa who sends it's minions to take over the ship, that's when things go wrong and because you don't have seatbelts, you jump. The ship crashes on or near an isolated island in a remote region of the Pacific Ocean.

I really want to write a negative review here because I have some exceptional design disagreements with the developers--HOWEVER, if given the choice between a thumbs up and a thumbs down, I ultimately have to tilt my thumb up (albeit with many caveats).
Essentially, the huge, ENORMOUS, shining issue regarding this game:
It's design team contains multiple world-famous Magic: the Gathering veterans, such as Conley Woods, Patrick Chapin, and Mr. Luck Skill Victory Luis "LSV" Scott Vargas. And, guess what? The gameplay is not only similar, but updated for the digital age with some mechanics that can only be done thanks to the advent of a digital space.
Furthermore, and this is ENORMOUS: the card collection rate, in my experience, is **exceptionally** fair. After a few months of playing, I was able to not only craft all the tier 1 decks, but also craft premium versions of several of them, just for giggles. In contrast, in a game called Alteil, that same time frame spent playing might result in one competitive deck, which was a mere whim away from getting nerfed away.
Essentially, while there are some severe design disagreements that I have with the developers at this point in time, it is nevertheless *readily apparent* that this game is being headed by a bunch of people that have extensive experience in playing the most complex strategic card game at a high level, that they love what they do, and it shows through the work they put in.
That said, as a caveat: in my opinion, the game is a bit too simplistic at this point in time--namely in that there feel like too few opportunities to really one-up your opponent, pull one lever instead of the other, and really make an outplay by using a card in a way that a lesser player wouldn't. Instead, most of the thinking is done outside the context of the game--mainly in deck design, as opposed to deck *piloting*. In an age of netdecking, reddit, the internet, and other strategy discussion, I'd hope that given the same deck, that two people could have wildly different results instead of there being slight differences.
At the end of the day, the gameplay is a simplified variant of Magic: the Gathering, for now. But with a very fair F2P model and designed by some very knowledgeable people, what have you got to lose?

An utterly♥♥♥♥♥♥game that lures you in by it's fun looking art style and temptation of cool units like any good tower defence, then promptly turns face, drops its pants and ♥♥♥♥♥ all over you when you lean forward to get into it.
The system works where you spawn troops from your truck for munitions, they race forth and attack the defenders base who can set up walls, barbed wire, mg nests, sniper towers, artillary, and AA, backed up by constant waves defending ground troops spawned from tents.
As time goes on a small timer in the bottom left gives you a random (random being the horror word here) boost of munitions to spend on units, or attack card like an air strike, gas, focus fire, rally or decoy to upset the enemy defence. The issue being, there is no pattern at all to this system, the randomness making one 3 red skull opponent (Meant to be very hard) very easy as you bounce from 1 air strike or gas to the next, creating a new path through the enemy defence and flanking. The next round you may fight a 2 white skull opponent, these are meant to be the run of the mill bases where the new players come to fight. The timer will not drop a single attack card, leaving the player with no control over their units, and no way to stop them from waddling in and being slaughtered. The random element kills it.
Now as we go on, we learn about this and we adapt, we bring in rarer attack cards to start to give ourselves a larger initial push into the enemies base before our power wanes. This in turn is blocked by some severe pathing flaws of our units caused by the defender, blocking their base off entirely with walls. In turn our units cluster, their mortars landing on their position, taking out groups of troops, before they finally tick into their attack animation and attack the wall. However this "Tactic" isn't quite over, the troops will cluster at the deepest part of the wall before trying to break through, so the enemy only needs to set up sniper towers and barber wire on the other side, and our troops will not attack until they clear the barbed wire, by then, there are none left, as these towers cleave through one man and into the next, causing collateral damage only stopped by 1 possible unit available to the attacker, the riot soldier, with his large shield and high health pool he can survive long enough to get over the wire, only to be glanced by a mortar shell, fumble the shield and be instant killed like the rest.
TLDR, this game had promise initially as a new tower defence/attacking moment to be enjoyed in short bursts, however has squandered their potential by their inability to stamp out bugs, exploits and the money grabbing tactics of exponentially higher unit costs.

This is a really neat game.
A lot of thought went into making this.  I believe it came out of a game development challenge where the creators had a very limited amount of time to put it together.  But they did a really great job of boiling the whole thing down to the core essentials and ended up with a very challenging yet entertaining result.
They did their research on firearm mechanics and created a control mechanic that requires a player to use more than just the LMB and 'R' key.  It's a rush every time you manage to survive a tense situation due to the muscle memory employed in manipulating the equipment.
The persistent death mechanic was also well-chosen and ramps up the intensity in a good way, making for a more interesting assessment of risk-versus-reward scenarios.  But it doesn't pose so much of a hurdle that it makes the game impossible.  When I finally 'beat' the game, my successful session was only about 30-40 minutes.  A totally reasonable time for a must-beat-in-a-single-sitting game.
The developers even threw in an interesting background story.  Even though you can ignore it completely if you want, the information is presented to you as you collect the cassette tapes required to complete the objective.
On a side note, I also encountered zero bugs the whole time I played.  Another example of the thoroughness and focus on the core mechanics and architecture.
Overall, this is a really fun, challenging, well-made game.  Hats off to the developers.  And a recommendation to any gamers interested in off-the-beaten-path style games, ESPECIALLY if you find it on sale.

Completed the game in 4.7 hours. The Final Station is about a train conductor piloting the train through a post-apocalyptic world. It has an interesting central idea and world-building effort, but is hold back by its linear and repetitive gameplay, and for its price, offers surprisingly little contents. On the railway, you play mini-games every 5 minuites or so to keep the train running; at the stations, you melee through 5 types of enemies to get the password through the level. The levels lack variety, barely giving you any motive to keep on playing. The campaign is short, unchallenging, and has virtually no replaying value. (both the path your train follows and each individual level are linear. only the password you need to find to pass each level is randomly generated.) The storytelling (conversations between passengers and the stations you stop at) felt insufficient, and is poorly written compared to many other games it resembles, such as Sunless Sea and FTL. The art is solid but feels generic. It's not a bad game considering the general experience, but is definitely a forgettable one among the many survival indies on steam.

It’s hard not to be impressed by the sheer scale. The Crew might have miniaturised the USA, shrinking states and cities so that they’re boiled down to an essence, making Chicago to New York a fifteen-minute drive, but this is still the most expansive open world of any racing game. It makes the Franco-Italian and Colorado settings of the Forza Horizon games seem tiddly, while Need for Speed: Rivals and Most Wanted can’t compare. The nearest open worlds would be the Hawaii and Ibiza settings of Test Drive Unlimited and its sequels – games you’ll soon find lurking in The Crew’s DNA – but even these can’t match The Crew’s massive landscapes for size.
These aren’t empty landscapes, either. The cities might not be accurate, but each one captures the most iconic architecture of its real-world inspiration, and a little of the feel. The freeways might not go on for miles and miles, but from the wild coastline of Northern California to the grasslands and forests of Dakota they traverse some incredible scenery. The streets teem with cars, buses, taxis, trucks and people. The tracks outside the cities are busy with wildlife, albeit some strangely suicidal critters. And everywhere you go there’s something to do, whether a full-sized event or a bite-sized challenge, that might see you slaloming around markers or speeding through gates in return for cash, experience points and car parts.
As with Forza Horizon 2 there are fast travel options that you’ll barely use, just because driving from one place to another is a rewarding activity in itself.
Nope, the world is undoubtedly the star of The Crew. If The Crew has problems, they’re the result of other things.
Pros :
- Vast open-world to explore
- Packed with events and challenges
- Enjoyable off-road missions
- Fun with other players
Cons:
- Missions can be exasperating
- Handling lacks grip
- Struggles to bring players together

One Sentence Summary - If you like pressing 15 buttons to shoot a gun, buy this game... otherwise, buy something else...
--REVIEW--
I simply cannot say that I recommend this game. It seems that this game was more of a tech demo than anything. Other than the "Tron" sounding background music, this game really doesn't provide any emotional connection with the player. The game simply starts... there is no story provided, other than the players having some sort of idea that they are running along some rooftops looking for cassette tapes. I assume these tapes give some sort of minimalistic story. I get the point that this was made for some 7-day FPS challenge, but they could have at least given the player some sort of story or motivation to find these tapes. The graphics are incredibly minimalistic, yet it runs poorly on my laptop, even on the "fastest" setting. I get much better performance playing something like Dragon Age or FInal Fantasy 13 than I would on this game. When I turned the resolution down to the lowest setting (like 600x800 or so), I got decent performance. You might as well do this, because you won't lose any graphical details... because there are none to lose. I believe this to be either a hardware compatability problem or simply not programmed well to run efficiently.
---PROS---
+Minimalistic/Non-existent story (if you like that sort of thing)
+Tron music
+Very "realistic" process of having to load and reload a gun.
---CONS---
-Minimalistic/Non-existent story
-No Tron motorcycles or discs
-You have to press way too many buttons to load a gun. There is no tutorial or simple explanation other than pressing the "?" button for help, and blindly pressing the buttons until your gun is ready to shoot.
-Graphics are very minimalistic (AKA- Didn't have time to add detail)
-The game runs extremely poor on a dual core laptop with 8GB ram.
-For the average game player, I think the gun loading process is extremely cumbersome... At least make a tutorial or arrange the buttons in a streamlined order.
---CONCLUSION---
If you like randomly generated worlds in games with no story, as well as tron music and hard to load guns, this is the game for you. For the rest of us, we'll be better off playing something else.

Red Dawn + Far Cry = Homefront: The Revolution
And that's a good combination. You play as an American resistance fighter based in Philadelphia years into a brutal occupation of the U.S by North Korean military forces. As a resistance fighter you'll be conducting guerilla warfare in the ruins around Phili, establishing bases, moving in and around heavily guarded areas, and pushing the KPA out. One block at a time.
Outside of no man's land, you'll be infiltrating walled up yellow zones where most of the civilians are forced to reside and treated like animals. Blend in with your surroundings and spread word of the resistance. And by "spread the word" I mean assassinate, sabotage, establish safe houses, and inspire the people to rise up against their oppressors.
The co-op component is a 4 player mission mode consisting of different missions carried out all across areas straight from the single player. No one really plays the online mode anymore, but it is possible to complete some of the missions solo with some practice.

Homefront The Revolution had an abysmal launch, being riddled with bugs, and was all-in-all one of the most underperforming AAA titles of 2016. A year after release though, most of these issues seem to be fixed up. I did encounter a few, once or twice during my playtime objectives would escort missions during the singleplayer bug out, and then during co-op the mission Triage would not spawn the enemies needed to finish the mission (happened to a friend as well), so it is not entirely bug-free. However, by and large this game has been quite polished up. I didn’t suffer any gamebreaking bugs (crashing, something that would force me to restart a playthrough, etc…)
I was disappointed to find out that it was not a direct sequel to the 2012 game, but more of a spiritual successor. The setting is still what I enjoyed from that game so it was not a huge deal to me.
Graphics for this game are beautiful, as most games that run on CryEngine are. All of the areas of the map look and feel unique as a result, which makes for a quite immersive experience.
Gameplay is extremely similar to Far Cry 3 and 4, if you found yourself enjoying the combat and game mechanics in that I would say that you would likely find the same things to enjoy here.
Story/Plot was ok, it is a pretty absurd premise to begin with (Korean occupation of the United States), so I would say that with that in mind I found it enjoyable for a playthrough. I did think that some of the characters could have been developed a little more (and some do during the course of the DLCs), and that the Koreans could have been used a little better by giving them a direct antagonist in the story.
Co-op multiplayer is surprisingly fun, definitely a nice addition, but I dont think its worth buying this game just for this alone as it is borderline impossible to find a match through matchmaking, If you can convince some friends to play it with you though, it is a fun time.
Overall I’d rate the game a 7/10. I was pleasantly surprised by how much I enjoyed this game, Sure it is far from perfect, but I enjoyed it and definitely got my money’s worth out of it. Especially with how cheap you can pick it up for now ($8 or thereabouts for the game and the expansion pass), I’d say it is more than worth it for that price.
Also, as mentioned above, there are three story DLCs, Voice of Freedom, Aftermath, and Beyond the Walls.

Voice of Freedom is a prologue to the story. Its short and adds a little bit of backstory, but is nothing special. 5/10

Aftermath is an epilogue to the story. Also fairly short, but enjoyable and ties up some loose ends from the singleplayer. 8/10
Beyond the Walls happens some time after the singleplayer. Is decently long, but adds the most in story content of the three DLCs. I found this to be extremely good and a great way to finish up the game. 10/10
