My thoughts on Banished:
Surprisingly addicting game! It seems so simple, and yet it has so much more to offer than anything that EA or Ubisoft have ever developed.
Your goal is to build houses for your people and give them enough food, clothes, firewood and other resources to let them make it through the cold winters. All you start with are ten people and some resources, and you're good to go.
Make sure they gather enough food for everyone, assign builders, build a school to teach the children, and gather enough firewood to prevent your citizen from freezing. Trade to stock up your storages with new fruits and seeds to be planted on your fields, build cattles, and expand your city with more and more houses, structures and farms.
But, obviously, the more houses you build, the more children will be born and the population will rise, and so will demands.
Your mission is to ensure that at every point in time your citizen have everything they need, because they'll starve, freeze to death, or catch themselves deadly diseases and within minutes all of your progress will be lost - so be careful and always watch your ressources.
This game is being developed by a single person, and as it is in early development, there still are lots of bugs, and the AI also could  need some work done.
Nonetheless, defenitely worth a purchase, even at full price.

If you take a certain amount of joy from watching your plans come to fruition, then I recommend Banished.
It is simple to understand but difficult to master. I am only in my 14th year, and the latest highlight was watching the 2 chickens I bought (for 100 barrels of ale) breed and become 26 chickens. This gives me more consistent food and that is good.
If that doesn't sound interesting, this is not the game for you.
The graphics are great and the variety of action is amazing in a game that as an amazingly small footprint.
There are bugs, glitches and weird behaviour, but nothing to distracting and somethings which could be part of the game.
Like when my farmers did not plant their crops one year. Could be that as with the orchards that occasionally need to be chopped down, my soil was overused. But without some notice I was left to assume that it was bug. Luckily my town survived.
These bugs could be devastating. Some will mention a fisherman starving while carrying food and yes I can see that as frustrating. But they should be able to get to their home to eat quickly or you haven't setup a very nice town. If you imagine them as robots that walk for hours to pick up an entire tree and return...wrong game. These people work for a while, then rest. If its cold they go in to warm up. Make the job easy enough that you could do it and your townsfolk will thrive.
The bugs that bug me, are labourers clearing trees from a building location, hauling the logs to a stockpile, putting them down and then picking them back up to take back and deliver to the same location. I understand the programming logic must be complicated for so many different sprites. But I wish they'd just leave it.
Otherwise, there is nothing that slowing down alittle and taking your time won't solve. You need to err on the side of caution. It took me 4 years of storing a little ale to get enough for the chickens. In the end it was all worth it.

I really want to write a negative review here because I have some exceptional design disagreements with the developers--HOWEVER, if given the choice between a thumbs up and a thumbs down, I ultimately have to tilt my thumb up (albeit with many caveats).
Essentially, the huge, ENORMOUS, shining issue regarding this game:
It's design team contains multiple world-famous Magic: the Gathering veterans, such as Conley Woods, Patrick Chapin, and Mr. Luck Skill Victory Luis "LSV" Scott Vargas. And, guess what? The gameplay is not only similar, but updated for the digital age with some mechanics that can only be done thanks to the advent of a digital space.
Furthermore, and this is ENORMOUS: the card collection rate, in my experience, is **exceptionally** fair. After a few months of playing, I was able to not only craft all the tier 1 decks, but also craft premium versions of several of them, just for giggles. In contrast, in a game called Alteil, that same time frame spent playing might result in one competitive deck, which was a mere whim away from getting nerfed away.
Essentially, while there are some severe design disagreements that I have with the developers at this point in time, it is nevertheless *readily apparent* that this game is being headed by a bunch of people that have extensive experience in playing the most complex strategic card game at a high level, that they love what they do, and it shows through the work they put in.
That said, as a caveat: in my opinion, the game is a bit too simplistic at this point in time--namely in that there feel like too few opportunities to really one-up your opponent, pull one lever instead of the other, and really make an outplay by using a card in a way that a lesser player wouldn't. Instead, most of the thinking is done outside the context of the game--mainly in deck design, as opposed to deck *piloting*. In an age of netdecking, reddit, the internet, and other strategy discussion, I'd hope that given the same deck, that two people could have wildly different results instead of there being slight differences.
At the end of the day, the gameplay is a simplified variant of Magic: the Gathering, for now. But with a very fair F2P model and designed by some very knowledgeable people, what have you got to lose?

I see a lot of new reviews...with a healthy dose of "not recommended". Invariably it feels like the HS kids just can't handle real variance and how to deal with it on a statistical curve. They see cool cards and want to play trash decks without any consideration of how to manage 75 cards with only 1 mulligan.
Too bad...l2p. There are so many exceedingly subtle adjustments you can make with the big 6-8 decks that at this point the options are, given the limited number of cards, quite impressive. I know I know...there are so many killer combos out there if you could just consistently draw a certain batch of 12-16 cards on the reg. It isn't going to happen, so stop trying to turn the game into something it isn't.
The great part of this game is that your win curve will constantly be dependent on your adjustment to the meta...and deciding when to move from 1 to 2 cards or 3 to 2 of another type. The cards people complain about (Champion of Chaos anyone?) often get wrecked once the meta changes, and are not OP until well, they are again.
Anyways, great game, and essentially f2p. I've spent $30.00 on the game and have every common card, every uncommon card, every rare card, and as an aggregate 38% of legendaries, with 30,000 shiftstone to spare when I need something new.  Try that with any other online CCG.

A game with interesting ideas that, unfortunately, never quite lives up to its potential. Its surreal world is intriguing and very atmospheric. Certain areas become truly creepy and unnerving. The actualy "plot" - such as it is - never really gets off the ground, however.  The story just doesn't go anywhere and ends abruptly. Lots of things are referred to, but it just never feels like a coherent story and there are so many unanswered questions that it just becomes bad design. Where is the other half of the game??
Gameplaywise, there are 2 parts: managing your train and exploring. The train is basically just micromanaging parts with simple controls and babysitting passenegers who are inexplicably incapable of feeding themselves. It's boring and feels like busywork. When you get off the train, it's a 2d shooter with limited ammo. Gunplay is serviceable but clunky. There are only 4 enemies and they lack a real sense of personality or menace. Other than that you just wander around and salvage stuff like in a thousand other games. The gameplay desperately needed something more, some sort of twist to make it unique and interesting.
The graphics, on the other hand, are often beautiful and sometimes haunting. Strange, mysterious backgrounds are around every corner. There are many intriguing sights and a variety of environments. I really liked this.
I also would like to point out how excellent the sound design is. The music is great and really sets a mood. Sound effects like rain, grass crunching under your feet, etc. are also good. Guns are not so good. The guns sound like peashooters and don't make much of an impact.
All in all, it's a short game (4 hours) that I would recommend only on sale if you are interested in a unique and atmospheric game that falls short on actual gameplay.

Giving this a "thumbs down" was difficult for me to do, mainly because space RTS's are probably one of my favorite genres to play.  As for what I don't like about it, the voice acting is horrid and the graphics aren't really reflective of modern day technology...the UI and camera controls (you can't rotate the camera and your zooming is limited) remind me a bit of Star Trek Armada from back in the day.  Base and turret building are present, but limited...there's just not a lot of building options here.  I do like the idea of building fleets and in doing so, your population cap will actually get smaller...at least that's how my experience went.  I essentially built ships until I hit my pop cap, hired a fleet commander and a fleet advisor and assigned them to the largest ship, then put them all into a fleet...then rinse and repeat.  There are three different factions and a skirmish mode, which I do like and appreciate.  I also like the wormhole/gate/sector system as it reminds me a bit of "AI War".
If the price were lower (say $5-$10), I'd give this a recommend.  As it stands, you can buy "Sins of a Solar Empire: Trinity" for $20 which has (in my opinion) better graphics/camera controls and more depth (tech trees, more resources, etc).

A fantastic open world racer, that may have minor ssues, but that does not hold it back from the finish line. The largest open world used in a racing game, spanning accross Ivory Tower's vision of the United States of America. From point to point the game is packed with a story that introduces and improves racing elements, skill challenges, head to head races, roaming lands that take you beyond paved road systems, and late game Faction Races that pit you against the whole world of players.
Negative aspects include client to server communication isssues, stats being incorrectly recorded at times, disruptions of online events, and inaccurate car mechanics. All of which have been stated as addressed in the near future.
Graphically, the game could use more on the PC side, as there is technology that goes unused due to console limitations. It does not look bad, but it is in no way eye-candy.
This game is not for simulation fans of the Project Cars style gameplay. This game is for those that want to jump in and go balls out across limitless road combinations.
All in all, an exccellent addition to people's collection, and has a bright future with endless room for improvement and additional content.

May contain spoilers.
In essence,
is a walking-exploration simulator of a man analyzing his own psyche. One aspect I like about this game is that there’s rarely any exposition. The narrative unfolds to the player through the mood, particularly its overt themes. For instance, part of one level involves finding the broken pieces of a picture of a pregnant woman, presumably your wife. Later you discover you hurt your wife – while simultaneously being exposed to dead baby props and jump-scares. Solve the puzzle and the story is short, but clear. You most likely hurt your wife while she was pregnant and she then most likely had a miscarriage. I say “maybe” because the game seems to be the first installment of a series so you never know what might change.
However, what really drives home this narrative is the creative level design. You play through roughly four different levels (reality and three depths of your unconsciousness) and they are all so unique. The overarching level planning really communicates the protagonists’ descent into his mind. The deeper you go, the darker the color palettes get, the weirder the sound effects become, the more surreal the environment appears and so forth. I will also quickly state that this game has the best flashlight of all Unity games hands down,
. It works just like a camera, and the clicking from “on” to “off” is immensely satisfying.
One aspect of this title’s well-executed atmosphere is its sound design. Instead of relying in loud thuds, open and closed doors or high-pitched string instruments, this title creates atmosphere by making commonplace sounds frightening. For instance, you’ll reach a dead end and will hear keys dangling from someone’s approaching pace through a rotten locked door blocked with wood planks – or you’ll hear like something is cracking its joints as you turn a corner until the sound evolves into something crushing a child’s skull. I also enjoyed the graphic designs. The two “monsters” that you face were horrific and the jump scares are off-beat enough for the player to get caught off guard here and there. But they’re not loud, they’re more in the fashion of a “glitch-in-the-matrix” type.
Overall,
is a fun title that I would not mind if it served as an example to follow. It's slightly above its price range but that's only a minor caveat. It’s one of the better Unity games out there right now and it has the potential to influence the genre like the Slender-Man series. That being said,
is a Unity title surpasses the expectations laid out by Slender-clones before it by avoiding the trope of collecting items while a tall, ominous silhouette follows you continuously until the end. It doesn’t revolutionize the field of horror-exploration, but it does enough to warrant its own merit within the Unity titles

I got the Freedom Fighter Bundle (+DLC) on sale and am impressed. If you like FPS games I highly recommend Homefront on sale
Bugs: I've encountered two bugs in 10 hours so far. The first was all non-music audio cutting out after a mission. This was fixed after reloading the checkpoint. The second was a black screen during normal gameplay. This was fixed by alt-tabbing. Neither issue has reoccured
Performance (1440p, specs below): On high/very high I average around 70 fps with a minimum of 60. The dusted zone saw drops to 55, but reducing shadows kept it above 60. While not great, this level of performance is acceptable to me and importantly there's no significant drops or stuttering
Graphics: pretty good overall. Little discernable difference between High and Very High. There's some good attention to detail especially in important characters' faces
Gameplay: most of the game is spent in decent-sized open areas where you perform main missions and side objectives. These objectives are either capturing zones or increasing rating by destroying vehicles, sabatoge, helping civilians etc. There's two types of areas: red zones and yellow zones. Red zones are hostile with no alarms. Yellow zones can spawn unlimited enemies during alarms and rely more on stealth. Red zones are more fun imo. Gone Home is a 2013 FP-Adventure game developed by The Fullbright Company. You play as the young student Kaitlin Greenbriar who returns home in Portland, OR after a year spent in Europe. It's the year 1995, middle of the night, and the house is empty. What happened to Kaitlin's family? You set out to explore in search of an answer.
Gone Home is neither difficult nor long. The gameplay is nigh inexistant and there is no replay value. It basically is a visual novel which is way more visual, resembling a movie, than it is a novel, telling a story.
Nevertheless, the story is highly emotional, while at the same time the atmosphere constantly switches it's tone. You never know what kind of movie you'll find yourself in next.
At first you think the disappearing of the Greenbriars might be of a supernatural cause. And then you realise there is no way for this to be true. But then again you start believing that there must be at least a ghost or two in the house as chills begin crawling down your spine.
The game keeps you wondering right until the very end.
At the time of it's release Gone Home was made fun of as a "Walking Simulator". There certainly is a truth behind this phrase. But whoever thinks this way is just too blind or ignorant to see behind the lacking gameplay.
I think that in one's life there are moments of clarity that make you think you understand the meaning of life. Sometimes life gives you such moments, other times media such as books, movies or video games does. This is due to their honesty/ sincerety considering questions you often ask yourself. They put you back on earth and they show you that you ought to be content with what you have.
To me, Gone Home is one of those moments.
Throughout the game you find all sorts of written information such as letters, birthday cards, bills, etc. All of them tell bits and pieces of the Greenbriars' difficult lives. It is up to you to decide what to find important and what not to read at all. Accorcding to your "choices" your understanding of the story changes a lot. However, the basic story is always the same. And indeed it is a tragic story that touches you.
According to your play-style, you'll need up to 120 min to finish the game. And then you'll probably never touch it again. Personally I don't see this as a disadvantage because it is an experience as incisive as Life Is Strange, which I honestly don't want to play ever again because it was just perfect the first time I played it.
The graphics are nice and the resolution is very high. Also, the audio and atmosphere are perfect.
I highly reccomend you to play Gone Home at night when you're home alone, preferably in the dark. Then you'll enjoy it even more.
So, is Gone Home a must-play? Yes, it is. It is a very special experience but unfortunately one that loses it's whole magic once you've seen it all.

Homefront: The Revolution is basically an urban take on Far Cry. There are similar animations, sounds, & other elements that make it seem like a re-skin of Far Cry 3. But even if it is, it changes enough from that game to make it a mostly different experience, like how Blood Dragon is a different enough game than Far Cry 3.
I never played the original Homefront, but my understanding is that the first game was a standard linear FPS. Early trailers for the sequel had me intrigued, but I never picked it up until there was a free weekend on Steam. I enjoyed it enough to justify the $20 sale price.
As mentioned, the game plays like Far Cry 3. It's a mostly open world (the maps are sectioned off into zones, but you can move freely between them when you unlock the fast travel points) taking place in the near future, in a Philadelphia overrun by North Koreans. You earn in-game currency by completing jobs (like taking out enemies with specific weapons, or photographing certain objects), and by taking over enemy bases. You don't upgrade your character, but the currency can be used to upgrade your gear, weapons, and mods. There's a bit of crafting in the game. There are 6 base weapons (Pistol, Shotgun, Assault Rifle, Crossbow, Battle Rifle, and Rocket Launcher) and each (except the RL) has 3 modes. Once a mode is purchased, you can mod that weapon on the fly. So the Crossbow, for example, has a basic crossbow mode, but also a "blunderbuss" and "flamethrower" mode. This is cool because even though you can only carry three weapons at a time (the pistol plus two others) you can basically switch between up to 9 different weapons without having to run back to a weapon station. In addition to the different modes, each weapon can have a few different attachments (scopes, suppressors, that sort of thing). There are also four different throwable weapons: an explosive, an incendiary, a distraction, and a hack tool (used to override locked doors or takeover drones). Each of those come in 4 alternates: throwable, remote detonation, proximity detonation, or radio-controlled car. The RC car is fun, but wish there were more interesting opportunities to use it. The throwables can be crafted from items you'll scrounge in the world—in trash cans, cars, desks, etc. But you'll also find plenty ready-made in stashes, or you can buy them from the gun shops. The in-game economy is a little weird, though. The money is used fine, as consecutive weapon upgrades are expensive. But you unlock weapon modes with some kind of units that you get from taking control of enemy strike points, or by winning over the populace (saving prisoners, destroying propaganda). Very early in the game I'd bought everything I could using those units, so there's no incentive to do tasks that earn you more, other than just to enjoy them or clear a map. By end of game I had 200 units left & nothing to spend them on.
While Far Cry 3 had plenty of vehicles, Homefront 2 only has motorbikes. And that's fine, though it would've been cool to really get to control one of the enemy armored cars or Goliaths. There are no bike races, which fits the narrative, but there are a lot of jumps, so it seems like racing on the bikes through the urban terrain would be fun. The environment itself is something the game does really well, and is the biggest difference from Far Cry. Areas of Philly are war-torn to varying degrees. Some sections (usually the "yellow zones," which are not actively hostile) are still standing, while the "red zones" are bombed out—one part of the city is covered in a deadly fog. But all the sections have a lot of interiors. At times it feels a bit like Fallout or Wasteland. If you like games with a recent post-apocalyptic feel, Homefront 2 does a good job at it. You won't find mutants or monsters, but plenty of urban decay. At a certain point the zones feel a bit repetitious, but each one makes an effort to add something new. Some are more vertical, some are more open. The zone that's full of gas seems like it was supposed to add a survival element to it: you have a gas mask, but it never needs changing, and the character puts it on/take it off automatically, so other than being a visual difference, the zone plays the same as before. Requiring the player to scavenge or build filters would've been a cool switch-up in game play. And back to the yellow and red zones: the game does have a bit of stealth in it. In red zones enemies will shoot on site. Yellow zones, however, are not actively hostile. Your character is on a wanted list, though, so you have to avoid being in direct view of enemies or security cameras. If you're spotted, an alert will sound, and you can either fight, or run to one of many hiding spots and wait for the alert to cool down. The game basically alternates between these zones as the story progresses. Yellow zone—then red zone—then yellow zone. While that does get repetitious, the different aesthetics of each zone kept it from becoming too much so. Compared to Far Cry 3, which was a real slog to complete with the two giant islands. Homefront 2 isn't nearly as bloated, and aside from some journals there really aren't any collectibles.
As far as the story goes, it's standard "action movie" fare. If you've seen either Red Dawn movie, you know the drill. Some reviewer said it would make a good game within the Terminator universe—just pretend the North Koreans are robots and you're a member of the human resistance. Personally it reminded me a lot more of the original V miniseries from the 80s. The story & characters are predictable and by-the-numbers, and ultimately a little anti-climactic. I don't know if any DLC will give the game an additional ending, but while the game does end with achieving a certain victory, it's far from the end of the Nork's occupation of Philly. Also, at a certain point in the game there's a point of no return. The game gives you fair warning, but you have to complete any jobs or strike points before the conclusion—after the credits roll, you can't go back and finish anything you didn't get to.
Glitches: I didn't play the game at launch, but heard there were lots of problems with the PC version. I had no real problems. It looks great and runs great. Never froze, never crashed. That said, there are a few routine glitches: the occasional NPC walking into a wall, or searching a bin that isn't there; an interior that is stuck with a "wet" overlay, as if it were outside in the rain; a job like "shoot enemy X with a shotgun" not registering when completed. Nothing game breaking. There was one enemy base that, oddly, could be entered before you were supposed to be able to. The base was empty, but you could hack the door, or break through an emergency hatch, and walk around. But then when you reach the part in the game that the base unlocks, and is now occupied, the doors can't be hacked and the emergency hatch is no longer accessible. The base was not required to complete for the story, but other players have had the same problem. It seems like the status of the base was reversed: the door should not have been hackable beforehand, and the emergency hatch should only have spawned once the base was ready for you to takeover. There is a workaround, though, which involved precisely jumping off a tiny wall with enough speed to clear a fancy. That's the biggest inconvenience I experienced.
I haven't played any multiplayer or DLC yet, so I can't comment on that.
Overall the game's a satisfying experience. Like a straight-to-Netflix movie that turned out to be better than expected. Or comfort food. When you want something familiar that hits all the right notes you want, but don't need an out-of-this-world, once-in-a-lifetime experience. $40 is a reasonable price for this, but it'll be on sale for $20 often. If you've got nothing else to play that will scratch this specific "B movie" itch, go for it.

A significant improvement over the first, LOG2 still retains it's almost brutal difficulty curve while progressing through the old-school dungeon crawler environment. If your key driver in an RPG game such as Skyrim is in its graphics, then you will be sorely let down by the presentation of LOG2. That's far from saying the game isn't pretty - but its more functional in appearance than blowing you away with graphical awe.
Where LOG2 scores very highly is in both character progression and feeling forever in fear of every creature that comes your way. Your original band of four ship-wrecked prisoners are woefully under-skilled and lack any form of equipment. In fact, you literally start with nothing other than a washed up branch nearby to begin with.
There are the usual race-to-class pros and cons. Amongst my group, I created a minotaur barbarian with high strength and attack. A female knight who has attained the ability as the groups' main potion maker sits alongside - protecting my much weaker reptilian rogue and my insectoid wizard at the rear. However, they all have their own unique roles to play in the group - and this is one of LOG2's big strong points. Skyrim's multi-skilled/multi-talented lead role is definitely not seen here. Your heavy hitters dish out damage and also attempt to absorb it - while the brain-boxes lie in second file and do their work from a safe distance.
LOG2 is a massively cerebral game. You can stand still for minutes at a time without concern of being attacked. It rewards lateral thinkers - those that think slightly out of the box and who attempt to intelligently work through a puzzle, rather than bash and kill their way through it.
Some puzzles are easy - while some are extremely tough to work out. But LOG2 provides a highly rewarding and enjoyable quest as you push on ahead. At the time of writing, I was approximately 8 hours into it - and I'll definitely be seeing this game through to the end.
For all those who want more of a thinking player's RPG - you certainly can't go wrong with this.

Foresite is a real time strategy game. In hindsight foresite is not  "Redefining Strategy in RTS". I was hopeful for foresite however at the start the game really did not shine the voice acting is bad and the tutorial is very slow paced and this immediately put me off the game. I stopped playing at that point however I decided to give it another try, I started a single battle and this was a much better experience to me. It plays like most rts games you have to develop your base, generate units, defend your base and attack the enemy base. The game doesn't really set itself apart from other RTS games your units each have unique attributes such as you can build large, slow, tanky ships, fast scouts, units specialized for structure damage etc.

Eternal is my new favorite digital card game, with the complexity of Magic: the Gathering and the polish and speed of other digital CCGs like Elder Scrolls Legends and Hearthstone. There's no excessive RNG like Hearthstone, and it's free to play (very generous for a f2p game) unlike MTGO. It's essentially taking the best parts of MTG and Hearthstone then merging them into a new game with its own interesting mechanics like warcry and the influence mechanic. Getting cards you want is also much easier, opening packs in Eternal grants you shiftstone (the equivalent of dust in hearthstone) so getting that legendary to use in your expensive control decks just got so much faster, and there's also a totem that influences how often you get cards from a specific faction (the equivalent of ESL's avatar system). If you love playing strategic card games you should totally give Eternal a try!
Edit : After playing for a longer while it's apparent that this game's card draw is a bit weird, I have to mulligan most of my opening hand because they contain 1 or no sigil at all.

Today's RTS options are rather limited and i was hoping Foresight would change this.
Sadly it dose not...let's get into it.
I am going to let you know from the start that the game feels rushed and unfinished. It feels more like Early Access rather then release material.
It has forced vsync... which creates mouse lag... in a RTS game this is not acceptable.
You can work around this... for nVidia users you can create a profile for the game in the nVidia control panel, and force vsync off. This will resolve the lag issue and unlock the frames.
There is NO controls menu.. so never-mind changing keys on a PC tittle... you can not even see what the controls are... and the tutorial dose not do the best job of pointing them out.
The voice acting in the game is nothing short of terrible... it would have been better with text only.
The graphics... are bearable for a tittle of this price but i seen better graphics on games that cost half as much.
The AI dose not prio attacking units from structures and it just mindlessly plunges ahead shooting the first red thing it comes across regardless of whatever else it has around. At least this is what i found from the first 3 missions which is all i could go through before being to frustrated to continue. This is mostly because of the awkward controls and the lack of information about the controls.
Because i did not play past the third mission i can not speak to the actual strategy in this game... what it prioritizes, what are its values or what approach it takes.
It's not all bad... there are some good ideas here.
The squadron / fleet concept is very interesting from my perspective and so is the sector mapping, the artwork presented in the cut-scenes is top notch! But all of these pale if the gameplay hinders the player.
I do not know why Strides rushed this tittle out...but i got a sneaking suspicion (the usual reason)
I hope they will be allowed to continue the development of this project and that in time we will get a decent RTS out of it (at least...)
For now however i can find no justifiable reason for spending 23 euro on this version...maybe if you are really REALLY passionate about RTS games...maybe then.
What else can i say... another sad day for RTS fans...unfortunately we kinda got used to it by now.

The best things about this game are the zombies and the challenge of finding new ways to conserve your ammo.
But the fact is, there really is no story. The two 'twists' I already had figured out as soon as the game provided enough context for me to guess them. That's frustrating in and of itself, since I always enjoy a good story and was looking forward to finding out some of the truth behind the world and the carefully crafted lies everyone's been fed. Then there's the fact that the grammar suffers horribly in translation, making parts of the game almost laughable. And then the ending... I'll just say it like it is: it sucked. It was a very typical nihilistic Russian story, so if that's your thing, have at it. But for me, it was a major letdown in every way.
TL;DR, It's a very short game, sparse on just about everything. And unlike SUPERHOT, that short and sparse format doesn't really work here. As far as I'm concerned, it has no replay value whatsoever (no, not even for the achievements).

Edit: I was dissapointed for a while that, while a couple of updates brought changes, they didn't seem to address some of the major flaws of the game. This changed with the recent update (1.18.2), as they implemented a counter measure to the infamous "mana-screw/ mana-flood" problem and they even expressed some thoughts on their approach. So, while i still think that more can be done, the devs have proven that they listen and try to respond, which i think is a good reason for further recommendation.
, Eternal is a must try for every digital CCG enthusiast and i think there's no reason for others not to try it as well. I bet, or at least hope a lot of people will get hooked by it.
of Eternal probably aren't the graphics or sound, they're decent enough, it looks nice and the sound probably won't hurt your ears, though i've muted it for the sake of my own music after little time and it could look a little better or worse, i think it wouldn't make much of a difference, because those aren't the core of Eternal's experience. I'd say, that's where the mechanics and accessibility of the game are.
: The Gathering definitely isn't farfetched. I've very actively played Magic for a couple of years some time ago and when i first played Eternal i immediately felt at home - which is not at all surprising, since the devs are Magic-players as well. Many mechanics are similar: The turn structure is almost the same, mana is called power, there's flying, trample is called overwhelm, haste is charge and there are many more in slight variations. So, if you really don't like Magic, you might not like Eternal, but i'd say you should still try, considering Eternal kind of looks and feels like the younger, sexier cousin of Magic, who offers some moves which feel familiar, but a bit different at the same time and who promises improvement during joyful consenting playtime, where Magic might feel like it's trying too hard to impress, just to grab your money.
often makes it feel a little slower than other recent CCGs and the resource mechanic can lead to frustrating bottlenecks in play if you heavily draw against the odds, but on the other hand i'd say there are a lot more possibilities to combo and build various decks with interesting strategies. I think it is rather well balanced, though there are certain cards which result in hefty power spikes and some i'd consider useless (as is often the case in most CCGs). But there is no card, deck, or strategy which can't be beaten by others, the game usually isn't decided in just a couple of turns and every turnaround can feel satisfying.
And, as rarely as it happens, i'd actually consider this game free to play, as you not only can get everything the game has to offer without paying anything, the rate at which you gain cards is actually pretty good, i'd say generous, which makes it possible to get strong/ tier 1 decks relatively fast and to experiment often.
And, well, if the current mass of positive reviews haven't convinced you to try and you haven't turned your back already because you hate CCGs in general, i honestly don't know what will change your mind.

If you enjoy magic the gathering and card games in general you will probably love this game. Some pros:
* Well developed client, everything feels smooth and responsive.
* Good graphics and sound. Even though graphics aren't a prio in a card game it doesn't hurt that everything looks and sounds nice. Artwork on cards are topnotch aswell.

* A big variety of really fun game modes. Who doesn't love to draft a deck from boosters, getting to keep all the cards you draft and also heap in big rewards if you do well? You can even do a smaller draft and play against AI only for a cheaper price.

All in all I have big hopes for this game in the future, seeing how good it is already.

The map is really diverse, and it's not filled with random content, you can explore for hours and you'll feel an amazing immersion, no racing game achieved this on me before. Contains all main USA cities, however if you're american, expect a few small towns you know to be missing (Orlando, for starters, is nowhere to be found), but it's the sacrifice you need to make with a game of this scale.
The graphics are also really pretty, and Nvidia's graphic features, completely opposite to other older games, does NOT ruin your framerate and performance and it amazingly improves the games' look compared to the console counterparts.

I've had fun with the game, even though I still prefer the fast paced nature in the older wwe games this is still a solid wwe game. I mostly just play the MyCareer mode, since it's the main selling point for me in the 2K games, and I'm still playing with a face run and a heel run.
Is it fun?
At times.
Is MyCareer repetitive?
Yes it is!
How's the creator suite?
Meh, not as expansive as 2K14. I enjoy making non-human characters and highly unlikely creatures that happen to wrestle. The good things I can say is the logo uploader, but somehow they make it really complicated to do. Entrance is the best so far, but it still needs more and use the PC to its advantage like custom videos, music and images.
How's Online?
Laggy, even worse when playing with more than 2 people.
How's the roster?
The biggest roster in a wwe game to date, but is still missing some great ones. I can name a few of my personal faves that are gone, but the majority of everyone's faves are in it regardless.
How's the fighting?
It's good if you want a sort of realistic wrestling gameplay, but playing isn't as fun as I had in 2K14. Everything feels too advanced such as the stats, skills, etc. I much prefer the basics and general options when making a character. The reversal meter is the best addition though.
Verdict?
If you want an online wrestling game to play, don't get it.
If you want to make wacky characters, you can, but very limited.
If you want a singleplayer experience, absolutely get it.

Spira is a world plagued by Sin, and it is up to a summoner and her six guardians to go on pilgrimage in order to defeat Sin. The player is given control of these seven character and their ultimate development, and must make it from game start to game end. If the player goes with the standard, usual, development, the game, while challenging, can be completed no problem.
I find the true value of the game is in replaying it, adding challenges like "No Sphere Grid", "Character-Only", "No Summons", "No Items", etc. Then it becomes a TRUE test of your mettle. (Also let's face it, all these challenges have been done before, and if you really get stuck there are guides.)

This unique game is for hardcore players who seek challenging puzzles that require fast reflexes, the soundtrack and the fun puzzles is what keeps you engaged for more and more puzzles, until you finally complete this very short game. It is a must have experience!

This game has a lot of good ideas about an open world racing MMO RPG (deep breaths) unfortunately not really executed well. Taking into consideration that this is an MMO, getting into a multiplayer game kinda doesn't work.
I've spent a lot of the time waiting for a match just for the game to tell me that no one is in the lobby, even though there clearly is, the same is true for Co-op. When you do end up in a Co-op match, you'll find out that the races were't even designed for Co-op.
The races themselves were boring with most of them consisiting of street races that are made up of mostly wide streets and right angle corners. The races do get get a bit more exciting out of the outskirts though. You race along mountain roads and offroad tracks that bring a bit of excitment to the racing. The handling model does help factor into fun and although its not Forza Horizon type handling, its still quite fun. All that and you can take in the scenery that usually an open world game can give you.
Speaking of open world, The Crew really is quite big. However, you don't really notice its largeness. You'd spend most of your time in Cities since thats where all the races happen. The cities really feel quite small as its very easy to find yourself at the outskirts by just driving about. You'd only notice the size when you are travelling to another city. Long monotonous roads cluttered by non interesting scenery and what seems like repeating landscapes (some trees- farm and repeat) for most of your journeys. No matter how fun the handling is, cross country trips are quite boring. Thankfully, mostly all of the terrain in the game are drivable so you can cut across the country if you feel that it brings some variety.
One of the biggest flaws of the game though is the graphics. It looks like an old game remade for IOS then remastered in HD for PC. If you don't run an NVidia GPU there would be some occassional lag and stutters if you run it at ultra with some Nvidia features that somehow only Nvidia GPUs can run ( although it is more forgiving than the Intel only Global Illumination features on Grid 2 and Autosport).
My conclusion, if you are excited for a open world racing game on the PC then you can give this a try but you won't really enjoy this for long. Other than that The Crew doesn't really offer anything much for a racing fan.

To all who gave this game a bad review on release, you probably had every right to. I wouldn't know its initial state as I bought it exactly a year after release. But either way, please consider what you've said and revisit it, because Homefront: The Revolution is a good game. Yes, the devs should have delayed the game, but give them props for sticking out when others would have abandoned it outright.
The game is more or less an urban Far Cry with North Koreans. So if you love FC, you'll love this. Capturing strikepoints (i.e. outposts) is quite fun. Some even require you to solve puzzles. I also love the in-game customization mechanic, yo can convert you assault rifle to an LMG and so on. Oh, and no regenerating health, either. And AI is competent: the KPA are NOT happy to see you and they will show it. You can, and will, die. A lot. And I'm suprised at the detail they have put in the indoor areas. You can enter almost every building, especially in the Red Zone. So don't be fooled by the reviews.
The story is, well, good also. The characters are also decent. What I hated, however, was the backstory. Who came up with idea of having the US military use North Korean technology? As if North Korea wouldn't turn them off with the push of a button. Oh wait...they did. Seriously, the backstory of the original Homefront was not only better, but believable. It's the only good thing about that game. Seriously, watch it.
Graphic-wise, it's neither ugly nor pretty. And it performs well, too. I played it on medium on my GTX 960M.
What I hated is that sometimes when you recruit Resistance members, they occasionally get stuck and/or block your way.. This can be solved by dismissing and re-recruiting them. Another problem is that sometimes KPA soldiers can spawn out-of-nowhere. Yes, they can be gunned down relatively easily, but still...
I have not tried the DLC yet, but I heard it's good. I will get it when it's on sale.
So, is it the game good? YES. Not great, but worth the price now.
Is the game fixed? YES. But please devs, either fix your game before release, or don't release at all.
Do I want a sequel? YES. And please learn from your mistakes.

(If TL;DR, you can watch my first and final impressions here:
I admit this game is very difficult and you might not like extreme challenges, but if a challenge is your jam, then keep rocking on because this is the strategy game for you.  Five Nights at Freddy’s 2 caught everyone by surprise when it was released and stands as a true testament of the power of sequels.
The premise is the same as the first game, keep the animatronics from ramming your body into an animatronic suit by religiously watching the cameras and keeping your eye on Foxy the Pirate; but there’s a twist.  Not only are you up against the original Fazbear Crew, you’re up against their sleek, new, state of the art counterparts on the stage ready to rock your world (and your ♥♥♥♥♥♥), a puppet that will jump you like mugger and the most diabolical animatronic ever to exist in the whole Fazbear canon: Balloon Boy, dispenser of balloons to kids by day and battery thief extraordinaire by night.  There wouldn’t be a good party without Golden Freddy either, so expect him in your future too.  You initially play as Jeremy Fitzgerald, 'summer job' intern at the ‘New and Improved’ Freddy Fazbear’s Pizza (circa November 1987).  The voicemail recordings were obviously older than the game alludes to since summer never occurs November in any part of the world. Being the night guard shouldn’t be a problem with our previous experience on the job as Mike Schmidt in the first game right?  That idea could not be further from the truth.
With no doors to protect you in a restaurant packed full of animatronics to the point of bursting out of the air vents into your room, you’re in deeper trouble than in any other game in the trilogy -even when you know what you’re doing.  Unfortunately I cannot review the game without explaining the mechanics so here goes nothing. Your main objective is to wind the music box in the prize corner to stop the puppet from jumping you like a stuffed animal; it doesn’t matter what the puppet is for or how something made from linen and stuffing can kill you, just keep it away at all costs.  Checking the office for unwanted company is your second priority, with an emphasis on shining your light down the hallway to disorient Foxy and the left air vent to stop Balloon Boy from stealing your flashlight’s batteries.  When someone is visibly in the room or able to be seen in the vents without the cameras, place the spare Freddy Fazbear head over yourself so none of the animatronics ‘mistake’ you as a bare robot endoskeleton and wait until they leave.  The mechanics function almost perfectly, but the premise they rely to do not necessarily make sense
The game mechanics pose many logical errors that can only be attributed to a lack of needing to be realistic.  The first logical error here stems from the way you wind up the music box in the prize corner, compromising my willing suspension of disbelief.  You wind up the music box by pressing a button on your camera’s user interface.  (I’m pretty sure graphical computer technology was not that advanced in 1987, but then again, they also didn’t have sentient machines either -so there goes any relevance to the real world starting right there).  Also with a world so rich with technology, why didn’t the staff just plug in a portable radio by the puppet instead or a continuously running motor or to wind the music box?  I’ll answer that rhetorical question with a non-rhetorical answer by saying it’s just a game and Scott Cawthon wanted to offer a greater challenge.  The same logical problems arise when you put the mask on.   Why can’t players do all the normal functions with the mask on? Is it that cumbersome?  Lastly, where do all the old animatronics get their electrical power from when there’s no charging station in the spare parts room? They can’t be powered just on the children’s love alone.  But who am I kidding in a children’s survival strategy.  There are many artistic attributes worth noting.
The eerie ambience of neglected office space has been replaced with the ambience of being new, clean and eerily too perfect.  The whole restaurant is spotless and the colors are vibrant aside from the spare parts room and the air vents.  The new ‘Toy’ animatronics are creepy as well, with porcelain-doll characteristics that come off as too friendly and lifeless, as Scott Cawthon intended, to creep the living hell out of us.  Balloon Boy and the puppet might be the creepiest of the bunch with balloon boy resembling a Lego version of Pinocchio donning a propeller hat and the puppet looks more like the convergence of a Studio Ghilbi production, Mardi Gras, and a sock monkey with its empty grinning mouth, bare eye sockets as well as brilliant colors.  Toy Chica even takes her beak off after leaving the stage and rolls her eyes into her head when she goes on the hunt. If being creeped out by things that look too happy is not your cup of tea, then we have good news for you.  The original Fazbear Crew are creepier than ever with broken limbs, damaged fur suits loose wires and enough bare metal to satisfy your post-apocalyptic fantasies.  Hell the old Bonnie has no face and the weathered Chica has a mouth assembly resembling a metal sandwich ready to bight your head off with after staring you down with its bloodshot eyes.  Audio cues turn up the adrenaline as players panic to find who is closing in as Balloon Boy cackles in the vents and the dreaded Mangle lurches and climbs its way into the room sounding like a faulty squad car radio.  This game is rich in detail; heck, Scott went the extra nine yards and simulated eye dilation when players take the mask off after wearing it too long since temporary blindness sets as the eyes adjust to the office lighting.  There are even shadow characters and death mini-games that offer more plot details than ever before. Nothing is perfect though.
The only problems that must be addressed are the sounds of robotic movement in the air vents (which currently are not in stereo and don’t vary in volume based on character distance from the player) and the lack of time I have to ward off Foxy.  The other issue that should be addressed is the statistical probability of surviving the 6th night.  The game is coded so winning the 6th night is not a matter of skill, but a matter of luck, as players are overwhelmed with too many characters to deal with simultaneously.  Each player's ultimate demise soon follows, chich can be very frustrating at times for a game with a sharp learning curve.  Foxy in the later nights is so overeager its jump scare animation can be superimposed over the wall when the timer for activating his animation hits 0; it would be nice if the counter that engages his animation was longer on later nights since resetting the binary timer with a flashlight can come milliseconds too late. I spite of these limitations this game is brilliant
This game offers almost everything.  An angel practically gets its wings for each extra bell and whistle offered in this game relative to all the others in the trilogy.  It marks the zenith of the Five Nights at Freddy’s trilogy satisfies most players desires in spite of its advanced difficulty on the earliest nights.  Could this game be better? Yes, but does this game leave more to be desired? Absolutely not.  The world was made a better place with this game and justify Scott’s recent financial/gaming success.  I just wished he conspicuously put the same amount of effort and originality into the sequels numbered 3 and 4 that came after this.

A much larger and mostly better version of the original game this sequel is a welcome return to the world of Grimrock. As the setting of the game is in the mythical island of Nex you as a player arent limited to delving in the dark, mossy dungeons of its precedessor but can instead explore and experience the great outdoors with such groundbreaking features as day and night cycle, diving underwater(no skuba included, at least so far) and fighting against the plant life in all of its ferocious forms (long live the industrial revolution).
After 14 hours of gameplay i havent run into any bugs or other bad experiences that would negatively impact the game and my biggest gripe so far might be that some of the puzzles arent immediately solvable after finding them. Combat is much better, albeit in the same style as the original, as the monsters arent so easily danced around anymore and you often find yourself forced to use your enviroment as a tactical tool to manage the encounters. And as both spellcasting and the skill system have received some tuning your characters arent forced to specialize into a single role anymore. Now it seems like you can have that greataxe-wielding insectoid berserker who likes to wear heavy armor while slinging fireballs around.
Overall its a good game so get it if you enjoy this kind of thing, and if not hey, why not try it.

Far and away better than the already really quite good original, what you have in Grimrock 2 is an excellent dungeon crawler style rpg - the focus being on combat and puzzle solving in a grid-based, first person fashion.
The combat is improved over the original, but it's still slightly wonky. While the AI is better, you'll still spend most of your fighting time exploiting its behaviour since a straight up fight will almost always end badly.
Where Grimrock 2 really shines, however, is in the exploration and puzzle solving. Gone is the multi-level, single dungeon, where you now have something almost reminiscent of legend of zelda; a roughly open world, where your progression is primarily driven by your ability to explore and solve puzzles.
And those puzzles, you say? Some of the best I've seen in games. While many are challenging, none have inexplicable leaps in logic, and every future puzzle is building on what you've learned previously. Clues are not as obscenely cryptic as in la mulana, but give just enough information for your mind to leap at the solution. There hasn't been a point in the game so far where I've been stuck with no-where to go, and yet many of the puzzles have me feeling like a genius on their solution. The balance of difficulty of the puzzles is meticulous.

LoG2 is a Tile Based, First Person, Dungeon Crawling, Puzzler (with combat.) I put the combat in parenthesis because while it is a prominent aspect of the game throughout, it is clearly not the focus of the game, which is the puzzle solving. The puzzles themselves get harder as the game progresses. If this is your first exposure to this type of game, it's likely that you'll find it relatively difficult as the puzzles do ramp up in difficulty rather quickly. Being a sequel I imagine that the devs are expecting that the majority of their players will have played the first LoG game in which the puzzles are generally easier and ramp up slower.
So now that I've covered what the game is, let's get into some nitty gritty.
The gameplay itself builds off of the first one, taking the core of the game and maintaining what it was, while making some distinct improvements based off player feedback from the first game. Monster AI has been improved so that monsters will try to counter squared dancing tactics (these are still effective, but sometimes need to be modified a bit based on what you are fighting). Monsters will also sometimes try to lure you to where they can hit you or even just wait you out instead of charging to their certain demise when you're hiding around a corner waiting to ambush them.
Each monster has it's own unique mechanics for how it moves and fights, requiring the player to learn the best ways to fight each one. Some monsters will leap behind the player, or steal your stuff right out of your hands, while others will actively dodge your attacks by jumping back a tile, etc. This is a distinct improvement from the first game where monsters were mostly the same, just moving from tile to tile to attack you as directly as they could and only flanking you by accident, now when they flank you it's on purpose. There are also several boss fights in this game unlike the first game that really only had 1 boss at the end of the game. Each of the boss fights feels like a puzzle in and of itself because of having to figure out how best to approach the fight. Not going to go into any more detail than that on them though as I don't want to give away any spoilers.
The dungeon crawling experience has been enhanced as well with the introduction of the great outdoors, with a full day and night cycle, with some things happening based on the time of day or night. The first game was entirely indoors, on top of that it was highly claustrophobic with narrow halls and low ceilings. LoG2 answers that by giving you multiple tiers of vertical movement on the same level and the openness of being able to be outside and see through the space between trees. About the multiple tiers, this adds an entirely new dimension to the game because this opens up the possibility for bridges that you can go over and under, pits you can drop down into and climb back out of, and ledges you can get up onto, all without changing to another map just because you went higher or lower than 'ground level' for the map you are on.
The original races were kept along with the addition of a new race, the ratlings. They also added classes, but with characters being centered around their skills, the classes are fairly fluid, offering advantages in the skills that the class would be good at but not really penalizing you if you decided to let say a barbarian learn to be a mage, or if you wanted a wizard to be able to wear heavy armor and stand on your front line. This opens up the party options and makes it so that there really is no 'bad' party composition. While some parties might be easier to play than others, any party can be made to work. This makes random party generation an interesting optional mechanic that you can take advantage of to give the game a bit more replayability.
The skills have also been refined since LoG1 so that each point in a skill is significant, making you noticeably better with that skill each time you add a point. Plus at certain points in skill development you gain additional perks, such as dual wielding light weapons, so that when you swing one light weapon it doesn't put both on cooldown, just the one you swung.
The story itself is 'hidden' within the game. You start off knowing nothing more than that you are shipwrecked and washed up on a beach. The story itself is delivered to you with that in mind, where you find notes written by the master of the island to you as his only real way of communicating with you, and you also find notes and other things left behind by others who were here before you, leaving the mystery of what fate befell them. The game's story stands by itself, without needing you to have played the first game, but players that have played the first one may notice small links back to it hidden on the island implying a deeper connection between the island and Grimrock than one might naturally suspect. That being said, while there is a story present, it is clearly not the focus of the game, which is the dungeon crawling itself and most of your experience is motivated by simply needing to survive on the island.
The game has a lot of secrets hidden throughout, most of which are found by discovering ways to access optional areas of the game. These hidden areas often contain powerful items that will have a significant impact on the game, but at the same time, none are absolutely necessary to progress through the game, they only make it a little easier to do so. Everything you absolutely have to have to progress through the basic game and get to an ending is offered in plain sight without the need for discovering secrets. I definitely don't recommend not looking for the secrets though as they will help immensely.
And finally, when you are done with the core game, or just want to pound your head against something different for a while, there is a dungeon editor included with the game so that players can make and publish their own content using the features included with the game and some ability to add in entirely new stuff. (I wont be going into detail on the features and capabilities of the editor in this review though as I have yet to play around with it).
Final verdict:
A worthy successor to the first Grimrock game that kept what made it great and enhanced what needed to be enhanced. A very good example of what the old school, tile based, dungeon crawlers are, and well worth the play if you enjoy the genre. Obviously not good for you if you aren't a fan of this type of game which spent about a decade in hibernation before the first Grimrock awoke the sleeping dragon... or cube as the case may be.

I still don't understand what is going on with the story. The clues you get from passengers on the train or from memos found in the world don't really piece together what is really going on. There seems to be a lot of influence from "Roadside Picnic", yet we are never really shown anything out of the ordinary beyond zombies or "dreams."
Ultimately these things aren't that bad considering the length of the game, but at the same time it feels like the game's length is also a detriment. It seems it is almost the wrong kind of game to tell this kind of story with, and that a top-down or isometric view along with some more interesting level design could have propelled this game to the top. Sadly, with the combat, controls and camera all working against the game's premise, the atmosphere can only do so much to lift it from a low score.

Overall, a great game. If it was not for the Micro-Transactions I would rate this a must play.
The game has a solid if somewhat relaxed RT Tatics PVP with you fighting player designed bases but computer controlled.
Thats it. Thats the gameplay. Doesn't sound like much, but then there are the upgrades.
Winning a match gives you munitions which can be used to upgrade your own base design.
A failed attack on your base by another player awards you with more munitions and other bonuses.
Which you can then use to upgrade your attacking force or your base again.
It is a constant game of figuring out where to put your resources next to help against that next attack. Or to make that next raid just that much easier.
If that was everything to the game, again. Must play. However, there are microtransactions.
You can buy extra munitions and bonuses that cannot be gotten through anything other then RNG for a non-paying player.
Can they buy anything you cannot get eventually? No, other then some cosmetics, which you do earn the "gold" (aka, $$ money) currency through RNG, if at extreamly low ammounts. So it is technically possible to get everything.
Does fighting people who pay cause an imbalance? Yes and No. It does not tell you the level of the player you are fighting. So telling if they are 30-50 levels higher then you or just shelled out 400$ is largely impossible. Unless they are slathered in cosmetics.
Have I fought people who clearly put cash into the game? Yes.
Did I feel the fights were harder? Yes. There was a noticible difference in what their base and units did.
Do I still recommend this game anyway? Yes. It is an extremely fun game that I try to play atleast once a day. Despite the Micro-Transactions this is a solid game that largely will put you against foes who do not feel impossible.

This review will contain some stuff i love, like, dislike and hate about The Crew
Prepare yourself
---
- The Map
The best map I have EVER seen in a racing game, and not the biggest, but the most diverse map I have EVER played on. It's that good. It would take a large amount of hours to completely explore the map. I still haven't completely expored it in my many hour playtime. It takes about an hour (if you are going very fast) tho get from one side of the map to the other. It just such a fun map to drive around, to take a road trip, and to see all kinds of fabulous landmarks throughput your journeys.
-Everything about the cars
All the cars have lots of detal, interior and exterior. They are all different to drive, and unique in their own ways. Also, all the sounds for the cars are the legit real life sounds, recorded from the cars in a sound studion. SO nice.
---
-Customization of car
The customization is quite good, especially compared to most of the recent need for speed games. The only problem is the customizations seem too concrete, there is no ability to add your own imagination or personal touch. Some stickers have different colors, but you can't change the color of a specific sticker. Also, each sticker goes on a certain, unchangable place on the car. You can make your car different than others, because there a large number of aesthetic parts and stickers.
-Car specs
I really like how the car can utilize many different utilities by changing the spec. There are 5 specs: Street, Dirt, Performance, Raid, and Circuit. They are all fun to experiment with. Some are great for the racetrack, while others are great for offroad trails. My only gripe about specs is that very few cars have the full 5 specs, most have 1-3 of the the specs. The starter cars all have the full 5 specs, so you will be able to have them all in at least one car.
-The story
It is surprising for a good story to be in a racing game, but in this case that surprise came true. It may seem cheesy and cliche to some people, but I thoroughly enjoyed it.
-The graphics
They aren't amazing by any means, but they are good. They capture american geography well (with a few minor hiccups) but there are many current racing games that have better graphics. They are definitely not bad though, they still make the game nice looking. The best graphics in the game are seen in some of the cutscenes. Legitimate movie quality cutscences.
---
-The "mmo" aspect of the game
Only 8 players in your session, and they players continually switch to different players, so, yeah, no. I still don't really know how to play with my friends, because there is no server choice, just places you in one.
-Not that many cars
There really should be more.
-Anything that has to do with AI
Other racers, cops, even NPC traffic. All equally annoying.
-Customization of your character
Nonexistent. Hopefully you are okay with the way you look, cuz you can't change that.
---
-ubisoft
-uplay
-ubisoft support
-uplay servers
-ubisoft bugs
-uplay bugs
-ubisoft glitches
-uplay glitches
-ubisoft in general
-uplay in general
Fortunately, ubisoft only published this game not developed, so it isn't UNPLAYABLE (i.e. ACU) a good company called Ivory Tower made it, which was responsible for some other open world maps (i.e. GTA 4) Some things about the game just seem buggy and unfinished, not because of Ivory Tower, but because of ubisoft. It just seems like with the many delays the game should be PERFECT but it isn't.
And now, for the thing I HATE the most about the crew, the following is a reddit rant that i put onto /r/The_Crew/ :
The good conclusion:
The game's main feature, a big map, is DEFINITELY true. The map, the cars, the graphics, all together make the game an great, interesting, and fun experience.
The bad conclusion:
The online, which was the other big feature, fails to deliver. There are many online problems and bugs that make some give up on the game. But I am not a quitter.
Final conclusion (tl;dr) :
This game offers an amazing experience, one that I have never seen in any other game. Simply being able to take a trip down a desert highway, explore a mountain, race around a city, and explore the entirety of the United states is something that no other game has ever done so beautifully.
Overall great game, beautiful map, beautiful cars, just some problems that need addressing. My rating is subject to go up if those improvements are made. The crew is definitely my favorite driving game, and it will never get old or boring.

Pros:

Good shooting mechanics
Detailed maps with believable interiors and exteriors
You can fight in war zones, or blend in with the crowd in more secure areas for some stealth gameplay.
You can recruit buddy's to follow you around.

Con's:
You have to press '0' to holster your weapon, which is needed to blend in in the secure areas. This action
cannot be bound to another key like most other controls can. I would have liked to have moved it over to 4 or something, since the gasmask auto equips anyway, and is kind of useless.
Sometimes, the areas you have to capture can have objectives that are too obtuse, like finding some medical supplies
around an abandoned hospital building, but it never tells you that they are on some windows up above, and you can only get them down by shooting them, or where you have to use a bike to power up a certain generator, but you don't know how to get the bike there.

This game (as of 5/27/17) is an easy 8/10 now that the patches have been released to correct the earlier performance issues.
Short Version: If you liked Far Cry 3, Half Life 2 or Red Dawn, you will enjoy this game as it draws heavy inspiration from all 3. Performance is smooth, though optimization isn't always great. Visuals are very atmospheric and gunplay is solid.
Long Version: I, like many, saw the Youtube reviews released on Youtube when this game first came out. It was buggy, sloppy and unfinished. Nobody in their right mind would pay $60 for a game in that state. However, Deep Silver did what few devs would choose to do: they refused to abandon the game. Over the past year, they have patched it numerous times and released some very competent single player DLCs. This game is now DEFINITELY worth your time.
In terms of gameplay, it draws heavily from Far Cry 3 and Half Life 2, with a dash of Crysis thrown in (it is the Crytek engine after all). Far Cry outpost-capturing returns, but there are always numerous ways to tackle a base, all of which are fairly creative and fun. The atmosphere is dark, dystopian and oppressive with numerous item stashes with marked areas and destructable obstacles, evoking a sense of Half Life 2. Finally, the gunplay is sharp and potent, with the Crysis modification system making a return. Explosions and physics are quite good, and destroying the APCs and nasty little robot tanks with your limpet launcher is very satisfying. Also, the R/C car + IED combo is a blast to use (pun intended).
No, the game is not perfect, and you will occasionally run across small glitches, though I never encountered anything game-breaking. Additionally, the characters are a little flat and I wouldn't call the writing original or spectacular in any way.
Disregard any review of this game made more than 5 months ago, as they are certainly not reflective of the game in its current state. Moreover, I can also say that most Youtube reviews of this game never even made it halfway through, as their weapon selection and the settings of their videos indicate to anyone who has played longer than that. I would take them with a grain of salt.

After finishing Homefront The Revolution, I couldn't help but feel a mixed opinion. While I strongly LOVE the overall theme of the game, I feel it is a bit of a wasted opportunity to show some truly amazing North Korean imagery and just overall... more! I'm not sure how to express myself, but the game felt bland as hell even though the theme of the North Koreans ("Norks", as the game defines them) invading the United States is a relatively amazing concept.
Let's start with the good. The graphics are very very good, to say the least. I've seen the performance and overall graphical quality on consoles and it is pure garbage by comparison to max settings on PC. It felt smooth, and it was very visually appealing. The shooting felt great, it was fast, gripping and satisfying. The weapons all have upgrades which actually make them much better, some weapons have high recoil but upgrading them reduces it. You can also press Shift to hold your breath while using any weapon. The game is of very decent length, clocking in at around 11 hours to finish the main story, (throughout the main story there are also secondary tasks you can complete for people in the environment, and some are pretty interesting but mostly it's just kill this or take a picture of that) and there are 3 other DLC story packs to keep you in for another 2 to 3 hours. The game has become amazingly cheap very quickly after its release, and I can gladly say it is worth it (on a sale). It showed me a very good time, even though the game was pretty repetitive. The game is also open world, and it is a great thing that it is open world, but I'm not really sure if it is worth it being open world when the game has such a cliché and dumb story (point of this is that they should have focused more on delivering a better story than this instead of another repetitive open world game). Most of the characters are very unlikable and they constantly yell at each other like morons. I sometimes felt good when some of the "good guys" died. Honestly the ending left me quite unsatisfied. While I don't want to spoil it, I just wish that wasn't IT. There is not much cool stuff about this game. I mean, imagine propaganda shows on TV in this game, Kim Jong Un (God, I wish he was here), anyway my point is, this game lacked any sort of creativity and just puts you in a Far Cry-esque world. Look at Wolfenstein 2: The New Colossus' "German or ELSE!" show. If things similar to that were in this game, boy oh boy would it be a hell of a ride. Honestly it's not bad, it's just very mediocre. You would have probably already played a game that is exactly the same as this game. It's fun, and the best thing about it is the background story of it, but even then it is a wasted potential.  8/10 for the amount of fun it gave me, but I really don't want to rate it more than a 7/10 for the main story mode. Which sucks cos I really enjoyed this game, from the start I knew I would love it and I did! However, the DLC does actually FINISH the story so definitely play those. With the DLC altogether I would give it an 8/10 overall, I loved the whole experience as a package.
To conclude, a summary: Bad storytelling as a whole (unlikable characters, etc) BUT DLC somewhat fixes things; a bit repetitive (depends on how much or how often you play) but it's overall very fun and the graphics are great. Soundtrack is very decent and performance is alright. 8/10
DLCs REVIEW: The DLCs definitely wrap the story up more and more and it makes me love the game more and more. The DLC story missions are better than any mission in the original story.
The Voice of Freedom DLC review: It is a pretty decent DLC, it felt very tense to play through but the 9-O are not a well-developed gang and they're kinda just there. It gives some backstory on how Walker saved the main character, so that's the best part about it. Same great gameplay and fantastic graphics are still present here. If you don't own the expansion pass, or the Freedom Fighter (complete edition) of Homefront: The Revolution, there is little content here to be very keen on getting. The DLC can take a minimum of 30 minutes and a maximum of 1 hour, difficulty level changes length. It sure was fun, and tense, but there was quite little to it. I do wish they did the story from the book they released with the original Homefront game (the book was also called The Voice of Freedom). Not bad DLC, a bit short, but depending on how much it costs (if it is £1.50 or below), I'd say it's worth it if you loved the game. I personally loved the game, and this DLC was a good addition to the game. It is linear, no open world stuff, and I advise you to play this DLC before starting the main campaign to get some more insight on how and what happened.
7/10 for this DLC.
Second DLC, "Aftermath" review: This DLC concludes Walker's story and gives Ethan Brady (the main character) a voice. So those are already two great things about this DLC. If ONLY Brady had a voice throughout the original story, it would have been so much cooler instead of a dumb silent protagonist. Brady makes snarky comments on what is happening, and his voice actor did a good job. It just shows so much more emotion in this character. This DLC also made us bond a bit more with the characters than the original story did, which is quite ashameful since the original story kind of makes you hate some of the characters (in particular the female character, already forgot her name). At the end of the game I felt unsatisfied as hell, since I didn't even know what the hell happened to Walker, but I'm happy I bothered to play this DLC since it took away my dislike for the story to some extent. The whole chapter is action packed, but I don't think it's any longer than the first DLC, "The Voice of Freedom". Overall, it is a great DLC but I DEFINITELY wish it was part of the original story. Also, we don't really get to bond with Walker all that much, but meh, at least it's good. Maximum 1 hour long, minimum 30 mins long.
8/10 for this DLC.
Beyond the Walls DLC review: Beyond The Walls is the final DLC for Homefront: The Revolution, that once again leaves off in a sort-of cliffhanger where the allies haven't necessarily won and the "battle just started". There was mention of NATO throughout the DLC but there wasn't much in it. I feel like this is yet another wasted potential, since as there most likely won't ever be a Homefront 3, in this DLC maybe all of Europe could have liberated America from the "Norks" (KPA - Korean People's Army) but in this DLC you blow something up that leads to a huge advantage in the battle against the Norks. It finishes Ethan Brady's story, but I seriously hope there is one more Homefront game, in which we get to see all out war against the KPA. Overall this story takes place on a farm environment and it looks very beautiful. The action was good, and once again like in DLC 2, Ethan Brady has a voice which made the game so much less boring. This was also the lengthiest of the DLCs for Homefront: The Revolution clocking in at around 1 hour. It was great and it really enforces how much better the DLC is compared to the main story, and really makes me wish the game wasn't an open world game in the first place, since such better linear story-telling could have been shown. This ending truly concludes Homefront: The Revolution, I feel like the DLC should have been part of the main story to begin with, so I do think maybe the game was rushed to meet a deadline rather than to actually completely finish the main story. Anyway, great DLC, enjoyed it thoroughly.
8/10 for this DLC.
