You, Kaitlin Greenbriar, arrive home on a last minute late-night flight from a year abroad, to find your parents and sister are missing. Someone you don’t know has left a strange answer machine message; they sound upset. You have to point and click your way around the house, find clues and access locked rooms and secret passageways, to discover what the shnaz is going on.
I love pathetic fallacy, so the atmospheric storm made my day. Plus, an early clue tells you the wiring in the house is ancient and bizarre, which explains why the lights flicker. I enjoyed unlocking filing cabinets, reading my family’s private letters, and making wild inferences from the way things had been left. The deeper you dig, the more you learn not only about your sister Sam’s secret, but also your parents’, er, issues and the strange great uncle your dad inherited the house from. Also, this is one of several recent games that is bringing it with queer, female main characters.
But… while you are free to piece together the secondary stories, Sam’s main thread is narrated at intervals, essentially as a reward for progressing to new areas of the game. This is fine - it’s a compelling tale - but not as satisfying as piecing the information together yourself. I was also disappointed with the mother’s story, which seemed clichéd and under-developed, and Kaitlin’s character was a shallow foil to the much more interesting Sam.
Worth mentioning: Sam’s essay on the human life cycle. Find it, read it. Genius.

Some details:
Updated graphics and environments. This game is super pretty. Come out of the dungeon and adventure outdoors in deep forests, shoreline caves, and other beautifully detailed areas.
Weapon and weapon skills redesigned. Weapon skills are now Light, Heavy, Missile, Thrown, and Firearms, so melee characters are less restricted by skill choice. Weapons now have special attacks built into them, which must be activated and use energy.
More flexible character creation, with eight classes and five races. Skills are no longer tied to class, so any class can learn any skills. Racial bonuses redesigned to be less obviously fit for particular classes.  Classes and races grant bonuses that can be built upon with skill and trait choices.
Smarter enemies for tougher, more engaging combat. No more easily dancing around enemies, as most enemies have the ability to attack to their side while turning to face you. In general enemies are quicker to attack and more often have special moves.

This game is a tile-based puzzle-RPG with lots of puzzles and quite some fighting. Graphics are very nice actually for todays standards, sound is ok. If you played the first LoG and liked it, you will love this one, it's improved in every way. If not, it may be worth your time if you like this kind of gameplay. You will be exploring multiple areas over and under the surface, while fending off monsters and trying to solve puzzles for treasures and story items. The puzzles are quite challenging at times, especially for optional rewards. I must admit, I had to consult the community a few times, but it is entirely possible to solve everything by yourself if you put your mind and some time to it. Some puzzle hints are quite cryptic, but with some thought and trial/error everything can be solved. The fighting is fun, you have multiple classes to choose from and nicely designed equipment that makes you want to have them all! There is a new race as well, so you could create an obese Rat farmer who gains experience by eating food and extra boni from cheese slices (lol), or an insectoid alchemist who fires giant cannonballs and grows mushrooms in her pockets (disgusting). Besides melee and ranged fighting, you have magic based on a rune system. But if you dont like that extra micromanagment, just make a party of 4 Berserkers and smash everything to a pulp. You can even change the character portraits with your own custom pictures, so visually you can have your dream party of Pokémon or whatever you fancy.
I got almost 40 h of gameplay out of this 20€ purchase, so it was well worth the money. I am actually more content with LoG2 than I was with Shadow of Mordor. It is a lot of fun and I recommend it to every RPG/Puzzle fan. For me personally, this is game of the year so far.

I can't say enough good about this game!  I think any fan of jigsaw puzzles would agree that this is a very well-done puzzler.
The puzzles pictures have a beautiful quilt-like feel (hence the name of the game, of course).  Graphically it's very pretty and the music fits very nicely.
There are a number of completion achievements that aren't difficult to get if you play through all of the puzzles.
The puzzles themselves range from easy to extremely difficult; you aren't provided with a guide picture but the game does place a small number of pieces on the board already to give you a starting point.  Which pieces are placed appears to be random, as restarting the puzzle nets you a whole different starter set.  This is nice to keep in mind if you have bad luck with which pieces are given at the start; you can always restart the level in the hopes of getting a better arrangement of pieces.  There is also a handy hint button if you simply can't figure out what to do, although there is a recharge time.
I got something like 30 hours of playtime out of this game by the time I finished all of the puzzles, and then went back to complete them all again with a perfect score (that is, no mistakes and within the time limit).  This feels like an immense amount of playtime for the price ($4.99) and well worth it, especially since jigsaw puzzles have (in my opinion) an inherent replayability.
100% recommended for jigsaw puzzle fans!

We've likely all heard the mysteriously enigmatic fairy tale called Alice In Wonderland as children, but what would occur if this fantasy story and its many zany characters were seamlessly combined with patchwork puzzle mosaics? We'd then have quite a compelling game on our hands aptly titled Alice's Patchwork, a relatively new release published by 8Floor and developed by Creobit.
The premise of the game itself is that you join up with Alice and her cohorts (found from both Wonderland and Looking-Glass Land) as you journey through many enchanting locations while assembling together patchwork scenes which are breathtakingly gorgeous, visually colorful, and also highly imaginative. Meanwhile the pieces themselves showcase incredibly rich and varied textures which further gives this game a hallmark of quality since quite clearly, much care & attention went into its creation.
The kicker here is that you must solve all of these puzzles within a set time limit since there exists a countdown timer, whereby you'll collect gold coins (in-game purchases) and keys (unlocking new levels and bonuses) upon solving each which wonderfully infuses an element of both suspense and reward into this challenge. However it should be noted that there also exists a "relaxed mode" setting in the options menu which disables the timer completely if you wish to maximize its casual-style attributes to their fullest, or perhaps even if you wish to practice with it first for a little while. In any event, the more optimally you solve the mosaic (in terms of both speed and mistakes) the more keys you will earn, which is a rather nice touch in compelling the player to perform at their very best.
The feature set of the game itself is rather impressive indeed! Because you'll easily enjoy hours upon hours of fun with it (over 10), with its more than 120 unique puzzles to solve, 6 expansive worlds, special quests, player ranks, and even bonuses to unlock. This is neither a short nor sparse play-through whatsoever, and I can only admire this aspect of Alice's Patchwork since its visually impressive yet challenging puzzles are something which you will definitely wish to keep coming back to time & again for the next sit-down with it. And make no mistake about it, the artistic merits of these mosaics presented here are nothing less than spectacular, especially for those who are aficionados of such eye candy in their games.
Another nice perk to be found is the hints bubble located in the top right hand corner of the screen, which is designed to help you along if needed, while being  purchased with the gold coins you win & collect. And believe me, in the later more difficult stages you'll come to appreciate this assistance because while it starts out fairly casual and relaxed to help ease you in, it gradually ramps up its challenge throughout at a fairly steady rate until you are being pushed right to your limits later on. This is fantastic to see because it will tightly grip your interest and not let go until you have finally completed the entire game, and a satisfying experience it is to be sure.
I must also say that the wide assortment of chosen background music is another glowing highlight to this game, because I felt it brilliantly captured the very essence of the fairy tale itself with its very classically themed arrangements and crisp/clear instrumentals, whereupon each individual instrument itself sounded very unique and charming...while also exuding a very relaxing and upbeat atmosphere as it should.
One final plus here, is that Alice's Patchwork has been fully Steamified with both achievements and trading cards included, and I might add here that even the cards themselves are rather impressive to behold when expanded to their full size glory.
The fusion of this particular fairy tale theme with such patchwork puzzle gameplay somehow works, and works fantastically. Furthermore, it felt very polished in all the right ways and is both very casual in character yet quite challenging at heart, meaning it will certainly have a wide audience appeal while also being accessible for just about all ages. I felt that its many positives far outnumbered its virtually non-existent negatives of which I didn't readily notice any glaring ones at all, thus I would easily recommend this masterpiece in a heartbeat for those with an affinity toward either Alice In Wonderland and/or those who simply enjoy casual puzzle type games. And while I still haven't finished every single puzzle within it yet, I surely plan to resume playing it much more so that I may finally solve them all in order to collect every single key to be acquired in the game. Because what they all unlock is a whole lot of magical fun in this truly hidden gem.
I'll enthusiastically rate this one 4.5 out of 5 stars.

Games like Final Station really make me wish there was a "Recommend with caution" button on Steam. I think the game overall is good enough to recommend, but this game isn't for everybody.
Pros:
+ Art and sound direction are pretty stellar.
+ The story, for the most part, kept me engaged. There are some issues with it though.
+ Gameplay rewards tactical play.
+ A lot of the levels contain interesting isolated stories of their own.
Cons:
- The gunplay is barely of flash game quality.
- There are segments where train passengers talk about about the story and world, but you're often too busy maintaining the train and/or their health to really listen in.
- As stated in the pros section, the story could use some tightening. It's left extremely open to interpretation with a lot of loose ends never getting outright explained to the player.
- Gameplay gets repetitive
- The game has no outright tutorial, meaning the player has to pick up everything for themselves. Sometimes this works to the game's favor, but more than once it kind of annoyed me.
Taking my sweet time and exploring everything, I beat Final Station in 4 hours even. The game is flawed in a lot of ways, but it is interesting enough that I'm willing to take a look at any other games this team may make down the line.

Developed by Elder Games and published by Merge Games & Headup Games, Meridian: New World is as much a homage to past RTS games and tries at the same time to set itself apart by adopting a few RPG features. It has achieved mixed results, but I have to admire the dev team’s dedication to this project. At one point, only one person was working on this strategy game. The Sci-Fi aesthetic and the several attempts at an engaging story, try to distract attention from the game’s few but significant programming flaws. This was Elder Games’ first game on Steam and they have shown an interest in making Meridian, part of an RTS series. As of 2016, a sequel to New World has been released. It’s called Meridian: Squad 22.

Meridian: New World tries hard at providing a good strategical experience. It offers a well designed tutorial and includes a story which pieces together the missions of the singleplayer campaign. It has to since, the game has no multiplayer option at all. Not even local co-op. You will have to contend with the less than stellar AI in custom map skirmishes, if you wish for a challenge outside of the main story. It has some RPG elements, if you can call the limited unit and base customization options by that. But speaking of the bases in this game, the micromanagement aspects involving both fixed turrets and units, can be a nuisance. If fact I found the game too easy during some missions, since the AI has pathfinding problems and even your own units struggle to reach the designated waypoints you set them towards.

From a graphical perspective, Meridian looks the part and the extensive use of different colors (especially in regards to the laser weaponry), matches the general feel of the game. It is very well polished for a game released in 2014. The terrain and foilage though, seems less diverse than the unit roster but that is a minor complaint at best.

The game’s sound department could certainly use an overhaul. While the musical score is decent, the voice acting has taken some serious dips in quality and general performance. There are in-game cinematics between missions which crop together a decent enough story. Too bad the voice actors deliver their lines with a somewhat lack of enthusiasm.

+ Classic style real time strategy.
+ Appealing graphical details
+ Steam Trading Cards & Achievements


- The AI pathfinding is troublesome at times
- No multiplayer
- Less than appealing voice acting

While Meridian: New World is most certainly not a boring strategy title, it lacks a certain depth and detail that make RTS games, engaging even after countless skirmishes throughout the time. It has a good looking unit roster, but It has no diversity whatsoever as far as picking a race or side within the game’s conflict. The lack of a multiplayer mode will also deter some gamers, which rightfully feel the need to test themselves against other players. I really wish I could have enjoyed this game more since I’m a strategy fan.

This was my grandmother's apple pie recipe. I have never seen another one quite like it. It will always be my favorite and has won me several first place prizes in local competitions. I hope it becomes one of your favorites as well!
Here is the ingredients for the dough:
2 1/2 cups all-purpose flour
4 teaspoons sugar
1/4 teaspoon fine salt
14 tablespoons cold butter, diced
1 large egg, lightly beaten with 2 tablespoons cold water
And for the filling:
2 tablespoons freshly squeezed lemon juice
3 pounds baking apples like Golden Delicious, Cortland, or Mutsu
2/3 cup sugar, plus more for sprinkling on the pie
1/4 cup unsalted butter
1/4 teaspoon ground cinnamon
A generous pinch of ground nutmeg
1 large egg, lightly beaten
Place a rack in the lower third of the oven and preheat the oven to 375 degrees F.
Bake the pie on a baking sheet until the crust is golden, about 50 minutes. Cool on a rack before serving. The pie keeps well at room temperature (covered) for 24 hours, or refrigerated for up to 4 days.
And there you have a nice looking, delicious pie for you and your family

I can't really recommend Receiver for the price of $5.00. The storyline is short and not compelling, the game doesn't run or look particularly well at all, and the gunplay is unique, but not enough to hold my interest.
The story is told through audiotapes found randomly throughout the game. I found it rather uninteresting, which in part is to be expected as the primary objective of the developer was to experiment with gunplay mechanics. As a result we have a storyline that just gives you a reason to collect audiotapes and shoot guns at robots.
The game did not run particularly well for me, and I doubt it’s a problem with my hardware. Clipping and pop-ins are fairly common. The environment is not textured so anything other than the guns you use look bland. The backdrop of a metropolis was a nice touch but overall the game was unimpressive graphically and technically.
The gameplay is centered on the gunplay. You are given a random gun in a random condition with a random amount of ammo. You can manipulate nearly any aspect of the gun including pulling the hammer back or loading bullets individually into a magazine, and each action requires a different key. It takes time to learn, but once you start to figure it out it becomes increasingly satisfying to quickly empty the casings out of a revolver and reload it. You fight two types of enemies, a flying taser robot and a turret. Different parts of the enemies react in different ways when shot, so accuracy is rewarded over speed. For example the strategy I usually attempted to employ was to shoot the camera on the turrets as ideally it would take one bullet, and they would no longer be able to detect me. Admittedly the gunplay is interesting, but in the end I don't think it’s capable of holding up the whole package.
Without a worthwhile story and weak graphics, the gameplay fails to make this game worth the $5.00 price tag. I'm glad someone experimented with gunplay to make this game, and if you can pick it up for a cheaper price or free, it is worth trying. Gun enthusiasts should also reconsider what I have said, because this game might be something you will find quite enjoyable.

I haven't played the predecessor, so this review is based on the quality of this game as an "old-school" RPG.
The game involves a great amount of time tediously scanning walls for very small hidden buttons.  I've spent about a quarter of time in game just retracing steps scanning walls; not my idea of fun.  Finding a hidden button/lever can mean the difference between progressing through content and being stuck at a standstill.  This could have been remedied by allowing the party to comment on hidden features similar to Might and Magic X.
Combat was rather clunky, especially playing a wizard.  I found missle weapons to be lackluster, and ranged combat in general was a hassle with projectile collection.  You can effectively kite mobs using melee attacks as long as you are quick enough to move to another tile before giving the mob time to attack.  Additionally, there is no way to track mob health; there are no hit point bars or visual cues.  There is no feedback regarding if a mob is resistant to certain forms of attacks; sometimes skills do 1 damage and then the same skill will do 20 damage (is it because of weak attacks or damage resistance?)
The only methods of healing are via potions and resting.  I made the assumption that one of the schools of magic would contain healing, but that was not the case.  No class healing really detracts from combat.
There doesn't appear to be any form of skill reset.  Given that you start the game clueless regarding the skills, items, and spells available, it would be great to have this available in some form.
Having played MIght and Magic X, I feel this is an inferior clone.  It does have some nice perks, such as unique weapon skills and interesting puzzles.  Sadly, the game is bogged down by unnecessary tedious tasks and clunky combat/skills.

Many say that Gone Home isn't really a video game, and I strongly disagree with that assertion. While it may not have an outlined objective to complete or complex puzzles to solve, it does have a definitive structure which the player must follow in order to experience the game's conclusion. And it is this because of this structure that I believe Gone Home is best categorized as a first person story-driven adventure game.
When playing this game, you will simply be interacting with one object after another, while exploring the environment, in order to unravel the mysterious situation which lies before you. And while there is much to explore and examine, Gone Home is not a game which requires great degree of investigative skill to finish. It is one that requires a bit of patience and a strong sense of curiosity though. Because while its overall length may not be long, you do need to take some time to carefully look around if you want to see the whole picture.
There is an incredible amount of detail throughout the entire game and almost every room you enter will reveal a key story detail to you. And because of the game's carefully organized level design, as long you explore in a common sense fashion, you'll never feel lost and the story will build upon itself in such a masterful and beautiful way; that by the time you reach its end, you'll wish so badly that there was more.
The reason to play Gone Home is not to achieve a high score or beat a boss, it is to experience a heart touching story. And I want to leave it up to you to find out what that story specifically is, so I won't say anything else about it. If you can, play the whole game in one sitting and go in as completely blind as you can. All you really need to know is that Gone Home is simple yet masterfully built game which will see your heart swell, and maybe even your eyes water, as you take in the lovingly crafted tale that it carefully sets before you to experience.

So, having logged 104 hours into the game and completed roughly 75% of the achievements, I figured I would sit down and write a review/recommendation for Banished.  Overall, this game is amazing.  It's got multiple (and I mean multiple) elements to consider in order for the player to achieve a healthy, happy, thriving community.  However, the basic mechanics are pretty easy to learn and the tutorials, while being somewhat bare minimum, are enough to at least get the player happily started on his own dreams of popuation building domination.  As I've played the game I've noticed:
- Having auto-pause on tabbing out is wonderful.  Some people may be annoyed by this, but since the player's population can go from happily frolicking through fields full of plums and cherries to attempting to cut down trees or mine rocks with their bare hands, puking their guts out and then trying madly to find the nearest hospital while shivering from the cold... all in a few moments on 10x speed... yeah.  Hurray for auto-pause so the population doesn't die while the player decides to load up youtube and watch a 2 minute video.
- Merchants in ships do not seem to use their spyglasses to look for supplies when deteriming which trading post to visit. When given the choice between a trading post full of workers and materials vs. a trading post with two lonely workers struggling to load 10 barrels of apples into an empty warehouse, guess which one the merchant picks fifty percent of the time? That's right!  He visits the seedy looking trading post with a few apples and completely bypasses the ten workers in the supply-laden trading post waving welcome signs and cheering. Sigh.
- One basket of produce left in a farmer's field over the winter somehow magically prevents that farmer from planting seeds or harvesting crops from any of the rest of his field the next planting season.  I realize the basket probably does take up five feet of space, but Mr. Farmer, honestly, you can just walk around it. I promise. Or better yet, take it to the storehouse so it is actually useable.
- All hunters in this game should be provided with a gps and a gun safety manual.  Hunters can produce an amazing amount of leather and venison in just one season.  Left to themselves, even alone in that huge mansion of a hunting lodge they get, one hunter can produce enough to feed a small army IF they are smart enough to find the deer standing outside the front door and not walk past them to aimlessly search for deer three miles away.  When they do eventually find a herd of deer, hunters seem to throw caution to the wind and take out as many of the cervine as they can, eventually hunting them to extinction and leaving no animals for the following several years.
- Actions taken by the populace of each city give the player a sense of a helpful, industrious community bent on serving others and helping with daily tasks.  This is awesome and probably would be the ideal scenario for any group of people who were banished to a remote location and forced to rely on one another to survive.  I love that farmers will help carry supplies to build houses, miners will sacrifice time and energy to carry logs from the storage area to a build site, and the local brewmaster will even leave the pub to help someone down the road carry his basket of fish to the storehouse as soon as he has extra time.  However, this is hell when the player's wonderful generous workers decide to help the person waaaay on the other side of the map, or to help clear a group of trees approximately nine hundred miles away, leaving their own jobs to stagnate and become unproductive.  Upon realizing that nine hundred miles was probably slightly too far to walk in one season, they then try to return to their homes and jobs, only to become famished and cold since they apparently left without coats or a lunchbox...or a tractor trailer loaded with all the stuff they'd need to not die before they got back to town.
- As it stands now, when building fields, orchards, and pastures, the player is unable to see how many workers will be required to serve at these locations once they are actually built.  While somewhat amusing, it is also pretty frustrating since this results in juggling workers back and forth unless the player has the size-to-worker ratio already memorized.
- WTB: the ability to toggle trees, stone, iron, and other terrain features on and off in order to be able to see what is being built where, to be able to plan roads that actually go in a straight line, and to have better city planning ability in general.
- Grats to the developer on coming up with some character names that made me laugh out loud several times.  I personally got kicks and giggles out of having three versions of the name "Orill" pairing up with "Colon" in the stone house I built for them and then surviving happily ever after presumably meeting each others needs quite well until their eighties.
- Every once in a while, even the most robust woodcutter needs to see the herbalist for a remedy.  This works quite well, until the player realizes that their woodcutter should have gone much earlier, because even though his information tells the player that he is visiting the herbalist, he is hallucinating since the herbalist hut has not been built yet and said herbalist will not exist for the next two years.
So, in conclusion, after a very long commentary and review, there are quite a few small tweaks to gameplay that need to be ironed out, but for a 1.0 release this game is incredible and impressive not only graphically but in its ability to release (for the most part) without a hitch.  I look forward to Banished 1.0.1 and beyond!

A very very good sequel worthy of its name. Legend of Grimrock 2 features many of the familiar mechanics seen in the first game, yet it improves upon the AI significantly, where they are less rigid in movement and are able to avoid your strikes or even counter-attack you as you move to their side, seemingly learning from your actions (a tactic commonly used in the first, where you strafe to their side and attack before strafing away). It features the grid-based movement and introduces new weapons, weapon attacks (special attacks) and a new race to boot. The puzzles are more interesting this time around and arguably the difficulty has been upped. Boss battles are exciting and there are many hidden areas for you to find, with each hidden area becoming more and more difficult to discover as its clues become more subtle. The maps have also been increased in size, where multiple paths can be taken for you to try out different puzzles, leaving you with the option to come back later if you wish. The visuals have also been improved and are quite impressive. A definite must-buy if you are a fan of the first game.

First thing first, The Final Station is by no means a bad game per say, I just don't think it's a 17 dollar worth of game.
But as per usual, I'll start with the pros and cons:
Pros:
1. Nice graphics, which is kind of wasted in terms of story potential. There is a lot of Chinese and Japanese characters in the background that could have been woven into lores and story that was left untouched. Such a waste........
2. Gameplay. One would think that the most challenging part of the game is when you explore an zombie filled station, but in my opinion the most challenging part is multitasking during the train ride. Which is a little counter productive. But overall, the game is at least challenging.
Cons:
1. Story. I've played the game from end to end. Fully explore and rescured every NPC. Yet, in the end I'm still not completely sure what the story is about. And apparently, regardless of what you did, you get a bad ending. Which kind of sucks a little tbh. But the biggest problem is that the story is just kind of incoherent.
2. Combat. This isn't strictly a complaint, but I thought the combat is a bit plain in that most enemy can be cced with simple melee attack so for the most part there really isn't much reason to use anything else.
In summary. If you can get this in a bundle or on sale, go for it; otherwise, I can think of plenty of other games that's way more fun for the same price.

Final Fantasy X is absolutely brilliant. It has my favourite combat system in the whole series: purely turn based (no active-time), with the ability to swap party members in and out mid-battle. This makes it feel strategic, and ensures you can keep your less-liked charactes caught up with the others without too much hassle. Summons are quite fun to use and important to the story, rather than just being spells with long cutscenes.
The music is fantastic, and the remaster comes with a completely redone soundtrack (though you're free to switch back to the original soundtrack at will). Other enhancements include upgraded graphics (of course) and a few cheats that you can either ignore, use to speed things up while grinding, or completely break in the game in half.
It's a great port, at a great price.
Oh, and you even get Final Fantasy X-2 as well. Which is... not as bad as some people say.

I have always loved city builders. I especially love the modern ones that allow players to track individual citizens of a particular town. That's very entertaining.
This game is attractive to look at. I built churches just to look at how pretty they were. Also the wildlife and naturescape is beautiful.
It is VERY addictive. Don't start playing unless you have a fair amount of time on your hands.
There are a few things that need to be fixed, though.
The production system, especially of food, is extremely frustrating. Every time you think you've finally figured out a way to get your citizens to actually grow food and then put it in their mouths to eat it, then grow more, they surprise you. I'd have over a thousand units of food sitting in storage, with farms, hunters, fishermen, and gatherers buzzing along, when suddenly, the amount of food available would bottom out to below 100 units, and the starvation would set in. And FAST. As soon as I saw that little fork-and-knife symbol above citizens, my heart would drop, because I knew that within (real-time) minutes they'd start falling dead, one after another, faster than they could be replaced. This left me with a catch-22: the food production industries had too few workers to function effectively, yet without them, more people would die, and the worker population would continue to shrink.
This spread to other industries as well. It's essential that you keep plenty of stone, wood, and iron available, yet it never seems like they're easy to get. Forget about iron and stone being readily available. It is at first, but takes an eternity to refresh (even now I'm not sure if iron ever DOES refresh). If you want a reliable supply, you have to build mines and quarries and foresters, but even then they're not really dependable, since supplies can still be low, and take up a lot of workers, which you're going to be shifting away from them in order to move workers over to the food industry, which inevitably you will do once the food supply begins its unavoidable descent. But then the food workers are going to run out of tools, which can only be made using wood and iron, so you're going to take workers away from them again to run the mines, foresters and blacksmiths, which is going to cause the food supply to slow down again, and the iron, wood and tool industries never really take off anyway.......
There are no ways to beautify the city. I missed this.
Lastly, it doesn't have much of a point. You build up a city, it either grows or shrinks (usually alternating between the two), and.....then what? There are no campaigns or goals. There's no way to "win". I got bored.

This is a fairly good arcade-like racing game with a huge open world which keeps my interest. I enjoyed Test Drive 1 and 2 quite a bit which is what influenced me to buy The Crew. I say it's a pretty good game even though for me there are some disappointments.
The biggest disappointment is there is no offline play. I can see they probably did not want hackers and such but it is still disappointing since Test Drive 1 + 2 offer offline play. If the online fuction dies then I won't be able to play without some sort of community support I guess.
I like how the textures are pretty detailed compared to the Test Drive games and there are many vistas that look pretty impressive such some areas show fireworks going off , very large bridges, detailed towns and cities, airports, a space shuttle, hot air balloons and quite a bit more. Though it seems to not look very realistic since the field of view seems to make everything kind of look like toys somewhat but it is unique, clean looking, and the lighting is very well done especially at night. The dirt roads look pretty bad though compared to other games and seems like it would have been easy to fix. Though it is nice to see animals and people in the world for added detail. The in-car view does look pretty good. The camara angle changes awkwardly a bit when using nitro though.
Sounds in general seem fine. I wish the car sounds were a bit fuller but aren't too bad. I do like how the sound does change when you are in the car itself.
The racing is pretty fun especially since you can take shortcuts and smash through things which adds excitement. There are mini games also which allow you to win car parts which is pretty neat.
For me this game is worth buying for the exploration because there are a lot of vistas, car parts, and such you can find throughout this very large map and the racing is fun too. The atmosphere of the world does feel a bit unrealistic visually but it does have it's own unique appearance which is nice. It is probably hard to be able to manage the time to create everything perfectly especially when making such a huge world.

You'll enjoy trashing the house you first spawn at in the game more than it's actual "story".

What to say about Guns UP...
As previously mentioned it is a very, fire and forget, real-time action, balance and odd pushing war game.
There is more strategy than some suggested but in most cases it's battlefield and enemy AI manipulation with no movement control other than the rally point card. The game has cards that include attack, defense, and counter measures, focusing fire, missile drops, decoys, tear gas, ect. You manage your munitions which are the resources that you consume to spawn troops/units, there are attack cards to increase munitions of course, as well as max army unit caps, and this is really the control aspect of your battles.
PVP defends are simply retaliation based and leave you a video source of your battle, it's a static process and one I'd like to see improved upon in the game the most. The option to defend in real-time and change the outcome would be great.
The base endless defend mode, listed as CPU Defend in 1 of 3 attack modes, is a fun and addictive. The base building has lots of choices and build stytles, a leveling system for each defense structure, and is very user-friendly to lay out.
There is a promotion system with upto 4 levels for each class of unit in your army, with a range of perks to boost health, damage, speed, ect. These perks cards. as well as attack cards packs, can be obtained through the real money purchase, battle rewards, and some are purchasable through in-game currency. The random chance of opening new card packs is fun, addictive, and reminds me of many other mobile type games.
A fun note to mention is the battle reward drops have some a real rare dropst that can have huge positive impacts for player experience, more notable than most games I've seen.
The game can get slower, between level 25 to level 35 as it grinds a lot harder, this this where a lot of players have peaked and lost interest, which adds to the grind of players to bypass in the ranking system. This is important because the game ranking system is based on the amount of dog tags obtained from player battles, that you gain or loss depending on the outcome. The good news is that the games pacing improves as you approach level 40 and higher. With a level cap of 200, and the amount of time I have already spent, there is a lot of room for more features and additional content. Some of the less active players who are not fully committed and still not as hooked on the game will find the grind discouraging.
The best way to counter the grind is to join an alliance, which has a couple ranks, alliance chat, but no perks other than you get to participate in alliance battles to help break up the repetitive gameplay of hunting low levels. Alliance battles are broken up into seasons, and last about a week and than take a break for a week,.They are still 1v1 combat, completely random and sometimes an inconsistent experience, favoring either side with unpredictable match ups. The difficulty and unpredictable nature does have a more rewarding feeling when you win theses battles, and alliance battle rewards are usually better. At the end of each season, the depending where you alliance finishes and is ranked, the prices can be very good too.
The pay to win formula has been well controlled and not a big factor affecting free play experiences, othere than large gaps from easy/medium difficulty and strongly difficult players add for inconsistent matchmaking at higher levels, but you are given a range of difficulty with 6 players each time and you chose who you fight, almost guarunteeing your win everytime. The game is instead, more of a pay to level faster and earn more in-game currency scenario, it does not have a huge impact in winning the battles or pushing the gameplay mechanics in more favorable odds. You may find however that being limited to only in-game currency and needing more time to obtain stronger attack cards limits the number battles you have with higher difficulty players in a certain timeframe. This is based on the amount of high levels cards that you can pay for instead of having to buy them with in-game currency or win them by chance with more successful battles.
There is no ganging up or bullying in the game, as the attack list is randomly generated based on your level, players can only specifically target other players on a friend list, but you can retaliate to any random player attack once and it will appear in your defend history.
Now for the bad part.
Although the game is very active and has a lot of support and even in-game events, it has not been progressing as much in development as I would of hoped by now, and suffers from bugs that become more apparent as you approach higher levels.
The A.I determines its path of attack, you have no control over your army and some players have exploited the battlefield object collision and automatic pathing to purposely have an advantage and break your experience and attacking abilitiy. Examples include infinite path looping, loops unnecessary paths to time out the player, too complicated to the point its almost impossible to beat some enemy bases, no matter the attack resources or units used.
The game has bugs, especially in CPU Defend mode, one the three modes of for you can attack in. The bug has been reported since February 2016 and they still have not resolved it and have players occasionsionally to often, crashing once they hit 15 or more minutes in-game. I have been disheartened and downright angry at the crashes as you lose progress, resources, new records, and monumental moments in your gaming experience, whch are immediately crushed.
So much potential, but I am not impresssed what the developers are allowing to slide, and have yet to fix, I am slowly losing my interest and dedication that could  been with a very long, active and healthy game commmunity. I would not be motivated to pay or invest money into this game. As a free title, totally recommend and my review score would be higher if they fix the major issues between crash and path manipulation.

The Final Station is a mixture of resource management and survival-horror: You have to manage your medkits, ammunition, the status of your train and its passengers you will pick up on the way.
The resource management is easy to do: check on various parts of your train to make sure that they don't overheat or so, make sure a passenger's health or hunger doesn't bottom out by either using a medkit or food, but don't go too wild with your resources as their limited by what you find in the wild and from what you can make.
The survival-horror aspect is pretty straightforward: shoot/melee any enemies encountered, watch your health, don't trap yourself in a dead end and make it back to the train. Now, some of the resource management affects this too, you will have very limited ammunition and in some cases more monsters to deal. So, use your environment when you can: sometimes chairs, toilets, and so forth will be throwable at enemies to save ammunition and in some cases you might find the occasional explosive barrel to help take out large groups of enemies or tough enemies. If you run out of ammunition, you will have to use melee hits or run away.


The controls are easy to learn, with about 8 keys and mouse or a controller, it's easy and the game will give you a quick rundown during your gameplay. I think the game was made with both keyboard/mouse and controller in mind due to the custom key mapping. Played both ways and found both easy to use and as far as controller use, I used both a Logitech F310 and a Steam Controller, both work perfectly.


The Final Station is of the pixel style with some non-pixel style backdrops, which both look wonderfully done and during gameplay just moves fluidly perfect. The art design for me, reminds me heavily of Tom Francis' Gunpoint, in many ways and I'm not knocking that at all, in fact I think because of the art design, I really kept tabs on the game when I randomly found it here on steam.


The Final Station music/audio is done pretty damn well. To specify, you are playing in a post-apocalyptic world, that's full of dread, fear and overall discomfort. Whether you are on your train or at a station, you get to hear it: the footsteps you take, the ruffle of grass, shooting your weapons, rain, or that random bird/dog in the background.
Music wise, it exists but not in a overall setting. Instead there is a focus on general ambience for the most part, but when you get ether an important area or point in the game you get to hear some of the game's light but enjoy music which give slight break from the general mood of the game.

I thoroughly enjoyed The Last Station and will fully recommend it to anyone: It has a interesting plot, easy to understand gameplay, nice music (which there is a soundtrack of!) and well, is fun to play.
I haven't had a chance to play the DLC, but will soon and will post a small view when I've finished it and hope it give more information of the world in the game.
Overall, The Final Station is a nice game and is definitely worth a play, so buy it now or put it on your wish list, but give it a try, when you can.

Receiver certainly is an interesting take on the FPS genre, but this time, the "S" stands for simulation.  Rather than your standard run and gun gameplay most FPS features, Receiver is much more deliberate where the focus isn't just on the shooting, but also on the gun itself.
In Receiver you must manage every part of the gun, the slider, the hammer, the magazine, it's chamber, etc. If you don't take care of your gun, or understand how each part functions you will die... a lot. The game does a good job at simulating what it takes to handle a real gun. Due to it's vast amount of controls there is a definite learning curve with this game. It will not play like other FPSs you've played previously.
The game is only $5usd, which isn't asking for a lot, but do know there are limited amounts of options, features, and content. There is only one play mode, only 2 types of enemies, and not much in the way of customization. Although the game does it's best to incentivize reply with it's procedurally generated maps, enemies, and load out, and each play through will be different from the last, but it will be "different" with a lot of very familiar assets.
Certainly the game is challenging, and at first may even be frustrating to some, but it's also very rewarding. Once you manage to get over the difficulty and control hump, the game will feel like none other you've played. Each kill feels like a huge victory, and the game does a good job at instilling a legitimate sense of tension and danger around every corner.
Overall Receiver is a quality product at a low price point. The content might be limited, but through the creativity of it's mechanics, there are also endless possibilities to play through.
Pros:
- Procedurally generated maps and load out offers endless play potential
- Very unique mechanics and concept
- Best gun simulation I've played (only gun simulation I've played?)
- Challenging
- Very fair price
Cons:
- Limited content
- Moderate visuals
- Large learning curve

For such a simple game, this one's done a great job of keeping my heart pumping quickly.
Pros:
- The gun mechanics are much more complicated in this game than most, which makes it very unique. Instead of simply pressing "R" to reload a weapon, there is a specific key that is pressed for every step of the reloading process (Removing mag, adding bullets to mag, inserting mag, cocking weapon, etc.).
- Your two enemies, Bots and Turrets, both have various hit boxes that, when shot, provide different effects. Turrets, For example, spin around in a circle scanning for the player, and if you fall inside of their sweeping scanner's view, they will fire on you. So shooting a turret in a certian spot may prevent it from spinning, but leave its gun fully operational, and able to shoot you if you walk in front of it; while shooting another location may leave the scanner untouched but render the gun itself useless.
- 3 or 4 different guns to choose from that all have different mechanics, strategies, strengths, and weaknesses.
- Maps are randomly generated.
Cons:
- The game is very repetitive. As your goal is always the same: gather the tapes.
- Graphics are awkwardly ugly
- Lack of enemies/weapons
- Slight learning curve for gun mechanics.
Overall, keeping the $5 price tag in mind, I give this a 8/10. Honestly I would say it's worth grabbing for the $5 tag if you can get it.

Played On: Laptop
Steam Price as of Review: $6.99
Total Time played: 40 Minutes
Review:
The next game on the wheel of morality is Meridian: New World, a RTS clone from publisher Elder Games that seems to take after the Starcraft style of play rather than the Command and Conquer style; essentially a foreign planet robot manned colonization strategy game with a surprisingly intuitive and minimal UI.  The only issue I have with this is that everything else about this seems done already.  The story itself (at least the first half hour) was fairly standard, and didn’t really feel very engaging.  The graphics, though pretty even at lower quality levels, seemed to get in the way more than anything else.  All in all, I would think that hardcore fans of RTS games would appreciate this, but really there are probably better ways to spend your time. Maybe after putting in a few hours, this game may have more substance, however that is not the context in which I am writing these reviews, so unfortunately, this is what we get.
Game’s Fate: Uninstalled.  When I want to play an RTS, I’ll go try Starcraft 2
Buy/No Buy: It’s Pretty and certainly seems to work, but i would wait till it’s on sale, and even then only if you are a big RTS fan already.

If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding pie recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.

Receiver is a first person shooter that takes on the challenge of bringing in realistic gun mechanics, and an environment that looks like it was made by a student in his/her first few years using 3Ds Max. While not inherently "bad"... Receiver isn't a game that will be enjoyed or appreciated by most people; that is why I'm giving it the down vote, to be honest I don't recommend or recommend-against playing this game, I simply didn't find it enjoyable.
You there! collect all the tapes! "who me? Why do I want to do that?" That's what I want to ask, but I'm not given that luxury. I collected only a couple tapes before getting tired of being murdered by the turrets 10+ times. Presumably you are collecting these tapes to uncover a mystery within the game and to understand what's going on inside the game.
First thing you do: Press ? on your keyboard so you can see what to do
Second thing you do: go through an acurete and realistic weapon arming proccess
third thing you do: run around and collect stuff on the floor
fourth thing you do: run into your first enemy and get yourself killed
Goal: To collect 11 tapes
The highlight for this game are the gun handling mechanics, you don't simply press "R" to reload, depending on the weapon you're using you need to press a button to change the cartage and then press a button to load a new one.
For the revolver, you actually need to open the revolver, take out the old bullets, and put in new ones. While very interesting, and highly realistic, the game is not very easy to learn and will require learning new tricks if you want to actually survive the game play.
I took down several of the auto turrets, there seem to be two kinds: Flying, and stationary. Both of them are really annoying if they spot you. If you get seen, you have a second to dodge around the corner. My instincts to shoot back usually ended up getting me killed.

No achievements (thankfully), unless you want to make them for yourself, I think collecting 11 tapes would be quite the accomplishment.

This is a review of the entire series. No I will not review all of them, because, no, I don't want to buy all of them and waist a good $30 on games I don't like.
Five Nights at Freddy's blew up over the past year. And for no good reason other than Markiplier played it. Though he plays a lot of games that don't get the same attention as this one. So why was this so popular, I mean every body and their mother made a video about the game and it's hidden story, that's just that, hidden. And I think that's what made this game so popular. Five Nights played on that fear of the unknown, until you quickly figured out that games mechanics.
I hate when people call this game the best game of 2015, it really isn't. I couldn't even really name one, though the Early Alpha Sandbox for Yandere Simulator (another game being made by a single person as an independent developer) has much more innovation put into it than all of the Five Night's games put together.
Five Nights at Freddy's uses jump scares, and that's all it uses. There isn't anything else that makes this game "scary" and at that the game isn't even scary, it's startling. The only time that the game is ever name stressful is when you're watching another person play it. And you can pick up the patterns that the animatronics use.
And the story is hidden. You shouldn't have to look for the story in a game that has one. There are plenty of games that just push you into the world without any explaination. And those don't need stories to them, a cryptic story is better than what Scott did. When you have to have the internet explain your story for you, you aren't doing your job correctly.

The Crew. An MMO racing game made by Ubisoft on a scaled down USA (minus Alaksa and Hawaii). Now, writing a review about this game would take too long, so IO made it into a pro and con list instead.
+ Entire scaled down USA to explore (minus Alaska and Hawaii).
+ 5 different car specs to choose from, each showing off an aspect of the huge map, and each with its own "story" (as such).
+ Runs on the same game engine as Test Drive Unlimited 2 (Havok engine), so physics feel mostly the same.
+ Car exterior customisation.
+ The need for grinding XP is non-existent. Enough XP is handed out by winning races and skills and finding landmarks that you'll almost always be ahead of the game (XP wise).
Now, as for the game not being made strictly by Ubisoft: it isn't. The Crew was also made by Ivory Tower, a company made up of people who worked on one of the three:
- Need for Speed
- Test Drive Unlimited/Test Drive Unlimited 2
- V-Rally
Ivory Tower was the company that came up with the idea for the game. They designed and bulit most of it. As for Ubisoft Reflections, I'm not entirely sure what they put in. I'm pretty sure the only idea they pitched in was the idea for Crew Credits (to get more money) and having DLC (for even more money than Crew Credits). As for the servers, I haven't had a problem with them. Whenever I've gone to play, the servers have always been up. I was on almost everyday on launch week and I never had the server problems like everyone else. It probably helps that I live in Australia, which means it's night in the US and everyone is sleeping and not doing maintenance to the servers. Also, as for the game crashing, I've only ever had it crash once, and that was when I changed the graphics settings to high for my computer to handle.
- Cop AI and catchup is too powerful, as no matter how fast you're going (e.g. 400km/h), apparently the cops can top that by at least 20km/h.
- Nitrous is weird i.e. your wheels spin when nitrous is activated. This can be troublesome at first, but once you get used to it, it can actually be quite helpful.
- Only sunshine and overcast weather, no rain/snow, etc.
- Bigger fleet of cars than NFS:Rivals, but still realativly small, but they add a new car every month or so. Also, not all the cars are listed on The Crew website.
- Barely any good songs. I was using my own song list almost immediately.
- Doesn't support EyeFinity properly i.e. the menu is a blank screen and the entire HUD is missing (only a problem on AMD it would seem. It works fine now that I use NVIDIA cards).
There are plenty more pros and cons to this game, but these are the major ones. all in all, this game is pretty awesome in most cases, but, like every game, it does have its problems.
Overall, I'm giving this game an 7/10.
Sidenote: there's a unicorn to find. I haven't found it yet, but I'm sure there's a guide on Steam to show you where it is and how to get to it.
[EDIT]
The new Wild Run expansion (release date: 17/11/2015 (America)) is going to change and fix some things listed above, both under the pros and cons section. Some of these include:
~ A HUGE graphics overhurl to make everything look prettier, add more weather effects, and increase the draw distance (i.e. quality of objects at a distance will be improved)
(avaliable to eveyone, even those who don't own the Wild Run expansion).
~ 3 more car specs: drag, drift and monster truck.
~ Although less realistic, the non-IRL car festival known as "The Summit" will be added, with festival style bases placed around the map.
~ Although less realistic, there will be playgrounds set up by The Summit festival for you to have fun in, and also monster truck specific playgrounds for testing and playing around with the new monster truck spec.
~ Bikes (avaliable in the original five specs. not sure about the new ones, though).
~ New cars (or so I've heard).

Not such a bad game. Yes, there are bugs, yes, some menus are incorrect or misplaced or the text in them is transparent and you can't read it. And so many missing things, even the most basic ones, like comparing the attributes of one of your players with another player in the world (i haven't figured out how to do that yet!). But, i like the managerial tycoon part of the game (setting ticket prices and expanding the arena) and the CORE of the gameplay, the algorithm of the match, its there, it exists, and its rather good. Still no 2D or 3D representation but only text commentary, but for me its OK, reminds me of the old times playing Football Manager 00/01. Also one good thing is that you can quit the game and save during a match, which is missing from FM for example. Also, the game is rather light with respect to system requirements, the loading and processing times are not so big (even for my low low end laptop). As other reviewers have mentioned, there exist a real names patch and a graphics patch for face picks, so don't be discouraged by the lack of licencing. I would give it a 7/10. Without doubt, a lot of work has to be done by the developers (who are Greek like me) as ti seems like an unfinished product, but the basic framework is set. If you like Basketball AND text sports sims with a flavor of tycoon elements, give it a try and be patient. For all the others, not recommended.

One word easily describes this game: thrilling.
It's easy enough to imagine what you think you would do a situation Receiver puts you in.  But, for those who have never used a gun, it comes across stressful, dreadful and filled with panic.  And that is was makes this game absolutely fantastic!
The idea is simple - you have a gun and off you go.  But it is more a gun simulator than a rouge-like.  Every part of a gun is modelled and must be manipulated to ensure you survive the levels.
So most of your time is spent asking questions like, "Is my magazine loaded? Safety off? Is there a round in the chamber? Will it jam? Is there a round in the chamber?".
And by the time you think you've answered those questions you've forgotten to aim and actually shoot the enemy in front.

Built a town for hours. It started to rain in the game, which is quite a normal event, but then something terrible happend.
A tornado came and wiped out my trade port (which had just been finished), a fishing dock, and 15 inhabitants - which was more than half of the population.
The ones who did survive were all over 70 years old or were only children. The old men and women stuggled to feed the younglings, but winter was coming. A shortage of warm clothing finished off most of the elders and sickly children.
However, some of the children and a couple of the elders miraculously survived the winter, and began to rebuild. The fishing dock was restored to its formers glory, and the bridge that had been under construction for many seasons, was finally finished. The bridge would bring in new resources with minimal effort. One girl joined the labor force, and produced warm clothing for the entire village. For many winters they survived, and the town population steadidly grew. Things were looking prosperous.
But the damage by the whirlwind to the town's infrastucture was too great. The fishing dock only yielded 2/3's of what it used to, and once again the adult population slowly starved to death while struggling to feed its children.
In an effort to feed my people, I ordered for firewood production to be put on hault. I sent the wood choppers to help the hunters and gatherers in a last attempt to keep this civilization alive. Not only did this not yield enough food, the entire population froze to death from the lack of warmth in thier homes. The blacksmith was the last to fall; he worked up to his last icy breath, stood still, then dropped to ground.
If you are a fan of brutal strategy games, then this is a must buy. Casual gamers need not apply.

Dark Souls 2 Scholar of the First Sin is the remastered and updated version of the original Dark Souls 2, featuring DX11 support, revamped lighting, enemy and item placement changes, and Lore and Character changes, even adding a new ending, all in all the definitive version of the game. (Also comes with all 3 DLC)
Now with that out of the way lets get to the actual game itself, Dark Souls 2 is obviously the sequel to Dark Souls 1, the fantastic 3D Action RPG by FromSotware released in 2011 (If you want to know about that game look at my review for it aswell). While that game suffered from a bad PC port, albeit easily fixed with a few mods, this game actually has a pretty good PC port although I'd still recommend playing with a gamepad. Dark Souls 2 is often regarded as the "Black Sheep" of the franchise and while for the most part it has trouble living up to its predecesor its still a fantastic game. The game went through a troubled development, switching directors halfway through and having to salvage the game they had instead of restarting due to time restraints, however the DLC and late game is noticeably better than the early levels. Dark Souls 2 enhances upon the gameplay of Dark Souls 1 however and adds quite a few nice features that make the games mechanics more intuitive, it also features IMO the best muliplayer of the series, Dark Souls 3 Included. They also take the story to new interesting places, the game features some pretty cool story and lore moments that compliment the first game rather well, for the most part, theres also quite a bit of throwbacks to Dark Souls 1 stuff that is kinda hit or miss but I quite enjoy the new stuff and feel it adds to the mythos. Overall while not being the Dark Souls Sequel people wanted Its still a great game with a lot of cool stuff in it.

So bannished is a interesting mixture of survival, town/settlement building and Tornadoes.
So you start with 4 or 6 familys and you have to use the population you have to build a new life in the wilderness you need to gather materials and build what you need to survive and hopefully thrive, so far so good and as you build up your population increases so you need more houses,woodcutters and food production to feed you people and need enougth fire wood to survive the random winters some are nice and easy and other times its rather punishing to keep people alive.
Once you get your first 100 people population is'nt a problem, if you don't manage to have a healthy and happy population they won't have kids and eventualy your people are too old to reproduce so the game is a proper balancing act of population and food production/stockpile to feed everyone.
The game has a interesting approach to peoples behaviour as you can have big problems made by your own people such as hoarding and over population which can cause you allot of problems if people start hoarding food and firewood others won't have enougth food or fire wood and they will become unhappy or mostly die in a harsh winter from starvation or hypothermia?
The fix you will need is markets as they make sure everyone gets what they need and it stops hoarding from happening so build a market and thats not a probem, or the oppposite problem you build to many houses or you have a mass die off and the younger generation move into the houses and  have kids before you know it you have 30 kids and you need more schools and they eat so much food and they won't help you gather or help produce more food until they adults and have been educated? I recommend schools as they work smarter and get more done with less accidents which is good!
With houses keep them spread out and linked by markets and never build like 50 or 60 houses it'll come back to haunt you when you least expect it.
Try to build multiple smaller settlements with 5 to 10 houses per place linked by a road with markets for supplies, as markets are awesome the vendors use wheel barrows and are super effient.
The game is really good and well made, the only thing i find is a bit much is tornades they are random and can end your game really fast, the other disasters are easy to fix such as disease easy, crops failing easy theres probably more i have'nt had yet so i look forward to dealing when it happens to my peoples.

Gone Home is a game about getting a chance to see the side of a family that they don't always show to the world.  Everyone has their own secrets, and as you play through, you will discover them through evidence that they leave behind.  Each character has their own story arc, and the game comes together at the end, justifying everything you've witnessed so far.
One of the great things about this game, is that multiple people can play through the game, which provides all the same experiences, but they may come away with completely different opinions of the characters.  This may either be because of missed or overlooked evidence, or even just bringing a preconceived idea of the character to the discussion.  Each character has a depth about them that makes them feel human and real.
This game is absolutely worth picking up if you see it on sale, but I wouldn't go so far as to put up $20 for a game with almost 0 replay value.

I really want to like this game.  It is quite a bit of fun but it has too many bugs and lazy programming with enemies that it just turns into an irritating and slightly unplayable mess.  Having enemies spawning next to you, allies despawn in front of you so more enemies can spawn on top of you.  Dead soldiers disappear into the ground so you cant loot them.  Areas bug and prevent you from moving through doors that are supposed to be opened.  Enemies despawn that you need to kill for a mission.  The main trouble with all that though is that it happens more and more over time.  What is the point of taking over a region if as soon as you get attacked in that area all allies that are now present immediately despawn so as to allow the computer to place enemies there, because it can only support around 10 units at a time.  Preventing you from actually having a decent battle, and devolving it to nothing more than you playing one man army.  For a game thats supposed to be about an uprising i find it terribly unimmersive when all your allies vanish as soon as there is a fight.  At its core this game is a pretty fun shooter, but its been done better else where and the additional material that could make this game stand out was not fully completed.  If your looking for a shooter to distract you for a little while go for it, otherwise move on.  One final note, this story is not a continuation from the previous game Homefront.  It is using the same concept but that is the end of the similarities.

Finally another F1 game that's worth its price! I must admit that Codemasters did a really good job on this one.
F1 2016 is - as the name reveals - licensed for the current season with all your favorite Formula One drivers from Hamilton over Grosjean to Haryanto. The graphics look almost lifelike and the different tracks feel like the real thing.
Positive:
- safety car and virtual safety car included
- stands and pit lane feel alive with an audience and the crews present
- pit garage is beautifully animated
- cars feel balanced
- training programmes during free practice provide motivation for collecting development points which you can invest for upgrades to your car over the season
- career mode is lots of fun
- animations before practice/qualifying/race add to the feeling of being a part of F1, as does the possibility to do a formation lap before race start
- weather changes are quite challenging
- very good damage models and collision simulation
Negative:
- even with a very good graphic card that can handle the settings on ultra, the game still sometimes loads stuff in the background and becomes rather bumpy, which sucks especially while driving through corners
- AI behaves rather erratically at times
- keyboard users are at a disadvantage at the tire wear training programme. The handling is too harsh if you don't use a controller or steering wheel
I haven't tested the online multiplayer yet, so I can't say anything about it.
All in all this is the best F1 game I've played since F1 Racing Championship. I can definitely recommend it to all racing fans out there.

Overall a decent game; it's not bad but it's not great either. Recommended when on sale (I got the Freedom Fighter Bundle for £8.99 - BARGAIN).
Graphics are pretty good and environments are really well designed IMO along with the KPA soldiers and vehicles etc. Characters could have used some refinement with their animations and development which is lacking (Dana deserved more screen time and way more development for sure, why no DLC of her back story!?). The story manages to carry you through to the end, again, not bad but not great either.
Gameplay's pretty much like Far Cry, free roam the map and capture enemy strongholds either by stealth or guns blazing with secrets and stashes littered about. It isnt open world like Far Cry is though, the world is seperated into several areas that you can free roam in and move onto the next area as you progress with the story. Each area has it's own look and feel with good atmosphere (especially Lombard; very Stalker/Metro 2033ish) that are the real stars of the show.
Shame it's bogged down by technical problems with performance (probably down to my FX 8350, turning settings down to low doesn't make much of a difference) and weird stuff like enemies literally popping in and out of thin air as they like. The gunplay could have used some fine tuning too IMO. Enemies seen to have pin point accuracy even from miles away with Assault Rifles but you? not so much. Weapon customization is okay but basic.
Mixed bag of a game that needed more time to be fully cooked. Worth a buy when it's on sale though, its a steal!

After the flops of 2014 and 2015, F1 2016 didn't disappoint me. Here's my pros and cons.

Even though I swerved only once to the right to defend, Hamilton rammed in there and spun us both out 3 times on 3 different occasions. The experience is not bad, but I came across an experience-ending glitch.
I began by playing lightly for a couple days then decided to really give this game a shot and dumped several hours into it at once. The game is very addictive for about a day, but has a few drawbacks to its long-term replay capability.
The basic premise is you get units which run on their own and you use different powers to assist them in their goal of defending or destroying a base. There are numerous upgrade options for your base and soldiers and a few options for powers and bonuses you can use mid-combat to help them. There are also several perks which you can upgrade and apply to your soldiers to make them tougher. You can spend money to get post of the upgrades but its not totally necessary to make you effective.
The sound is average for a game like this and the music is only okay. Not surprising for a free game so its not a massive letdown.
The biggest problems with this game are in its actual gameplay. Your units have the AI of a pong game, attacking relatively useless targets when you have a massive bunker blasting holes into your lines which they could attack instead. You have to use specific powers to tell them what to do so everything is mostly run on rails, which kills a lot of the "strategy" aspect this game could have. There is an excessive amount of random chance in this game as well. When your units arrive they move in an unpredictable manner, they just wander in a random direction which at times can even be backwards just to go behind certain points of cover instead of moving to the forward lines as fast as possible. Simply put, the game is not really a strategy game. Its far more like a tower defense game trying to be strategic.
I managed to use the very simple mechanics and get to an over 1000 point base but when I returned to try it out again the game refused to begin, sitting on an eternal loading screen. There isn't anything else to say after this because as far as I'm concerned there are much better games to play that do similar concepts even better. Ones which I dont have to worry about not starting again.

The game from the outside looks like team-management for basketball team, like FM for football team. The basic features are there : the team management, the facility management, contract management, etc. There is also training management, finance management, and basic management stuff that should be in any sport management game. The problem in this game is not on features, but on its execution, that is what I have to say. As in FM game, the management aspect in this game revolves on managing your players, notably their training, contract, and general condition. You can also manage your team, which revolves on how to improve your facility, what players you want to draft in this season, what players you want to sell this season, how to gain income from sponsors and tickets, and others. The game also have match management, at least in theory, because during play I always got an error when trying to resolve the match manually.
Sadly, the game don't work. There are too many bugs, too many things unfinished. I am talking about unfinished, not unpolished. For some games (notably tycoon games) some things could be unpolished, looks clunky, but the functionalities are there. A lot of stuff on this game have zero functionality, not to mention lots of game-breaking bugs.
The UI is bad. Here are few things that I found as unacceptable :
- It's hard to navigate to a particular player.
- On the player screen, his physical stats, his offensive stats, and his defensive stats are divided into three different screens, which requires you to switch back and forth to view this player from all angles.
- You don't know how much money on-hand you got now. You can view it from the finance overview, but that only tells you about budget and remaining cash after the budget year, not your cash now.
- Everything is hard to be navigated. Too access a specific information you have to go 3-4 clicks, while in similar games 1 click or 2 click is suffice.
- There are no explanation when you are building something. The game only gives you the cost and the picture, but nothing else. Tycoons can't make decision without critical information, this game fails to deliver information.
There are options on this game to publish certain team snippets, for example "Red Sox is looking for a new manager" in Facebook. Why with Facebook? Is this game like those farming game in Facebook, where we pester other people for help? Bad decision.
If you draft the players, the screen suddenly changes background that you have hard time figuring out the text. There are problems when trying to play match manually, all matches must be played automatically. Why put the button there if it can't work?
The only redeeming factor is the art of the facility (one scene only) is quite good. No other arts existed though, because I can't play the manual game, and like tycoon games, art is limited. Tycoon games is mostly about UI, art can be followed next.
Not recommended, this game is unfinished. Unfinished. Unplayable. Not fun to play.
