tl;dr I dont normally review games but this is one of the strongest titles I've ever played, quite literally outstanding.
On the playtime: 3.8 hours without touching the DLC, but they were incredibly dense hours. Just know what you're buying.
I personally prioritize gameplay when I'm thinking about video games critically, so most narrative driven games fall flat. Games like Mass Effect, Gone Home, and Bioshock Infinite all seem like wastes of time to me. Doesn't matter if your story was written by a critically acclaimed author, if your gameplay is♥♥♥♥♥♥your game is♥♥♥♥♥♥ Despite my usual preference to talk about gameplay the most, this game deserves particular attention to its narrative.
Take characters for instance, understood by most writers to be the building blocks of good writing. Cmdr. Shepard is one of the most uninteresting characters in the history of fiction (sacrificing any depth for trite player input) and the protagonist is only one of the scores of boring characters in the ME series. Usually video game characters feel contrived and obvious projections of the developers' personal beliefs or tired archetypes. With plot based exceptions, The Final Station's characters avoid these traps.
The narrative style also sets this game apart from many of its competitors. Most narrative games will assault the player with character traits and world building that don't really develop the overall tone at all. I can't provide any examples for this since they're so forgettable, but I notice them in the moment when I'm playing and it's incredibly distracting. Instead of telling the player what the world and characters are like by yelling at him/her, The Final Station leaves subtle hints that the attentive player will be rewarded with. It really comes down to "show, don't tell," and this game does very little telling and a whole lot of showing.
Then there's the motifs, the colors that the artists who wrote this game used on their canvas. Zombies are tired, especially to me, but this game has twisted the traditional approach of zombies into something new and refreshing. Insider v. outsider also makes an appearance, but it isn't hamfisted like other games might approach something of contemporary controversy. Without getting into substantial spoilers, the inner X-Files freak in me absolutely adored this game, and I'm sure the developers drew some inspiration from the show. Being a conductor means the player is exposed to a variety of areas, which on the one hand provides the illusion of freedom while still literally railroading them, adding to the game's overall claustophobic tone. Also it's got some Asian characters (font not people, but the people are probably Asian too, it isn't really important what their race is) and cool looking machines so you weird anime people might find something enjoyable there. [edit2: if you think Evangelion is cool you'll enjoy it for more than just having mechs] [edit1: I saw another reviewer mention Roadside Picnic and I just wanted to include it in this section. Going into an unknown malice is a favorite motif of mine, also found in House of Leaves]
Back to the gameplay however, I'd say that it's really above average. At its core it's a survival/resource management game, where you have to scavenge and weigh your costs/benefits of keeping certain people alive. The platformer combat is alright, but I found myself gaming the stair/ladder system from about midgame onwards. Once the enemies weaknesses were known to me I kind of missed the mystery of not knowing, but I feel that with most combat based games. It's definitely a game I would recommend taking each fight slowly and cautiously, all rushing will get you is gameovers. I always try to take time to give games like this a little review.
After traveling from station to station and transporting one mysterious parcel after the other for the government, I found myself heading up a mountain to get the blocker code that would allow my train– and my four injured passengers– safe passage to Metropole. In my pistol, I had three bullets. In my bag, two med kits– both of which I needed to save if I wanted my passengers to make it to the end of the line.
Blood stains the hallway I walk through. The dining room is suspiciously clean, but as I open the door, human shaped monstrosities race towards me.
This isn’t a battle, though; it’s a puzzle, and I have three moves in the barrel of my gun.
Quick Run-Down:
This game costs about $15 on steam, but regularly goes on sale for $5.
It’s about 4 hours long when you’re running at a brisk pace– I could see someone who’s a completion taking 5 to 6 hours to complete it.
It’s a 2D shooter/platformer (though I’d consider it more of a puzzle platformer).
The Good:
Really easy to pick up! This game is welcoming to “casual” and “hardcore” gamers alike, providing a wonderful atmosphere that’s not overtly terrifying. A lot of what you know of the world comes from reading, so if you’re not a fan of that kind of exposition, you’ll be in the long haul for the 2D root-n-toot-n-point-n-shoot gameplay.
I mention the fear factor specifically because I, like many of you (probably) are tired of paying $60 to be jump-scared or thrown into a maze filled with gore. This game lets you experience creepy comfortably, so even the most squeamish among us can have a good time without needing to turn it off every ten minutes.
Also, one of the most important things for me when I play a game is the soundtrack. The Final Station doesn’t have a lot of tracks (it doesn’t need many for it’s four hour campaign), but the songs it brings to the table are atmospheric and eerily beautiful.
The strongest points of the game as a whole are the narrative, worldbuilding, and quirky characters. I’m a total sucker for a good story, and this game kept me interested through the entirety of it’s short runtime. It throws a few twists at you throughout, making sure you’re always guessing and wondering what’s around the next station.
The visuals are also surprisingly engrossing, even though they’re 8-bit.
Some would call the game-play repetitive, as you alternate between a combat section, a travel section, and safe hubs. I didn’t find that to be the case, but I was focused more on chasing down the story than I was on the way the game played. I never caught myself thinking, “Oh boy, another enemy that I’ve killed 20 times.” It was always, “Oh, man! I need that item, but I can go two ways– if I pick this chair up, maybe I can do x,y,z…”
That’s why I call it more a puzzle platformer than a shooter. The enemies are lined up in such a way that they impede progress, but you have limited ammo, so you’ve really got to think about how you’re going to handle them. This keeps you highly engaged throughout the campaign.
The Bad:
Gunna lay it out here. If I’m going to pay $15 for a 4 hour experience, that experience better be absolutely fantastic or have a high replay value (like Undertale!). The final Station is good– maybe $10 good– but it’s definitely not worth $15. You’ll play through and enjoy the story once.
However, I’d argue this isn’t one of those games you can sit and watch a let’s play of (which is strange, given the linear nature of the story). It wouldn’t have had the same feel– part of the game is interpreting the events that happen and stringing them together in a way that makes sense to you. Once you have an assumption, it colors the rest of the game as you go through it. Watching someone play it with commentary would ruin the effect, I think.
The inventory system in this game is… well, I’m almost afraid to mention it because it’s barely a “system”. You can hold two guns. The game tricks you (genuinely, 100% tricks you) into dropping the best gun in the game, letting you think you just picked up a third. This really made the end portion of the game difficult for me, and they absolutely did it on purpose.
Also, if you’re a fan of open-ended endings, this game has one. There is a finite end, but wrapping your head around the entirety of the story is a tough task. I’ll tell you, all the pieces are there, but the last half-hour starts to get tough to follow. I personally understood the ending well, which is why I enjoyed it. Other people felt it ended abruptly, so play at your own risk!
(If you played INSIDE, which is a game I hated, know that this ending is in a similar category but by no means as frustrating.)
Verdict:
Buy it when it’s on sale! I got it for $5, and it provides a great narrative experience that reminds me of the old point and click adventure games.
If you like the atmosphere of…
INSIDE and This War of Mine,
or the gameplay style of…
Night in the Woods,
you’ll probably like The Final Station.

Some of the reviews of this game seem way too premature from where I sit. Some people have missed the point of this game entirely. This is a car RPG if that makes sense. You have different classes of cars which you use for different situations, whether you're free driving or on a mission. In each of those classes, you work on improving whatever cars fit into each spec. Customisation for visual preference is good. Lots of body kits, paint jobs, decals etc to apply. There isn't a huge variety of cars (like GT or Forza) but definitely enough.
Teaming up with friends is fun if you're a similar level otherwise it's something I avoided until I hit max level. Once you're at max level, there's plenty of end game challenges to complete, players to battle, cars to improve and areas to explore.
I cannot stress how much seemless terrain there is in this game. Driving from one side of the country to the other, up and down the coasts, through the mountains and all around gradually blends really well. Very few world bugs.
If you're into cars, this is definitely worth a play. The single player campaign is decent on its own but really exists to show you all the variety the game has to offer. I've spent ages just cruisin on highways, finding random secluded rally tracks, crossed barren plains, doing laps at famous race courses... it goes on and on. I'd suggest you get a mate to play with you on voice chat. I'll be playing this for along time.. the good really outwieghts the bad. So far... 8/10

What LoGR2 does different than LoGR1:
-a wider variety of areas (swamps, beaches, castles, forests, and [don't you worry] more dungeons! And they are BEAUTIFUL)
-non-linear exploration. (or at least more than before. think, 6 paths you need to complete but you chose the order and can backtrack)
-vertical multi-level elements
-a simpler, faster potion crafting system
-more class types
-a fifth species of character
What 2 still has from 1:
-loads of monsters (most of them new [and more variety than even before], but you see some familiar faces)
-loads of loot
-loads of satisfying puzzles!

Nice retro music and graphics, if that's your thing. But that's about all this game has going for itself. As for the difficulty, there is hard, then there is unfair. This game leans heavily toward the unfair side. "Hard" can be something like Super Meat Boy where you can plainly see all the challenges in front of you, and it's up to you to be skillful enough to pass them. VVVVVV's version of challenge is to punish players for not being psychic. It's trial-and-error gameplay at its worst. Your vision is limited to 1 tiny screen at a time. Get to the edge of the screen, and you appear in the next one. If you happen to be falling (up OR down, in this game) you go very fast and if there just happens to be a pit of spikes in your path, you die and there is little you can do other than remember they are there during your next attempt.

First Impressions Review:
I think WWE 2K16 is an improvement over WWE 2K15 but it still has a lot of issues.
What's Better:
1) Create-A-Diva: '15 left out Diva creation '16 brought it in. Nice to know that 2K stopped being sexist.
2) In-match optimization better: I no longer have the stuttering and performance issues during the match as I did with '15.
3) Story Mode: They added a LOT to story mode, including rivalries, allies, picking which championship you want to go for, who you want to invade, all sorts of stuff! It's still got a grind factor, but there's a lot more depth in '16 than there was in '15.
4) Match depth: There's a little more in-depth match mechanics like the various grappling mechanics which involve a back-and-forth mini-game of who can find the "sweet spot" first. But the game doesn't really tell you how to set that up...
What's The Same:
1) Graphics: Virtually the same engine. The audience is slightly improved. Superstars and the scenery are pretty much the same. Maybe some minor improvements...
2) Overall fighting mechanics: Same huge sets of moves that are hard to perfect and remember
What's Worse:
1) Submission: The submission mechanic is horrible. The system works like this: The defender has a blue bar, the aggressor has a red bar. The aggressor wants to have their red bar inside the defender's blue bar to fill up the circle in the center. If the circle is filled, the defender taps out. If it becomes completely blue, then the defender kicks out. Sounds fair, right? WRONG! If the body part is undamaged or fully damaged there's no real adjustment to how the mechanic works. It's all skill-based. I can understand that the bars should initially be based off of the wrestler's skills. But as the match goes on, there should be an equalizer. If you damage a body part, the aggressor should have an equalizer to help them get the submission win. What's the point of damaging a body part if you can't even take advantage of it...
2) AI Kick-Outs: The AI kicks out ALL THE F*CKING TIME! An opponent I was against had no health, no stamina, just got Finishered, but STILL KICKED OUT BEFORE 3! Dark Souls 2 Scholar of the First Sin is the remastered and updated version of the original Dark Souls 2, featuring DX11 support, revamped lighting, enemy and item placement changes, and Lore and Character changes, even adding a new ending, all in all the definitive version of the game. (Also comes with all 3 DLC)
Now with that out of the way lets get to the actual game itself, Dark Souls 2 is obviously the sequel to Dark Souls 1, the fantastic 3D Action RPG by FromSotware released in 2011 (If you want to know about that game look at my review for it aswell). While that game suffered from a bad PC port, albeit easily fixed with a few mods, this game actually has a pretty good PC port although I'd still recommend playing with a gamepad. Dark Souls 2 is often regarded as the "Black Sheep" of the franchise and while for the most part it has trouble living up to its predecesor its still a fantastic game. The game went through a troubled development, switching directors halfway through and having to salvage the game they had instead of restarting due to time restraints, however the DLC and late game is noticeably better than the early levels. Dark Souls 2 enhances upon the gameplay of Dark Souls 1 however and adds quite a few nice features that make the games mechanics more intuitive, it also features IMO the best muliplayer of the series, Dark Souls 3 Included. They also take the story to new interesting places, the game features some pretty cool story and lore moments that compliment the first game rather well, for the most part, theres also quite a bit of throwbacks to Dark Souls 1 stuff that is kinda hit or miss but I quite enjoy the new stuff and feel it adds to the mythos. Overall while not being the Dark Souls Sequel people wanted Its still a great game with a lot of cool stuff in it.

So, here's the deal. You have this one game, made by a team of many developers: coders, designers, managers, associates, support, marketing, people who make textures, design AI, design multiplayer elements, people who work on network code etc, etc. Months and months go by, (Read: Much) more than a million dollars is spent. Hype is skyrocketing for the upcoming game these people are working for. As the days go by, the slow drip of media is let loose to the public and they are devouring it, because the game looks great.
Finally, after months of waiting and hard work, the game is released and boy is it broken. Where did all that money go? What were the developers doing all that time? Why is there even multiplayer in a single player game? The end result of all this work, is Sim City. And it blows. Really bad.
Then you have Banished. A simple game, made entirely by one guy. The budget for this game palese in comparison to the turd  EA puts out, and get this, Banished is a revelation! The gameplay is smart, deep, and the best of all, it works as it is designed to work. The music is beautiful in its simplicity and elegance, I'm not bombarded with messages to "Go online" for a single player game, I'm not harassed to buy DLC content, the game is definitely not a resource hog, and you can tell actual thought went into this game.
Not to say thought didn't go into making Sim City. On the contrary, so much thought went into making that game. Too bad all that thought was made up of horrible, terrible, no good ideas that were put in place to help EAs bottom line.
Listen, I'm not the one to bash a mega corporation for the sake of bashing a mega corporation. I'm vocally anti-piracy, and not only that, I actuallly enjoy some of EAs games. But when you do what EA does, specifically everything in the last five years, to try to make playing and enjoying their games as painful and un-fun as possible, the odds of having a success, at least in my eyes, approaches zero.
I'm sorry that this review was more of a review of Sim City than Banished, but I feel that Banished shines especially when placed next to its convoluted and stupid counterpart, Sim City. Its everything its brother isn't, and more.  There is so much to do in the game, you may never find yourself bored. You'll have a blast while playing, too.

Brace yourselves for No-Man's Land, Soldiers. This world war isn't the world war that everyone likes to talk about, but it is worth slamming some money on the table for an experience that makes you feel like you're there in the trenches; avoiding mustard gas and waiting sharpshooters if you attempt climbing over the mounds of mud and dirt.
This game is immersive; be it with the ambience of gunfire and mortars, death animations and screams, authentic regalia and weapons, and I feel the best part is that the Germans actually speak German instead of English with an accent. Sehr gut, ja? The same goes for the French, so when you are making your way through the trenches and hear multiple voices speaking German you know you are in for a fight.
The graphics are a thing of beauty. My primary counting machine doesn't have the highest performance, but I have played it on a buddy's computer and it is marvelous. You can stare out over the wire and smoke while looking down your weapon sights and wait for movement of advancing lines, picking off Brits and Germans alike. There's loss of limbs via grenades and mortar strikes, writhing bodies you'll mistake for still alive enemies, and Flammenwerfer units ready to douse you in flame if you don't keep your distance.
Trying to lone wolf is ill-advised, working together as a unified group can get you the most points and win battles. Sticking with your commandant is a must too, he'll give out orders for flanking and for attack positions; as well as call in artillery.
This will sound bad, but killing in this game has never been more satisfying. Especially if you don't have a scope on your rifle and you lead your shot over a great distance away. It is hard to kill. I have a higher death count than kill count just because of how good the snipers are, but to me that makes my kills all the more worthwhile; due to how difficult it is to not get killed before you raise your rifle butt to your shoulder to zero in on a target.
I recommend this game foremost because of the historic authenticity, which is something you can't really say about Battlefield One's weapons in multiplayer; since they use too many automatic weapons and prototypes. The only downside is the player base not being great in number. I sometimes have to switch to the European servers. Even though it has been ported to Play Station now, not many people know about this gem and it saddens me. This game is worth every penny.

If you are using a gamepad, such as an xbox controller, steer away from this game. Although the game itself for the most part seems like a good game, it is unfortunately ruined by a very high input delay for gamepads. I have tried every combination of the (quite limited) control options to no avail. The core issue seems to be a very low saturation on the rate of steering input. That is, try moving your controls from far right to far left, it will take several seconds before the game reaches far left which you can see from the visual response of the steering wheel. Unfortunately, it is so slow that it is impossible to counter-steer if you have a bit of oversteer. You don't really feel the car and can't make any quick adjustments, which just ruins the immersion. A very conservative and predictable driving style is necessary just to keep the car on the road.
From the discussion I've read, driving wheels do not seem to have this issue as the game input is one-to-one with your steering wheels angle. If this is what you're using, I'm sure you'll enjoy this game. It's unfortunate what seems like a small fix for Codemasters completely ruins the game experience for me and many others. I've gone back and reinstalled F1 2012 which just feels so much better. There is some steering rate saturation here as well as is natural for gamepad inputs, but it is so much faster and feels much better. My recommendation is stick to 2012 or 2013 until Codemasters fix this issue - if they ever do. Meanwhile I urge the developers to add options for the input rate saturation and any other parameters that the game uses for gamepad inputs.

When I first tried to read up on the scale of The Crew I had found forum posts talking about the time it takes to cross the map. Hearing times ranging from an hour to over two hours I was disappointed when I made it from Northeastern Maine to Malibu, California in just under 40 minutes.
But it isn't just about the quantity of width, it was about the quality that expands to the north and south as well. Whether you even choose to do the campaign missions, there can be dozens of hours of pleasure found in traversing the country in Street spec cars. They did a great job capturing monumental structures such as the Golden Gate Bridge and Mount Rushmore or landmarks like the Bonneville Salt Flats and the Grand Canyon.
The map itself doesn't feel copy and pasted either. Each section does seem to have its own unique features. Whether it be the snowy roads of the Rocky Mountains or the winding and elevating roads in the Giant Sequoia Forest, or Las Vegas towering over the horizon, it is worth going and seeing what The Crew has to offer.

Me Giving a Bad Rep for this game doen´s mean that I wouldn´t recommend it all, but the thing is: The game has too much going against it to really recommend it.
The game throws you right into the Actionand it gives you some nice cars to play with right from the get go and within the first few hours of gameplay you get to drive cars from 4 of the 5 Spec sets so you can get a glimpse of what lies ahead. And you can do all that either on your own or in Co-Op with a Crew of either some random people or with your friends. The game tries to tell a story about revenge and stuff, but it is so narrow with unintresting characters that it makes Fast and Furious look like The Godfather in comparsion. However I do like the variety in gameplay, you get to drive some races, escape the cops every once in a while, take down a target, destroy some boxes for reasons or just try to get to the finish line within a timelimit. All that both on- and off-road.
I also like the huge map, you need roughly 90 minutes to get from New York City to Los Angeles, and just to make sure that you don´t get bored during your road trips you get tons of little Skill Challenges all over the Place, these range from jumps to Race Line challenges and you can win parts to updgrade your car and money in these challenges. The Map itself is basicly a compressed Hollywood Version of the entire USA (not Including Alaska and Hawaii) without all that boring stuff. It´s the first time in an Open World Racing game that I don´t feel that the game world is limited too much.
You can visit tons of famous Towns and Landmarks, the map also Includes some, honestly bad, recreations of real life racetracks, you get everything from the time Square to the Hollywood Hills, you can drive up the Pikes Peak or reach insane Speeds on the Boneville Salt Flats, you can Visit Mount Rushmoore, the Swamps in the Southern Regions, take a road trip along the Route 66. You get the point.
The Car Handling takes a while to get used to, but once you figured out how to drift around corners it gets much easier because you would have to slow down way too much to drive around corners the regular way.
However here is why I don´t recommend it, and uPlay isn´t any of the reasons, I don´t mind it too much. The game requires you to be online all the time, if the servers goes offline for whatever reason or you loose the connection the game throws you out of whatever you are doing, even if that means that loose your 3 Hour Progress into an almost 4 Hour long race. However there is no real reason that the game has to be connected to a server at any point because you can do everything on your own. Also the game is NOT an MMO in the classical sense, while in Free Drive you randomly drop In and Out off Online Lobbys, players inside a Lobby can Invite others into their Crew and play Story-, Faction- and PVP-Events together. A Crew can have up to 4 Players and all 4 will Drop In and Out off the Sessions together. While it works, it almost feels like a gimmick to me.
I have a feeling that the car Levels and Perks don´t mean anything, at least when there is AI Involved. The game has some of the worst rubberbanding AI I encountered in over 20 Years of playing Racing games, even with cars close to Level 900 you can´t really drive away from the Low Level AI in the earliest Missions th game has to offer. When Playing PvP the Car Levely do Matter, however a goog driver can still beat a car that is 200+ Levels above him when the other driver isn´t that experienced. The whole concept is untransparent, you never get a feeling that all the carparts you collect even do anything.
Also it throws you the Option for Microtransactions in your Face every time you are anywhere where you can buy stuff within the game. You can get everything without ever using them, but I get a strong feeling that you don´t earn money fast enough in the game so they can sell more micro Transactions.

VVVVVV is an amazing journey through space and a mystical dimension trying to desperately save your friends and get back home safely. The gameplay is excellent and the retro graphics really make an impact even in their simplicity. This is by no means a long game. In fact I finished it in less than two hours in my first serious try. The thing is, you shouldn’t really expect anything else from the game. It’s a super fun bite-sized goodie with a lot to offer if you just give it a chance. The game is pretty simple and straight forward. There aren’t many mechanics but mastering the few there are is a challenge in itself. The soundtrack by Magnus (SoulEye) Pålsson is magnificent. It keeps you pumped up for the action and keeps the flow of the game up even if you happen to die 50 times in a single room. Overall, if you like retro platformers, this is a must buy. It’s not quite a masterpiece contender since the length barely gets you started with the game and the gameplay is super simplistic. Still, you’ll definitely get your money’s worth out of VVVVVV.

Original Journey is a shining example of why I love indie games and support talented indie developers. I've had the privilege of playing both the pre and post release builds, and I was astonished on both occasions with the quality of the entire gaming experience. This is exactly the type of video game review I like to write, one that highlights a truly hidden gem.
Original Journey is a 2D side-scrolling adventure RPG and shooter with roguelike elements. In regard to gameplay, the game is what I would consider simple but not simplistic. The beginning of the game alerts us to the nature of our character and this company of vegetable-like "Ato" who are on an as of yet undisclosed mission in this strange place. The game proceeds very much in a linear fashion, one area after the next, one objective after the next, so it's virtually impossible to find yourself "lost" and unsure of how to proceed. As we venture into the forest, we find procedurally generated levels with their own objectives/quests, resources and enemies, and each more difficult than the last.
During gameplay, we unlock a variety of weapons and suits, each unique in function and benefits, and find a variety of loot utilized for upgrades. This is where the roguelike elements come in, because when our character dies, it respawns back at base, and we can then venture out again. However, we will have lost whatever items were in our cargo hold at the time, so frequent trips back to base to store loot are a must. This is a game with definite "rinse and repeat," but I never found it boring or unnecessarily difficult.
In regard to time commitment, I have over 21 hours into Original Journey, but I completed the game content available in both builds more than once, so this can easily be completed in one 3-5 hour gaming session, dependent upon how much exploring you do. It can also be completed in short increments, saving your progress to revisit at a later time, so this is not a game that requires a huge commitment on your part to enjoy.
Graphically, it's beautiful, a muted color pallette allows the player to focus more on the striking hand-drawn artwork and less on flashy graphic effects. I found the graphics very refreshing actually and consider it to be an excellent example of what an ambitious creative team can accomplish.
The soundtrack is another plus. It's not at all overpowering or annoying. It's actually quite impressive, and sound effects can alert you to hazards. However, hearing impaired players and those who prefer to game with little to no sound will still be able to enjoy the game by relying on visual cues.
Developmentally, Original Journey is solid. I did not encounter any game breaking bugs at any time, and never encountered any kind of bug or glitch once the full release was published. There's plenty of content to enjoy, and the controller mechanics were spot on. Shooters are one of many types of games where poorly developed control schemes can ruin the entire experience for a gamer, but I can assure you that is not a factor for Original Journey. Game progression is steadily paced, and the levels, while not complex, are certainly enjoyable and don't inhibit the progressing storyline.
Original Journey also has definite replayability. Because the levels are procedurally generated, with resources, enemies, and even supply drops varying from one playthrough to the next, and because the player can choose weapons, turrets, and suits, and also control turret placement, the game can be revisited at anytime. I've yet to play through the game in exactly the same way twice.
Overall, I definitely recommend Original Journey, especially to gamers who enjoy shooters, roguelike/roguelite games, RPGs, and adventure games. There is much to appreciate and enjoy aesthetically, but that aside, the gameplay is truly enjoyable. In fact, I'm holding out hope for additional content or even a sequel. I enjoyed it that much.

I have loved sports management games for years. Basketball ones are not common, so I was excited to try this one, and even more excited when I saw how huge and detailed its database and game world was.
Unfortunately, the game is let down by some basic failings. The accuracy of the simulation is not that good, which is a problem when the game is built around numbers. My team often racks up more offensive rebounds than defensive rebounds,  and hardly any assists (which may be due to the European system).
Coaching options are also irritatingly limited. Have a star player and want to give them a lead role? Have a great long-range shooter and want them to focus on those shots? You'll have to set them *every game*; there's no overall strategy screen. In a long season and want to skip some games? You can't even set a depth chart.
The database is definitely praise-worthy, and being able to simulate so many leagues across the world is a fine feature. It's just a shame the rest of the game doesn't do it justice.

Receiver has some very fun gun mechanics that make the game very enjoyable to play. If you're asking yourself whether you should buy it, there's only one answer: YES!

If you are looking for a game with a fully-developed storyline, intense combat, and beautiful artistry, Original Journey from publisher Another Indie and developer Bonfire Entertainment has you covered. In this space adventure, you play a rookie soldier of the Ato alien race, which has just landed on the monster-ridden Planet Shadow on a desperate mission to save its home world. To prove your worth, you travel deep into the depths of Planet Shadow and complete missions assigned to you by the Captain and other Ato officers, facing an impressive variety of lethal creatures and collecting precious crystals along the way. The intense amount of work and creativity that went into designing this game is on full display, from the intricate layout of the Ato’s home base to the exquisite hand-drawn pencil graphics. As a gamer, you are completely sucked into the screen and transported to a different world.
One of the reasons why Original Journey feels so real and, well, original, is because it truly makes you feel in control of your own individual character. Although there is a basic narrative to follow, you are still free to make decisions and explore the world at your own pace. As mentioned before, the Ato’s home base is a maze full of different rooms and workshops, from weapon arsenals to suit armories to your own character’s personal room. You can also hitch a ride from a friendly flying droid called Vacuum Baby and strike out on your own journey, fighting monsters and collecting supplies that you can later sell at the home base. Furthermore, you can upgrade and buy new weapons and suits as you stock up on crystals, which can give you a distinct advantage in harder missions. Another unique aspect of the game is the ability to make decisions that affect the outcome of the game; for example, you can choose whether to learn extra information from the database, or whether you want to accept another character’s business offer. This independent decision-making makes the gameplay more realistic and interesting, and it feels empowering being able to determine your character’s own destiny.
Even the battle scenes in Original Journey showcase immense creativity and variety. Every fight is unique, with diverse monsters that all look and attack differently. The terrain changes every time, too—sometimes the ground is smooth, while other times there is thorny vegetation that can inflict as much damage as enemies do. As you acquire different weapons, you will discover that certain guns are better suited to fight certain monsters, which makes combat all the more stimulating. On certain levels there are also other Alto warriors who provide you with backup and even pay you crystals in return for helping them. I found that in order to preserve your health, you must constantly hold back and let the monsters come to you. I had some trouble with that initially, but battles became much easier to win after I started doing that.
In conclusion, Original Journey is stellar in its story concept, game design, and artistic composition. It struck the perfect balance of serious and yet fun, complex and yet user-friendly, dark and yet beautiful. I would absolutely recommend this game, and it definitely ranks among my favorites!

First off all, this game was rather fun in the first hours.
-----------
Pros:
- A good example of "got a bit of time, lets play something casual" style of game.
- The developers seem to take a more active stance on resolving bugs compared to other free to play mini-games ive seen.
- The artwork and graphical effects are quite nice.
Cons
- Tedious grind if you do not want to purchase anything
(As common in quite many free to play  games)
- The game mechanics for base building and matchmaking are unbalanced and are being
effectivly (ab)used by players. This is reinforced by the game being a F2P model and thus
needing a "good" motiviation for the  player to become a payer.
- Even without abuse of the pathing, the AI soldiers (Esp when you are attacking) is atrocious,
leading to defeats just  because the soldiers stumble into chokepoints, FIRE and crossfires
without the player being unable to do anything*
- There were plenty of bots/cheaters on the steam version, take a look at the game´s own website and forum.
*And no, the "Rally" Order is not a good workaround. It is not reliably available, makes the soldiers IGNORE everything till they reached the area marked, and the order itself takes up an attack card slot at the match start.
--------------------
Before i stoppped playing, my base strenght was something around 1k.
You can pick from a group of randomized opponents, each having a difficulty rating dependant on base strenght and (i hope) win/loss ratio.
The more powerful your opponent, the better loot/rewards and chances for higher grade rewards you get.
My starting setup (Grunts;Medics;Flamer/Ranger) easily overran not-well designed bases with 1,2 and up to 1,4 k, with liberal use of the (purchable with ingame-currency) card packs giving attack cards.
Occasionally, i would "rent"  a rocketeer (higher tier, expensive unit) for one match, for ingame currency,  and roflstomp 1,5k bases along with my normal setup.
And then there were PLENTY of bases around 1k, even 800 or lower base strenght, which were impregnable to my forces.
Those bases belonged to veteran players/people spending a good amount of money on the game.
---
Simply because the AIs pathfinding can be easily abused to split the soldiers up, the base building can be easily used to create chokepoints (which is a quite effective tactic) as well as abusing the base strenght not taking a few important factors into account;
There is 1xBunker and 2xSniper tents listed,  and once on the map, those base defense structures are upgraded to the highest tier possible, making them very hard to take out with the units available below level 15 or 18.
There are veteran units ("Randomly" promoted units during attacks) which carry over as troops to be used at will and during defenses, and meeting quite a few players around 1k base strenght with veteran units composed of Riot Shield soldiers, Snipers and various normal units upgraded to heroes  makes early-game armies evaporate.
Then there are cards that can be attached to the HQ, spawning groups every X seconds or when enemies are closing in.
There were plenty of HQs with base strenght around, and under, 1k which had three or more of those card-types equipped. (E.g. Spawning a group of 1xMedic and some troops, or a mixed bag of sniper, grenadier and co, AS WELL AS heroes and paratroopers)
And every unit-type (available to the player, not "rented" for a match) can be equipped with perks to permanently boost stats.
The very same enemies around 1k with high-est tier base defenses had high-grade perks on each unit, thus increasing the combat power by a large margin, compared to everything available to starting out player on level 14,15.
All of the above is available for real life money, thus adding a very visible pay to win factor into the game.
-
My biggest contention is that there were too many players "on my level/base strenght" with very good, expensive or paid for assets, who seem to deliberaty hold their base strenght down to keep around the "lower levels" in a PvP game, with an  unbalanced setup.
My second biggest contention is the pathfinding. As long as there is no "RTS" like controlling, even just setting waypoints, or ability to at least order troops to only fire on buildings, soldiers, or closest enemy, this game isnt really enjoyable.
As soon as you watch your soldiers pour into a chokepoint despite you having cleared up another path, or watch soldiers shooting a mortar or bunker instead of the sniper tents activly killing them, or see a group of riot shield veterans setting up behind a wall/barbed wire maze, you´ll understand.

Original Journey is Shoot-em-Up, Adventure game game that features light RPG and Roguelite elements.
You can find a bit over 30 minutes of gameplay with commentary here:

You play as a Rookie Ato, a small plant clone that uses armor to move around. Your homeworlds core is failing and you have come as a grunt to the planet Shadow, to retrieve the Origin Stone that has the ability to save your homeworld.
The games RPG elements include a leveling system based on experience gained from killing monsters. Each time you kill a monster it will provide you with experience, drop a number of crystals (that are the games currency and also regenerate life when collected) and there is the chance that it will also drop an item. These items range from various materials needed to craft the games weapons and armor, ammo for your guns, to upgrade chips that provide your armor with a minor benefit. On leveling you will improve the games 3 stats - health, weapon damage and luck (to improve item drops).
The Roguelike part is the stages. Each stage is a self contained island, with obstacles that either are static and you take damage from touching them, ones that you can destroy, rocks and the like that block shots but are destructible, and floating clouds that are platforms. A range of enemies will spawn and the goal is to kill them, with each island getting progressively harder. The player needs to choose between increasingly better loot or returning to base and starting over. If you die on a run, all loot gained will be dropped at that level. You get one chance to fight your way back to the dropped loot - but if you die again or abandon your run, then those items are lost.
Weapons are purchased via items collected in your runs. You can carry 2 at a time, but can only fire them separately. Each gun has their own ammo amount, which can be randomly replenished from enemy drops or by returning to base. The weapons are broken up into 3 tiers - with tier 1 consisting of a grenade launcher, mini gun, shotgun (your starting choices), sniper rifle and sword. Weapon damage is linked to your level, so weapons scale with the character.
Finally there are the armor suits. The look of the armor is mostly cosmetic, but different armor types provide a bonus to the 3 player stats. Armor is also broken up into 3 tiers like weapons, and in a tier the only difference between armor (apart from cosmetic) is how it allocates its stats bonus. Tier 1 armor gives 4 bonus points which just vary their allocation based on the armor chosen. Armor also has a chip slot - these are collected from enemy drops. Chips provide small bonuses like extra health, extra ammo capacity for a certain weapon or a minor regen.
The art style is very nice, with hand drawn elements. The animations are smooth and the muted colour scheme suits the game well. The music and sound effects are also good - but the game does not seem to have an option to mute music or audio which I feel is lacking.
The game recommends playing with an Xbox controller, and other controller support will be coming apparently.
I have found it to be an enjoyable game which can get very challenging. After 3 hours I am about 25% through (according to the game percentage). I am still in the first zone but believe I am close to getting to the next - so hopefully I will get 12 out of the game, which I feel is fair for the price. Your playtime may vary depending on skill.
Overall I am happy to recommend this game.

Long story short: This is what deus ex would have been if it was done by the director of fight club. Minimalist, beautiful, hard, mesmeric. Utterly recommended.
----
Now more detail: Receiver is a minimalist and realistic FPS. The game features 3 different models of guns: a S&W Model 10, a Colt M1911, or a Glock 17. It also features procedural levels (generated from patterns), and randomized placement for enemies (of which I've seen two different types, so far), items and objectives. That way, you never get the same experience twice. In addition, you spawn with a random selection of items, which can make the game difficulty range from moderately easy to very hard, depending on what you get.
The idea behind the game is to be as close to a realistic gun handling experience as it is possible with a keyboard and mouse. It means that the game maps to the keyboard/mouse a lot more interactions with the gun than existing titles, and also, does so with much greater details than usual FPSes. In addition, the difference in the power of each gun is very noticable, making the experience feel even more authentic.
A must have.

I was extremely excited when I first saw the preview for this game. So excited that I immediately got a Steam account, found the game, and bought it. I downloaded it and began playing immediately, and at first it seemed absolutely fantastic! I couldn't believe how well done everything was. The graphics are great, the maps enormous, the interface, music, and gameplay are all fantastic.
However, as I continued to play, I found that there were still a lot of wrinkles to be ironed out, should the developer decide to take the time to do so. The most glaring problem, by far, is the food-shortage issue. As soon as your adult population breaks the 25 - 30 mark, you will inevitably find that if you don't have EVERY SINGLE ONE OF THEM producing food, you will wind up with an unmanageable food-shortage. Very soon, your people will begin to starve and die at an alarming rate. Either that, or you'll do what I do and transfer almost three-quarters of your workers over to food-production. Which of course leads to massive shortages on other essential resources, like wood for your fires, iron to make tools with, etc...
Now I believe that the solution to this is supposed to be to educate your children so that they are more productive when they reach maturity, but if you do this then they will not be able to work until they are 20 or so - rather than going to work at age 10, if they are uneducated - which leaves you with another kind of shortage; a shortage on workers. It's all extremely frustrating because there seems to be no way to balance the equasion, so you are pretty much doomed to failure.
This is just my experience of the game. I think that if these issues were ironed out, it would be all-around awesome.

Annual sports franchises are difficult to know when to jump in. Have they just update the drivers and car liveries, have they broken what worked before or worst of all have they stripped out all but the most basic features.
F1 2016 takes the promise of a next-gen F1 game that 2015 failed to deliver and improves in almost every way.
I'm not an online racer so career mode is where it is at for me. This is not only back but has been seriously upgraded. Teams can now be developed so seasons do vary with Mercedes not always staying on top. As part of this they have managed to make one of the most skipped parts of the game, practice sessions, now mean something as this is where you can earn upgrade points. The challenges in the sessions make sense, are fun and teach you about the course and an F1 car.
None of this would matter if the racing wasn't up to scratch but Codemasters have made it very fun to race. The cars handle as you would expect with the margin between sublime cornering and spinning out of control so close. The game maintains it's excellent assists systems which you can dial back as you gain more experience someone just starting out can find their balance. I tend to race with a controller and I've never felt like I get less of an experience.
Finally it seems this year Codemasters are really pushing this game to be as good as it can be. I've already seen 2 changes to the game that I expected not to see till 2017. Lots of people were finding there was too big a gap between 2 difficulties so Codemasters introduced a new level to bridge the gap.
So in summary this is one of the great years for this annual franchise. Maybe next year will be even better but I don't think you can go wrong jumping in this year.

Finally a decent F1 game from Codemasters.
Pros:
- Nice graphics.
- A very interesting and immersive career mode with lots of features: Character customization, car development and actually workable R&D tests and many more.
- Very decent physics.
- Tyre wear seems not to be scripted anymore.
- Improved voice recognition (The engineer finally understands my Greek accent :D).
- You have more control of your car (Manual starts, manual slow down at the pit entry, chose if to repair damage or not etc).
- More strict and fair penalty system (It still needs some work though).
- More sensitive car damage and a small improvement in damage model.
- Better online experience with less lag and less aliens :3.
- More customisable races (Scripted weather, race time etc)
- A realistic race weekend with tyre choices and all the practice sessions.
Cons:
- Driver faces are terribly designed. My eyes are burnt!
- Damage model should be more detailed. Suspension damage for example does not exist. It's only wheel on, wheel off.
- Physics need some improvements too (They are not bad though).
- The info menu right down is not so easy to use (Sometimes I lose my focus to the race because of that).
- A.I. should be a little bit more aggressive. Especially in higher difficulties.
- The engine failures happen very often which is not reallistic.
- Virtual Safety Car's and Safety Car's pace is terrible and very unstable. Also the delta during these periods is completely♥♥♥♥♥♥as the A.I. go slower than it. Furthermore the A.I. slow down instantly which is really dangerous if you're right behind them.
- The jump from Expert to Legend difficulty is still an issue.
- Mid Session Save is buggy. When you load a Mid Session Saved race I just get a freezed black screen.
What the game misses:
- Dedicated servers!
- Manual pitstops.
- Detailed damage model as I said above.
- Gearbox failures and any other similar to that.
- ERS!
- More difficulties and a detailed difficulty menu (Like A.I. pace, aggression and mistakes).
In conclusion: It's worth to buy it but not for 50 euros. Maybe 30-40 euros would be ok (At least in my opinion). It's the most completed F1 game from Codemasters so far. The first game after F1 2013 that keeps my interest more than a week and without getting bored. They've made some serious♥♥♥♥♥♥for the first time! 10/10 IGN

Me Giving a Bad Rep for this game doen´s mean that I wouldn´t recommend it all, but the thing is: The game has too much going against it to really recommend it.
The game throws you right into the Actionand it gives you some nice cars to play with right from the get go and within the first few hours of gameplay you get to drive cars from 4 of the 5 Spec sets so you can get a glimpse of what lies ahead. And you can do all that either on your own or in Co-Op with a Crew of either some random people or with your friends. The game tries to tell a story about revenge and stuff, but it is so narrow with unintresting characters that it makes Fast and Furious look like The Godfather in comparsion. However I do like the variety in gameplay, you get to drive some races, escape the cops every once in a while, take down a target, destroy some boxes for reasons or just try to get to the finish line within a timelimit. All that both on- and off-road.
I also like the huge map, you need roughly 90 minutes to get from New York City to Los Angeles, and just to make sure that you don´t get bored during your road trips you get tons of little Skill Challenges all over the Place, these range from jumps to Race Line challenges and you can win parts to updgrade your car and money in these challenges. The Map itself is basicly a compressed Hollywood Version of the entire USA (not Including Alaska and Hawaii) without all that boring stuff. It´s the first time in an Open World Racing game that I don´t feel that the game world is limited too much.
You can visit tons of famous Towns and Landmarks, the map also Includes some, honestly bad, recreations of real life racetracks, you get everything from the time Square to the Hollywood Hills, you can drive up the Pikes Peak or reach insane Speeds on the Boneville Salt Flats, you can Visit Mount Rushmoore, the Swamps in the Southern Regions, take a road trip along the Route 66. You get the point.
The Car Handling takes a while to get used to, but once you figured out how to drift around corners it gets much easier because you would have to slow down way too much to drive around corners the regular way.
However here is why I don´t recommend it, and uPlay isn´t any of the reasons, I don´t mind it too much. The game requires you to be online all the time, if the servers goes offline for whatever reason or you loose the connection the game throws you out of whatever you are doing, even if that means that loose your 3 Hour Progress into an almost 4 Hour long race. However there is no real reason that the game has to be connected to a server at any point because you can do everything on your own. Also the game is NOT an MMO in the classical sense, while in Free Drive you randomly drop In and Out off Online Lobbys, players inside a Lobby can Invite others into their Crew and play Story-, Faction- and PVP-Events together. A Crew can have up to 4 Players and all 4 will Drop In and Out off the Sessions together. While it works, it almost feels like a gimmick to me.
I have a feeling that the car Levels and Perks don´t mean anything, at least when there is AI Involved. The game has some of the worst rubberbanding AI I encountered in over 20 Years of playing Racing games, even with cars close to Level 900 you can´t really drive away from the Low Level AI in the earliest Missions th game has to offer. When Playing PvP the Car Levely do Matter, however a goog driver can still beat a car that is 200+ Levels above him when the other driver isn´t that experienced. The whole concept is untransparent, you never get a feeling that all the carparts you collect even do anything.
Also it throws you the Option for Microtransactions in your Face every time you are anywhere where you can buy stuff within the game. You can get everything without ever using them, but I get a strong feeling that you don´t earn money fast enough in the game so they can sell more micro Transactions.

This is one of those games that looks like it has to be either poorly made, or terribly boring. In reality, it's one of the best simulators that I've ever experienced. As you run your restaurant, you're forced to balance pleasing the customers, and pleasing the health inspectors by keeping up with upkeep. All actions are made simple, but not so simple that they can be done without thought. Unlike some games which feature cooking, you're not given simple "Cook" and "Serve" buttons. Instead, you are most often left to assemble dishes with simplified "one key = one ingredient" style combinations (e.g. PSCR PSCR PSCR makes a lasagna [Pasta, Sauce, Cheese, Parmesan]). It's simple in theory, until the lunch rush leaves you hectically trying to push through order after order, all while balancing the need to wash dishes and toss out trash. There's no deep story to the campaign, but somewhat forced menu changes and the always random orders will ensure that days vary heavily and keep you on your toes. Overall, it's well worth the pick up. 8.5/10

this review is special designed for people who like LG 1 and aren't quite sure to buy it.
I played LG1 with much pleasure and was so hyped when they announced LG2. I thought even if LG2 would be the same like LG1, it would be (imo) a great game.
But what they have done is such an amazing polished game. Here my favorites improvements:
1. New Skillsystem which is imo much better than LG1, because you have more freedom and could try some different ways of leveling.
2. The new class: Alchemie. I love this one. To have with him much more herbs aka potions is such a great thing.
3. New monsters, and more than one bossfight (first in the first 2 hours of the game, second will be the final boss...maybe there are even more ^^)
3. No more empty flasks (maybe some others don't like this decision but i like it)
4. Spells, you don't have to take all the scrolls with you or use other sides in the internet. Learn the spell and Tada on the Traits Rooster you can always read them.
5. Overall the new way to cast spells --> really great game design. They beware the feeling of LG1 but this way it is much more like it used to be :)
6. New Tooltips on weapons, special the description which attribute will improve the damage
7. Outdoor, Indoor, Day and Night Cycle --> Overall much more variety in dungeon design (ladders!!)
8. And i don't know why but i have the feeling that the fights (so far 7h in the game) are much more different between two monster arts. I use much more movement or all ways of making damage as in LG1.
9. New Map + and the new signs to make notes --> Great idea. Obverall the map is so much better.
10. Digging. This way there are a new way to find secrets.

The Island of Nex, a worthy successor to the dank Grimrock mountain....
In all fairness, Legend of Grimrock 2 takes the old formula from the original and evolves it in all the right ways. The main difference in the game is that instead of the sequential level design of the first game, LGR 2 has a more horizontal layout that allows more organic exploration then simple sequential levels. This does not confine the secrets (the many, many mind bending secrets) to simply the designated "dungeon" sections of the island either, in addition to simple little caches and puzzles on the island surface, you can find riddles and clues that can lead you to buried treasure chests, which was a great touch and encouraged backtracking (which was not much of a pain, the island has a small hub that links the major wings together). One flaw would be the diving mechanic, some tiles are covered in water and your party cannot stay in them for long without drowning, coupled with the fact there can be underwater enemies and your attack is disabled when underwater, you can get pinned into a corner and be unable to get out, resulting in you needing to load a previous save.
The combat has been polished greatly from the first, rather then gaining perks that would allow for a random chance of a special attack, the weapons themselves have special attacks noted in their discription that can be activated by holding the attack button (at the cost of some energy/mana). All the spells from LGR 1 make their return, as well as some more interesting ones, but I do believe that more spells should have been implimented. However, the requirments to cast the spells have been reduced as a result of a simpler leveling system, so your mage is no longer a "one trick pony".
The leveling system was revamped from the original, all skills now only have 5 levels instead of 50, and you gain one point to spend per level. One thing of note is that your stats now level automatically (but can be enhanced by drinking special potions) depending on your class, which can be a bad thing if you really want full control over your characters' growth, but not everyone does so its more of a neutral point. The skills also have milestone perks and per level upgrades, similar to the original. Overall the leveling system was streamlined rather then completely changed.
One mechanic that was greatly expanded was the alchemy system, which acts as the party's healing. There are more ingredients, more potions and the potion interface is similar to the spell casting interface so it can be used in combat with ease (something the first game needed badly). Your alchemist can also make bombs which act as one time spells with additional effects (freezing the enemy, setting the ground alight, etc). The greatest alchemist can even cheat death, if you find the correct recipe that is.
Overall, there are more items, more enemies, more ground to cover, more dungeons to dive into and more secrets to uncover. I would give the game a 9/10, it would be a perfect 10 if not for the annoying water sections and the lack of very many new spells. A great game, if you liked the first one, get this one, if you never played the first one, consider getting this one, the stories are independent and the second one is a bit stronger gameplay wise.

Simply put, this game is awful to actually play. If that's all you need from a review, you can stop here. If you want to know WHY this game is awful, keep reading.
1. Storyline
The story is pretty uninspired. It's not completely terrible, but it's nothing you haven't seen before. Maybe it gets better, but I couldn't get too far due to numerous frustrations before I dropped the game. The voice acting is at best, average. WIth woodenly delivered lines, and dialogue that could have been written by a chat-bot.
2. Gameplay
This is the main problem. An average to below average plot/voice acting can often be made up for in gameplay. Unfortunately these developers seem to have forgotten how RTS' work.
Problem 1: The perspective and selection of units.
The angle of the game, and the awful awful unit boxes make it very difficult to get all your units, or select individual units, or really do basic things quickly and efficiently. Did you miss on of your units when trying to select it? Well screw you player! Because now you have NOTHING selected. Isn't that great? There are several abilities in the game that you are to use on a singular unit. This is difficult and can cause issues. Anyone who is used to a well made RTS, and want's to micro and control army effectively is in for a bad time. This however, is not the only contributor to that bad time.
Problem 2: The (lack of) pathfinding
You know when you play a game, and sometimes your unit happens to go a weird way around the map to the location you sent it to? Usually doesn't happen that often, and usually isn't a big deal. That's not the case In Meridian: forgotten mechanics. Do you want to move somewhere specific? They will eventually get there. Not together, not in a timely manner, but eventually. Just hope there are no enemies to fight.
What happens when there are enemies? Well I'm glad you asked! See, if you run in to an enemy, while moving around the map, chances are everyone in your dumb as hell army has separated into squads of 1. Thankfully, the enemy AI will just put them out of their misery. Now, it is possible you'll actually have your army together and want to attack. One of the basic moves in an RTS is to Attack move. In almost every RTS ever made, as soon as an enemy is in sight and range, the guns start blazing. In "Meridian: What LSD trip made us think we knew how to make a game", you will find, at almost every occasion, your units running directly at the enemy without firing. Without realizing that they are NOT some sort of kamikaze unit. Without deigning to obey your commands in a remotely satisfactory manner.
Thanks to these amazing mechanics, you often need to retreat to try to herd your dumb struck army in to a semblance of a group so you can actually play the game. In most RTS' retreat is a viable strategy. In "Meridian: Oh my GOD does anyone know how to walk?" this is nigh impossible. Retreating involves attempting to move away from the enemy. In the unlikely event your units actually manage to walk away from the enemy, you will find them immediately attempting to engage the enemy. The worst part is, the terrible pathing and AI means that they will have half trying to get back somewhere, half who are going the other way and get stuck on eachother, and no one actually firing on the enemy OR retreating. The target acquisition range is just absolutely nuts. It doesn't make sense. I've had units react to hostiles WHO WEREN"T VISIBLE YET. You are a train driver, taking passengers and cargo to their destinations. And that is as simple and conventional as this game gets.
Everything else, and there is a fair amount of it, is a tale of otherworldly threat and horror and that is all the detail I can give you without breaking out some spoilers. I can say that you will go through the game finding snippets of information here and there and that, while the game never actually tells you exactly what is happening around you, you will find enough for your own theories.
The game breaks into two separate phases. The train game, where you maintain the train and see to the passengers' needs, and the scavenge game where you loot the wreckage of abandoned towns and stations for the materials you need.
The Scavenging game is good. The videos and screenshots show a side-scrolling shoot-em-up but, in reality, the pace is slow and careful. You cannot see what is inside a room until you open the door and that provides plenty of tension and scares as simple homes can turn out to be full of monsters or empty. You shouldn't expect to just blast your way through with a shotgun, ammunition is always scarce. This game makes you think about each house, shop or bunker tactically and does it in a natural way. You will fall easily into the rhythms of the scavenger.
The Train sections aren't so good, unfortunately. On each stretch of rail travel, there will be some part of the train in need of repair. The repairs cost nothing but take up your time and attention and this is where the game falls a little for me. While you are running up and down fixing brakes or ferrying medpacks to the passengers, the passengers are talking about the world and who the protagonists are, but you only hear them when you are in the same carriage as them. I feel that I have missed some story beats simply because I was having to leave the room to get stuff done.
All in all, I do not regret having this game in my library (got it on a Humble Bundle). I got through the main campaign in about 3.5/4 hours. A solid 8/10 for me, the story is just that intriguing.
_______________________________________________________________________________
The DLC is another 3 hours worth of content and doubles down on what the game does well. You still have the Travel/Scavenge phases, but the Travel has been stripped down to exposition, crafting and character details. No repairs minigames, and that is a good thing.
The Scavenge game has been improved with new monsters types and, since the DLC's plot involves a new character and new journey, you will be seeing more of the world, piecing together more of the backstory. And the backstory is great. It builds on the foundations of Final Station very well.
The DLC takes my rating up to 8.5/10, if that means anything to you :)

I tried to put myself in the mindset of the target audience when I was playing this game, but even when I did, I found that there were a few disruptive problems that make this quite inaccessible.
The main problem, as pointed out by most of the reviews that don't recommend this game, is that you need to pay for membership to get past level 10, something that is often popped up in your face while you play once you hit that level. This wouldn't be a problem if a lot of the content was blocked to those below certain levels, making this a game that can only really be enjoyed in the long-term if you pay for a membership.
The second problem that I found fairly intrusive is the janky jump and collision physics. There's a minigame where you have to collect fruit and avoid some demonic, spiky balls. If you touch these, you are sent back until you hit the next solid object; this means that if you jump while touching this, you are sent rocketing into the sky for a few seconds before hurtling back to the ground. This could be potentially very disorientating for a child playing.
The third problem is one can't aim to collect certain matierals for crafting, since they are all given as random drops when completing missions. This means one can't really aim to make a certain thing to create for their home, which then makes the crafting system quite pointless.
Overall, this is a nice game in terms of aesthetics, but I couldn't recommend it for children as an introduction to gaming or MMOs, or even just for anything in general. I didn't pay, so I don't know all the features, but it seems a little broken as it stands.

From hero to zero in minutes.
The balance in this is superb. Everything suffers cause and effect. Too many sheep creating too much wool that fills the barns that prevents the harvest that causes the people to starve is just one example. SO just build more barns yeah? Then wood becomes scarce and the toolmaker runs out. So no tools are made and you run out and nobody can do anything. Including the toolmaker! Scrambling around grabbing every bit of iron and wood to make tools so you can harvest so the people don't starve. Or freeze to death!
A wicked dev made this and he's a clever one. I've spent a long time looking for those little exploits that circumvents game logic and give me an "I win" button but I can't find one. Even the data that might give you clues to what is going wrong (or right) is cleverly hidden despite appearing to have lots of data at your disposal.  After many hours of losing your perfect cities, again and again, you will understand what I mean here.
Not that it matters. There is an evil monster lurking in the background of every game.
Meet "The Cascade".
It's that horrible nagging doubt in the back of your mind that the map you've just spent hours, even days on,  is doomed. Death for all is inevitable.  You *know* something is not right and you try to overcompensate but you cause supply problems elsewhere and create even more problems.
And your whole town dies. Quickly.
As your cemetary fills up, you madly juggle the myriad of tasks each citizen must undertake until... NO... he/she died too!!  After the cascade crash of most of population, you may be left with enough to regrow but be careful now. You need to make the corrections to prevent it happening again. Can you? Will you?
You won't.  You will reseed another map and start all over again, ever the wiser. "I'll put the farms over there and the fishing huts here and the market here and the mine there and the church here and.... and.... and....."
You'll die anyway. It's unavoidable. It's inevitable.  Unsustainable growth will kill you. Every time.
A lesson for us all perhaps?

First, this game came before battlefield one and is a game that i consider a more accurate representation of war. While equally enjoyable, battlefield one focuses on open world batles that seem far fetched compared to the trench centric battles that actually occuered in WW1. Verdun even goes as far as to simulate the Christmas truce which i think shows more dedication in simulating what it was really like.
Other notable things include
More historically accurate weapons (that lead to a different dynamic of warfare compared to more generic shooters)
more attention to detail: things like barbed wire catch players leaving them vulnerable to being shot along with territory restrictions being cleverly hidden with a deserter mechanic (you are shot if you try and go outside the realm of the map)
Less computer strain: Compared to BF1, your computer is going to have a better time handling/processing verdun than it would BF.
Regardless of comparisons to BF1, Verdun still is overall a game that encapsulates WW1's trech warfare feeling and one which i can fully recommend.

How the mighty have fallen.
Five Nights at Freddy's 1 was incredibly terrifying and quite difficult, but the reason why it was terrifying is that it went to great lengths to build up atmosphere and made it hard for you to know if an animatronic was coming for you until the last minute, and the reason it was difficult is because it would scare you into making frequent mistakes just because you're so nervous. The basic game was actually rather simple, but the framing device made it made it seem hard.
Five Nights at Freddy's 2 seems to have forgotten how to be scary. Where FNAF's animatronics evoked the unintentional creepiness of shoddily-made Chuck E Cheese characters, FNAF 2's new animatronics are shiny and cute and the only thing remotely frightening about them is their malevolence. Meanwhile, the old animatronics have been turned into mangled messes, abandoning the unintentional creepiness for deliberately freakish appearances, but this loses its fear factor very quickly because it just feels like it's trying too hard. What's more, the fact that the Freddy Fazbear head is a trump card against all but two animatronics -- and a trump card you can never ever not have available -- means that the two animatronics you can't use it against are the only ones that really matter, and everyone else is just annoying.
Now, FNAF 2 is certainly very difficult -- that part hasn't been lost. But it's difficult in the wrong way. FNAF 1 was hard because it stressed you out into making mistakes. FNAF 2 is hard because it gives you so many different things to manage and pure luck alone will determine whether or not you can manage them. A charitable interpretation of this might suggest that it's trying to evoke a different kind of horror: the futility of our illusion of control in a world where so little actually is in our control, a world where any one of us could do everything right in life and still get killed by a drunk driver or something out of nowhere tomorrow. But I'm not feeling charitable, I'm just feeling frustrated, and besides that kind of horror doesn't fit well with anything else in the atmosphere of the game, so no, it's just making the game hard for the sake of being hard because it wasn't scary.
Get this game only if you REALLY want to know the story of the series, because the one good thing it does is expand on the lore. Outside of that, it's a pretty bad sequel (or prequel, as the case may be) to the original.

Can't say how I feel about this game. There are two conflicting parts in it for me that really make recommending this game hard for me:
THE GOOD:
The gameplay is probably one of the greatest representation of how a walking simulator should play. There's a huge mansion to walk around to your heart's content and interact with the objects in every room. The mansion feels lived-in and pretty detailed in all aspects. The graphics aren't TOO realistic but so much thought has been put in little details scattered throughout the house that it felt truly unique and rewarding to explore.
Once you start exploring, you'll come across the story of the empty house and slowly but surely work your way up to the reasons why the house is empty when you arrive from your trip. This leads to the only negative aspect of the game.
THE BAD:
I swear I've read better lesbian fan fiction written by my 14-year-old niece than the stuff represented in here. The main character which is the primary focus of the story (who is also the main character's younger sister) is Sam. A punk-rock loving teen rebel who doesn't know the difference between the stains in her panties and the strawberry jam on her toast ....and thinks she's a lesbian because her parents probably didn't give her enough attention and the new highschool she's moved to doesn't regard her as a royal princess.
So she does what most teens do when they feel they're under pressure: going gay (well, to give credit to some of the more creative ones, they could go bisexual).
I don't know if this was a dark cautionary tale written by parents for parents with rebelious teens or by actual horny, shallow teens who want to express the diversity in probably the most woefully controversial and important subjects on the western youth's general mindset: sexuality... because that's the only freedom they feel they have.... I guess? I don't know whether to take the story seriously especially when it turns out to be a faulty, shallow and unexciting romance without a solid basis for a good story.
To be honest, I don't care after Gone Home's ending because I feel exhausted after tagging along with the game which promises mysterious twists and turns and puts me in a very interesting environment for around 3 hours just to keep slapping me left and right with its ovaries and finally unload its full load of estrogen on my face.
On the other hand, if you're into walking simulators or want to experience the interactive bliss which can be achieved through this genre, by all means check Gone Home out. The detailed environments and the general atmosphere was what pulled me towards finishing it.

isn’t a game in the traditional sense; it’s an interactive young adult (YA) novel. The graphics and sound effects are OK, and the voice acting is excellent. For what it is attempting to be, it succeeds more than it fails.
: there are two important things you should consider before buying
.
First: it’s short. Since you can complete it in only a few hours of playing time, if you want to buy it, I’d suggest waiting for the Steam summer or holiday sale.
And second,
has an in-your-face progressive political slant. Think
, except that Margaret is a budding SJW. To say any more would spoil it, but the bottom line is that unless you agree with left-leaning politics (including feminism and gender politics), you probably won’t like this game.
’s progressive politics are why its reviews are so polarized. Left-leaning reviewers—which describes most professional reviewers in the gaming industry—hyped
like it was Half-Life 3, solely because the politics of
neatly aligned with their own prejudices. This created a huge backlash from non-progressive gamers, who felt that
didn’t live up to the hype that had been generated by all of the progressive-leaning reviewers.
Unfortunately, neither viewpoint is accurate.
isn’t Half Life 3. It’s not even revolutionary, really. But neither is it bad at what it is. It’s a cute, short, visual YA novel, written specifically and unapologetically for a niche market (feminists and SJWs). If that describes you, then you will probably enjoy
. If it doesn’t, you probably won’t. Purchase it (or not) accordingly.

I loved Gone Home.  I'm a little surprised by some of the negative reviews.  As long as you have the right expectations going into the game, it is a fantastic experience.  This is a short, interactive story about a family dealing with a number of issues, and the process of discovering exactly what has happened to them.  The narrative is revealed gradually as you explore a vacant house, and the game effectively builds suspense as it plays with your expectations about what you're going to find.  The soundtrack and '90s setting also enhance the experience tremendously.  If you're expecting a lot of action, or in-depth puzzle solving, you're going to be disappointed.  But if you're open to simply participating in a well-crafted, mysterious short story, you may find Gone Home to be as moving as I did.
