RTS, otherwise known as Real Time Strategy has become quite rare in today’s day an age. Oh, there are a number of offshoots, but very few modern day RTS that still hold to the core root of the genre. Sadly while Meridian comes close, it still misses what I personally consider a true RTS.
First the pros:
PRO’s
1.	Interesting set of weapons each with their own unique attributes. While fun, they do become redundant when all are unlocked.
2.	Decent enough graphics. Cut-scenes are adequate with a few neat space shots.
3.	So-so story, and a few unique missions that are out of the norm. Adding some variety.
4.	Audio is well done.
5.	Voice actors actually fit their role and put the appropriate emotion behind their lines.
6.	Turrets and normal structure building expected of a RTS.
7.	Missions where you have a locked group of units explore and fight maps. Requiring a certain level of timing and strategy.
8.	Special orders/powers are always fun, and actually influence the game quite a bit. Especially on certain maps.
CON’s
1.	Units are incredibly limited by the end of the game. Very little variety.  With only 1 species/faction.
2.	Story is so-so by the end, neither impressive nor a failure. Could have used something unique to spice it up.
3.	AI programming can be very annoying. Example, send a unit to fight, but there is not enough room. So the AI sends the units around the entire map if necessary, rather than what most RTS do in pushing units forward so they can all shoot. If there is no route, they pile up waiting for the unit in front to die.
4.	Long excursions, units will chase enemies to their death. Which requires the player’s constant attention in order to avoid pointless losses.
5.	Some incredibly irritating missions, where the game locks you in place and forces certain actions without the options of a true RTS. For example, rather than a normal unit cap that only requires a little cache (or whatever the game wants built), Meridian has map locks where special expensive factories must be placed in unique zones that are not available on every map. Otherwise the unit cap is locked to under 10 – 20 units.
6.	Mission completion usually entails exterminating an enemy’s every structure and unit. This can grow irksome when fighting multiple opponents, and a waste of time at the end. Where all you can do is cleanup of the map.
While the game has a number of irritations, it also has some positive RTS draws. For the price, it is more than worth a purchase. I can only hope the developers will add some interesting content in the future.
I give it 3.2 out of 5 for the overall gameplay, skirmish, and campaign.

Lots of potential buried under poor design decisions. I remember when this first came out way back when, I was really excited for it and then incredibly disappointed by the ending. That feeling more or less holds up now - the first couple of missions are great, with a cool "international peacekeepers" concept that's pretty unique, but then the story very quickly departs from that and becomes a convoluted mess that never makes any sense and ends on a sequel hook cliffhanger with no real explanation of anything that's going on. The game was a bomb and a sequel never got made, so the story ends up feeling like complete nonsense. It feels like the game went through several rewrites and the different plots ended up being sloppily patched together to make missions fit in the end.
Speaking of missions, they become unbearably boring and articifially difficult about halfway through, making the game an overlong slog that's absolutely full of padding. The unit variety makes tic-tac-toe seem deep, with every unit in the game introduced within the first few missions, and the AI spamming forces of roughly 80% anti-aircraft units in the late game in order to render all of your air support completely useless (and thereby upping the difficulty considerably, since not only do you effectively lose air support, but the enemy's AA is also great anti-infantry and decent anti-armor.) This is made even worse by the terrible AI - poor pathfinding is more or less expected in RTS games, but Joint Task Force has painfully bad and often harmful pathfinding, with units running themselves repeatedly into obstacles and getting stuck or directly into the enemy and getting destroyed, even when a shorter, simpler, and safer route is available. Combined with the fact that your units will often refuse to perform automatic reactions like they're supposed to, such as firing on nearby enemies or healing injured allies, and the game just becomes a micromanagement nightmare that's not worth the effort.

Couple of notes for people who are completely new to final fantasy:
1. You don't need to play FF1 - FFIX to understand everything. FFX is it's own standalone title
2. This is an RPG (role playing game). The combat, though extremely deep/ strategic, is turn based with average battle lengths ranging from 30 sec to 10+ min (end game stuff has very long battles).
3. This game is long. Standard main quest at full speed will probably take at least 30-40 hours. So strap yourselves in for a long haul (bring tissues)
4. The story is very linear for the first 10 hours or so. Eventually it will open up allowing you to revisit places.
For People who have never played FFX but have played other FF games:
1. FFX in my opinion is top notch in story and combat. Although the combat is turn based rather than ATB, it rewards slow and strategic action. There aren't notable OP abilities that will make the game ridiculously easy (unless you use cheats).
2. Soundtrack is top notch (as per usual).
3. People have voices in this game (WOW! That's so cool! No more text boxes!)
4. Lots of end game activities to spend another 40 hours on. (Quite a bit of grinding though)
5. FFX-2 is ATB system though a little lackluster story wise (compared to FFX). However the combat is pretty fun.
Notes for people who have played FFX:
1. This copy of FFX is International/ Pal edition. So if you played only the NA verison, then know that this copy of FFX has a lot more end Game Material. Penance and Dark Aeons.
2. This game has cheats!
3. You already know what you're in for. GO BUY IT!
Overall:
This game packs a ton with content and combat depth. Very enjoyable customizable item system as well as the Sphere Grid allowing for even more character customization. Ultimately, the soundtrack and story will draw you in and keep you playing. A must have for the RPG lover.
Final Fantasy 10/10

This is a very fun first person shooter.
When it first came out it got horrible reviews because of game-breaking bugs, but thankfully subsequent patches have fixed those issues.
You play as a resistance fighter battling against the occupation of the USA by a hostile North Korea. Actually the enemy was apparently originally supposed to be China, which would have been a lot more credible, but it was changed to North Korea to avoid controversy (sigh). Overall the storyline was well done however, and the voice actors did a great job.
The gameplay makes you feel like the underdog, which is exactly what a resistance fighter should feel like! You'll quickly learn the value of stealth because there's an essentially limitless amount of bad guys but you have very limited resources to fight them. Actually fighting them can be a net loss when it comes to resources expended (even if you win), so often it's best to just avoid battles entirely. You have to pick and choose your battles, stay under cover and out of sight, and avoid superior enemy forces.
The underdog mentality is further reinforced depending on what kind of zone you're in. Red Zones are essentially free-fire zones with roaming enemy patrols and strongholds that can be captured for the resistance. Giant enemy airships have to be avoided; if they spot you they'll sic a large enemy force upon you. As you crouch and hide in a darkened basement as the huge enemy airship thunders overhead it's pretty much the epitome of feeling like "the underdog." Awesome!
Yellow Zones are the other kind of zone. Here there are no airships but there is a global alarm. You have to blend in with the civilians and hide when the global alarm is raised. Example: If you plant an improvised explosive device in the road and an armored car drives over it and explodes this may trigger an alarm.
The game takes place mostly in the post apocalyptic ruins of the city of Philadelpia. There's a large number of missions, many of which are open ended and can be approached in different ways. There's also a neat weapon customization system. With this system you can modify your guns as the situation develops. For example if you decide you need lots of close range firepower you can change your basic pistol into a submachine gun, but if you decide you need to be stealthy you can change it into a silent pneumatic pistol. Cool!
The graphics are AAA quality. Music is unobtrusive and appropriate; I'm sad they didn't include the soundtrack with the game.
There is also a multiplayer co-operative mode. These are a set of missions separate from the single-player campaign designed specifically for co-op with up to four players. Co-op gameplay is significantly different firstly because you get random loot; so your character's gear loadout will invariably have different strengths compared to what your buddies are sporting. Secondly, there is an RPG-like skill system, in which you earn skill points and have to choose how to invest them -- will you go heavy on stealth, or just ignore stealth entirely and choose brute force combat skills? The choice is up to you, and the randomization of the levels means there is some amount of replayability.
There are some minor bugs still in the game, mostly relating to not being able to complete optional missions involving taking pictures with your character's camera, but I encountered no game-breaking bugs. There are also 3 DLC's which are high quality and help flesh out the single-player campaign. I paid $12 for the game plus all DLCs, and felt that was a good value for the 40+ hours of entertainment I got out of it.
If you like first person shooters you'll like Homefront: The Revolution!

A delightful simple story. Gone Home seems to have been on a fence over the years, because some people love it, while others act as if it is cheap.
I turned out to be one of the people who loved it - and I played this game long after tons of people argued on all sides, so it wasn't like I necessarily went in blind. Despite that, Gone Home held up quite a bit. I can understand that it's not necessarily a "game", as the term "walking simulator" has been used for years now. But at the same time, that doesn't mean that it isn't nice or fun to play.
You are essentially learning a story while reading documents, exploring and finding little objects and pieces, and also listening to journal entries. Very simple, easy to do for the most part. But it was still very enjoyable.
From my perspective, games like this one are just a newer/different way of reading a book or short story. And I like that, so long as things are put together well: Gone Home certainly was. There's not really that much to puzzle you, but it was fine because everything I came across was interesting enough to me. The house is really nice looking and its hidden passageways certainly kept me intrigued, especially with some of the more odd things you find along the way. There are some key points in the family story that are easy to miss if you do not find enough of the items as well, so you definitely have to keep on your toes.
In any case, Gone Home is something that I think some of my personal friends would enjoy to go through, even if it is a short little tale. Some people seem to flat out hate it - and I think a lot of it boils down to people just not liking the style, as they were looking for more game-like material instead of just piecing together a story. People who claim that there isn't a story, however, are... Well, I hate to say it, but it's true - "wrong." You can simply read someone's guide of the chronological log of the documents and things you find to see the story here.
Whether you like the story or not is another question.
For myself, I went in knowing the style of Gone Home and enjoyed it.

A very worthy sequel! I have sunk quite a few hours into it so far, but not completed it, so these are my impressions. I am assuming you are familiar with the original Grimrock's game mechanics.
Shipwrecked and shackled, your four prisoner party washes up in a locked cage on the beach of a mysterious island. After you break free and fight and puzzle your way through the initial enclosed area the game sprawls out before you. Unlike the original game which was linear, you can pretty much go where you want. But tread carefully, as some sections are a lot more difficult than others depending on your skills, equipment and spell knowledge. The world of Grimrock 2 is tightly designed with little wasted space and there is always something close by to be slaughtering, solving or salvaging. There is something about it that is reminiscent of the Zelda games.
The default party has a decent mix of skills, with two melee damage dealers, a wizard, and a ranged firearm user. Yes, Grimrock 2 has boomsticks. Skills are not exclusive to any class now, and can be customized as you see fit. So if you want to add some fire magic to your barbarian Minotaur, you can do that, though clearly their casting efficacy is not going to be up to a pure wizard/battlemage's build, and generalizing your skills could lead to a weak party. There are numerous additions to classes over the last game, including an interesting looking "farmer" class that levels up by eating rather than killing.
Somehow I managed to play through the last Grimrock with the automap disabled, but in Grimrock 2 the area is so much larger and more open that it would be difficult to explore properly without making notes. The automap feature fills in detail as you navigate the world and allows annotation with multiple symbols that can be set as markers for those locked chests, doors and unsolved puzzles you need to return to. It is very easy to pan and zoom around the map.
The atmosphere is spot on whether you are navigating the woodland by day, listening to the birdsong, or moving in the marshes with everything shrouded in a thick green fog, toadstools silhouetted in the distance. I was surprised to see that there is a day night cycle and enjoyed emerging from a dank dungeon into a glorious sanguine dusk. If you find adventuring by night too inconvenient you can sleep through it, though you will burn through your food stocks quicker doing this.
Combat has been refined with enemies needing different tactics to beat effectively. Some will require more thought than just circle strafing and hitting, with them capable of setting counter-attacks if you try this or plain leaping over you and attacking from a different side. Magic casting has been polished with you dragging a gesture over the symbols rather than selecting them individually. This makes casting a little slicker and more fun to use. Melee has been improved with the addition of a power attack. If the weapons skill requirements are met, the power attack can be used and unleashed at the expense of a large hit to your energy pool.
Grimrock 2 is a joy to play. It is fun to explore the game world, solve puzzles, and slaughter monsters, gradually becoming more and more powerful. The game is a clear recommend to anyone that enjoyed the first game in the series and the old dungeon crawler classics. Perhaps the grid-based movement is a little antiquated for some, an acquired taste, but it is a taste you should strive to acquire.

Game has fun concept, the combination of tower defense and tower offense makes for a fun experience. The execution was lacking, though. In-game the mouse becomes very hard to control, accelerating and decelerating much slower than I would like while playing.
The game also lacks strategic depth that was very simple to include. The game includes several different types of units to send out to attack the enemy. Most of these units end up being roughly equivalent though. Tanks vs runners is effectively a choice as to how long you want to wait as they usually end up reaching the end at roughly the same success rate. Swarmers are useless since each swarmer costs the same amount of your unit cap as others. Yes, they bunch up more from the beginning, but other units have this property as well. Any unit that attacks things will also end up bunching up because the units will wait for their attack.This means that swarmers, while cheaper, and a nice place to start have no use later in a match. Having these set roles for what stage of a game to use swarmers or tanks or runners or whatever else causes the game to follow a very set path.
The towers are also very similar. Yes, you have the AoE towers vs the single target towers. Within the single target towers, there are supposed to be towers that are good against soldier types and towers that are good against tank types. In the end, the anti-tank towers also serve as the best option for anti-soldier, leading to a very boring set up being optimal.
Great concept, terribly executed. I would suggest finding other tower defense games to play.

Although this game does require you to attack as well as defend, that isn't enough extra to save it from everything else. The voice acting is a crime against humanity; the tower selection isn't imaginative; the campaign is terribly easy - just spam cheap units as soon as the game starts and away you go. There's a lack of strategy and fun.
Multiplayer isn't much different. It also plays rather poorly on slower connections, despite the minimal amount of data that a tower defense game needs to pass back and forth. What is it doing to choke my friend's pipe? I don't know, but it's unnecessary.
I'd advise against a purchase even if it is deeply discounted and you're a tower defense fan.

The Final Station is a fairly easy 2D survival horror game packed full of atmosphere, moody ambience and music, gorgeous pixel art, questions and not many answers in a world where humanity is on its way out. In a way, by setting, it borrows heavily from post apocalyptic anime, Half Life 2 and 2D survival horror that reminded me somethat of Lone Survivor.
The game itself is divided in two segments: You are a Train Conductor and between stations, your job is to ensure your passengers (surviving stragglers you picked up along the way of your long journey) stay alive by feeding them or bandaging them. You also have to make sure the engine stays funcioning by performing menial minigames on the train's different indicators. Sadly this part of the game sufferes from whack-a-mole gameplay and tis a pity, becasue it would have been better pacing to let you silently contemplate the world and the situation of your pasengers' conversations than be running around patching people up, no time to even read what they say.
The other part of the game is exploration of the towns and places your train stops at. This is the main bulk of the game - bullets are scarce and mobs are plentiful, and soon enough you get into the rythm of dispatching them in the most bullet-economical way. Combat is fast but simple, and most encounters can be solved with a little wit, so there is a puzzle element to the combat in how you approach it, and unfortunately this makes the game somewhat easy.
What hooks you is the setting, watching the world slowly die, picking up notes from houses you explore. Each station offers a new setting - a prison, shopping mall, small towns, an abandoned mansion, and each town is chock-full of notes that give flavor to the games main enigma, which is what the hell has happened, and what the hell is what remains of humnanity doing to survive. The stilted and dodgy translation makes the plot difficult to follow at times but I found that was part of the charm, the mystery that surrounds the game, and even in its final moments, not all questions are answered and much is left to interpretation.
So, BUY, SALE or FORGET? Well, it is also a relatively short game at 5-6h a playthrough. If it had cost me 15 bucks I'd be a little disappointed, but at 6-7 (its current price on the Humble Bundle) its a no-brainer. I'm already eyeing the DLC and eager to dip into more of this beautifully crafed, enigmatic world on its way out.

The Final Station has sat on my wishlist for quite some time, now that I own it I can see that it's not the game I thought it would be, if I looked into it more this game it would never have made it onto the list. Usually a game triumphs in either a good story or good game play, Final Station falls short on both accounts.
The story is very confusing, 5 mins into the game and I already felt that the story was a little off and trying to hard to be something complex without taking the time to explain it to you properly. As I mentioned above how you have no time to read conversations on the train, I think this probably explained the story a lot more, but I don't recall reading even one chat bubble while on the train, I was to focused on keeping everyone alive. All throughout the game I was waiting for the big reveal of what is going on even after the game already ended. If someone asked me what the story about this game was other then shooting "zombies" and riding on trains, I would honestly have no idea what to say.
The game play gets old real fast, to the point where I was just rushing through levels as fast as possible as they presented no challenge and all had the same goal and 5 or less types of enemys (The DLC added more with better variation). I would think most people could finish this game in under 3 deaths, as their are no overly difficult encounters, other then killing yourself with an explosive barrel you are holding while trying to open a door. The collection of money felt really pointless, as you get enough of everything by just playing (maybe only purchase food and gun mods) and you only get the option to use that money twice?? (I forget). Gun mods are also pointless as they only make an easy game even more easy.
The DLC that was very unnecessary... I played about 4 levels and then dropped it, as it had an even more uninteresting story and even more painfully easy repetative game play.
This could have been a great game if it had better story telling and if they added new goals and enemies to keep levels fresh, The Final Station just doesn't live up to its concept. Also gold star for you! If you actually managed to read this ramble of a review.

-Not a huge fan of the new submission system, but it's still better than mashing buttons
All in all 2K16 gets a solid 8/10, possibly going to 9/10 after they clear up some bugs in updates and remove the 30FPS cap on cutscenes

Banished is, to put it simply, excellent.
Careful planning is rewarded, but not a gaurantee of success. You must be able to react well to potential disaster. There is a surprising level of depth here, with settlers getting their own names, and the age of all living objects (and some nonliving) being tracked at all times. Each character has a name and family. They live, and work, and eat, and sleep, and love. They even become sad when their family members die.
The lack of any "action" is just fine. If you want to build a mighty army, play Age of Empires or Total War. If you want to forge a dynastic realm that will stand the test of time (and constant incestual marriages, you Zoroastrian fiend you!), play Crusader Kings II.
But if you want to architect a thriving settler town in the middle of the wilderness despite freezing winters and the occassional disaster, Banished is your game.
The one problem with Banished is that its very easy, after you learn the pitfalls, to set up your village and then just let it go for hours at a time, even on 5x speed. That initial learning period, and the hours spent architecting your mighty village, are well worth the $20.
There is, of course, the option of creating your own goals. This is where people who enjoy Minecraft and CKII will enjoy the game. Some players will decide that there settlers are vegetarian, and will eat no meat. Or they're xenophobic and never conduct trade (that's a tough one!).
Banished has plenty of room for growth, but its already a great game.

Couple of notes for people who are completely new to final fantasy:
1. You don't need to play FF1 - FFIX to understand everything. FFX is it's own standalone title
2. This is an RPG (role playing game). The combat, though extremely deep/ strategic, is turn based with average battle lengths ranging from 30 sec to 10+ min (end game stuff has very long battles).
3. This game is long. Standard main quest at full speed will probably take at least 30-40 hours. So strap yourselves in for a long haul (bring tissues)
4. The story is very linear for the first 10 hours or so. Eventually it will open up allowing you to revisit places.
For People who have never played FFX but have played other FF games:
1. FFX in my opinion is top notch in story and combat. Although the combat is turn based rather than ATB, it rewards slow and strategic action. There aren't notable OP abilities that will make the game ridiculously easy (unless you use cheats).
2. Soundtrack is top notch (as per usual).
3. People have voices in this game (WOW! That's so cool! No more text boxes!)
4. Lots of end game activities to spend another 40 hours on. (Quite a bit of grinding though)
5. FFX-2 is ATB system though a little lackluster story wise (compared to FFX). However the combat is pretty fun.
Notes for people who have played FFX:
1. This copy of FFX is International/ Pal edition. So if you played only the NA verison, then know that this copy of FFX has a lot more end Game Material. Penance and Dark Aeons.
2. This game has cheats!
3. You already know what you're in for. GO BUY IT!
Overall:
This game packs a ton with content and combat depth. Very enjoyable customizable item system as well as the Sphere Grid allowing for even more character customization. Ultimately, the soundtrack and story will draw you in and keep you playing. A must have for the RPG lover.

Banished is one of, if not the most hardcore city builder out there.
You won't thrive in this game, you won't build a massive succesful city with thousands of people, and you won't casually start building as fast as you can and live to tell about it. You will fail hard and start again at least a few times before getting the hang of what you need to do for survival.
Survival is pretty much the word for this game, in that aspect it is arguably more in common with games like Haven & Hearth than SimCity. You have to balance out your workers between gethering food, resorces, tools, clothes, etc. depending on many variables like the weather or map changes. For example, growing crop in a farm may give you tons of valuable food during the spring and summer, but will bite you in the♥♥♥♥♥and grow absolutely nothing during the harsh winters, meaning you will have to replace your farmers to do something useful like chopping firewood to heat your people up.
Most of the game's interaction with the player is through tables and selection manues (which are shown only if you toggle them on), and you can speed up, slow down, or pause the game while adjusting these settings. While it may be tempting to speed up the game to gather stuff faster, it will be every amature's downfall, since the adjustments to the situation must be constant and require the player's attention at all times.
Honestly, despite all that the game is surprisingly relaxing (when you are not worrying your people will die of starvation). The toned down ambiant music is calm and soothing and the visuals are bright and vibrant. The game manages to be both relaxing and engaging at the same time, while making you truely appreciate your workers and your town after all they have been through.
Banished is not easy, But with it's challange it is greatly rewarding. So prepare to start a game, get hooked, lose your town to the forces of nature, and start again better than ever.

Well, a huge amount of time has passed since I tried Dark Souls 2 for the first time, but I want to review this game because I'm playing again in these days.
Y'all know what Dark Souls is, so I will not spend any time to say obvious things about this game and I'll try to do a comparison between DS and DS2.
You know this is a Souls, you know this is hard. Isn't it?
Well...to be honest this probably is not entirely true: I found DS2 to be the easiest Dark Souls I have ever played. There are only 3 good boss fights, while all the other are trivial. Few traps. Few danger.
What about the level design?
In the first chapter all the areas were logically connected and there were a nice amount of shortcuts to bring you faster to the main hub. In Dark Souls 2 you have a teleport function that let you jump from bonefire to bonefire. This is wonderful, right? Wrong! Thanks to this now all the areas are randomly connected thanks to corridors/elevator, with no shortcuts and without that feeling of cohesion.
And all those wonderful characters?
All gone. Only 3 characters are really well made, with a nice storyline and a nice quest (Pate for Quest and story, Lucatiel for story...well, can't find a third character right now ^^").
Most of Souls player says that this Dark Souls is the worst for this problems and other more, but I must disagree with them. This game has good things too, like a better gameplay. There are plenty of weapons, when on the first chapter only 2 weapons were actually useful. Your character's response from your input is really nice, with no random rolling or getting stuck on an invisible wall while rolling.
For this reason I do recommend this game. In my opinion those downsides are little things you have to bear to have a smoother gameplay.

I’ve tried. Seriously. I tried when it was released and I tried after the 1.0 release. I really wanted to like this game and give it a bright review, but I couldn’t.
Let’s start with the obvious one. The whole marketing campaign was built upon the (false) fact that the game was done by one people. It gained some attention around the early access release solely because of that fact. When the only good thing that you can quote (or you think worth quoting) from a major member of the game press is, “One Guy Shouldn’t Be Able To Make Meridian: New World”. There is something clearly wrong with your game or your marketing people. Sadly, it turns out it’s the game itself.
Sound. For me it was an instant no, I had to turn it off from the menu as soon as I heard a few seconds from it. Highly generic electronic music without a soul. The same thing about the soundtrack (I own the contributor edition), nothing unique there. The sound design itself is bad. All the voices feel mechanical, artificial. I don’t know if it’s because of the voice actors (there are some “celebrities” on the cast, so probably not) or due to some unexperienced sound engineer. Honestly, I don’t care, the result is simply awful. The same is true about the actual in-game sounds, they are like something from a bad sci-fi movie from the 80s. Or something that a cat would produce if put it in front of a midi keyboard.
Graphics. The game falls short there to. I don’t expect the same quality visuals as from AAA RTS games like wargame or starcraft 2, but I was expecting at least a minimal amount of good taste from the designer. No, it doesn’t exists. Some effects are overused, no consistent style across the board and the GUI looks like if it’s done by somebody who discovered a few cool tutorials for photoshop. (quick fact, the same problem is there with all the games from the developer, all the UIs are a joke)
Gameplay. I could have lived with the other two being bad or amateurish, but not this one. The few missions I’ve played are just simply boring. No tactics involved whatsoever, the whole base / army management is clunky and badly done. No zoom functionality (erm, 2014, guys!) and all the game mechanics clearly shows that the developer has almost no experience with modern (and actually good) RTS games.
Writing. The story feels simple, the cut scenes doesn’t support the whole flow of the game, and completely useless (why then?). Dialogues feel forced and unnatural (the bad voice acting makes it even worse), and the game tries to be too much like other games, providing unnecessary story sections, where you can wander around the ship, but it only makes all your choices and answers feel completely weightless. The best example is the first mission. You wander around on the planet for like 2 minutes, then immediately you are switched back to the ship’s view and now you are talking with your crew. The “flow” is too erratic and not enjoyable.
Multiplayer. There is no multiplayer. It’s 2014, guys.
So, shortly. Don’t buy this game. For it’s normal price you can get entries from way better strategy games (wargame series!). If you have a few bucks to burn, and you want to support an indie dev, then it’s up to you. But as a game product, it falls short badly.
If you don’t believe me, just look at the reviews. When the game was released, it had a very positive standing (early access gamers tend to be way softer when it comes to reviews), but as soon as it reached a wider (and more critical) audience it went down to mixed.

Verdun really is a great game. I haven't put as many hours into it as some of the old pros, but I think I put enough into it to have an opinion on it. It's one of the very VERY few world war 1 shooters and yknow, it's probably the only one to actually capture the feel of the war. Long distance, in the trenches,  fearful to poke your head out to shoot because the enemy has just as much of a chance to kill you. One shot is usually an instant kill too. All the weapons, while similar, have a distinct feel and accurately portray the weapons of the time. Each gun has its own reloading animation and way it shoots, and manage to feel all quite different despite being 90% bolt action rifles.
The animations are okay for firing and reloading, but some might seem a little janky if you're picky. The sound design, while very good for the 'corpses' and the gunfire, leaves something to be desired in other aspects. Worldspace, atmosphere, etc. The game can feel unfair at times because some ♥♥♥♥♥♥s like to hole up in an area on your spawn with a mounted MG, and some guns are OP (♥♥♥♥ everyone who uses the RSC), however, these things can be relatively easily overlooked. Like I said, it's mostly skill and I don't care how OP your machine gun is, one well placed shot can kill anyone and drive the enemy team out of a foothold.
You'll often find yourself firing at pinpricks in the distance smaller than the iron sight itself hoping it's an enemy. Just as much, you're hoping that the muzzle flash and noise of the shot doesn't give away your own position. It's brutal, but it's fair and honestly probably my favorite shooter. If you want a break from the run and gun Call of Duty ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t and want a realistic, enjoyable, skill based shooter, this is it.
The developers of this game obviously care about the history involved as well, the guns being quite accurate to real life and the maps all taking place in historic battle sites. I hope this developer does more like this in the future (pls do a black powder era shooter similar to this).

You will need:
Yeast - 2 Tbsp
Hot-ish* water - 2 cups
Bread flour - 5 cups total, 2 for the sponge and 3 for later. (NOT regular flour)
Sugar - 2 Tbsp.
Salt - 2 tsp.
Oil - 2 Tbsp.
3 loaf pans
Quick-read thermometer
Oven pre-heated to 375
*Hot-ish means between 95 and 115 degrees F.
This recipe uses what I call a "sponge." The sponge will activate the yeast and get things started; getting the yeast warm, happy, and ready to go
Start by mixing the hot water and the flour. Then, add 2 Tbsp. sugar, 2 Tbsp. oil, 2 Tbsp. yeast, and 2 tsp. salt.
Knead by hand.
Let this sit for about 8 or 10 minutes. Assuming your water was hot enough, it should be nice and bubbly.
Now you need to add about 3 more cups of flour. I added a little less this time, it really depends on the humidity and how exact your measurements were in the sponge step.
Once it gets too tough to stir, flip it onto a clean floured surface. Now, knead away, adding flour as you do so.
Knead the dough for 8 or 9 minutes. As my Mother says, it should be the texture of your earlobe when it's done kneading.
When you finish this part put it back in the bowl and cover it with a slightly damp towel.
let the dough rise in a warm place for about 45 minutes to an hour. the dough should be about doubled in size by the time it's finished.

The Crew is an amazing achievement of a game. Especially by Ubisoft, which I keep forgetting they made the game. It's an open world (literally, the entire United States at your disposal) racing game with an arcade-like control scheme and a wide selection of vehicles. There are thousands of missions, side quests, mini games, and PVP lobbies to enjoy and they really do pull you into this vast open world game. I have driven across the United States many times in real life and they really capture alot of the beauty our country has. It's not "exactly" a representation of this country but its got its landmarks and alot of things I reconigize (like the oil fields and empty backroads in Amarillo texas and the swamps through the south in Louisana and alot of the beautiful wooded areas and mountains of Maine). This game is very addicting and I have over 17 hours of gameplay. It's hard sometimes and its mostly those hairpin turns and the traffic that♥♥♥♥♥♥me off the most. I keep on having to retry alot of the challenges because I'm shooting for that gold medal. The way it grades you during the main missions I don't like very much because in the end, if you win and you're in 1st place, you should automatically get a gold medal. I don't know how it grades you but I keep getting bronze and silver medals even if I win 1st place in the main missions. There are also hour long missions that take forever, so I reccommend that if you're not playing with friends, play those missions in solo so you can pause the game and take a break after holding down the R-trigger for a half hour or more. When it says "1 Hour" in length, it really means it too. I still have a long ways to go, I'm level 35 and I own a handful of cars (I bought out all the Mustangs since they are my favorite cars and I think I got an F150 too) but I wish there was a way to sell or trade vehicles between players because each car is unique when you start unlocking parts for them and there is a wide selection of parts and add-ons so there will never be an exactly identical vehicle for as long as this game survives. I wish more people would buy this game or at least get it when it's on sale. It is worth the $60 and the fact that its an online open world racing game without a monthly fee just makes it all the better. I hope they come out with alot of DLC for this and maybe expand the map across North and South America and maybe even make a sequel that will take us across the world to other countries too. I highly reccommend this game to anybody who loves racing games (I usually suck at them but after playing this game this long I've gotten used to the genre alot more and I've even improved my skills in games like GRID 2 and NFS Rivals).

To make it short:
"But why?" I hear many of you cry.
I own F1 2010 and 2013, and have played every demo for the games that I didn't have.
So, why do I love this game so much?
- The handling of the cars just feels

I have never had so much fun experiencing such high performance realistic driving models. I don't know. I never drove a F1 car myself, but if I could, I would imagine it behave exactly like this game suggests.
- The presentation is really, really good! Apart from the overall superior graphical quality, you feel like really being a participant in one of the best sports there is.
- What I personally find most interesting about F1, is the tactics. And maaaan, this game is nailing it. You are able to accurately adapt your tactics to your driving style and your engineer even suggests possible changes of tactics, reacting to current race events (such as change in weather, safety car, or other cars with unexpected speeds are observed - do you want the same tires?). This is very useful and expands your F1 gaming expierience by a lot. You even have the chance to test your personal tyre usage on the track, adapting the race tactics to you personally, which is nice.
Another great thing about F1 2016 is that you see how much dedication the devs put into this piece of software and how much of badasses and racing game developer extraordinaires work at this studio. There is so much love to detail!
Of course there are bugs.
But you know what? Almost weekly updates do a great job fixing them. I once encountered a sound bug. 7 hours later it was fixed.
The only real thing which disturbs my experience is some kind of unbalanced AI. You know, at track A I have absolutely no problem winning, whilst on track B, I hardly manage to make it into top 10. But that's nothing that cannot be tweaked over time. Maybe I'm just a noob who likes certain tracks more than others and my own performance is varying so much.
But I will keep this review updated as soon as something changes.
Cheers!

Overall, a decent game. Story isn't half bad, the map is HUGE (some races literally take well over an hour to complete, and you don't even see 25% of the map in those races), and there are a few really cool cars. The level of detail in this game is incredible. I'm not a fan of the butchered geography of the United States, but they (for the most part) captured the feel of all the different areas of the country. It really does feel like I am driving across the prarie of my home in Wyoming, the east coast really looks like the east coast, and New Mexico looks like New Mexico. I am impressed. I'm a racing game junkie and I love this game. The multiplayer is phenominal and I love the incorporation of MMO style to the game. I would have to say this is probably the best racing game since the first Need for Speed: Most Wanted came out on the original XBOX. The challenges that are spread out throughout the game definately keep things interesting and alleviate some of the hum-drum-ness that accompanies the long drives in this game.
However...
There are a few bad things to this game. Some of this is nit-picking, but I feel like the main points are valid complaints.
1. The AI cars are nearly impossible to beat. They accelerate harder, go faster, and recover from crashes way faster than you ever could. If you want to take first in almost any long distance event, you had better make sure your car is well over 100 levels higher than the game recommends or you won't have a chance in H-E-double hockey sticks to ever hold first long enough to come in first. Same thing applies to the police and hitmen trying to run you off the road. They are stupidly fast and hard to dodge.
2. The scoring system. The game makes it nearly impossible to take a gold medal in an event. You need to hold first place for over 90% of the race, not hit like anything and come in first to take the gold. This is an extremely hard scale to beat, especially when you factor in the god-like AI cars (that can be well over 100 levels below you and still accelerate harder and have a top speed of literally one or two mph faster than your car) and the questonable physics engine (more on that next paragraph) The missions where you ditch the AI cars are also difficult to take gold in becuase you simultaneously have to do incredible amounts of damage to the cops and evade them quickly. If the mission goes over like two minutes you won't get gold, no matter how much damage you did to the cops. And its really hard to get away from them and damage them because hitting them seems to make them mad and harder to get away from. It just really seems like the scoring system is heavily stacked against you.
3. The physics for this game. Especially when it comes to off-road vehicles. I don't know of anyone who would want to drive well over 130 mph off road. Going this fast lends itself to some incredibly difficult handling off road. The game was very well designed, map wise, but the off road vehicles were not. They are too bouncy and hard to control. Going up hills is a challenge when all the car wants to do is spin around and go downhill. If you hit one slight bump wrong while going 120+ (and you will, believe me you will) you will 90% of the time lose control of the car. It takes very, very fast fingers to keep your car from hitting anything and crashing. Driving in first person (which is the only way I can drive without hitting everything [the car angle throws off my perception of how hard I'm turning]) is nearly impossible off road due to all the time your car spends with its nose way in the air from hitting something. I feel like having the game go a more realistic speed off road AND not just floor it when you try to give it gas would do wonders for the off-road specs. They did a really good job imitating the slipperiness of dirt (I grew up driving on dirt), so it should stand to reason that they should have an option, at least for when you are not racing, to accelerate like a real person would. Heck, that would be great through the whole game. Stopping and turning around is a lot harder when all your car wants to do is peel out.
Fortunately, there are not a whole lot of Raid spec missions, and you don't spend a lot of time off-road. Looking past these few flaws, I love the game. It's a refreshing take on the racing genre and I can see myself easily pouring over a hundred hours into this game.

Set in the world made famous by Majesty, in Ardania, you are the king. Some arrogant noble causes trouble by sending militia to attack you, so you slash back by building towers to defend your castle and sending various troops to counter-attack. Campaign takes you through Ardania to find the culprit of the attacks on your cities. Sounds cool enough, but unfortunately, you probably shouldn't get too excited.
Defenders of Ardania is a mix between Tower Defense (TD) and Reverse TD. You can protect yourself by building towers, but ultimately, you win by destroying the enemy castle(s) by sending out troops. Troops are quite strong: a single tower can hardly destroy a wave of enemies, so you either need to build more towers in clever spots or, which is usually easier against AI, destroy the enemy castle quickly.
There are about 5 different types of units and towers, none too different from other games of the genre. Some units can attack other units (rather weakly) and others can attack enemy towers. There's some strategy involved in placing the towers, as you are limited in the number of towers depending on the level. You may also direct your troops using a waypoint (yep, a single one) or place bounties (akin to Majesty but costs nothing) to focus fire on certain enemy. What is interesting is that your troops gain experience: using certain type of troops makes them stronger.
Later on, this feels indifferent though: it was always easiest just to either (following is a couple of killer strategies for campaign)
This worked in almost every map: While AI can build towers to counter your troops, it's not up to these kinds of attacks.
Also, while there are three races, you can only play humans in the campaign, the rest restricted for AI and multiplayer (which I've yet to try: servers are empty though). Every race has its own towers, troops and spells, which is cool, but with mere single campaign, the game feels unfinished: there really should be a campaign for each race.
Story is quirky and and full of nerdy jokes, puns and references, so at least it does not take itself too seriously. You do have to endure some quite bad voice acting along the way (I'm looking at you, Kilia the Elf!). Playing it through lasts about 5-10 hours, probably less if you can come up with winning strategies faster. I guess it might be worth it for the amusing ending. :P
While not entirely bad, there are many better TDs out there: this one fails to fill its niche in the reverse TD. So if you just kind of like TD genre, stay away. If TD is your hot chocolate, by all means do get this one but do yourself a favour and do so when it's on sale or bundled.

Personally I enjoyed this game a lot. It's comparable to games like Lone Survivor, Uncanny Valley, and Claire, and if you enjoy any of those types of games you'll love this.
However, I should probably state that there are some pros and cons for those who don't know what I'm talking about.
- A great soundtrack. It's atmospheric but easily something I can listen to outside the game as well.
- The story is a wild ride. There's a lot to unpack in the story, but unlike something like Claire it isn't clear what's going on as soon as the game opens. I especially love the world the developers created.
- The art direction is solid. The pixel graphics look nice, and while I think the sprites on the characters could be a bit less generic they do all look different and are easy to read. Until the DLC I didn't find myself ever mistaking one enemy type for another. I especially adored the backgrounds when moving between stations.
- There really isn't much gameplay in this. You've got two different games packed in one here; In one you're managing your train as you go from one station to another, and the other game follows you running through increasingly defunct shooting galleries with story notes all throughout.
- The game's short. To me, $10 = 1 hour of play and with the DLC I've spent $20 on this. With 7.5 hours spent on the game it's more than enough for me, but do others that may be too little. The DLC is fairly long too, as it took me 2.3 hours.
- The story that is there isn't easy to parse. Games like this love to tell their stories in bits and pieces, allowing you to fill in the holes. Combine that with the bleak atmosphere brought on by the story, and it may turn some people off. This isn't a story that will provide with many answers or happy feelings. The DLC does end up complicating some things as well, but does provide a lot of much needed detail on certain characters.
Overall, if you haven't play these types of "basically a point-and-click but also not" types of games this one is a great way to start.

When I first heard this game’s title I immediately thought of Majesty 2, a medieval sim game that takes place in the land of Ardania. Though Defenders of Ardania is related to the Majesty franchise it surprisingly shirks its predecessor’s medieval sim genes and instead fits firmly in the tower defense genre.
Tower defense games have been around for quite a while and every year there are tons of them released as indie titles and mods. I was curious as to how developer Paradox Interactive would tackle this particular sub-genre of real-time strategy.
Like many such games, Defenders of Ardania has you slugging it out with an AI or human opponent to try to wipe out each other’s base. You set up towers to defend your building against enemy troops while simultaneously sending out your own armies to destroy the opposition.
Following in the vein of Majesty 2, Defenders of Ardania is filled with bright colors and has a nice style to it. But sadly the graphics aren’t that polished and the game seems to use the same engine as Majesty 2.
In addition to borrowing graphics, Defenders’ music also uses the same themes as that of its strategy-game counterpart, which was filled with sweeping orchestral pieces. The voice acting, however, is rather horrendous. Aside from your stalwart Advisor the characters, such as Kilia the Elf, will grate on your nerves. The character sounds like an old woman who talks rather slowly. In fact, if I couldn’t skip the dialogue at the beginning of each campaign I probably would have stopped playing.

Banished is one of, if not the most hardcore city builder out there.
You won't thrive in this game, you won't build a massive succesful city with thousands of people, and you won't casually start building as fast as you can and live to tell about it. You will fail hard and start again at least a few times before getting the hang of what you need to do for survival.
Survival is pretty much the word for this game, in that aspect it is arguably more in common with games like Haven & Hearth than SimCity. You have to balance out your workers between gethering food, resorces, tools, clothes, etc. depending on many variables like the weather or map changes. For example, growing crop in a farm may give you tons of valuable food during the spring and summer, but will bite you in the♥♥♥♥♥and grow absolutely nothing during the harsh winters, meaning you will have to replace your farmers to do something useful like chopping firewood to heat your people up.
Most of the game's interaction with the player is through tables and selection manues (which are shown only if you toggle them on), and you can speed up, slow down, or pause the game while adjusting these settings. While it may be tempting to speed up the game to gather stuff faster, it will be every amature's downfall, since the adjustments to the situation must be constant and require the player's attention at all times.
Honestly, despite all that the game is surprisingly relaxing (when you are not worrying your people will die of starvation). The toned down ambiant music is calm and soothing and the visuals are bright and vibrant. The game manages to be both relaxing and engaging at the same time, while making you truely appreciate your workers and your town after all they have been through.
Banished is not easy, But with it's challange it is greatly rewarding. So prepare to start a game, get hooked, lose your town to the forces of nature, and start again better than ever.

It's a rare treat to find a city building game that isn't focused on fighting, soldiers, wars or monsters, and espceially not one that manages to engage you so well. In Banishedl, your enemy is Nature itself, along with the cruel reality of trying to survive in this harsh, unforgiving world. The learning curve will absolutely take time and likely see your people and towns die off as you fgure the game out, but at the same time it's brilliant at displaying information in a manner that is concise, relevant, and easy to consume.  There aren't a thousand menus and as many things to build, which to some may appear too simplistic and dumbed-downed; however, I believe these are positives that make the game easy to approach, but very difficult to master.
There are several ways to build your town in order to fulfill your people's needs, and the game allows your to assign specialized jobs to help keep your people focused on the tasks you ned done most. Overall, this is a wonderful game that will punish you for being greedy, for trying to expand too far and too quickly, and sometimes despite all your hard work and cautious preparations, Nature comes and burns down your homes or blows away all that remains like the Big Bad Wolf.
I can see myself enjoying a great deal more time with this game, and hope to bring my people a flourishing society!

Tidus is the only positive person in spira, everyone else is resigned to an inevitable death at sin's hands. Sin, who is basically an unstoppable kaiju, serves as our main antagonist throughout, Sin is death, and more importantly, he's treated as a sort of "Ultimate force of judgment" nothing can stop him, and while nobody tells you from the onset, the whole game is secretly one long deathmarch to an ending that isn't meant to be happy.
this, in my opinion, is exactly what makes tidus so special, he's the sole ray of hope in a world that lives on rules based heavily in shafting people. from khimari, who lost his horn, to lulu, who lost her boyfriend to wakka, who can't win a single game of blitzball and whose team hasn't won a damned thing for ten years, to rikku, whose entire race is hated, reviled, and basically outcasts. this game has some very dark themes lurking just beneath the surface, and may be the most depressing final fantasy title in existence. even tidus isn't immune to "your day is going to be ruined" syndrome, though he weathers it better than most.
basically, this is a game that focuses on valuing life with the constant and certain presence of death, spira's metaphor is quite fitting.
gameplay is tight, the sphere grid is...wierd, but that's fine I guess.
Basically if you just want to experience one of the bleakest worlds in final fantasy history and one of the more uplifting stories about changing one's fate, this is the game for you.

Meridian: New World is a Real Time Strategy single player game.  The
music is very well done, and adds to the highs and lows of the combat and
story.  The graphics and the story combine beautifully to create a visual work
of art.
One issue I have noted in this game is in the user interface.
The map is nicely done, and I had no issue with the moving or management of
troops, but there are small problems like having to click on the scene to
move individual troops.   There is a level of micromanagement that has been
integrated into the system that makes the action of moving troops more
complicated than it needs to be, which becomes more and more of an issue as you
progress through higher levels of difficulty.
The level design is done quite well.  The missions provide small
variations with specific goals that breaks up any feeling of repetitive combat.
What hurts this game is the lack of a proper tutorial;  you are just thrown
into the action without proper knowledge of the interface.  As the levels get
larger, and you have a larger army, you need to have tight control of your troops
and a workable strategy with how you  progress.  The AI in this game is very
poor, where sometimes a troop that you tell to hold position will decided to
attack anyways, making any advanced strategy near impossible as you have to
babysit your troops to make sure they don't go off on their own.  It is
extremely frustrating.
The game suffers from many minor annoyances;  I go into more detail in
my video, but small things like not being able to bind to infantry barracks to
one key, or not being able to build buildings if there is a troop in the way,
and the continuous swarming of the enemy that doesn't seem to have a unit cap
while you are limited by resources all add up to a not fun experience.  The cost
of troops to the amount of resources available in the game is unbalanced.
Overall, I can't recommend this game due to the combination of so
many small annoyances that all add up to a frustrating experience.  The game
doesn't respect you or your time, and isn't worth your money.

I'm a huge sucker for restaurant time management games such as Diner/Cooking Dash, Papa's Gameria series, etc. Out of any restaurant time management games I've played, this one is the most unique.
It's highly customizable where you get to pick up to 6 different menu items each with varying difficulty and drawbacks. They can be as stupidly easy as slapping on some condiments and calling it a day, and others are very meticulous as to what order its ingredients need to be in.
Needless to say, this game gets super complicated super fast. It's very fast-paced and it gets really hectic later in the game. It makes the game challenging and that's what makes it super fun. Don't think the main game is hard enough? Finish the main game to unlock the New Game+ that is way harder.
There are new challenges every week that are ranked against other players, and you can refine your abilities even more with the new Battle Kitchen mode. There's lots to do with this game and it keeps pulling out new features that'll make you want to come back.
I highly, HIGHLY recommend this game if you like time management or cooking games. You won't get a game like this anywhere else.

Defenders of Ardania is Paradox's new take on the Tower Defense genre. Although set in the same universe as the majesty games you probably won't notice as the majority of the lore, units and locations is of much the same generic fantasy staple as 99% of the rest out there.
Defenders of Ardania takes on the genre in a way we mostly see from PvP focused Tower Defense games by letting you not only manage the defense of your own keep through Tower placement and ability use but instead of making victory based on the simple passage of time you have to send units yourself towards the enemy keep and past his towers to secure victory. This a great mechanic for multi-player but unfortunately it hamstrings the AI in the single-player campaign quite badly as it simply does not build fast enough or responds fast enough making most of the maps a breeze to win by simply rushing fast units with little concern for your own defenses.
A rather weird income system that never lets you run out of money for more than a few seconds at a time and hard limits on both towers and units only compounds this problem, making the first 5 minutes of any map the only minutes that really matter and any game that progresses beyond that because a rather dull slugfest where you sit around with an impenetrable defense, spamming the same units over and over waiting for their experience to go up enough so that you can unlock a more powerful hero version.
Defenders of Ardania is not a very inspired game, the gameplay mechanics do not lend themselves to single-player very well and although some entertainment can be found in the game's multi-player component the lack of anyone actually playing it online means this is only viable if you do it with friends. There are many better Tower Defense games out there, Sol Survivor even has a multi-player mode with pretty much the same mechanics as this, only not quite as broken.

This was my first game I owned on Steam. I'm happy to say that this game is well deserving of that statistic. It's unique gameplay and amazing soundtrack make this one of my favorite indie platformers ever.
You assume the role of Captain Viridian, the cyan-colored protagonist whose spaceship has become trapped in an alternative dimension thanks to dimensional interference. Viridian must now explore the dimension to find his five lost crew members and the cause of the interference.
This is a platformer that feels unique. The biggest difference between this game and other platformers is that instead of jumping, you invert gravity, causing Viridian to flip between upside-down and right-side-up. You'll have to flip gravity and walk across both floors and ceilings to make your way through the game. It's an open-world game. It can be a bit difficult to navigate your way around even if you're using the map to help you, but this never felt like too much of a problem. There's also 20 trinkets to collect for those that want more out of the game.
If you're a fan of 2D platformers, this game is definitely worth checking out. The soundtrack is amazing. and the gameplay is even better. You'll find yourself raging at some parts, but overall it makes for a fun indie game. It's biggest negative would be that it's rather short. It only took me about four to five hours to complete the story. The story wasn't anything special, but it was sufficient. The gameplay and soundtrack is what gives this game it's charm and makes it well worth the $5 that it costs.

Not so much a game as a proof of concept. Generally, gun handling is something that's completely hidden from a player - boiled down to a "hit R to reload". That's great for a lot of reasons, but this demo explores what could happen if you actually made players "handle" their weapon - slotting bullets to magazines, managing magazine locations, loading/unloading into the gun, making the sure the safety is off,the firemode is correct, the slide is forward, and a round is chambered. Even better, shot placement on an enemy has different effects - you can disarm, blind, kill, or immobilize enemies depending on your shot placement.
But let's be clear, it's not much of a game. Sure it has an objective and endgame, but it's uninteresting to play for more than a couple hours. Too often you're placed in a map that has dead ends, or you're given an impossible situation where you can't progress without getting by 4-5 enemies that are all covering each other.
I'm recommending it because I think it's a good thing for people to play. It shows a cool concept in action, and how fun handling the weapon (moreso than just "hold R to reload"), and hitting an enemy for more effect than just "kill" can be.

The Final Station, and its DLC The Only Traitor is developed by do my best and published by tiny Build games, and is best described as a post-apocalypse, 2-d side scroll, pixelated dungeon-shooter game. The plot varies from base to expansion, but generally follows the idea that you are a survivor looking to find refuge in a monster/zombie plagued world. Gameplay holds 30 different levels in the base game and about half as many levels in the DLC, leaving playtime around 4-7 hours to finish both storylines.
Gameplay- You start off without a tutorial or really any idea of what you are going to be doing, so it is best to look at the controls in the start menu. The controls are the keyboard and mouse, and you can play using a controller if you wish with the only qualm being you can’t aim that well. When it comes to aiming you have to be careful not to shoot wildly because it is easy to miss headshots and consume ammo. Enemies are a bit fast to approach especially in quantity so the best strategy is to be walking backwards from danger or escaping onto ladders. At first ammo seems a bit sparse but eventually you do start to horde it. In the DLC the melee attack is improved and could solely be used rather than a gun. Both games have a mix of enemies that require a little bit of strategy or blind courage (depending on personal choice) but they never seem to reach a hard difficulty level or become too much to handle. Regardless if you do happen to die, you aren’t sent back to far back usually and can make better choices given that you are aware of what lies ahead. Perhaps in total the gameplay is not quite as hoped to be with the repeated motion of looking for a code and looking for food, though the DLC does feel more open world and more choice based. The base game does start to lose its excitement the further you go in and keeping a set path and set enemy count. It could be improved if the enemies were randomly generated along with randomly generated loot.

If you enjoy speedrunning, or if you like the idea of speedrunning but have always been too intimidated to try it, then this is the game for you.
In 10 Secong Ninja X you're tasked with killing all the enemies in the level in as few seconds as possible. This requires not just good reflexes but good planning ahead skills, since most of the time you have to find the optimal path and enemy killing sequence to get a good score. At times this even reminded me of puzzle games, since as the levels get harder you really have to incorprorate the environment/pull switches/kill enemies in a specific way/etc to win. And of course there's always the challenge (and ultimate satisfaction when you get it done) of doing the EXACT right thing at the EXACT right time and 3-star perfecting a level. It's really quite the rush!
Despite the difficulty I think this game is very welcoming to casual players (like me!) mainly for two reasons: First, you definitely don't need to get all 3 stars in a level to progress. While you do need a certain amount of stars to unlock the next world, it's a very reasonable amount that feels fair, and it's even easier to achieve the more levels you have available. Second and most important, by playing a minigame you get a number of tokens which you can the use to get hints for the levels. This shows you optimal path I mentioned earlier and in a way shows you the answer to the "puzzle" of each level. I personally found the hints extremely helpful, and it really cut down on any frustration I might have felt otherwise. (Be warned though that the minigame gets increasingly more difficult with time, so don't waste your tokens!)
As expected of a game like this, both the controls and the animation of the playable character are very
smooth and crisp. You'll always feel like your little ninja is doing exactly what you wanted him to do, and any mistakes come from you not pushing a button at the right time. The graphics, while simplistic, are very colourful and pleasing to the eye. The game even has a cute little storyline that is surprisingly funny!
And as for the playtime, obviously a game where levels are done in a few seconds is not going to last many hours. However, 10 Second Ninja X still feels like it's brimming with content. There are six worlds with ten levels each, and later you can unlock yet another four worlds with legacy levels, plus a few bonus levels. And that's not even taking into account the marathon mode and of course collecting every single star. According to Steam I've only played this for 3 hours, but it certainly felt longer, and even though I'm done with the story mode I'm definitely planning on going back and winning a whole bunch of stars.
All in all, a very enjoyable and challenging game that's worth the money. Recommended!

I didn't play that much of Meridian, and with good reason.
The game is a smaller, uglier, less polished version of Starcraft, only instead of fighting interesting alien races and monsters in chilly, dark settings, you're fighting space marines and mechs in some of the most uninspired-looking arenas I've ever seen in a modern strategy game.
As an RTS, Meridian ticks all of the boxes, but that's it. It struggles to reach the heights of better RTS games, such as Red Alert 3, Starcraft 2, Dawn of War, or just about any major 3D RTS game that has hit the market over the last ten years. The game has no aspirations, no distinctive qualities.
The variety in units and buildings is♥♥♥♥♥♥poor, and the skirmish match customisation options are just laughable, failing to even match up with RTS games released back in the 90's. The sound effects are basic, with guns and cannons emitting ugly 'ping' sounds, instead of something meaty and believable. The progression system and the in-game special abilities are interesting additions to the formula, but the abilities themselves are so slow and inconsequential, you'll have no reason to use any of them during a match save for some of the more powerful ones.
Campaign-wise, from what I’ve experienced, you're stuck mainly with defensive objectives. I didn't play beyond the first four missions, so I can't comment much on the storyline, other than the dull voice acting and the lifeless setting of Meridian.
The only prop I can offer to this game is the inclusion of a map editor, which is a feature that has been exempt from many recent RTS releases. However, given that you have no real reason to invest much time in Meridian, I doubt anyone will create anything truly spectacular with the editor, since the game's online community seems to have stagnated over the course of development.
Meridian is unremarkable, sharing the same basic gameplay elements and graphical palette as Starcraft II, only that it is nowhere near as fun to play. As an RTS, it's okay, but that's all it is. It's just alright. Average. Run-of-the-mill. You could name any well-known RTS game released since 2004, and I can guarantee that it plays, looks, and sounds better than Meridian, not to mention that it's probably retailing for around the same price, too.
It’s nice to see a new RTS game on the market, but we need more innovation than this.
Meridian: New World gets a 4/10.

While the visual design is strong and the developers do a good job of evoking mystery and tension, Final Station is ultimately 5 hours of tedious gameplay with no payoff.
The game does a good job of creating suspense and mystery, but none of its plot threads are ever really resolved, and the mysteries are never really explained. Up until the end credits rolled, I was still expecting something to be revealed that would help tie together what I had learned. I had listened as best I could to all the passenger conversations, read all of the notes scattered through the game, and still have no real understanding of what happened.
There are two types of gameplay - both simplistic and tedious. Firstly, train journeys involve running up and down the train to fix machines and delivere medkits and food to passengers; this means you miss out on the conversations between passengers, which are the only remotely interesting feature of the journeys. Secondly, exploration and combat sections are extremely predictable, requiring you to use the slow, tedious punch attack and environmental objects to conserve ammunition, as not enough ammo is provided to get through all of the enemies. There is no meaningful variation in enemy types, and with just three attacks to choose from (a pistol which you rarely have ammo for, a shotgun which you will never have ammo for, and a limitless punch) there is no meaningful strategy.
Overall, I found the game disappointing. The narrative elements and strong visual design hooked me quite effectively, and made me want to slog through the game despite the tedious gameplay. Unfortunately, without any real payoff at the end of the game, it feels like I wasted my time.

Writing a recommendation for 10 Second Ninja X is easy. If you like twitch action games, then you'll like it. If you don't, then make sure to avoid it.
You're a ninja who has 10 seconds to clear every level - ie. kill all the robots with your three shurikens and your sword. Of course, doing it in ten secs gives you a miserable one star rating, if you want 3, then you need to be much faster, generally a 4 or 5 second ninja. For that, you don't only need to be fast and accurate, you also need to make sure your battle plan is good.
In a game like this, control accuracy and level design are everything, and the creators of 10SNX got these perfectly right. Visuals and audio are fine, but who cares? :) The action is superb, and while there aren't so many levels, the replay value is immense as reaching 3 stars on most levels is anything but easy. It may be a niche game, but in that particular niche, it's about perfect. Recommended!

Banished is a very well thought game about town management and survival. You take control of a small community of outcasts and attempt to keep them alive as long as you can in a verdent but harsh environment. You will have engineer your town to provide the necessities of life not only for your workers, but also for those too young to provide for themselves. Those needs include shelter, fuel, food, clothing, tools (non-fatal) education (non-fatal), medical services, wells for fighting fires as well as sourses of wood, stone, iron and other resourses for the production of said items and for the growth of your town.
It is the first game I have seen that has penelties for not expanding your town regulaurly. As your population ages, your older workers will die off and, if no new childeren have been born for some time, you may run low on citizens old enough to work.
(Adults will move into new houses and begin raising children if new houses are avaliable, but older adults can't raise children)
in addition to the need for basic nesessities and growth, your workers must walk to their place of work, meaning that you must make sure enough housing is nearby for them to live in (but they will exchange jobs automaticaly to minimize the legnth of their walking paths)
There is also the ability to trade with other towns for needed resourses and unlock new types of food by trading.

Banished is the closest thing to a town simulator I have ever witnessed. This isn't your typical city building strategy. Where other games would have you build until you're broke, Banished takes a very different approach. It's all about the resource management. I'm not talking about money and energy, or making sure everyone has plumbing; I am talking about food, warmth, shelter, the real necessities. These are a few of the things you will have to balance, ranging from gathering supplies, to making sure you have enough hospitals and physicians to keep your citizens healthy. And although there are no villians in this game, you struggle against the elements and your own planning.
That being said, Banished is a game that requires patience and a lot of forethought. It is a very relaxing chess game of planning and preparation. I DO NOT suggest this for the casual gamer, as there is no true goal nor any quick paced action. If, however, you would like to see if you could lead a city to autonomy from just 1 house, this is the game for you.

Joint Task Force is a real-time strategy game from HD Publishing.
In Joint Task Force, you don't get to build a base unlike any other RTS out there, but instead you have to secure a landing zone to deploy your heavy forces. Light forces such as infantry can be deployed directly near your officers via helicopters. Vehicles will need soldiers/crews to operate, and their effectiveness will increase if the right crew mount them. Soldiers that operate a vehicles can also be killed even if their vehicles still intact, which makes capturing enemy vehicles possible. Officers can also call in an airstrike or cruise missile strike.
The graphics are great and awesome for an old game and the effects are very good. This is the first strategy game where I see ragdoll effect is featured. Unit collision is also a big matter here, as unlike most RTS game out there, vehicles and tanks almost cannot collide with one another. Even on very low graphics setting, somehow the game still looks good.
The downside of the game is, the skirmish game is somewhat boring, as the AI is quite stupid. The skirmish setting are also bugged, as there are some setting that makes you win or lose instantly when the game not even started. Multiplayer are also dead I think. I haven't been able to play multiplayer.
Joint Task Force has great potential to be a great game, overall the campaign can still give you some hours of playtime. I recommend this.
Rating 6/10
