A touching story told through artifacts and diary entries. Meditative and compelling. If you like things that fall closer to the interactive fiction end of the spectrum, it's a good, relatively bite-sized experience.

At the moment, in early access, the game is very much pay-to-win and extremely unbalanced...
-Crates cost way to much to open, forcing you to buy gold, and they can give extreme advantages to players who pay their way through the game.
-Attcking in PvP is pointless because Choke-points and Grunt/Sniper spam can wipe out armies without contest, and when you compare standard player offence to what CPU defence throws at a base, you can understand why players have very little chance to win even if they are attacking a base with a low powerlevel.
-The only upgrade to units is in perks, which can be won as Cards, but upgraded three or four times before they are worth while. Perks can also be bought, which, once again, can give players a huge advantage.
-Alliance battles are pointless. They pit you up against completely random enemies who seem to be much further along than the attacker/defender, much more so than standard PvP attacks.
-Units are expensive to unlock, Veteran units are pointless at the end of the day (unles you stack vetran units like snipers so that you have 5 on defence,) Heros basically have to be payed for, Attack cards dont provide enough time/damage to break choke-points, which in turn mulch anything you throw at them (and attack cards can't be "upgraded" in the traditional sense, making them less effective as your opponents prgress through the game.
The game has a ton of potental. It's a great idea backed by an amazing art style and unique base-building (without a build timer,) but there needs to be a ton of rebalancing before I would even mention this game in conversation, let alone recommend it.
That said, this post is being made during it's early access stage, so we can hope to see a huge list of changes before its complete release.

Some of the best memories I have playing video games come from the Original release of Dungeon Lords. I have always played with at least one friend.. never play this game alone..
The endless struggle to escape the hell that was Fargrove is still vivid in my mind. In the original, the skies were always overcast, likely due to the massive burning pit they must have had for the endless corpses of thieves, rats, bats, and snakes that sprang out to attack around every corner.
In multiplayer the bugs were...features and you learned to save often.. or you suffered. Map holes were traps for those foolish enough to venture near... you learn quickly to invest in the backflip ability if you want to make it out of holes, or the map itself.
Some people tend to try to break games, as a way to shake the chains of order that oppress us.. do not do this.. you will succeed with Dungeon Lords, and you will be sorry.
That said, this is one of the only old game steam re-releases I would advocate buying. Whoever it is that put this on the steam store actually fixed a lot of the issues the older versions had. If you wanted to play multiplayer with the original you had to become very familiar with third party save game editors just to progress through the broken quests. Now, in our game of four people, one who joined in late, we are probably 70% of the way through the game with not a single game breaking bug. (woo?)
Sure, there's plenty of network issues, crashing, loot whoring, and minimap confusion, but nothing a few ethernet cables and a beer or ten can't fix.
I really do enjoy this game. Don't let the missing polish derail you, there is a lot of really great/funny voice acting, a book's length of story dialogue, and a lot of character building/customization. Play over LAN if you can.

I have been playing The Crew for about 2 hours.
From a racing simulation point of view, the game lacks in various areas such as handling, physics, drivetrain, shifting. All vehicle handles nearly the same, with more or less understeer. Gearbox is odd, and slow while shifting/down shifting, handbraking is slow. On road, cars rarely spin out, but when pushing them to the limit, the cars will throw the rear end out, but refusing to turn. There are three modes of driving: All Assistance, Sport, Hardcore. All assistance would include ABS, Traction, steering stability, etc. Hardcore has less traction and less steering stability. Drifting is a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥on keyboard, but manageable on Sport and Hardcore mode.
Tuning is simplified and a lot easier for the general audience, nothing too complicated. Parts are found during runs and story events, Gold, Silver, Bronze, each adding x amount of additional car level. Level cap for players is at 50. Level caps for cars are at 1299.
From a car enthusiast point of view, for those who just wants to collect and drive the cars, and tune (not in-depth tuning), this game is great. story pretends to be deep by being vauge.  it isnt a bad story but it is not nearly strong enough to carry the game alone.  Dont kid yourself, you might see screenshots or summerys and hear teh buzz words "explore" "manage train" "keep survivours alive" and you might think that these are cetral parts of this game.... you would be wrong.  it is a simple side scrolling point and shoot game.  no puzzles, no mazes. completely linear. really easy. wastes your time more often than not pretending to have mechanics besides walk toward the right and sometimes click the mouse.
"keep your train operational"- this is not part of the game. there are 4 completely unchallangeing mini games that you do one of between stations, the mini game just serves to keep you occupied while npc's talk. no challange at all.
"look after passangers" - mostly they do fine on there own, there are some that get hungry and some that bleed forever... buut... there is no resource management at all. you get much more food and medicine than you need without looking and if you look you will swim in useless resources whoes only purpose is to speak the plot at you while you coast between stations.  like the mainenance mini game, passenger management is a way to keep you standing next to them and listen to dialog.
"explore"- every map works like this: walk right, eventualy find locked door walk up or down, walk righ again. shoot or punch anything that comes to kill you, reach end of level and find peice of paper with coad on it. turn around and walk left until back at train. que train dialog and unfun mini games.  exploreation is absoultely not part of this game.
"make sure you can reach the next station"- seeing as you can kill most enemyies with no bullets and you can run past everything if you want to, and seeing as your train requires literally no effort to reach the next station once it is moveing and there is never any obstical between stations. and you cnat choose which station to travel towards... uh.... the only way you arnt reaching the next station is if you turn off the game...
"collect money"- this is just odd. the whole game you collect money from the stations you visit. passangers pay you. you can sell stuff for cash... but there are only two places to spend cash in game and really the only thing you buy are two newspapers and then optionaly some food and medicine (which you have tons of anyway) really i just dont understand what the point of the moeny is...

A game made by Russians - a rare occasion nowadays. Russians make the weirdest, most peculiar games I ever had pleasure to play.

Perfectly functional just not anything exciting. The combat works, sort of feels like a 2D Resident Evil Four, but without limb targeting or any tention because theres no death penalty and you can restart levels or checkpoints whenever you want. Really good level design, but it's just not that exciting. It ties into the games themes, that this is a dying dreary world where the concept of fun got shot in someone's backyard. Which is a shame because the shooting is fairly tight and with the right framing device could really stand out among other "metroidvania" titles. It's not quite metroid or castlevania though, you acquire powerups by buying them a store or from saving one guy. There were a couple neat little secrets sprinkled here and there but held only plot elements or ammo/supplies. I sort of even like how there are three guns total for the whole game because they're designed tight and the levels are built around them. The melee attack is a nice touch but the game is missing some kind of dodge/roll, but at the same time doesn't really need it, since backstepping and charging your fist solves most 1v1 encounters and you're not often caught short for ammo.
The Train segments were a nice cooldown from the survival horror day to day. They're a task management deal where you have to check on passengers blood and hunger levels while also pressing various buttons around the train. Though once you figure out that the malfunctioning equipment has sparks coming off it and anything else you can ignore it gets broken like fine china in a wood chipper.
Graphically, the game looks alright. It’s artstyle matches the tone but it’s nothing to write home about. I liked how it doesn’t rely on crazy sci-fi towers or giant crystals to make it’s scenery look nice, and I recall some very picturesque fields. The artists for this game definitely specialise in landscapes because the sprite and level design are a bit chunky and screw around with perspective occasionally. That and the enemy design is just the kid from limbo on protein shakes.
Plot was interesting, well written if a little predictable. Felt sort of like if the Guardian from Destiny rolled up instead of the aliens in independence day but the government was somehow less competent. It takes a more character focused narrative, one element I like is you're not meant to get invested in the characters, which means that they don't have to be written in a likeable manner. The dialog came across as very human, if a little memey because of the translation issues. Though there is a bit of a problem where the chump you're playing as his own story but it's impossible to be invested or give a sh!t because he's a silent protagonist without any character. Endings a bit sh!t but hey it's about the journey.
Overall I'd recommend getting this on sale, It's a good game, just not very exciting, new or innovative. But maybe that's enough, and i respect the developers for drawing a line about what they wanted to make, and not adding any unnecessary padding or dumb sh!t. And in the Indie market thats a ♥♥♥♥!ng diamond in the rough. Thats a ♥♥♥♥!ng country in the EU without more than ten billion dollars in debt.

Welp it's just more of the Final station. a couple tweaks in the main gameplay department, some new enemys and a new minigame that isn't a minigame.

After playing it for three days, doing some skirmishes and getting to the last current mission (Mission 5 at the time of the review), I have to say I am very impressed. This game is really simple, but in a good way. Almost no learning curve to the basics of this game. It reminds me of Command and Conquer and the first Starcraft put together.
Pros:
*Even with only about 8 (I count the fighter and heavy fighter as one) units total, it's diverse.
-3 Units (infantry and bomber) only have 1 available weapon.
-1 Unit has 4 (Fighter/Heavy Fighter) weapon choices
-4 Units have 5 (Light/Heavy Vehicles) Choices
-(I count tier 1 and 2 weapons as one because the upgrade replaces the tier 1)
*For an RTS it has a pretty good story to it.
-In between missions you can walk around your ship and converse with the crew, run training simulations, and read about various parts of the game.
*Optamization
-As stated in another review, there are virtually no loading times. My rig is a 4 year old gaming laptop and missions and skirmishes load up in less than 5 seconds.
*Fun campaign
*Good graphics
-The graphics are really good for how smooth it is, even the cutscenes are really good looking.
Cons:
*No way to zoom in or pan the camera.
-Normally I play supreme commander, so I don't really care about panning the camera, but being unable to zoom in and out can be a minor inconvinience at times.
*Short campaign
-As fun as it is, it was over too soon, BUT!!! it is only on mission 5 so far. The dev is still adding missions in as the game progresses
*Only one faction
-I'm not even able to really speculate on whether I feel there would be another faction or not. It's too soon to tell but I don't see why there wouldn't be plans for one.
*A little buggy
-I had a start up error, but the crash report was very detailed and provided multiple troubleshooting ideas to solve the problem and they worked. This is an early access game, so bugs are to be expected.
*Pathfinding
-The AI pathfinding cand be really bad at times. I.E. I send a scout to one corner of the map and it cuts through and enemy base on the opposite side of the destination. Still good for the games current stage.
Neutral Points:
(These are neither good or bad, just some features that some people might like and others may not)
*Snipers can outrange defense turrets
*Defense turrets function like the NOD Turrets in C&C 3: Tiberium Wars (There is a central hub that is linked to turrets)
*A rank up tree (level up, get perks)
*Halowars Deathmatch style unit cap. You increase your unit cap by building structures.
All in all I do recommend this game. More so if it is on sale.

They are getting better with this version for sure. I like a lot about it but find that it fails to deliver the smoothness I look for in the graphics, particularly with the anti aliasing effects making everything look a bit jagged in the distance, and for me personally, this is a deal breaker and find that sims such as iRacing have much better AA effects in place. Graphics are not everything of course, and I find the graphics in F1 very decent, although found no way to improve the AA to a satisfactory level even on ultra settings.
I wanted to love this game though as they nailed it with all official teams and tracks, which is very cool. No on else out there has the lisence to F1 but codemasters. The career mode seams to be very indepth and well made as well as unique, although the character animations are very cartoon like which puts a damper on giving the game a simulation feel, but the wide array of options settings for the cars and view and such are nice and give a simulation depth. The force feedback seems much better than past versions as do the physics, so well done there.
Better AA and better frame rate optimization may have kept this game in my library rather than ending up as a refund. SO close, yet so far away. If the lack of smooth edges in the distance and overall doesn't bother you, or if your system does a better job than mine smoothing them out somehow, this may be right up your alley if you're really into F1. But for me, close but no cigar quite yet.
Perhaps next season they'll perfect it and I'll be back with a stellar review...until then....

If Codemasters thought the last 5 iterations of the F1 franchise were a step forward, then this latest one is a rocket to the moon forward. All I can say is that this is the game fans have been waiting on for years. If you are skeptical, I can't blame you, but this is an absolutely outstanding game that brings in features that the community have been asking for. Formations laps, manual starts, pit entries, radio messages to your engineer, it's just crammed full of immersive features that are necessary in an F1 simulator. Unlike previous titles, the track evolution, tyre wear, temps etc are all noticable on performance and managable in a realistic manner. Aside from the occasional crashes which have been and are being patched out (I have already seen a noticible difference since 1.3), there really is nothing I can fault in this game. Finally this franchise is heading in the right direction. Now we just need to hope Codemasters continue this progression and add even more immersive features i.e manually pulling in to your team's garage and pit form the pitlane and driving to your grid position. F1 is no longer just the pinnacle of motorsport but the pinnacle of motorsport games.

Gone Home is a relatively short narrative game where you play as Kaitlin Greenbriar, who returns home after a trip throughout Europe.  Upon arriving, you see a note from your younger sister taped to the front door telling you not to go digging around for answers and that she'll see you again someday.  Upon entering the house, it appears that nobody is home and you begin your journey to uncover what happened while you were away.
What really got me first in this game is the atmosphere.  It's not a horror game but it certainly can feel that way sometimes with the thunderstorm booming outside, the darkness that envelopes entire rooms, and the creaking of an old house settling.  The unease as you explore the mystery surrounding your family works well in tandem with the overall story.  As you progress along, you'll turn on lights to combat the darkness and both figuratively and literally, shine light on the mystery your pursuing.
The story in Gone Home is certainly one that I think many of us can relate to on several different levels.  Almost everyone has gone through the turbulent, confusing, and emotional teenage years and regardless of your age, I believe those memories still resonate with people on some level or another.  I think that is where the charm of this story truly comes to fruition as you navigate through your sisters personal thoughts and conflicts; the innate understanding of what being a teenager entails.  While your sisters' story is the main driving plot, there are other stories to be discovered not only about yourself, but your parents as well.  All of this combined makes for a very compelling fictionalized family.
Gone Home takes place is the mid 90's and the recreation of common household items are calls back to that era, with CRT TV's, VHS cassette tapes, audio cassettes, etc.  I was amazed by how authentic I felt this place to be and the little details placed throughout certainly drives that point home.  The random notes, pictures, print-outs, etc also feel very authentic and further develop the idea that you're in a real place inhabited by real people.
Personally, I recommend this game to anyone curious.  It may be short, but the authenticity of its characters and world is incredible.  For me it was somewhat of an emotional roller-coaster as you discover what has happened to your family and compelled me to pick it up again after several months to experience it once more.  The second time through, knowing the story, I opted to enable the commentary which gives you insight into the creation and ideology behind the game.

[gameplay & story spoiler alert]
The player starts out as a 21-year old female character called Kaitlin who has just come home from an overseas trip to find a house absent of both her parents and her 18 year old sister Samantha. The game starts by placing Kaitlin outside the main house under the shelter of a the front porch while the rain belts down and a chaotic storm rages violently through the night. The front door is locked and she must search the immediate area for a key. While the game is focused on discovery, this beginning often has the player feeling like they are playing a horror game and that rushing is essential. The storm and flashing lights inside certainly do not help with this aspect, although not long into the game, the player moves on from that feeling to a surreal and immersive story.
You can’t run, you can’t jump and you can’t hide. Why? Because you don’t have to. The atmosphere is great and almost everything can be interacted with. From discovering  a super soft brand of tissues, to finding the Kaitlin's dad’s dirty mags underneath copies of his book, detail is everywhere. The story however, focuses more on Samantha and how she ends up running away with her lesbian girlfriend. Everything is told to the player through voiced dialogue after finding certain letters and notes written by Sam.
The level design is amazing as well, secret doors/cabinets are scattered throughout and can be found by updating the map after finding sketches/notes from Sam. But that’s not even the best part, they were always there to begin with so technically the game can be completed within minutes. Although then the story gets forgotten of course.
Cassettes can be found and played, notes with codes are tucked under hidden doors in the wall, books have covers and blurbs, including authors, and letter completely irrelevant to the story about the dad’s adventures can be found everywhere. This game has everything a player could want…. Apart from content…
And I don’t mean content as in what you can find, there’s lots of that, but as in gameplay time. I took my time playing this game, and I looked at everything I could find. But even after all that my first run through the game only took about 70 minutes, that’s barely over an hour. And it’s got no replay-ability. I mean, sure if you rushed the first time and missed a ton then it’s a nice idea to play again looking for everything, but I only missed about 1 or 3 irrelevant letters as far as I could tell.
Don’t get me wrong it’s an amazing game and I love it, but what it really needs is to last longer. I’d love to see another version of the game with more story, maybe expand on the parents story, or even more on Kaitlin’s travels.

You get more points for the more stuff you do with your squad, promoting team play. Unlike Verdun's competitors (Battlefield 1), the hit models are more realistic, as any rifle shot is pretty much a one-shot. Unfortunately, numbers could go down in Verdun due to Battlfield 1, but this game provides a great alternative.

Receiver is an interesting firearms simulator video game but it falls short of it's goals with poor execution. I suppose you get what you pay for. Don't always expect just $5 to get you a good video game.
GAMEPLAY: You spawn in a random location with a random pistol with a random amount of ammo. The goal is to find six randomly-placed casette tapes in a randomly-generated map with randomly-placed robot enemies (taser-bots & stationary machine gun turrets). There's ammo randomly placed around the map. You must manipulate every part of your gun with your keyboard. There's no lean feature, so you must expose your entire body in order to get a few shots off at a robot. Considering that you die no matter where you are shot, this becomes extremely problematic. The randomly-generated maps don't fit the gameplay well; you can easily get stuck in odd places thanks to the bizzare level design. Stairs are nightmarish.
PRESENTATION: The game is full of plain, blank textures which have no depth whatsoever. Low-detail textures can look good sometimes (see: Unturned) but this game is trying to create a realistic apartment complex. Without the textures, though, every surface looks like plastic. The skybox is low detail and ugly as sin. The sound effects and music are good, but unfortunately, do little to correct the visual sins.
STORY: Hardly any story at all. The little story you can get is from the randomly-placed casette tapes. It's just a guy reading from a script in the most boring and monotonous voice thought possible. It sounds like he just got up at 6:30 AM and didn't have his coffee yet.
THE VERDICT: You should really shell out some extra money in order to get you a better video game. This game doesn't teach you much about actually fighting since there's no human enemies. You can learn how to work a pistol, but if you're the kind of guy who finds this game interesting, you should already know how to use a gun.

Receiver is a fun little title that is held back by a system of pure luck.
Upon first getting this game, it is a fairly confusing first romp, fiddling with your pistrol as you try to understand how it works before venturing out to find your first sentry and HOPEFULLY killing it, or at least hittng a vital part and breaking it in some way that allows you to either get away alive or make things unwinnable. The gun system is by the most interesting part of this game, and the main selling point of it: There is no "Press R to reload" in this game, ammo doesn't magicly appear in your clip.. Heck, you might not even have an extra mag, meaning reloading requires you to go through the effort of putting in each bullet into the mag, provided you even have some bullets stored away.
Really, I wish more games had such a deep gun system, where you have to manually reload the realistic way instead of just pressing R and making a new magazine poof into the gun. however, it is a shame that such a system is wasted here...
While it is fun to fiddle with a gun in this game, what holds it back is how the game is played.. The goal of the game is to collect a certain number of tapes while fighting off robotic sentries in a randomly generated series of buildings. However, what this quickly boils into is a game that is nothing but pure luck if you win or not. The world is so randomly generated that it is possible that it could spawn an impossible situation that makes the game unwinnable.. Other times, however, it might just give you all the tapes right near the start, although this is rare.. From what I heard, it isn't worth it, though.
So what about the combat? Surely it must be fun. And it is, provided you only are fighting ground-based sentries. But the moment you come across a flyer, kiss your progress goodbye because the blimy little robotic dinks will kill you so fast it baffles the mind. You will tremble in fear the moment you hear their buzzing down the hallway, maybe even try and find another way around, because no matter how hard you try, you can't beat them.. Not without either getting insanely lucky or throwing half your ammo at it.
This is because of how crazed their movement is, the flyers flying in such a wobbly way that it makes it hard to hit them, let alone once they start charging you.. They shake so hard that it is like staring at a very angry blur. This makes it very hard to hit weakpoints, and the fact that they are melee based makes it worse, since you have no way of protecting yourself against the speedy hunks of junk unless you run like a bat out of hell and get lucky enough to avoid them. Wouldn't be so bad if it weren't for the one-hit death system.
Combine random generation with such unfair enemies and you get a game that oftentime, no matter how hard you may try, you will never be able to beat. Not because it is hard, but because the game tends to play unfair, sometimes going the extra mile to make sure you suffer your fair share of cheap deaths. A shame, really.. Were it not for the bullish systems in place, this game woulda been great.. But alas it is held back by some real unfun flaws.

If you're a fan of RTS games, ala SC2 this game might just be for you. Is it StarCraft II??...well, no.
But this game puts a few interesting spins on the RTS formula that make it really interesting and fun to play. Instead of producing a standard unit and upgrading offense/defense from an approriate facility (this game has this feature aswell for unit specific upgrades), any weapon upgrades you research for your units can ONLY be applied when they are created. For example, you can Research upgraded cannons, rockets, lasers, railguns etc. that are purchased with the creation of your new unit (varried costs). Cannons are strong vs infantry, Rockets apply area damage, Lasers have increased range and Railguns jump to nearby units.
Also, Commander abilities add alot to gameplay (a SC2 comparison would be hero powers, but they are only usable when you have a hero and only with hero in range). Meridian's 'Commander' abilities are usable anytime and anywhere on the map not affected by fog of war. These powers do come at a cost in the form of an regenerative energy bar and vary from Direct Damage to Healing to Increased build/production rates. These abilities are trained with points you acquire when you level up.
No Multiplayer (yet at least), some pathing issues and at times questionable voice acting are the only minor concerns with this title.
NOTE: This game was for the most part made by ONE MAN in 2 years. Damn impressive.

I liked the story and environments in this one, a nice tropical summery atmosphere, like it feels nostalgic playing it….like I would feel that way anyway, but also like one of those memories you might have, of like that great summer with friends when you all stopped Sin from killing everyone every decade, and managed to bring the eternal calm. I mean that was a particularly good summer.
For someone like me this remaster is great, I really love the game boosters for this, where you can give yourself as much money as you want, the auto battle system and the ability to speed up time. I’m sure purists might hate that, but f*ck grinding, you can grind using these boosters in a quarter of the time it would normally take, although if that’s how you play the game the whole way through you will get stuck at the end. It’s important to know the battle systems and how they work or you’re gonna have a tough time when it comes to the end bosses.
Also Blitzball…wtf, dude I still suck at it *shakes head* I’m sure I could eventually master this mini game, but they messed up the starting difficulty on that one, and I couldn’t be bothered to see it through, I wasn’t enjoying playing it, and it wasn’t worth my time just for the achievements.
This is a really good remaster of a classic game, I think every RPG should have those boosters, or just not make you grind like a motherf*cker. The game is locked to 30fps, honestly, for turn based RPG’s it’s fine for me, 60fps doesn’t add that much to this kinda gameplay, so I was happy enough with the performance.
What did they do! WHAT DID THEY EVEN DO! So the first 10 to 15 hours of this game are really horrible. Tonally it seems totally off. It makes sense from a story perspective I guess, in that in the last game they had won, so when you start out with Yuna, Rikku and new girl Paine, for some reason they have formed a band and sing at concerts. The story gets better and serious after those first 10 hours though, so if you stick with it past the horrible reintroduction, it becomes a lot less stupid and light hearted, and there are stakes again later on.
Yuna for some reason now uses guns. In the first FFX Yuna was a summoner who could call up Aeons that are like these mythical creatures that can fight for her. For story reasons she is unable to do that in FFX-2, so instead they added this dressphere system, where they combined the abilities the Aeons had in the first game with the costume you wear in this one. Two of the costumes Yuna wears are gun related ones. I never got used to Yuna using guns throughout the game, I found that sh*t really jarring with how her character was and acted in the first game.
I actually liked the battle system in FFX-2 more than the first one though, they added an active battle system (you can set it to revert back to the original system if you want). The boss fights also seemed more balanced and easier than in FFX. To be honest I auto battled throughout most of the second game lol It only took me like 27 – 30 hours to finish the second game by doing that. In fact I only stuck with it to see how the story played out. Then again I’m more of a story centric RPG person, so if you are into turn based fighting there is a lot to like about the system used in FFX-2.
Most of the areas are all just reused from FFX, there were a lot of tedious puzzles you had to do in FFX, thankfully you don’t have to redo them, but there’s these annoying piano puzzles at the end of the game that I watched a youtube video to get passed (if you fail the piano puzzle you have to fight a monster for 20 or 30 minutes, and you might not even win the fight, so you need to really complete the puzzle to have an easy time)

There’s actually a third mini game included in the remaster called X-2 Last mission, which plays like a roguelike game. I played the first level of it and lost my gun and died. I restarted it and I still had no gun and was killed….so yeah, don’t think I’ll be playing that. There’s apparently 100 randomly generated levels for it though (you have to make you way up the building to get a prize or find out a secret or something)
Overall, for the amount of content you get in this remaster it is worth the price and then some, granted I probably wouldn’t have bought FFX-2 or the mini game on their own, but they are nice to have all the same.

I try to go into a game with a positive outlook on it and base my decisions on how the game community, developers and moderators portray the overall feeling of the game... Now, this game is a "special case" ordeal. I've been playing since its original release  when warface used its own launcher (prior to
taking over the publishment of the game and it came to steam for a population boost) And i've steadily lost interest in the game.

*- PvE is amazingly well crafted with the difficulty ramping up steadily based on how your team is set up and how your equipment is prioritized.
*- PvP aspect keeps players from getting bored
*- Items can be awarded for doing well in-game
*-You can purchase a weapon permanently if you like the weapon.
*-Free to play
*-Regular updates including large content buffers like new PvE maps and special events which require tokens to play (personally i loved the zombie mode involving convoy support)
*- Heavily biased towards Pay to Win
*- Moderation is abysmal, normally ending with you being banned from the match if you're regularly destroying the enemy with less than 10 deaths (especially if you're using a shotgun)
*- Games are extremely unreliable (both player and connection wise). Glitches plague the game's stability with constant crashing to desktop. On top of this the crash-reporting system is just as bugged causing the error report to fail regularly when sending it in to the support desk.
*-Weapons are insanely priced for non-paying users.
*-Integration to steam was sloppy (may have been fixed), using not only the steam launcher but also the
launcher, making it basically download Warface
before you can play it.
*-Long standing bugs are still prevelant and are not being patched. [problems like flying corpses, moving around when dead as a player, glitched floors on major events/missions etc]
*- Severe moderation restricting player communication in the forums [their forums not steam, steam is toxic even with moderation.]
*- Players will leave the match if they don't get a support unit they want (and will refuse to play it themselves)
*- Players will leave if they lose the match even once leaving you undermanned on hard missions.
*- Severe toxicity in game chat
*- hackers (as with most multiplayer PvP oriented games)
*- abusive mods who kick/ban if they're regularly killed. (as with most PvP oriented games)
*- Bots/inactive players (again, a normal ocurrence online.)
Overall i don't have alot to complain about in this game. It's a great addition to Steam and really needed the boost in players, as Warface was starting to stumble on its own launcher. It can only get better from here.... hopefully.

Having spent around 30 hours on the game before this review I can say I've explored most of the game features now. Without a doubt this is a big leap forward on last years edition, graphically it's about the same, but FIFA get away with that every year too :P The real star in this years edition is the large roster and much improved creation tools, and gameplay tweaks to the controls (some such as the submission system are a bit of a faff but in fairness it's better than button mashing to win) , and revesals are vastly improved upon (you can see the shock as you power out on the other players face... hilarious). A lot more expressive animations and better cutscenes and comebacks this time around.
Pros - Big Roster full of classic WWE era charcters, All DLCs and unlocks included free, better creation options, smoother gameplay, expanded and improved controls, loading times are massively faster than 2k15 at the price of a bigger 40gb install size, replays are much better now (in last years game they often showed no relivant action), career mode now has more things to do. Entry cutscenes are still poorly optimised and cause terrible frame drop... even though once the match starts it's fantastically smooth.
Cons - Still no Diva career mode, Diva roster is improved but still missing many big names like Chyna (Thankfully there are plenty on custom downloadable area), some of the controls are still a bit sluggish and faffy to use (Submissions for example), Custom photo importing is still very poorly supported.
Overall - Must have for Wrestling fans.

As much as I'd like to give this game a positive review, there's a couple things that make parts of this game unplayable. Now I've been looking forward for the "upgrade to f1 2015", or you know, a complete version of that game. And this game does do that. By implimenting the career mode (and all of its nice little quirks), the game has some definition other than just time trial and quick race. The offline AI are alright, they let you attack pretty easily as to avoid a collision, but actually defend a little bit.
My main problem with the game is the online AI. You might think this is one problem who cares, but to me it's extremely prevelent considering I like to play with my mate, but the online AI have something to say about that... We are playing on legend so if it isn't hard enough to keep up and overtake, the AI will literally break poorly (either into you or early in front of you), and completely ignore your existance if you're not the host. Even if you are th host, it's not as good as single player AI, which once again, are just OK.
In closing, this is a great single player racing simulator if you like Formula One, but the online is shotty at best at the moment, and Codemasters are literally on vacation 10 months out of the year, so I won't be expecting much of a patch for these AI anytime soon.

Being the sequel to the original Five Nights at Freddy's, Five Nights at Freddy's 2 provides almost the same fear factor the original game had, but adds new features. The game is a good sequel to the original game, but lacks some of the fear factor that the original had, for example; the Foxy jumpscare is supposed to be coming from the hallway, but when you're looking away from the hallway, he jumps from the wall. The game does have a more complex story than the original game had, and expands on most of the original story showing the events in many ways showing all the incidents that took place through Freddy Fazbear's, and the game's ending has a huge twist.
Story:
The story is very deep in this game, maybe even deeper than the one in the original game, and instead of hiding the secrets; it throws them right at you through minigames. Even though its pretty direct, its still hard to understand the game's story in the end; making the game oh-so-more mysterious.
Verdict:
This is a pretty good sequel, but is noticeably not as good as the original. It has a twist ending, and is an amazing game. This doesn't hide all the faults though. If you liked the original Five Nights at Freddy's; buy this. If you didn't; then don't buy this.
Rating:
8/10
+ Deep Story
+ Scarier than most of the other games in the series
+ Awesome Jumpscares
+ Newer Features
- Game's fear factor gets old a little after getting all jumpscares.
- Formula is still a little worn out.
They focused more on making the game difficult than actually making the game good.

I have been playing this game for a few years now. It is a beautifully made game. At first, it will seem like some classes, or one side (the Nazis) is over powered and unbalanced, but as you play and gain skill, or at least experience, you learn that the game is, indeed, very well balanced. Two players with similar skill are most always a fair match, regardless of class or side. In fact I would say few, if any games, have achieved the level of balance across the great diversity of classes as this game has. The models -character and weapon- are also very well done, and the ballistics of most of the guns are as close to realistic as possible. The only downside I have seen -if it can be called that- is the small community of players. Sometimes there may only be a few servers with players, but it does not detract from the gameplay or plain fun of dinosaurs with guns. This has become my favorite game over the years, and will continue to be -even with the M1 carbine being slightly OP.

I really loved this game. Maybe it's the atmosphere of "exploring empty, creepy, supposedly haunted mansion during a thunderstorm", maybe it's the 90's nostalgia, maybe it's the nuanced way of exploring what could be a sensationalist theme... Maybe it's all of the above? All I know is, when I finished it (after about 2.5 hours of exploring the house), I had goosebumps everywhere. I agree with the other reviewers that I wish the Mom subplot had been explored a little more (I feel like Dad got a fair arc, if a bit one-dimensional), but I love how Sam's relationships with Lonnie and her sister were developed and explored. It made me remember my own uncertain, tentative teenage years, in the best way. The love story is thoughtfully and delicately wrought. I have to admit I actually laughed out loud when I discovered a *certain* note around the house, and the response to trying to reread it was "no, no no no". I think the best way to sum up this review is still: "Goosebumps. EVERYWHERE." I'll probably play again, and this time try to find any and all things I missed or skipped over the first time.

Steam says I've played an hour, but that is all that I could get through in this "steam edition". I have played hundreds of hours in this game in the previous CD-Rom edition.
I really resent what Steam did to this game. Nobody who played Dungeon Lords in the past would clam it was problem free. Enemies would randomly attack you every ten feet. The dialouge with NPCs was cringey and often had grammatical errors. Playing as an Urgoth was literally impossible without a work around, as they couldn't fit through a doorway at a point in the main quest (I would have to make a new character, open a LAN game, complete the task, proceed as the Urgoth, ugh). The NPCs of Skuldoon sounded like racist stereotypes of black southerners. It had issues. We get it. But at its heart it was a great game.
I thought the Steam edition would fix these mistakes and keep everyhing that was good about the game. Instead, nohing is fixed, and everything that was good about the game (the experience system, the classes) is simplified into a pointless endeavor. The random encounters were always ridiculous, but in the steam edition I was running into enemies that decimated me as soon as I took ten steps out of the original spawn.
This game was fun. It was campy, a stereotypical dungeon crawler/save the princess game and thrived in this role. The game mechanics were honestly perfect for a mid-2000's game. But by far the most redeemable quality of the game was the experience system: seeing the last skill needed for a tier three class highlighted in gold after farming billions of exp killing minotaurs was a priceless experience that has been removed from this edition. Not worth the $2.50 I wound up spending.
Steam, I would easily shell out $50 for an unedited Collector's edition. Until thta becomes available, I want to make it clear to all fans of DL: Collectors Edition that this steam game IS NOT what you are looking for.

Receiver is one heck of a free game (was a giveaway). You are placed into a randomly generated texture-less world. Your objective is to collect tapes. You need to shoot or avoid sentry guns (there is only ground and air). It is a one hit kill’s type of FPS game, so it can be challenging.
The title of the game is somewhat of a pun and has no relation to weapon mechanics. As you collect tapes you hear a recording of a guy’s voice (sounds like Lone Wolf). He tells you the situation of what is going on. The story is freakish in the way that it gives meaning to the texture-less level with basic 3D models that you are strolling through. Each time you die and have to start again, the recordings are played in random order, which means eventually you may have a great understanding of the story even though you have not even made it halfway through the game.
I’ll also quickly mention that the soundtrack also is very fitting and gives an atmosphere to the levels. It reminds me of Islamic prayer type of music sounds like in the film Black Hawk Down.
The most interesting part of the game is undoubtedly the weapon reload mechanics. The learning curve is not too steep in my opinion. It will help to just crouch down somewhere upon first play and fiddle with the buttons on your keyboard to understand how to reload your gun. There are two different reload mechanics to learn … the semi-automatic pistol (Glock and 1911 if I remember correctly) and the dirty harry revolver.
It is just cool. I find myself pulling back on the slide to eject the bullets which all go onto the ground. You pick up all the bullets which goes into a reserve (like your pocket). Then you need to put the bullets back into the magazine one by one, but you cannot do that before holstering your weapon (because you need two hands to fill a magazine). Then you need to draw and put the magazine back into the weapon. The first time you pull on the trigger, it may not shoot anything because you need to pull back on the slide again to load a bullet into the chamber. All this is an OCD persons dream come true.
The magnum revolver is a little simpler. Although you start to notice a difference when running low on bullets, you need to make sure you spin the cylinder to align the bullet filled chambers with the barrel. And because there is less bullets you are always having to pull on the ejector rod.
With all weapons you have a safety switch which is useless and you can pull back on the hammer for extra readiness. You can also turn on smart tooltips which highlight what you can and cannot do with button presses.
I find the randomly generated levels made more sense compared to say Hellgate: London which did not make sense to me and felt more like a selling point gimmick. There are sections that you will familiarize yourself with. So even if the level is randomly generated, you know what to expect in each section anyways. So that is definitely a positive for a game that could have just been based on a single static level design.
One thing that I find stupid (and I am not 100% sure about this) is there may be a random luck factor when disabling sentries. It is actually the one thing that has really put me off the game. All sentries supposedly have these weak points. But if you shoot a sentry exactly at a weak point that disables it in one round and then try it again in another round, it will not work. And you can tell because when you get close to the sentry you can see where your bullets have hit exactly. Sometimes you can disable a sentry from a distance that looks like a pea on your screen with one bullet … sometimes you have to fire three shots at a sentry that fills up a quarter of your screen just to disable it. It makes no sense to me. I really hate luck factors in games.
The last thing I would like to mention is this game could have been great. I mean really big. But it is clearly unfinished and from what I heard was part of a competition in designing a game within a week. The thing this game lacks is arms, hands and textures applied to everything including the weapons. But seriously this game could have been amazing! I can actually visualise many FPS games that could utilize this mechanic. Tom Clancy type of games in particular, but even the Battlefield series. The reason why I mention this is because it is one of those revolutionary ideas that gets put out too quickly and is drowned by games with too common typical boring one button reload mechanics and nothing new (albeit finished). I really do hope to see something better made in the future with this idea … not everyone in the world just wants to gun down stuff on the screen senselessly. This is a needed option!

Failing to take out the turrets and/or robots quickly will result in a quick death, they will attack you with precision and you will die after one or two hits. Everytime you start a new game the map (and audio cassettes) are randomised so that adds to the replay value.

This has been a great little game.  I've played several of the ski resort games and this one has been my favorite one so far.  Yes there are some minor parts about it that will aggravate you from time to time, but for $10 they are trivial.
Some suggestions for the developer:
Add in things like hotels/condos/etc.  They could function just like parking lots, but would add more flavor to the game
Make it so that the cable cars and aerial trams can cross unpassable terrain.  That's kind of a silly restriction.  I can't imagine why my huge aerial tram can't cross over that tiny round red spot that is on the side of hill.  Just make it so crossing unpassable terrain adds a little to the cost.
Rethink the "no objects under ski lift thing.  Especially for snow cannons.  That really doesn't make sense.  I've been to many resorts that have had buildings under ski lifts.  Especially cable cars and aerial trams.
The above things shouldn't take too much coding to implement.  The other thing I'd love to see you add is terrain modification.  The ability to make minor changes to terrain would be awesome in this game.
Thanks again for making such a great game.  Don't let my suggetions make you think I didn't enjoy it.
AI and level design leave much to be desired, but overall it seems a good RTS for an indy company without Blizzard or EAs unlimited bank accounts.

Neverending Nightmares is frantic, it's horrifying, it's short.
The game has you play as Thomas, an asthmatic man who is trying to break out of his nightmare.
There are a few different paths in the game that will decide how the rest of the game and story pan out, there are a total of 3 different endings and it significantly changes the levels you'll play.
One more thing to note about this game before diving into the pros and cons is that it is symbolic for different psychological issues such as depression and OCD.
Overall
Pros:
-Design is the strongest point in this game by far, the game is designed to symbolize these mental issues and does very well on it. In addition colors in this game are used very powerful and highlight key elements and themes in this game
-Gore, This game will make you feel uncomfortable. There are so many great horror visuals in this game and Thomas ends up going through so much in his journey. My favorite for the game that gives a clear example is when
again this game will make you feel uncomfortable which when buying a game like this is honestly what is wanted.
-Enemy design is delightfully horrific and fair, each chapter will have their enemy(some will reoccur in later chapters)that is fairly straight forward on how to deal with. The game also scales in difficulty so it never feels like a total cakewalk.
-Choices matter and aren't obvious, avoiding spoilers in the game certain actions are required to achieve certain endings. The choices won't ever be as simple as "Press A to save/Press B to kill" and are done by actual actions.
-The progression in the game takes form of frantic jumps after a major event that end up throwing you back into your bed every time highlighting the title Neverending Nightmares
-Game is properly punishing, it won't set you back to the very beginning, instead it reverts you to the closest bedroom to try again and still fits the narrative of the story. One complaint I have with some games is that there is no sense of danger which considering the genre horror isn't enough there needs to be a threat and punishment which this game does fair.
Cons:
-Thomas has Asthma which injects a stamina system into this game, if you run for more than 5 seconds Thomas will start wheezing for about 20 seconds. Fits the theme of the game but his Asthma doesn't really serve for more outside of a stamina system outside of one character interaction.
-Very short, All three endings took about 2 hours to beat. This also includes every achievement since there are 4 of them.
-You have minimal choices, In the Pros section I mention choices matter and they do... when they happen. There are really about 3 or so major choice areas to save which won't even come up until
For this game I'd definitely recommend it, It's biggest issue is it didn't expand enough on what it did right and that's okay. Just consider the game may be called Neverending Nightmares, but it's more like 2-3 Hour Nightmares. The game wants to take you through the mind of a man who is going through some major issues and it does that very well. In this game you'll want the best for Thomas and you'll go through hell to make it happen.

Poor hitboxes, completely changing how rolling/dodging feels, godawful enemy placement, the list goes on.
Constantly being hit by attacks that simply DID NOT hit you is nonsense. This is not a matter of timing rolls properly, this is getting hit by an attack that visibly was not close to hitting your character.
Not that timing rolls even matters anymore. In Dark Souls 1 (and 3), you have a pretty decent number of invincibility frames. While the max number of i-frames in this game is higher than in 1, it's squandered by the fact that the amount you actually get is tied to a stat you need to level up. Given how expensive leveling is in Souls games, this is quite annoying. You're forced to waste levels on a stat solely to make your movement actually bearable. Another issue is that if your roll is not perfect within a few frames, you still take damage. Not full damage, it seems, but you're still being hurt despite playing the game in a way that you SHOULD be playing.
One of Scholar of the First Sin's selling points was adjusted enemy placement to add a new challenge, but it seems like they decided that a "challenge" consists of fighting 12 of the same enemy over the course of two rooms. This whole game is bursting with these artificial difficulty moments, where the challenge is based not on skill, but on cheap nonsense.
Some people would say to a person like me that I just need to "git gud," but you can't get good at a game that punishes you for not playing with 100% accuracy at all times.

I own an older version of this game.
Though as it's been YEARS since I last played it, I don't remember a whole lot of it. I just know it was an OK game. Not the worst, but not the greatest either. Hell I didn't even know they made a Steam version! I only noticed it when a friend recently bought it when it was -75% off. So I grabbed it as well, sat down one night and just played through it.
Playing the old version, there was some problems. Graphically it was average, and could barely keep up to 20FPS, the draw distance wasn't that far, the controls were a little clunky, and the difficulty was insanely brutal if you weren't playing a Tank build, at least for me. Back then I think I ended up making 4 different characters, and the only one that was able to not die was my tank. Playing anything but made the game really difficult. Compared to the old version, this version is alright. This game runs at a smooth 60FPS, the graphics are polished up a little bit, they added/fixed some of the control problems, cleaned up/improved the UI, fixed the difficulty, etc.
Though this game still has some problems. The major one is when you are in game, there is no possible way to view the "options" menu. You have to quit to the main menu to be able to change anything. There isn't even a pause option in this game. When you open up your menu's or even the save/load screen, the game does not pause. This is annoying for a reason which I will explain.
This game has a "random encounter" feature to it, where almost anywhere you are (other than certain buildings/stores) there may be a random encounter... or in other words an enemy or group of enemies that want to kill you. This can range from a thief, to a swarm of bats, or a horde of goblins. This is even possible in the middle of town! Combine this with no pause menu, you can be looking through your inventory to sort your bags or add your stats from your level up, and you can be jumped. In this version the chance of having an encounter is really high. There is an option to set how often this happens, but as stated you can't do that in game.
Another issue, partly from how the game was built, is that when you are in big areas (not in caves/dungeons/towns) you will experience "mini loadings" here and there. This tends to get annoying when you are running down a path, then suddenly stop for a "loading" for a few seconds, then continue on for about a min before you are hit with another "loading". Again this is partially on how the game was originally built, and don't think it would be possible to remove it.
Now, this is probably the biggest fault of the game, but the map design/world design, is just horrible at times. The first few hours of this game is by far the worst thing about this game. There is no store in the beginning for you to unload your junk, and is impossible to go back to the first area after you leave. It takes a few hours to get into town, and it's a rough ride as well. You will be fighting big groups of goblins, and have WAY more loot than you can ever carry, so you have to leave most of it behind. On top of that, in order to even be able to get out, you will be fighting a strong Ogre boss. In my playthrough, I was only level 6, and the Ogre boss was level 12. The game can be cheap, so be warned. Even after you get to town, good luck finding the stores/guilds as there is no navigation or sign posts telling you what is where, and no NPC's will tell you either. You will get lost in the town.
Like I said, it's not the worst, but not the greatest either. But it IS fun to play through. I didn't really want to play through it again (as there is no achievements, so I don't really wanna waste too much time on it again) as I just replaying it just for fun and Nostalgia sake. Growing up poor and not really able to go and buy new games all the time, so you had to bargain bin shop, this is one of those games. For the many flaws, it's still a fun adventure to play through this old 2005 game.
Just like the old version, there is 8 player coop... But apperently it doesn't work well, as it's direct connection to the host. I never tried it out, but then I never played online for this game originally.
Pros:
- Runs smooth
- Old school RPG with some interesting ideas
- Fun to play
- Improved difficulty
- Steam Traiding Cards
Cons:
- Little pricey
- The game takes 3 steps forward, then 1 step back compared to older versions
- Poor level design
- Story is average
- Difficulty/Random Encounters are still a pain
- Mini "Loading" in large areas.
- Controls/camera can be clunky at times
- Multiplayer net code is old/doesn't work well
- No Achievements
For $15 it's a little pricey, especially for an older game that didn't do well like this. If you are interested, wait till it hits -75% or more.

Gone Home is probably not what you will expect it to be, which is part of why I loved it so much. It is quite short and not especially in-depth, but there are plenty of interesting things to be seen, found, and done in Gone Home, and above all, it tells a story.
I quite recommend it as an artistic experience, and in particular, a shining example of how games can do and be that while still being a game.

The Steam Edition of Dungeon Lords appears to be an earlier, crappier version of the game. I am giving this a lukewarm positive because it's hard to get over the disappointment of having gone backwards with the game, despite the fact that this is a classic rpg.
For anyone who wants an amazing DL experience, try to find the Collector's Edition (not sold here). There you will find better graphics, less sticky terrain, tougher monsters, more skill choices, better spell effects, more strategically-placed terrain, better equipment balance, a completly different system for learning/using magic and skills, and a 100% better game. You will also be able to jump on top of buildings and large terrain features with ease in the CE version, giving your character a decided combat advantage and place to recover.
The CE version has been out of print for awhile, which is why I'm recommending this version instead. If this is the only version you can find, then it's still worthwhile---but you will have to put up with clunky controls, which shouldn't be a huge deal once you get used to it. This version looks like Morrowind graphically, while the CE version looks a bit closer to ES: Oblivion (though not quite).
What makes this game truely amazing are the fully-detailed towns, enemy types with distinct personalities and differing tactics, incredibly well-thought out dungeons, and interesting quests. I doubt I will ever forget the Elven Test, the Isle of Moon Dogs, the creepy Sword-of-Shanara-like Trolls, running through hordes of enemies with mass effect spells, or the final battle with the Witch Queen and her minions.
The goblins have differing personalities, and are funny to watch. Towers of crystal magic have winding external staircases which trap you when squads of an advancing enemy army are keyed to your presence. There are multiple magic systems (arcane, crystal/rune, and nether/voodoo magic). You can sneak into a dragon breeding ground to recover dragon eggs and artifacts, or to surprise the nesting dragons. There are water-filled sewers, ancient tombs, dungeons full of traps, elven forts among the treetops, wizard towers, castles, an army encampment with endless skirmishes, a hidden Thieves Quarter, and other fantasy tropes which are oozing with their own unique style.
All in all, a very fun game. I just wish it was the CE version.

Edit (2016) They have sold a "complete edition" when there is more content on the way, so you can pay once for the game with the season pass, pay again for the content that doesn't come in the season pass, then pay one more time for more content not included to be released. To hell with this game.

Me, I checked and played the 'new' content for a few hours and unninstalled it again, personally I can't find any improvement worth a buyback into this game since my gripe is the terrible driving mechanics alongside the bad physics. I remain true to every word I wrote in this review.
I had high hopes for this game, I played the betas, followed the forums and pre-ordered it. Then I forced myself to like it and play it even after I was completely frustrated by everything I'm about to say.
I DO NOT RECOMMEND THIS GAME AT IT'S CURRENT STATE AND/OR PRICE TAG.
Before the ugly : THE CREW is not a complete mess, there is the possibility of having a great amount of fun playing this game depending on what kinda of player you are. One thing it gets right is the map diversion. Every spot, every city or zone as they say, has it's own feeling and design, it's unique, and driving around the map with a friend is sure entertaining. but that's it. if you're not the person who enjoys cross country trips or american cars, there is not much for you here.
Entitled as "MMO CAR-PG" but you can't develop your character, not a single aspect. In theory, every player has the same exact character, solution? Let's hide other player's driver. and that's it. Let's say you play against remote controlled cars, for immersion's sake. you CAN'T call it an mmo, without character development, the best you'll get are perks, nothing really groundbreaking. but we have cars, don't we?
There are 30~40 cars and all of them seem unfinished, except for the first ones. because you know, "first impressions are always the most important". the first five cars have all the specs available, street, dirt, performance, raid and circuit. other cars usually have 2~3 specs only. so you wanna go crazy off road with that expensive car? too bad. also, most cars are American, so no luxury here. what's most stupid is the unbalanced performance cars have, the starter vehicles run faster then the most expensive car in the game.
But driving gets better as your car and player level increases, right? No. That's an excuse for the handling in the game. It doesn't get better. I have 1299 ( Max level ) cars and with assistance off, they just don't grip on the road as the default low level mustang does. With assistance on, it's just "drifting". The crew should have stayed as a street racing game only, the street tracks are okay, the handling on street is OK. but when it goes off-road becomes soap ( and not in a good 'Dirt game' way of soap ), on circuit the game just doesn't have enough decent physics to feel solid, and while climbing mountains with raid spec... I wish you good luck trying not to roll 900º in the air after hitting that small rock. this game is unpredictable thanks to it's physics, you never know how is your car going to react to crashes so expect for the worst and try avoiding collisions. worth adding : some elements break, some doesn't, and in this game this is not okay because when someone tries to cut their way trough some houses, the fences breaks. When you're doing the turn on a corner, well, the fence it very likely to be the most solid virtual object you'll ever find.
Progression is BROKEN, I had to try various missions at least three times due to disconnects that WIPED my progress, my statistics are currently like this " main missions complete : 167% ", and the rewards are ridiculously unbalanced. Let me explain this : I leveled from 1 to 50 in ONE DAY AND A HALF doing no more than 60 PvP matches, 10 or so story missions and some exploration. Yes, I reached maxed level on an MMO in basically a day. It gets better, I was being rewarded 16k bucks every time I finished first on a PvP match, and when you are disqualified because you couldn't get to the finish line in time, well, TAKE THESE 16K BUCKS ANYWAY. You just know they didn't really put any thought into the game's progression when all it takes from level 49 to 50 is 2 races in 10 minutes.
The customization feels incomplete, some categories are there with no parts to purchase for you car, get used to the "No part available in this category" message. the stickers are single color only and there isn't variety among those, expect to see everyone using the same 2 flame stickers or racing stripes. the real car performance parts are available with a grind of challenges after level 50 which is not very cool given the insane difficulty of some challenges, but don't worry, it doesn't matter how fast your car is...
AI CHEATS, it goes off track and spawns in front of you, It rams you constantly and the Catch-up is ridiculous. there are some gifs on Polygon's review of the crew if your interested.
The story is not good, you bounce trough one generic dialog to the next and I couldn't connect to any character of this game, I couldn't care less to be honest and not skipping cutscenes was a challenge at times. At the end of the main story you are rewarded with a mix of every CGI they made for the game, which felt very very lazy.
And I could go on, there is the server instability problem, the always online "DRM", the NAT problem that causes online atrocities, the lack of mirrors promised by launch, no weather system, the "crew joining different lobbies" bug, the "Hitting someone back at 20mp/h and flying like when hit by a giant on skyrim" bug, the "I regret the money I spent buying this game" case and the first time I actually emailed steam support to ask about their refund policy.
I'm frustrated. I just wish I could go back to those TDU2 Times.
tl;dr
+ Every area is unique and has it's own feeling.
+ Driving with friends can be fun

The Crew is one of those racing games that you just have to play even if it has Ubisoft's name on it. Let's get all of the BS rumors out of the way by saying UBISOFT DID NOT DEVELOP THIS GAME!!!! Ivory Tower developed this game with the ability of having 60 FPS at the start and yes it does have micro transactions but earning in-game cash is super easy. This game isn't tanted with Ubisoft's bad pc port mojo. This is a super stable game and I occasionaly experience a crash once or twice a day.
So gameplay, how is it? Well the gameplay is well how any Need for Speed from Underground 2 through Carbon but with a twist. This game has RPG elements thats similar to Need for Speed World but is not purposly asking you to empty your wallets into a pay wall. It is open world and the world is really huge. It is close to 50 in-game miles and it will take you a long time to get you there. You have a level (50 is a max) in which you level up by doing story missions (yes it has a story), skill challenges, PvP events, and faction missions. The story missions is what it is labeled as, missions that's part of the story. The skill challenges offer a way to gain car parts (more on that later) and get some experience for doing it. There is also a leaderboard so you can compete against a person's ghost and see if you can get to the top of the leaderboard. PvP events are what it is labeled. You go against other players and you can choose to fight for your faction or just free-for-all. Faction missions are where you get a lot of money, faction experience in which that adds everyday you login, and some chunk of experience. They also have one hour long races and one that goes up to 4 hours
What are these car parts you mentioned above? Well those car parts give your car a level as well ranging from 0-1299. The car parts consist of a motorcore, air system, diff, tires, weight reduction, and more. There are five classes of cars and each car class is different to each other: There is Street, Dirt, Performance, Raid, and Circuit. Street is your step above stock. Dirt is something you would see from a World Rally Championship. Performance is your step above Street but is almost stripped out. Raid is something you see from the Dakar Rally and yes they have trophy trucks. Circuit is something you see from Grand Touring ot 24 Hour Le Mons racing. The car is completely stripped down with weight saving and high performance in mind with the ability to take corners.
Well since this is a driving game, how are the physics? The physics can be odd but if you work around them, you can win a lot of the races. Drafting is a thing so use it when you can. The cars will tend to bounce off of things like bumper cars and it focuses a little on drifting.
Hows the car customization? It is what you would expect from a Need for Speed Most Wanted and Carbon game. You can customize the interior with your choices of aluminum, carbon fiber, mixed aluminum, and mixed carbon fiber. You cannot place stickers anywhere you want to though. They have presets which look cool IMO.
Car selection? How big is it? Well IMO it is small but it will slowly expand with DLC. The car list consists of 58 total cars but at least they have trucks.
Final thoughts? Well I am enjoying the game. I am enjoying every bit of time I have put into the game. I would recommend everyone getting the Season Pass since they are going to add more cars. January 2015 is going to be their first DLC which should be an interesting one. I did wish they have given us the ability to move around the stickers rather than give us presets and working mirrors in the cockpit (yes a working cockpit). This game I believe will set a new standard on the illegal arcade street racing genre that was leaving a sour taste in my mouth because of the way Need for Speed has been going and from the look of things, it isnt going to get any better. You just have to play this game to know what I feel about this game. I have been dying to play a game thats open world with similar car customization as Need for Speed Most Wanted and Carbon but isn't trying to make your wallets screem and this is the answer my friends.
UPDATE: Next Tuesday of updating this review, they are adding three more cars into the game if you don't count the Mini Cooper non-street edition we got at launch. In The Final Station you play as a train conductor 106 years after an alien invasion. On this particular day it seems like the world might be facing another invasion, and you are tasked with taking important defense materials to where they are needed while also finding any survivors who may need help. While the games main story isn’t much to write home about, each station and survivor you find has their own story and I found those to be very entertaining. Unfortunately, the act of experiencing them could use some work. I remember once I had a group of survivors in the train argued about a conspiracy surrounding the First Visitation. I was enthused with the conversation, but I was only able to get bits and pieces of it as my attention was diverted and NPC conversations kept going even while I wasn’t able to pay attention to them. Because of this I didn’t really experiences a lot of these stories as fully as I wish I had. Not knowing how those two survivors worked out their conflicting feelings on the truth behind The First Visitation annoys me. And that’s not the only story I can say that about. The late game makes up for this a bit with a pretty great piece of environmental storytelling and an ending that is rather heart breaking. You could speed through the story like an express train through a vacant station, but I enjoyed taking the scenic route.
Gameplay is split between taking care of the train and it’s passengers and exploring towns and stations. The train sections are the low point, as most of what you do is some light puzzles making sure the different sections of the train aren’t drawing too much power. Not a bad idea for a core mechanic, but so little goes wrong at any one point that these sections feel like busy work. I was never rushing from one section of the train to another, instead I was casually strolling every now and again. Taking care of the passengers isn’t much better. You have to keep track of their health and hunger, but the ones who need it the most are almost never worth the effort. There were times I’d find myself wasting all my health packs on someone because they offered the best rewards only for them to die anyways due to reopening wounds. Or, maybe that was due to the fact that a train conductor was playing nurse. None of this is bad, I just wish it was expanded upon more. As it exists right now these sections feel more like they are there to give the player something to do between missions. But, with just a little more work they could have really added a lot to the core experience. For example, if too much went wrong and the player ignored it, what if the train broke down, forcing them into an impromptu mission to find replacement parts? What if as passengers died the others began to decide it was in their best interest to take their chances on their own? Minor additions like that would have helped the game greatly.
Combat and exploration fairs better however. Most of the places you stop are deserted and overrun with zombie like people infected by an alien virus. You have to go out and look for the code that disengages the locks on the train to get moving again, while also looking for supplies and survivors. I never found these sections to be hard, but they were enjoyably suspenseful. Rooms are blacked out until you open doors or windows, so you never know what’s coming your way until it’s right there. And like in most survival horror games, health and ammo is always scarce and hard to find. Because of this, even when I knew I could shoot my way through an area I still moved with trepidation through each location.
The only complaint I have about these sections is that they don’t evolve enough throughout the course of the game. The scope of the towns and stations you explore increases, sure, but you’re doing the same thing each time. With this making up the bulk of the game play, some mechanics changes every now and again would have been appreciated. The enemy variety does help with this to an extent, but one or two big shakeups to the formula would still have gone a long way. As is, the combat still manages to impress, but playing for extended periods gets tedious.
The visuals and sound design never failed to impress however. Not only does the game look fantastic, but if you take the time too look at the back grounds there are some pretty damn gorgeous back-drops. Add to that the sparse use of music and you get that classic survival horror feeling of isolation. Most of the games sound track is just your footsteps echoing on whatever surface you’re walking on until a fight breaks out. When music does come in it’s either disconcerting or somber, matching the games tone perfectly.
The game was tense when it needed to be and was engaging throughout the four hours I spent with it. It may not scare the pants off of you like some other games and you may not find yourself going back to it once it’s over, but I definitely recommend giving this a look. The Final Station gave me a good few hours of tension and that’s all I wanted out of it. Some aspects of the game left me wanting more, but that’s only because what’s there was so good to begin with. It might be a bit of a bumpy ride at times, but this is still a train worth catching.

At the first glance, The Final Station looks like an interesting survival/horror game and after playing it I have to say to buy it when it’s on sale if you are really interested in getting it. With what you get in this game you will be severely disappointed if you buy it at it’s 15 dollar price.
Gameplay in this game is very upsetting. I expected to be challenged and have to manage my resources while exploring abandoned towns and outposts but I ended up purging the area with nothing but my fists and rarely using my ammo. Also medkits are useless because when you die you spawn right back where you were in some spots.
The Train bit are the weirdest part in the whole game because it’s one of the crucial times to take in vital info about the story, but You need to fix the train because it’s falling apart, The passenger you picked up from your last stop is bleeding all over the train floor, and two of your passengers will die of starvation if they aren’t given a box of crackers! I hardly read all of their conversations too concerned about everything else going on.
Those are my really big gripes with the game. It was never the less interesting and I loved some of the environments in the game. Characters were pretty cool even though some of them are a little forgettable. The towns were pretty fun to explore (even though you get a handful of towns to explore) and have some pretty interesting areas.
The Final Station is a weak survival/horror game where you will end up with plenty of resources to keep yourself and your passengers happy. It’s an okay game but I wouldn’t recommend for it’s gameplay. Probably for it’s story but I don’t know much because the goddamn fan needed stabilizing.
TL:DR - wait for sale if you’re really interested.
