This game is fine. I don't know why all of the whiny PC gamers are the only people to write reviews. Some of the reviews had me worried about buying it, but the worry is all hype. Some people don't have the slightest clue what it takes to develop a game. Just because you learned a few Java functions doesn't make you a developer. Games don't just appear from magic.
Now to the review. This game is an arcade style of racing. If you are a fan of Need for Speed, Midnight Club, Burnout, etc. (I know some of you can barely remember those titles), you will love this game. If you want a simulator style racing game, go play Forza. The servers are a bit haywire right now, but that's normal for an AAA title (BF4 anyone?). The waypoint GPS is one of the best I've ever seen, although sometimes the GPS takes you off road to get to hardball, but I figure it's trying to get you there as fast as possible. The rearview mirror isn’t functional (NASCAR 98 anyone?). I don't know why they didn't implement that. Maybe it will come in the future. The Gold Edition is definitely worth every penny. You get some cool cars off the bat and more to come with the season pass. If you are too cheap to buy the season pass, you still have some good cars to choose from. The guys complaining about having to buy the season pass to get free cars, refer to the "games don't appear from magic" statement. I don't get why you think everything should be free in life. Maybe your liberal parents should've taught you better.
You crash a lot if you are going 200 MPH. But you are soon back on your feet, or tires I guess. The damage to your car in free roam goes away after some drive time. The servers stutter some, but not bad at all. It seems to happen more when I go to LA or LV, but these are two of the biggest cities in the game. Overall this game is worth it. The graphics aren't the best, the mechanics are arcade style, and the driving is fun. That's all you need. Plus it's a MMO! It’s styled just like AC games. So if you know how to navigate that map, you are good to go. Hopefully this curbed some of the worries you might have from reading the nit picking, "I want my cake and I want to eat it too", reviews. It's a fine game... I can't praise it any more than I already have.

Imagine Metal Gear Solid mixed with Rainbow Six, along with the undertones of the world controlling you. This might be the best idea for Receiver. The game is very barebones in gameplay, but it's exactly that element that changes how you play the game compared to other first-person shooters. This is hardcore FPS at its finest, and you'll be shocked to know just how much work you need to put in to get through it all.
It has a roguelight element to it, which to this game, means you have a small variety of guns that you will spawn with, along with a specific quantity of ammunition, as well as magazines, based on the weapon. The equipment also has randomized properties. You may need to prime the weapon, you may need to turn the safety off, you may need to ensure that your six-shooter is full in all barrels. It goes a long way, and over time, you'll be adapted to this, which shows another element that the game has: it disciplines you. You WILL die if you neglect one detail, so don't overlook
.
Speaking of dying,
. You will probably die a lot. That's because it's a one-hit kill game. You get hit at all, it's over, and you start anew. Doesn't seem new, huh? Well, admittedly not, but there's several details the game focuses on for you to succeed. Specific hit zones on your enemies. Blind spots. Corners, timing, even your gun has an arc after a certain distance that warrants you be a bit more methodical... Until you're spotted. Now you need to find and hit their weak spot. Miss the spot? Pray your next shot doesn't. It does? Say goodbye. And that is yet another element:
. If you don't, you risk missing the shot.
There's actually a few weak spots on all your enemies, and it sets a slight dynamic for how your enemy is defeated, and what happens next. You can shoot out the tazer on the cyclone bots, and that may leave you annoyed to hell and back as they fly around, distracting you and wasting your ammo as they fly around you, and through you, which is disorienting as all hell.
You must be tactical, conservative, watchful, and completely aware. Your ammo can fade quickly, your magazines will be emptied rapidly, and if you don't run when you need to, you'll screw up, and fail to reload as you attempt to. The controls go a long way to emphasize that as well. It definitely doesn't feel traditional, which makes sense, because it isn't. It isn't even comparable to games like Takedown: Red Sabre or Insurgency. You go at one speed, and crouching does little except expand your mobility among the level. The focus is completely on your location relative to the enemies, and your defense/offense.
Remember my explaining the game in layman's terms? That sets the story's tone too. The story is as such:
Sounds crazy right? Well, it is. And again,
Die, and you start over. Admittedly, it's a short game, but it's the difficulty and effort required that makes it worth it all. This game will not mess around. It's kill or be killed, and the game will make sure you are killed most.
Final note, the game runs in the Unity3D engine, and surprisingly, is very bad in performance. I am shocked to know I get frame drops at 720p considering my specs. I've played Unity3D games that seemed far more demanding, and subsequently, perform much better than this game. Optimization faults, maybe? Either way, it isn't absolutely jarring, though framedrops can be bad if you find yourself in a risky situation.
Overall, Receiver is probably the best hardcore FPS I've played this year, and probably of all time. It is simple, it focuses on the gunplay and strategy over all things, and bar controls, I can jump into this game and lose myself trying to make progress. It is an excellent grab, and if you didn't score it from Humble Bundle's free summer games, I think it is work every penny.

An excellent addition to the F1 series by Codemasters. The last one I played was 2013, and having read the reviews for '14 & '15 I was glad to have missed them out. Short review: I would highly recommend this game to anyone who is a fan of racing sims in general, and obviously to those who like motorsports. This is the game we've all been waiting for.
What immediately strikes you as you jump into Career Mode is the amazing feel of the cars and the sense of detail within the simulation. The set up of the car, in combination with the tyres, temperature, fuel weight and engine setting all play a significant factor on how the car performs. It can be a little daunting at first, but in practice there are three 'practice programs' that help you learn the tracks, and how to conserve your tyres, and what sort of times you'll need to achieve in qualifying. These programs continue to be of use even for those who master the car and track as they provide R&D points which can be used to upgrade the car as the season goes on. As such, as your season progresses, other teams may catch up with you, or you may leave them behind, and the likes of Mercedes are not guaranteed to dominate season after season.
The races themselves are fantastic: the AI, whilst not perfect, provides an enjoyable, consistent challenge. It's certainly the most lifelike AI I've ever seen in a racing game. I've seen three cars attack corners at the same time, all exchanging positions, and I've been overtaken through late breaking etc. The AI can sometimes be a bit timid and give you too much space on lower difficulties - but once you start playing on expert, the AI really does provide an almost human like challenge. The biggest issue with the AI is that the jump up to the next difficulty can feel a little too much at times. This means that you might find yourself overachieving on one difficulty setting, but really struggling on the next difficulty up. The implementation of sliders would greatly help with this problem, but it is unlikely that we'll see such a system any time soon.
By putting the damage setting to 'simulation' you'll witness fairly frequent (virtual) safety cars. In my last race in Canada there was two SCs following two crashes on T1 and T2 of the first lap, as well as for a mechanical failure late in the race. The SCs helped me conserve my tyres, so I was able to use a 1-stop strategy, which helped me finish in 3rd with a Renault, whilst my teammate got 5th. Other races haven't quite gone so well: at Monaco a rainy start called for intermediate tyres, but I was too quick to jump to slicks when the track dried and I lost quite a bit of time, finishing outside the points. Basically, anything can happen in a race: good fortune or bad luck, so you'll find yourself doing well some races but poorly in others - and the AI likewise struggles and benefits from certain conditions. This makes career mode far more enjoyable, since it's unpredictable and realistic, making the game very replayable.
The graphics are very nice - not had any trouble with them following a couple of patches and updating drivers. This isn't an area of the game I'm usually too fussy about, but you can really see the effort Codemasters have made with the game, and it really does enhance the experience. I would say, however, that the sound of the game could do with some work. Bugs have made the sound a bit wonky at times, and the levels are not quite right, especially when passing other cars who are in the pits. Codemasters have already patched many bugs and addressed most issues, so I'm fairly confident that these issues will no longer be relevant in a few months time.
In addition to career mode there is custom championships and time trial, although I haven't touch either game mode yet. There is obviously multiplayer - but I've never enjoyed racing games online, so again can't comment on that.
To round this off I would say this is the best F1 game yet, it has fantastic replayability, graphics and gameplay. The simulation is the best it's ever been, and the practice programs are extremely useful tools for teaching people the tracks and how to drive quickly and smoothly. Whilst the difficulty settings could do with some tweaking and a few bugs in the sound department ironed out, this game is undoubtedly the new benchmark for the F1 series and is as good as a game we could have wished for.

I'm gonna make this very simple. If you value action gameplay and mechanics over all else, this is going to be your favourite Souls game. More so if you are into PvP.
All the mechanics in this game are built on systems. You don't have dual wield as a "special" stance of a specific weapon, you have a dual wield system that works with ALL weapons and is quite complex.
Unlike the first and third games, shields are bad in this game so you are forced to learn how to dodge or you can't get past even the first boss. Poise is also not very important except for PvP against a few weapons such as rapiers and longswords.
Parrying is slower, however you get a larger parry window which, combined with the slower more predictable attacks makes parrying a lot more about prediction than about reaction time. It also makes parry spam extremely ineffective.
Most movesets are standard, based on the class of the weapon with small deviations such as alternative running attacks, or special heavy attacks, but the moveset itself is complex, depending on the hand you wield the weapon with.
The biggest difference in the combat between Dark Souls 1 or 3 and this one is that in this one you can't change attack direction after you attack, or you can but only a little. That completely changes how you have to think because once you commit to an attack you opponent can easily get behind you and punish it with a backstab. This type of punishment was possible in the first dark souls because backstabs were instant but it isn't possible in the third one because backstabs are delayed and you can change attack direction really fast. In DS1 and DS3 you can attack forward and then do a 180 turn and attack behind you very fast, this makes dodging around an opponent useless because he will be able to track your movement and attack you with ease. This difference means fights are slower but closer, you don't have to keep distance between you and your opponent because you can almost always dodge his attacks. This also completely eliminates the possibility to spam attacks, it just doesn't work and is very easy to punish. You only attack twice in a row in this game if you land the first hit, because your second hit will almost always miss otherwise.
The magic system is also good and not only viable but often better than melee, at least for PvE content. In PvP magic is just a game of attrition, trying to overwhelm your opponent with various random spells, hoping for him to make a mistake. Miracles are very good PvE wise because most monsters are vulnerable to lighting. Pyromancies don't have enought casts for PvE but are very good for PvP especially if you free-aim your shots. Sorceries and Dark Sorceries are excellent for PvE due to high number of casts and high damage and are ok for PvP as long as you don't rely solely on them. There a of course a few exceptional spells, such as forbiden sun, dark resonant soul and the various aoe spells which are very effective in PvP when used correctly to supplement good melee.
Also elemental weapon enchantments work great and stack with temporary magic buffs which makes elemental melee builds almost on par with quality build classes.
This game is hard. I don't mean "hard" for people that don't play Soul's games, I mean this game is hard even for hardcore players. Until you learn how dodging works, you will have a very difficult time.
I personally don't recommend the Scholar of the First Sin version over the original one as it's much harder, especially in the beginning areas, and it really screws up the pace of the game.
The story is less impressive but also less intrusive. There are no scripted deaths, or puzzle bosses in this game, every boss you fight is a more or less fair fight that you have to win with your ability to read your opponent and dodge his attacks. Also, most bosses don't have a second phase where they change into a different boss. If they have a second phase it's subtle, except for Dark Lurker.
If you've never played a Souls game you should know that Dark Souls games don't have a real story, it's just bits and pieces of information that you can, if you choose to, interpret as a cohesive story. In Souls games, the mechanics, level design and atmosphere combined are the story, so from this point of view this game tells a very good story.

Gone Home is an atmospheric walking simulator that can be finished in a mere hour if you don't search through everything in this grotesquely huge house in the suburbs.
.Gameplay.
The game is presented in first person perspective. You move with wasd and left click to pick up and examine things. You can turn objects by holding down the right mouse button or toss what you're holding by left clicking again. Going through the house, you'll read various documents and letters that explain just why the house appears to be abandoned and you'll solve rudimentary puzzles by gathering numbers for combinations to open various locks. Nothing too strenuous or difficult.
.Premise/Story.
You are Katie, who has just returned home from a trip abroad. You need to figure out where the hell your family has gone and you do so by looting everything. Cupboards, lockers, secret panels--nothing is safe from your prying.
The story of where your little sister, Sam, has gone is cute and features the taboo subject of being a lesbian. Please refrain from rolling your eyes I am aware that this was published in 2013. There are a handful of little subplots, but the game play just isn't interesting enough to even take the time to piece them together.
.Atmosphere.
This was the game's strength. The desolate sound of rain battering the old house, creaking floorboards, and that lightning bolt or too that catches you off-guard just adds to it. For me, who hates horror, it was entirely creepy and I had to play with the lights on.
.Soundtrack.
Unimpressive. The ambient sounds were very good. The music was quiet and just sort of faded into the background. The cassette tapes littered through the game were just plain awful.
.Bottom line.
I can't, with a good conscience, recommend this--especially with a 20USD price tag. If you can get the bundled version, this may be good if you're looking for something short with cards.

Banished is a really fun city-building game. You quickly want to keep your people alive and happy since they are basically your main resource. Food is not terribly hard to come by so long as you have a decent amount of crop fields. The need to trade for the different types of crop and tree seeds gives something to strive for though it can be a little frustrating to get livestock due to price and the rarity of the actual merchant (there is usually only 1 merchant selling them and he/she only comes once in several years). There is no combat in the game so if you only like city builders with some aspects of combat then look elsewhere. Despite my overall reccomendation of the game I have 2 main problems with it.
The AI: When you order land to be cleared every laborer and worker who is not currently doing something goes to clear the land. Farmers in the Winter also like to do this and be on the opposite side of town when spring planting is in need and by the time they walk back it is often late into the season or even early summer resulting in food issues for the entire town. I also frequently see villagers march all the way across town for something that is in the barn next door to them. This is more of a tuning issue and doesn't break the game, you just need to be careful.
Simplicity: The beauty and death of Banished is its sheer simplicity. There is no real tech tree to the point that you can build anything with the same few resources. There isn't really anything to strive for other than just making your town bigger, for the sake of it being bigger. There is also no real difference between crops. Some may grow a little faster or slower but in the end they don't have much of a difference. There is not 1 crop that grows better in wet years and another in dry so there isnt a big reason to expand beyond a few crops for diversity in your villagers diet. The same goes for the different orchard types. There isn't much depth in general to the game but at the same time there is no annoying need to build this 1 building for a random resource to build one building and then its never of use again.
Overall Banished is a good game to eat up your time but it begins to lag in late game as the end game tends to be more farms->More Houses->More People ->More Farms... as well as more woodcutters and foresters.

Verdun.
If you're here, you already know the premise of Verdun, therefore, I'll focus on the more nitty gritty.
Verdun takes the approach Battlefield One does not; it attempts a realistic and almost nihilistic approach to multiplayer and the game as a whole.  Although classes unlock and your character picks up skills as he becomes battle hardened, there is minimal player progression compared to the obious measures of level in games like Call of Duty.  Weapons do not differ vastly in things like power or accuracy based on a player's level, instead, they simply have their own strengths and weaknesses like the real weapons.  In Verdun, you can expect your character to act in a realistic manner and unlike most other FPS games.  You will reload at a painfully realistic speed.  You will struggle spotting target through iron sights at distant ranges.  You will be painfully aware that your character suffers from human limitations and does not posses the magical powers found in most other FPS multiplayer characters.
Pros:
-WWI games are rare, well done WWI games are rarer
-Realistic weapons, uniforms, sounds, and "feel"
-Maps truly capture the atmosphere of WWI
-Realism in strategies and methods
-Don't charge each update of new units, weapon packs, or maps as DLC and instead just provide them as updates
-Good graphics, great sounds, good music

'Dungeon Lords Steam Edition' - maybe another way to call it would be:
'Okay boys, Dungeon Lords Take #4: Let's try not to screw it up this time. Lights, camera, action!'
___________________________________________________________________________________
First the good part': This time it seems the developers care for the game as they released their first patch after the release. This one adressed several problems in MP - unfortunately the SP seems mostly untouched. So now it's important to see if they release more patches to fix bugs and glitches or if it was a one-time wonder.
'Fans' of the old Dungeon Lords:
This version is better than 'MMXII' but if there was a bug or glitch in the original version it's quite possible that it is still there and wasn't fixed. However the game is more accessible (there are e.g. finally tool tips for skills and spells), a quest log gives you some hints where to go and the randomized loot is quite interesting - so there are several positive changes. However maybe it would be better to wait some more weeks and see if the developers now actually care for their game and support SP and MP it or if it will be abandonned once more.
'Newcomers' who have never heard of or played the original game:
It's probably better to skip this game, there are better RPGs out there. It has its own charm (quite trashy and retro) but to find the positive things you have to dig deep in a game full of bulky and weird systems and design decisions.
___________________________________________________________________________________
Oh Lord, that game is like an undead, It was a bit rotten the first time it was released in 2005 (and full of bugs), afterwards it came back in an 'improved' version (still a buggy mess) and some years after it returned from its grave with the 'MMXII' version (did I mention the bugs?) that had 'improved systems' (official claim) and some nice function additions - however at the same time they also screwed up the once good leveling and magic system and removed interesting features like identification, the whole exploring aspect or the penalty systems. I regretted buying this game quite fast.
Well so now here's the Steam Edition that is based on an improved 'MMXII' version and should finally act as a 'complete and finished' version. So do all good things come in... fours?
First there is to say that the original game was neither very good nor very polished but it had its own charm. 'Dungeon Lords' provided some very interesting concepts (e.g. the nice character and class system that I still remember in very good ways), challenging dungeons with good puzzles, interesting secrets (like the 'Demon Key' from 'Naga Temple') and had a great 'retro' feel. It wasn't very special but back then it entertained me quite good despite the many flaws.
Seriously there was a ton of bugs, terrible game design decisions and glitches: awful animations, missing loading screens, absolutely empty cities and buildings, nearly everything was unfunctional, figuring out stuff was made in hell (tutorial or explanations of the items/spells/skills... what's that?) and it felt like a bulky mess overall.
However I enjoyed it for quite some time back then and I still remember my badass Ninjutsu-Nethermagic character (Rogue + Mage class combination) in a good way.
Unfortunately they changed the game a lot back in the 'MMXII' version: they e.g. swaped the skill system for a cookie-cutter version, the new magic system was 'boring' and much stuff was still not working as intended. Anyway the worst thing was that they abandoned the 'new' game very fast and didn't care for updates or fixes for the problems.
Together with some others I voluntereed as tester and translator for the german version and spent many hours with translating the tool tips and looking for glitches and bugs (trust me, that list was long) but in the end it didn't even matter (many hours were wasted back then).
So now there's this 'new' version and I've been looking at it with a lot of critical thoughts in mind. However I thought 'Can't be worse than the last version' and started another 'adventure'. That was some hours ago...
... and I can say it's better. Way better than the MMXII version and in most parts better than the original version. I didn't encounter any huge bugs or crashes (the small ones they belong to the game like heat to fire), they finally added necessary options and higher difficulties, changing your weapon manually is possible once again and the map's hidden again.
Besides there is also the good stuff from 'MMXII' like the way better interface, hotkeys for spells and items, randomized loot and tool tips. They improved the weird systems to make them kind of okay (I'd still kill for the old character and class system) and overall it's running quite smoothly (in comparison to the 'whole time stuttering' and the awful loading times of the earlier versions'...).
________________________________________________________________________________
So... can I recommend the game? Well that's a difficult question.
The 'Steam Edition' version is definitely 'okay' and way better than the last one but it's necessary to see what the developers will do with all the feedback and the information they are now able to get from the players. Will they fix stuff (e.g. the problem with the lines/voice of NPCs: if you click at a person several times he will repeat his whole dialogue that many times. That's absolutely awful ingame) or abandon the game like the last version? They released one patch that adressed the MP but I would prefer improvements to the SP.
In addition it's 'Dungeon Lords' - that game was a special kind of trashy RPG and will stay that way no matter what you'll do. The animations are awful, the world's empty, the story has more clichés than an 80's movie, the technical aspects are totally outdated, it feels horrible in so many ways...
... but damned, I still kind of like it. It's such a special game. In a way somebody would say 'Oh he's such a special boy'. I'd rate it a 6 out of 10 (maybe only because the original version was one of the first RPGs I've ever played and there are some good memories besides bugs and glitches...)
I trend towards a recommendation, but mostly for players of the original 'Dungeon Lords' who didn't already hate it back then. However the recommendation depends totally on the question if the developers are willing to continue the support for the game. Else it will fail the same way as its 'parents'. There's much stuff to fix but deep down there's potential for a nice entertaining oldschool RPG. Maybe you should wait grabbing it until the developers show that they now care for their game and support it with fixes and patches...
And for most of the others ones, who have never played or even heard of 'Dungeon Lords'  (probably 85%): Skip it, there's better stuff out there. Way better stuff. There are too many bad design decisions and bulky systems to bother with until you may see some positive aspects. However the RPG has definitely potential for some hilarious and funny times - and if it only be due to bugs, glitches or weird things happening and you raging about everything.

I mean there's just so much here that screams "I can be good if you let me" but the devs clearly had no idea where to take the game. Much of the game is hidden away so you'll need to be prepared to read information online on which quests to take for which classes/guilds and heraldry but most of the guides are kind of outdated. One I read had stat requirements for the classes which I can only assume was for the classic as this version has no such requirements. The game won't tell you that you will pick a total of 5 classes. Two classes come from the original 4 (Fighter/Adept/Mage/Rogue), Two from Secondary Classes (either upgrades or hybrid classes, roughly 20), and then One final Third Tier class which is an upgrade of one of the secondaries you chose (excluding the Shadowlord Class). This is mind blowing to me and sounds like insane fun. The problem is that the classes past the original 4 ONLY GIVE NEW SKILLS. New skills are not new spells, new skills include the ability to use polearms, plate, dual wield, etc. The Third Tier classes give a passive buff and one diabolic skill which is specialized to that third tier class.
The problem that comes out of this is that getting a new tier 2 class is nothing. The fact you can choose two tier 2 classes is a joke because you'll be able to get the skills you want from a single tier 2 class and the second one you choose will likely just be for the tier 3 upgrade.
Spells are only learned by the first two classes you pick Warrior-Rune, Adept-Celestial, Mage-Arcane, Rogue-Nether. However! Mage also has the Nether skill so you can already purchase Nether spells (or find them) making a Rogue rather useless. The Rogue starts with extra skills such as pickpocket, sneak, and dual wield. The former 2 are worthless and dual wielding is learned by most classes later on.
Skills are things such as Athletics, Armor (Cloth, Leather) useability, Sword Fighting, Arcane Magic, etc. It's supposed to be used to increase these abilities and some of them (such as those you fight with, sword/arcane/rune/nether/celestial) can upgrade on their own. Some like Atheletics you have to spend skill points on.
At every level up you get 3 stat and 3 skill points. (It appears you also get skill points on quest completions but I'm not 100% on that)
Now I get that this is won't be agreed upon by everyone, but to me the better way to have handled this would be to TAKE AWAY the stat points that players get. Skills should no longer passively level as you use them. This causes a change in the game. Stat points are allocated as you level up dependent on the race you picked. Classes should now offer stat bonuses to your character which makes it far more worthwhile to go get new classes. Now that skills have to be actively leveled on their own, it would need to be lowered to level them easier (or give more points per level).
The way the game is now with skills is that you'll end up level 20 and invest all your points in Arcane to only have it level 18 at best. Most of the game lies to you like with Honor, claiming to lower prices and increase EXP but does no such thing. Diminishing returns are pretty huge on this game imo, maxing one stat means jack all and I could hardly tell any of the stats even did anything. I had roughly 70 STR (increases Weapon Damage) and was hitting for next to nothing. I spent another playthrough maxing INT and found out the joys of how it doesn't help level skills any faster.
I like that they removed the stat requirements, it made all the races viable. But females >>>> any other race simply due to the extra heraldry they get for the womens guild.
It's okay, I have a lot more problems with it (HALL OF LOOOORDS) like with the randomly spawning goons that swarm every inch of towns and rolling hills. But it'll entertain people for a few hours before you can't stand it anymore.
Like certain parts of the story that require you to run back and forth across a huge godforsakenly empty map. Have fun.
(And don't anyone tell me Moonstones. As it is even if you know the code you have to activate it manually once first, AND EVEN THEN you can't just TP from just anywhere.)

Receiver is more or less a proof of concept that actually comes off being a reasonable game. The primary focus is on mastering gun control. This includes ejecting the magazine, filling it with bullets, replacing the magazine, engaging the slide, and turning off the safety so it's ready to fire. It takes some getting used to, but it's not that difficult after a little practice.
The game part ends up being a permadeath environment where you search for and collect audio tapes while trying to avoid being shot by randomly placed turrets and flying drones. The player spawns with one of three guns that may or may not be ready to fire, a random number of bullets and magazines, and sometimes a flashlight. The one aspect that makes this game engaging is that you always have to be aware of your gun state, especially how many bullets you have in your magazine before you decide to engage a target. Ammunition is scarce making shots that much more valuable. The turrets and drones are quite tough which, combined with the weapon control elements, makes for some very cautious gameplay.
Make no mistake, Receiver is certainly rough around the edges. The environment isn't randomized; only the enemies and audio tape locations. The graphics are not interesting, nor optimized. It feels laggy at times. It can even unfairly spawn you with no gear or in a bad spot. However, it does master the element of weapon handling. It can become quite intense if your magazine runs dry while a drone is hunting you down and you need to pull off a precision reload in the moment. And for that aspect, I give it a thumbs up.

Final Fantasy X/X-2 HD Remaster on PC is probably the definitive version of both games for you to play.
Final Fantasy X for me is one of the best JRPG's of all time for various reasons: the world of Spira is rich and diverse; it has a great story, even if sometimes some things don't make much sense; the cast is rich; the combat system is old school, but that's the reason why i like it: turn based combat; to win battles you'll need different strategies even for normal encounters; leveling up through a grid allows for more customization; the soundtrack is simply amazing. Although there are a few things that i don't really like: idle party members don't gain AP; the minigames are crap (except for blitzball); the areas are mostly corridors, and there's no airship; you still can't skip cutscenes (why?). But still, it's a great game that alone deserves you to buy this collection. And you get all the international version content (extra superbosses and a X-2 prologue). It's worth it.
And then there's Final Fantasy X-2. As a whole, i actually like this game, but i understand most of the criticism this game has: it's a fanservice cashgrab; the map is mostly recycled from X; it has almost no story, and what's here isn't much interesting; it's mostly a side-quest galore (but better that the ones in X, although blitzball here kinda sucked for me); the cast is less interesting; the soundtrack sucks (with some exceptions). It seems that the best thing this game has is the combat, going back to the ATB system and adding a class change mechanic mid-combat. It has a lot of options, but for me it's almost pointless, since most of the strategy from X was removed. With a few exceptions, you can beat most of the game by just using the normal attack and healing with Hi-Potions without too much trouble. But despite all this, it's still an enjoyable game, only not as good as X. And this international version adds a lot of content. First, there's the creature capture where you can capture and use monsters in combat, even if you don't have control over them. Leveling them up unlocks a mini story with a cutscene. Many monsters have cutscenes to unlock, and if you watch them all there's around 4-6 hours of extra movies. They are silly, but made me laugh.
Secondly, there's the Final Mission, a rogue-like dungeon turn-based game that serves as an epilogue to X-2. And i was surprised by it. It's not a minigame, but almost an entire game that will take you around 10-20 hours to beat. It has an incredible amount of depht for what it is. It starts easy, but becomes hard if you don't have a solid strategy. Fortunately, there's plenty of good options, and i enjoyed playing it.
This remaster also adds an audio drama epilogue, and it's bad. It's 30 minutes of screwing with the story of X. Just terrible. This PC version also includes some in-game cheats like superspeed and auto-battle (great for grinding) and an auto-save that saves you a lot of trouble, trust me. It makes the games a little easier, but they are optional. It has a 30 FPS cap, but it works just fine. It will run on almost all PC's, and i never experienced slowdown or a crash. The download size is big though. In the end, this is a great package that includes 2 entire games (one great and one good) and a lot of extras including an extra game. On your PC. And the price is also fair for what you get.

If you are a fan of psychological horror, this a fantastic, albeit short game can deliver a lingering sense of terror that few games in the genre can seem to pull off.  The developer of this game created it with the intention of creating a feeling similar to that of when he had struggled with obsessive–compulsive disorder and depression, and a feeling of bleak hopelessness is ever present thanks to the atmosphere of this game.  The hand drawn artwork of the game is simple yet effective in creating tension.  There is a lot of repetition both in gameplay and visual art, and while that may at first seem like a bad thing, it is used to make some of the smallest differences seem more jarring and uncomfortable and only add to the haunting atmosphere.
Controls are a similar situation.  Movement is slow and while there is a run button, your character has asthma and tires out very quickly.  This mixed with the narrow corridors makes every enemy encounter terrifying as you try in vain to out run or out maneuver them.  The story has your character continuously waking from on nightmare into another, sometimes from performing the correct actions and other times from not, and since there is no 'Game Over' screen, there can be many times that you are unsure if you are doing the right thing or not.  This system adds to the feeling of hopelessness and with three different endings, there is some draw to going back through and if things could be different.
Over all this is tense and atmospheric horror game that successfully instills a sense of dread and hopelessness, which may turn some players away, but is worth at least one play through for the impressive experience.

FarHomeCryFront is a fps with rpg elements. Kind of like. You guessed it any Ubisoft game you ever played. But... It reminds me a lot of Dying Light if you hold the zombies than anything else. And where are the  cheese steaks?
The story is there. It is not great, kind of like Dying Light but a little better. You are a person who gets kidnapped with the intent of murder, freed then kidnapped with the intent to murder, then freed to help the second kidnappers kill people. What are you resisting? Who cares, just grab your gun. Indepence!!!
Since this is an open world game I should touch on the world itself. It's very well detailed, the civilian npc all give off a oppressed dirty life. All the enemies look the same. There are many interiors to hide in, like Dying Light. The map size is kind of small, but given the level of detail and clutter in every ally it suits the game fine. This game takes place in the City of Brotherly Love. Philly. Philadelphia is a great choice for a game world. I wish other devs would try something different cities from the typical L.A. or NYC. I wish they accually had the Philly accent and characteristics of loud and abrupt people,or atleast had some sports team references.
So gameplay. It is like Far Cry. There is mild parkour, guns, and dirt bikes. Seriously if you do not like Far Cry. Just don't. The guns can be modified, but I would have perfered more variety off of real guns.
Graphics. Well first off there are a lot of options here to tinker with. The visuals when turned up look incredibly good. I mean one of the best looking games out there good with a some Sweet Fx. The textures, lighting, and draw distance are all top notch. The down side is this game is demanding. I run a 1080ti and 2160p will give me drop under 60fps on high settings with shaders on medium. Drop to 1440p and Ultra+Sweet Fx is no problem. Still once you get it running well it is smooth. The facial animations are incredible and there is a lot of detail to render. Though the shadows on low or medium res are ugly and trees could have been done better. There are also a lot of bugs. Fires burning on nothing.
Sound is there. Like the story it's not bad, but not great. The voices seem so middle america. Phily is a city where you will here ebonics, loud people yelling things like wooder or crayola crowns. Seems like a missed opertunity. The music is another miss. Licensed music could have been a nice addition with the likes of Boyz II Men, Will Smith, Chubby Checker, Hall & Oats Jim Croce, the Roots, DJ Jazzy Jeff, ect.  There is a vibe to Philly and they did not capture it. If they did the game world would feel so much more lived in.
So for what I paid for this game I can not complain. This is a good game and a great buy for under $15.

It was creepy for most of the game but by the time I got to the branching paths near the end it was just a slog to get through. I wouldn't have minded if the story itself was solid and connected; above almost nothing else I LOVE playing a game with a strong narrative, however for me, I didn't get that either. The game deals with mental illness, insanity, love and loss both within and without... but it just kind of throws things on the wall and hopes that they resonate with the audience. Quick scenes being flung at you without relating one to another is par for the course in each nightmare. I'm quite certain some people will get something out of this that I didn't, specifically because of the vagueness, but I think that audience is select and few. Overall I'd say it's a Glass of Milk/10

Having beaten every boss in Dark Souls, Dark Souls 3, Demon's Souls, and Bloodborne, it's no doubt that the Soulsborne franchise is one of my favorites of all time. That being said, this one is arguably the weakest in the series. However, that does not mean the game is bad as It is actually still a very solid game. The difficulty in this game feels a bit on the unfair side of things, and the game punishes you more than it should when you die (lose 5% of your max health every time you die down to 50% max life, restored by using an item that feels far harder less common than it should). Early on there are many challenges that feel a little bit to steep for new players, even by Dark Souls standards. This game is also siginficantly longer than the other Soulsborne games, so much so that it sort of overstays its welcome.
While I enjoyed and completed the other Soulsborne games solo, I eventually caved in and did a co-op playthrough with one of my friends who was in a similar situation as me. The game became much easier than before, and I ended up enjoying the game significantly more than I did alone, and deaths felt less punishing because I could just beat the boss on my friend's world to regain all of my life.
This version of the game is also one of the smoothest games I have played to date. Even though my monitor only supports up to 60 fps, I feel like I am running this game at 200fps. I don't know how good the optimization is, as my computer is far more powerful that this game's recommended requirements.
All in all, I would recommend this game as long as you aren't afraid of a challenge, and/or if you have a friend to play through the game with.

Recommended but with one GIANT catch:
For everything the game does right, I love it. The city building aspect is intuitive and brilliantly done, but the game would have been better named something like "waiting to die". The game play in the first 20 minutes of a map is about as intense and involved as the game gets. After that, it pretty much drops off and becomes redundant. The entire purpose of the game revolves around keeping your population moving forward without stalling to what will eventually, many hours later if you can be bothered to play long enough, the death of your village. Why? Iron. If you play one map long enough, you WILL eventually run out of iron, both surface and minable iron. Once this happens, you will run out of tools. When this happens, it will trigger a domino effect where you people stand around pulling their puds until they finally starve to death. Your only hope of survival at this point in the game is relying on traders to bring you iron and tools, but by this stage in the game, you really aren't doing anything but watch the seasons go by. After a solid 10+ hours of playing what starts out as an awesome game, it becomes a bit boring and pointless to play.
The game would have benefitted greatly from mulitplayer and conflict/combat via pvp or AI (either in terms of enemy villages or simple marauding barbarians). The creator of the game doesn't have any interest in adding these things, so the game really has no where else to go from here sadly.
So why am I recommending the game? Because for all that it does right, it's worth the play. At $20, I'm not entirely sure it's worth it, so if it ever goes on sale you'd be a fool not to buy it. If you consider $20 a fair price for 10-20 hours of entertainment, it's worth the price of admission.

This review is mainly for people who played the original game back in 200X.
I played this game back in the day when it was chock full of bugs, empty towns, characters that were void of any interest and a multiplayer system that would cause the game to crash...
And you know what? I loved it.
For some reason there was a charm to the way that the game allowed you to stand there, shooting your bow for 20+ minutes to kill enemies that were never meant to be fought at your level, finally killing them and gaining hundreds of thousands of experience points. The game also rewarded you for playing on harder difficulties by rewarding more experience.
I remember doing backflips in full plate armour over mountains to reach areas that were meant for the final hours of the game. The way I was able to increase my speed so my jump attacks would shred the enemies like a wood chipper was also hilarious.
The game's mechanics made it fun, giving you the ability to use whatever spells you find as long as you had the proper ingredients, equip whatever weapons and armour you wanted with penalties if you didn't have the required stats and of course the magical power to pause the game in any menu and wait for your stuns and debuffs to wear off while the myriad of enemies politely wait for you to check your stats or find that spellbook that you really need.
If I were to give it an honest rating, it'd likely be a 3/10. It wasn't a good game at all, though it was fun and hilarious despite all these shortcomings. I would compare it to movies like "The Room" or "Spiderman 3", as I don't think either of these movies are good, though they're hilarious fun.
Now to describe my experience with the steam edition. The cool starting menu was taken out, which made me frown, though I can get past that. My character was a Zaur fighter, much like my previous playthroughs which eventually became deathlords by the end of the game. They give you starting rune spells which I found kind of strange, though they were useful. As I killed my first few groups of goblins, I noticed that I couldn't equip bows. "But... But why, though", I asked. Later I realized that the only spells I WAS allowed to use were the ones given to me by leveling up, making it seem like a bad singleplayer version of a tab-targetting MMORPG. When I finally got to a shopkeeper, I sold all my junk weapons and armour, ending up with over 10k gold (which for some reason is noted with a $ sign). I was able to buy everything I needed at any point because nothing costed enough to make a dent in my wallet. I remember in the old game there was a weapon called the giant battle axe, which required 35 strength to use without penalty. I ended up chopping through enemies like they were made of chocolate with it, despite my strength score of 20. The point at which I was no longer able to handle the changes was when I arrived at the council of ancient elders. You see, in the original game, you could stand there hacking away for minutes on end and take out these huge health boss ghosts and get loads of exp. Now they're level 80 and I can only hit them once every few minutes...
In short, the core game is still there. The issue is that the core game was the worst part of it and they changed all the charming bits of it that I liked. If you actually enjoyed the story and were annoyed by the bugs and glitches, this is for you. If you enjoyed the old game because of how stupid it was in spite of its serious tone, I'd recommend staying away from this one.

You see a lot of games coming out these days dealing with end times, the moral dilemmas, but they leave you out of that "survivor" state where yo u're also fighting against your environment, as well as dealing with the fact the world is crumbling around you.
A huge amount of minor details, tons of mini-stories, characters, interactions, discoverables, etc. allow this game to have a surprising depth I didn't expect when I jumped in figuring it was something akin' to an endless runner.
thoughts:
Art 10/10, though there were many dark scenes,most things were easily discernable, great backgrounds, huge amount of detail to items fore, and background. This came in to play extra for me as i've a bit of color blindness so picking things out can sometimes be problematic.
The pixelated style definitly didn't stop these guys from making things look  great. Theres a distinct feel you get depending on where in the game you are entirely based off your environment.
The little touches, like the extra frame when you're readying a melee attack with a weapon, showing you in that braced position, viewing the gun from a different angle, it almost looks like the gun itelf is in 3d at that point ,just breathes life into it. kinda like those little battery powered fake sleeping kittens that pretend to breathe. (besides the point)
Gameplay: 9/10, Controls were tight, weapons and interactables behaved well. Minor issue with me giving a medpack to somebody, but them dying anyways, but solid gameplay, tight controls, everything behaves "as you'd expect" you're not left baffled by why a thing did what it did
GAME FEEL: 10/10 as i'd stated, it really nails in that end of times end of humanity feel, evokes deep thought, but keeps things light enough that it still feels like you're playing a platformer.
I'm in no way good with ANYTHING spooky, so a few times i found myself turning back, waiting a little make sure its safe before nutting up and forging onward. Atmospheric, the music and sound direction is well done, really pulls the feel of the game together.
Closing Notes: Again, i'm just loving the sheer amount of discoverables, details, little notes you find, they really flush out the world, and the characters as at a glance, things seem kinda "Flat" (get it? 2d? eyyy) but still, if you have an afternoon / evening to burn, this game is really great for that, it really draws you in.
I picked it up on sale and felt not only did I get my money's worth, but then some, and therefore am gonna be gifting a few to my friends for them to enjoy too.

I need to update this review. I had been messing around with the windows Icons for a while. Some games have problems with Win 7 and Win 10 due to the fact that the Operating Systems has changed the way the Mouse Device Context works and sometimes you have to reduce the game into windows mode to get the mouse cursor to work with the mouse. That happened with the game "Titan Quest." But, I could not find such feature on the Dungeon Lords icon on the startup bar. So I went directly to the DL Steam Edition application exe. file and right clicked and brought up the properties panel. Went to the Compatability tab and changed the compatability mode for Win XP Service Pack 3 and checked the boxes for Disable display scaling on high DPI settings and Run as Administrator. That fixed the problems. So far, the start of the game came out without a hitch.
I actually like how the options and charater creation had been rearanged and looks alot better than the original set up UI. Now, hope the game plays as well, or even better, than the Collectors Edition was. Really loved playing this game.
BTW, when you start with the messenger, before you move anywheres, save the game. Then go to the chest that is behind the ruins wall and open it. If you do not get the bow, keep reloading and going to the chest untill you finally recieved the bow. After that, get on the rock that is west of your area and get on it. Keep on shooting the enemies and building up your acrobatics as well as some other needed skills ... acrobatics, on the 4th level will let your character make a jump backwards
flip so he can get on the rock much quicker before more enemies come. This can build your skills up as well as collect money and other items that will help you in your quest. Yea, it will take some time to get all that up to snuff, but it's worth it.

It's a simple game that's built around handling a gun.  Instead of just "point to shoot, R to reload,"  The game gives you simple to comprehend keyboard commands to do everything you can imagine when it comes to weapons.  With the Revolver, my favorite weapon, instead of "R" and now your clip is emptied and new bullets put in place, you press E to push the Cylinder out to the side, V to use the bullet release, which sometimes you have to tap a few times for all the bullets to fall out (a realistic scenario), Z to load bullets in one at a time (No speed loader clip), and R to replace the cylinder.  They also have a mechanic (works most of the time) where you can use the scroll wheel to spin the cylinder.  Albeit there's only 3 (maybe 4, don't remember off the top of my head) pistols that you can spawn with, each one is mechanically different, and requires you to learn how the gun works to effectively use it.  It's a difficult, thought oriented shooter, which is rare on it's own.  And here's the best part above it all:  They mastered it perfectly.  Yes, I know the Graphics are cheesy, yes I know it has only 2 enemies, yes I know it's very simple.  However, the Cheesy Graphics play into the storyline if you listen to the audio tapes you collect, the 2 enemies fit that bill as wel.  And the games simplicity is where it gains my love for it.  Instead of making the game as complicated as Battlefield 4 with all the whirling twirling exploding heads for just the reason of "We want to push the boundaries of gaming" they chose to make it simple, defined, and to the point.  You are not playing this for crazy shootoffs with your friends.  You are playing it to see how well you understand some of the simple mechanics of a pistol.  If anyone who reads this enjoys shooters, I would take the time to play this game.
Definitely worth it. <3

The Final Station achieves everything it sets out to do, with no small amount of finesse. Mechanically tight and satisfying, melancholically atmospheric, and a narrative that sets you as a minute but emblematic element of a large, intriguing and purposefully obfuscated world.
The gameplay is split into two distinctive elements. One is exploring an environment for resources, snippets of story, and passcodes needed to progress while combatting zombie-like creatures. The combat isn't difficult, but rather asks you questions, which finding the answer to is satisfying without being punishing. While I don't particularly enjoy punishing combat anyway, my appreciation of how combat feels in The Final Station is in it's tonal consistency with the narrative. The feel and progression of the combat mirrors that of the emotional narrative. It feels laconic and rhythmic, almost meditative as you come to terms with the slowly unfolding and declining world. This element of the gameplay feels satisfying not just in and of itself, but especially so because of how it compliments the narrative and tone, contributing to an overall game that is more accomplished than the sum of it's parts.
The other element of the gameplay is akin to plate-spinning, keeping parts of your train and your passengers from breaking down, which while not as satisfying as the other gameplay elements, does do the same thing in terms of feeling consistent and complimentary to the narrative. However, it is also complimentary to the exploration and combat element. It punctuates the exploration and combat sections, which breaks up the gameplay and gives a sense of space and lets the game breathe. In this way it reminds me of the relationship between traversal and combat in open world games, whereby the traversal punctuates the combat, building tension and giving the player room to shift their focus, and giving a sense of importance to the combat.
The narrative is more emotional or tonal than it is driven by character or plot. Aside from the fact that I think this has been done very effectively in The Final Station, I think this focus is very clever on the part of the developer. Personally, I have found that videogame narratives are typically weakest when they are driven primarily by character or plot, especially when compared to other mediums of narrative fiction such as film or literature. There are many reasons for this, such as the burden being beholden to gameplay mechanics, a lack of artistic talent or vision in studios, but I won't digress. The fundament of The Final Station's success is that it relies on and explores the strengths of the medium. The game achieves a satisfying, affecting, and resonant emotional and tonal narrative through the complimentary uses of gameplay and world-building, with sparing use of plot and character. All of which would be for nought if that narrative was not interesting, compelling, believable, or satisfying.
The narrative of The Final Station is successful because it eskews another weakness of videogames as a medium, in my opinion. That weakness being the use of grand, epic stories with the player character at the centre. This trope in videogames has been as bland and unsatisfying for as long as it has been in film, the medium it borrowed the trope from. Particularly satisfying in The Final Station, however is the fact that more than just avoid it, it is uses this trope as a foil, and borrows it's cache to do something more interesting. In the game, the blockbuster, epic, sci-fi story is happening just out of sight. It does so literally at times to do so figuratively, with the high budget scenes from the trailer happening just after you leave or before you arrive. In one particularly emblematic moment, what is happening in the blockbuster is literally to big for you to see as you pass by. This contributes to the sense of helplessness and pessimism of the emotional narrative, but also says something about the experience of ordinary people in the grand narratives of our world. Things really are too big and complex for us to comprehend. We are not the key players in the great games of history. We are largely powerless, changing ourselves to adjust to the world around us rather than changing it, spinning plates and just keeping our heads above water until the inevitable and categorically unepic moment of our passing.

Games rarely consider the details of ammunition. The amount of rounds a player carries shows up as a number in the interface, and reloading requires nothing more than tapping a button. Actually handling and managing the bullets that go into a gun is a complex task, however. Receiver, an first-person shooter (FPS) from Wolfire Games, wants to remind us of that fact. Unfortunately, it never makes it clear why we should care.
Receiver drops the player into a randomly-generated set of rooftop rooms and tasks him with recovering 11 tapes of droning narration (without subtitles) and that explain the game's story. The player begins with an unpredictable loadout including one handgun in one of various states and some ammunition. The player may also start with a flashlight or, if his gun is semi-automatic, a spare magazine or two. He must then move through the multi-tiered linear world looking for the tapes, which can be frustrating since one can go through at least nine rooms in a row without encountering a single one. I myself haven't managed to get all 11 in a single playthrough before dying.
The game only has two kinds of enemies: a stationary gun turret and a flying drone, both of which can kill the player with a single hit. Each has some associated visual cues, but most of the time the player will need to hear their alert chirps to know when he's been spotted and when it's safe to move. The distribution of enemies changes, and on rare occasions they can be avoided. Because enemies are difficult to evade and pickups can be hard to see, however, killing everything in a room is generally the only option.
Receiver started as a response to a seven-day FPS challenge and definitely feels like it, from its spare graphics to its room-entry stutter. The hook for the game is that it presents the process of actually reloading the firearm in a significant level of detail. The HUD has no ammo count, and bullets do not magically fly from the corpses of your enemies into magazines the player can swap out every time he takes a breath. Rounds must be gathered manually and loaded into magazines by hand, with the gun safely tucked away. If there's no spare magazine, the player has to eject the empty, refill it, then shove it back home again. The only way to know the number of bullets remaining is to remember how many have been fired or check by eye.
Receiver fails to establish that the complexity of gun handling matters. The detailed reloading scheme doesn't speak to the story, the aesthetic, or the other mechanics. Receiver doesn't treat aiming or shooting the weapon with the same carefulness it reserves for reloading, and doesn't fiddle much with the basics of movement, yet running and shooting are the core verbs of the game. By making the world randomly generated, the developers give up the opportunity to design encounters where efficient reloading matters. As a consequence, becoming more skilled with the game's most intricate systems doesn't make a player any more likely to succeed. Receiver's complex gun-handling mechanics are irrelevant in the context of its larger design.
That's a shame, because the larger design has nothing to recommend it. The perfunctory story and low-poly world of Receiver aren't interesting to explore in their own right, much less when one must overcome the game's unforgiving difficulty. The choice to generate the world randomly might add replay value, but it also adds much to the frustration level while costing the game the ability to present rewarding encounters that highlight its unique mechanics. Receiver has a neat idea at its core, but that didn't translate into an interesting game.

Even though the game wasn't what I expected, I still enjoyed it all the way through. I found the story to be a little WTF while going through it but at the end I think it came together nicely.
I thought it was going to be about using a train to build up a group of survivors, stopping at dangerous stations to gather up supplies to make the train bigger/stronger/etc. That is not what this game is about.
You go from station to station, you do have to keep survivors alive during a brief travel minigame (it's not hard once you get the hang out it), but at each station you drop people off and pick up new people. You also venture out into the stations to gather supplies, it's a bit of a 2d platform shooter (if that's the right terminology). You don't build up the train, nor do you build up a big clan of survivors.
Overall the gameplay is okay but what kept me coming back is the atmosphere and story. Bad Things are happening and as a lowly train operator you get to see/know a bit more than Joe Average but things are still a little mysterious and sometimes confusing. I usually prefer gameplay over story, but the gameplay was decent enough and the story was my kind of thing, so I enjoyed this one from start to finish.
That being said, some people won't like the story. Thing's aren't always plainly spelled out, and some people might find it cliched, overwrought, nonsensical, etc. Everyone has their own taste and in a story focused game it's a lot harder to say "XYZ is good" like it is with gameplay.
In the end I think it's quite a good game but some people will still hate it and it's kind of hard for me to tell which side of the fence you'll land on.

I played a lot of Starcraft, and Command & Conquer in those days when internet gaming was pretty much non-existant.
Years had passed and I was into the wonderful technology of hardline internet gaming.  I had played a tonne of Unreal Tournament and at that time I was introduced to Counterstrike.  Boy, let me tell you my world changed from that point and I was instantly hooked.  Every boy wants to play with real guns, and this was it!
I played CS for years before Steam, and Counterstike Source came along.  I bet I would have logged 2000+ hours of gaming with all of the CS's together.
I loved playing Source, I spent my hard earned money for 2 years going to a network gaming cafe before buying my own cpu and copy of it.  I remember playing people online and they'd always complain that I was hacking.  A lot of times I would have a 9-1 kill to death ratio.  Yes, kids hated me, but my clan of friends loved me.
So, long and short of it all...Honestly, I do have an addictive personality, but gaming is far from harmful compared to drugs and alcohol.  I admit, Counterstrike, SAVED MY LIFE!!!!

Having beaten every boss in Dark Souls, Dark Souls 3, Demon's Souls, and Bloodborne, it's no doubt that the Soulsborne franchise is one of my favorites of all time. That being said, this one is arguably the weakest in the series. However, that does not mean the game is bad as It is actually still a very solid game. The difficulty in this game feels a bit on the unfair side of things, and the game punishes you more than it should when you die (lose 5% of your max health every time you die down to 50% max life, restored by using an item that feels far harder less common than it should). Early on there are many challenges that feel a little bit to steep for new players, even by Dark Souls standards. This game is also siginficantly longer than the other Soulsborne games, so much so that it sort of overstays its welcome.
While I enjoyed and completed the other Soulsborne games solo, I eventually caved in and did a co-op playthrough with one of my friends who was in a similar situation as me. The game became much easier than before, and I ended up enjoying the game significantly more than I did alone, and deaths felt less punishing because I could just beat the boss on my friend's world to regain all of my life.
This version of the game is also one of the smoothest games I have played to date. Even though my monitor only supports up to 60 fps, I feel like I am running this game at 200fps. I don't know how good the optimization is, as my computer is far more powerful that this game's recommended requirements.
All in all, I would recommend this game as long as you aren't afraid of a challenge, and/or if you have a friend to play through the game with.

Recommended but with one GIANT catch:
For everything the game does right, I love it. The city building aspect is intuitive and brilliantly done, but the game would have been better named something like "waiting to die". The game play in the first 20 minutes of a map is about as intense and involved as the game gets. After that, it pretty much drops off and becomes redundant. The entire purpose of the game revolves around keeping your population moving forward without stalling to what will eventually, many hours later if you can be bothered to play long enough, the death of your village. Why? Iron. If you play one map long enough, you WILL eventually run out of iron, both surface and minable iron. Once this happens, you will run out of tools. When this happens, it will trigger a domino effect where you people stand around pulling their puds until they finally starve to death. Your only hope of survival at this point in the game is relying on traders to bring you iron and tools, but by this stage in the game, you really aren't doing anything but watch the seasons go by. After a solid 10+ hours of playing what starts out as an awesome game, it becomes a bit boring and pointless to play.
The game would have benefitted greatly from mulitplayer and conflict/combat via pvp or AI (either in terms of enemy villages or simple marauding barbarians). The creator of the game doesn't have any interest in adding these things, so the game really has no where else to go from here sadly.
So why am I recommending the game? Because for all that it does right, it's worth the play. At $20, I'm not entirely sure it's worth it, so if it ever goes on sale you'd be a fool not to buy it. If you consider $20 a fair price for 10-20 hours of entertainment, it's worth the price of admission.

I'm very disappointed that I have come to the decision to not recommend this game. I tried to justify a recommendation so many times through my playthrough, but in the end, I simply cannot.
I would like to start with the positive qualities of this game. The sound design is amazing and the graphics and animations are very unique and interesting. It succeeds in creating an intense and terrifying atmosphere despite its story book artstyle.
I was absolutely in love with this game for the first thirty minutes, however, the experience got bogged down by bad design choices and over indulgence.
There are two enemies of a horror games, boredom and frustration, and unfortunately, this is exactly the two flavors that remain in my mouth after my playthrough.  The game makes a hard turn from disturbing imagery to challenging puzzles, which was a bad choice.  In each stage, there is a unique type of monster that blocks your way, unfortunately, it is only one kind of monster.  This game would have benefitted greatly from adding one or two more types of hazards and each environment. However, it is the puzzle design that I found so frustrating.  A good puzzle game will teach you the tools necessary for you to solve the puzzle and then throw a curveball. In a good puzzle game, the player should be constantly flipping between the feelings of the puzzle being easy and the puzzle being impossible. But this is not what happens in Neverending Nightmares. Instead, it turns into a pixel hunt, where you are trying to find the little trick to each puzzle by peering through the  murky sketches. An example of this:
I had to resort to watching YouTube Walkthroughs, and the Youtubers frustration cemented in my mind that this design was flawed.  In a horror game like this, you should only be dying when the game decides it's important for the story. But, there is a mixture of scripted deaths which push forward the narrative and cheap deaths from failing to avoid an enemy that led to confusion and, eventually, took the atmosphere and horror out of the game.
Furthermore, the game is relatively short. My first and only playthrough ended up being roughly 1 hour and 40 minutes but there was probably 45 minutes of content. A little bit more restraint in the level design and the number of rooms and encounters would have greatly helped tighten it up.  I found myself throwing my arms up and asking the game what it wanted me to do.  There are multiple paths and endings, but I will not be going back to explore them.

Even though the game wasn't what I expected, I still enjoyed it all the way through. I found the story to be a little WTF while going through it but at the end I think it came together nicely.
I thought it was going to be about using a train to build up a group of survivors, stopping at dangerous stations to gather up supplies to make the train bigger/stronger/etc. That is not what this game is about.
You go from station to station, you do have to keep survivors alive during a brief travel minigame (it's not hard once you get the hang out it), but at each station you drop people off and pick up new people. You also venture out into the stations to gather supplies, it's a bit of a 2d platform shooter (if that's the right terminology). You don't build up the train, nor do you build up a big clan of survivors.
Overall the gameplay is okay but what kept me coming back is the atmosphere and story. Bad Things are happening and as a lowly train operator you get to see/know a bit more than Joe Average but things are still a little mysterious and sometimes confusing. I usually prefer gameplay over story, but the gameplay was decent enough and the story was my kind of thing, so I enjoyed this one from start to finish.
That being said, some people won't like the story. Thing's aren't always plainly spelled out, and some people might find it cliched, overwrought, nonsensical, etc. Everyone has their own taste and in a story focused game it's a lot harder to say "XYZ is good" like it is with gameplay.
In the end I think it's quite a good game but some people will still hate it and it's kind of hard for me to tell which side of the fence you'll land on.

So, The Crew, by Ubisoft.
It's a very nice idea, join friends and complete missions in high preformance cars. Sounds like The Fast and the Furious right? Joining a crew for sertain missions and for PvP is realy easy, leaving said crew is aswell. The missions in PvE are easy, even Solo.
The game has a short storyline by which at the end you are the Boss (V8) of a street racing gang that has gone international criminal orginasation. You achive so by means of driving missions using various vehicles like street cars, high preformance sport cars, dirt cars, trophy trucks and circuit speed demons. You can free ride unrestricted trough the USA freely switching between cars and explore a lot of sites, the game gives in game curency as a reward for visiting sight seeing area's and provides one or two lines of background info. Also you can get involved in police chases, and hamper other players that are being prosued.
The gameplay gives of a friendly arcade style feeling. The cars look real good and tons of costumization is available. The world you dive in is done quite good and I especially like how the road surface affects your grip. Rain and snow don't do your grip any good and the various type of vehicle will respond differently to it. Unfortunatly the road does need work, small bumbs and missalignments in road surfaces cause unecpected bumbs and jumps, or crashes if using a circuit car, and cause grip loss, sliding and other automotive mayhem. Something your computer controlled opponents don't seem to be bothered by.
Doing the faction missions, which only help with cashflow or so it seems, the opponents are of about the same level as you are, making for an intresting challange, if not for the unfair behaviour of the game favouring against you. Which i found frustrating and annoying at times.
The game as purely a racing game gets boring quite quickly after you have maxed out your personnal level and some cars you like to use. Doing the same "test", a mini challange, can get you rewarded with the best possible parts for your ride. The lvl 50 parts have 4 different bonusses so again, costumize and find the best setting. Making sure that cars that have maxed out still have a bit of difference in them. All sounds good right?
Yes, the game in istelf is quite good, be it short, and your reasons for playing it will mostly be becouse of your friends list. Gamers are friendly mostly but crews in PvP can realy ruin your day by having one or two members take out the competions and having their friends win easy. Well within the rules but not fair play.
The game has promise, and loads of DLC is indeed promised, including more cars and area's to explore. Most will have found the Mexican border crossing by now. But at the time of this writing, is not open yet.
Conclusion,
If I make the game sound in general not bad at all, why not reccomend it? Well, there's this one thing in the way of hours of fun gameing with your friends. Crashes, not in game car crashes but gamecrashes, computer crashes, network crashes, server connection interruptions, explained errors, unexplained errors, known errors that will give you a code and ask you to submit them. (the location the game suggest is the Ubi website but i couldn't figure out where to put them in.) In 60 hours of gameplay I calculated an interruption would take place on average every 3 hours of gameplay. Fairly annoying and other than the occasional lagg not very accepteble in this day and age. I don't think my PC has ever crashed on any other game besides The Crew. Save for windows update butting in but no-one can blame any game or develloper for that right? I won't at least.
So The Crew might seem as a must-have, but it isn't. So even if you still want to buy it, refrain from buying it together with the Seasons Pass untill you are satisfied with the game.
So, end of rant and pardon my English! (Yes, it's meant to be English)
