This game is just fantastic. Have you ever wanted to scrach that classic fantasy itch for some grand wizards with epic names pronouncing "Evil" in a silly way?  Or huge monsters smashing everything around them with wooden clubs? Or maybe giant red dragons spitting fireballs at you? Then this game is exactly what you're looking for.
You are either a Human, Elf, Dwarf, Lizard or one of the creatures of the forests called "demigoths" (Furry things), who is either a Warrior, Priest (of sorts), Mage or Rogue, each having various different abilities and mulitple ways to build his character. Like for example as a Rogue, you can either use a bow, axes, daggers or throwing weapons, and may only pick 2 at a time all while you get to level things like summoning power, lockingpicking skills, sneak skill, etc. making 1 class feel more like 3.  On top of that your character has the usual stats like Agility, Strenght, Intellect, etc. which you get to increase every level.
Once you know what you want to be, you just jump into the world. It's a visible 2005 game, the best way I could describe the graphics is that they look like Vanilla WoW but better in every way. I really doubt you will have any problems with them, for 2005, they look amazing. And some of the really well made models and enemy facial animations made it age well.
There are some other things that make the game look like an MMO. The action bar (where your abilities are placed) looks 1 to 1 like an MMO action bar, the way you level and gain experience and the way you get new loot and equip it are also identical to an MMO. The similarities really end there however. There aren't any quest markers, or tab-target combat or pointless mobs or grindy quests.
Infact, the combat and the overall gameplay experience you will have really makes me love this game. There is just something about how the arrows fly, how the throwing weapons get stuck in the creature until it dies, how powerful spells feel really powerful. That something is something rare and amazing, something that you could play hundreds of really popular RPGs and never find, something that makes every hit you deal in this game feel great. KNOCKBACK! Yes, this game has knockback. You know how in Elder Scroll games like Skyrim, you just take up your sword and slash at the opponent while he is slashing at you, making it a dull cut or smash fight until one of you suddenly falls down? Or how shooting fire at them will cause them to just stand there until they fall down dead? There is none of that here.
If you have 2 daggers and you are stabbing someone your size with them, they will get knockbacked with every single hit, making it look like you are actually doing some damage, same goes with arrows, spells, axes, maces, whatever! Every single hit feels like it counts. I know it seems like a small thing, but it makes the combat much, much better. Combine that with crazy monster abilities, like Trolls killing you in one massive blow or goblins on huge stake launchers. And you will find that combat will often be great fun.
The quests include great puzzles, nice storylines, and they will never hold your hand. Most of the time you are given very little actual information and have to figure it out yourself. Like early on in the game where you told to find this Elven village, yet were never told where it is and just have to randomly walk off into the forest. Probably getting attacked by wolves and all kinds of beasts instead.
There are of course bad things, which, I might add, are often completely overblown by some people, bugs were common and would often prevent progression, I haven't run into any so far, and the hope is that they removed them all, but you can never be sure. On top of that, quests provide TOO little information in certain cases, like this Vampire who will tell you you should meet her behind a mansion on the south side of a town, I've been running around for hours and couldn't find anything, that is a case where a quest lacking information didn't lead to more attention or immersion, but just confusion and a waste of time. The quests can be very badly written sometimes and just feel awkward, but that might be likable to some. The game was unfinished when it was released, and you can certainly see it some areas.
Good:
-Combat is really good because of knockback and aiming.
-Classic fantasy theme
-Plenty of ways to play and build your character
-Great graphics for the time
-Good quests that never hold your hand
-65~ hours worth of gameplay
-Large amounts of different enemies
-Plenty of loot and abilities
Bad:
-Sometimes badly written quests
-The possibility of bugs remaining
-Certain quests that provide TOO little information, leading to waste of time doing the wrong thing.
-A few unfinished areas in certain places.
Make of it what you want:
-Mobs seem to endlessly respawn in certain dungeons
-MMO-like action bar that you need to press
Overall, buy it if you want an amazing old-school kind of Fantasy RPG experience. It could have been better, but by the end of the day it's a great game that is simply fun to play.

The Final Station is simply what it is supposed to be - with a damn good story.
The graphics is nice. They are not the super detailed pixelart, but it does look good. Backgrounds looks super nice.
Combat is not hard at all and simply requires a tiny amount of planning.
So it is by no means a hardcore pixel shooter. More like relaxed fun combat. Some like that, other do not. I do.
It is made up in train-sections and map-sections
Train sections is (to my suprise) much easier than I had expected, though it got a bit hectic in the end.
You basically take care of ur passengers (food/medkit), while tending to different 'problems' on ur train.
The problems is very basic. It is more the food/medkit part, which u need to conserve carefully.
Some did not like this part, as they said it was too easy. I liked it, as I hate super hardcore difficulty. I just want to relax sometimes.
Map-sections is what I liked the most. Each time ur train stops at a station, you enter some sort of map. It can be a town, building, underground facility - whatever. Here you run around killing enemies and looting for resources. Food and Medkits is what u really want (to take care of ur passenger). This is a major part of the game, if not the main. You also find new passenger and information about the world (books, notes and such). I never used Medkits for myself and always saved each and everyone for my passengers.
Story is actually really really good. It is not directly told, but if u read stuff and pay attention to the environment, then you'll get a good idea of what is going on.
The game is re-playable once, if u ask me. I am going to do it for achievements and the fun of it. Sadly it does not really support a multiple re-runs, as u do not get ur end game items with u. There is no New Game+ so to say. You just restart everything. This is why I do not agree with the price. The game is not huge enough for that price tag, yet I do not regret buying it. So if u have few coins left and want a game u can play for days, find another one. If you have money to spare and want a really goood, but small adventure, they buy it.

The Crew is the first MMO to do something different and use cars and driving instead of the usual aray of fantasy characters.
It is an enjoyable mix of arcade/sim style racing with the added online benefits - namely being able to join and crew up with as many as 4 of your mates to race and cruise all over the USA.
Strengths are definately the enjoyment you get out of messing about with your friends whilst in your hotted up car, the graphics are good for next gen but for the PC it could be better, 60 FPS on PC runs smooth enough, the sound effects from the cars are nice and beefy and last but not least the size of the map and drivable area is absolutely massive.
The weaknesses are - its gets a bit laggy from time to time, there are not nearly enough visable players online making it not really feel like a MMO (at least not yet), not enough races on offer and the button mapping system is frustraiting when trying to really customize it.
The final verdict after 42 hours of playing time is despite its flaws it is an addictive driving game especially when cruising around with mates but no substitute for a real racer (wait for Project Cars).  This is well worth your money if you intend to play with friends online and like a massive map of the USA to drive around but if you want a hardcore racer to post times and compete against mates then this will only annoy you.

This is not a game for everyone so wether someone recommended this game or not is almost entirely based on their taste in games and as such introduce some bias. That being said I will now impart some of my bias upon you. Reciever is an interseting game to say the least: no fancy graphics, minimal to no story, and a difficulty on a level of reality unobtainable by another game in this genre. Where Reciever truely shines is its delivery of narative through gameplay. There are a few (11 to be exacy) tapes throughout the game that have recordings on them that help explain the basic premise (the  goal of the game being to collect all 11), but the entirety of the feel and the lessons this game imparts (as any game worth its salts has at least some knowledge to impart) are based in its mechanics. This game takes guns very seriously: they kill. You take one bullet in this game and you die. Not to mention, as many comments will tell you, they ain't easy to operate (E, ~, 2, 3, ~, Z, R, F to reload?). Which leads to the conveince of theme. This game is hard. It is almost pointless to expect to win with any sense of ease; which is exactly what the narritive delivers. Without spoiling too much, you can essentially die endlessly in this game. A never ending cycle of death, failure and pain. Sounds like a message to me (not to mention the recordings speaking of a dystopian society). This coupled with the game's core mechanics being gun manipulation means that the narritive is almost entirely non-verbal, which is fantastic. Again, I do not reccommend this game to everyone (it is rather artsy and only made in a week), but is excellent for what it is, and I hope we can all learn something about guns from something other than Battlefield, CoD, Halo, etc where they're just tools. I wish you a good day, and thanks for listening to my ramblings on :) Cheers!

Receiver is not a game that everyone will like. It takes the FPS genre to a much higher level of realism. It has no difficulty settings, checkpoints, game save or HUD for that matter.
You start the game in a random room inside of a building. You don´t know who you are or why you´re there. Equipped with a 1 of 3 diferent firearms (a Glock 18, a Revolver or a 1911 45. cal Pistol), a flashlight(that you may not get on spawn but be able to find later), and nothing else than that you must find out what is going on.
When walking around the building you will find  turrets or flying robots that will try to kill you. You can fight or run, but in some areas you will just have to go trough them to progress.
You will eventually find orange sound tapes that will tell you why you´re there, how to get out, and how to effectively fight the robots and turrets. In order to finish the game you must find all 11 tapes scattered around the building.
The game mechanics will be hard to understand at 1st, but in time you will get better at it. And if you don´t like some of the controls you can change them from the Launch Menu.
You don´t have sights in the screen so you must aim to shoot properly, there are many commands for what you can do with your weapon, and the reload process must be done manually.
Ammo is in pretty short supply, so you got to look around in the building and find bullets, equip it in your magazine (or barrel) and put in your inventory(in case you are using a pistol), then have it ready to reload in combat.
Also this game is made with the Unity engine, so don´t expect anything fancy here.
The game itself is great and addictive, but I until the crashing issues are fixed, stay away from this.

Heyyo, so Homefront: The Revolution may have had a shaky retail release, but in its current form? It's pretty good. The framerate is solid for me (i7-3770k @ 4.2GHz & MSI R9 390 @ 1100MHz with no extra power delivery) and with everything on high minus ambient occlusion and particle effects I can maintain 60fps most of the time.
One thing of note off the bat? Even when you have maxed out all your upgrades? You still can't take much of a beating... but in a sense it's a good thing since you're technically a guerilla fighter, so trying to fight too many enemies at once will cause your hitpoints to drain quickly, so it's always best to try and only take on a few at a time or to just run away... so it's not like Crysis where you have this badass suit of armor and can just mow down hordes of enemies.
The part that impressed me the most about this game? The acting. Voice actors are all good and the animations are among the best out there. The detail put into the main character's models are also really impressive. The way Parish's unbuckled vest actually sways when he moves being the highlight of quality in character models. You can definitely see the love put into them.
My second favorite part of the game has to be the gun handling mechanics. The way you can customize your gun is done really good much like Crysis plus the way the gun handles in and out of aiming mode is nice. Essentially when you're shooting from the hip the gun will spray a little widly unless you buy and equip a laser sight which helps you figure out where it'll aim at the hip. When using your sights to aim? It will recoil a little and using a foregrip is genuinely helpful. Of course, you can only customize your gun with either a sight or a foregrip so depending on your gameplay style for said weapon it'll vary on how you want to set up your gun. The fantastic part about gun customization? It's also per-gun conversion kit. So using your assault rifle with certain attachments can differ to the limpet launcher conversion's set, so changing on the fly between conversion kits isn't annoying.
Oh, I guess I should mention each gun has two unlockable conversion kits (minus the rocket launcher. It fires rockets so I guess it does what it needs to heh). So your pistol can be just a regular pistol, or get a machine pistol coversion kit or the "Pneumatic pistol" which allows for charged shots that deal a lot of damage but with a slower rate of fire. This conversion kit gameplay mechanic is damn handy and the animations for the swapping of parts is also really well done.
The other parts of the gameplay are all really well done such as the different thrown weapons and the crafting of throwable devices too. The RC car for explosives is great as a prime example... my only gripe with the gameplay being the motor cycle gets stuck on all kinds of things. It's an annoyance but meh, just get the upgraded run speed gear and then don't worry about motorcycles. :P
Oh, and my third favorite thing? Time Splitters 2. There's an arcade machine easter egg in the prison section of the game at the top story inside the fighting arena's building where you can activate the arcade machine and watch the intro to Time Splitters 2 and even play the first few levels heh. It looks and runs damn good on PC and makes me sad the game never did get a PC release so I guess this is the closest thing you can get to playing it on PC without an emulator heh.
The storyline? Eh, it's ok I guess. You're pretty much just fighting to release Philadelphia from the Korean People's Army. The main part of the storyline that shines like I said was the acting and I always looked forward to seeing those in game cutscenes which were well done.
The only real downside to the game is some bugs, namely the audio bugs. I've had the KPA on red alert and went to hide in trash bins and Brady (your character's name btw) breathes heavily... and sometimes when I exit said trash bin? He'll keep breathing heavily and drown out any gun shooting sounds and everything else and the only way to fix it is to access a gun cabinet which saves your game then quit to the main menu and resume your save. The only other bug that's truly annoying is like I said with the motorcycles where they get stuck on things but meh, upgraded sprint speed gear and sprinting everywhere was fine with me. :P
So with all that said? Yes I feel I got my money's worth on this game. I haven't bothered with multiplayer since tbh I rarely play multiplayer FPS games these days since I tend to stick with World of Tanks for my multiplayer fix.

Introduction:
If you are watching F1 grand prix including the practice sessions, and qualifying sessions and allways wanted to be in the shoes of some of the drivers from this year or in the future, this game will suit you.
Carreer mode:
F1 2016 includes all of the drivers and teams from 2016, and have a deep and engaging carreer mode lasting 10 years/sessions from 2016-2026 . In the carrer mode you can choose your tire strategy for each race and customize your cars in alot of ways to help you beat the opponents in the practice sessions and qualifying.
Practice sessions:
The practice sessions have alot of detail, including team-objectives where you learn how to save your tires and how to drive on the apex of the circuits. After you have completed the team-objectives you will earn funds, which you can use on various parts of the car f.ex. a better engine, more optimized fuel-systems , chasis-development etc.
Race:
After you have completed both the practice sessions and the qualification, you can choose to run a track parade, where you can increase the temperature of the tires.
The AI cars race are very good, and have been improved from 2015, so f.ex. you will have less accidents with other AI-cars at the start of the race. There are 7 difficult levels you can choose from for the AI cars: "very easy" to "ultimate".
Graphics: 95 /100
The graphics of F1 2016 is improved from the earlier version and includes a full time-of-day, so you can f.ex. see the sun go down and lights turn on. The game includes dynamic weather effects, so you will have to change tires in mid-race if it's raining. The tracks have alot of detail and have more details than F1 2015.
Sound: 85 / 100
Sound is very nice with alot of details, like the sound of rain on the hood, the abillity to hear the other F1 cars engines both on track and in pit etc. The cars could have a better engine sound though.
Performance: 95 / 100
On my old Phenom 955 with 8gb of ram and a Nvidia GTX 960 I have around 39 fps with ultra settings and I haven't noticed any lag like there was in F1 2015.
Overall: 92 /100

A good PC port, if lacking in graphics options such as model, object and environment detail, but is a much better improvement over the previous game. I'm not a wrestling fan, but even I love this game, with its vast customisation, game modes, character roster and sheer amount of replay value is incredible.
Running at a locked 60 fps, WWE 2K16 sees the return of many favourite game modes, like create-an-arena, create-a-diva, match types, a whole new career mode and much more. The graphics seem better than WWE 2K15, especially with the character models and costume textures. Gameplay wise, I'm loving all the match types and going into the options menu to change rules, game hints, blood on/off and so forth. And speaking of, I also love the new mini-game-like QTEs that happen when actions like a pin, or grapple, occur. It adds a simple layer of 'fun' on-top of what is already a fun, meaty game. I love making my own movesets with my characters, making an entrance for them, and an arena for them to battle in. It's just incredibly fun and you'll be here for triple digit hours with it all!
I haven't tried online, so this is an offline review. Having said that, a couple of things I want to see added in for the inevitable sequel is better audio design. What I mean is - I want to hear the occasional character scream or grunt as they pull off certain moves; giving it immersion by proportioning realism onto what is already a realistic game. Also minor, yet near-essential things like hearing footstep noises, climbing the ladder/cages, more variety in 'punch' sounds beyond the generic slap noise. And finally, better flowing commentary: it's quite jarring hearing the commentary suddenly cut-out to talk about something else I'm doing without finishing the previous sentence.
Overall, as I said, I'm not a wrestling fan at all and I doubt this game will turn me to one, but I'm very much enjoying my time with this game. Perhaps a little more violence wouldn't hurt with enhanced persistent character damage, floors being scuffed and whatnot as per real wrestling. Having said that, this is a much better, improved, real letter to the fans that were left disappointed by the previous iteration or like me, just lost interest after so many features were dropped.
Recommend to people who enjoy sports, brawlers, RPGs, simulators and action. Worth the £35 asking price? Definitely!

I actually preordered this game, but I haven't had a chance to play it until recently because of time and life issues. I really had a blast playing it and finally completed it. The characters were interesting and very well voice acted, and I loved the story. It is basically the movie Red Dawn, (the remake) mad into an open world FPS with fantastic art and environments. It's a very living city where you have to inspire the hearts and minds of the people to rise up for their nation and freedom. It had a very patriotic feel to it and was just a lot of fun to play. The only real negative I can think of was that the dialogue had too much cursing for my taste, but that is a personal preference. One of the best challenging Action RPGs that you'll find in the industry.
From what you already know- it's both frustratingly and excitingly difficult that trains you to adapt to the games mechanics and rewards you on your intuition and stratagem. True to a real-time action title.
That said, as an RPG title, you can always make the game easier in various ways- such as grinding for Souls (which is both EXP and Currency) to allow you to chose how to make the games difficulty play around your preferred gameplay style: LEVEL UP your base character to improve your survival chances and overall damage, or purchase NEW EQUIPMENT to change your fighting style to try new ways to progress during a challenging section. Alternatively you can use mechanic-changing equipment such as "the ablitiy to hear if an enemy is nearby"- at the price of a equipment slot to keep the game balanced, etc. For RPG fans who crave detailed battles and great loot, you'll find a lot of joy taking this all in.
As a last note, as it tries to mix both RPG and Action Adventure together, the game does try to forcefully push and prioritise Player-Strength (learn to get better, rather than just "level up"), but does offer Avatar-Strength (your character will get stronger even if you don't learn how to defeat the opponents) to keep the difficulty in match with you. So if you keep dying on a section after killing the same enemies repeatedly, those enemies stop appearing after a certain amount of deaths (to make progression easier and fairer). However, if you desire a truly challenging experience, Covenants (game mechanic-changing teams to join) are there from the get-go to offer options such as "Harder Enemies that will always come back", and "AI Assistance when in serious danger from other Players", that'll keep the experience changing continuously, even after your 1st playthrough.
The reason you hear about Dark Souls so often is because in this current game industry, it really is a game that's worth checking out and being inspired from, from both a consumer and a designer point of view.

One word Review: Overpriced.
Without spoiling the plot, I can say that Gone Home is a very unconventional, and unorthodox walking simulator. It's not likely that you've ever played another game like this, and while you might have your own assumptions of what to expect, Gone Home will likely fool you with it’s misdirection.
What the Fullbright Company has managed to do with the Unity engine is quite impressive, creating a mansion where virtually everything can be picked up, inspected, read, or examined, even if it's completely irrelevant to the story. The deluge of seemingly insignificant items may fluster you into thinking you've missed something useful, but trust me, you haven't.
The game's atmosphere is mostly horror based, although I'm tempted to reuse the word: misdirection. The downpour of rain, accompanied by thunder and flickering lights creates a very tense, suspenseful abience. Played at night, with a headset, and you’ll find yourself jumping at shadows and fearing the dark.
When it comes to the story itself, Gone Home is very short, allowing for just over an hour of gameplay, possibly two if you take your time. For this reason, I highly recommend you buy the game on sale, just to avoid being burned.
For what the game offers, and the experience as a whole, I enjoyed it. I just don't agree with the twenty dollar price tag.

If you're looking for a game that you can sprint through and brag about 'winning', this is not it.  There's nothing to fight, no conflict, no 'boss level'.  It's just you, your house and a lot of memories.
'Gone Home' starts on your front porch.  After a year overseas, you've come back to find the place empty.  Your sister is gone, your parents are out somewhere, and all you have in the way of information is audio-tapes, notepads, school binders and letters.
I don't fault others for calling this game 'bland' or 'uninteresting'; certainly, there isn't anything in the way of 'action' or 'adventure'.  What it does have, however, is a lot to say about family -- the one you're born into and the one you create for yourself.
Take your time.  Read the letters.  Listen to your sister's story.
Sometimes, we all need someone to just listen.

Simply put, Banished is a town builder where the goal is to have your village thrive. It's The Oregon Trail meets Sim City. From a handful of families to hundreds of people, you re-create how the ancient settlements of a few people became the burgeoning cities of today.
The game itself has a few simple mechanics and a very stripped down UI which can be viewed in individual parts. The graphics are acceptable (nothing too amazing), and the controls are intuitive. It may not be your cup of tea as there is no win condition and there's no real economy building, so if you are interested, take a look at some game play videos which go over the game as they help illustrate how the game is played and how it feels.

Instead of writing an essay on how good or bad this game is here's my conclusion for it:
POSITIVES:
-Very large map (basically a mini scale U.S.). Takes about 2 hours in real time to make a loop all the way around it.

NEGATIVES
-Freaking Ushit
-Rubberbanding of other players.
-Overpowered AI where if you mess up they jump like a mile ahead of you in a couple seconds and it's hard to catch back up to them.

The Final Station is a story based game with a lot of repetetive levels. You are a train conductor going round to many places throughout the Second Visitation. You need to survive, bring as many people as you can to their destination, keep control of the train and listen to wacky conversations.
Audio - The Audio brings a little horror to the game as you can hear footsteps, gun shots and not much background noise. Not the best thing that shines in this game.
Gameplay - The goal of the game, in my view, is to bring as many people as you can find to safety (either to a protection unit with guards or a random place). There are crafting mechanics but not a big variety like finding metal and making a rifle. You can get 2 guns through the start to the near end, and a useless rifle at the end. There is no value of replaying this game and I do not see much to do in this game. If it wasn't for the good graphics, this game would recieve a bad recommendation. The Story is alright but the ending is horrible. I do recommend it if you are willing to play a one time game that can last from 4 - 7 hours.
Graphics / Visuals - What can i say? I bet that just designing a building in a background (around 600px) would probaly take around about 3 weeks alone. This is greatly shown that the developers took more input into graphic changes than the actual storyline and gameplay. I think you can expect the greatest art while riding in the train.
+ Incredible and Satisfying Visuals
+ Decent Horror Audio
+ Nice mild jumpscares
+ Crafting System is smooth
+ Scavenging system is alright
+ Great Variety of monsters (not just the odd 3)
- Not a decent story
- No Replayability value
- Short
- No Endless mode or anything.
Overall, 6.5/10

Last year we finally got a WWE licensed wrestling game on PC in over a decade, but it was a fairly mediocore game. 2K16 is a huge step up from that - It reintroduces many features that were missing, has a much larger roster and online is greatly improved.
In fact this is one of my all time favourite pro wrestling games. If you're a fan of the old school Smackdown or N64 games then beware that this is a much more simulation focused game. It's a lot more slow paced and more unforgiving but that allows for more strategic gameplay. With stamina you can't endlessly run away, and you may have to decide to rest a little following a big move rather than hitting another with no stamina left for a quick pin. There's also limited reversals this time and THANK GOD. FINALLY matches aren't just an endless chain of reversals anymore.
If you dislike any of that then everything can be customised; turn off stamina, reversal slots, adjust finisher damage etc. Also this year's game brings back features like Create An Arena and a much improved Create a Wrestler. (You can create females again! Yay!) The roster is massive and includes past and current wrestlers including some from NXT. Entrances are the best I have ever seen and are now completely seemless which allows you to interfere during your opponent's entrance! Awesome!
It still suffers from Yearly Franchise Syndrome™ which includes plenty of minor bugs and glitches and some strange roster ommisions like Sasha Banks and Charlotte even though Blake and Murphy are somehow in the game. And for some reason you can't use your own entrance music even though you could do it in the last gen console games. Commentary is also as bland as ever and feels like it hasn't improved since Smackdown Vs Raw 2006.
However it is entirely modabble! There was tons of great mods last year from updating wrestler's attire and entrances to entirely new arenas, and this year is no exception. Check out
for tons of great mods including tutorials on how to mod the game to

This game is a high contrast picture. It has some AWESOME game design marred by shitawful implementation that makes the experience on the whole very unenjoyable.
The pros:
- The graphics look quite frankly amazing even on lower settings.
- The roster is humongous.
- The customization options were largely improved over WWE2k15, including the inclusion of custom divas.
- Career mode is fun, but...
The cons:
- The lnput lags. And i don't mean a bit. I mean that a game where your winning or losing a match (escaping a pin) is based on a timing minigame, has a solid half second of input delay. That is unplayable. You can still win if you get used to it, but it's terrible for a company like 2K to not even be able to code a decent input manager.
- Reversals are ♥♥♥♥ing impossible. Let's be real here: nobody knows ALL the moves to this game. There's just too many. Even if they did, they'd not be able to spot which is being done in time for the reversal window to matter. Hence why the input delay, coupled with the fact that sometimes the reversal prompts just refuse to show, or show too early/late, is again a huge problem that needs addressing ASAP. Considering i've read various sources saying it's been there since 2014, i'd not hold my breath for a fix.
- The AI cheats. If you have limited reversals enabled (Don't) the AI will ignore that if you're gaining too much on it. It also kicks out after the second or third finisher in a match. And we're not talking Undertaker versus Sting on PPV here, we're talking jobbers on a normal show night.
- Lip synching in the very few dubbed scenes is comedically bad, but nobody gives a♥♥♥♥♥♥about that.
In summation: The game designers for this game put a lot of effort into building a simulator. The fact that the match is graded on its entertainment value is an awesome idea that makes losing feel like less of a failure, if you at least managed to get a good rating out of the match, the strategic choices when building a moveset and stats combination are as deep as it gets, then whoever programmed the whole thing took a giant steaming♥♥♥♥♥♥all over the very obvious effort and ruined it with ♥♥♥♥♥♥ AI and Input.
Good job 2K.

One of the best challenging Action RPGs that you'll find in the industry.
From what you already know- it's both frustratingly and excitingly difficult that trains you to adapt to the games mechanics and rewards you on your intuition and stratagem. True to a real-time action title.
That said, as an RPG title, you can always make the game easier in various ways- such as grinding for Souls (which is both EXP and Currency) to allow you to chose how to make the games difficulty play around your preferred gameplay style: LEVEL UP your base character to improve your survival chances and overall damage, or purchase NEW EQUIPMENT to change your fighting style to try new ways to progress during a challenging section. Alternatively you can use mechanic-changing equipment such as "the ablitiy to hear if an enemy is nearby"- at the price of a equipment slot to keep the game balanced, etc. For RPG fans who crave detailed battles and great loot, you'll find a lot of joy taking this all in.
As a last note, as it tries to mix both RPG and Action Adventure together, the game does try to forcefully push and prioritise Player-Strength (learn to get better, rather than just "level up"), but does offer Avatar-Strength (your character will get stronger even if you don't learn how to defeat the opponents) to keep the difficulty in match with you. So if you keep dying on a section after killing the same enemies repeatedly, those enemies stop appearing after a certain amount of deaths (to make progression easier and fairer). However, if you desire a truly challenging experience, Covenants (game mechanic-changing teams to join) are there from the get-go to offer options such as "Harder Enemies that will always come back", and "AI Assistance when in serious danger from other Players", that'll keep the experience changing continuously, even after your 1st playthrough.
The reason you hear about Dark Souls so often is because in this current game industry, it really is a game that's worth checking out and being inspired from, from both a consumer and a designer point of view.

After playing the Original Dark Souls, I was hoping for the sequel to live up to hype and its name. To be completely frank, it did not. The game has many, many flaws that initially can be overlooked because it’s a Dark Souls game, but it just becomes more and more apparent as the game goes on. The story is unbelievably un-cohesive and really poorly written. The combat system was clunky, with many of the stats just ripped apart to be more “realistic”. Speaking of, it’s so “realistic” that a massive lance hitting you should stagger you? Oh no, not the mobs. You however have the poise of a newborn giraffe with a broken leg. Awful, bloody awful level design. I mean seriously, tight corridors and huge enemies I can deal with I guess. By mass amounts of poison, nearly invisible enemies, oh and lets not forgetting that enemies start to stop spawning if you kill them enough. The hell is that? Seriously, why on freaking on earth does an elevator on top a freaking MOUNTAIN end up INSIDE a volcanic castle!? What the hell. Ultimately I HIGHLY, HIGHLY discourage anyone from playing this. The bosses are all humanoids who can be blitzed easily, and the only memorable boss was the Executioner’s Chariot… What happened? Seriously. And that damn ending. Man, if I wanted some idiotic ending like that I’d play something else, not Dark Souls… Unbelievable.
Plus if you're a PC player? Hah, good luck with some of the attack variations. I literally had to bind a macro together to do several abilities because the designers of the game put them on the other side of the keyboard and cannot be rebinded. What a disgrace.
Do not play unless, idk, you have too much free time. Better to watch paint dry on a wall. And if you want the 'Souls' experience, do yourself a favor and either buy Dark Souls & Dark Souls 3 or watch someone a youtube.

Brief history lesson: Heuristic Park released version 1.0 of Dungeon Lords in 2005. It received patches in the classic sense - update files that you download, execute, point toward your install folder and let it to the work. These patches, however, didn't do much as far as I'm aware.
My history with it was that I got the Collector's Edition, a special rerelease which fixed several bugs and had a new character class and a tonne of new content! I found it when I was rather young at a dollar store. I didn't know why an RPG of such scale was in a dollar store, but lo and behold! I get back home, pop it into my Windows XP computer and give it a launch. The game was buggy, with spells like Freezing Touch and Burning Hands not working, and all sorts of great stuff.
I originally wrote off the acrobatics system as faulty, however it didn't tell me that you needed certain ranks in the Acrobatics skill to use certain dodge rolls and flips. This was pretty nice, albeit unexplained. Perhaps the Freezing Touch and Burning Hands problem was a matter of the skill system too? I don't know.
The matter at hand here is that the game was rereleased in 2012 in the form you see now. It was entirely reworked: An engine overhaul, new systems, fancy effects, a point-and-click mode, etc.
The original version of the game always had co-op, through LAN or internet play. Now, we have Steam for eight-player co-op.
I'm going to highlight some of the main differences between the versions here:
The spell system: In the original, you could usually find spells out in the wilderness as loot, and depending on your starting class you may have started with one or two. As far as I know you may have been able to put ranks in any type of magic skill and use it, but I may be wrong. In this Steam Edition, you get one spell per level, and each class seems to have a certain type of magic they use, that they learn each level.
The skill system: In the original, there were many types of skills, and you could rank up in any one you pleased using a skill point. In this version of the game, your skills gain experience in a similar way to how you level up in The Elder Scrolls or Final Fantasy II: You use something, it gains experience. You gain skill points every level, but if you use one on a skill, it just gives it an experience boost, and will not guarantee a level up. I'm personally not much a fan of this.
The graphics: The game now has fancy bloom and fog, and WORKING particle effects! The UI is a little less polished than it originally was, but I still find it enjoyable.
The multiplayer: Hoo boy, is this game a hoot to play online. The bugs or simple obscurity of practically EVERYTHING in this game makes this game a laugh to play with others. The Collector's Edition is absolutely riddled with bugs or quirks, while the netcode works well. Saves are confusing, but the bugs and problems make the game hilarious! I have yet to test the game in this Steam Edition, but various skills now apply to your allies as well as yourself. It creates a new dynamic that wasn't present in the original.
The verdict: Not mentioned above: The physics of this version aren't as... Tight, so to say, as the original/Collector's Edition, and the old spell system was quite nice. This version's difficulty seems much easier than the original's, and in the first dungeon alone I leveled up five times more than I usually did in the original! This isn't so much a problem, but it's interesting to say the least.
If you want a solid RPG and don't mind the price tag, get this version! If you want a laugh and a more solid system (WHEN it works) then play the original or the Collector's Edition. Either way, it's an RPG on the PC with cooperative multiplayer. A+ From me!

Have you ever sat cross-legged with your left hand on your cheek, searching for that hidden gem RPG among the crowd? Congratulations, you may have just found that. If you're a fan of Bioware's old RPGs and older games such as Summoner, Severance, Enclave, Deathtrap Dungeon, Die by the Sword and the Elder Scrolls games there is a high chance you're going to really enjoy this one. Dungeon Lords is an old, but obscure, aged yet playable third person CRPG. The game supports unlocked framerate and fps in-game (unfortunately the menus are 23fps locked), which already puts half of modern PC ports to shame. For a 2005 remastered port, this is impressive. Now, what differs this game from other RPGs even ones considered masterpieces is what the game offers and how it presents itself.
Those games I listed? Combine them together, imagine they poly morphed as one game and grew up with just one parent. That's this game in a nutshell. The game offers real time combat with hotkeys, status screens, doll-like inventory, real-time changing portraits, and much more, which would take me beyond the word limit to list. Dungeon Lords also offers a point and click mode, which brings the cursor on-screen so you can play it like a traditional MMO, or you can just stick with the default action control system. The bog standard difficulty mode is there but in addition to a random encounter chance slider. No, that doesn't mean your world transitions into a "battle mode" ala Final Fantasy, it just means the chance of random mob spawns. There's options for view distance, individual audio sliders, camera smoothness, mouse sensitivity + inversion... it goes on.
Now, the meat of the game. It's a 2005 game so it will lack modern polish and care, hence the single parent bad joke I made. Some animations, sound effects, the voice acting and the general ware and tare feel of the game is quirky and aged, HOWEVER, I actually think this compliments the vibrant art scheme of the graphics in a strange and twisted way. The graphic fidelity isn't high as you'd expect, but they remind me of Morrowind and Neverwinter Nights 2, to compare. Just don't expect lots of NPCs and text boxes on screen all at one time.
The game features a class system, m/f, different races and starting kits kind of like Dragon Age. If you're aware of Bethesda games they offer freedom, go anywhere, do what you want. Well... this game has that, too. You can completely ignore the main quest and go do your own thing and now with up to eight player co-op, this will be immensely fun. Yes, eight players with this Steam version. Modern RPGs struggle with just two. Cool isn't it?
Back to gameplay, there's your typical cooldowns for spells and skills, you attack spam with clicks and opposite click for shield blocking. This is where it reminds me of the Summoner and even the Dark Souls games. It has that sort of "personalisation" feel to it, the roleplaying has emphasis and it feels like you're going on a medieval adventure. The game's atmosphere in certain dungeons really has that Dark Souls and Severance aesthetic and eeriness. Speaking of, since this is an old CRPG with some Dungeons and Dragons rulesets, the game feels traditional and does nothing more to innovate beyond that. Which can be seen as good or bad to you. The game has your main quest, side quests, towns to barter and learn rumours from, and dungeons to go explore for loot. There's orcs, skeletons, crows, atypical mythical beasts to fight, the sort of stuff that's commonplace in fantasy lore.
Don't get me wrong here, this isn't the best CRPG out there and PERSONALLY I do think it can match Bioware's old material and hell even beat older CRPGs like those wave of DOS ones from the 90s. BUT. And I mean BUT. Dungeon Lords feels very unpolished, as said, mixed in with a lack of hand-holding and a truly investing story, you might find yourself becoming bored quickly if you're looking for that "different and unqiue" RPG experience. Although, the game does differentiate itself amongst other CRPGs of the same genre. However, Dungeon Lords is your traditional and tried-and-true from start to finish. There's no forced romance, no deep epic companions or dialogue and quotes that will eventually end up as memes, dialogue wheels that don't actually effect anything and a voiced protagonist. But what you're getting is a quirky yet enjoyable CRPG that is built around:
-Customisation
-Roleplaying
-Freedom
-Old school feel
If any, or all, of those concepts interest you I urge you to check this one out. I've beaten both versions of this game, alone, and I love it. However, I'm aware that it won't appeal to everybody DESPITE the game having tuns of options to mess with like a girl and her make-up. So please, if you enjoyed this review, check the game out and have fun! Give a friend a call, try the co-op and thanks for reading! Now, you may uncross your legs and place your left hand on the desk. :)

- Interchangable soundtracks
- Custom resoultions
- Timescale
- Encounter Rate
- FMV skipping
I recommend this game to anyone new to the Final Fantasy series, those who played the PS2 version, and anyone looking for a great turn-based RPG.

Receiver is... meh, it is not a terrible game nor is it a fantastic game!
The game was developed by Wolfire Games (the same developer as Overgrowth) for the 7-day FPS challenge, and I must say for 7 days, they have created quite a stable game.
The gun mechanics and the realism of the gun handling is amazing, the animations for the guns are fantastic, well done to Wolfire Games!
BUT the game has some serious issues:-
The level of difficulty: The game is really hard, from beginning to end, once you die, it resets everything (kind of like a rogue-like game), it is randomly generated, the enemies are really hard and annoying and the tapes that you have to  collect are very hard to find. Once you found a number of tapes and you get killed, you lose everything, which can be quite annoying, as the enemies are difficult and sometimes just appear out of nowhere!
The controls for the guns: They are extremely awkward, I can understand why they did it, because in real life, to handle a gun, it takes time and practice, but for game it is pretty annoying, the game does help you with a list of controls, but if you run out of a magazine with one of the game's enemies running after you/shooting at you, I don't think the list of controls will help in dire need of refilling a magazine with ammo, whilst focusing on the game and the list of controls (not for me anyway)!
Level design: Although the levels are quite good, they can get really confusing and it put me off after a while
Ammo: Ammo is really scarce, and you can hardly find any ammo anywhere, once you lost your ammo, and you meet one of the enemies of the game, your ♥♥♥♥ed
Compatibility: The game is awful with compatibility, the game is developed with the Unity3D engine, and its frame rate just drops drastically in some areas, whereas other Unity3D games I've played, run fantastically on my gaming PC
Level of detail: The level of detail (excluding the gun designs) is bland, and very incomplete, I can understand for a 7-day development time, but Wolfire Games could of after the game finished the 7-day FPS challenge make the game a bit more detailed, but it seems that Wolfire Games just abandoned the game after they finished the 7-day FPS challenge
Now to the recommendation, for its full price, I would not recommend it, BUT if it is either in a sale, price drop, giveaway, gift or even given to you as a free game then I would recommend it.

This instalment has several glaring problems:

That being said, this is still a great game with plenty of cool things to discover. Just be aware that it is not without a few glaring problems.
TL;DR - It's the worst Dark Souls game (IMO), but it's still a Dark Souls game. Definitely worth a purchase.

A worthy sequel to Dark Souls 1. Another desolate and deadly world to explore. 'Scholar' sports improved graphics and different enemy and item placements from the original Dark Souls 2. It also includes all three DLC packs incorporated into the game. Those who played the original DS2 will be in for a few surprises.
This game punishes arrogance and carelessness so proceed with caution and learn enemy movements and wait for an opening. There is nothing quite like the feeling of FINALLY taking down that seemingly impossible boss after being defeated several times in a row. The rush is exhilarating. Highly recommend this game to those who like a challenging game based on exploration and combat. The difficulty can be a shock to newcomers but the ambiance, world design and tense, nailbiting combat keeps you coming back for more.
Also, though it's not my cup of tea, this game does have a very active and vibrant pvp aspect. So those into co-op or pvp will be sure to appreciate fighting off invading players or teaming up to take on powerful enemies. Various factions in the game called "covenants" award players for various tiers of participation in co-op or pvp.
Final Verdict: Very challenging but rewarding experience.

It's no secret that Five Nights at Freddy's was a complete success. The game was like none other I nor anyone else in the gaming community had seen before. This works quite well and works an all but two animtronics: Foxy and the Puppet who all talk about later. Newly found appreciation for Dark Souls II has been acquired with this re-work called 'Scholar of the First Sin'. Approximately two years having not played Dark Souls II and after I had moved on to Bloodborne and Dark Souls III - finally, I decided to go back to see how it has changed and hopefully improved. I have come to realise the new placement of items and enemies works way better than how it originally did. For example, I really loved the new placements for the Suspicious Shadow enemies. They were originally only featured in New Game+(almost certain) and that, in my opinion, was a waste. They are really fun to fight and obtaining their gear was pretty satisfying. Also, the addition of the Forlorn Dark Spirit is a good one - he has an interesting background albeit not much is known. I've been invaded five times and received his gear and scythe. I think he is fun to fight but Drangleic Castle is by far his toughest encounter; try to move to a more open room. As for The Pursuer haters, are they not meant to pursue you? It is silly to think they only have a small handful. They aren't that tough, anyway.
The new NPC antagonist is really cool, won't spoil too much but it raises just as many questions as it gives answers. Well, maybe not even so. PvP is still pretty great besides the ridiculous lag backstabs but I don't get that so often. I am pretty surprised that I still get summoned a lot - getting the Sun Sword was easy! The DLC still remains to be the best part of this package but I'll admit that I really started enjoying this game after the halfway point - just before Drangleic Castle and onwards.
I will keep my gripes with this game such gripes being the 'Agility' attribute - I need to phase through every attack nonsense. Not smart design. Also, 'Soul Memory' still continues to just be horrible. All in all, this is a great game and I think all Souls fans should get this and doubly so if you've still yet to play Dark Souls II in general. I bought this as a $12 upgrade from the original a while back - I don't think that's so bad. $50 is fair for full price if you've yet to play, in my opinion. However, it has been significantly discounted many times throughout the past year and a half. I would just wait a few months.

This game is rated as a "simulator" and while you can run a triple monitor surround with a stearing wheel (mine is the G27) with flawless rotation and actuation time from the game to the wheel there were several, and I mean several issues that I had hoped Ubisoft could have fixed because its not very difficult to fix but they are again just being lazy.
First off it doesn't seem to matter however you tilt my wheel to barely make a turn while letting off the gas the game refuses to understand basic physics, if I tap a car that I am passing you have a chance to get randomly thrown about 50ft and turned around or flipped in a wreck setting you back about 6seconds if you get the wreck cut screen, or depending on how bad it throws you 3-10 seconds.
Second, if you are driving a Raid vehicle (one designed for extensive offroad use) you can tap a small rock and while in real life even a four wheeler could easily go over this rock without any problems your high performance off road beast gets thrown around like a piece of paper in a air cannon.
Third, the game itself isn't consistant with what it tells you that your getting upgrades on. On my Zr1 Corvette set up for circuit I can be running 220+ miles per hour and turn my wheel and start drifting into a wall which then flings me 50ft (as stated before). I go out and find a mini game get a tire upgrade and kept playing until I got a tire upgrade with a grip upgrade in a gold metal (so I should have better grip with better tires now right?) Wrong. So very wrong. While I had the chance to go to Daytona Beach and drive a NASCAR through their training course you can pay for a day of training and drive with a co-driver, I was driving at 150mph. While driving my Corvette (after my tire upgrade) I hit the circuit and couldn't seem to keep a measely 200 mph when before I was easily holding 200 consitantly.
Fourth, this is a very minor gripe but a gripe none the less, while playing this game Ubisoft has put "Gold Metal Cars" in during the mini game challenges while driving along the road. While I can be in front of this so called "Gold Metal Car" and have a perfect score when time runs out I will complete it with a silver metal. What the f**k?
Though there is a few good points in the game, most of the stats for the cars (stock anyway) are pretty close to accurate in real life, and while the game doesn't give you a good perspective of how fast you are driving the acceleration is almost on point with most of the real life cars as well. This feels like a silly review to write because I'm pretty sure most people who care about Final Fantasy or JRPGs in general have played this game by now especially since most of the reviews on here are just raving nostalgia. For me it's no different really: it’s a fantastic game, I played it as a kid, I loved it then and I love it now, same as the rest. But to add to that I will say this to those who maybe haven’t tried Final Fantasy or the JRPG genre themselves.
FFX is probably one of the most approachable JRPGs out there. If anyone were to ask me where to start with the genre it would probably be this game (or Persona 4 if they are into anime and would therefore be more attracted to how quirky that game is). The graphics, gameplay, setting, story, and soundtrack are just so good and inviting that I think it's a fantastic place for someone to get into the genre. I think this gets overshadowed a lot by everyone’s obsession with FF7, and while I love FF7 myself I just don't think that it is the greatest starting point in 2016. FFX still manages to look and feel impressive despite its age and I think it has a lot more power to draw newcomers in because of it. The world of Spira is full of intoxicating fantasy atmosphere and imagery that you can really get immersed in.
Just take the risk and give it a shot if you’re looking to try something different out, or maybe thought FF7 looked too dated to approach. You may or may not end up liking it but in my opinion this is a very good game to take a chance on if you’re looking to pick a JRPG to try out.

Receiver is an INCREDIBLY challenging game. You will hate it and love it at the same time.
You play an unnamed protagonist navigating through various indoor and outdoor areas in a structure located in an unnamed city. Many of the rooms are guarded by randomly-placed sentry turrets that shot you on sight, or helicopter/taser sentries that fly at you when you are detected.
You come armed with one of three different handguns, all of which are nicely-rendered. Each one is operated in a realistic-manner that may be off--putting to the gamer used to relading by simply pressing the R key. In this game, reloading could involve five distinctly-different operations, depending on the gun you happen to have on you at the time.  The sound effects of the guns are nice, and have an authentic feel to them.
The environments you travel around in are randomly assembled, and comprised of flat-shaded textures and occasional lights. The assembly of the rooms means that you occasionally find passages to nowhere, but that doesn't really detract from gameplay. Repetition is high, and some of the rooms/areas are confusing, but since you are just passing through, it's not really a big deal. Your goal is to locate ammo and tapes, and the threats are there to stop you.
Audio is pretty good, with a couple of notable exceptions:
1: the helicopter sentries are loud enough to be heard from one room over, but it becomes difficult to pin down their locations based on the audio alone.
2: The sentry turrets also make sounds while they rotate, but you can't hear them until you're almost right on top of them. Their sounds, as well as the helicopters,  also pass through walls/floors at the same volume level. This aspect of the game is bothersome if you are searching a room. I prefer to play the game with the music silenced so I can try to hear the threats before they spot me, and often I find that I am shot dead before ever hearing the servo motor of the turret that nailed me.
3: The audio tapes are well-voiced, but remind me a lot of the sort of thing you might find on a webiste run by fringe-science/conspiracy theorists. After playing for a few hours, I completly silenced the tapes because I became bothered at having to hear them over and over again. Kudos to the devs for allowing this option in the settings.
The main goal of the game is to find all 11 tapes, and "absorb" them by listening. Listening occurs while you continue exploring, so that's a good thing. I did find a couple of small problems with the exploration/survival aspect:
1: Sometimes the game allows you to access an area that does not have an exit. The only option is to exit and restart.
2: You are assigned a random firearm and random loadout upon starting. Rarely, you will find yourself without enough ammo to eliminate enough of the threats to be able to find more.
3: (Extremely rare) you begin the game in the direct line of site of a threat, and get killed immediately.
For a game created in a week as part of a contest, the developers have done an admirable job! The simplicity of the design and the addictiveness of the concept keeps me coming back over and over again. I've only managed to get as high as 4 tapes before being mowed down by a threat in a moment of complacency. The game forces you to be on high-alert at all times, and punishes relaxed attitudes brutally. You will learn to use expletives effectively, I guarantee.
Worth every bit of the 5 bucks it currently is. Get it. You'll be glad you did.

I just
about how the devs have continously supported the game and patched away most of the issues that ruined its launch. It's a shame it went so poorly, because now that it's fixed, I've got about 3 hours in and I'm happy I picked it up.
It's a guerilla warfare simulator. It also happens to be a well-optimized one with good visuals (albeit somewhat dreary), along with all the AAA regalia we've come to expect these days: crafting, weapon mods, parkour, skill trees, vehicles to ride.
Gameplay features the usual modern shooter tropes and ultimately proves to be more than a little derivative of Far Cry 3 & 4 and their imitators. You'll be taking out outposts and strongholds, clearing caches, and drip-feeding on loot while steadily advancing your weapons and character. It's all somewhat rote, with the notable exception of the on-the-fly weapon modding, which is rather nifty- you can convert your pistol to an SMG instantaneously in the field, for example.
Yet, as I do my busywork clearing the map and putting off the next objective, I'm enjoying it as much as I dared hope if not more. It really does provide a compelling simulation of urban guerilla warfare. I feel outnumbered, like I need to be cautious, but haven't had any frustrations, other than those that were my fault. After 2+ hours I have a new gun and some attachments, have cleared a few enemy hangouts, earned some duckets and everyone likes me. That's about all I was expecting.
Ultimately nothing will stand out as terribly original or groundbreaking, but everything is excecuted well and competently: the environments are a bit bland but rendered very nicely, and the story seems very basic so far but serves the setting nonetheless. War stories are rarely as exciting as a video game, making this story probably closer to real life than most. So I forgive it. It's told clearly and competently enough that I think it's fine. If you do yourself a favor and approach this game from the right perspective, you will probably have fun. You're playing through a war. No glamour, no shiny medals. Just surviving and taking back your homeland. Good enough for me.
Make no mistake, I'm the type who enjoys worldbuilding, story and exploration equally if not more than mechanics. This is not the kind of game players like me usually get very taken in by-- but I think it's very good. I'd recommend this anyone who's in the mood for a solid AAA shooter, something to buzz through and enjoy for its strengths, and then maybe forget about.

After years of playing it both on console and PC i finally write down this review for what i consider an incredibly good game that, unfortunately, doesn't stand much of a chance when confronted with the other titles in the serie (including Demon's souls & Bloodborne)
It's kinda tough to review this title, since there are many points to take on count.. what does it better than DS 1; what does it worse; is it worth for people who have DS2 vanilla to upgrade to DS2 SOTFS?
I'll first say what i think of DS2/DS2 SOFTS compared to Dark Souls 1:
1) DS2/DS2 Scholar definitely controls smoother..but not better, and only in some instances:
animations are less "clunky" (not that they were bad in the first one, but this time they're even better!), this doesn't necessarily means that the controls are better tho; i definitely, by far , prefer DS1 in this point, and DS3 & Bloodborne are the clear winners.
The way your PG moves around and directs his attacks is incredibly slow, feels imprecise and unresponsive,especially with ultragreat weapons.
Dodging is weird, since it's extremely smooth from start to finish, but only a portion of the whole roll animation is composed of i-frames, unlike in DS1 where your rolling lasted an instant and looked very "mechanic"..but at least you knew perfectly the duration of it's i-frame (also: there is a stat in DS2 that you have to level up to increase those i-frames..one of the worst choices about the leveling process in my opinion)
Too much attention to the animations meant some downgrades in other departments such as the movesets..there where sooo many movesets in the first game,if you took 10 random weapons you probably had 5-6 different
movesets, instead in this sequel you can count 'em on 2 hands probably..a mace is just like an axe, a small axe is like a great axe, an halberd is like any pole weapon ecc ecc..and this is in my opinion a disgrace
2)In the graphic department it looks better than the first one by a mile..and SOTFS is even more brilliant.. but unfortunately, in my opinion, the locations have less personality..
They look gorgeous: Majula, Heide's tower, The Dragon sanctuary ecc are jawdropping, but once you explore them they're less memorable than the firelink shrine, anor londo, or the borgue of the undead (not sure if that's how it's called in english, i played DS1 in Italian)
they're much less detailed, with most of the rooms/areas you'll encounter being empty spaces with nothing interesting to see and, in some cases, VERY ugly low res textures copy  & pasted every 2 centimeters.
3)The soundtrack is where i have no doubt..DS1 takes the cake. The only part of DS2 where i purposely waited to beat the boss just to listen to the music is the final boss of the DLC "Crown of
the Iron king" (i'll don't write his/her/it's name for spoilers)
4)Story/Lore: I'm sorry but this has no match..the overall concept is good, but some parts angered me for reasons i can't say cause of spoilers.
I guess everyone at this point knows the HUGE plotholes (well..loreholes) that just can't be interpreted either way..unlike the first chapter, were those few uncertain points were obviously left open to interpretation here there are obvious contradictions that make absolutely no sense.
5) less atmosphere..in DS1 you felt like an ant in a gigantic world, a world with hundreds and hundreds of centuries of history, and the world was the main focus, it's the real protagonist!
DS2 tried to have a compromise, even from the initial cutscene the attention is totally focalized on you, but the rest of the game isn't.. usually in an rpg you have to go with one or the other:
you center the whole game around the protagonist or around the world/events. Fromsoftware tried to do both and missed.
Also, the decision of letting you teleport from the start of the game (which unfortunately they mantained in Bloodborne & DS3) is ia huge step back.
Ask any player; i'm sure i'm not the only one who says that the best memories from Dark Souls 1 are present in the first half, when you still can't teleport..how cool it was to have to memorize the map and shortcuts? And what about the fear of committing too much to a path because, if you wanted to go back, you had to backtrack the entire way and battle again everything? That was one of the best sensations a videogame ever made me feel.
I guess in the end the teleport was kinda necessary since this game is so much larger in scale than the first one..but that's a whole other problem in itself: it didn't need to be this big.
Don't misunderstand this; for me the bigger a Dark souls game is the better..but DS2 is big, but too spread out and, in the end, most areas feel like they're big for the sake of being big..no interesting secrets or details in most cases..just empty rooms and terrains with some enemies here and there.
6)General difficulty: Ds2 is kinda easier than DS1 for 2 simple reasons:
A-You still got your limited "Estus Flasks" as health replanishment...plus many more items that you can buy pretty much from the beginning..they have some disadvantages, but you pretty
much have infinite "medikits"
B-Bosses are stupid, and the ones that are challenging can be called that because of some cheap stuff like some boss battles where you face multiple opponents with the arena being not suitable for maintaining a constant eye on all of them..or a couple of bosses that will oneshot you everytime (thankfully the worst one has been semi fixed in SOTFS, because in Vanilla was simply stupid)
Apart from bosses,you will definitely find some frustrating parts, but they're more annoyingly hard than challengin. Rooms full of 10 enemies that can kill you in one hit and will just do a bee line following you, casters that have
infinite spells and have so much range that you (literally) can't see them (this too has been SLIGHTLY tweaked in Scholar)..where did the beauty of the 1v1 go? I think that the most memorable parts of DS1 were the single fights you had with the most threatening enemies like the black knights! We were all scared of them at the beginning! (then we learned to parry and they became clowns..)
Enough. All that said DS2/DS2 Scholar is an AMAZING game, it simply has problems and it is just a step behind the first in my opinion.
I obviously didn't mention some common "annoyances" you'd find in any "Souls" game that i finally accepted and don't mind anymore...enemy weapons killin you through walls, enemy AI ecc ecc
-----------------
Now: Is it worth to upgrade from DS2 to DS2 Scholar of the first sin?
I did it, and i'm glad of it.
It really surprised me in some points, and there were many occasions where i had to re asset my way of playin because of the numerous changes.. crucial items are placed elsewhere, the pursuer
pops out in places i'd never imagined, invasions happenin more often ecc
plus it's a little bit more balanced than DS2..some areas that were too easy/too frustrating have been tweaked in a good way, but it doesn't change the fact that if you summon more than 1 player to co-op boss fights/areas.. you'll be ruining 99% of the fun since it becomes a complete cakewalk..even boss fights like the fume knight (definitely one of the
top 3 hardest boss of the entire game) become almost impossible to fail.
Cheers from Italy : )

When the time comes to sequelize something - be it a movie, a book or, well, a video game - the creators of the new "product" always have a major dilemma to resolve.  Namely:  How similar or different do we make it from the original, "hit" product?  If you're James Cameron and you're directing the sequel to a super-slow-moving Ridley Scott film, your answer might be to make a slam-bang action movie evidencing every war movie cliché in the handbook.  If, on the other hand, you're David Fincher, you might instead opt to make something at least slightly more akin to the original, albeit with a decidedly larger cast of characters and thusly more bloodshed and mayhem.  Scott Cawthon, the creator of the first Five Nights as well as this one, seems to have MOSTLY opted for the latter of these two options, but I'm not entirely convinced he should've changed things even as much as he has...

The true genius of the first Five Nights was that it preyed upon what I will call "itchy trigger-finger syndrome".  That is to say, the game creates such an extraordinary atmosphere of suspense that, as soon as the player tells themselves that they haven't checked on the cameras recently enough, or convinces themselves that there MAY be something standing at the darkened doorway which will get them if they DON'T hurriedly close said door in the next milli-second...they give in to that panic and do precisely what the game wants them to do:  Waste the precious POWER which is the only thing which stands between them and Freddy Fazbear violently stuffing them into an animatronic suit.  Another way of putting it is this:  The nerves-of-steel player who could show the restraint to NOT do anything, except when absolutely necessary, was the one who could most successfully survive through each night.

Like a lot of sequels, this one decides to "amp things up" a bit by making things more frenzied and complicated...but more complicated doesn't always mean "better".  In the first one, you only had to monitor the cameras and the "blind spots" just outside your security room's two doorways, and close either of the doors when you deemed it necessary.  In this one, you have to keep an eye on not two but THREE possible points of entry for the misguided muppets - with NO doors and only a Freddy mask you can pop on to keep you safe when an intrusion DOES occur - whilst also checking the cameras and ensuring that a remote-controlled music box in a far-flung room doesn't wind all the way down.  Add to this a SHEDLOAD more potential animatronic aggressors, coming at you from all sorts of angles, and it's hard to argue that the raw, beautiful simplicity of the original hasn't been lost somewhere in the translation.

Now, I know that many of you will view this as an "improvement".  In an age of "bigger is better", this will no doubt please many people MORE than the comparative subtleties of Freddy the first.  But for me, well...let's just say the first one was maybe a bit more about NERVES, and this time it's a bit more about...REFLEXES?  You tell me...which of those two is SCARIER?!  What's more, and it's possibly just me, but I just didn't find the character designs quite as seamlessly spooky as they were the first time around.  That perfect blend of cute 'n' creepy seems to have been lost, if only a little.  But again, if Mr Cawthon had simply kept the exact same designs as the first game, there would have been RIOTS IN THE STREETS, wouldn't there?  Or at least a bit of blood on some bedroom walls.  It's like they always say...you can't please EVERYBODY...

Look, I'm still giving this one a REALLY high recommendation, because most of the appeal of the original is still intact, and some of you will no doubt PREFER this to the original.   It's just not as fresh the second time around, and the "improvements" aren't necessarily a step forward so much as a step, well...mostly SIDEWAYS, if you want my opinion.  Which you clearly MIGHT, if you've managed to read this far into this rather long-winded review (bless you, bless you).  For those who loved the original:  Expect much of the same, only kinda different, and kinda more complicated and kinda more "busy" and "epic" (if that's your thing).  Oh, and it's also HARDER, as if the original wasn't hard enough!  For those who haven't played the original:  Play that first.  This is way too crazy a place to start.  The original's really quite, quite crazy enough, and the premise will probably make more sense if you start there anyway.  I'm still looking forward to checking out the third one (and apparently there's a FOURTH on the way!), but as is often the case, I'm left wondering if maybe this world would be a better place if people just learned to leave well enough alone, rather than just grinding things needlessly into the ground.  Alien: Resurrection, anyone?!

Verdict: 8.5/10.

Um... yeah. It's not a good sign when I've only been playing the game half an hour and i'm already bored.
The developer did a pretty good job building the atmosphere, but it feels like all it's used for is jump scares. The most I can say is at least it isn't one of those fricking flash games where you click on this thing five times, this thing once, once on the first thing, and then are rewarded with a really cheap jumpscare.
Game play is excruciatingly repetitive. It is a clever gimmick that instead of "dying" you wake up, and it was utilized well during the first bit of gameplay, where you wander around an empty house waking up every time you see something particularly horrifying. I also love the black and white color scheme, with interactable objects having different colors to them. This was a godsend, and I didn't have to wander around smashing the interact button in front of everything that looks slightly unique.
Trouble was, this is a walking simulator in the worst sense of the word. And I like walking simulators! But whereas in, say, Gone Home you are walking through a house that's loaded down with secrets and personality and notes and Bikini Kill and Le Tigre tapes, in this game you are just walking. Periodically jogging for a bit. Hiding in plain sight for a moment. Followed by more walking. There aren't notes. There are barely any other people. Even when the game did something I thought was really neat (introducing the girl with black hair from the trailer/game icon as your sister by showing a picture of you with her, then telling you her name by showing your character react to her tombstone, which reads "beloved sister") it goes and ruins it by having the character wake up and immediately have a conversation with his sister about how she is his sister.
And I get where the game is coming from, I do. It's about mental illness. Mental illness is all about repetition, whether it's the good kind of repetition like stimming or the bad kind, like chronic unwanted thoughts. But when that's all there is to the game... life is just too short, you know?

As one of my games with the most hours put into it, I can definitely say something about this game.
Firstly, the graphics are starting to age in comparisson to newer games, but it has more than enough thatn whats needed to play. Graphics don't make a game, gameplay does.
Speaking of gameplay, point 2: Fun. Addictive. 60 hours in and I'm still mostly just zipping around blowing stuff up and off-roading sports cars. Make allt the more awesome that you can buy fancy stuff from the black market at any given time.
Next point: the world. Quite nice looking, a bit plain, but realistic. And yet just colorful enough not to be boring. What makes this look so much better thatn CoD or some other shooters is that there's lots of green, and a few colorful cars and people now and then.
Mountains are realisticly scaled, giving the world a large and open feel. And nothing is more satifying than testing sports cars' durability down the side of the larger ones.
Finally: story. I'm not big on story lines, especially when it comes to action focused games. Games like Dear Esther do it nice, but in a game where the fun is suposed to come from shooting things up, I have to admit that any story that gets in the way of gaming just fustrates me. Luckily, this game has the option to skip almost every single unnessecary animation. And I'm sure the plot line is somewhat thought out, as I've picked up pieces of it, but not enough to know why the heck I'm doing anything that I'm doing.
But that's what makes this game great. Action. Addictive, explosive action. Sorry, plotline, I'm busy headshotting commanders with my 9 mil' and blowing up army bases with rpg's.
EDIT: Forgot one key part of why this game is so addictive. It does a damn good job of making you feel pro. Even if you play on hard, you have more abilites and weapons than the enemy, and killing large amounts of people (or covering vast distances) in short times gives you the feeling of power and liberty.
