I've clocked in quite a lot of time with Cook, Serve, Delicious! , and can attest to its addictiveness. It is a game which places you under the stress of following repeated sets of instructions at a sometimes rapid pace. The setting is that of a restaurant where you, the head chef, must develop your instruction-following skills to exceptional standards.
The presentation is pretty straightforward and functional, with the art style cartoonish without sacrificing the necessary detail. The humour is quirkily offbeat and in places (primarily the food descriptions) mildly satirical. If you get gripped by addiction like I did you're likely to be annoyed by the music after awhile, although the sound effects are vital for you to be cooking at your best: difficulty can be applied by simply muting the game.
Although the game tries to enliven the cookery grind with betting, health inspections, tournaments and a rather bland dating system, the core elements remain unchanged from start to finish. I doubt the creators could have done any better without essentially building minigames from the ground up. Regardless, this is by definition a title of limited scope.
I do recommend this title, however given the aformentioned shallowness I also recommend buying it when it's on sale.

Look at my hours. I've spent enough time in this game to give you an honest review. Note that I will likely continue to play the game, despite the negative review. But for NEW players, I suggest otherwise.
The lag; this is just atrocious. The developers don't force players to play on servers of their own region, and the lag kick threshhold is extremely high. You'll have someone in every match that seems like they're hacking, but they're just lagging like a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. Sometimes you'll get disconnected in the middle of a match, even a ranked match, and lose everything you did.
The language barriers; It's pretty difficult to find English speaking players in a match together. I'd say maybe 10% of the players I've come across speak English.(Which includes broken English) I attribute this to the game not forcing players to play on their own local servers. What you end up getting stuck with is a match filled with people that can't listen, can't speak, and can't co-ordinate anything. So if you're expecting even a hint of a tactile approach, don't. Form a premade with your rl friends instead. You'll get better results.
The 'money' gear; You can buy armor in this game with in game currency (W$ for short.) W$ can also be bought with premium currency. So lets say you want to spend $20 and buy a sniper rifle that usually takes weeks to get to.. well, guess what, you can. The worst part is the armor. Armor in this game gives various bonuses. Like -20% to head, or resistance to flashbangs, or higher run speed, or even the ability to resist the first shot from a sniper rifle. Yes. you heard that correctly... What players with the funds seem to do, is they go and stock the hell out on gear and weapons and absolutely dominate the field without earning that right. They bought the right. It bugs the hell out of me personally. I think RL money should not go towards anything except cosmetics or maybe reasonable boosters.
The wtferry; This game runs well on potatos. It's not a super demanding game, and it can be scaled down if need be. An issue I see with that, is this is one of the highest downloaded f2p fps games on Steam right now... and you get stuck with a very odd amount of players that seem to have never played a first person shooter before... And not the kind of noob where you're just like "Ugh, l2p. Git gud newb." but more like... why in the bloody hell is he shooting a lamp post. Oh. He's out of ammo. Finally. WAIT NO DON'T THROW THAT *boom*." that kind of thing. I've entered several games (both co-op and vs) where players will sit at the edge of the map and shoot at the sky, or the out of bounds zone... It throws me off, and I really don't know why it's happening. I haven't seen this in any other game before. It reminds me of when I hand my 4year old niece the xbox controller. Or my 45 year old mother, really. It's baffling. Hence 'wtferry'.
The HORRID anti-cheat; this one won't be as long. The anti-cheat system seems to be a very rough beta for what they intended in the beginning. It's faulty as all hell, and will give you false flags on many, many things. Let's name a few I've seen. Fraps, Overwolf, Steam overlay, Curse, GeForce Experience, AMD Catalyst, Razr Gamebooster, Teamspeak, Raidcall, and any remote-desktop applications you may use. There are many more, but I haven't come across them. It's irritating to say the least.
No love for the snipers; The classes are Rifleman, Medic, Engineer, and Sniper. Pretty basic of this type of game. Each class has a primary weapon, a secondary weapon, and grenade or grenade like utilities. They each also get a special equipment item simple called their 'special'. Rifleman gets a distributable ammo pack, medic gets both a defib, and a med kit, engineer gets both an armor repair kit and a claymore, and sniper gets... nothing. Not a single thing. I don't really get the design idea behind this. Maybe there's something I'm missing, and it would make sense why they did this if I just knew, but as it stands, this♥♥♥♥♥♥is dumb as hell.
With all of that being said, I've obviously found areas in which I enjoy the game. It's a free FPS in the voice of Battlefield, but singing a song from Call of Duty. I may continue to play this game in the future, and you bet your sweet review reading♥♥♥♥♥I'll be playing this when they fix the lag issues.

Quite a few things are different from DS1, one thing in particular that I first noticed was changes in speed.
Con - Firstly, Estus no longer refills your health instantly, but rather it slowly fills up your health over the course of ~1 second. Still quite fast, but it does get annoying when you die right after you heal, just because of how long it takes.
Pro + Con - They also changed the speed at which you consume items (including estus), now it seems to take only a fraction of a second longer than DS1, it's not that bad of a change as you can now use some items while walking (albeit at a reduced walking speed), but also makes you consider when to use an item.
Pro - In terms of character movement, it feels waaay different compared to DS1, but in a good way. Feels a whole lot more responsive and fast. I personally used a steam controller in my playthrough and those buttons on the back are a live saver when it comes to locking on and sprinting.
As for general game design.
Con - There are a few levels which I feel are poorly designed, they just threw an unnecessary amount of enemies into it. Some levels literally only have 2 enemies just copy and pasted a couple dozen times (cough* Dragon Shrine cough* Iron Keep). There are also a few areas which don't really serve any purpose other than to access a completely different. It's true that not every level needs a boss, but it should at least serve a purpose. That being said, I feel most of the levels are pretty good, only a couple of them will leave a bad taste in your mouth.
Pro + Con - DS2 is a lot larger than the first game, so it's difficult to pinpoint exactly where you need to go without looking it up, BUT, once you actually know where you're going it's insanely fun, Especially in NG+.
Pro/Con - Ability to warp between bonfires right from the start. I know a lot of people may not have enjoyed it, but part of the fun in DS1 was the trek from place to place, and only after you reached a certain point could you warp. I feel this should have continued in DS2 as the ability to warp is a nice thing to strive for.
Overall a really fun and challenging game, but I can see why people don't like this one compared to the other souls games.

If you like restaurant management games, then you will enjoy this one.
The aesthetics are nice, the food art is well done and the background city view from your window changes with the day/night cycle very seamlessly. The music is okay, I play my own while running this game.
The controls are very straightforward - you can use the mouse and/or keyboard. The key bindings are very intuitive (usually first letter = key you have to press; ex: b for bacon), and you can change them around to suit your playstyle. The learning curve is minimal to moderate, the main difficulty comes from juggling tasks efficiently in order to maximize your score multiplier (perfect days give you cash bonuses). Once you get used to the key bindings (highly recommend using primarily the keyboard vs. the mouse as it can be significantly faster) you can complete your orders very quickly.
The tutorial is nice and quick, and there is always a guide to the right of the screen when you are completing your orders. In the preplanning area, you can practice with any of the food items to see if you'd like to add them to your active menu. There is quite a variety of food available, and you can upgrade certain foods in order to charge more for them. Some items require you to have additional equipment, like a grill for your hamburgers.
There are also restaurant upgrades like a tip jar or light snacks to increase the time your customers will wait for you to take their order before leaving. Customers do not have a happiness gauge (you can take their order even when their ticket is almost empty with no penalty) - what matters is getting the order perfect. You cannot go back if you make a mistake, so balancing speed accuracy (speed-accuracy tradeoff lol) is critical to success (and perfect days).
Rush hour usually occurs during lunch time and dinner, giving you a boost to customer intake. Different foods have pros and cons - for example, if you have more than 3 "fatty" foods, then you will get a negative rating to your "buzz," which determines how many clients enter your restaurant. Other foods may not generate tips and/or have menu rot (they decrease in popularity and generate negative buzz if they remain on active menu for more than 2 consecutive days). The baked potato takes much longer to prepare, however, it also has a modifier to tipping - generating higher value and more frequent tips.
A good game if you enjoy restaurant management, reminded me a lot of Cooking Mama. Give it a try if you are interested.

I'm sorry, but this is one of the most boring and uninspired horror games I've ever played. In the hour and a half it took to get through the game I kept hoping for Anything mildly interesting to happen, but in the end I just felt like I had wasted my time.
You play through a series of nightmares that all consist of walking through corridor upon corridor in such groundbreaking and refreshing settings as ~an old, abandoned house~, ~a psychiatric hospital~, and ~a graveyard~. I expected there to be some absurdity, maybe some surreal looking areas - these are nightmares after all - but there was hardly any to be found.
Occassionally you will come across monsters that you have to get past to get to the next boring corridor. Some you need to hide from, some are blind but will attack if they hear you, etc. Pretty standard horror game mechanics, nothing new here either.
Now, I could live with the boring gameplay and paint-by-the-numbers horror elements if only the game had an interesting story to tell, but even the story is about as trite and clichéd as they come. In the description it says the game was inspired by the creator's struggles with depression and OCD, but I didn't see anything that gave me any insight into what it was like to deal with that.
I say this as someone who's struggling with mental illness myself, and am a little dissapointed that you'd use that as a selling point for something that only ever comes across as yet another horror story about some guy fighting monsters in a surreal alternate world because of a traumatic family incident. It never feels personal at all, it just falls flat.
Also, apparently the game has multiple endnings, but it gives you no reason to want to replay it, so I don't know what the point of that even is.
If you want to play a game where it feels like you're fighting mentall illness, play Knock Knock. If you want to play a game with a similar quirky children's book style, play Fran Bow. Both are much better horror games.

Gone Home is a unique game released in 2013 for windows and in 2016 for the Xbox One and PlayStation Four. The main character, Kaitlin, has just returned from a year long trip around the world, but when she gets home, no one is there. Then the game begins and the player has to explore the house looking for clues to what had happened, and why no one is home.
This whole game revolves around this mystery, leading to some interesting storytelling. In a way the whole game is almost like a detective game. When searching the house the player will find different items, such as books and notes that they can read. Everything in the game world can be picked up and manipulated. I’m not going to give anything away here, but when I figured out what happened in the year that passed, it blew my mind. After learning more, I started to relate more to Sam, Kaitlin’s sister. It enlightened me as to how a  specific group of people become who they are. It is rare for a game to become so understandable, and relatable so quickly. Needless to say the story is really well done, and the main reason for playing this game. Every member of the family has something unique and interesting to learn about, with secrets hidden around every corner.
The design of the house is really intriguing. It feels like there are remnants of the past everywhere, that are just waiting to be explored. Although, it does seem a little bit big for it to be a normal house. This is forgivable, because everything that is in the house is really interesting to explore. The game is anything but linear. Since the entire game is based around searching for clues to the past, players will often find some things others did not, or have a relatively similar, but different experience.
Despite all of these amazing factors of the game, there are many flaws. For me personally, these flaws do not out way the overall good of the game, but for some they might. To begin, the game is not a traditional game. There are no enemies, monsters, or any real antagonist. As you would expect this leaves the game with very little tension between characters. For the most part, the story is primarily told from Sam’s point of view. Depending on how you view storytelling, this could potentially be great or awful. For me it worked, but I felt that it was very one sided, especially with the audio logs. Everything that is there is really inspiring, informational, and emotional, but to me it would have been interesting to hear more audio logs that were not part of the main story. There are many side stories that could have been fleshed out more.
Additionally, there is a great deal of reading. Similar to Phoenix Wright, your experience with this game will greatly depend on whether you enjoy reading a lot of text in games. To me, this game seemed a little too reliant on text. Without much tension I found it hard to engage with the game at times. I would get bored because there was not much to do other than reading. I think more audio logs would improve the quality of this aspect of the game and make it more interesting.
Another, major flaw of the game is its lack of time and replay value. The game only lasts about two hours. It took me only an hour and a half to complete, but yet the developers are charging twenty dollars for this experience. This would be fine, if there was some replay value, but there is hardly any. After I finished the game, I had no intention of going back to play it again. It is good, but not worth playing again. Because of that, this game is definitely not worth the price. I got it on sale for five dollars, and that is probably the most that I would pay for it.The game is good for what it is, but very few games justify the price of twenty dollars for only two hours of content.
Overall, the narrative and storytelling in this game are great, but all of the problems that come with it may cause the game to not be worth it to some people. For me this game is an interesting and creative spin on traditional methods of storytelling. Additionally, I think that this is an important game for the community as a whole, because of its strives to turn the tables on traditional methods of interaction and storytelling. However, because of its many flaws and oversights, I must give this game a two out of five. That is not to say that it is a bad game, just one that will only appeal to a niche audience. Your experience with this game will ultimately depend upon whether you enjoy new and unique ways of storytelling, a lack of enemies, and being able to piece the story together with little help.

I really enjoyed Neverending Nightmares.  The Edward Gorey inspired artwork is perfect (perfect emulation of Gorey's works and perfect for the gameplay style).  The soundscape builds anxiety and reminds me of the terror of hearing something but not knowing what or where it is.
As far as the story, you get out of it what you want.  You can look for deep hidden meanings in the artwork/paintings, level design, monsters, and brief dialogue or you can just enjoy it as a true Nightmare without context and dreamlike. It doesn't beat you over the head with plot.  (I truly just wanted to experience the world because of the artwork.  I wasn't demanding a deep complicated storyline - which is there.)
The only thing I wanted that the game didn't provide would have been more subtle changes in the backgrounds (shadows move/objects change or fall etc.). There were a few, but I want more.  I like looking at the screen and thinking Did I just see that?
There are parts of the game where the mechanics may frustrate people. Thomas doesn't run for long at all (which makes sense, ever had those dreams where you try to punch but can't? I attribute his slowness to things like that)  In this game, getting killed doesn't set you back far at all so trying to avoid death again is easy in that aspect.
I recommend this game (if it is on sale).  It's a short playthough if you want to just get one ending.  It has some really creepy moments. I'd probably buy a sequel to it if they made one.

(Note: this review is for X only, not X-2, but should largely apply to both).
Nicely done! I give this 8/10. The graphics are basically the same as the original, but crisper, and even a modest GPU is quite adequate.
What's really great is the set of gameplay enhancements (e.g., Turbo, No-Encounter). For those of us who play for the story rather than the combat, they allow combat to go much faster, and often be avoided altogether. The only down-side is that these enhancements require a keyboard. For those of us who play in console mode in the living room, this could be a problem. The Steam Controller solves this by allowing mapping of the necessary keys to an on-screen pop-up menu (a number of these configurations are available from the community).
Auto-save (which happens at area transitions) is a major plus. No-Encounter can be combined with auto save and/or the "normal" save points to effectively allow you to save at any point in the story.
The only fail is Auto-Battle. All it does is cause every character to automatically use their default physical attack, which in magic users is generally useless. This method generally gets you killed for battles against enemies anywhere near your level. It only works well against much weaker enemies, where the amount of AP gained is too small to be worth grinding this way.
Most of the problems in the original game remain, of course (e.g. long cut-scene sequences). The biggest design problem is that most of the side quests don't become available until the end of the game, and are quite difficult. They also add nothing to the story. Now that I've reached that point, the story is effectively done, apart from what promises to be a predictable conclusion, so I've decided to set the game aside indefinitely.

Look at my hours. I've spent enough time in this game to give you an honest review. Note that I will likely continue to play the game, despite the negative review. But for NEW players, I suggest otherwise.
The lag; this is just atrocious. The developers don't force players to play on servers of their own region, and the lag kick threshhold is extremely high. You'll have someone in every match that seems like they're hacking, but they're just lagging like a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. Sometimes you'll get disconnected in the middle of a match, even a ranked match, and lose everything you did.
The language barriers; It's pretty difficult to find English speaking players in a match together. I'd say maybe 10% of the players I've come across speak English.(Which includes broken English) I attribute this to the game not forcing players to play on their own local servers. What you end up getting stuck with is a match filled with people that can't listen, can't speak, and can't co-ordinate anything. So if you're expecting even a hint of a tactile approach, don't. Form a premade with your rl friends instead. You'll get better results.
The 'money' gear; You can buy armor in this game with in game currency (W$ for short.) W$ can also be bought with premium currency. So lets say you want to spend $20 and buy a sniper rifle that usually takes weeks to get to.. well, guess what, you can. The worst part is the armor. Armor in this game gives various bonuses. Like -20% to head, or resistance to flashbangs, or higher run speed, or even the ability to resist the first shot from a sniper rifle. Yes. you heard that correctly... What players with the funds seem to do, is they go and stock the hell out on gear and weapons and absolutely dominate the field without earning that right. They bought the right. It bugs the hell out of me personally. I think RL money should not go towards anything except cosmetics or maybe reasonable boosters.
The wtferry; This game runs well on potatos. It's not a super demanding game, and it can be scaled down if need be. An issue I see with that, is this is one of the highest downloaded f2p fps games on Steam right now... and you get stuck with a very odd amount of players that seem to have never played a first person shooter before... And not the kind of noob where you're just like "Ugh, l2p. Git gud newb." but more like... why in the bloody hell is he shooting a lamp post. Oh. He's out of ammo. Finally. WAIT NO DON'T THROW THAT *boom*." that kind of thing. I've entered several games (both co-op and vs) where players will sit at the edge of the map and shoot at the sky, or the out of bounds zone... It throws me off, and I really don't know why it's happening. I haven't seen this in any other game before. It reminds me of when I hand my 4year old niece the xbox controller. Or my 45 year old mother, really. It's baffling. Hence 'wtferry'.
The HORRID anti-cheat; this one won't be as long. The anti-cheat system seems to be a very rough beta for what they intended in the beginning. It's faulty as all hell, and will give you false flags on many, many things. Let's name a few I've seen. Fraps, Overwolf, Steam overlay, Curse, GeForce Experience, AMD Catalyst, Razr Gamebooster, Teamspeak, Raidcall, and any remote-desktop applications you may use. There are many more, but I haven't come across them. It's irritating to say the least.
No love for the snipers; The classes are Rifleman, Medic, Engineer, and Sniper. Pretty basic of this type of game. Each class has a primary weapon, a secondary weapon, and grenade or grenade like utilities. They each also get a special equipment item simple called their 'special'. Rifleman gets a distributable ammo pack, medic gets both a defib, and a med kit, engineer gets both an armor repair kit and a claymore, and sniper gets... nothing. Not a single thing. I don't really get the design idea behind this. Maybe there's something I'm missing, and it would make sense why they did this if I just knew, but as it stands, this♥♥♥♥♥♥is dumb as hell.
With all of that being said, I've obviously found areas in which I enjoy the game. It's a free FPS in the voice of Battlefield, but singing a song from Call of Duty. I may continue to play this game in the future, and you bet your sweet review reading♥♥♥♥♥I'll be playing this when they fix the lag issues.

It's a bit grindy. I find myself spamming my attacks against difficulty 1-2 enemies and I still can't really upgrade my HQ for larger army supply. Two hours and eight levels in and I've largely been using the same handful of units and tactics. My base is a lot more badass than it was and so far that's the only sense of progress I've been able to attain.
What is the game exactly? Pretty much as advertised. It talks about some Tower Defense elements and there is the periodic defense at play but most of my gameplay was spent on the attack, which acts like a classic Tug-of-War that you might have played on flash game websites in the past. There's some tactics to be had, like managing supply and when to use which units and spamming one type may not always serve you well. You also get airstrikes and smoke bombs that will help you weaken defenses (I personally aim for sniper towers as soon as possible) so there's more nuance than just seeing if you have more dudes than the other guy.
Yes, there are some hefty microtransactions but it doesn't beat me over the head with them except for the exclamation point on the store page going "NEW OFFER, GET IT NOW AND IT GOES AWAY IN THREE DAYS". Other than that, most of it is cosmetic but there is a pay-to-skip-progress mechanic at play.
At the very least, there's no "pay to wait" mechanic here. You can constantly play to your heart's content, as long as you can handle some grind.

Ever since Cook, Serve, Delicious! came out on Steam, I followed it around. I tried trading for it a few times, but was unsuccessful. I gave up hope of getting the game since I was saving up my money for another thing at the time, and I forgot about it. A few months later, I was delighted to find the game in Humble Bundle- I almost instantly purchased it, and I have to say, even though I got it for a dollar, I would gladly pay the full Steam price for it.
So far it's been incredibly fun. The concept is incredibly simple; press a letter key, and you plop an ingredient onto the dish. This quickly turns from easy to hard. You have to press the buttons with speed, memorize which ingredients go with which key, and juggle multiple tasks at the same time. The gameplay becomes even harder during Rush Hour (usually during workers' lunch breaks and at the end of the work-day), since multiple customers enter at a time. You can customize what you have on your menu each day, so you can theme your restaurant if you wanted (for example, a classic burger/fries/soda restaurant).
Overall, it's small and simple, but turns into a huge, incredibly hard game. At the time of writing this review I only have 2-ish hours, and I'm already in love with the game. You can expect to see my played hours steadily rising.
EDIT: Now I have 28 hours compared to the 2 hours at this review's writing. The game has only gotten better, and New Game+ provides an even bigger challenge. Oh, and Battle Kitchen just came out, which is awesome. BUY THIS GAME NOW.

Very few games have ever disappointed me as much a Gone Home did. After reading all the critic reviews of how amazing this game is and the interesting description for the game, I had fairly high expectations. The description for the game leads you to believe there will be an interesting mystery as you arrive at your home and no one is there. I really expected a game where I would be at the edge of my seat trying to figure out the answers to the mysteries of the game all the way up to the very end. This obviously didn't happen. In the first 10 minutes of the game, things are quiet interesting. Trying to figure out where everyone is and why no one is home keeps you in the mystery of the game for a little bit. However, after searching the house and progressing in the story, Gone Home quickly becomes less and less interesting. Not only does it become increasingly annoying to move around the house, because your character is incredibly slow (I swear she is part snail), but not even half way through the game you will figure out the entire mystery.
[Spoilers below]
(Once again, spoilers) Really, the mystery isn't hard at all the figure out and once you do, you will be disappointed. The big GIANT reveal is that your sister is just a rebellious teen that has run off with her lover. After about the half way mark of the game, once I figured it out, I kept thinking this can't be it. This cannot be the amazing mystery critics raved about. I was wrong. It was the entire mystery. Even as a story on it's own, it's nothing unique. Almost every single teenage that has ever lived has gone through a rebellious stage. Many run away just like the main character's sister. It happens, it's nothing new or intriguing and it is especially not something worthy of making a mystery game over. If the story was to realistically progress, I guarantee that the main character's sister would be back home going to school. She may still dream of what could have happened, but it was a stage. She will grow out of it. In the story, she talks like she is special and that she truly has found her true love and what she plans to do for the rest of her life. However, this is exactly how all teens in the rebellious stage feel. This part of her story isn't special or unique. After her hormones balance out, things would change. It's a cycle of life.
My expectations were crushed by this uninteresting and easy to figure out mystery game. Gone Home: The Snail Simulator is one of the few games that I am ashamed to have in my steam library.

My name is SynificHD and I am a YouTuber who uploads many gameplay content, such as this game.
This review will show my thoughts and opinions towards the game, also including a link to the game for you guys to check out and hopefully enjoy; and give you an insight of the game!
The game "Gone Home" is a first-person walking simulator, where you play as a girl named Kaitlin Greenbrair, who arrives home from a holiday trip, only to find out that no-one is home; the house is deserted and you are to solve the mystery to why the house is empty.
The game is "Narrator based", where you find diary entries that belong to your sister Samantha Greenbrair, as you explore around the house you eventually uncover strange events that eventually lead up to a dramatic ending.
"Gone Home" is a very 'emotional' game that requires you to sit through a lot of dialogue to understand what is happening in the household. As a walking simulator it features many basic concepts but the story does take a rather sharp turn towards the end that makes you rethink everything you have been told. This game would best suit people who are open minded to most situations and interests - "I hope I worded that correctly..."
I recommend this game to people who enjoy basic walking simulators that are narrator based which features minimal puzzles, and involves sitting through a lot of dialogue.
At the time, recording was an issue and like ive mentioned in another review of mine this would be easier to record now. I would give this a 7-8/10 being that its a game full of lots of dialogue which makes editing more of an issue having an unnecessarily long video.

This is going to be very long, but I am very passionate about this. Long story short, I do not think this game is worth $60+ I would consider it closer to a $30-$40 game. Very stable, especially for Ubisoft, and I enjoyed myself.
When this game was first announced at E3, I was so excited. It appeared to be close to the game I'd been hoping for years ago. I have always been a fan of racing games, and over the last few years I've been underwhelmed by the options on PC. I was quick to pre-order The Crew despite my displeasure with Ubisoft and Watch_Dogs especially. When I played the Beta for The Crew, I was met with a stable game which was nice, but there were little things that bothered me. First and foremost was their approach to many of the landmarks of the US. I live in Las Vegas, so once I finally got there, I was underwhelmed. I feel like GTA San Andreas had a better looking Vegas than this game does. I then noticed that Mazda Laguna Seca was on the map also. Laguna Seca is one of my favorite Tracks ever, so I had to see it. After my initial woes with Las Vegas, I was mildly worried. My fears came true, and this point I was legitamately upset.  If you are going to take the time to put a track as Iconic as Laguna Seca in the game, at least do it justice. The Corkscrew, a sweeping S curve, with a 3 story drop, is flat in the game. plus the bump just before the corner turns into a jump at any speed greater than about 50 mph. I understand they can't capture every single part of the US but for tracks, especially those like Laguna Seca, at least make them like the real thing. Car selection is very limited comapred to most other racing titles, but you can go through the entire game with your starter car. there really is no need to spend money at all. I beat the game only spending 2200 on mirrors for my Ferrari, because the Italian flag decal didn't really fit withthe rest of the car. All class upgrades are paid for and individula parts are awarded from skill challenges. unless you want to drive a different car, or make the ones you have prettier, there is absolutely no need to buy anything. I am not very ggod at games in general so I found some missions to be very frustrating. The takedown missions in particular were an annoyance for me. trying to chase someone down and inflict enough damage was very difficult for me. As were the Smash missions, hit a certain number of container within the time limit. it would take me over an hour just for those missions, mostly due to physics (more on that later). The story was pretty much what you would expect from a racing game. Not super indepth, lots of random missions that you have to do with no real explanation of why, but it does have a rather logical progression, and moves at a decent pace. I played through the entire campaign solo, and the only time i interacted with other players was occasionally having a head on collision mid corner. now that I beat the story I might look more into Faction missions, but for now, I found the online function to be more of an annoyance than anything useful.  Overall, I would say that from a game play standpoint, I wasn't really disappointed.
From a technological stand point I was.... I'll say satisfied. In 24.6 hours of play the game only crashed 3 times. As far as servers go, the only time I had trouble connecting was when they were performing server maintanence. Visually, this is actually a very good looking game. If it weren't for the 60 fps lock, and the strange Depth of Field effects I wouldn't have any complaints. Honestly, playing at max settings (motion blur and depth of field off) I was playing at 3140 x 2160 on my  GTX 980 at a stable 60 fps, and gpu usage was only at around 70%. I would have liked to be able to fully utilize 144 Hz that my monitor is capable of, but for whatever reason they locked it to 60. Not a deal breaker for the vast majority of consumers, but it was mildly irksome for me. Normal road driving is quite satisfying, once I turned driving assists to hardcore, I was quite content with the handling. The collision detection baffles me though. there is no consistency as far as what constitutes a full crash and what is just a glancing blow. I had times that I would ram into the back of a pedestrian vehicle by more than half of it, and my car would just "glitch" to one side and I wouldn't lose more than a couple mph. other times there would be a couple of feet between my car and the pedestrian vehicle, and I would crash. I tried to figure out why, but never really could. The most ridiculous aspect of the physics is most apparent once you unlock the raid class. These vehicles are designed to go offroad, over large objects, and jumps. Every time I tried to go off a jump, the physics would react in a way that I can only call alien.  I could get practically no distance, or I would have insane nose up manuvers. worst of all was the tendency for the car to spring up to one side if only one tire went over a large rock or object. If your vehicle goes past a 90 degree angle the game treats it as a crash, even if you end up landing on your wheels again. If you did end up making it off the jump well, the game trys to keep you flat, most of the time, so more times than not I would end up taking an awkward bounce and spin out. This was completely unnatural to me. and it was so random I couldn't compensate for it. If the game was trictly on road, this wouldn't be a problem, but there are so many missions, like the smash missions I mentioned before, where this comes into play, and it is very frustrating. At the end of the day, I was able to work around these issues, and beat the missions, but I could never really achieve the score I wanted because the physics would mess me up. But i do have to give them credit, not once did i experience a glitch, much less a game breaking one. Just 3 freeze and crashes that I can't really explain, but since it is always online, server based, I didn't lose any progress.
Overall I would give The Crew a 7 out of 10. It held my attention the whole time, and I found satisfaction in completeing missions. the overall experience was quite good, it had it's faults, but nothing was ever major enough to put me off of the game entirely. I would say wait for it so go on sale for 33% or more, and you'll get your moneys worth. For that reason, I do recommend  this game.

. I fully expect riots in the near future if we survive this winter.

Banished:
Sort of a city builder and a survival game. You need to build a town for a couple of people, and make sure that town grows and stay alive.
What is special about Banished unlike most of city-builders, is that EVERYTHING is unlocked from the start. There is no "research" and something like that. Now, you might think that this will make the game easier, or very short, but it really doesnt. If you just build everything from the start, you will die quickly.
Now what's the difficult part? Well, the amount of s*** you will need to deal with all depends on what you choose on the start. the "difficulty" option only really metters for the first couple of years. The other options, like weather, disasters and such, are what really metters.
Every citizen needs food, a warm place, A HOUSE, and to be healthy. If you dont think ahead, it will be difficult to keep the town alive.
Also, there are many dengerous stuff you need to avoid: Non-healthy citizens can start diseases. Non-happy citizens will work A LOT WORSER. And idiot citizens, again,dont really do their jobs.
Now, wheres the fun? The survival. keeping your city/town alive is fun and can be pretty difficult. There are always new problems that pop out, you need to be ready for everything. This game is also amazingly relaxing...
So, you got 20$? What the hell are you waiting for? Buy this game! Even if you dont like city builders you might have fun with this one.
Heck, this game will also get mod support soon, so you can expect a lot more to come.

I love this game. The people who play it are nice and will give you tips early on. There are 4 modes, all of which are great.  The main mode is called Frontlines where you try to take trenches from the enemy and defend your own trenches from their assaults. The squad system works well and you have to cooperate with them if you want to get anything done. It does get frustrating when you have to fall back or else you are 'executed for desertion' though but I think the mode would lose its structure if the mechanic didn't exist. Another game mode is the Rifle Deathmatch, a free for all, rifle only mode. It is great for practicing your skills before going into Frontlines and is really fun as a stand alone mode too. Team Attrition is a gamemode where your team starts out with a certain amount of lives and when you run out the match ends. You get to use any weapons in this mode, whether it is the flamethrower, a shotgun or a tiny little knife. It is fun to cooperate with your team to take out enemies and move into the trenches. The last mode is squad defence; It is like Frontlines except you don't get to attack and the enemies are bots. You get to fight wave after wave, shooting down the bots as they desperately try to sprint into your trench. This gamemode is perfect to play coop with your friends. This game is great and that is why I recommend it.

I have played a lot of racing games from sims to arcade racers, and I have not found a better racing game. This game truely has it all; two tracks, bayous, jumps, cities, MILES upon MILES of roads. The scope is simply amazing. I have seen some people say that this game lacks detail because of the size, but I simply don't think thats true. Going through my neck of the woods (Michigan area) I can clearly see they nailed the look and feel of the state, and I think the pure size only enhanses the experience. As for the handling think heavy Need For Speed influence with maybe a hint of Burnout. Definitely not a game for the people who are simulation master race, more of a fun game for everyone else who just loves driving for the enjoyment. There is nothing more satisfying than logging in with some friends and just cruising across the Rocky Mountains or flying through the Vegas dunes, and thats why this game is so good.
As for the bad, there isn't a whole lot. My main complaint would be with the AI being able to hang with you even if your car is rated over double theirs. However this makes the game more challenging, so its not really much of a con. Also the disabiling missions aren't very fun. They are all doable since the AI takes the same path every time, its just annoying the first time you hit them and they have 6 health and you have to chase them for 60 seconds only to love tap them and kill them.
Pros:
- Great arcade driving feel
- Huge world
- Cruising with your friends across America
Cons:
- AI rubber bands hard even if you have an insane car
- The disabling missions aren't fun
Overall: 9.5/10

If you are looking for a solid multiplayer experience with your friends, do not buy this game. At the moment, the multiplayer aspect of the game barely works, and ironically, forming a crew with your friends is nigh on impossible. The singleplayer is solid enough, though gathering enough cash to buy new cars is a bit tedious.
Edit: As of now, the multiplayer does seem functional enough for me to edit this review. While I cannot speak for the crew aspect (since none of my friends are interested in reinstalling the game so I can test it), PvP does seem to work fairly well for the moment. However, I was disappointed in the lack of variety in some PvP races; most notably in the Perf spec races. There is only one viable car to race with, the LaFerrari, forget trying to race with anything else because you will with most certainty lose.
In the Street spec the Skyline is heavily favored, though it hardly matters what car you pick since most are fairly competitive. Sadly it is a spec that people rarely want to race with.
As for Dirt spec races the Skyline is again favored by most players, though a skilled player should be able to stay with the pack in pretty much any car, granted it has all platinum parts installed.
Raid is my favorite spec, but only because most cars in that class appear to be relatively balanced. What car you choose to race with appears to matter the least in this specific spec. As long as the car you choose has all platinum parts, you should be just fine with pretty much anything.
And finally we come to the Circuit spec, and here the car does matter. From what I have seen you have three options in this spec. The Circuit Hotrod, the DLC Cadillac Escalade (I wish that was a joke) and finally the Alfa Romeo Competizione. The Hotrod is free, so that is what I recommend you get.
When in a PvP lobby, expect to play a lot of Circuit and Perf spec races since these appear to be the most popular. And maybe once in a blue moon, you'll get to play a Street spec race.

That said there are a lot of gaps in the storyline open to interpretation and the forums are buzzing with threads with titles like WHAT DOES IT MEAN?
Overall very satisfactory and fun. The only complaint I have is that the levels are not procedurally generated so after a single playthrough you can storm through the levels knowing which rooms you can bypass and which enemies are going to assault you next. That being said, a second playthrough to help piece together parts of the storyline you may have missed would not be remiss.

This is a review of FFX-2:
Short version : It's a great and happy game full of positive energy. It's a direct sequel from FFX and i advise you either to play or read the plot of FFX on the web, it's not mandatory but it'll help you link the two games and characters for a better gaming experience. You should also watch the ETERNAL CALM cutscene from the launcher, it gives you some minor info. For me it's a good, fun and positive game. If you're feeling down play that game :)
Long version (may contain SPOILERS about FFX):
After bringing the Eterenal Calm to Spira, Yuna took a 2 years vacation and is now is part of the Gullwings, with Rikku and a new character: Paine. The Gullwings are sphere hunters. Spheres are a sort of memory recording device. Your HQ is the airsphip of Brother, Rikku's brother. From the start of the game you can go anywhere in Spira, Hotspots will be marked on your map telling you that there is a sphere to recover there. Each hotspot is a mission (if i remember correctly), when you complete all current hotspot missions you go to the next chapter of the game. BUT if you go only where the hotspots are you'll finish the game pretty fast (it as several endings) AND YOU'LL MISS MOST OF WHAT THE GAME HAS TO OFFER.
To way to go to get the 100% completion is to visit EVERY location everytime you change a chapter. Don't worry it's not tedious, You just play the game and see how the story and the "little" stories of the people of SPIRA unfold.
There are 19 classes called "Dresspheres", basically garments that give you warrior, gunner, thief, black mage, etc abilities and stats. Every round you can change your dressphere by pressing LB or L1 and bring up a "garment grid" showing how you can chnage your dressphere based on the grid you chose and the dresspheres (classes) you put threre. I think each character can have it's own garment grid. If you still don't get what a grament grid is fear not (! ^^ ) look for garment grid images in your browser. I have to say that despite this explanation the system is quite easy to use and this class swap system offers alot of tactics and FUN. There is also a beautiful animation when the girls change their class, it can be shortened or turned off.
You can also capture monsters and make them fight in your party instead of the girls, its up to you.
The game runs at 30fps and honestly it doesn'bother me at all, it doesn't even look that it runs at 30 fps and if I, the guy who can't stand not having 60 fps enjoys the game then so can you. When you play the game you forget about this stuff, it's simply fun to play and the game's job's done.
It got FullHD textures, and other video settings: Vsync, Texture quality, Anisotropic filtering, Shadows setting, Antialiasing, Color correction, Anti Aliasing (Post filtering), Unsharp mark (?) and Ambient occlusion. The game looks really great, sharp and colorful even for an old game. I'm pretty sure it will run even if you have a low end pc.
It also has an autosave system indepedent of your manual save slots which is pretty useful, you just play and play and play ...
You get 2 big games + bonuses (Last mission) for a budget price it's a good deal and a good game. Those are both AAA games of their time that have been very well remastered.
Go for it! ;)

The Crew is the 2014 textbook definition of polarizing, even before it released. On the one hand, it is an open-world racing game, giving you the opportunity to drive from one end of the United States to the other. On the other hand, Ubisoft.
This polarization extends in-game as well. One minute, I could be screaming at the screen because I failed a raid mission for the fifteenth time: My car had forgotten how it was supposed to work and a tiny rock about two pixels in size sent it careening sideways into fifteen trees like the world's worst lumberjack. The next, I would be driving through the snowy Rockies with the sun shining on my face as I drifted through a corner, pondering whether it was possible to operate the steering wheel with my massive erection.
It's a beautiful game with an adequate roster of cars (58 cars including Season Pass, possibly more to come) and wonky physics and I've loved every second of it.

Purchase if it's massively discounted, but it isn't worth the current price.

A lot of disappointment with this one.   I think some of it is residual from some release bugs.  I had a problem getting it to launch.  I checked online for ideas, and I switched off my iobit protection services, and that got me up and running.  No, people shouldn't have to seek out solutions that way; after all, my other games work fine; so I can understand how people could get really frustrated by that, especially when they're eager to play.
That said, it also took me an afternoon to realize I was essentially playing FAR CRY, but in an urban setting.  It uses the CRY ENGINE, the controls, binoculars, targeting, capturing, and MAIN MISSIONS are almost alike.  That's not a bad thing, because FAR CRY is fun.  So is this game.
It's not original, really.  But it is done well.  I haven't seen anywhere near the excellent story telling or characters of FAR CRY 3.  In fact, your own player isn't voiced.  That's kind of a big deal right there, and very different from FAR CRY, and not in a good way.  But I'll tell you what!  Get in there and start fighting, and see if you aren't having every bit as much fun as you do with other games.
As far as performance goes, I have a GTX 970, 4690k, and 16G RAM.  I can't turn everything on without ruining the performance, but I can select HIGH and add more features from there without taking a hit on the frame rate.  And this is a good looking game!
I recommend this one, now that it is apparently past its buggy stage, to anyone who likes shooters.  And you can grab four AI soldiers to fight along side you.  You need them, too, or you are a DEAD MAN.
Have fun.  And guys, it may not be perfect, or better than some of its predecessors from which it is derived, but someone did a helluva lot of honest work on this, and I'd like to say, "Thanks," and "Kudos," on a great game.
And now, I've gotta get back to the carnage (sounds awful, doesn't it?  What's wrong with us?) ...

Have fixed a vast majority of the bugs, delievered even more story content for it and made it a actually fun and fresh shooter to play. Here is my review:
GAMEPLAY:
+ Satisfying shooter play, and Gun customization
+ Multiple ways to approach each Strikepoint, use the enemy's equipment against them with hacks, make a suprise explosion, go in guns blazing, or go in with stealth.
+ Fun puzzles to solve in a variety of ways.
+ Recruit AI to fight with you
+ Good progression pace in terms of getting new gear
- Clunky Driving, felt like it was meant to be played on foot only.
STORY:
+ Story satisfies my desire for a game about American perserverence in a ficitional invasion of the United States
- Wish it went more in depth to what was happening elsewhere in the U.S.
+ Later DLC additions added voice acting for Player's Character Ethan Brady.
- Doc Burnett's character doesn't fit into the story. He offers little significance and most of the time just comes off as annoying. People die in war, and he plays the pacifist like laying down and taking the abuse from the KPA is going to solve thing. But yet being a pacifist had already decided to help the resistance which fights and kills the KPA.
+ Satisfyingly opened up the possibility to a sequel with the 'Beyond the Walls' DLC
MULTIPLAYER:
+ Is actually really fun, it presents a challange and encourages teamwork.
+ Great customization for different types of roles with gear/weapon selection
+ Progression seams at the right pace for using in game currency earned through missions
to buy everything you need.
- Multiplayer can be sparse. I had times where I tried nearly all day to find a group, and other times where I fell
into a group and played a few rounds. This isn't a problem on Dambusters end however.
RECOMMENDATION FOR DEVELPOR:
***Should a sequel occur, and with the latest jump into new technology. I hope you guys will consider exploring an even larger part of the U.S. expanding on the story you guys have already built. And if in fact you do that, offer a better
vehicle system that is more polished and refined.
***Also consider an procedural weapon generation system akin to Borderlands or the Division. A resistance with low resources will spawn a number of homemade weapons/modifications that could be fun to play with, given realistic restrictions placed on the procedural system.
SCORE AND RECOMMENDATION FOR CONSUMER:
*** The game in current state as of 3/14/2017 is easily worth a 75% or above overall quality rating. You cannot go wrong getting this game, especially when it goes on sale. However consider buying at full-price to show more support toward Dambuster as they'll get more out of their percentage cut of the sale.

I love this game.  It's kinda what I've been waiting for.
I've played others, like Stronghold and Age of Empires, but...I wanted a game where you could do the building, and not worry that once you've got a great town...an army comes along and nukes it.
Some people have called Banished, a 'brutal' game.  Because just when you think you've got everything under control, something happens and it's just...over.
Like, a fire or a plague will hit, and wipe out your villagers.
I've had a plague, and with a hospital, it was dealt with...no deaths.
Fires though...are another matter.  This game does have some bugs, but for me...fire is the biggest downside.
I have 7 wells in my village, and 2 rivers either side...1 building caught fire, and over 10 villagers rushed to it...grabbing water from the wells AND the rivers...and yet, my village burned down.  Either the game is designed to do this on purpose, or it's a major issue.  If it's a purpose thing...then this game loses my respect.
I like games with realism...so, 10+ villages fighting a single house fire, all with water, next to a river, with 7 wells handy...that fire would NOT stand a chance.
Not one villager died of cold, but with most of my resources gone...took 5 years for the village to die...but die it did.  187 villagers, and at the moment, it's got less than 20.  I could get it going again, but...another 'disaster' and it'd just finish the town off.
I'm all for bad things happening...but not to this unrealistic extreme.  Which is why on my next village, I'll be turning disasters off.
But yeah...fantastic game, with a few bugs in it...which I'm sure will be dealt with eventually.

A fun and addictive fast-paced game, which will put you on edge in fear of messing up just one tiny button press, or just being too slow for your own good.
This game is all about reacting as quick as lightning and having a wide understanding of the recipes you are able to follow with your current ingredients. Each time a client enters your restaurant, you will have to deal with them as quickly as possible before they get tired of waiting. Following their indications, you will have to press a very specific series of keys in order to fulfill their order, while other clients begin to get impatient and are about to quit your restaurant.
Many factors influence how well your establishment will be doing, not only in general but also during each day.  Depending on your menus and achievements during the day, your restaurant will have more or less popularity throughout the different days you will be playing. Different times of the day and some events make your restaurant's popularity vary during the day itself, having some small peaks in clients at some points. However, this does not compare to the Rush Hours you will be facing twice per day, having clients beginning to stack behind the counter and orders accumulating 4 at a time.
Overall, highly recommended for players who want somewhat of a test of their reaction and memorization skills; not recommended for a casual and laid back experience. This game can be arcade-ish, but it's definitely not too casual in a relaxing sense.

This is a very solid singleplayer city-builder. I have not played many other city builders simply because the blocky graphics (who wants to build something if it's going to make their eyes hurt?), or way too intensive micromanaging turned me off.
This game is simple. This game is easy. This game is elegant with a beautiful soundtrack. That is until a single fire ravages through your urban center destroying any sense of unity your village had. Then---DEATH SPIRAL. Death spirals are so intense, as you watch graveyards fill before your eyes and entire professions become void of workers. Pulling out of one is near impossible, but if you do it is an accomplishment worthy of song.
There are however some drawbacks:
1. Gameplay is more or less managing a set of spreadsheets, drop down menus and building stuff to your best ability-then observing the outcome.
2.  Starving people will walk past barns and markets FILLED TO CAPACITY with food and starve to death on the way to their house, come on people grab a peach at the market and don't die.
3. So many houses... In order to keep a population growing you constantly have to build houses leading to the before mentioned urban sprawl, eventual fire, disease, lucky tornado and/or food shortage leading to DEATH SPIRAL.
4. Glitches: By scheduling to demolish and then canceling the demolish order graveyards are 'emptied' of bodies even though gravestones remain allowing infinite burials on one small patch of land (useful glitch but still a glitch), Livestock walk underwater between pens instead of taking roads, lag starts to intrude with populations over 1000 (gets bad around 1400) and Gatherers are incredibly OP compared to other starting food sources.
5. Do What??? Once you have a town going you may feel a sense of emptiness at having 'conquered' the game and unless you are willing to go after the achievements that sense of pointlessness will remain. However the achievements for this game offer interesting challenges instead of the standard 'get-all-the-things' sort.
So overall it is a good game but there is a steep learning curve and, unless you like to achievement hunt, limited replay value, but for all that it is an addictive game into which I have sunk dozens of hours and have a few more left in me.

I'm sure most of you have already watched movies such as the Fast and Furious, right? Now, who wouldn't want to roleplay as a bunch of street racers out cruising on the city with pimped-out rides fighting for bragging rights?
The Crew is an open world, online multiplayer arcade racing game that lets you crew up with people to challenge others all over five major areas in the United States. That single line alone got me hooked enough to take the game and see for myself. After several hours clocked in, I managed to pin-point a few things that make this game great, at the same time notice a few issues that could be resolved in the future hopefully.
The Pros:
- Probably one of the biggest selling points of this game is the fact that it's open world. They weren't kidding when they said, "If you can see it, you can drive there" part, with a minor exception from the world's boundaries. From busy streets, to wide highways, to rocky mountain tops, to the vast fields. You can race, or chill-out, practically anywhere given that you have already driven to that spot before. To add to this, the game allows you to warp anywhere with minimal to no loading time whatsoever. Always a plus on my book.
- The rides aren't limited to your typical street racer tuning. The game has several specifications that works on certain terrain and objectives. It allows you to customize your ride to best suit the situation at hand, like dirt specs for off-road challenges, and raid specs for heavy duty pursuits. A large chunk of the pimping-out option is available as visual customization for your ride, allowing drivers to make unique rides that they can show-off to others, or look awesome winning in them during races.
- This is a multiplayer game after all, so what could be more exciting than racing as a crew? Imagine cruising down the streets as a 4-man team out looking for trouble or a challenge. Visualize being chased down by cops while your crewmates dive right in to clear a path for you. Or you could just troll people around and block busy streets just for fun.
The Cons:
- No game is perfect after all, especially during its first launch, so don't expect too much or you'll just end up disappointed like some. While the game is labled as an MMO, players are divided into "sessions" much like RPG games have "server channels". Most of the time players see only a handful of people in their current session, sometimes no one at all. While I have no idea what are the maximum number of players per session is, it would be nice if I could see 20+ drivers or so in every coast. Not too much though, or it would be chaos. Some people are complaining about not being able to see their friends in-game as well to crew up, which is quite a let down.
- AI in this game is quite annoying in my opinion. First of, the term "rubberbanding", in reference to the elasticity of a rubber band, means that car A will not move too far away from car B in most situations. For example, you're in a race wherein you're in first place. The 2nd place AI will "rubberband" its way towards you no matter what situation it gets stuck in. It will suddenly dive towards you at ridiculous speeds even if it had just recovered from a crash. It works both ways when you're the one at 2nd, the 1st place AI seems to slow down a bit to allow you to get back into the race. Imagine the "rubberbanding" on police vehicles, chases aren't as exciting as it should be. In fact, it's difficult and down right scary.
- The physics and controls on this game is a little off, I think. I mean, yes, driving at high speeds have this tendency to lose control obviously. But the handling and recovery is just too darn difficult.  The vehicles tend to spin-out easily, lose traction and so on. Let's not get started on the police, especially when they decide to break in front of you, they turn into a solid brick wall you can't possibly push aside. On the plus side, however, these cops really know how to do pit manouvers and stuff. And I think the handling of the cars can be remedied with the right car parts. Just expect to have a hard time at the start though.
All in all, despite the ups and downs, The Crew is still a fun game to have, especially if you love the challenge and the thought of having one awesome ride as an avatar. It's barely a week into release and I'm sure we can expect better things to come from this game. If you're debating on picking this up, my personal opinion is go for it.  I mean, why not? It's not a bad game, but it's not the best either, but I'm sure this game has potential to get up there on the list.
Hope to see you guys on the streets. Later.

So, there have been some mixed reviews about The Crew.  Most of them comparing this game to other games like Forza Horizon 2 (Amazing game) and the NFS series.  Remember, this is its own game.  Take it for what it is:  an arcade style racing game with the capability to connect with others in an open world setting.  In that sense, the game completely delivers.
I haven't encountered any bugs or issues except for one disconnect a few days ago.   I also think a few of these reviews haven't given the game enough effort.  They're complaining about not getting gold/platinum parts or that people can pay for them.  Absolutely they can pay for them, but they can also be earned.  That's part of the challenge and the parts are wtihin reach.
The car list isn't extensive which is a bit upsetting and Ubisoft should really release them instead of making us pay.  That would really be my only complaint.  Tons of customization is available and the story line really isn't that bad.  I actually enjoy the cutscenese inbetween moving from city to city to try and build the 5-10 reputation and get to Coburn.
It is also worth noting that as you progress, new race modes are made available and features to immerse you further into The Crew such as factions and different classes.
I honestly believe some of the backlash is from the other Ubisoft launches this year that were subpar, but this game is exactly what they state it to be.  I recommend The Crew.  It's a great game.

This will be a two part review, as this includes two games.
FINAL FANTASY X HD:
First off, I should say that I have not previously played this game at all. Not the SD version or this remaster on console. I went into Final Fantasy X with very little knowledge of it besides the fact that I have played other Final Fantasy games before. As I'm sure you will read from many other reviews, the PC port is actually really good. There are a decent amount of options, not that any modern PC would have problems maxing this game out. I did play this game with UnX (you can find it in the guides section of the community hub.) UnX is a mod that adds support for other mods and adds some more technical features. I reccomend playing the game with this. The main reason I got the mod was so I could have Japanese voice acting with English subtitles, as that is not an option without this mod. Trust me, the English voice acting sucks, play it in Japanese. The only gripe I had at first is that the game is locked at 30fps, but in the end THIS IS NOT A BIG DEAL. Everything is animated for 30fps since this was originally a game from 2001 for the PS2. So if you try to uncap the FPS it would cause a ton of bugs and destroy the game. Someone is working on a mod for 60fps, but it is probably taking a ton of work. In the end the 30fps looks fine.
Let's get into the actual game though. The battle system is kinda a mix between the ATB system and a turn based system. When it's your turn you can act on your own pace, meaning the enemy won't attack if you have control over the menu, but you or the enemy can attack more than once in a row if you have your agility up. Overall the battle system is nothing too out of this world but it's all in good fun. The leveling system is a little different than other games. Your character doesn't have a "level" you gain AP from fighting and you can increase your stats through a sphere map thing. Each level grants you the ability to move forward, and you unlock stat boosters with spheres, which are items you get from battles.  It's similar to Final Fantasy 13's leveling system, if you have played that game.
Other than that there is an amazing story and a beautiful world to journey with. I really enjoyed the story and I see it as the reason to play this game really. Of course, I won't really talk about the story because I don't like spoiling stuff. The less you know before you play the better it will be when you do.
I really enjoyed this game and if you are a fan of the FF games you will enjoy it as much as I did.
If you played the original and are thinking about reexperiencing this game. this PC release is the way to go.
FFX-2 HD: This game is fun but not as good as X. The battle system is an ATB system this time around. There are no limit breaks or summons. There are only 3 party members. The game is a lot shorter and uses a mission system. I liked the story as it was a continuation from FFX, but that is really the only thing that kept me going tbh. I played the 13 series before this (FF13, FF13-2, LRFF13) and I can say that FFX-2 is the root of what Lightning Returns ended up being. FFX-2 and Lightning Returns are both mission based and they both also have a clothes changing system. Basically you can find and unlock different dresspheres and you can set up a grid for each character. You can switch between different dresspheres mid battle. These will change your stats and avaliable abilities. This is very similar to Lightning Returns Final Fantasy 13 if you ever played that. (which I loved that series btw) Overall FFX-2 is not an awful game by any means, but it's soundtrack and plot was nowhere near as epic as FFX and you could probably skip out on playing it and still have buying this game worth your time and money.
Oh yeah, there is a third game in this. It's called Final Fantasy X-2 Last Mission. It's like a turned base tower crawler thing. It has like 60 floors you have to clear, which I assumed will be awarded with another cutscene. I didn't really bother with this one. I probably never will.
Overall FINAL FANTSY X/X-2 HD Remaster is worth $30 for just FFX alone in my opinion. I've spent a little over a week now playing this and it's been a fun ride. (yes I finished both in that time, I'm on summer break what else am I to do?)

Standalone, Darks Souls 2 is a good game and fun to play. But 1 and 3 are much better.
PROS: More Dark Souls. Who can argue with that? It's like being offered more slices of a delicous cake.
CONS:
The level design is needlessly punishing when compared to the others. Look no further than The Gutter and Black Gulch and their endless statues that spit poison. You spend more time destroying statues than looking out for enemies and traps, which there are plenty of.
Instead of making enemies more challenging, they just decided to make every area a 6v1 gank. Unlike Souls 1 and 3 where you could avoid ganks by luring enemies out 1 by 1 with a bit of common sense and clever item use, the enemy agro range makes that less that possible. Thus, most areas play out like a Benny Hill chase. There are even several bosses that are just a mob of common enemies. It's not fun, it's just tedious trying to cut them down one by one without being mobbed to death.
Weapons degrade faster than paper under a jetwash.
Invulnerability frames on dodging and speed of estus use is tied to a stat, which means without leveling up "adaptability", dodge rolls are pointless and sneaking a cheaky estus into a boss battle becomes a liablilty rather than a tactical decision.
A minor gripe but many bosses are badly designed. There are some really good ideas there, like many bosses have elements where you can make their fight easier by triggering switches or destroying things in the areas beforehand: E.g. There's a boss you fight in total darkness, but you can turn on lights by finding a key to unlock a room where you can light a torch to illuminate the arena. That being said, several bosses just try to capture the lightning in a bottle that was Ornstein and Smough and make the fight a gank. Hell a few bosses are literally a mob of common enemies. It's kind of sad.
All in all, I do enjoy Dark Souls 2 but I'd rather play 1 and 3.

Banished is a town-/village - building simulation with some refreshing new ideas, spiced up with some long-lost components which were not seen in this genre in the last few years.
Whatever you build or command, it has effects for at least several (playing minutes), if you don't fast forward the game speed constructing several buildings can easily take 15-20 minutes, based on their location and the materials needed.
The workers have to clear the construction side from rocks and trees, have to bring the materials to the spot, and after all this the construction itself can begin. Since your workers are not only workers but also human, they got to do lunch-breaks, or go home to warmup from time to time if the temperature is low.
Banished simulates much more than many other games do, not only the single working processes of the workers, but also their life outside of work - getting food and firewood for their homes etc. is simulated for every individual villager (a thing the big "Sim City" didn't manage to achieve).
Interesting fact: The game was crafted by one (ONE!) developer, this man kicked some big game studios' asses.
The graphics aren't up-to-date of course, but they are still nice to look at, especially considerung ONE (i cannot stop to mention this) single person took care of all aspects of the game.
The game isn't perfect, but it is getting patched constantly and also will get mod-support soon, which will make the options and possible content explode.
If you are into the genre, dare to give this little gem a chance.
And please- eventhough it's DRM free, buy the game. People who invest that much of their freetime, taking the risk of all that time being lost because their game gets lost in the abyss of the videogame market, deserve it.

Verdun is the WW1 game I've been waiting for all my life. This game is also in a league of its own, there is no other WW1 FPS game that depicts what it was like as well as Verdun does. The accuracy and detail of this game is simply incredible. The uniforms, the guns, the weapons, are all based on real life, nothing here is fictional, it's all based on the real thing. You have the Germans, French, British, Canadians, Belgians, and Americans (so far). Team work is important, you have squads of 4 players and each member is its own class. In fact, since each team type has its own unique weapons and abilities, there is actually an enormous amount of 'classes' available. Frontlines game mode is PvP multiplayer with the attackers and defenders taking turns to invade each other's trenches. Squad defense is a horde mode/wave survival thing (which I enjoy the most), and a couple of other modes like rifle deathmatch which is a fan change of pace but a lot harder to find players for.
Playing this game has taught me that I really don't know much AT ALL about WW1 and that's even after watching the documentaries. As it is made by indie developers, it doesn't have the polish of AAA shooters, but with support I'm sure a Verdun 2 in the future will be huge. Even as is, still very good, and I highly recommend it. To add to this, the community in this game is great, I mean seriously great. Have not once heard or read anything toxic. Chatting about WW1 movies, shows, real life war discussions mid-battle just adds to the enjoyment.
It's not all sunshine and rainbows though. Some of the biggest issues are
- low playerbase, especially in Australia (can barely fill a server on Frontlines mode)
- some game modes don't get played at all (or extremely rarely)
- movement feels clunky
- developers are very slow to respond to bugs, and have allegedly abandoned supporting some game modes like Squad Defence
- low TTK, as in most of these bolt action rifles are instakills
I love how people hate it because it involve Ubisoft, while the game is made by Ivory Tower mainly and Ubisoft	is just act as publisher. *sigh*
Although the repetitive elements are everywhere in this game, I'm still giving a positive feedback simply because that this game gave and give me a lot of fun.

This is a package containing two of the most polarizing games in the Final Fantasy franchise: X and X-2. Since they're packaged into the same game effectively, I'll try to break it apart into two tl;dr reviews.
+ Strongest gameplay of all major FF entries
+ Solid story and atmosphere
+ Sphere grid
+ Minigames (Blitzball!)
~ Sphere grid
~ Customization
- Characters
- Late game exponential scaling
- Corridor gaming for 20+ hours
The shining gem of FFX is combat. It uses another evolution of the ATB system used throughout the FF series, but this particular iteration is fully turn based. You have an infinite period of time to determine what your strategy will be for each particular character, which allows for actual strategy outside of spamming the attack button. In conjunction with this is the sphere grid system, which allows for a variety of upgrade paths for your characters. If you want 8 black mages, then you can damn well have your 8 black mages. The only thing that truly separates the characters are their overdrives, so take that as you will. The major downside to this system is the exponential scaling; it works marvelously throughout most of the game, but once you hit the endgame content, stuff just skyrockets. I maxed out everything but luck and I couldn't even touch half of the end game bosses, but 1 shot the final boss like it's nothing.
Two big staples of FF games are to have a fantastical world and endearing characters; the world is pretty interesting, but the characters just fall kinda flat. It was Squenix's first foray into voice acting, and it was preeeeeeeeeeeetty bad (the laughing scene notwithstanding, that whole cringeworthy section was intentional). Rikku is universally praised, but the rest... Not so much. Tidus, the main protagonist, is a bit of a loud mouth cry baby, while Yuna, the leading female, is fairly shy and soft spoken, so the people that the audience want to become attached to don't tend to share common traits with them.
Otherwise, blitzball is good enough to be it's own separate game. Seriously, its underwater handball soccer or some crazy crap like that. Lightning dodging for a key item to unlock a super weapon's power sucks more than anything since getting 1000 consecutive jumps in FF9. The chocobo balloon catching and bird dodging mini game is pretty damn frustrating, especially because it's mostly RNG whether you get enough balloons for the constant barrage of birds right in your face to be worth it.
Last point, there is basically no exploration until after Zanarkand, which is the last area before the end game content, meaning that you have to heavily invest into the game before you ever get the freedom to go do whatever the crap you want and have to spend 20-30 hours before being able to formulate a true idea of whether you like the game or not.
Overall, it's a very solid entry in the franchise and made a very strong step forward in terms of gameplay, but is mostly lacking in the charm that makes a FF game. I give it a 8/10 because I have yet to see a combat formula beat this one in any game, much less the FF series.
