The game features an enhanced career mode that takes place over ten seasons. Specific race goals are dependent on the strength of the team, and driver rivalries develop over time. A very neat feature is practice objectives: performing specific tests (like learning the track, conserving tires, or going on a qualifying run) will earn research points that can be spent on upgrading car parts. It is a welcome feature that gives a purpose to practice other than simply turning laps. In addition to the career mode, single seasons, quick races, time trials, and online multiplayer with full twenty-two car fields are available. A number of minor new features (the Azerbaijan street circuit, new Haas team, a formation lap, manual race starts, manual pitting, and the safety car) are also added for this year’s version. Racing physics are plausible, including tire wear, handling, and damage. Driving assists can be adjusted to support a wide range of player abilities, and flashbacks can be used to rewind time if needed. AI drivers are appropriately aggressive. F1 2016 is a slick, feature-complete simulation perfect for the racing aficionado.

By all accounts, Homefront: The Revolution should have never seen the light of day. The game passed through at least four developers and three publishers before its final release in May of 2016. With that kind of development hell, it’s frankly amazing that the game even came out and even more shocking that the game is even good.
Having played Homefront: The Revolution in March of 2017, I cannot speak to its supposedly rocky launch. When the game released, it was met with a wave of discontent and uproar about everything from performance and glitches to being flat out broken. There were even people claiming this to be “The Worst Game Ever Made”. First off, let’s dispel that hyperbolic nonsense, in no universe is Homefront: The Revolution “The Worst Game Ever Made”. Homefront is shockingly competent given its development history, not that its history gives it a pass by any means, but I do think it’s important to look at it with context.
As far as the actual gameplay goes, Homefront plays like an urban Far Cry. The long and short of it is that if you enjoyed Far Cry 3 and/or 4 then you’ll probably enjoy Homefront. It has all of the trappings of a Far Cry game: open world, climbing structures to reveal part of the map, light crafting and customization, etc. There are some aspects, however, that I think Homefront does better than the Far Cry games. Climbing towers in the Far Cry games are usually pretty straightforward but in Homefront, it’s often a puzzle that must be solved. Rarely is a base or tower a straightforward affair. I often found myself circling the building multiple times to find my pathway up. This little wrinkle made a normally mundane process a bit more rewarding. This is also in part due to the excellent traversal. This game gets first person movement right, and is some of the best feeling in any FPS I’ve played.
Running around and capturing strongholds was quite satisfying as I think the free roam nature of this game is its strong suit. In fact, I think the best compliment I can give Homefront is that I never even used the fast travel feature. Compare this to a game like Mafia 3 which was utterly painful to play by the end because of the lack of fast travel. In Mafia, there was nothing to do between your destinations whereas is Homefront there’s always a pack of enemies right around the corner ready for a firefight. This emergence is really where Homefront shines.
The gunplay in Homefront: The Revolution is properly meaty and all the guns have a heft to them that feels satisfying. While I enjoyed the ability to customize my weapons on the fly, it would have been nice to have an extra weapon or two. The weapons, and the world, do have a nice sense of patched-togetherness that you would expect out of a crumbled Philadelphia.
I haven’t mentioned the story yet because, well, it’s pretty average. I like to play a lot of games primarily for the story but Homefront: The Revolution was not one of them. While not bad, the story was pretty boilerplate revolt and uprising stuff. There’s nothing here that you haven’t seen before. It’s enough to string together sequences but don’t expect a gripping thriller here.
I’ll speak briefly about the DLC since I didn’t give it much playtime: skip it unless you really loved the story. I found all three of the story DLC’s to be subpar of the main game mostly due to the fact that they’re extremely linear. Now I’m not opposed to linearity, in fact I often prefer it to open worlds, but Homefront’s strength is in its open world. When you change the element that it does best, it’s going to suffer. Again, it’s not terrible, but it’s nothing that I would recommend buying unless you’re dying to get more of the story, which they do expand on.
Despite its tortured development history, I think that Dambuster Studios managed to make a pretty darn enjoyable game in Homefront: The Revolution. The game has no right to be as fun as it is but its mechanics come together to create scenarios that remain enjoyable throughout its 13 plus hour campaign. While I would not recommend it at full price, I think that there is great fun to be had here if you can snag the game while on sale. While doubtful, I would love to see another entry in the series.

I really don't like the FPS lock. The gameplay while repetitive I managed to keep engaging by stirring up chaos and trying to not die. The graphics aren't horrible. The vehicle controls are horrible though.
You gas the bike and let off for even a split second and it all but stops dead. Turning tilts the entire camera and any damage taken knocks you off. If you jump off the bike, it stops almost in place and you fly forward.
The way the game spawns NPC is not engaging. It does not make the game more fun. It breaks immersion heavily. I've had several instances where a NPC literally spawned infront of me and I saw it. There is no magic here. For all the transparency of this horribly executed mechanic, the game feels gutted and forced.
I'd be willing to bet the reason this game stayed alive was largely tied to the size of the game world. The game world is well done. I really enjoy the exploration and level design for this title. Not a fan of the same 12 NPC showing up throughout the entire game. Apparently they didn't have it in the budget to afford a greater variety of NPC.
My only complaint about the game world design, it's too open. Not too open-world. The city for instance, the streets are much wider than they should be. The buildings are far wider apart than they should be. I get that war has torn the city apart, but even the areas seemingly spared feel spaced out.
This game would have benefitted heavily from a better cover system. The peek function and shoot function over walls gets glitchy in that I've had my gun stop animating infront of me after using it and I've had the character stop aiming for no good reason simply because of how the animation interacts with the cover system. That said, you can't shoot around corners at all and that's unfortunate.
The game is worth getting for $15 tops. If you do all of the side missions and explore a lot and listen to dialogue and just enjoy the landscape....If you really try to immerse yourself in the game world, it could give you a solid 20 hrs of content.
The story is garbage, so expect to play this game with your own narrative in mind and tie in the main theme into your own theory of how the game works.
Replayability: None. I barely wanted to finish my first run through this title, despite the positives I mentioned. Eventually it feels like work and the story is so worn out and used with bland characters that you feel nothing for their plight and even start resenting some of them for their immersion breaking platitudes.
TL;DR
Buy it on sale for $15 when it pops up. 20hrs of gameplay. Feels like work. Characters are bland. NPC are cloned ALOT. Story is horribly written. Dialogue is uninspired. Mechanics are buggy. Run-And-Gun is forced. Game world is beautiful, if not a bit more spacious than it should be. Good game to waste time on, but not worth sacrificing a family order of KFC for.

WWE 2K16 is awesome, simply awesome as a PC wrestling sim. Runs A LOT better than WWE 2K15, solid 60FPS in game at High settings with 8X MSAA. Gameplay is a little sluggish compared to the previous WWE games, but it helps control the pacing and makes it feel like a true WWE broadcast. Graphics are also improved a lot over 2K15, from the hair not clipping as much, to the sweat effects.
Very big roster, it has a Superstar or Diva for everyone . It has the obvious choices like John Cena, Randy Orton, and Stone Cold Steve Austin, but they even added the more obscure Superstars, Divas, and tag teams like Enzo Amore and Big Cass, Alundra Blayze, and Harlem Heat.
2K Showcase follows Stone Cold Steve Austin, but I haven't touched it very much as I am not interested in the story, but for what it has it's great.
MyCareer is also a major improvement over WWE 2K15. Instead of having you embroiled in meaningless rivalries ("B! Blade! anyone?), you get to pick your path into the WWE and what you want to do with your career. Absolutely amazing, worth the money by itself.
I would say if you have the money OR have not played WWE 2K16 on PS4 or Xbox One, definitely pick this up.

Whatever happens, I won't be missed..."
"I thought that might be you. You haven't changed a bit, have you? Heh heh. The longer I am here, the more madness I discover. A wretched place, indeed, but not without traces of its former glory. What could have caused such degradation? Ah yes, I have not thanked you for humouring me the other day. This is for you. Of course, I've no idea what it is. Our land of Mirrah is surrounded by enemies, and constantly at war. There is only one way up to Mirrah. Join the Order, and prove yourself in battle. My familly had little fortune, and no name. I had to carve out a piece of the world by myself...with two things. My sword, and my loyalty to my Lord. I was raised to wield a sword from birth. Life was hard, but I never gave it a second thought. I had swift success on the battlefield, and quickly attained respectable stature. And then...I..And the I came here...to...Have you heard of the Undead? These poor souls affected by the curse. An Undead gradually loses his humanity, until his wits degrade completely. "Still on the road, are you? Sorry to have burdened you so. This is for you, by way of an apology. I've found my thought growing hazy. My memories are fading, oldest first. "Oh...you...My thoughts...are very...scattered...What is this curse? The question rings in my mind, but I haven't the focus to answer it. Loss frightens me no ends. Loss of memory, loss of self. I would sacrifice anything, anything at all for this. It shames me, but it is the truth. Sometimes, I feel obsessed...with this insignificant thing called "self". This game is okay. I really can't say I had "fun" playing through it but thinking back, it was decent, I don't exactly regret playing it.
I was excited when I started the game, I love adventure, exploration, narrative and story-based games. You start and everything's dark, I figured maybe it was going to be a bit of a scary game.
But it's not.
You turn on the lights and that's it, it stops being dark. You never meet anyone and nothing really happens except from you gathering notes around the house to figure out where everyone is.
You can pick up and interact with almost every objects in the game. So when I started, I went around to pick up and inspect every single thing I could find. The thing is, it's useless. There's nothing to it. There's no real "puzzle" or anything in the game, there's only very few objects that you do need to look at.
The game can easily be finished under two hours. Probably half that or even less if you're not like me an inspect every single corners of the place. The story is... Okay. I kinda liked the narrative and I was really curious to know how the story would unravel. Except there wasn't really much to, I was pretty let down in the end. I figure out the "plot" about halfway through the game then just felt like it dragged on until the "big reveal" where I was like "Oh okay yeah that makes sense... That's it?".
The game's description makes it sound like something paranormal is going on but I wouldn't ever describe what happened as a "mystery". This "mystery" was mildly interesting at best.
Now don't get me wrong. It's not like I cringed listening to the dialogue, it wasn't badly written. The story is not BAD. It's just that it's so minor on its own. It does touch subjects that some people might be less comfortable or open with or that some people could relate more to. But the things this game discussed were pretty obvious to me.
Clearly, a consirable amount of work went into this. But this game is in no way, shape or form worth 22$. I feel bad because of the work that went into this but it just wasn't all that entertaining. You can buy all 5 episode of Life is Strange for the exact same price and these two games which are story-based are on astronomically different levels. I got Gone Home (and the soundtrack, so the 28$ edition) as part of the Humble Indie Bundle 15 which I spent 10$ on. ...Let's just pretend that those 10$ were for all the other games and not this one. I would buy 10 copies of all 5 episodes of Life is Strange before I would spend 1$ on this game, I mean it.
But... Considering I essentially got this game for free... It was okay. If you did get it for free, play through it but don't search around too much, there's not much to find. Finish the game and don't play it again. It's better in your memories than it is while you play it.
If you really want to play an overpriced walking simulator though, go buy Dear Esther instead. It looks better, sounds better, the narration is better, the story is actually interesting, the plot is a actually a plot and it's half the price (yet still too expensive for a 1h game).

Well, I finally got around to playing this and... it's alright. I enjoyed Gone Home, but ultimately it suffers from its format and a price tag that is not justified by the, at most, 2 hours of playtime you are going to get out of it. I got it out off a bundle and I think I got my money's worht out of it, but if I had paid the price listed on the store page I would be annoyed.
Let's go back to why I think the game doesn't really work: notes. Here a note, there a note, everywhere a note note. I am supposed to believe that Sam strategically placed scraps all over the house so that her sister would find them when she comes home? No. It just doesn't work. Hey, narrative game designer! Yeah, you! Lay off the notes! Find another way to tell your story unless the note leaving actually makes sense as a mechanic. Note leaving is the found footage of game design: when it works it REALLY works and when it doesn't it is annoying, gimmicky and the sign of a low budget. The note leaving that does work in Gone Home? The parent's professional and marital problems, but that's a small part of the story.
The second problem is that I don't think interactivity really made the story or experience any better. Exploring the house adds some level of suspense and in producing a little dread in the player as they piece together the story, but the absurdity of th note leaving wrecks that part of the experience. Furthermore, what few puzzles or other mechanics placed in the game aren't particularly well tied to the narrative experience. Contrast with Brothers: A Tale of Two Sons where th mechanics are very tightly woven into the narrative. Gone Home would likely have worked better as a novella written in first person with a possibly unreliable narrator.
Gripes aside, Gone Home is well put together. It has one of the better narratives in this genre of games and it is overall a positive experience. I wouldn't spend $20 on it, though. $8, I think, would be the upper end of fair. Get it on sale if you haven't played this yet and are interested in these kinds of games.

The Final Station, while true of most indie games, continues to prove that the depth of a game has nothing to do with fancy graphics or complex mechanics. You are a train conductor. You fix the train. You have to stop at the stations. You have to get the permission code to continue on. You don't choose your route, nor your passengers. But inside your little metal box, the world around you is changing, violently. And sometimes, paranormally. Or is it?
The Final Station does a very good job of setting up the protaganist in his role. You MUST get your cargo to its specified place. And with the Second Visitation, many people are left stranded, hunted by mysterious creatures that seem to only hunt people. BUT, rescuing survivors is your ORDERED second objective. What causes it, why the world functions as it does, and theories on just what is going on abound, but no-one seems sure for certain. The plot, not to mention the fan theories, abound and leave one with the ultimate question of humanity:
Why?
This game also features a small crafting system supplemented by a scavanging system, but your wits are far, far more important to your survival and the survival of your passengers. It can take days to get from one safe station to another, and you must ration out food, as well as medical supplies from your own stock to the survivors. Some are heavily wounded and require constant care. But are they worth it, ultimately?
My only complaints are that some of the grammar in English is very occasionally hard to follow, sometimes an NPC will be talking into a radio, and it is hard to distinguish the difference between if they are talking to you, or not. But there is a sense of eavesdropping that goes with it, that adds to the mystery of the story.
Which is my only other mixed complaint. I do, genuinely, love the story. The futility and joys of some of your actions can be profound, and you are as much a passenger on your train as much as the people and cargo you take. But that cargo can go on to drastically change the story, while you watch from your little metal box. And ultimately, the plot is unclear as to what the actual struggle was.
(IF YOU DO NOT LIKE CLEARLY NARRATED STORIES, THIS IS NOT FOR YOU)
However, if you take your time, explore and read everything, use your wits and observe, this game is well-worth the asking price. I look forward to seeing a continuation, but the mystery holds its charm.

Well, that was The Crew...
After about 42 Hours ive seen the most things, beat the Campain and most of the Challenges.
I bought "The Crew" with Hope for a Game that would be as entertaining as "Test Drive Unlimited 2".
If you played that before, you will notice the similarity, many parts of TDU2 are also in The Crew.
Sounds good right? No, not at all.
What they both have in common is for example that the Police Cars are either always faster than you, regardless if you drive 100 km/h or 300 km/h or give up after 100 meters for no reason at all... Also the AI and Catch-Up-Systems during Races are equally bad.
Other than that,
Test Drive Unlimited 2 had probably over 130 different Vehicles, from many different Brands
In Test Drive Unlimited 2 you had 1 small and one big Island as Gaming Worlds, Ibiza and Hawaii.
When the Servers at Test Drive Unlimited 2 are down, you can keep playing your Savegame in Offline Mode.
Test Drive Unlimited 2 offered a lot of things to do, you were able to go to a Driving School before races, to make Racing Licenses, to buy Houses, Cars, Bikes,Furniture for your Houses, you were able to customize your Avatar with clothes, Haircuts, Makeup, Accessoires. Also there were more design options for the Cars as well.
It was possible to go to go into the Houses, walk around, similar to "The Sims". You could visit other Players homes, take Photos, there even was a Casino where you could play Blackjack, Poker, Slotmachines with other Players... and a few other things.
While i played The Crew, i often asked myself how awesome the Game could be, if it was also developed and published by Atari and Eden Games.
Ubisoft delivered, as expect, another Game that feels unfinished, like they stopped the developing Process at the Late Alpha Stage and just published it to cash in, for next Years "The Crew 2"?
For example, you sit inside your Car, the Driving Mirror and Side Mirrors dont show anything, They are just grey.
Same goes for the Racing Wheel Instruments. They were supposed to show Speed, Gear and RPM, but they also just show you a fantastic grey bitmap.
Only a few Cars have an Animation for a Gearshifting Character. Inside most of the Cars, the Avartar just keeps his Hands on the Steering Wheel and the Gears shift magically.
There are probably a few more little annoyances, but those points are already unnecessary
I would expect that from an early 2005 Game, but not from a 2014 release.
The Things i liked about The Crew,  were the incredibly detailed surroundings.
You see NPC's walking around, like a beggar moving his belongings in a shopping cart, Prisoners knocking stones in front of a Prison, Planes and Helicopters flying around ... and many more realistic Daily Life Events.
The Map is filled with Wild Animals, they move a bit strange, but are still a nice addition.
Also the Animated Sky looks really nice.
What else is left to say? Yeah. The Cars.
While Test Drive Unlimited 2 had a very good balance and Car selection, The Crew's Cars are very unbalanced
The Crew got a bunch of overpowered and ugly (My opinion, yes.) American Muscle Cars.
They look like they weight 5 tons, have the aerodynamic values of a Brick Row House, but got a surreal good handling and can easily outrun a Lamborghini.
Thats just plain dumb.
Besides that, there are a handfull european and asian Cars. But yeah they are the minority in this Game.
The Handling of the Cars alltogether is good, mostly. The Handling of the Offroad Vehicles can be very frustrating.
For sure this wont be any fun playing with Keyboard and Mouse.
All together i would say, "The Crew" has nice looking Cars, but it isnt the big next Generation Racing Game that was announced and promised.
Its good for cruising around with Friends (If youre lucky enough to get a connection..) , to find out a few things about the United States, but in the Main Category "RACING" it lacks a lot.

My answer to if/why you should you get this on steam if you've already played/own the original playstation 2 versions off of steam: Final Fantasy X was one of my favourites of the Final Fantasy franchise *both for the storyline and for the extras such as the celestial weapons and dark aeons*- so I was super excited when it was released on steam to play with ease on the laptop. The release offers extras that do help the game to be smoother- with you being able to speed up the gameplay- (good for moving quickly), and change frequency of enemies (I love activating extra encounter mode- it means no more running in circles for Tidus trying to buff the character's levels- making buffing/grinding much easier, but no encounter mode can also be great for quickly progressing through the storyline). For those unfamiliar with the game or who don't have the official walkthrough the achievements that steam offers give extra hints on different things to be unlocked, and reminders to old players.
If you're dedicated to Final Fantasy X the first time you play through FFX2 you will likely be disappointed at how much the characters have changed from the original - however it makes sense that with people's hope and lives changing so much from the events of FFX people's character has changed a lot (with Yuna being less dedicated to following her father's footsteps and now trying to find herself for example). However, it is nice to have a sequal addressing how the events of Final Fantasy X have changed Spira's stability and viewpoints (eg: people's attitudes to Yevon and the Crusaders, what happens to Seymour's followers *the Guado*, etc). But after the potential intial annoyance and character changes you're likely to appreciate it for the way it wraps up the storyline nicely and has some fun minigames and challenges. The dress-sphere system of X2 at first took a while to get used to - but on reflection it means that instead of focusing on different characters to get new skills you just change your character's skill-focus-set/outfit.
Over-all I'm very happy to have purchased this :D -
PS - my review was in a way so as to try avoiding giving away spoilers for those new to FFX/FFX2.

: Sandbox [FPS/Sci-Fi/Thriller/Dystopian]
: 9/10
: 8/10
: 9/10
: 10/10
: 10/10
The Good:
-- Fantastic visuals
-- Responsive and optimized
-- Immersion. The alternate, dystopian reality where North Korea becomes a technological powerhouse and supplants America as the World Police during the Space Race Era is fascinating.
-- Philadelphia comes to life as it is laid to siege by the KPA (Korean People's Army) forces using APEX technology. The oppressed citizens always have something to say, and their behavior modifies accordingly based on changes you make to the area. It really is a nice touch, in that you have a growing sentiment of rebellion and revolution always accompanying your campaign progress. You really do feel like what you do for The Revolution is making an actual change, if only for a digital world.
--Speaking of citizens having something to say, so do your enemies(who fluently speak Korean and scream out Korean explitives and battle commands when you're in the s**t). And your brothers(and sisters) in arms in The Revolution. The sound work and Foley studio work is incredible in Homefront--one becomes easily enveloped in the game's ambience and aural charm.
--Soundtrack and music. I have a high regard for The Homefront's audio work(at least, a majority of it--explained below in The Bad). The mixture of 80s synth, haunting strings, and bass work is very reminiscent of Darkwave Electronica, but without the imposing nature of the more hardcore aspect of the genre. It's a very subconcious vibe that is incredibly mellow with just enough intensity (that piques at absolutely the right moments, ie. combat) to keep you in a savage yet sensible lull as you defend America from hostile intent(basically, it kicks♥♥♥♥♥to shoot stuff to).
--Gameplay. There's a lot to do, but not in a Grand Theft Auto sense -- more in a Far Cry sense. You have main missions, some sub missions, and then a couple variations of collectibles. Finding these increases your influence throughout a district or zone, and increasing influence encourages citizen rebellions, uprisings and takeovers (but you'll be the main catalyst and also the main Rambo-style hero doing the taking over)
--Gunwork and explosives are tangible and fun. Some shooters have the problem of their weapons not feeling like they're actually making an impact when the bullets hit; Homefront has no such issue. There's a lot of fun weaponry and upgrades to play with, and each one is not only significantly strong in its own unique way but they also FEEL like they're signifcantly strong when using them. In shooters, that feeling is important -- it's an aspect of game sense that I feel helps keep your skill in check. If you can't feel your shot, it's like coming without actually feeling the ♥♥♥♥♥♥.. it just ain't right.
--Story is fast, intense, and decently written. Lots of "why are we here?" moments and reflections in a broader sense (hence the exercise in existentialism) married with an action-driven narrative makes for a memorable experience.
The Bad:
--The voice acting leaves something to be desired. This is the bad part of the sound that I was mentioning. The first few ingame cinematics are actually pretty good(like the Walker rescue scene during your torture), but as the story carries on we meet characters who just don't always deliver their lines or act convincingly enough. But it's not bad enough to detract from the overall experience.
--Lots of sameness when it comes to gameplay, but if you are an avid shooter and like Far Cry/Bioshock style games than Homefront's sameness really shouldn't annoy you or assuage you from playing.
--Needs more weapons. While Each weapon has 2 subweapons, I wish there were still more options, like swapping out the default loadout with a loadout of our choosing from a mored varied selection of guns (Being restricted to 4 main weapon types feels a little too God of Warsy for me, I prefer my sandboxes to be sandbox in every aspect, including armaments)
I really can't think about much that I disliked about this game. I can't speak for it at launch, but I can speak for it now, and it's a hell of an experience. You'd do yourself a disservice but not grabbing it when it's on sale.

Then the story itself was intriguing to me, as someone fascinated with dreams and nightmares who experiences a lot of both the premise meant the game was bound to interest me.
Yes, the game is rather short, but I don't think that's necessarily a bad thing. I often enjoy short games, they can be just the thing when you fancy playing something but have other things going on. It also keeps the game from being repetitive, in order to make this game longer a lot of new creatures and endings would have needed to be added, by which point the plot would run the risk of getting stretched too thin. I feel like Neverending Nightmares strikes the perfect balance for those who don't mind if a game is short.
As far as how scary this game is, that'd depend on what gets to you, for instance, for a person afraid of dolls a large portion of this game would be very creepy. For me there were other things that would creep me out, I'm afraid of the dark and stairs make me very uneasy. They have covered a lot of based and there were a couple of bits where I jumped (although I'm admittedly easily startled).
Lastly, I'd say that while I definitely recommend this game to people who don't mind a short psychological horror experience that isn't action-oriented, if you are sensitive to imagery or references to suicide or self harm then this game will likely not be for you, so basically, player discretion is advised.

Outstanding game. Short, not terribly difficult, and the hunger mechanic aboard the train really doesn't make any sense: Otherwise healthy people will literally starve to death on a train ride between towns that takes less than a day to complete. It's obviously there as busywork, to force a greater level of interactivity, but it's a wasted effort. Setting aside its fundamental silliness, it also distracts from more important elements of the game, particularly the dialog that takes place between passengers while the train is in motion.
But the station exploration, while almost perfectly linear, is incredibly intense at times, and there are brilliant moments of visual storytelling as well. It's powerful, even if it doesn't always make sense. Discovering the real nature of my secret cargo, for instance, absolutely blew me away. I hadn't been sufficiently inquisitive when it was loaded onto my train, and so when the truth became clear it was completely out of nowhere, and legitimately shocking. Combat can be tense, too, because ammunition and health are in such short supply. It's possible to craft them, and the game is paced well enough that it always seems to be generous at just the right moments (or maybe I was just lucky), but most of the time I felt like I was on the cusp of running dry.
As you can see from other reviews, the ending is a point of contention, but I think it fits with the overall tone of the story. It's very weird, and no explanations are given. I can't say I'm happy with it, but I was compelled to think about it too, and that's not a bad thing. If you want a tidy package wrapped up in a bow and labeled in large, easy-to-read print, you will probably come away unsatisfied. But if you can live with ambiguity, and like kicking around theories and ideas with your fellow gamers, you won't find many stories better this one.

This game was a masterpiece of ambient storytelling. The game mechanics both inside the train and out were simple and unobtrusive, while the dialogue was enticing and interesting. There is a vague sense of something far beyond your grasp, and small pieces of it are fed to you as you play, not only leading you onwards but giving you time to mull over what you've learned.
I never felt there was an unwinnable situation or unfair scenario, only something brought by my own ineptitude or negligence. Level designs were intuitive and branching but never misleading, and expertly minimized any backtracking. Combat felt smooth and manageable yet tense and surprising, even after many iterative encounters.
In all, the few flaws I found (translation errors, slight annoyance at upkeep on the train) were more than made up for in this highly polished game. It has a special place in my collection as a quirky and decidedly inventive style of game. I highly recommend it to anyone looking for an interesting story and entertaining gameplay.

first a little introduction: I love Forza Motorsport 4, used to play nfsu:2 etc back in the day. experience in rfactor, gtr2, raceroom and tried out asseto corsa and next car game.
some people are negative for no reason. maybe they are the type of people who don't even bother to look at their settings. maybe their pc is half a decade old. maybe they expected a different game from what it really is.
I expected a game not as realistic or hardcore as a real sim. slightly more arcadey than forza and that is exactly what I got. (to clarify, forza is one of the more relaxed racing sims I know handling wise)
I have played the crew with a xbox360 controller, a Thrustmaster Run'n'Drive and a Logitech Momo force feedback racing wheel. the handling feels pretty good on hardcore. as with any game I had to mess with the settings a bit to get it nice feeling, but that is to be expected. Grip and lines are pretty controllable and when you get a feel for it it's pretty easy to recover from a hairy situation. But you will also crash often and hard, trying to get that gold medal or not paying attention to traffic.
this game, like any good racing game, requires solid and precise input to be fast. especially with force feedback on dirt or off-road, the car can be quite a handfull. the differences in suspension between the classes are also very noticeable. with force feedback turned up all the way off-road is pretty doable in raid or even dirt, but with harder suspension the wheel will fight you for control on bumps and jumps. on the other hand, a raid spec will often understeer and lift one or two wheels when driving hard on road.
The big open world is really awesome. you can drive to a huge amount of places and a cross country or round trip takes a LONG time. In gta 5 i was pretty dissapointed about the lack of tight driving roads on that map. Luckily Ivory Tower did not make the same mistake. the game is filled to the brim with not only highways and country roads, but also big mountain passes. Be it dirt, snow, or blacktop, it´s all there.
It´s true the landscape isn´t the prettiest close up, but the quality of the roads and sheer size of the map easily make up for that. the different landscapes like field, forest, desert, mountain, hill, swamp etc. all feel like a world in themselves and seeing the landscape fluently change around you as you drive cross country is really cool. It all looks pristine until you get really close (and slow), so that´s usually a non-issue.
the first few days there were some connectivity issues but they have significantly lessened after they did a few server patches. I hope they will keep this up and keep their promise of rapid and frequent updates / patches.
The Crew is a very good game with the potential to become the greatest racer of this time. It finds a middle ground between arcade and hardcore handling (with assists it's very easy to stay on the road, on hardcore you have to be precise, and sport is somewhere in between.)
We will have to see in about 3-6 months if Ubisoft and Ivory Tower can live up to their online promise, but even if you would leave out pvp this game is worth it.

PS4 and PC players can play this game together. I mostly play this game on the PS4, but i do sometimes play it on PC as well. For me this game is one of it's kind. I have never before seen a war game like this.
I will now tell the good things and the bad things about this game. Reminder that i'm a mostly PS4 player and my name is Kumiankka98.
GOOD
+Build your own base and army with Mutions only. You can't upgrade buildings or any other structures with Gold. You get mutions by playing the game, so Mutions are like the in-game free currency that you get by just playing the game. Mutions are used for upgrading / buying buildings or buying Standard units.
+Build an army that fits your playstyle. Max amount of different units you can take to battle is 6 thou. I like to take Grunts for the damage dealing and the rest are support units that help the Grunts. There are many units Standard and Hero units. Standard units are good and not inferior to Hero units.
+ Join an alliance and play alliance wars! The better the score that your alliance gets in the alliance war the better the reward is! So join an Alliance for free card packs! Also chat with your alliance friends and discuss different strategies with them.
+ Chance to get Hero units from successful base defence reports! I got 2 Hero units from base defence reports. So build good defences. You might get lucky.
+ Not really a p2w game. Hero units are not any better then the Standard units. If you ask me, some of the Hero units are very weak. Mercenary, Sharpshooter and Chemist are kinda weak in my opinion. Ranger, Flamer and Sniper are way better then their Hero counterparts.
+ Whole lot of different Perks for your units. Improve your units with different perks. Try Grunts with Fire rate and reload speed perks to make them little machineguns or try accuracy and damage perks to make your Grunts little snipers.
+ Never seen this type of game. Nothing like the Clash of Clans or rest of the crappy mobile games. This game does not force you to buy Gold. There is no building or upgrade time. So when you have gathered enough mutions you can just simply upgrade a structure and it's done. You don't have to wait for anything.
+ Special events like the Halloween event and the Christmas event.
BAD
- Hero units are kinda hard to get. Either you get lucky and get them free from a defence report or you put real life money to buy Gold and open card packs. Unit crates take 25 keys to open and it takes long time to gather those 25 keys. You can also open to crates with Gold and i don't really like that. Crates should be Key only things.
- Hero Perks are very hard to get. You can get them mostly from Unit crates. So i suggest you don't waste your keys on anyother crate then the Unit crate. Remember that.
- There are bugs in this game.
- You can buy card packs with Gold to get Hero units or Perks quickly if you don't want to grind them without putting any real world money in this game. Good thing there are the Alliances thou. Join them to get free card packs after the Alliance war season ends. Remember to practicate in them.
- Need more ways to get Keys. Right now they are very hard to get. Some missions should award players with Keys.
In my opinion Guns Up! Is a good game and you should try it. Challenge yourself and try not to buy Gold. The best feeling is when you get an Hero unit and that you didn't even pay real world money to get them! Tell your own ideas and opinions about how to improve this game and make it even better. Join the Guns up forum.

- Even the populated territories are rather sparsely populated.
Using any explosives is cumbersum and especially not something you should do in full combat since it just takes to long to take out the approbiate explosive/tool and then use it and then to change back to one of your weapons. - The extra sidemissions called "jobs" are super tedious and it simply makes no sense that you can only take on four at one time. Wich i sad because some of the ideas, like taking pictures of you fellow freedome fighters are super interesting. The game just doesn#t do anything with it.

A massive word of warning if you're interested in creation. Though I've long stopped watching wrestling, I've always had a soft spot for the games. In particular, the creating of wrestlers has always been a rather large attraction and major selling point. However, despite 2K16 having a seemingly very robust creator wrestler, it is let down by one, fatal flaw. You can no longer import or have any sort of custom soundtrack. The music that is already in the game is what you have to use.
Let me repeat that. YOU. CANNOT. HAVE. CUSTOM. ENTRANCE. THEMES.
If you wanted to try and create Alex Wright and have him come out with his WCW theme, forget about it. Wanted to create a character from another game and have them walk out to their theme, nope. Frankly, this is disgraceful and removes a large element of fun from the game.
It might seem like a silly thing to rage about, but I'd wager for a fair few people, this is a big turnoff. Honestly, had I known this, I would have never, EVER, bought the game.
Sadly, I can't even refund it. So I can only look on in sour malcontent as this piece of software squats on my hard drive. Hopefully, some kind soul will create a mod which enable this a critical feature. And the fact I even had to type that sentence is rather obnoxious.
Shame on you, 2K. Shame on you!
*Extended*
This is my first wrestling game since 2K14. I had no idea they'd removed this feature from 2K15, as I avoided that game given all the negative reports. Again, it seems like a silly thing to gripe about, but once you've had the option to have a creation walk out to a certain type of song (be it serious or silly) you don't want to go back. It just help establish an identity for your creation.
I mean, honestly, if I can't have wrestlers walking out looking all serious and moody to the Pokemon tv theme - what is the point?
No long can I have Nintendo vs. Capcom vs. Sega vs. Sony wrestling abominations walking out to their respective themes - le sigh -

As gaming matures so does it’s themes. In recent years there has been a slew of more or less interactive games about mental illnesses, perhaps the most discussed being Depression Quest.
Neverending Nightmares is also said to be based on the developers own experience living with ocd and depression, but where Depression Quest was a choose-your-own-adventure text based game this time we have a proper adventure game.
Or what at first glance looks like a proper game. Yes there is a character to control and progress to be made but don’t be fooled to think there is much more gameplay here.
The whole game consists of walking endless corridors, sometimes opening doors or clumsily trying to avoid a few monsters.
The striking art style is admirable, in still pictures it resembles some crude underground comic from yesteryear and in motion the facial expressions and body language of the main character helps transfer a feeling of utter despair and terror as you blindly navigate the endless corridors.
But here also lies it’s main problem - sure the atmosphere is there but it’s not used to tell the gamer anything, the story is non-existent until the very end.
While I can sympathise with the design decision to keep with the theme of a looping, never ending nightmare it also takes away the incentive to keep playing as you are not given any reason to do so. In the end it was an empty experience more filled with boredom than horror.

A dreamlike exploration of living with mental illness, Neverending Nightmares gets a lot of mileage out of a rather constrained setting. Even before the branching plotlines and multiple endings, the game's trio of primary settings offer more than enough dread to deal with.
Despite its admitted inspiration in struggles with OCD and depression, Neverending Nightmares opts for a more metaphorical take on its subject matter than anything literal. The game looks at what such struggles feel like, or felt like for the creator at least, through the lens of horror rather than attempting to recount the experience directly. The bulk of the game involves waking up to an eerie, foreboding environment that only slightly changes with each return to supposed consciousness. Every wakeup is followed by a new attempt to find a way out of these increasingly imposing scenarios, searching each area for new tools to progress and usually ending in an unexpectedly horrible way. As things progress, human-but-not-quite creatures join the environment in trying to stop you, but never quite to the point of being a showdown. Even though this realm is apparently your own mind, you have no real power here.
The game's monochrome visual style is striking and memorable, with some interesting techniques used to add gloom and otherwise obfuscate areas when necessary. The only color that comes into play is red, which is used selectively but liberally for gore when warranted. The soundtrack is subtle, but haunting, and what few sounds the handful of enemies make when you encounter them are enough on their own to make it clear they should be avoided.
Neverending Nightmares does a great job of managing difficulty as well. Puzzles often rely on a bit of wandering at first to trigger certain appearances, but don't feel overly drawn out. Enemies are easy enough to avoid in most cases, with later encounters taking a bit more strategy, and the consequences for failure feel justified but horrifying. As things increase in difficulty and complexity, levels offer checkpoints to keep repetition down.
The multiple endings aren't overly numerous, and I liked how it wasn't entirely clear which one, if any of them, was the "real" ending. As you finish the game, a level map unlocks, showing threads between what you've cleared thus far and making it easier to figure out where you should be looking for alternate choices to enable different progress. All in all, this is one neat little horror package, and the connection it has to the developer's personal experience makes it that much more worthwhile.

- Graphics: 7 / 10
- Performance: 10 / 10
- Storytelling: 7 / 10
- Possibilitys: 10 / 10
- Server-Onlinetime: 9 / 10
►
The Graphics of this game are pretty good and well done for a racing game being that big. But compared to other titles released today not the best and detailed one. Not saying that they are almost perfect for a game like this, its still not the best it could be.
Shader is well done, also the Antialising. Textures are well but not that detailed and a little bit "spongy" if you are looking close to them. However, its a well done composition of textures and it´s nice for the eye.
Due to the fact, that this game has a dang big world to explore and the graphics are pretty nice the performance is incredible. I was surprised that this game runs on a very low quality computer of a friend very stable and well.
You got almost every time the amount of fps you loocked in the options. (30 or 60)
Nothing more to add. Perfect performance for a game like this and for a game of this generation.
The game has a OK story but it is pretty long and has it plots and twists. Short cutscenes, short dialogs.
I´d had it rated lower if it does´t have a playtime like this. If you play casual you can come through the story in something like 25 - 30 hours which is very long for singleplayer/or coop story without using the extra things and PvP a long time.
The Crew offers a veeery big world to explore. To get from the west to the eastcoast you are driving something like 2-3 hours if you are fast. Also you got additional to the Storyraces and PvPstuff a tons of tests/skill mini missions where you can test your skills in some small disciplins. Escape fast, drive fast on a road, climb a hill and so on. If you want to get through everything you are going to have some 100 hours.
In addition The Crew offers a very good Tuning system. Optic tuning is back in business in a little bit smaller version of the "Need for Speed Underground 2" tuning possibilitys. I have three reasons why I would recommend not buying F1 2016.. yet?
1) This should obviously be driven with wheels and pedals, and Codemasters haven't made that a comfortable experince. There are huge deadzones on both the brake pedal and the throttle pedal. It's especially bad on the throttle. I've simraced for about 8 years and I've never experienced such massive deadzones. There's an aproximately 30% deadzone on the buttom of the brake, and a 25% deadzone on the buttom AND top of the throttle. I have no issues in any other of the racing games/sims that I usually play. This should be easy for Codemasters to fix but it's appalling that such core settings aren't made properly from the start.
2) The shiftlights cannot be moved. The last F1 game I bought and played was 2011. It really borthered me that the shiftlight indicators couldn't be moved. I suspect the reason for that is that they need to port their games to consoles, but that's speculation. I wasn't really surprised to see they're still immovable, it is Codemasters afterall.
3) The sound is absolutely messed up. Even using the "full soundscale" setting, sound is messed up in a couple of ways. The most obvious is that the other cars are waayyy too loud. Way louder than your own car. Also, there seems to be too few sound channels to handle all the noises when you're running in a large pack of cars, makes the car sound like robots beint brutally mistreated instead of expensive racecars.
The game has a lot of potential. I hope codemasters patch the game. The physics are decent, the grapics and framerates are good. I'll change my review once I find the game in an acceptable state.

Ugh.  No.  This game is a damn mess.
It's beautiful and has an incredibly large map.  That's what saves this game.  Really, it's beautiful and the map is god damn gigantic.  But forget everything else in this game.
It has built in DRM.  Yep.  Uplay it is, folks!
This game is incredibly glitchy.  Here is what I've come across:
I HATE the side missions for upgrades.
1) Do NOT do the side missions.  The missions where you have to hit specific targets, the game will ALWAYS spawn traffic and a car will stop right ontop of a target.  I've had 18 wheelers stop in the middle of a target....how the heck am I supposed to hit the target?!  You will frustrate yourself to no end.  Slalom is pretty great because you don't have to specifically hit anything, just be on either side of a target and you're good.  The precision missions, forget it.  They will spawn targets that are too small for your car to get through and you'll lose your modifier bonus, making it next to impossible to get a gold ranking.  Forget scramble, just don't even bother.  None of the cars handle well enough to do the missions.  I mean, it's POSSIBLE to do the missions, but you'll slam your fist through a wall or put your controller through your screen long before you complete the mission.
2) If you're using a controller, for some reason the game loses track of the steering.  Seriously.  You'll go flying through a corner and your car won't turn at all.  You have to swivel the analog stick in a 360 a few times to get the game to recognize your steering again.  I've used an Xbox One controller, and a PS3 controller with MotionJoy, both controllers had the same issue.  I've tried different USB ports, both USB 2.0 and 3.0, same deal.
3) Every car handles pretty much the same, except for muscle cars are tanky and non muscle cars have slightly better turning, compared to muscle cars.  That's it.
4) First person driving mode (where you can see the steering wheel and the driver's hands) is glitchy as hell, it will constantly flicker like you're trying to look out the back window.
5) I don't know if this is just because I have two monitors, but when you start the game, it boots Uplay, and you have to start the game through uplay.  First, it takes forever to boot the damn game and when it does, it boots the game in the background, minimized.  WTF.  And when it does, number 6 happens....
6) Sometimes it will boot the game in a glitchy fashion and you'll only get 2 FPS.  Seriously.  You have to alt+tab out of the game, and then maximize the game again to get the game.....focused?  I don't know.
7) Because the game is always online, you can be in the middle of a race and KABLAM you'll slam dead into someone who just logged in.
8) Because it's always online, if you sit at an intersection (they seem to be spawn spots) in a city, someone can spawn right on top of you.  Repairs to your vehicle are expensive, that's why I'm bringing this up.  You will have to pay for repairs to your vehicle because the game spawned a vehicle either right in front of you while you were driving or right on top of you.
I have the music turned off so I can't comment on the music.
The graphics are phenominal.  Someone had commented that your car is your avatar.  I somewhat agree, you can modify just about everything, but there's certain cars in certain classes that are significantly better than the rest, so everyone is going to spam those cars.
The races themselves are great though.  The handling is never bad enough to not be able to corner, even as a tanky muscle car.  I really want to say just do the main missions and enjoy the story (which you could see coming a mile away) but you have to level up your car.  Long jump is stupidly simple.  You learn really quickly to get a 3 mile start before the jump and you'll fly and get a gold every time.  Same with speed missions, just start a million miles away and you'll be going so ridiculously fast you'll get gold every time.  So this combined with the Slalom, and you'll be alright.  The other missions, you'll pull off a bronze hopefully and you'll get a part here and there.
What saves this game?  It's beautiful, the map is amazing and the fact that it's always online so you're always playing with other people, even if you do the missions solo, other people will inhabit your world.  You're never alone.

I didn't buy this game at launch because I was worried about how it would turn out. I sort of refret not doing that. Although the game isn't the greatest thing ever it does renew my faith that Triple A games can turn out good. If you look at Triple A games from from the last 3-5 years the all seem like cash grabs and lack a lot of polish and content that even indie developers are including nowadays. The weapon customization is really good. It is similar to the Crisis games but evolves upon that, as it allows you to completely change how a weapon functions. You can change an assault rifle to a lmg or or battle rifle to an antimaterial rifle. In addition to that you can also equip your weapons with a decent amount of attachments.
The game is sort of similar to the Far Cry games (which I really enjoy) in the sense you are taking over an area and the way the game plays out. The game also includes elements of the Crisis games as I mentioned along with almost Sabetour elements with destroying enemy compounds and key components.
Overall I would highly recommend this game for its interesting story and its well designed gameplay.

Fixed the durability but bugged the AI. Enemies now tend to go randomly aggro across the whole map, and the enemy placement is absolutely horribly unbalanced and cheap for single players.
Also, the Agape Ring. Low lvl Invaders with endgame gear are back. I don't know what the hell they were thinking when adding that. 99% of times it's just a free kill for the invader. Where's the fun and balancing in that? It was stupid in Dark Souls 1 and it is stupid now.
Fascit: Either you play Co-Op or don't even bother buying the Scholar of the First Sin Edition. It's simply balanced for Co-Op play, with singleplayer not in mind. Co-Op is great, mind you, sure, go ahead and buy it if you have friends you can do some jolly co-op with, but it's no excuse for the singleplayer being almost unplayable if you're not a professional, it's just too heavily biased towards the Invaders due to the agape ring, and mobs due to their horrible placement and huge numbers attacking you at the same time. The devs concentrated all about making high level PvP and Co-Op more balanced, and forgot all about the singleplayer experience.
Sure, Scholar of the First Sin Edition fixed a lot of things for PC users, but it also made a huge amount of others things worse, both on console and on PC. Alas, I can only recommend this game if you don't have a console for the original version of Dark Souls 2 due to the durability bug on PC, whoch sadly makes the original Dark Souls 2 almost unplayable for PC users.

If you're reading this, it's safe to assume that you have an Internet-capable device with all of the modern comforts that typically implies. But what if you didn't? What if you were forced out of civilization as you know it, to live in the wilderness? How do you think you'd fare? Banished asks those questions, opening with a dozen or so outcasts seeking to make their way in the wilderness. It's a humble setup, but the game is masterfully constructed with dozens of interlocking mechanics--the perfect foundation for a stinging emergent narrative and a focus on empathy in the face of a Malthusian world.
People, more than anything else, are your vital resource. They need homes, food, decent clothes, tools, emotional support, medicine, and more. Every mechanic, every building you can place, and everything else you can do relates back to that central theme of survival. If you can't gather enough food, your people die. If they're stuck outside for too long, or don't have warm clothing, they die. Each time you fail as their leader, you're reminded of the loss with a grating sound and a yellow gravestone. These serve as a one-two punch to punish you for failure because losing citizens makes it that much harder to keep up the resource flow. One fewer worker means you can't gather food, stone, wood, or anything else as quickly. When children die, it's even worse, though you likely won't know it for some time. As your population ages, you eventually lose more than a few citizens to old age, and the best way to replace them is to give your younger citizens houses in the hopes that they'll reproduce and bolster your future numbers.While the process of survival is never-ending, holding out against the elements amid the hostility of the untamed natural world is a small but powerful personal victory. Villagers have names; they're born, grow up, and eventually die under your intense supervision. Banished reinforces the human drama with its brutal difficulty and negative feedback loops. It's fertile soil for some of the most remarkable emergent storytelling around. With relatively few, well-designed mechanics, the game weaves a powerful tale of empathy and desperation and is a high-water mark for narrative elements that mutually reinforce mechanics. Even better, this is a very human story divorced from the Western tropes common in the loosely imperialistic messages of other, similar games. It's just you, your people, and their strong desire to live.

This game is more of an atmospheric horror than a 'jump-scare' horror. There are, maybe, two or three jumpscares. It's slow-paced and repetitive, which, I think, work really well for the game. You pay close attention to all these tiny details, like blinking and shadows, and all the paintings convey all these interesting thoughts. The game makes you wonder "Why is this here?", "What's going on?", "What does this mean?". I spent more time wondering about the enviroments and the events than being afraid, and I'm still trying to connect the dots of the game.
One thing you're going to notice is that almost all the reviews have a short playthrough time, me included. There isn't a lot to play through. The game is very short. This helps the game stay suspenseful. If you're looking for a game to sink 100's of hours in, this isn't the game for you. You'll want to replay it to acheive all possible endings,  but the replaying time isn't long. The short playthrough time creates a tense feeling for the whole game. It should be added that there are absolutely no loading screens in the game, so you never have any release or rest from the tension.
The game is also very heavy with symbolism. The paintings, the art, the ages, the enemies, the colors, they all seem to have unique meaning. I found myself sitting in rooms, staring at the windows or the pictures, or hiding from enemies to observe them, trying to figure out what it meant, how it reflected the character.
The art style is somehow simple and complex. The characters look cartoonish, as does the enviroment, but it still has great detail. A lot of effort went into the design, as everything is hand drawn. Items that you can interact with are colored, like the bronze doorhandles, which is an interesting mechanic that helps negate confusion.
As for the horror elements, I really didn't find the game scary, but there is a LOT of gore. As previously stated, the enviroment is monochromatic, consisting of just black and white. One exeption to this is the blood, which is red. And, oh boy, there is a lot of red. It's similar to 'The Human Centipede 2' in this way, where in that movie, only the blood had color. This causes the blood to stick out and have a drastic impact on the player. I don't want to spoil anything, but as the game goes on, the amount of blood increases, and you get this feeling of dread, like you don't want to go on, but you want to find the cause. This gives me a tense feeling, but not a scared feeling. Gore has never been a scare factor for me, but it might be for you.
Tl;Dr: I wholeheartedly reccomend this game. It's packed with symbolism. It's short, but tense all the way through. It looks beautifuly frightening and sounds amazing. It's not terribly scary, but it's quite immersive.

This seems like it might be one of those games where the story is the star and that deep story is told in subtle ways both by the characters you meet and the environment you interact with, and it certainly tries to do so, but fails miserably.
The first, and most glaring, issue is the terrible translation.  While in many games this is not that big of a problem, when a game is trying to tell a story in as few words as possible, the ones they do use need to be on point.  These were anything but.
The second issue is how the player character engages in dialogue, by which I mean he doesn't.  This is one of those games where you interact with anything that highlights, and when that interaction is a person, you talk to them, but that dialogue is always one sided.  You never see what your character is saying, which when combined with the bad translation, makes it hard to understand what is going on.  Too much of the story is lost this way.
Finally is the gameplay on the train.  The game is set up to give you a large amount of exposition on the train by overhearing the conversations of the passengers while you go about your job of keeping the train running and the passengers healthy and happy.  This is a great idea and the concept really reinforces the idea that you're just some guy trying to do his job, not an action hero.  But this is the main way for you to get the story, and the minigames required to keep the train running prevent you from being able to see that dialogue.
When you're forced to choose between playing the game and understanding what the hell is going on -- and I literally found myself saying "What the hell is going on?" because of all this -- playing the game wins out, because, hey, you can't progress unless you play the game.
Once you've decided to play these minigames and not hear the (badly translated) story, the quality of gameplay becomes all you have, and this is mediocre at best.  The minigames are terribly repetitive and simple, but take a lot of time.  The main game is rather good, but becomes rote quite quickly.  Nothing novel or clever comes up, no special puzzles appear where you have to figure the right way to take out the enemies, it's just the same "save your ammo, aim for the head, punch if you can" every level.  It becomes a slog quite quickly.  An easy slog, but a slog nonetheless.
The idea seems like it could have been really great in a Papers, Please sort of way, but gameplay decisions and terrible translation mar the execution.  Pass on this one unless you can get it for $5 or less.

In
, you play as an older sibling returning home after a year abroad. During your absence, your family has inherited and moved into an old manor.
The entire game consists of exploring the house and discovering the story at your own pace.
lets you enter one family's personal space and uncover their lives. You'll find notes, drawings, or various objects in drawers, underneath beds, everywhere.
This unprecedented realism is also present in the story. Things that would seem boring in your typical bro game, like childhood friendship, coming of age, or marital problems, are abundant in
. This game has some top notch character development despite the fact that all you do is rummage around a house. You can’t help but be interested in the lives of this family. It’s so much more real than any other game.

Yes you, I see you cringe a bit. Get out, this isn't your game.
...The rest of you still here? Good.
VVVVVV is a retro-esque game that is short (about an hour if you're looking for everything), difficult, rocking, and a teensy bit bizarre. The highlight of this game is it's spikes, there are about as many spikes as there are in I Wanna Be the Guy!. Its other highlight is the flipping system. You see, your character can't jump, only flip gravity (and at one point if you're aiming for getting all of the Trinkets, you're going to loathe this fact) and along the way many little features are tacked onto this ability. The thing is: it works. VVVVVV is a game that could have come out on the Atari but made for a more modern audience. In short, it's difficult (and short), but lovingly so.
Don't attempt getting all of the Trinkets unless you're a maschoist like I am. It is agonizing. Type Vidi, Veni, Vinci or Prize for the Reckless on Youtube. You'll see.
A short, but memorable, unique and personal experience. Goosebumps.

Knowing that Homefront The Revolution had loads of development troubles from THQ dying, Crytek refusing to pay their employees (And STILL not doing so at the rate that they're self imploding), going from a basic sequel to the original with its crazy ambition of wanting to be an open world Half Life 2 and the reading the reviews at launch, I went in with the lowest of expectations, but I was pleasantly surprised. It isnt a great game by any means but its really undeserving of its "WORST GAME EVER" title many people give it, as it has merit and is still better compared to the original game. That said its got some flaws that make it difficult to recommend at its current price tag of $43 CDN, though if you can get it and the DLC included at a heavily discounted bargain bin price tag its certainly worth a look since it feels like a successor to THQ titles in that its flawed yet can be enjoyable, just dont go in expecting much.

Pros
Looks and runs great
The stories found through collectable journals are interesting
The world itself is genuinely interesting and has a great atmosphere
At times the game feels like an awesome mix of Crysis and Half Life 2
Provides a lot of bang for your buck
Loads of weapon customization options
Cons
Characters are fairly bland and forgettable
Though the game aimed for an open world Half-Life feel it feels more like a mixture of a modern Ubisoft game (The blander ones) and Crysis in that it can get repetitive very quickly
Can get repetitive very quickly
Story DLC is more enjoyable than the base game which isnt bad but its annoying with their short length + pricetag
Music is generally forgettable and bland, would benefit more from a soundtrack used in the DLC which feels appropriate for an action game
Though its focused on guerilla combat you'll either love or hate the fact that you die very easily
And the most disappointing of all is that it feels really safe without much new you havent already seen before, or taking some interesting mechanics from things like Metro in terms of a cracking gas mask/ammo as currency. Its pretty vanilla.
Though in fairness Dambusters really seem commited to turning this game around, and if they provide the same care they've given this game recently for future projects or sequels I could get a real kick out of it.

A lot of people think that Kool-Aid Jammers are just for kids, but I disagree. They're my particular favorite when it comes to pouched drinks, on top of others like Capri Sun. While they may not be as healthy as the others (but then, none of them are particularly healthy, really), I've found that Kool-Aid Jammers have a stronger flavor than the other brands, and don't have that watered down feeling that some of the others have. My personal favorite flavor is Cherry, and it's usually the only flavor I buy - there used to be a Cherry Limeade flavor that was better, but they seem to have stopped selling those. Kool-Aid Jammers might not be the best drink you could get, but they're good, fast drinks for when you want something with a stronger taste than water but want something more hydrating than a soda, with the convenience of a pouch meaning you don't have to take a lot of time away from your game to grab one.
The reason I'm talking about Kool-Aid Jammers instead of Neverending Nightmares is two-fold; not only did my Kool-Aid Jammer outlast the game, but I also found it more interesting. Nevending Nightmares is a game that puts up a nice face in terms of atmosphere and art and sound design, but quickly falls apart when you actually play it. The game is, as the title implies, about a character experiencing neverending nightmares. You wake up in your bed, walk through one of three environments, and at the end something kills you and you wake up in the next nightmare. This goes on for about one hour (for a game called Neverending Nightmares, it sure does end pretty quickly), and then the game ends. Every now and then it'll bring in mechanics familiar to horror game fans, like a monster that you have to hide in a closet to avoid or an enemy that you can't sprint by, but these are few and far between and the enemies are so basic that it doesn't even feel like an effort to avoid them, let alone anything that might make you feel nervous around them. The only reason I even know what they do when they catch you is because each of them do it at least once in the scripted next-level death. The art style is unique, and the audio is well-designed to boost the atmosphere (though the special "headphones" sound option it encourages you to use seemed more like it was meant for bad headphones than ones more suited for gaming, and on my Gamescom 780 it just pushed all the sound to the front speakers of the headphones instead of giving a good surround experience), but so much of your time spent in the game is spent just walking past almost identical rooms over and over until you finally stumble upon the thing that kills you, and it's just not very entertaining. I'm not saying I want some PewDiePie youtube fodder game full of jump scares, but it's just hard to stay invested in a game with this little substance.
There are apparently three additional levels that I missed leading to two different endings (though I have no idea what I did to "choose" the path I ended up on, since there isn't really anything in terms of dialogue or obvious story), but after seeing how long and tedious the final nightmare in my branch was I really just didn't care enough to see the others. I really wanted to like this game, but in the end I just found it extremely repetitive, and while some games make good use of down time to build up the atmosphere for a payoff, this game just feels like nothing but down time, leading to an unsatisfying conclusion that just leaves you wondering what the point was. Neverending Nightmares currently costs $15. A 10-count box of Cherry Kool-Aid Jammers costs $1.88. You can do the math yourself.

So this is the first review I've ever written, something compelled me to do so and here goes! These are my thoughts on the game which may or may not reflect others opinions on the game, read several reviews if you're unsure!
Verdun is a WWI shooter and in fact the only modern WWI shooter that delivers what it delivers: A gruelling trench warfare experience with a lot of people running around, dying en masse and battles often ending in draws. Great
* The combat is harrowing, blood, guts and death will be all around you and it can be very immersive.
* The Devs are actively joining games, playing with the community and hearing people out about their requests and answering their questions.
* The weapons are diverse in their own simplicity, there are many many different rifles, machineguns and other gadgets for you to utilize.
* When playing with an even oponent it's extremely satisfying to finally being able to hold on to a trench by the skin of your teeth.
* The maps are varied, even though it's simply just trenches, but foliage, scenery varies and is a pleasant mix rather than just fighting in the brown mud.
* There are some shining examples within the community, giving tips and tricks for general survival and are rather pleasant when conversing. The community is rather balanced, teethering towards the positive and nice side.
* Hit registration and lag will leave you incredibly frustrated when you die behind cover or when you see enemies in the distance teleporting several meters at a time when running, making it difficult to pick them off.
* The blend between realism and arcade blends rather poorly. Kill feed and hit markers clashes with the one shot kills and the feel of the game. The random "Bolt in wrong place" that'll get you killed at the most inopportune times and as far as I know, there are no ways to prevent that from happening, no way of making sure the bolt is in it's right place before getting into combat or the likes. Taking you very little time to cycle a round into a bolt action rifle, but taking even longer to pump a new shell into a shotgun or simply cocking  the hammer on a revolver leaves you scratching your head wondering if the soldiers themselves even realize they're in a war.
* The lack of autobalancing: Entire teams of level 100s against a few leaves many games feel like an impossible battle to win: since they have higher level squads and more experienced players. And a general unwillingness to compromise and even out the teams permeates throughout the more experienced players as they seem to prefer leveling their squads from evening out the fight. There'll also be situations where players from the losing side joins the winning side whenever possible.
* Movement is rather clunky and WILL leave you fifteen meters into no mans land without stamina making you a extremely easy target for the enemy. Having to rest for 5-10 seconds between 20-25 meter sprints make very little sense when the movement speed is barely increased above a generous trot. Granted there's a weight to the gear on the soldiers but the general sluggishness in many of the soldiers movement makes you feel like you're playing actual great war veterans, over 110 years old and with osteoperosis wracking their body. There is no way in dropping quickly to the ground when you recieve fire (most often you'll just drop dead with a -Zuck- noice, even when a mg has been firing on you for a while). There is very little urgency in the soldiers movement or actions, as I stated earlier; kind of like they're unaware of that they're in a war.
--------------
But at the end of the line: I think Verdun has a lot to offer, despite it's drawbacks and one can only hope that with constant improvement there'll be a game that'll iron out it's kinks and give you a more polished experience. But then again, nothing is polished in war, nothing is polished in the trenches of western europe and that, is something that Verdun captures very well! It's immersive, despite being frustrating at times. It's fun, despite it leaves you feeling cheated at times. It's addictive, even though it has some drawbacks.
Just like any other game.
Do you like shooting? Do you like fun? Do you like a sense of dread?
If so: Buy it! Play it! Support the Devs.
