Since this package includes two games, I will review them separately:
Final Fantasy X was originally released on the PS2 around the turn of the new century. The game was well received; it was Square's first FF game on the PS2 and it was also the first FF game to feature voice acting. Fast-forward more than a decade and today we can enjoy it on the PS3, PS4, and of course PC. Does it hold up to today's standards or is it an anachronistic classic?
The player takes the role of a young man named Tidus. You find out within the opening scenes that he's a blitzball player (combination of soccer and American football, but underwater). Soon after he gets warped to another world (Spira) and he must find a way to go back to his. Ultimately, his "fate" becomes entangled with the denizens of Spira and he, along with several companions, must face a greater evil.
The story sounds like typical JRPG fare - a group people must stop some evil from destroying the world. However, it's really not that simple and the plot develops "organically". What I mean is that the main antagonist doesn't just appear out of nowhere and now only this specific group of people must stop him because why not. The game also goes more in-depth on real life subject areas such as racism and religion compared to its predecessors. Since a lot of the plot centers around a pilgrimage from temple to temple there is some resemblance to the Chinese tale, "Journey to the West" as well. It's difficult to go into details without spoiling certain things but overall the story is decent and well written.
Most negative reviews back in the day centered around the linear nature of the game. Indeed, there is no world map your characters can travel in and when you do get the option to travel freely it comes down to a menu and selecting the areas  to teleport to. There are some hidden areas but overall there isn't much to explore once you reach the end. The story is progressed by going from point A to point B (as mandated by the glowing red arrow on the mini-map) to trigger a cutscene and/or a boss fight. Rinse and repeat and that's pretty much it for the main story.
Departing from the iconic ATB battle system, FFX introduced the CTB system. It is a turn-based battle system in which the Agility stat plays a huge role. The turns of your characters and enemies are displayed on the right hand side during battle and so planning ahead and manipulating the turn-order is key. After battle your characters gain AP points and you use these points to increase their stats and learn abilities on the sphere grid. That's right, there are no traditional character levels in this game.
The HD remaster of FFX is overall good. More attention was paid to the main characters while many NPCs look very "doll-like" in cutscenes, but the background environments are detailed and bright. The textures may not always be the best but they do look clean. The music was composed by the legend Nobuo Uematsu and it's simply amazing. I highly recommend the original score and not the newly arranged ones. Unfortunately, Tidus and the main female protagonist's voices are just...well, bad. The delivery is very inconsistent and there were many times the mood was ruined in a cutscene due to inappropriate delivery. Just search "Tidus laugh" on Youtube and you'll see what I mean. The other characters' voices are pretty decent most of the time though.
Besides the campaign the main draw in FFX is the "Monster Arena". Here you can fight superbosses with millions and millions of HP. Additionally, there are the Dark Aeons and the hardest superboss in the game, Penance, for you to topple as well (originally only found in the International version of the game). If you are looking to collect all the achievements then you'll be in for some major stat grinding. It took me over 100 hours.
FFX-2 was the first direct sequel of a flagship FF game. It was released 2 years after FFX and was developed for the PS2 as well.
This time around the player takes control of Yuna, a young woman who is traveling with two other friends. They are "sphere hunters", basically people that travel Spira to uncover its history. Considering this is a direct sequal to FFX, saying anything more would spoil the plot for both games. The tone of the story is a lot more light-hearted compared to FFX. There are some really silly NPCs and ridiculous missions. In the end you're still stopping an "ultimate evil" and all that.
Okay here we diverge from FFX. I guess Square paid attention to the complaints about the linear format in X, so the player has access to all the areas in the game from the beginning. It's still just a menu but you are freely to go wherever you want. Unfortunately, the areas are recycled from FFX so exploring new places and hoping for larger maps are out of the question. The game is composed of 5 chapters - completing enough story-related missions in each chapter will conclude it. So you can do some sidequests and then go back to the main story or just rush through the main story quickly. Although if you want to get all the achievements in the game you'll pretty much have to do everything and then some (more on this later).
The traditional ATB battle system is back along with character levels. Character classes or "jobs" are also back with unique abilities that can be learned through gaining AP. A character's job can be changed in battle by changing their dresspheres (their clothes) on the garment grid. Doing so can activate special bonuses such as increases in core stats or gaining access to abilities. Overall the battle system is quick and effective and allows for a large variety of styles and strategies.
Again, the HD remaster looks good but not fantastic. The main characters, environments, and especially the monsters are nicely detailed. The problem, similar to FFX, is the same lack of polish to many NPCs. The music is overall...not good. This time around we get a new composer and everything just sounds underwhelming. There are some key pieces that are quite melodic but overall the music doesn't do it for me. And the voice acting...well, it's more or less the same quality as FFX.
There is a 100 floor optional dungeon in this game and also the Fiend Arena to sink your hours into. I can't comment too much on the Fiend Arena because I didn't really go through it - there aren't any achievements associated with it, surprisingly. Speaking of achievements, there is one really tedious to obtain: Sweet Perfection. This requires you to get 100% completion of the story and this means basically doing a lot of random sidequests and watching scenes without skipping dialogue and other small bits and pieces. If you want to get this in one playthrough you'll HAVE to follow a guide. I followed 2 guides at once and I still only got 99.8% in the end. I cleaned the last 0.2% up on my NG+ run but still. Also, you'll have to go through FFX-2 Last Mission as well to get the rest of the achievements. Last Mission is a separate rogue-like game that is accessed through the main launcher.
If you never played these games before I highly recommend you give them a try, at least FFX. If you have played these before then you know what to expect just with better graphics. Also, unless you played the International version back in the day, this time around you get to experience the Dark Aeons / Penance in X and the Fiend Arena in X-2. Personally I enjoyed FFX a lot more because of its story, music, and overall tone of the game. However, the job system in X-2 is really well done and is reminiscent of classic FF.

Poorly made, but very fun. It plays exactly like a Far Cry game but in a more urban and futuristic area, with two types of areas, red zones and yellow zones. Red zones are basically open, all out warfare in the streets, you still have to play stealthily but you'll find that you can take a much more head on approach to things there. Yellow zones are much more policed areas where you'll actually find some civilian life and less destruction. Because of the heavy presence in these areas, you'll need to move much stealthier and more quietly, taking to side streets and avoiding cameras and enemies. The game has the same system of capturing points and claiming areas for your side that is employed in Far Cry, slowly liberating area after area to your cause. The game also has one of my favorite weapon customization systems, all the guns are incredibly modular and there are three configurations for each weapon. An example is that you can slide the top and the clip out of your pistol and put on smg parts and basically turn it into an smg. Also, all of this has animations, from sliding on a scope to screwing on a suppressor. The game has a really nice story and atmosphere, it really gives you the feeling of being a guerilla revolutionary fighting back against an oppresive regime. The overworld is very ambient and reminds me heavily of the Infamous games. The combat a mixed bag, guns have kick and feel like they have actual weight to them when you fire. There is no regeneration and health packs are scarce, adding a degree of challenge and required thought when you go into a fight. Sadly though, the AI in this game is abysmal. Enemies seem to completely lack object permanence and will often just rush you head on without attempting to use cover. Because of the fact you die in just four to five shots, I often find my self getting killed by enemies whose positions I can't see. This game is also very unstable, although not as much as people let it out to be. I have so far only experienced one crash, but I'd assume that varies depending on your PC. Overall, this game is pretty fun and worth purchasing if on sale, I got it for ten bucks, but probably not worth it's full price tag. I give it 7/10.

I don't understand how this game has such a low rating. I thoroughly enjoyed it. The story is good, even if some of the characters are a little annoying... that pacifist doctor especially. The ending was satisfying. More than can be said for Far Cry 3/4, which this game has been compared to. I will say that Homefront does tread the same path as recent Far Cry games, but I think it does so very well.
Some criticisms though. The weapon modifications are interesting, but the interface is a bit tedious, and it takes time to do it, so you can't do it in combat. The LMG mods into a very cool grenade launcher, but due to the slowness of the interface, you can't just mod over to the grenade launcher when you get surprised by an armored car, so you rely on your regular explosives to take it out. This is unfortunate.
I didn't encounter any major bugs while playing the campaign. Once I had an RC car explosive get stuck in terrain, and the mod interface gets glitchy at times, but these are minor things. No crashes. Ran it on medium graphics settings, 1920*1200 on an Nvidia 960, and had a mostly steady 60 FPS.
Also worth mentioning: This game has the most satisfying sniper rifle ever. KABLAMMO! It'll take out heavy infantry in one hit. It's not silent though, so plan for that.
Verdict: Buy.

Dark Souls 2 is a great sequel to one of my favorite games. First of all, I highly recommend that you play the original Dark Souls before playing this one. There is really no reason to play 2 before 1.
So assuming that you have played the first one, 2 improves upon some things but also makes some big mistakes.
Combat is for the most part the same. There are slight changes to rolling when locked on, iFrames, and there is also a new move called shield break. The main difference with combat is the edition of power stancing. Power stancing makes dual-wielding more effective by being able to attack with both weapons (if they have the same attack type) when you have 150% of the required stats. Personally I wasn't a huge fan of this change just because I feel that it made rolling essential even earlier than rolling became essential in Dark Souls 1. Nonetheless, I still had fun dual wielding katanas. I just sort of missed having a shield.
One thing I loved about Dark Souls was the non-linear world. Dark Souls 2 has a beautiful but unconnected world. 2 gives you the ability to teleport to every single bonfire you light from the beginning of the game! In 1 all of the areas connect with shortcuts back to the hub area. I still remember the first time I went down the elevator from the church back to firelink. Dark Souls 2 has none of this, the ability to travel to all bonfires removes the purpose of short cuts back to the hub. Because of this crucial mistake, the world of Dark Souls feels very linear and unconnected. This was my main issue with the game. It's not a deal breaker but it is just a bit of a shame.
Other than that there are a just a few minor changes such as losing health everytime you die. That one isn't much of an issue just because the items to reverse it are plentiful and the ring of binding helps a lot if you know you are going to die a lot. Also I just want to add that the DLC included in SOTFS is phenomenal.
Overall I loved this game and highly recommend it if you enjoyed the first. For the most part it is just more of the same amazing DS gameplay.

I've felt the need to write the Dark Souls 2 review from scratch again, but this time I will say what Dark Souls 2 did right as a Dark Souls game.
The main issue with this game is its name, "Dark Souls 2". If this game had been called "Undead Adventure" no one would've had any issue, but that's not its name, it has Dark Souls on its title, and those two words mean things that this game mostly fails to get. I used to hate on this game too much, I still think it's horsecrap, but I recognize some REALLY REALLY good things this has, though people use to remember more easily the REALLY REALLY (REALLY) terrible things.
Some lore and game moments are very memorable and even shocking.
- After spending the whole game searching for the King, finally find him and see he has already gone Hollow was very impactful. Banished is game about a community trying to survive the harsh nature. There are no enemies, no conquest, not even a true possibility to amass wealth like in other sims. It’s just your villagers and their struggle to survive.
For the most part this struggle to survive is really intriguing. At the beginning you will fail, and most likely your first village will either be soon a ghost town or crippled through too many deaths, that a restart is the better idea. The most pressing dangers for your villagers are starvation and freezing and these are the ones, that define the whole game. Other dangers like sickness oder disasters (e.g. a tornado) are either too rare or too weak to play a significant role. Before writing this review I have played for around 8 hours and have only encountered a handful of sick people and not one disaster has spawned.
However feeding your people and making sure they stay warm will be challening enough to have fun, at least in the beginning. Depending on the difficulty you start on, you’ll either have seeds to start farming immediately or you will have to make due with gathering, hunting and fishing. To manage this you will have to build gatherer huts or hunting lodges, but you also have to make sure, that your laborors cut enough trees so your woodcutter can build a supply of firewood for the winter. At the same time you need enough builders to build houses for everyone and storage barns to store your food and other produces.
You’ll have to maintain a balance between the different jobs, so that everything gets done, in quite a similar way to Dwarf Fortress and it’s various clones. In contrast to a lot of these games, the Ui in Banished actually helps you to do this and is very well done. It’s easy to find anything you want to build and you can not only turn on or off various menus shown on the screen but also drag them around in any way you want them. This in collaboration with the very intuitive and easy to learn hotkeys make Banished one of the easiest to learn games of it’s genre.
Maintaing said balance is really engaging and fun, you constantly ponder if you have enough people working on producing food or if you can maybe change a few jobs to produce more stones, so your builders will actually be able to build one of the way too many projects you started. Or maybe you just want to assign a few villagers as herbalist in case someone gets sick only to notice that your woodcutter just died while your at low supply of firewood and there is no laborer to replace him.
Sadly after a while this fun subsides. It is quite easy to come to a point, where it is hard to fail, if you just have enough people producing food. And since there are only a few jobs outside of the basic food/wood/stone procudicing ones you soon run out of options for your people to work with. And the more you grow the more it feels like a replay of the previous steps, just get more food and a bit of firewood and build more houses to grow your city, just like before.
It’s not that the journey to this point isn’t fun, is genuinely is. But the journey is way to short. In other games a new kind of challenge would appear, in e.g. Dwarf Fortress  you would have to fortify your fortress against enemies or would just start a huge project of mining a giant dining hall with flowing lava to keep it warm. Or like in the old Caesar or Pharao games from Sierra you’d have a whole bunch of different jobs and buildings more to last for quite a while.
In Banished however the endgame is quickly reached and it basically consists of just more of the same.
I haven’t talked much about the graphics or the sound, which is mostly due to both of these parts are just good enough. The graphics are pretty enough, but not so much, that you stop to look at them. The seasonal change of the weather and the land is nice, but the rain and snow effects are a little bit too thick and get in the way sometimes. The sound effects are nice and give the village a nice living feel of people really working, but nothing really memorable comes to mind.
In conclusion Banished is a good game. It’s not as good as it could have been, but considering that as far as I know most, if not all the work for this game was done by one single person, it is quite a feat. If you’re a fan of city building games or liked the premise of Dwarf Fortress, but didn’t like the obscure UI, you should check this game out, but don’t expect to be entertained for hundreds of hours. I certainly don’t regrett buying it, but will put it aside in hope of future updates to rekindle my interest. If you want to have a number i would give it a 7/10.
One last word of advice: Consider buying directly from the developer at
, if you’re from a country with € like I am. You will profit from the exchange rate and get the game a bit cheaper and you will get a Steam Key and a DRM free version as well.

Actual gameplay is your basic bunny-hop shooting simulator. Everybody jumps all the time. Somehow people will hit each other. Hit detection seems way off, and all guns are wildly inaccurate and have oddly short ranges. MGs overheat after 2 seconds of firing. Grenades appear in mid air in front of your character before sailing off in a seemingly random trajectory.
Graphics are meh.
Dinosaur classes are completely broken. Several of them don't have guns, so enjoy chasing enemies that are bunny-hopping backwards as they riddle you with bullets. Most people seem to just play the human soldiers, removing the shred of uniqueness this game possessed. Often they have convoluted tactics in order to be useful. The Compy, for instance is a suicide bomber with a pathetically weak normal attack and almost no health, but must kill enemies in order to make the blast more powerful. This is nigh impossible and about as much fun as it sounds.
There are the expected modes, team deathmatch, king of the hill, etc. Unfortunately, with so few players, there is pretty much only one populated server up at any given time.
In conclusion: The game isn't very good and its servers are all but dead, but at least I got to shoot a T-Rex in the butt with a flamethrower.

Description: Banished is a Medieval, city builder simulator. You are required to manage your building materials (iron, stone, wood), your crafting materials (coal, iron, leather, wool), your sustenance (fruits, meats, vegetables), and the general well-being of your population (alcohol, cemeteries, churches, herbs, hospitals, schools). You must provide tools (iron and steel), for your laborers to work faster and cloths (hide, warm, and wool) to keep them warm in the winter months. While your populations education may not seem to do much it increases the work speed and carry weight of your population, which is a big deal.
Review: I have greatly enjoyed playing Banished. It is very relaxing, pretty, and the achievements can be difficult to obtain (although they require some seriously playtime). I would have to say that I prefer Banished over most of the other city builder simulation games. It is also intigrated with Steam Workshop, if you don't like the base game then download some of the fantastic mods!
Pro's: Smooth gameplay, excellent graphics, calming, achievements are challenging, requires thought and planning, Steam Workshop!
Con's: Few buildings, some occasional bugs that are annoying, 10x speed not fast enough (I wish I didn't have to say that, but 10x is really too slow when you've "master" this game), tornadoes are super rare but annihilate your town (nuclear launch detected), AI population runs into said tornado, “AI can't firefighter” (Seriously, the AI handling a building on fire is similar to watching Magikarp trying to splash you to death). With so few buildings it really loses progression rather early. The challenge is to figure out how to manage a large colony, as small colonies can manage with only a few buildings.
Content: 6 out of 10. (Steam Workshop 10 out of 10).
Controls: 10 out of 10.
Gameplay: 9 out of 10.
Graphics: 8 out of 10.
Story: n/a
Sounds: 8 out of 10.
Soundtrack: 8 out of 10.
Replay Value: 10 out of 10.
Overall Rating: 9 out of 10.

The Final Station  - Minimalist story telling at its finest!
As always, Ranks are done by + or -, a title with +Title+ is extremely well done, a title with -Title- is poor, a +Title- is good and -Title+ is okay, and lastly a =Title= means no complaints, no major comments, it works.
The Final Station follows a simple forumula of being a side scrolling action adventure game. Contra style gunplay (though without all the zanny guns) melded with a semi metroidvania style of exploration, limited to the location that you are visiting, a location that you cannot return back to once the train has left that station.
Combat is simple as well, you point your gun in the directrion of your crosshair, and fire.
The only 2issues I have overall here, is that combat in certain locations, really puts you in a pinch, almost unfairly so with the little speed demons, or exploders. Giving you next to no quarter while having to combat these nasties gets harsh at times! Certainly a challenge, but one I wish they would place about a little better.
My second issue is the overall lack of variation with the zombies. Seeing that the devlopers decided to give these lower lifeforms a black silhouette, I think we could have gotten a few more creature designs aside from shambler, armored shambler, midget runner, and exploder. The addition of a tank, or wall/ceiling crawlers would certainly add to the atmosphere, and more importantly, what about animals? Again we have an end of world style scenario with gas changing humans, yet animals never seem to truly be affected. This might be un purpose, but I feel that too many developers skimp over the animals.
I give it to this tiny team for having put so much into this game. The artwork is extremely well done. While characters come off a minimalistic, they seem to present a wide range of emotion in their little pixelated selves.
The world itself is incredible, from venturing forth into town, to riding the train and watching the background as story elements play out, or the world passes you by! I really want a train screensaver just so I can put it up on my tv and just watch the world pass by in all of its apocalyptic action!
The contorls are basic and easy, using both keyboard and gamepad, though I will say, I favored the gamepad in this case, more of a preference to the design and style of the game. Controls were sharp, snappy, and very reponsive. There really isn't any more I can tag on to how easy the controls are.
The games Atmosphere (including story) is amazing! This game utilizes the Mad Max policy in story telling. It tells a story by showing a lot of the world, but forcing very little information to the player. More than anything, we gather a lot of story telling by finding clips and pieces of evidence, or from the minor conversations that our fellow survivors/passengers have on our train.
It first comes off as a simple alien invasion scenario, with the human race desperately trying to build the ultimate weapon in order to safeguard humanity. It is more than that, it is very deep and very thought provoking if you are able to read between the fine lines of the game!
Now on to the minor thoughts, as great as I am loving the story and its atmosphere, I feel it gets a little weak in some of the interaction. A lot of interpersonal conflict builds up with apssengers to then be quickly blown off. I feel this confontation should continue to escalate, but then it is asking the programmer and writer to add in more to the story :O
Also I wish we could have seen earlier evidence of people transforming, we already know its people, so watching a few tragic scenes would have been quite interesting, but again that is just minor thoughts.,
Yes, that is a double plus good folks :P
Though it utilizes free sound packs and such for its foley effectsd, it is very balanced, and coded in very well. I've not complaints as to the atmosphere it helps build, with dogs barking in the background, or the sound of war reaching you as you ride along in your train.
The music is powerful, again, it adds to the worlds atmosphere, building the stress of the situation, or the sadness that follows with the loss of towns behind you. The OST is certainly worth getting especially with the added bonus of the artbook, showing the development and the imagination the artist has put into this game!
The level design is pretty basic, as it is with most metroidvania style games. You've ladders, doors, stairwells. All common ingredients, and we see that the world, or at least the towns we go to, follow a rather basic design, when it comes to our Engineers own visitation.
The design is  good, its middle of the road, and sadly with this, I feel it could be so much more. My favorite location has to be the unknown train yard, with the tentacles embedded in the train, or the other abandonned housing location where we find out what happened to the populace hidden in their underground bunker.
I would have liked to have gone into these bunkers too, as a source of exploration and curiosity, or found more locations where scientist are sudying the unknown aliens and such.
Even with its very VERY minor flaws, The Final Station is still a superb game that I would recommend to anyone. There is rumors in the grapevine of an expansion, and I surely hope to see that come to life!
I do hope the developers take the time to really stretch the levels out and apply some of the more unknown alien phsyiology within them, something we have seen throughout the game itself.
As well, the train, I want a screensaver of the train just going from place to place! The atmosphere of just watching the world pass you by is phenomenal!
To  Oleg Sergeev ,	Andrey Rumak, I bid you a job well done, and please continue creating gems like this one, and never lose sight of your own imaginations!

A lot of negativity regarding this game for a few reasons I'd like to cover:
1. No replayability. I agree with this, the game fails in this regard, but as is such for most visual novels and games that revolve primarily around its story as opposed to ones that focus on the gameplay itself.
2. Overhyped. True, this is problematic when it leaves you feeling that you have failed to get the same amout of pleasure out of a game in which you were expecting to get. However, this is not the game's fault for not living up to expectations set forth by another person.
3. Very few controls, all you do is pick stuff up. True, this is not a game for people who have no patience, no love for a story, or people who need explosions to be satisfied. This is essentially just an interactive story, not much different from a movie or a novel.

I completed this game in roughly 2.5 hours, going through every single drawer and reading every letter of every scrap of paper. I overall enjoyed it, and I'd like to cover some pros and cons from an objective, non-biased standpoint.
-Emotional. During the game I felt moments of sadness, moments of happiness, had some laughs, and said some stuff aloud. A story is done pretty well if it can elicit such an emotional response.
-The environment was pretty nice, I enjoyed a lot of little details, like occasional unremoved price stickers and typos/writing mistakes
-The characters are pretty richly devoloped, and though you never meet them you get a feel for how they act and think.
- I very much enjoyed the narrative, It felt emotional and real.
- Short. While it can be argued that many games of similar size would be much longer due to accomplishing tasks, fighting enemies, questing, or solving puzzles and what not, but it just feels short.
- Purpose. I could not determine the purpose of having to go on a house adventure to find out what happened, perhaps its just me, but the entire game seems like an unneccessary undertaking.
I'd say if you would enjoy a neat story, wait until a Steam sale and definitely grab this game ($20 is somewhat steep for this).

I've been asked recently by a friend how Warface was. I hadn't actually tried it before - at one point I got about 10 minutes into installing before deciding against it - but now that I've seen it doing semi-decent on Steam I've decided to give it a go for a few hours and make a review for friends. I now have one hell of a headache.
Bear with me, this is a little long so let me start of with: "THIS GAME IS NOT GOOD", if you want to see why then look down.
First a little background on Crytek, the developer for the game: Their primary product is CryEngine which has only been utilized in two major franchises. First, the original Far Cry game and its spin-offs. Second, Crysis. Since the success of the original Crysis, Crytek continuously upgrades the CryEngine and tries to sell it to other developers. In my opinion the last iteration of the CryEngine that was good was also the one that the original Crysis ran on, and apparently most studios agree because only studios strapped for cash and unwilling to use the Unreal Engine will go for the CryEngine.
Crytek are in fact running themselves into the ground with their blind efforts to increase brand awareness and sell their engine; in 2014 it was discovered some staff weren't paid for months on end (according to eurogamer). Their games are reduced to fancy attempts to market the CryEngine as the company strategically cuts all ties with award winning, money-making franchises to instead sell their engine. This misguided vision running the company shows in their game, Warface.
W A R F A C E (announced: 2010, released: 2014)
W A R FrA m E (announced: 2012, released: 2013)
It's hard not to find parallels between two gun-toting action co-op games, so let me say this right away: I'm /not/ saying Warface is a clone of Warframe. In fact, the name Warface was chosen (before Warfame's name was announced, as shown above) to appeal to the Chinese market the game was originally developed for. That said, there is a major parallel between both Warface and Warframe's PvE, that being the 'dungeon crawling' aspect.
Digital Extremes, the company behind Warframe, self-published their game at extreme expense to the studio because no publishers would 'buy' a PvE dungeon crawling shooter. One of the primary concerns expressed by publishers was the repetitiveness: how do you keep players engaged when they do the same mission 5 times over? DE figured that out: You generate the missions procedurally.
Warface on the other hand, is built around that one single flaw that nearly killed Warframe before it had even started. It's simultaneously as deep and repetitive as an arcade (literal, real life arcade) shooter. Its quality is enough to keep you engaged just long enough for you to put some money in, then you'll get bored of it a little later. PvE aside, the PvP might be engaging but if you prefer PvP you should be picking up a title from a more reliable stuido and publisher.
Again, as said above, Warface is at its core yet another attempt to increase brand awareness for Crytek and the CryEngine. It's practically a monetized tech demo, and the gameplay holds about as much depth as one.
Where I can say yes, you should try a game like Defiance (from the same publisher, Trion), I can't stress enough that this game isn't worth the data usage to download.

Overall it's a must buy if you like F1 racing game.

At this point I have completed the game and played all the DLC content that has come with it. The only thing i was not able to experience was the multiplayer due to lack of people playing it.
I purchased the game + freedom fighter bundle which came with all the DLC for about $11

I feel like you are not punished enough for death in the game as i was frequesntly able to just run and gun while single handedly killing hundreds of KPA securing objectives in each zone. You can recruit AI resistance to fight with you but I never found it needed. If i did die I simply was just sent to a safe house with no real penalty and able to do the mission again. The open world is also very repetitive. The same style of missions over and over to secure a zone and compell the average people to resist.The gun play in the game is decent feels smooth and kills are satisfying. the game does lack where it comes to performance. I dont have a top of the line rig but i feel like my amd 480 and I5-6400 should have been able to run it at the High setting that were recommended. However the game still looked very good at medium setting getting a steady 60 fps.
Where this game really shined for me though waws the story. it had a bit of a slow point in the middle but overall it was solid. The writing was good the setting felt fitting and the backstory was a little far fetched but you could see it. The DLC were also very nice. one is more a prologue and the other two take you to thge events after the main campaign, allowing you to countinue where you left off.

Description: Banished is a Medieval, city builder simulator. You are required to manage your building materials (iron, stone, wood), your crafting materials (coal, iron, leather, wool), your sustenance (fruits, meats, vegetables), and the general well-being of your population (alcohol, cemeteries, churches, herbs, hospitals, schools). You must provide tools (iron and steel), for your laborers to work faster and cloths (hide, warm, and wool) to keep them warm in the winter months. While your populations education may not seem to do much it increases the work speed and carry weight of your population, which is a big deal.
Review: I have greatly enjoyed playing Banished. It is very relaxing, pretty, and the achievements can be difficult to obtain (although they require some seriously playtime). I would have to say that I prefer Banished over most of the other city builder simulation games. It is also intigrated with Steam Workshop, if you don't like the base game then download some of the fantastic mods!
Pro's: Smooth gameplay, excellent graphics, calming, achievements are challenging, requires thought and planning, Steam Workshop!
Con's: Few buildings, some occasional bugs that are annoying, 10x speed not fast enough (I wish I didn't have to say that, but 10x is really too slow when you've "master" this game), tornadoes are super rare but annihilate your town (nuclear launch detected), AI population runs into said tornado, “AI can't firefighter” (Seriously, the AI handling a building on fire is similar to watching Magikarp trying to splash you to death). With so few buildings it really loses progression rather early. The challenge is to figure out how to manage a large colony, as small colonies can manage with only a few buildings.
Content: 6 out of 10. (Steam Workshop 10 out of 10).
Controls: 10 out of 10.
Gameplay: 9 out of 10.
Graphics: 8 out of 10.
Story: n/a
Sounds: 8 out of 10.
Soundtrack: 8 out of 10.
Replay Value: 10 out of 10.
Overall Rating: 9 out of 10.

First impressions? I spent 50 minutes creating my Waifu.
I've played Fashion Souls: Prepare to be Fabulous Edition and Dark Bourne Three.
I'll be comparing all three throughout.
Three feels too fast and too fluid, it's not like you're playing a human, it's BloodBourne's engine, and that's what makes it a terrible Souls game. It's still a good game, but it's Dark Bourne 2.
One is a older game, and I love it to death. It suffers from lots of jerkiness. There's too much jerky; You're jerky, the hollows are jerky, and so is your skin.
Now, DARK SOULS™ II: Scholar of the First Sin.
I fell in love with it immediatly. This feels like a Souls game. The repair mechanic isn't something you ignore. In One, I never had to repair my weapon with repair powder or spells. In Three, it may as well not exsist. They should've toned down how fast weapons break down, but I'll just carry repair powder and throw that into my sword and the eye's of a occasional hollow.
The combat in DARK SOULS™ II: Scholar of the First Sin, is excellent. Weapons have a real feeling to it, going through the motions. I was battling a hulking orc thing wielding a mace, and it came crashing down. I rolled away, but the screen turned blurry, as if the weapon was something to be warry of getting hit by.
The sound effects could've used more work, it's a mixed bag of noises; both good and bad.
Movement. This is a difficult one since people have perferences. I like this games' movement. I feel as if I'm controlling a real being. DS3 was too fluid, DS1 was really stiff, DS2 had it on track. If DS3 had taken all the good from DS1 and DS2, we would've gotten something amazing. Turning around, swinging my sword, rolling, back-stepping, it felt genuine. I really love it. I really, really do. I expected a ugly, stiff, and problematic game. It's not.
Now, here is an issue, getting attacks by a mob of enemies. It's not as bad as some people claim, but it pays to go slowly and not aggro everything in a kilometer radius. Parrying feels satisfying, as does everything else you do, but it's difficult to pull off the riposte if there's nearby enemies. You don't get the i-frames until your foe falls onto his♥♥♥♥♥and pathetically raises his arm to ward off the on-coming critical. That means you can get attacked and lose your chance to stab their eyeballs out. I would speed up the animation of falling to the ground—or offer different types of ripose animation for the sake of diversity.  If I were part of the team making this game, but that's not the case. Backstabs are odd, and I'm still experiminting with the game's mechanics.
Healing seems more fair than 3s' estus heal. DS1's heal system felt right as well. I would've used the average heal speed of both DS2's and DS1's heal speed. It's a tad bit slow in DS2, but combat is much more intuitive and slow-paced—in the traditional Souls Fashion. (That's a pun, laugh you dirty casuals)
I love Dark Souls, so I have my bias, do keep that in mind.
People new to the Souls series don't know what to get first.
DS1 -> DS2 -> DS3, it actually doesn't matter, but I('ve) played it in the order of DS1 -> DS3 -> DS2. There's no interconnecting story besides subtle references.
Dark Souls is not difficult. Once you've played one of them for over ten hours, you get the hang of how to handle it. If you've ever beaten or played another Souls game, all the others' hardly seem difficult. Unless you are incapable of learning or have some type of learning disability, I would stay away. Unless you're willing to fight that disability?

This game starts out promising. With a fantastic art style and great ambient soundtrack it sucks you in, immerses you in its nightmare horror setting. But soon you realize there isn't much else there.
The gameplay basically boils down to blindly walking through spooky rooms and corridors until you reach the end of the nightmare and you wake up in a new slightly different nightmare consisting of more rooms and corridors. Occasionally you meet one of several different types of enemies, each requiring a different strategy to get past, be it hiding in a closet, sneaking past or just running away. Once you figure out how they're easy to avoid. Most rooms are just empty though. The backgrounds look nice and detailed but only very rarely is there something you can actually interact with, and usually it just means a close up view of the object. Every now and then a loud noise will try to startle you, together with spooky or disturbing imagery. It tries to scare you, but personally I was never scared or even startled.
Like this it continues for the 1-2 hours it takes to beat, and to be honest it's way too long for how little of interest actually happens. By the end my thumb was tired from having to constantly hold right on the left thumb-stick. That's what you'll be doing 90% of the time, just walking to the right.
There is a vague story. A girl died and haunts your dreams. The game drip feeds you some bits and pices of the story throughout the game but mostly leaves you with no story developement until your reach the very end of the game where you might find out what really happened, or not, based on a couple of branching paths in the game. Fortunately there is a "nightmare select" menu so you can go back to these branches and choose a different path if you wish.
Bottom line, it's a game with a nice art style, good sountrack and atmosphere. But it fails in the gameplay and story department. It might be worth getting at a discout but otherwise I wouldn't recommend it.

Don't let this game deceive you. It's a pretty challenging and addictive little game that has a lot of charm and is a lot of fun. You  basically run a restaurant and have to prepare and cook food for customers.  The game is broken up into a day where you will try and serve as many customers as you can while trying not to get there orders wrong. Sounds easy enough but try doing it with recipes that require more complex preperation and trying to serve 8 customers at once.
The game has a wide variety of recipes which you can buy and upgrade and before each day you can customize your menu. There are also additional challenges you can do like catering missions or competing in an Iron Chef competition. You also have to do chores as well as preparing meals and this adds to the challenge.
The game is really nicely animated as well with decent music and gives the game a lot of charm. It isn't a game i found i could play for long time though. I found it better for maybe a quick 20 minutes to half an hour at a time as it can start to feel repetitive at times. It doesn't help that you have to do at least 20 days before being able to upgrade your restaurant which makes the game feel a little dragged out.

- Easy game to pick up and play but a difficult one to master, providing a decent challenge.

The Bad

Overall this is a nice fun game perfect for jumping in and out of when you've got a few minutes to kill which is also accessible while still able to provide a challenge. 8/10

This is quite an impressive little game taking on world builder giants such as Simcity and doing a fiesty job at that. Although in the city-building genre, it's emphasis is more on survival than simply expansion. Instead of building and bloating a population, you focus on a handful of families at first, with the initial challenge to build shelter and services using the resources that lay around them.
It is rather microcosmic in nature and if you are a fan of micromanagement, you will go ape over this.
Its UI is neat and practical, its graphics crisp and delightful. A pleasant change in this genre that makes every decision count. Make a mistake or poorly plan and it won't be simply a few people leaving... you may quickly find out how insidious starvation can be.
If you enjoy starting communities from scratch with a purpose beyond just filling the map, you will easily get hooked on this great game. It's not a bad effort from a single developer.

VVVVVV is a game that transports my brain 30 years back in time to my childhood. In many ways, it looks like something that could have existed on the Atari 2600, but that's not really true - games didn't exist back then that were this polished, either design- or control-wise. So this is really the best of both worlds for people like me: great nostalgia value, but also designed to look and play great for modern times. But what is VVVVVV, anyways? It's a 2D exploration platformer with only one character action - the ability to 'flip' gravity up or down. You might think that having only one mechanic would really limit the game's playability, but it doesn't. There are enough fresh twists sprinkled throughout the game to keep it interesting from start to finish (around 3-4 hours for the main quest). It's really a brilliantly designed game, with just the right amount of challenge. This should be a no brainer for 2D platforming fans, and especially for those who grew up gaming in the 80s.

Gone Home is a game beckoning players to solve its mystery. The moment the player walks into the empty house he or she is drawn in by the stillness of the vacant home. So begins a search to figure out where everyone has gone. The search never leaves the house, but the house is incredibly large and tightly-packed with subtle clues and objects to flesh out the plot. Gone Home doesn't require the player to do any more than explore, so if you're looking for anything more than a story-driven exploration game I'm afraid you may be disappointed. However, Gone Home commits to what it does, and it's that commitment that makes it a wonderful game.
On paper the story would seem lackluster, but it's the feeling and voice-acting of the narration of notes littered around the house that help give the game life. You begin to see that all the characters involved are deep and relatable even though you will never lay eyes on them. As you sift through all the belongings of your family you'll become closer with these people that have a lot more going on than you realize. It makes you wonder how much someone could get to know you just by going through your own home. As creepy as it sounds, Gone Home is a game that makes the player think about how these relationships are affecting each other, and ultimately affecting the end portion of the story.
Honestly, it's the sound design of Gone Home that heightened the experience for me. The sounds of an empty home during a thunderstorm were oddly chilling even though I knew I had nothing to fear. The crisp dialogue is perfectly cast, and the actors did an amazing job. This is one of those cases where great writing and acting come together to create something truly great. The soundtrack, however, really hit home for me. It's beautifully done comes in at just the perfect time for emphasis to what's happening in the story. I have the soundtrack on my phone as we speak, which is only something I do with the my favorites.
I love simple walking simulators that allow you to relax and enjoy a great story. Gone Home is well made, and there's a lot of love in it. If you enjoy a good story with relatable characters and a little exploration, you should pick this one up. However, be warned that Gone Home only lasts a couple hours unless you REALLY dig deep into the environment. As much as I love it, I would suggest getting it at a discount.

There's some music stuff too, I won't go into it too much here. Overall, I was moved by the story and enjoyed the exploration, even if it's a bit slow at times.

This is by far the best F1 game in a long time!
Feels like the Force Feedback has been completely rebuilt and feels good, although once controlling the car steering feels loose until you hit the full steering lock left/right. It's like your calibrating the wheel real time. Not sure if that's to simulate fresh tires or not but it certainly is interesting. I end up off track more times than not because pit assist on rejoining track will suddenly give you control right before a hard turn.
Control mappings from wheel show controller buttons for on screen menu navigation even when a controller isn't plugged in, no don't show off you're a console port! Sense of speed feels good, and careful throttle application is required exiting turns no matter how fast your going. Maybe a higher downforce setup would mitigate this, would make sense just haven't tested this yet. To me it feels like the F1 series magnifies every small mistake, something that I'm not neccessarily a fan of but it does make it more challenging and fun to master.
In race settings you can enable formation lap, then you can try to get your tires and brakes at optimal temperature, and it feels simply amazing having full control of the car following the pace car around the track. Problem is you don't get to pull up to your grid spot as control is taken away, then suddenly a quick screen flash which seems to refresh the grid for the start of the race.
I'm truely impressed here, I just wish they would redo pitting entirely giving you full control and take the car off rails entering and leaving your pit stall.
Even with all it's problems as is, F1 2016 shows potential to be truely epic. 9/10

Dark Souls 2 is a great sequel to one of my favorite games. First of all, I highly recommend that you play the original Dark Souls before playing this one. There is really no reason to play 2 before 1.
So assuming that you have played the first one, 2 improves upon some things but also makes some big mistakes.
Combat is for the most part the same. There are slight changes to rolling when locked on, iFrames, and there is also a new move called shield break. The main difference with combat is the edition of power stancing. Power stancing makes dual-wielding more effective by being able to attack with both weapons (if they have the same attack type) when you have 150% of the required stats. Personally I wasn't a huge fan of this change just because I feel that it made rolling essential even earlier than rolling became essential in Dark Souls 1. Nonetheless, I still had fun dual wielding katanas. I just sort of missed having a shield.
One thing I loved about Dark Souls was the non-linear world. Dark Souls 2 has a beautiful but unconnected world. 2 gives you the ability to teleport to every single bonfire you light from the beginning of the game! In 1 all of the areas connect with shortcuts back to the hub area. I still remember the first time I went down the elevator from the church back to firelink. Dark Souls 2 has none of this, the ability to travel to all bonfires removes the purpose of short cuts back to the hub. Because of this crucial mistake, the world of Dark Souls feels very linear and unconnected. This was my main issue with the game. It's not a deal breaker but it is just a bit of a shame.
Other than that there are a just a few minor changes such as losing health everytime you die. That one isn't much of an issue just because the items to reverse it are plentiful and the ring of binding helps a lot if you know you are going to die a lot. Also I just want to add that the DLC included in SOTFS is phenomenal.
Overall I loved this game and highly recommend it if you enjoyed the first. For the most part it is just more of the same amazing DS gameplay.

I've felt the need to write the Dark Souls 2 review from scratch again, but this time I will say what Dark Souls 2 did right as a Dark Souls game.
The main issue with this game is its name, "Dark Souls 2". If this game had been called "Undead Adventure" no one would've had any issue, but that's not its name, it has Dark Souls on its title, and those two words mean things that this game mostly fails to get. I used to hate on this game too much, I still think it's horsecrap, but I recognize some REALLY REALLY good things this has, though people use to remember more easily the REALLY REALLY (REALLY) terrible things.
Some lore and game moments are very memorable and even shocking.
- After spending the whole game searching for the King, finally find him and see he has already gone Hollow was very impactful. Just like when you get to his memories and talk to him, while he was still alive. All that lore with His kingdom and the revenge of the giants, just like the giants' memories are something that really fit within the Dark Souls terms.
- There's this memory where you get to see a stone dragon just like the ones from the Dark Souls 1 cinematic, I don't exactly know the lore explanation for this, but I pretty much see it as a dead dragon on the overworld, just before the Age of Fire begun, when the dragons were being exterminated, and this dragon being one of them, now lying down dead in the ashen land surrounded by the archtrees.
The DLCs are the closest this game is to (being a good game) being as good as Dark Souls 1. It ranges from ok to great depending on the location. And I have had quite a fun exploring some of these locations. The issue is that everything this game does right, except for one or two things, were already done right in the previous game. So it's not like this game has anything special. But again, I have had quite fun exploring certain locations, and (mostly) the bosses were kinda improved too.
OVERALL. This game has some close moments to being as good and fun as Dark Souls 1, those were the parts I enjoyed the most, if not the only parts I enjoyed. But again, this game has many many more flaws than good things, cheap level design, enemy placement and boss design being the worst ones that may ruin the experience between lots of other terrible things, that made playing this game quite a torture to me. I'd much rather play Dark Souls 1 or 3 again than this game. So I cannot recommend to any Souls fan. Though, if you are more of a casual kind of gamer that looks for a challenging (but cheap) experience, you may find joy playing this game. I personally haven't, though not everything about this game is wrong, as stated above.

Almost any other Real Time Strategy Game boils down to one question: "How fast can you expand?"
'Banished' chops the legs out from under that philosophy.  Expand too fast and your population explodes, quickly consuming all your resources and irrevicably crippling your economy.  But, of course, if you expand too slow, you will never have a population too begin with...
It is a balancing act so delicate that the first sign of complacency spells disaster.  The only thing not critical is time.  You will forget it is time to eat, time to sleep and even time to go to work.  The first time I sat down to play, 12 hours vanished without hardly looking up.  So take a hint, set an alarm clock.  It is an excellent game.

Neverending Nightmares has a remarkable art style that can pull off both unsettling and innocent, but a great art style doesn't make a great game, and particularly not a great "horror" game. The game does have a foreboding atmosphere, I suppose, but at a certain point in the first half hour of play, you develop a rhythm to the game play. Your character has asthma, so can run in only EXTREMELY short bursts. This is not developed or particularly meaningful in a story context, so it honestly feels like a ploy by the developer to make you uncomfortable. You don't want to run ever because what if you need it when an enemy appears??
It's an interesting premise, and it works well....for 10 minutes. After that point you know when the "horror" will appear. You are no longer engrossed in the atmosphere and the grotesque art. You are simply walking. And that walking lasts a LONG time. It feels as if the developer believed that uncertainty as to the incoming danger would last throughout the whole 2-3 hour experience. It does not, and as a result, the tediousness of walking and never running just bothered me, quite frankly. Was the art phenomenal? Yes! Was the game enjoyable? I suppose for a bit. Do I recommend it? Unfortunately not; it just doesn't do enough of interest to me to recommend.

This game should be called Neverending Jump Scares and Walking. Seriously, all you do in this game is walk, very slowly I might add, and trigger jump scares. The devs added the capability to run but your character can't run more than 10 sec so I guess he's asthmatic.
This game is clearly a personal message from the dev on something happening in his life but that's all it should be, a message, write in a journal and don't make games dude. Good:
-Artwork is fantastic! I really loved the pen and ink feel. The black and white set a very good creepy tone and matched well with the story and setting.
-Music and audio matched up well with everything and felt original for horror music.
-I enjoyed the creature interactions and really liked killing my character off just to see what happens.
Bad:
-At times the artwork was so overwhelming with so many lines especially in the forest. There was nothing creepy about the forest walking scene because I was so frustrated at how long it took to get through WAY TOO MUCH WALKING and how busy the artwork was.
-Boring story. I get the story, I understand it, it was just boring. The characters weren't interesting and the endings were dull.
-TOO MUCH WALKING! Unless I can get something added to the story or some intersting scenes from walking away from the main objective then don't let me walk there. Out of all the cells you could peek into, only one did anything, and that was a very predictable jump scare. If exploration doesn't do anything then stop letting us explore. As a player I expect to find something when I go somewhere, but in this game you don't see anything unless you go towards the main objectives. It's like having a game where the very last room out of 100 has a boss fight but the game lets you enter all other rooms 1-99 but they are empty. What's the point?
TL;DR
I'd give the game a 4 out of 10. It's not something I'd reccomend to anybody unless they simply like original stories regardless of quality.

*SPOILER* There's a note you find, written by Terrence's dad (Katy and Sam's grand dad), wherein he congratulates his son on being published, but then rips him apart for the trite banality of his book series. He urges him to find a real, honest voice, as opposed to jumping through hoops of convoluted nothingness and tropish crap. You realize that Terry has been going back and forth, trying to discover this voice and with no avail. How does that fit in with the game? It was real, it was honest. No ghosts, no alien abductions, no seance to reveal the spirits. Just a simple story of a family in turmoil. A wife who is messing around on her husband, an alcoholic dad who's lost his talent and passion of writing, their relationship with a troubled teenage daughter and the daughter who herself is also struggling to find her real voice. Believe it or not, and as soap operatic as it all sounds, the way the game approached the narrative (having you drive the narrative through simple discovery) was really unique and fun.
If you love platforming puzzle games and old school graphics and sound, this game is for you.

First off - ignore the haters.  If you're not sure whether you'll like this game, there's a number of demo videos out on the Internet that give you a breakdown.  If you're here, you probably know what this game is about a little bit.  If not, spoilers.
As a game, the delivery and overall experience is solid.  I found there was one place where things didn't quite click together for me, and I needed to check a walkthrough.  For an indie game, that's a pretty clean track record.
Up front you should know that it's mostly a narrative experience with a focus on story.  There are some light horror aspects, but mostly it's about a young woman uncovering a lot of hidden truths about the history of her family - not just her sister, for the record - while looking through her house.  Specifically, the focus is on her sister's story, and what's happened since the silent protagonist left for college.
People who are focusing too much on the sexuality aspect are probably ignoring the fact that this was perhaps the first major game to feature and focus on a believable gay character.  It's important that way, which is why the narrative itself is fairly simple and rote, without delving too much into the characters outside of that.  I also thought the narrative was a bit simplistic and ended a little too early, but when you realize that this game essentially started a conversation in gaming (and that the developers probably ran out of money) then you pretty much realize it ends right when it should.
So.  Do you want to experience a little bit of LGBT history?  The game that started the conversation? Do you want a really good story about coming out, a fun, light narrative mystery? You're in the right place, buddy.
Or are you already familiar with the issues of LGBT youth?  Are you not feeling that you want to get "preached" at?  Are you feeling worn out by the recent flush of gay representation in media? (Note: The game is not super preachy, although many have quoted dissatisfaction with the ending.) If so, this game is worth a look - it's fun, and novel, but maybe wait until you're more ready for it, or pick up any other narrative game since that has featured gay characters.  Life is Strange is my current favourite.

Verdun is a great game for anyone who is a fan of Military games and the First World War but is willing to play a more realistic game than battlefield 1.
GOOD POINTS
The devs have put enormous effort into player models and the maps but also they taken care to have distinctive classes for each nation even if some are clearly better in battle. The game runs smooth and looks amazing at max graphics however i would warn players with bad computers that the experience wont be the same because at lower graphics setting the game doesnt look that good. One thing i enjoy is the one shot- one kill approach the devs have taken which is a refreshing break from games such as Battlefield or Call of Duty where it takes several shots to kill a player.
BAD POINTS
I have a few problems with the game however they are not massive. The first one is that at certain times during the day it is hard to find servers with many players in. This therefore doesnt make you want to play the game as much. The second problem is that the respawn times on this game can be as high as 25 seconds which is a very long time to wait. Also i think the core gameplay would benefit from variety in objectives while playing because in the main gamemode you can spend a very long time just advancing, then retreating, then advancing again without that much enjoyment. It would be nice for side quests maybe.
OVERALL
To conclude i think Verdun is a very good game for a reasonable price in the steam store and it is highly underrated as a game and i feel like it deserves a higher user base. It has a dedicated userbase and if you enjoy slower, more tactical combat this is the game for you.

Well done Codemasters! You really stepped it up this year.
Reviewed after around 13 hours of gameplay incuding a quick race at spa, 4 rounds of career mode (full qualifying, full practice, 50% race) and a few online sprint races

+ Beautiful Graphics, more realistic styling than F1 2015
+ Good A.I, racing is slightly worse but they make many more strategy decision
+ Safety Car
+ Virtual Safety Car
+ More options for speaking to the engineer
+ Multifunctional display is miles better than is previous games
+ Very detailed R&D development
+ Good character models
+ Characters are voiced well
+ Commentators have more varied commentary
+ Laptop function is cool
+ Good testing programms
+ More A.I difficulty settings
+ Variable race strategies
+ Improved damage model, including wheel tethers
+ Personalised 10 year career mode
+ Ability to upgrade your team so that it is improved on overall standing
+ Multiplayer connection is greatly improved
+ Manual starts
+ Formation Lap
+ Physics are much less arcadey than they where last year, much harder to drive
+ Much better and more realistic kerb physics
+ Very good wet weather driving physics
+ Includes all 22 drivers, cars and liveries of the 2016 F1 season
- Car sounds are a mixed bag: Honda sounds great, Mercedes sounds pretty horrific, Ferrari and Renault both sound ok
- Sometimes the damage model is still too forgiving
- Target times for practice programms are sometimes too high
- A.I. are faster in qualifying than the race and even faster in practice
- A.I. set some unrealistic times in practice and qualifying, for example being high up in a not so great car on the slower tire
- My wheel (Logitech G27) is sometimes reset to 900 degrees during sessions for no reason
- Online penalty system is still a mixed bag
- Warming up tyres and brakes on the formation lap seems to be irrelevant because the game resets the grid fully before the race start
- Car models seem a little off

Good game, but a lesser Souls game. Don't let this be your first Souls title, I'd recommend you only give this a go once you've had your fun with all the other Souls games - Demon's Souls, Dark Souls, Bloodborne and Dark Souls 3.
More than any other Souls game, you really need to research the game heavily before making any major decisions. For instance, if you join the Covenant of Champions(referred to from now on as COCs), you may assume through what the game tells you that it's just a clan dedicated to doing cool stuff, unlocking Awestones when you beat hard enemies. In reality, it takes away your ability to play the game cooperatively, it raises enemy health and damage output a ton and you get invaded more often. I had no idea, so I spent around 50 hours absolutely despising my time with Dark Souls 2. I thought it was poorly-designed, that the devs didn't understand the difference between a crushingly brutal game and a satisfyingly difficult game. I punched brick walls repeatedly, bit my hand, came really close to committing awful violent atrocities, all that jazz, but when I made a new character and researched COCs, I found out that my whole experience had been sabotaged. Normally it's not the horrible game I experienced when I was in the COCs(seriously, avoid that group like the plague).
Even at a rock-solid 60 FPS, the combat feels less fluid and satisfying as the console Souls games, which ran at an unstable 30 FPS. It feels kinda floaty, yet clunky and heavy. To be clear, the combat is still superior to most third-person action games, but it just can't compare to any Hidetaka Miyazaki-designed Souls game.
Give it a try if you see it on sale and you've already had your fun with Dark Souls. It's worth experiencing, just expect to read lots of strategy guides and wikis if you want a decent experience. And stay the hell away from COCs. No one should ever join COCs on a whim without researching ahead of time.

I really wanted to like this game. I really did. And I tried my best to fully immerse myself in its dark atmosphere, playing with headphones, taking it slowly and all. It worked well for a few minutes, but then...the game ended. After less than two hours, it was over. And the ending was abrupt, weak and somewhat inconsistent. There are multiple endings, yes, but they are simply determined by which path you (blindly) choose in the last few sections, there are no big puzzles or significant choices to make during the course of the game. And seeing all of the three endings doesn't really make things better. They make everything confusing and nonsensical at first, they become clearer after putting a bit of thought into them, but still you are left with a sense of something missing.
Neverending Nightmares is not an awful experience to endure, on the contrary it is filled with undeniable inspiration, but as it is it's a totally rushed and incomplete work. And that saddens me a lot, because it's a terrible waste to see a title with such a beautiful, deeply unsetting visual design and so much narrative potential fail to deliver something up to the expectations. It would have taken so little to make this game really beautiful and worth playing that I really cannot condone the way it's been presented. And it's just a terrible pity. I'm giving my thumb down with the highest reclutance this time, but I have to.

Now I know that is a touchy subject and before you attack me, I have had my bout with depression. I've taken anti depressants and gone to therapy. So without to much pretension I feel I'm capable of commenting on the subject with some clarity and sensitivity.
It seems to me that everything here represents some facet of depression while maintaining an over the top hyperbole that goes beyond a simple euphemism. Such as the fact the character walks so very.. very.. slowly and is constantly out of breath. To which I'd say this is more allegory to the crushing weight of the world and simply existing being so overbearing it's difficult to just move you body alone. And narratively speaking this comes across well. But mechanically, we may be reading the same book but we are not on the same page.
This goes further into the having to repeat rooms (it does checkpoint nice, as the title would suggest you tend to have waking nightmares) because of the monsters that kill you instantly and in ways that are not super pleasant to look at all the time. Why are these monsters are there? Well, it seems the developer wanted it to be open ended as a design choice. I have my story, my ending, my interpretation and that's what I'm sticking with. I do not recommend going back in or really even the first time.
I should mention it's “Not Recommended” because I feel that anything over what 'you the reader' thinks, lets use the idiom, 'a drop in the bucket' is just not worth it at an hour and a half of mediocre content.
Now back to the depression aspect. I don't feel as though this represents MY OWN experience with depression. Its was far more mundane then anything this extravagant. It was more like, why bother getting out of bed, why bother changing/cleaning my clothes, no one would notice. Then you sort of stare blankly at things and watch other people live their lives wondering how they ignored how pointless things were, couldn't they see it? Were they living in a bubble?! And it went on like that for awhile. It still creeps in once and awhile. But I digress. Perhaps I'm way off base and this person did have an experience much closer to what is depicted here. But all that said, this isn't worth the time or money in my own very humble opinion.

You know how sometimes in movies and TV shows, they have these sequences where the main character gets up and everything's a little bit off? They go around and stranger and stranger things happen, and then a big shocking thing happens and they wake up? Neverending Nightmares is an entire game built around that concept. And if that doesn't sound like much of a game to you, well, you'd be right.
The game opens with your sister dying and you waking up. You lead your character through a darkened, monochromatic house in search of... nothing, really. You proceed through the unsettling halls because nothing would happen if you didn't. Eventually you'll find your sister again, and something horrible will happen to one of you, and then you'll wake up again. The cycle continues throughout the game, with the environments becoming steadily darker and more unfamiliar. This part admittedly works really well, forming a genuinely tense atmosphere. The gorgeous art and animation sets the tone perfectly, and you never really feel completely safe, even after you divine the flow of the game. Neverending Nightmares does a fantastic job of mimicking actual nightmares, at least in terms of aesthetic.
The problem is that there really is no more game to it than that. You'll come across enemies from time to time, but all you can do is hide from them and then scamper past once their backs are turned. There are no puzzles aside from permutations of "find candle to enter dark room" roadblocks. Exploration won't gain you anything aside from some slightly different scenery, as all paths still lead to the same inevitable conclusions. And that's the true killer of Neverending Nightmares, that everything about it is inevitable. Each nightmare is the same hell of wandering dark halls and weathering jumpscares and shambling monsters. Your reward for navigating the gauntlet is some terrible shock scene and a sudden awakening into the next.
It's one of those games that seems to do exactly what it set out to do. Neverending Nightmares does indeed trap you in a seemingly never-ending cycle of wandering halls and avoiding monsters. It just does it in a far more tedious and uninteresting way than your own mind would.

The damage model adds a genuine sense of peril to proceeding as on higher settings a light knock will damage your wing and heavier contact results in the immediate departure of one of your wheels... If you have bought previous Codemasters F1 titles and being disappointed then buy this one with confidence. Codemasters have upped their game and it is a must buy for sim racers and F1 fans alike.

First and foremost, I will say this. I wanted to wait until I got at least 10 hours into the game to write a review for it.
This is a simple review, and I won't go super in-depth, I'll tell you the things this game does right, and the things it does wrong.
Firstly. The gunplay, and overall gameplay is pretty phenomenal for a F2P shooter. My buddy convinced me to play the game for the first time, and I was pretty skeptical but after giving it a shot, I'm convinced this game has the best gunplay of any free FPS out there, as far as I can tell. The only free game I know that competes with this game's gunplay is APB: Reloaded, but that's a 3rdPS.
There's no sense of team work in this game though. No VoIP, and even if there were, your team mates probably speak a different language. It's best to play in a party with some friends because unlike some games that you pay for (Dead by daylight, looking at you), it's actually possible to play this game in a party without getting a headache from sitting in queues for 25 minutes. It's almost instant, every time, without failure.
The worst part about the game is by far, without doubt, the map design. Almost all of the maps are far too simple. There's no complexity to any of them. They're basic af. Secondly, every map panders to spawn campers. Anybody who has played a solid FPS game before (CoD4, CS1.6, CS:S, CS:GO, Rainbow Six: Vegas 1/2, or really any well made shooter) is going to be able to spawn camp for the entire match in this game. You'll easily end up with a score of 45/<10 in team deathmatch. Your games will likely empty out quick.
The only other bad part I've noticed about the game thus far is that it takes VERY long to rank up. Very, very long. Attachments cannot be bought. you have to unlock them. The good news is that this is permanent. Most guns I've used are permanent too, but to be fiar there IS a in-game shop that has guns that aren't permanent I think.

Counter-Strike: Source is one of those games that you don't really buy for the core gameplay; if you want a pure CS experience, Counter-Strike: Global Offensive does a much better job and offers ranked matchmaking for more competitive players. Some people buy CS:S in order to play Garry's Mod and all of its custom game modes properly, but I would urge everyone to buy and play CS:S for all of the custom game modes that the community has developed and refined over the last decade. Sure, most of the game modes have been ported to CS:GO, but they usually aren't as polished or even fun as they are in CS:S.
One game mode that I absolutely love is Surf, which is what approximately 95% of my hours in both CS:S and CS:GO have been dedicated too. If I'm playing this game, chances are I'm surfing on one of the KSF surf servers. But even if you don't surf, there are plenty of other game modes that you can lose hundreds of hours in, if not more. I am honestly recommending this game purely based on my experiences with surfing. Good game, but a lesser Souls game. Don't let this be your first Souls title, I'd recommend you only give this a go once you've had your fun with all the other Souls games - Demon's Souls, Dark Souls, Bloodborne and Dark Souls 3.
More than any other Souls game, you really need to research the game heavily before making any major decisions. For instance, if you join the Covenant of Champions(referred to from now on as COCs), you may assume through what the game tells you that it's just a clan dedicated to doing cool stuff, unlocking Awestones when you beat hard enemies. In reality, it takes away your ability to play the game cooperatively, it raises enemy health and damage output a ton and you get invaded more often. I had no idea, so I spent around 50 hours absolutely despising my time with Dark Souls 2. I thought it was poorly-designed, that the devs didn't understand the difference between a crushingly brutal game and a satisfyingly difficult game. I punched brick walls repeatedly, bit my hand, came really close to committing awful violent atrocities, all that jazz, but when I made a new character and researched COCs, I found out that my whole experience had been sabotaged. Normally it's not the horrible game I experienced when I was in the COCs(seriously, avoid that group like the plague).
Even at a rock-solid 60 FPS, the combat feels less fluid and satisfying as the console Souls games, which ran at an unstable 30 FPS. It feels kinda floaty, yet clunky and heavy. To be clear, the combat is still superior to most third-person action games, but it just can't compare to any Hidetaka Miyazaki-designed Souls game.
Give it a try if you see it on sale and you've already had your fun with Dark Souls. It's worth experiencing, just expect to read lots of strategy guides and wikis if you want a decent experience. And stay the hell away from COCs. No one should ever join COCs on a whim without researching ahead of time.
